Honestly, I think the people giving positive reviews for this game have vested interest in the game or something.  Most of them sound very forced and don't give any substantial reason as to why the game is good, other than "it's fun" or "the devs are nice."  The game simply isn't very good.  It just seems like a game that you'd find on any free flash game website - but far rougher around the edges.  For example, there's actually no end to the levels (I had to read the other negative reviews to figure this out) - when you get all the way to the right side of the level, there's just an invisible wall that prevents you from moving any further.  In the Streets of Peril level, on the far right side, you actually get stuck in a small area on the dirt because the game prevents you from jumping for some reason.  In the arcade levels?  You just instantly die when you go too far.  The entire game has just such low production quality - and it definitely seems like one of those "first try" game efforts that might have come out of a project course in high school.
To be frank, I don't think this game should have been released on Steam.  It would never have passed the quality controls of previous years.

This is what happens when people get used to overpriced games. They see a good game for $1 and start getting suspicious. Endless Space is not the typical type of indie greenlight game trash that floats all over steam. It's a good well-developed game. Also, I hate all that "for $1 anything is good lol" reviews. So I decided to make a review myself.
The game isn't perfect. ES may be not the right choice for a newcomer to the 4x genre. It is very rough on edges and lacks proper tutorial.
Some tips for beginners.
1. Beware of pirates and random events. Events mostly negative and can be very harsh. Both can be disabled in game settings.
2. AI cheats on all difficulties starting from normal, and it likes to spam ships. Be prepared for war. However, unlike Total War series, here the AI is not so prone to backstab you. You will probably see when and why if it gets pissy.
3. LR kinetics rules.
4. For me, the most complicated thing to start with this game was a tech tree. It took me hours to figure what the final goals of my research should be. But then I just gave up and started to pick from those technologies which I could research at the moment and which would be most useful as of right now.
5. "The lines to the new systems looked wavy and I didn't know which research would let me pass it."
Those are wormholes. The game didn't explain it well. But you need to unlock Applied Casimir Effect tech from the Exploration&Expansion tech branch.
Overall I rate this game as a solid but average 4x strategy with its lowest in simplistic combat, rudimentary diplomacy.

Some people give this controller a bad review. I've had this controller for almost 2 years. I purchased this in excitement when it was first released. I actually pre-ordered it to be precise. This controller hasn't let me down. It took some hours to get used to playing with but it is now my preferred controller using steam over an xbox or ps controller. It's customized setup makes it the perfect controller. Some games you have to tweak the controller for your play style, which is fine in my opinion. When you take the time to setup the controller to your preference, it makes game play very enjoyable. Even my girlfriend prefers using this controller over a mouse and keyboard. That says a lot when she is not a gamer. It makes the controller the best experience you can possibly have. The only cons I can say about the controller is the fact you have to use double A batteries for the wireless feature. Most new controllers have a built in rechargable battery pack. I did resolve this issue by purchasing rechargable batteries. I use 6 and just have the other ones charging incase the ones I'm using die.

If you're using this as your only controller, I feel it is a pretty solid choice, though you'll occasionally find yourself wannting something more traditional. This can make the learning curve a bit steeper and more frustrating, but you can work through it.
If you're using this controller as an option alongside a more traditional controller, it really shines. I've owned the Steam controller for about 6 months at this point, and find that I prefer it for about 90% of games - that includes shooters, rpgs, adventure games, and even fighting games (after a lot of experimentation and adjustment.) The only real problem in this situation is forcing yourself to experimnt outside your comfort zone, instead of instantly falling back to your traditional controller for many games.
The bottom line is that this is a very comfortable and flexible controller, capable of doing many things that a normal controller cannot do. In exchange though, you're going to need to learn to set it up to suit
preferences, and your preferences are going to constantly change over the first few months as you grow accustomed to the controller and develop more precise ability with features like gyro aiming and fine trackpad tweaking.

This is a very, very good game. It does the original justice, and that is a big achievement. The visuals still look good, but it's the gameplay, story, voice acting and the choices you have to make that put this game way up there. The choices range from play style (stealth, FPS, non-lethal), what upgrades to get, what path to take in a certain area, to morality. The combat is fun and rich, from grenade/gun combo's to takedowns (tip: get the multiple takedown aug when you can).
Cons?
- the security/biometric scan in a particular area takes annoyingly long and you have to pass through several times
- the sniper rifle seems a bit broken in some points; headshots doing far too little damage (no-scoping worked better)
In my entire playthrough, doing pretty much every sidequest, these are the only two things I can think of that annoyed me. In a game this big and complex, that should tell you enough. Now go buy it.

The jist of director's commentary:  this thing we wanted to do would have been awesome, but it didn't work out, so you're playing the thing we put together in a fraction of the time to make up for it.
Play with commentary off for you first play through for sure. Don't make my mistake.  A decent game still.

I haven't played any of the previous Deus Ex parts at all, so I can't say anything about their connections. Regarding Human Revolution alone I can say that it is a game which I still favor a lot.
It is set in a unique cyberpunk-world with many problems that are two sides of the same coin. The protagonist, Adam Jensen, unwillingly gets stuck between these sides. During their gameplay the player has the ability to choose between different actions and dialogues Adam can have. Thereby the story can be customed, but still has a linear plot.
The missions can be performed either stealth or action wise, whatever you prefer, although in my opinion some of them have a similar layout (as in "infiltrate this area, find this/ eliminate this, come back in one piece"), but all of them were still exciting and interesting.
I sometimes struggled with Adam's personality, aka his way of coping with and reacting to situations, but considering what he went through and that this probably simply is
I do sympathise a lot with him.
Human Revolution will definitely always be one of my favourite cyberpunk-games.

TL;DR: Mindblowing for flight sims, great for first person games, decent for FPS, driving, and turnbased strategy, bad for RTSs. Customization and related community features are amazing. Try the old Star Wars flight sims and marvel at how great it works.
So, the Steam controller - quite a controversial thing. I have owned it for about a year now and I think I can finaly give a verdict after playing a variety of genres, for which I will highlight a few games.
The controller is very different from the standard models and requires a good amount of getting used to just because of its shape, that isn't even considering the trackpads that replace d-pad and one analogue stick. Haptic is not as neat as with X-Box controllers, as clickpoints are a lot harsher. The trackpads do feel great, though, thanks to the vibrating feedback.
The controller has a good amount of buttons with backside paddles that I love and have always missed from my X-Box 360 controller. It also comes with a gyroscopic sensor, but I haven't tried it, yet.
Final verdict for hardware: Great functions, not ideal in form. I don't really care, but you might.
The controller works through Steam, which can be annoying, but also useful, as you can apply configurations to any game you want and they work without any input lag because of how they are applied. Speaking of configurations - here is where you truly get your moneys worth! The amounts of customization possible are mindboggeling. Want to aim using the gyro-sensor? You can do that if you are brave enough! Need more buttons than there are on the controller? Put them on virtually on the one of the trackpads (this one actually works superbly if you don't overdo it)! For many games there are excellent community presets you can download so you can benefit from all the customizability without having to work through the overwhelming possibilities yourself.
I played through the Talos Principle using the steam controller and liked it a lot. The trackpad is comfortable for camera control and the rest of the controller works like you would expect.
However first person games have an issue with precision - not needed in that capacity in Talos Principle, but critical for shooters. There I tried a session of TF2, which was just awefull. Then I tried Republic Commando as single player game, which was alright (excellent for the coordination, even, thanks to a neat trackpad assignment), but became pretty frustrating on higher difficulties. Maybe with a lot of relearning you can become decent at shooters, as it is a lot more precise than a stick will ever be, but it probably isn't worth the effort. Singleplayer works at casual difficulties and it is preferable to stick-aiming.
So great for general first person games, useless for multiplayer shooters, neat as a sofa-tool for singleplayer shooters, if not ideal.
Here I only played Rocket League, with mixed results. On one hand the driving works just as you'd expect and the camera movement was better than with a stick. However in Rocket League you also need to be on top of using your abilities, and the button placement at least for me just didn't work there, because my thumb tended to be on the trackpad for the camera and then had difficulty finding the relatively small (~20% less than X-Box I'd eyeball) XYAB-buttons again.
Driving in general great, driving that involves simultaneous camera controll and abilities not so much.
I haven't tried an RTS (well somewhat in a similar vein I tried a round of DOTA and had a miserable time, can't imagine that getting better with more units to controll), but I can't imagine it being great. What I did play was Civ V and it works well. The trackpads make for comfortable handheld mice, and you don't need much more for Civ. The few hotkeys that you do use you can map to the various buttons and be happy. I will also lump Hearthstone in here as it likewise just needs the controller as mouse and works perfectly.
Great for turnbased strategy!
Oh boy, here I go: It is perfect! Really. Flightsims need two thing, a stick (check!) and lots of buttons. The second department is where all controllers before this failed in one way or another, either having too few buttons or not having them usable. Well, enter the trackpads and cry tears of joy. You can make them behave like a grid of buttons which will be displayed as overlay over your game (where you can also give them actual labels so you don't have to learn the keybinds before playing). Crossing a border between two buttons causes a light bump that helps you find the right one quickly.
I have played Star Wars TIE Fighter with a setup like this and it works like a charm. Every command I can desire is availiable. Where before I had to put at least two functions on to any button with my X-Box controller and still was not able to have everything I needed to comfortably play.
If you buy this controller for anything, it is this. The possibilities are demonstrated so well here.
Personally, I love it. Playing TIE Fighter in a sofa-setting blew my mind. I am rather sad that because it isn't popular there is never going to be a game build from the ground up to utilize all of its possibilities. Fortunately it actually is great at what it promises, bringing desktop games to the sofa without making as many compromises as with traditional controllers, while also performing well enough at the tasks associated with those. The community features help a lot with the overwhelming amount of customization. It is not perfect for some tasks, but usually good enough so if you can only afford one controller, you wouldn't be wrong picking this one.

Sometimes It can be difficult to evaluate whether mediocrity should be thought of as an offense to the pedigree of an established series or an excuse to enjoy its own moments. Welcome to Moreytown is brimming with potential to tell a story about an interesting setting/premise that feels squandered not only as a piece of fiction but also as an interactive one. Beyond the simplistic crime-fiction narrative, there is so little of an author’s voice to make it sufficient to judge the quality of his writing. The best thing I can say about the story itself is that it’s an anthropomorphic narrative that feels neither tainted nor corrupted by its intended audience, something that I cannot say about major publications nor minor projects.  If there is anything strictly positive about Moreytown it is that it is enough of a teaser to want to invest into the Moreau series, which is what compelled me to purchase the Moreau Omnibus as I hope these books delve further into its merits.
It should be noted that Welcome to Moreytown was my foray into the “Choice of..” games followed by Choice of Robots. This was intentional as I wanted to have no expectations of what these games offer before playing a highly-regarded one gifted to me as my barometer. As a result of this approach, I believe this provided insight on how and why choices in “Choice of…” games are effective. While I do not want to approach this review with the “Good Game, Bad Game” attitude, this approach will make it sensible for people to understand the differences in quality as well as draw out for the developer where Moreytown can improve and to provide an example in action. (This won’t include spoilers of either game if you are concerned.) While these games may feel like comparing apples to oranges, both games tell linear narratives with different approaches to reward choices.
Moreytown suffers from superfluous decisions that add nothing to the story you create such as your species, your romantic interests and your flavor text of meaningless actions. Even with some decisions being based on species’ stats and preemptive measures like preparing for a fight, the overall journey is not one shaped by the player. Conditions have little impact on future choices, stats remain stagnant beyond the romance opportunities, and the only real decisions that have payoff are the different results at the end. The greatest pitfall of Moreytown is how it is the role of these romantic side-activities and the multiple endings to satisfy the player’s curiosity as you play, which makes the decisions you accumulate all too meaningless because the plot ignores them.
In contrast to Moreytown, Choice of Robots is a linear narrative that tells the accumulation of your decisions about the robot you create, providing meaning in the moment and in the future. This focus is more beneficial because the flavor-text has immediate results on the story you create, and the accumulation of ever-changing stats adds value to moments such as teaching a robot empathy by playing video-games. The overall script remains largely intact like Moreytown yet all these additional touches, including alternative scenes to chapters and multiple endings, tells a more personal story. This does not even include the romance opportunities that challenge the player to value whether to spend more time bonding with another person or their own robotic creation.
Each game’s systems are virtually identical, so illustrating how Moreytown can create its own ideas, such as balancing the “pinks’ (humans’)” support’ and the moreaus (non-humans), would make all decisions tell a more dynamic narrative. The ending itself should not be the destination we sought after but the moment to reflect on what decisions we made that led up to that final moment.
As much as I may appear to harp on Moreytown, it’s out of passionate constructive criticism because the world it sets up is the one thing that made me invested enough to read more about it. The world around Moreytown is one inspired by The Island of Dr. Moreau after nations have invested in scientifically questionable projects to create anthropomorphic animals for war. Eventually these experiments led to a civil rights movement to establish a constitutional amendment recognizing their humanity with all the same inalienable rights, and integrating them into society is the challenge the game always teases will be the main dilemma. Except the story itself has nothing to do with this set-up.
Instead, the plot is largely focused on events after all these initial problems were established, taking place in the moreau slums years later where the events that led up to the story have already been set into motion with you as a bystander borne from the past. This game’s plot is a clear example of a narrative that did not ask itself the question, “Is this the most interesting part of the story? If not, why are we not reading about that story?” What we get in its place is a simple crime drama with exposition around these more interesting events with a clear emphasis on the writing taking a backseat where a niche audience is meant to excuse its shortcomings. Perhaps the point of not setting it into the past was to intrigue new readers to check out the author’s other works, yet that shouldn’t have resulted in a creating a subpar piece of interactive fiction to entice people to go read books.
Again, I want to reiterate that the narrative itself is entertaining enough on its own to excuse this game from receiving more ire because I don’t believe it was done out of malice, more so from ignorance. This interactive fiction feels like a novel writer trying to write a game like a book, failing to see the innate differences, and the execution of its storytelling and of its choices proves there were misconceptions made about what the audience values. Unless you wish to support the developer’s game itself, it seems more preferable to read his stories instead because they are likely to be more entertaining with a writer set in his own environment where he knows his rules and limitations. Hopefully lessons learned from Welcome to Moreytown will inspire the writer to give interactive fiction another chance in the future to give the game its proper justice.

I wish I could write a neutral here. This game wasn't bad, but compared to most choose your own adventures, it's a bit short and could be seen as disappointing. I give it a thumbs up simply because I still personally enjoyed it.
If you enjoy anthropomorphic characters, that'll probably be the thing that'd bring you to this, as you have a lot of species options. The plot itself seems intruiging, though it's a bit rushed in execution. The romance system, or lack thereof, is probably my biggest complaint, even though in many choose your own adventures romancing a character is as easy as not being a♥♥♥♥♥♥to them, deciding you like them, and they automatically requite your feelings, other games mask this better, drawing out your time with the character to make it feel more fleshed out and excusable that they just happen to feel the same way. This game pretty much made it so that as soon as I decided I was interested in the human reporter I saved from thugs, went to her apartment and flirted with her, I was quickly in her pants and got an acheivement for it, twice in fact, though that might have been a glitch.
The premise is fairly decent, you have to investigate gang activity, a lunatic cult, and terrorism in a future where humans experimentation on animals has resulted in a future with sentient, anthropomorphic animals. This becomes an aspect of society with racial tension between humans and non-humans, as well as having a fleshed out exposition that shows how these anthropomorchic people, or "moreaus" live their day to day lives.
The one thing I really felt rised above some other choose your own adventure games, despite the bad pacing, was the ending. My ending, without too much spoilers, made it apparent I could have made some other choices to bring a better outcome to Moreytown had I made better choices. It made the endgame at least feel like it was important, where a lot of games you can fool around the whole time and still get the best ending by clicking the obvious correct choices. Here I got a bittersweet ending, that didn't punish me too much for bad choices, but still made me feel like I could have done better, making me more curious as to where I made my mistakes.
I'd recommend buying this game on sale if you like choose your own adventures and find the premise of anthropomic animals and humans living together in a world of high racial tensions, and measuring your moral choices in society fighting a cult threatening your neighborhood. If money is no object to you, however, or you have a lot of games you want to try out, I would pass on this game for something with more bang for your buck.

I can only really recommend this for multiplayer, as the single-player AI is frankly atrociously-handled.
The multiplier bonuses as listed on the Endless Space wiki are pretty telling:
Putting aside the fact that, going by those figures, Newbie difficulty seems to be the
, I shouldn't need to point out that simply buffing numbers is a lazy method of introducing difficulty, nor should I have to explain why. It's a matter that's been discussed ad nauseum for a large part of the medium's life.
There's also the matter of a territory/resource-deprived AI still somehow managing to churn out a considerable amount of firepower. I don't know what's sillier, pulling entire fleets out of Hammerspace, or the fact there are apparently people who deny there's anything fishy about this.
I mean, if you're okay with it - maybe you just like having more stuff to blow up - that's totally fine. But at least be honest about it.
With a group of human players, I could see this being a fairly enjoyable (if very lightweight) 4X. It's not necessarily BAD, there's just not a lot to it. If you're willing to go to the trouble of organising lengthy multiplayer sessions with this kind of game, you're probably also willing to get your teeth into something a bit more substantial.
I'll still be playing this a bit to see if I warm up to it, but as of the time of writing this, I'm doubtful.

Review:
Pros:
+ Combat is absolutely brillaint.
+ Gameplay feels smooth.
+ Things despawn at a very slow rate. For example: You can set a helicopter down at one end of the map. Run to another end and back and find it right where you left it.
+ You have character appropriate abilities.
+ Violent, and gory. Very, very graphic. (If you enjoy gory games.)
+ There's an option to replay the campaign with previous campaigns unlocks. <3
Cons:
- Graphics are a little dated. Max resolution is 1280/800.
- Story is short, and a little lacking.
- Entire game is essentially a copy of Radical's: "The Incredible Hulk. Ultimate Destruction."
- Very gory, and violent. (If you dislike, or are disturbed by gore.)
- Voice acting was bad. (Though better than the second game, I will mention.)
- End game feels repetitive. You run around killing the same hunters, soldiers. Destroying the same bases, and hives. After you're fully upgraded. End game Prototype feels a lot like endgame GTA. You just run around and kill things.
If you played the Hulk Game I mentioned in the Cons. Then realizing the fact that it was essentially copy pasted from that game will ruin most the experience for you. Though if it is on sale. I would pick it up.

The king of FPS returns with lightning quick gunfights and a killer soundtrack.
DOOM has quite possibly the greatest FPS singleplayer campaign in over a decade with tons of secrets and optional objectives. The level design is a highlight as well, ranging from big sprawling arenas to dark maze-like dungeons and everything in between. The game gives moments of quiet time in between fights for you to breathe a bit and solve some switch-based puzzles. The weapon arsenal is huge as should be expected, and each and every weapon can be upgraded, most of them in two distinctively different ways. You can customize your Doom Slayer to fit your playstyle, or if you're a completionist like me, 100% all the levels to reach godlike power.
The multiplayer is very enjoyable too. I found it to be highly reminiscent of old arena-style shooters like Quake III Arena and Unreal Tournament. There are loads of different gamemodes to choose from including capture points and freeze-tag combat, the old classics like Deathmatch and Capture the Flag are of course also here, although CTF has seen some alterations making it more resemble american football. Loadouts are customisable with 2 main weapons and additional equipment like grenades or mines, there are also runes that give you a distinct advantage in an area of your choosing. In this respect it could be likened to a mix between Quake III Arena and modern Call of Duty games, although the main gameplay is definitely leaning more towards the older style. Health kits, armor and super weapons like the BFG and the Gauss Cannon still spawn into the map, so map control is still highly useful. Some modes also allow you to collect a Demon powerup to become one of the game's many powerful demons. Taking down the current demon drops the powerup once again and allows you to transform into a demon of your own for the remainder of the powerup timer. This results in an often frantic game of cat and mouse, but where taking down the goliath is highly rewarding.
Lastly the game also supports custom maps and even campaigns which can all be built inside the game's engine itself. Creating maps is very simple once you get the hang of it, and there are multiple tutorials to guide you on your way. I'm very impressed to see such support for community creations, and thanks to the powerful tools there is some high quality user created content out there.
Id Software definitely delivered this time!

Hey, you like Choose-Your-Own-Adventure games? You a Furry? Well I think this game's for you. Okay now that we've got the obligatory Furry joke out of the way, here's the review:
Welcome to Moreytown is basically if Zootopia was a darker and grittier noir story, but also had human characters along with the anthropomorphic ones. You start out the game choosing which species you'd like your character to be, each one has advantages and disadvantages, some are stronger and slower, other's are smaller and faster. The story starts with your character discovering that their apartment's on fire, upon escaping you discover your apartment fire could be leading to a much bigger threat that could shake Moreytown to its core.
Well, the main selling point for a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure game is its story, so how's the story? I personally really liked this game's story. I liked learning about this world of humans and "Moreys", as the Anthros in the game are called. The mystery is interesting, if not a little predictible towards the end.
I also liked how the game takes advantage of the fact that you're playing as an animal, with certain heightened senses. At the beginning of the game you choose a sense you want your character to have that's more powerful than their others, and that affects how the game describes certain parts of what's going on in a scene. If your character's strongest sense is their sense of smell, then the character will describe the atmosphere at certain points in the story by what they pick up in scent. There are also several fights your character gets in in the game, and the outcomes of the fights are dependent on your character's size, strength, and agility, and the combat choices you make that are geared towards their strengths and weaknesses. The game also has romance options, as most choice-based games do, but they're optional, thankfully.
Though the game has some decent replay value, I do think the story could have been a bit longer. I've played two or three other games published by Choice of Games, and both were a lot longer than this. In fact the story is so short I'm afraid talking about it too much might spoil it. But the plot is interesting enough and seeing as the game is only $5 (and even less if you get it on sale), it's hard not to recommend it to anyone who's curiousity is even a little peaked by the premise.
If you think you'll like this game based on the summary on it's store page, you probably will, I definitely enjoyed seeing where the plot was taking me, and seeing what different paths you could take to complete the story.
I'd give Welcome to Morey town a 7/10, it's not one of the greatest games in Choice of Game's library, but I enjoyed it too much not to recommend it, and might even look into the author's other printed works that take place in the same universe.

This is a choice-of-games game; so again before you buy this you can check out the demo to see if you'd like it. The choice-of-games brand is accompanied by many reoccuring problems, such as the games being really short and many choices not mattering. The first one at least is also affecting this game; even if you take lots of time to read through everything you'll be done in like less than 2 hours and have a good overview of the games content and what the other routes might be even after one playthrough.
As another warning beforehand: this is a furry game. If you are really uncomfortable with reading about an anthropomorphic wolf wearing jeans that accentuate her curves then this is not a game for you. But since this game is on steam, there are no explicit sex-scenes, so there aren't going to be any surprises if one would judge this game based on stereotypes.
The game itself is written by S. Andrew Swann. Recognize that name? Unlike many other CoG-author's he is actually a writer with more than two decades of experience in that field. This game is based on his Moreau novels. I cannot really say anything about the novels since I haven't read them but they certainly seem more interesting than the material many of the other CoG games authors have been using.
The basic gist of the story is that mankind created animal-people to fight their wars for them. These people are called "moreau". But since they made the mistake of making these guys sentient humanity realized that they have to treat these engineered organisms like humans.
That is where the story begins and your player character is one of these engineered animal-people. You awake to a chain of unfortunate events and are left outside of your apartment with nothing but yourself. From there onwards the chain of unfortunate events continues. The beginning of the story actually left me quite amused - even anticipating what disaster that is worse than the last could strike the character now.
Some have complained about a lack of direction in the story because of that. But under your fur, claws and teeth you're just a regular dude with not much else going on. I feel like this game has been written for people who have never read the novels, so there isn't really much "end-of-the-world"-stuff or other complex political/socioeconomic/social/... topics that are being talked about.
In fact the game tries to tell you the differences or difficulties of humans and moreaus in other ways. The moreaus colloquially refer to humans as the "pinks" which again left me with a chuckle. The protagonist does describe things around him in a personal and sometimes offensive way but not to what I felt was too obtrusive. In fact in the story the player character even starts wondering why the moreaus are using that term to begin with since that black person they saw in that moment wasn't pink.
It's moments like these that I actually came to really like this story; there are lots of details and lots of very small things that happen (i.e. the PC describes the tail wagging of another character after they're agitated or they describe the smell of a human) that remind you what the world and the player character are.
Unlike many CoG games this game does not force social issues down your throat. You can but do not have to become an activist for your people. This is actually refreshing to see after having read through Zachary Sergi's works or Eternal Sea where you just could not avoid these topics, and not just that, you had to deal with these issues without really having an option to select a side.
So, are there faults to this game? It's short, even too much so. When I was done I felt like that the story barely even started. The story that is being told does actually have an end, so you're not left with a cliffhanger just so you buy the sequel.
Do I recommend this game? It's hard to say and I wish there was a "It depends" or other middle option here on steam. That little that is already there was pretty enjoyable and good. Is it worth it to spend $5 on this game? Perhaps but you can actually get one of his books for that price which probably has more content than this CoG game.
If you are interested in just buying a CoG that isn't terrible this is a good buy. If you are just interested in the story and don't mind supporting the author with a little bit more cash then go for it.
But in all fairness I have to say that $5 is too much for this while Choice of Robots sells for the same price which has a ridiculously large amount of content.
With this little content this game even feels a little like an ad for the novels, but I have to admit, it did its job: Now I do want to check out the novels.

EDITED REVIEW AFTER 6 MONTHS:
I am changing this review because the game and the developer have both shown a lot of improvement. First let me say that the developer is human and it's not an easy job. Gamers are quick to espouse their opinions and rarely offer the same degree of politeness expected in person. It can be very hard to hear harsh criticism from strangers when you have shown the bravery to share your art with the world at large and sometimes hurt feelings can lead you to make rash decisions. In this case the developer has matured and taken the criticisms to heart. He has stopped censoring opinions and put a lot of hard work into his game. It shows and it is appreciated. I now support this developer and look forward to his future work. I would also like to apologize if I offended Jake from Statefarm at any stage of the process.
WARNING: Another developer who deletes negative criticism posts and bans users for them. Avoid this game and developer at all costs. The User CashPanda and myself have both had forum posts with negative, but constructive criticism deleted as well as being banned with the following message "You have been permanently banned from all The Lost Battalion: All Out Warfare discussions.
You were banned by a The Lost Battalion: All Out Warfare developer.
Reason: "Toxic behavior""  There is NO ROOM on Steam for developers like this.
I am having trouble recommending this game for any reason. I am a huge supporter of indie games and can usually find a redeeming idea or element of execution, but here I have no hope. The whole game is less functional and rewarding than ANY game you will find on the free flash game websites like Armor Games, etc. This game is merely a series of static screens consisting of one length scroll right, one left with endless waves of stupid enemies that come along. There is no point other than try to beat your score. As if that wasn't bad enough, it's wonky and unpredictable. Jump up and down a few times and you will randomly ending up in "the mud" and instantly die. Walk to the right and you might end up in the mud and instantly die. It's incredibly bad at this point and while I do believe in cutting low priced games some slack, I would tell my friends to stay away even if it was free. This is a course in how NOT to develop games. This team seems to have failed to develop a concept or design document even though they have been working on this for "8 months". I do not have any interest in being mean or hurting the feelings of this team but this type of production has no place on Steam. It is damaging to the overall quality of the platform when an aimless team sells something that an average newcomer could make himself in 5-7 days with Game Maker. Developer, please consider taking your game down from the store until you have a concept. This is in response to the only post on the forum at this time which is from you asking us from gameplay ideas. This is NOT how to make games. I wish you better luck in the future, please study our industry a bit and learn the steps to making a game that is going to be enjoyed and appreciated by others if not a commercial success.

Mechwarrior online is an awesome game and the fact that it’s free makes it better. Now one thing that needs to be made clear is that MWO is not like other first person shooters, it has a big learning curve. For one thing there is no healing, and no respawning. What ever damage you sustain will stay with until the end of the match and if you die then that’s it, no respawn (except faction play but that’s later down the line). So with both of these factors MWO becomes a slow pace game that favors good tactics over skill. Also don’t worry about how many kills you get in a match instead worry about how much damage you dealt to the enemy, the game rewards you more for damage over kills. Last note I recommend watching this youtuber named Kanajashi. He offers training videos and he does a series where he plays the game completely for free. This is helpful to new people and people who want to spend little to no money on this game. Mechwarrior is by far one of my favorite games. If you’re just starting out, stay strong, this game is harder to learn than other games but once you learn the ropes then this game becomes a lot of fun.

Quick Pro-Con Lost
PRO:
-The movement. I mean god damn, does it put games like Titianfall and the latest cawadoody entry to shame. The entire game is played with an exo-suit that makes you feel like you've got an ACME rocket-powered skatboard welded to your feet at all times. With the hilly structure of nearly all of the maps, it's like the worlds most dangerous skate park - but with guns and Capture the Flag.
-The weapons. Don't expect too many traditional pew pews in Tribes. This game is fought primarily with high-velocity explosive frisbees. Spinfusors are the name of the game, and learning to use one is easy, but eyeballing the trajectory, distance, and speed of your enemy as they go screaming across the map and scoring a hit is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to master. Weapon variety is enough to keep you happy, and each one has it's own little purpose.
-The classes. Old Tribes players will disticntly remember nine in total, but with recent updates it's been shaved down to three; light, medium, and heavy. Don't worry, this is probably my favorite new feature, as it allows more creativity in creating them. Classes are simple, light means go fast, heavy means big armor, and medium is a balance between the two. With the new additions, you can really carve out your niche in the match. Want to have some heavy offensive ordinance AND be able to deploy a turret now? You can. Want to carry a crossbow and a Jackal at the same time? No more class restriction on that. Chaingun AND Heavy spinfusor AND Fractal Grenade? Yep, that too. The sky's the limit.
-The graphics. Not on par with a triple-A 2016 release but still really pretty if you crank everything up to max, and can still be set low enough to play on a toaster. The gameplay is the focus here.
-It's free. What more could you want?
SO-SO
-Cannot be played through Steam, so your favorite dank meme name is a no-go.
-Serves can get a bit underpopulated, but that's not bad in my opinion becaue you see a few famailiar faces from time to time.
CON:
-Learning curve is a bit frusturating. 20 hours in and I'm still getting my behind kicked.
-May be dead as a doornail in a year or two.
-I can't think of anythig else.

TL;DR: Mindblowing for flight sims, great for first person games, decent for FPS, driving, and turnbased strategy, bad for RTSs. Customization and related community features are amazing. Try the old Star Wars flight sims and marvel at how great it works.
So, the Steam controller - quite a controversial thing. I have owned it for about a year now and I think I can finaly give a verdict after playing a variety of genres, for which I will highlight a few games.
The controller is very different from the standard models and requires a good amount of getting used to just because of its shape, that isn't even considering the trackpads that replace d-pad and one analogue stick. Haptic is not as neat as with X-Box controllers, as clickpoints are a lot harsher. The trackpads do feel great, though, thanks to the vibrating feedback.
The controller has a good amount of buttons with backside paddles that I love and have always missed from my X-Box 360 controller. It also comes with a gyroscopic sensor, but I haven't tried it, yet.
Final verdict for hardware: Great functions, not ideal in form. I don't really care, but you might.
The controller works through Steam, which can be annoying, but also useful, as you can apply configurations to any game you want and they work without any input lag because of how they are applied. Speaking of configurations - here is where you truly get your moneys worth! The amounts of customization possible are mindboggeling. Want to aim using the gyro-sensor? You can do that if you are brave enough! Need more buttons than there are on the controller? Put them on virtually on the one of the trackpads (this one actually works superbly if you don't overdo it)! For many games there are excellent community presets you can download so you can benefit from all the customizability without having to work through the overwhelming possibilities yourself.
I played through the Talos Principle using the steam controller and liked it a lot. The trackpad is comfortable for camera control and the rest of the controller works like you would expect.
However first person games have an issue with precision - not needed in that capacity in Talos Principle, but critical for shooters. There I tried a session of TF2, which was just awefull. Then I tried Republic Commando as single player game, which was alright (excellent for the coordination, even, thanks to a neat trackpad assignment), but became pretty frustrating on higher difficulties. Maybe with a lot of relearning you can become decent at shooters, as it is a lot more precise than a stick will ever be, but it probably isn't worth the effort. Singleplayer works at casual difficulties and it is preferable to stick-aiming.
So great for general first person games, useless for multiplayer shooters, neat as a sofa-tool for singleplayer shooters, if not ideal.
Here I only played Rocket League, with mixed results. On one hand the driving works just as you'd expect and the camera movement was better than with a stick. However in Rocket League you also need to be on top of using your abilities, and the button placement at least for me just didn't work there, because my thumb tended to be on the trackpad for the camera and then had difficulty finding the relatively small (~20% less than X-Box I'd eyeball) XYAB-buttons again.
Driving in general great, driving that involves simultaneous camera controll and abilities not so much.
I haven't tried an RTS (well somewhat in a similar vein I tried a round of DOTA and had a miserable time, can't imagine that getting better with more units to controll), but I can't imagine it being great. What I did play was Civ V and it works well. The trackpads make for comfortable handheld mice, and you don't need much more for Civ. The few hotkeys that you do use you can map to the various buttons and be happy. I will also lump Hearthstone in here as it likewise just needs the controller as mouse and works perfectly.
Great for turnbased strategy!
Oh boy, here I go: It is perfect! Really. Flightsims need two thing, a stick (check!) and lots of buttons. The second department is where all controllers before this failed in one way or another, either having too few buttons or not having them usable. Well, enter the trackpads and cry tears of joy. You can make them behave like a grid of buttons which will be displayed as overlay over your game (where you can also give them actual labels so you don't have to learn the keybinds before playing). Crossing a border between two buttons causes a light bump that helps you find the right one quickly.
I have played Star Wars TIE Fighter with a setup like this and it works like a charm. Every command I can desire is availiable. Where before I had to put at least two functions on to any button with my X-Box controller and still was not able to have everything I needed to comfortably play.
If you buy this controller for anything, it is this. The possibilities are demonstrated so well here.
Personally, I love it. Playing TIE Fighter in a sofa-setting blew my mind. I am rather sad that because it isn't popular there is never going to be a game build from the ground up to utilize all of its possibilities. Fortunately it actually is great at what it promises, bringing desktop games to the sofa without making as many compromises as with traditional controllers, while also performing well enough at the tasks associated with those. The community features help a lot with the overwhelming amount of customization. It is not perfect for some tasks, but usually good enough so if you can only afford one controller, you wouldn't be wrong picking this one.

Well haters gonna hate but I love this thing. Now I can play games with no controller support like a champ, but I've found this controller fills more than that one, small niche. For retro gamers, this pad of joy has that extra click on the triggers like a Gamecube, a gyro so good you can use it like an IR pointer (amazing for WII emulation and lightgun games) , and the mapping of functions withe HD haptics means that a trackball style control for games like Centipede and Missle Command is available. The mapping of buttons to the D-Pad touchpad with the "click required" option turned off can give you a super fast D-Pad for retro-fighters too. For the hardcore gamer the tricks are endless. Map your run button to the outer edge of your pad for auto run on the outer edges of movement, one button less to think about and very natural. Use the right pad like a  mouse  so that a full 180 is a quick swipe, then add quick aim accuracy with the gyro's. Done right this controller can leave a lot of other players looking like they are standing still. I'm just scratching the surface, this things deep and it does require a few hours of study to get the most out of it. But, with so many great guides out in the world wide web, it is worth it. I'm amazed at negative reviews for this pad, RTFM guys, this is the most compatible and configurable controller in the world, learn to use it before slamming it. If you can't be bothered to put in the time, buy an XBox pad instead and stick to games that support it. If you have a couple of hours and can be bothered to learn, than this pad will reward you well.

Let's get something straight, this contoller is advertised as a halfway point between controllers and keyboard + mouse. It's not good at being a replacement for keyboard + mouse. However, as a contoller, it excels. It's wonderful for platformers, racing games, 3rd person rpgs, and anything else you could imagine a contoller being good at. It does all that with amazing customization options, and thats the main reason why I reccomend it over an xbox controller. If you dont like something about how the game controls, even if it wasnt made with the steam contoller in mind, you can change it. Other bonuses are its insane battery life. I've put somewhere between 80 and 100 hours on a single set of batteries and they still aren't showing signs of dying. Also, especially on a sale, it's cheaper than an Xbox controller. Finally, the flaps in the back. I love them sooo much. They're very good for routing them to buttons that are usally on controls you dont want to take your thumbs off, or controls like dashing inplatformers that just make sense with them.
They seem like such a glaringly obivous innovation that should really be on all controllers.
TL;DR - Don't buy this for advertised reasons (a compromise between controler and KB+M) buy it if you want an excelent controller
Edit: I have somwhere between 120 and 130 hours on the controller and still haven't replaced the batteries once.
It's a good controller, but the only thing I dislike is the sensitive pad to move the camera. Wish it was a stick.

I've been using it for 6 months and finally just defaulted back to an old 360 controller. It's definitely an upgrade in precision over other controllers but the problem is that two analogue sticks can't be beat for certain genres and PC games have wide support for Xbox controllers. To top it off the the SC is not sturdy at all, in terms of build quality and feeling of use it ranks below the dual shock controllers (xbox>ps>SC). You're best off with a Xbone controller in all likelyhood because using this for shooters and strategy games etc is a gimmick so better just use m&kb. And this really isn't comfortable or reliable for casual singleplayer games imo.
For exact nitpicks: the shoulder buttons are hardassed clinky pieces of plastic that hate been pressed, the face buttons are overly small and scrunched next to eachother, the palm grips curve forward and force your thumbs into a sort of claw grip on the pads which is not a relaxed position (although that is kinda required to make touch pads work), the pads become a deteriment if your fingers get sweaty/wet because then a traction is formed, the triggers feel hollow and lack the gun trigger feel of 360 triggers, no dpad, its impossible to find a good feeling camera setting for 3rd person games (worst cases so far Darksiders 2 and Mad Max), clicking the pads makes the controller echo through it's hollow inards adding to sense of low quality, and the start and select buttons are very shallow and far from the center of the pads.
Controllers are a big influence on my sense of how a game plays and the steam controller thereby sullies my opinion of many good/solid games.

I've had this game back since mid 2011, and it's made up a significant amount of my childhood. I grew up with Roblox and Minecraft as well, but I have to say this game was and is the most memorable and fun to play. I have an accumulation of almost 10,000 hours in this game, including the many years I've played the demo. However, there's still many other reasons I love this game than just my playtime.
There's a lot of good things to Blockland. Some of the things are:
While there are a lot of good things about Blockland, there still are some of its cons, such as:
Building -
- Very simple and straightforward, yet can still get very sophisticated and detailed
Events -
- Fairly simple and easy to understand; a few points decked for moderately low event limit
Graphics -
- Very satisfying lag to quality ratio
Physics -
- Horrendous; hit boxes are very inaccurate, vehicle physics are easily wonked up
Overall -
- Mainly good experience;
community; fantastic building and event system; final verdict is
.
Overall, I have fairly positive feeling towards Blockland. The building, events, and minigames (all vanilla) are easy to get the hang of and can really express creativity. The scale of how great these buildings can get is much higher than Minecraft AND Roblox. While the singleplayer and creativity experiences are good, there is still the community you'll need to worry about. A large number of people are trolls or swear a lot, and it may be hard to govern players sometimes. There's also the fact that Badspot (the owner, also known as Eric Hartman) doesn't really care about Blockland's development anymore, so updates aren't coming anymore. Those aside, there is still a lot of greatness to experience in Blockland and is still worth $9.99USD even if it hasn't even reached its full potential. I would highly recommend Blockland to anyone looking for a game to build in or a sandbox to play around in.

I will start with that I enjoy all the 'choice of' games I play so the recomendation comes from a general level of tolerance and enjoyment from these games.
This one in particular had a nice concept and fairly well presented story.
With that said I have just finished the game and boy does it have serious flaws that should be seen if you wish to purchase this game:
1. It is very quick, it felt like I was jumping into experiences extremely quickly. I understand there is that constraint but it bounces through maybe 5 plot point over 3 days and then you're done.
2. There is a lack of deeper lore and character backstory or maybe just less than I am used too.
3. There are perhaps the wide range of customizables that are linked to these games but boy were they surface level.
4. This is the last and most important, I don't know what motivation any character from the baseline would have in this whole thing, I just can't believe someone would act so rashly and completely.
Buy if you like the concept and fancy a quick (less than 2 hours in my 1st playthrough) of a 'choice' game, otherwise if the price is to steep for that just leave it, probably end up just a bit disapointed like me.
1st review so thanks for those that read this and I hope both the author and publisher move onto better things.

TLDR: It’s a fun game if you like strategic thinking FPS's and slower moving mechs from the Battletech universe.
MWO is a deep game with a very steep learning curve. You play as a slow moving mech broken into 4 classifications (light, medium, heavy, assault). Light mechs are faster, with less armor and weapons, and usually used for recon, harassing, skirmishing, and flanking, they’re not frontline fighters. Mediums fill a category where they’re in between everything else, they can be fairly fast and tanky and have a solid punch, so they end up getting to engagements faster and moving to assist bigger slower mechs; they’re usually strikers, skirmishers, and support mechs. Heavy mechs are exactly that, heavier, slower but with more armor and weapons; they’re usually strikers or supporters. Assault mechs are the biggest mechs with the most armor and weapons, many are used as the tip of the spear to push into enemy lines, but they need to be protected from lighter faster mechs flanking them, not all assaults are cut out for frontline use. Unfortunately, it’s up to you to figure out what mech plays which role best based on its strengths and weaknesses.
Mechs have hitboxes (2 arms and legs, center and side torsos), you need to go through the forums to find the specifics. You’re trying to shoot through your enemy’s armor and destroy the structure in that location (e.g. destroying the center torso or both legs will kill the mech), but you can also do criticals that will destroy components in that location, like weapons, etc. Components include weapons, ammo, sensors, engines, heat sinks, etc. Weapons come in extreme, long, medium, and short ranges and are broken into three categories: ballistic, missile, and energy. They operate out to optimal ranges where damage falls off to nothing past its maximum range, some with a minimum range before they do damage. Ballistic weapons produce low heat, are heavy, reliant on limited ammo, and have a fairly good front loaded damage or DPS. Missile weapons have medium heat, are medium weight, also require ammo, and can do a lot of damage but you can equip deterrents; long range variants require a lock on for consistent damage, luckily there is technology to help quicken, keep, and make locks. Energy weapons are light, hot, and most have burn durations. If you get too hot your mech will shut down or you can override that and cause damage to your mech’s structure. The mechs have an extensive amount of customization, based on hard points, engine, armor, and structure type as well as visual customization. There’s also an extensive skill system. You also get to figure out what how to best use your weapons and work as a team.
There’s a very small basic tutorial, but the rest is left for the players to brutally discover. A lot of statistics are slowly making their way from the forums and into the game but plenty of things aren’t displayed in-game. There are 3 game modes: Quick Play, 12v12 objective play that usually ends up being a free- for- all, where you can use any mech, regardless of affiliation; Comp Play, 8v8 free-for-all; Faction Play where you have to have your drop deck setup (4 mechs, and an additional light or medium mech) for scouting missions and objective play – you need to click fight now after going into Faction Warfare and then pick whether you’re scouting or going into the fight cue, in the fight cue you chose which mech you’ll drop as each time you die. In Faction Play, you also need an affiliation (Clan, Inner Sphere or Merc pledged to either). Games have a max time of 15 minutes except for Faction Play, where it varies on the game type. Most matches last 2-10 minutes, depending on the skill level, tactics, and communication of the players.
It’s made in CryEngine so it’s very resource heavy and not optimized, but can run on older machines. The company developing it is very small. The game is kind of its own beast compared to prior titles, primarily because it doesn’t have a single player campaign and they don’t utilize or explain the lore. The same company is also making MechWarrior 5 in a different engine. MWO has been up and running for 5-6 years and been on steam for a year or two. They started the game set at 3025 and it's currently set at the end of the clan invasion, but they're moving the timeline and tech up to 3067 era this month. Monthly, new mechs are released and the game is rebalanced. F2P comes in with buying the newly released mechs with a 6 months period where it’s not released for in-game currency. You can use your hard cash to skip grinding for in-game cash or outright buying mechs, they also sell a lot of visual customizations, and you can buy premium time which gives incresed money and experience. Everything is balanced so there doesn’t ever feel like there is a pay-2-win factor going on. All-in-all the community is less salty than other competitive games and pretty inviting and helpful. I enjoy playing and have played since closed beta. There are a lot of legacy features that have no function anymore but are still in the game, like Tiers and the Ready button. Be prepared for some confusion when going into the game, but again the community is great. They really need to hire someone to interface with the community instead of their CEO, since he frequently says something that sets the community in an outrage. The game has a horrible UI and needs a serious optimization pass, but most of the problems are smaller in nature. I think it’s still a worthwhile game and if it sounded interesting download it, it’s free.

Okay. TL:DR: Okay game, has flaws, fun tactical combat, takes some time to make progress, free to play, in game purchases.
To be in more depth:
MWO Is a tactical futuristic battle simulator where you, as a pilot, control a giant vaugely human shaped robots, called  BattleMechs. Your `Mech pilots somewhat like a tank, with lower torso legs, and an upper torso, no strafing, whatever direction your lower torso is facing is where forward is. There are 4 types of BattleMechs, Lights, Mediums, Heavies, and Assault `Mechs. Lights have low armor, quick movement, and weaker weapons. Assaults have very tough armor, are much slower, and have very heavy firepower. Heavies and Mediums lay somewhere in the middle of the spectrum. With that summary in mind, here are the pros and cons.
Pros :
Fun gameplay,
Large variety of play,
Interesting combat,
Large tactical play,
Tons of ability to customize,
Lots of holiday events.
Cons :
Large grind aspect,
Distinct meta, (Meta meaning whats the best and used the most)
Expensive BattleMechs,
Very select few of good weapons.
In the end, I do recommend this game because of there being very few games like it. Its a fun unique experience, and I do hope everyone gives it a try.

This is the worst controller I gave ever laid hands on, and I hate it.
The haptics work, the analog stick feels better than most of the ones I have tried, saving configurations to the controller is convenient, and the fact that it works out of the box as an Xbox controller for any game with full controller support is nice.
The whole point of the dual trackpads was versatility and customizability, however the controller has neither. Configurations can only be tweaked through Steam's Living Room mode, and who ever used that? The trackpads can be configured to use a "button" or "directional pad" mapping, but in practice, can only be mapped to mouse or keyboard commands, which is worthless for most gaming needs. I want to reconfigure my gamepad settings. If I wanted to use mouse or keyboard commands, I already have a far superior set of peripherals for those purposes.
Additionally, while I will admit that I am unconventional in preferring the PlayStation button layout to the Xbox, he layout on the Steam controller is the worst of both worlds, with your hands stretching to reach the most often used controls, and shoulder buttons running together confusingly so that you have to think about whether you're pulling the right bumper or right trigger.
Finally, there is no documentation of use. The setup guide tells you everything you already know: plug in the dongle, turn the controller on by pressing the "steam" button. The controller actually can be paired with additional dongles, but the only reason I know this is because Valve sells them separately. this functionality is not documented anywhere in the instructional materials, not the configuration utilities.
Ultimately, the Steam controller is an overall vastly inferior experience to using an Xbox or Playstation controller running on 3rd-party drivers (when necessary), both of which are also more ergonomic, and what your software will be expecting to take orders from anyway.
Has good potential, but it's not easy to get a hang of. Looks like a powerful tool, though.

The reprogrammability of this controller is incredible and while the software may crash every rare chance, the hardware is beyond incredible. Having the capability to remap every function for each of the controller's button, touch pads, double-button triggers, and even a gyro can create great customization of controlls! The gyro works great for fine-tuning aiming for games like Resident Evil 4, games with long-distance weapons and lack of mobility, and even steering, though I doubt it can replace a steering wheel hardware.
Let me add that I don't think this controller will ever replace the current Xbox/Dualshock controllers and their functionality. But if you are an enthusiast and feel like getting anything neat during the Steam Summer Sale or something, I'd get it and try it out. Personally, as someone who plays MMO's on PC, I love remapping the controller so I can play MMO's when I'm grinding through leveling areas of gathering mats for crafting or something from the bed on a weekend. I can't see myself take on hardcore content with it, but I love grinding out content with it!
Nevertheless, if you want to experiment and have some fun with this controller, I'd definitely consider checking it out!

Background: I love city builders and have wanted to try this twist on the genre for quite some time.. and then Humble Bundle comes to the rescue. Have played the base game with none of the expansions.
Impressions: This is such a hard game to give a fair review too.. and it's not that it's a bad game... it just has a  frustrating element to seemingly balance out every good one.
The biggest issues are with the tutorial poorly describes the two systems it covers and does very little to prepare you for the deep-end when it finishes. To really play with any degree of success it's essential to watch some tutorials videos online and read some fan sites to get information on just how the transport systems work.
There's so much game play and it's fun to build thriving economies but so frustrating when you cant see why your city is failing or when one poor choice has you scurrying back to the last save you made till you save before placing every single building.
The Good:
*Decent graphics and sound, not amazing but more than adequate.
*Nice touches like seeing individual people travelling around the network.
*A range of transport options that are nicely animated.
*Pre-order bonuses are now free in the inbuilt store.
*Intelligently connecting lines gives satisfying results.
*Growing a city really feels like you are making a difference.
*Creating routes requires some thought and the campaign makes you think more as you progress.
*Campaign is really fun, if disjointed, as you town hop back-n-fore.
The Bad:
*Steep learning curve and terribly inadequate tutorial.
*Graphics and sound don't wow you but aren't irritating either.
*Despite a range of transport several systems feel too much alike.
*Campaign missions are repetitive, boring and lack vital info.
*Ticket pricing and wages are lacking depth.
*Despite dozens of information windows some feedback just isn't available.
*Setting timetables is a chore, even with the copy function.
*Building/Stop upgrading is initially confusing.
*Very limited modding options, which could have been really fun.
Recommended for:
City builders and god game people. Certainly for teenagers as there's little to wow a younger audience.
Conclusion.
7/10. I so badly want to give this an 8/10 but the problems in the base game stop it being as fun as it so nearly was.

So I have been reading through the negative reviews of this game and I've noticed a lot of those reviews are from people who have played the game for years. I would like to start this review by stating that I have played this game for years as well, I bought it some time in August, 2011.
I still enjoy it.
The glitches:
It's one of those games where you don't need glitchless gameplay to enjoy. I don't think I've come across one glitch that would make this game less entertaining to play, for example:
- A car crash could result in both cars flying in opposite directions at extremely high speeds
- If you jump at a certain angle at a block and hold the jump button, you do a "super jump" which increases possibilities with parkour
- if you press a movement button ("W" for example) and press your "sit" hotkey at the same time, your character will be locked in that animation (one animation makes your character look like he/she is humping the ground)
each of these glitches, along with a couple others I haven't mentioned, actually enhance the gaming experience.
The building/addons:
To add on to that, the building in this game can be made better by simply going to the forums, or BL Glass, or another RTB clone and downloading a few brick/color/tool addons. The community has been making a lot of really cool stuff that can make the game extremely fun in terms of bricks, weapons, and gamemodes. There are even map addons (the thing that some people are complaining were removed from the game) however it's mainly for nostalgia for the older players, but it's still an option.
The gamemodes:
Blockland also has minigames/gamemodes that you can play, which is where you essentially put your builds into action. One that comes to mind is Fortwars, where you create a base and fight other players with your creation. The base can be whatever you want: maybe a floating castle, or if you're not feeling very creative, a box on the ground with one entrance. That one is the best example because it's a gamemode about building and putting your build into action. It's a nice feature because what good is a creation if you don't do anything with it?
This paragraph is just me defending Badspot:
[I also feel that some of the community is giving Badspot a hard time because he stopped updating the game. I went and found the release date for blockland, which was sometime in 2007. Then I went and found the release date for his last update, which was sometime in 2013, meaning he has spent about 6 years constantly updating the game. I just felt like saying that as a lot of people seem to be getting the wrong idea about him, saying he "abandoned" the game. He has put in so many hours into making this game, that we only paid for once, as good as he could, and people are complaining. However, I will admit that there are some things he could've done better for the community, maybe keeping an eye on it every once in a while, and there are some criticisms that I do agree with, but he's human like the rest of us. Everyone makes mistakes, when thousands of people are constantly keeping an eye on what you do, I can't imagine it makes it easier to not make mistakes.]
Enough ranting, back on track (The community):
The game's community is suffering somewhat, people are leaving the community, not as many people are joining in, but it's still active. The blockland community has been saying that it's dying for the past couple of years now (really after the last update) and it's still got players online, daily. I will not deny that a large amount of the community can be rather rude for no reason, but I have met some great people who play this game and have formed lasting friendships from this game. In fact, about half of my entire steam friends list consists of people I met on blockland.
Conclusion:
Overall, this game is nice, definitely worth the $10 it is right now. I still think it's worth the $20 I got it for, but I wouldn't complain with half the price. It's a nice game if you like creating things, while having a laugh at silly glitches. I would not recommend this game to people that dislike building.

After endless (pun intended ;-) ) years searching of a game that would be better than Master of Orion 2, I came to a conclusion, that there is none. However other space strategies can be fun on their own merits and ES is one of them (but get the DLC, cause it makes the game a lot better).
The good stuff:
- good automation of colony management (needed in late game)
- enforced keeping of diplomacy treaties ("let's call cease fire, but gimme those 5 techs, 1 turn later, haha I changed my mind & I'll kill you anyway" - this doesn't work here)
- interesting background lore and story
- good variety of races (12), some quite unique
- big tech tree
- waging war costs money (literally, doing battle actions costs game cash, which has an interesting effect on strategy)
- pretty good AI opponents (they have problems with taking over systems on the lower skill levels though)
The bad stuff:
- lack of tactical battles (the DLC gives some nice new options for battles, but still they are very non-interactive)
- quite small array of ship design options (e.g. a ship can have only 1 of each kinetic, beam and missile weapons in 1 configuration each, can't have 2 different beam weapons)
- espionage doesn't exist (I think)
- not everything is covered by tutorial and the game manual
- rarely some bugs show up
Overall, a good game, worth playing.

TL,DR: Great idea, terrible implementation.
There is nothing that disappoints me more than lost potential. When I heard about this game, I loved the premise. Be an evil god! Leaping through the city, unleasing your unspeakable power on the hapless citizens! And sometimes, that's what I got. Most times however, what I got was a buggy, lazy, difficult-to-control mess.
I have some ideas what happened here. 1) The open world's so big, and there's so many missions and events and kaka, the designers didn't put all the effort they should have into polishing and playtesting. I can't help but contrast this game against something like Portal, that's small but perfectly tuned. I didn't expect THAT from Prototype, but I would have happily swapped a few missions and events for more time taken working the bugs out of the others. 2) From what I've read of other people's complaints, this is a really lazy port. The fact alone that this started as a console game explains some of my frustration, as there are simply too many options mapped to too few keys, leading to frequent raging when I meant to do one thing and something else happened.
I did finish the game. I finished nearly all of the events. And I'm not just calling a game bad because I sucked at it. In events where I actually felt like I was fighting NPCs instead of gameplay and glitches, I did fine. I got gold in most events, some on the first try. My frustration wasn't from lack of skill, but from things like...
*There are kill missions where you are supposed to use a certain weapon or power. Half the challenge is keeping the game from defaulting to kicking and jumping attacks that won't count towards your score.
*Sometimes no matter how much I selected the whipfist, I wouldn't transform into it. No other power had this problem (Until the final boss, where I kept getting locked into previous powers and being unable to change them for a minute or so).
*I beat an event with four seconds clearly left on the clock and it said I'd failed it.
*Watching my character destroy infected water towers, yet the game says they hatched before I did.
*Game gives you incorrect advice on how to proceed with a helicopter mission: "Hold TAB and flick mouse to select another detector"
*I lost track of the number of times NPCs killed off a Web Of Intrigue target before I could get to them. I lost an event MULTIPLE TIMES because of this.
*A Consume Event icon on my map; no event or marker in the area when I'm directly at the spot. Followed by a Consume Event marker floating in midair with no corresponding event.
*I consume a target in an event, the game says the target died and doesn't count it. I was IN the animation of consuming it!
*Accidentally hit escape during an event; this aborts the event instead of pausing the game.
*Targeting is gambling. Most of the time my attacks would hit just fine, but sometimes the game would decide that I'd much rather punch a helicopter than the Hunter I targeted.
*Sound was really low, even at the highest volume.
*Was supposed to protect a tank. Control was taken away from me while the game played a cutscene. During this cutscene, hunters attacked the tank and crippled it. I had absolutely no way to stop them.
*Boss battle against a Supreme Hunter. Suddenly "Objective Completed" without me having done anything, leaving me feeling cheated of a good fight.
*I had to kill 100 enemies for an event. At 99 kills, the game stopped producing NPCs so I lost the event.
*Timed kill event located in an area with tons of low fences, preventing me from getting to enemies or enemies getting to me.
*Frequently getting stuck inside tanks despite clicking 'E' tons of times.
*Lost a Movement event twice because the game suddenly put me in my armor, which meant I dropped out of parkour and lost precious seconds trying to get the armor off.
And you know what? I could forgive all of that, but the final straw was how TWO CUTSCENES THAT OCCUR DURING MISSIONS WILL CRASH THE GAME, MEANING YOU WILL HAVE TO START THOSE MISSIONS ALL OVER AGAIN AFTER YOU RESTART. The cutscene plays; fade to black; game is completely frozen. And it wasn't just me: I saw many, many people on many different websites describing the crash in The Stolen Body and Men Like Gods. Supposedly it's a corrupted audio file. It's unforgivable that this hasn't been patched by now.
So yeah, there were moments of occasional triumph. I liked a lot of the powers, the whipfist especially. when the game worked, it actually did feel pretty damn great. But those moments were rare. This was a game where 'flow' should have happened way, WAY more than it ever did. I got this for five bucks during a Steam sale and feel ripped off.
Also, I'm gonna be hearing those bedamned military alarm sirens in my sleep for weeks.
