Whether or not the game is worth it to you comes down to how late you were to the party. If you're a new recruit, this game may well appeal to you. At its base level, it's a solid shooter. Uninspired and stuffed full of really, really bad game modes, but solid. Killing 'Mechs is satisfying. Sticking with a team and working together is essential, and rewarding when things go well (they don't always, but that's all just part of the fun).
But if you're new you also won't know the extent of what has been lost. This game was once quite special. It was more than a "solid shooter." It was Mechwarrior - or at least, a game very nearly worthy of the Mechwarrior name. There was a lot of variety in the builds you could make. Tweaking 'Mechs between drops was a game within a game.
It was great fun if you allowed youself to ignore the "Min/Max" crowd. The various chassis were different in form and function, possessing "quirks" that made each and every one unique in some (mostly minor) way. The various weapons had their own strengths, weaknesses, and specific applications they excelled at. I've played this game since the beta. I must have logged hundreds upon hundreds of hours. I loved it.
All that, though? That's all been lost. The game has been cruising slowly towards homogeneity for years - now, finally, at long last MWO has achieved it. 'Mechs are no longer unique in the slightest. They're just configurations of weapon hardpoints that differ slightly in arrangement. They all handle the exact same way, and have the same speed ranges (light, medium, heavy, and super-slow assaults - read: missile bait). They no longer have weapon-specific quirks.
Speaking of weapons, they're all the same now too. That wasn't always the case. Now they're all differently-colored variations of the same damage-over-time track beam. That goes for projectile weapons, too. Everything is the same friggin' stream weapon with no variation or nuance whatsoever. That even somehow goes for missile weapons. EVERYTHING is - maddeningly - a damage-over-time stream, which is what the kids today call "balance." All you do is pick your color. Would you like it to be a blue laser, a green laser, or a yellow stream of p...missiles?
This is the biggest failure the game has brought to bear. The weapon classes were once distinct until forum dwellers somehow convinced the devs that anything not a damage-over-time stream was unfair. Heavy hitting projectile weapons featuring deflection and drop? Nah, forget about it. Make it a laser. They "balanced" the game by completely stripping it of all nuance.
And then there's the "skill tree" - their attempt to make up for the homogenized 'Mech chassis. It's your typical idiotic grind. Waste X hours so you can accrue enough Y to activate nodes on a grid so you can get +2% Z. Any 'Mech can be "anything" within the confines of this system, if you're willing to grind madly to do it. See, the game  used to be about convincing people to buy uniquely-designed 'Mechs. Now, apparently, they lack the talent/resources to crank out new chassis, so they're shifting away from that and now they've based the game upon convincing you to shell out to bypass the massive grind now that every unique chassis is just a blank slate tied to a skill tree.
If you're new, you also won't know the joy of having all your progress essentially wiped by the implementation of this skill tree system as I have. It used to be that they encouraged you to "max out" your chassis bonus by buying multiples of the same chassis type. Now all that's out the window, and all that grinding is essentially reset to make up for the new grind. Not relevant if you're new, but who's to say they won't simply flip a switch and do it again? It was really just a way to "restart" the game for the old guard and get everybody back to grinding and spending real cash in the absence of new content.
Oh, did I mention this game has been in a state of null development for YEARS now? Yeah, while the lead dev constantly threatens to terminate the project unless it proves to be a continual "viable revenue generator." Real passion for the project there, eh Russ? Par for the course, I guess, but it's notable because the developers have been trying to jump ship on this game multiple times in the past. When Star Citizen proved a flash in the pan, PGI jumped up and said "ME TOO! I WANT IN ON THAT!" with a kickstarter of their own, practically out of nowhere, comprised of hastily thrown-together concept art and promises of a huge universe to explore, yadda yadda. The backlash was so overwhelming, the pandering SO obvious, that they stuck their tail between their legs in shame and the space game project died quietly with no further mention.
Point? Simple. This game is just a job for the devs. A grind they don't really care about, and would obviously have done with if they got the opportunity. There is zero heart in this title - it's a shell without a soul. You'd have to have been there from the begnning to really understand just how bad MWO is compared to its much more colorful, much more nuanced original versions. I think the devs DID care back then. This was their job, after all. They needed it to succeed. But now that they've got what cash they could, it's obvious they simply no longer care. The forum dwellers (maybe 20 guys who live to complain about "balance") essentially run the game now, and patches are nothing more than numbers tweaks in the .xml made to cater to the whining of the vocal minority. The community is freaking awful, by the way. Don't you ever threaten THEIR game by complaining.
It's a terrible, terrible shame these fools have such a cherished IP in their hands. It really is.

MWO is a PvP-only game billed as a mech sim and more or less delivers on that promise. Some in the community would say it leans farther toward a slow-paced FPS than a giant walking tank simulator, YMMV. The gameplay itself is tight: wildly varing opinions on weapon and tech balance aside, things usually work as they're promised to and most things look/feel/move in a believeable way; most of the maps are "decent" though invisible assets due to lazy texturing can cause problems at times and many maps end up as a NASCAR race around a central object; there is a nice variety of weapons and mechs (though some chassies are locked behind a pay wall) so lots of opportunity to play around for casual players - there's a big tech update coming this Summer that will add to that variety.
If you're just trying things out, the initial free mechs are servicable but since you can't customize them you really need to put considerable time into the game before you can earn the money to buy your own and really get good value for your time. I wouldn't say this is a game that casual players will stick with long-term. The learning curve can be brutal (visit the official forums or Outreach HPG on Reddit for advice) and the grind daunting (this is a FTP game, after all). But if you're willing to put in the time to "get good" and also grind out the in-game currency to actually purchase and customize your mechs then MWO is a satisfying appetizer while Battletech/Mechwarrior fans wait for a more substantial entry in the series.
Ignoring the typical FTP game complaints, my biggest gripe about MWO is the lack of gameplay content. Currently the player population can chose between a Quickplay queue where available players are dropped into a 12v12 deathmatch and a Faction Play queue where players do almost the same thing as Quickplay but with marginally more lore-based reasoning - Faction Play is allegedly meant to represent the in-universe war over planet control. Although both queues contain sub-gametypes that are supposed to change up the battle style, most games just end up being death matches - there is usually little incentive to play for objectives in the objective-based gametypes. And it's been like this since the game's inception. The shooting aspect is mostly great, PGI has done a very nice job on that end despite their questionable decisions elsewhere, but shooting alone gets boring.
If it matters, the game also lacks connection to the Battletech lore. Not a big deal to some folks, but I would really enjoy more fluff. There are lore-based factions that you can join, and we fight over a map of the Inner Sphere in Faction Play, but that's about the extent of what PGI has put in. There's no flavor text accompanying mechs, planets, or factions and they've made no effort to include any lore in in-game events or official communications. I guess PGI has left that to the players who want to role play - it's pretty clear they don't care about it themselves unlike the folks at Harebrained Schemes (currently putting the finishing touches on a new Battletech strategy game). Keep in mind there is no single-player storymode so it's not as if they've stashed the lore elsewhere.
Gripes aside, MWO has good gameplay for people who like to shoot giant death machines with lasers and delivers a bare-bones Mechwarrior/Battletech experience on the side if you're willing to put in the time. You can get by without paying real money if you sitck around long-term, and there is an active albiet small community.

This is my all time favorite game. Bought it on the 360, beat it three times, and bought it again on the PC so I can play it some more. The loading times and graphics are far improved from 360, but the stuttering in between menus and dialogue options is really annoying. Nonetheless, this game is my favorite game of all time because it exceeds in almost every category that can be used to describe a piece of art.
1) Story - 10/10
2) Soundtrack - 10/10
3) Dialogue - 9/10
4)Ambient/Environmental Sounds - 8/10
5) Level design - 10/10
6) Locations - 10/10
7) Creativity/originality of the game world and its citizens- 10/10
8) Exploration/ traversal - 10/10
9) Variety of combat/use of environment 10/10
10) Length/replayability - 10/10
11) DLC - 9/10
12) RPG elements - 10/10
13) Side quests - 10/10
14) Game play mechanics/combat - 9/10
15) Difficulty - 10/10
Overall: 9.7/10 - the highest rating I have given a game
1) The story is full of twists and turns and has characters and events that you care about. Your actions have consequences and your choices feel like they are important, and sometimes difficult to make.
2) The soundtrack is one of the most brilliantly composed pieces of music I have ever heard in a game.
3) The dialogue of the main characters of the game is very well scripted and makes you think about what the characters say; however random citizens/civilians/enemies have pretty dull/boring dialogue in comparison.
4) Albiet having somewhat limited sounds, the environment and ambient noises are very convincing and make you feel like you are apart of the world.
5) The level design is very well fleshed out giving the player many different options on how to approach the situation, although stealth/hacking/exploration is usually the most rewarding.
6-9) The environments are rich and traversal is fun, with tons of things to discover, even in the smallest of environments. The locations you visit are gorgeous and creatively designed. The game world feels unique in a seemingly saturated genre. The combat and environment exploration is rich and diverse. There is NEVER only one path you can take. There is never only a single way to aproach any situation or combat instance.
10) The length of the story + side quests + DLC is very long ranging between 15-25 hours for a single play through. The replayability is amazing, due to the diverse level design; playing through a difficult area in one play through may be a breeze next play through due to a hidden area in the environment/dialogue option.
11) The DLC in this game is actually one of the best DLCs I have played, due to its ambition and its concept; rather than going for a generic DLC cash grab, it addresses a minor plot hole in the original game and fleshes it out into its own little story, then when finished, the game continues where the plot hole would have been unresolved before.
12-13) This game allows you to make Adam into the character you want him to be, specializing in things that interest you. I could see some of the side quests in this game being marketed as entirely separate DLC if this game were published in this day and age.
14) The mechanics and combat are very well designed and make the game have good variety in the way situations can be handled.
15) And finally, this game is tough as nails, especially on the "Give me Deus Ex" difficulty (how I recommend playing DE:HR). Adam is only a human and getting augmented did not just suddenly turn him into super bad♥♥♥♥♥who can take down crowds of people and tear apart rooms of machines. He is still human and will die in just a few shots if you're not careful.
Anyways, this game is worth purchasing to anybody interested in any of the aforementioned categories above.

I use this PS4 controller for a few games on Steam for this reason, but with the vast majority I use the Steam controller for its versitility.

TL:DR; Not for people with a short attention span - you need to commit to learn the game, around 2-5 hours. Though I still highly recommend it.
So here we have a 4X Space-Based Strategy game with about the same complexity of Civilization V (Base Game).
I highly recommend this game to anyone with some patience and the will to learn a new game, as Endless Space is not easy to jump right into.
The Tutorial is a series of text-based prompts with pictures; remeniscent of a wikipedia instead of an in-game tutorial, this coupled with a few 'ease-of-life' features (such as the Waypoint system) not being included in the tutorials make for an experience and a half when it comes to learning the game. Once you get the hang of the early game, however, everything else simply falls into place and all comes together. Between myself and my friends, we became competent in the game within 2-5 hours of playing (without the tutorial).
In terms of difficulty; Pirates tend to give people a hard time, but can be disabled in 'Game Settings' just before starting a new game. The AI controlled Empires unfortunately 'cheat' at higher levels, gaining bonuses to their entire economy which grows exponentially with difficulty. That being said; after playing against them for a while, you'll begin to notice patterns in their behaviour and countering the AI becomes trivial after a while.
Combat's not too complex; you do, after all, play the role of the Emperor. When 2 fleets clash, you're only able to select a 'battle action' for each of the 3 rounds. (Basically cards which give bonuses and negatives based on what your opponent chooses - some increase a specific defence, while others may empower your ships' weapons).
The game is pretty, cinematic battles which take place in rather stunning space-scapes, beautiful galaxy maps with subtle animations in the background, dynamic changes to planets based off of which anomalies befit it and how much population is on it.
Well, if you've read this far you're likely patient enough to learn and enjoy Endless Space, also thanks! Your dedication is appreciated!
Regardless, I beleive this game is most fun with a few friends, though most of the time I've played has been in singleplayer. I also Highly recommend Disharmony - Endless Space's only DLC, it adds a few features that really help the game among other things, as well as adding a couple more layers to combat.
P.S: In the Galaxy map, hold 'Ctrl', click on a system you own, click on another system (you don't have to own the second system); Congratulations! You just set a system waypoint, now whenever you create a ship in System A, it'll create a fleet as soon as it's done and move to System B.

Rush for Gold is your typical resource-gathering time management game with the most basic mechanics. It has no remarkable features, but that also means it is a harmlessly pleasant, enjoyable little casual title.
Gather food, wood, gold, and coal, then use these to clear obstacles or to build production buildings… this basic time management formula changed little over the years, and Rush for Gold: Alaska sure as heck does not want to mess around with it.
Using a tested and solid foundation has its merits: we know exactly what we are in for, even if we see most gameplay mechanics within the first few stages. The real strength lies in these said stages, because team created 40 fun and interesting levels where the nice layouts and small size help to keep the boring walking distances in check.
The clock can be rather unforgiving, especially with the somewhat slow resource production, but there are no penalties for using timeless/casual mode. I would recommend that mode anyway, since it helps to cement Rush for Gold as a modest, yet still entertaining casual game.
It's a simple but good time-management, with the option to play without time limit.

Rush for gold: Alaska is a cute (there's hardly any better word to describe it) time-management strategy game set in Alaska during the years of the Gold Rush. The game may look childish (actually it is :)), but that doesn't mean it can't be enjoyed by adults. Its difficulty is pretty well set and it does require some basic strategic planning skills.
According to the story (yes, there's one) we play as a young woman whose family business has gone bankrupt so she seeks fortune in Alaska, to find gold, in order to pay the creditors. Our first job is to help sorting out baggages at a train station (where everyone seem to have lost their stuff) and by doing so, we receive the recognition of the town mayor, who asks us to be his assistant and become the leader of the gold diggers.
The game consists of 2 major locations: the town overview, where we can decorate the settlement, which is just for show, there's no actual gameplay here and the mission area, where we have to perform various tasks. In these missions we have to collect a given amount of the 4 resources (gold, wood, food, coal) or build/repair a building within the time limit. These resources can be traded at the corresponding merchant (for example gold for food at the Indian tent). To each task we can assign workers, who return to the town hall after their job is finished. The number of our workers can be increased by spending food and naturally more workers mean more assignable duties. After a worker finished his task we have to manually collect the resource by moving the mouse cursor over it. That is not all however.
There are various risks and hazards, the main one being the time limit. As we progress, we receive several forms of aid which we can use once in a while: speeding up our workers' movement and efficiency, freezing time and also resource packages. The use of these helps are compulsory to get maximum amounts of stars for each mission (these function as ingame achievements and are also necessary to decorate the town). Also there are simple obstacles blocking our path which we have to remove: these vary from fallen over trees to hungry bears, all which require certain resources to get rid of. Wolves and bandits are the most dangerous of them all, they can scare the workers thus making us lose valuable time. Our heroine is the only one who can chase the wolfs and the bandits away with her revolvers (later on we can recruit a sheriff, he is the best in dealing with the convicts). It is rather strange though that a young woman has to protect the entire group from these dangers...
Everything is controlled by the mouse, there's no need to use the keyboard at all. The gameplay consist of clicking and moving the cursor on the right spot in the right moment basically. Of course as I said before, there's a minimal amount of strategy involved. Hint: the berries reproduce, so they are a constant source of food and therefore should be our primary target at the beginning of each mission.
My main problem with the game was that it becomes quite monotonous towards the end (even though the last mission does present us new elements). There are some bugs present, that can affect gameplay, like the one where we may lose precious materials, when our heroine is interrupted by wolfs or convicts, while she is on route to a trading post and the resources about to be traded has already been deducted from us. We can circumvent this however by always cleaning our path, right before conducting a trade. Likewise, another minor problem is that the resolution has to be manually reset every time after launching the game. Also there are some small grammatical errors.
There are 40 missions altogether, 10 for each season. All the maps have a different look according to the given season (in the winter scenario for example there's a quest where we have to clear the railroad from the snow). The graphics is cartoonish and of simplistic design, but the characters are well animated and funny looking, with beautiful, colorful scenery full of trees, flowers and waterfalls. The music is what you'd expect from a game like this: fitting westernish music, that'll most certainly cheer you up.
The game is one of those few cases that's entertaining for adults and small children alike. The fact that it's a casual game is both a blessing and a curse: I would have liked a bit more variety, but I also enjoyed it greatly as it used and combined the scarce elements it possesses. I would recommend it to anyone who'd like a quick relaxing experience within a cheerful and charming game.

Renegade Ops is one of those games you want to play when you got enough from complex mechanics and stories and simply want to have fun – this basically is a blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up simulator.
The whole story about a mad pyromaniac who wants to destroy the world, while you’re part of a squad which takes things in their own hands cause the governments are incompetent, is a pretty clear homage to some of the simple 80s + 90s action movies. Avalanche Studios themselves also have a reputation for over-the-top games – those guys developed the Just Cause series after all.
Honestly…there’s not much more worth to mention about the story: You follow the evil Inferno over the globe to sabotage all his plans and secret facilities. This mostly involves driving around and blowing stuff up – the plot is purposefully silly and simply works to give you a reason why exactly everything around you is exploding. In between missions you get comic-style cut-scenes which tell you what’s going on.
So let’s get to the main and most important part of the game: the shooting!
Equipped with a machine gun which gets stronger by collecting the blue weapon power-ups, you mow through groups of enemy infantry as well as all kinds of vehicles. For tougher enemies like tanks or the rare bosses you have a stronger secondary weapon: either rockets, a railgun or a flamethrower – in contrast to your main weapon, however, their ammo is limited and has to be replenished by collecting the red power-ups.
At your disposal stand a total of 5 vehicles (or rather: characters, which use different vehicles; you can even play as Gordon Freeman) which differ only in looks and special ability – they’re all equipped with a MG and can choose between the three special weapons. The mentioned abilities are for example a short time of invulnerability or an airstrike on nearby enemies; those can be quite handy in some situations. By leveling up your current character you unlock a couple of upgrades which for example increase your health, boost your special ability or let you start a level with one of the special weapons already equipped.
Sometimes the game also gives you a helicopter to control which, however, can’t be upgraded and is only used a few times in the whole game – usually you’re controlling your car, only.
Your main objective in pretty much every mission is: drive to a certain place on the map and destroy everything there (and on the way, ofc) – pretty straight-forward if you will. From time to time the game gives you (optional) side-objectives like freeing prisoners (by shooting at their cages) or collecting relics (by first shooting the boxes they’re in) – you see, great quest design here. These side-objectives usually only give you additional high-score points and rarely serve any other purpose.
The only times you need to employ something like strategy is when facing for example tanks which have a weak spot at the rear that can be exploited by circling around the vehicle OR of course in one of the few boss-fights. Though usually avoiding to get hit and simply holding down the left mouse button solves most problems – blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up is the main theme of the game after all.
As you can very clearly see by just watching some gameplay (or my video, *wink wink*): Renegade Ops is really great looking. You drive around in varying landscapes (the DLC adds snow maps) with lots of details and partly destructible environment (for example huts, fences n guard towers). Where the game really shines are the visual effects, starting with the dust-clouds while driving and of course ending with the explosions and fire effects caused by you blowing up enemies.
The sound effects are doing their part to make you feel pretty badass; the soundtrack and voice actors on the other hand are good, but nothing special.
In a couple of reviews here you will read about control issues – and yes, driving with the keyboard can be a little bit unintuitive. You can switch to “tank-controls” in the options which some people prefer – or use a gamepad but then suffer from less precise aiming. However, in my opinion it’s not “completely unplayable” as some people claim: after a few minutes you get used to the controls and shouldn’t have any major problems finishing the game with mouse n keyboard (which I did, and I’m still fine).
Well, Renegade Ops certainly isn’t a very deep game, there’s no great progression system, the story is pretty basic and you don’t have a wide variety of weapons to choose from.
But if all this doesn’t bother you and you just want some over-the-top action, this game probably is right up your alley – it’s simply a lot of mindless fun. If alone or in coop with up to three friends you drive around in great looking landscapes and blow stuff up while hearing cool one-liners and fighting an enemy which may be from one of the old James Bond movies: Crazy vehicles, world domination – or rather destruction – and hidden bases on ships and in mountains.
For fast and action-packed shootouts and highscore hunts, you should definitely pick-up Renegade Ops and enjoy the chaos.

Stunning graphics which while wearing headphones really make you feel like you are one with the environment.
Amazing sound fx and a killer soundtrack to keep you on your toes and pushing through.
Despite all of this, I am not playing on a ridiculous rig or anything and get stable fps.
Don't let the first couple missions fool you, there are so many secrets in this game it's almost silly.
The main character has some silent, quirky sass to him which makes the cutscenes a nice fun break from the brutality.
The option exists in game to monitor pretty much any part of your graphics unit without 3rd party tools.
I haven't tried it yet (still playing the campaign) but with their SnapMap mode you can make and publish, or play custom missions to keep this game feeling worth your money even after you have found everything in the base content.
Spoiler:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Cons:
=================================================================
If you are a casual gamer who enjoys shooters this game may be too fast paced.
It's just a bit of a nit-pick as it hasn't slowed me down yet, but the ledge grabbing doesn't always work and may lead you to believe an area is not traversable. Always pay attention to the map and keep trying if the area seems noteworthy.
The game has a PVP arena mode, however in my experience it has really put me off. I'm not saying everyone will hate it, but I wouldn't pick this up solely due to it being a feature.
Gameplay con spoiler:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I have yet to finish the campaign so I may update this review as I go, but as it stands right now this game is probably one of the best single player shooters I've played to date, and I would highly recommend anyone who is in the market for a good one grab this game. As well, as opposed to a lot of single player fps the gameplay in this title makes it quite the nice tool for sharpening and honing your fps aiming skills.

I've played many tycoon games. I like this game and finished the campaign for it. It's not difficult to win once you get a feel for what the different transport types can support and how to space them out to give good service(hint: try following a grid, <5 minutes round trip for any one line). It can be very relaxing, even when you're doing poorly, and there are plenty of options for setting up a complex network even without the DLC additions.
I have two issues with the game:
The first is that track and stop placement can be tedious and error-prone, depending on which type of transit you're working with. Although the majority of the time, you want your tram and trolley lines(which are built at street level) to either continue straight ahead or take a 90-degree bend, you have to carefully click each road segment and scroll each time, which, combined with the low visibility of these constructions, almost guarantees that you mess up and fail to link one of the segments and then have to go back and debug it when the game tells you the route can't reach a stop. There is no tool to simplify this construction phase, even though the game can adequately plan the entire route for you when you use buses on existing roads - so you may spend a LOT of time squinting and clicking. Similarly, when building underground roads or metro lines, there is no way to view through the roads, which means that when you go to add stops, you have to either work extremely hard to position the camera to see through a road, build around the road, or tear up the road and add it again.
A lazy player is going to want to build only buses, watertaxis and underground metros that consciously avoid overlapping the road.
The second problem is with the city growth model. To induce growth, all a player has to do is build new roads with sidewalks, and improve overall transit service. The player doesn't get any control over what types of zones appear, even though they're relevant to decisions about transit scheduling and peak service. This makes city growth feel very "one size fits all" - the growth is generic so you have to build generically - and since you can add roads anywhere that the terrain will fit, the simplest growth strategy is rinse-and-repeat: build a new metro line, and build roads on top of it. When I discovered this it  detracted from any sense of individual character amongst cities. Growth can be turned off, at the expense of making the game feel more like a static "fill in the blanks" exercise.

This is an amazing game that uses blocks and events to build games within the game. I started playing about eight years ago and probably had over 1000 hours before the game hit steam. One of the things that upset me about the game was that RTB (return to blockland) was shut down.
Return to blockland was an ingame overlay type system (similar to steam). It had a large add-on (mod) system that would allow you to download any add on you liked without having to leave the game. It basically served in the same way the workshop works in garry's mod.
With the shut down, blockland gradually declined. There is a great community still in the game but, you would find it difficult to find a time when there are 100+ players on the servers.
However, someone made an RTB replacement named Blockland Glass. The system has most of the features of RTB (and some RTB did not) and contains an RTB archive of all those add ons that can no longer be found on the blockland forums.
The game is pretty old at this point being around 10 years, but that means that it can run on some very old computers. Because of this, the game is great for playing with friend sas even friends with near aweful computers will be able to run it smoothly (with shaders off).
On top of that, the game does not require port forwarding to host an online server. This means that you and your friends can host and build your own online server for free (if you and them have the game).

I will admit, I am a slight sadist and evil when it comes to games like this. If it involves doing some very cruel things for fun like assimilating others into your memories to accumulate more knowledge and power, then I'll do it without hesitation.
This game is for those like me. Those who need a wide open area, a neat selection of awesome powers to pull off various ways of killing enemies and a whole lot of time!
The selection includes:
Whiplash - Whip your enemies and tear them in half, cling onto helicopters and pull yourself to them or hit them several times from far away even while in mid-air and cause them to plummet to their doom.
Musclemass - Wanna play more normally, on foot, beat the living snot out of people and send them flying? You can do just that and plenty more!
Hammerfists - Pounding things into the ground sound like your style? Send tanks into the concrete with each smash? Do an elbow drop from several feet high and do devastating damage when you land? This is the one for you!
Blade -  Sever your enemies in a clean half, swing your blade around and around, tearing those apart around you, sending heads and limbs alike flying.
That was just the abilities you can use. You can do so much more like:
Thermal vision - See enemies through smoke and obstacles at the expense of decreased vision range.
Infected vision - Highlight those with the BLACKLIGHT virus as well as military units.
Keep in mind it muffles all your other senses like hearing in order to focus on his sight.
You can also disguise! Assimilating others will not only restore your health but you will take on their appearance! Convert into an everyday citizen or even the military! Act inconspicuous amongst the enemy, take down important targets, stay out of their sight and certain equipment and they won't even know you're there!
One offensive and defensive power may be active at a time. Using any of your powers while disguised completely negates the current disguise.
There's also a really fun mechanic called Devastators. You need to be in Critical Mass (a state of almost dead or the complete opposite, having excess stored biomass and increased health). They include:
- Tendril Barrage: Fires impaling tendrils from your body in all directions.
- Groundspike Graveyard: Erupts massive spikes from the ground all around you.
- Critical Pain: A single beam of hardened biomass protrudes from your hands to severely damage a single target.
While you sprint, you automatically hop over cars, barriers and other obstacles without loss of momentum. You will also knock any humanoids aside without stopping if they get in your way.

Prototype is a game that I mostly consider very underrated that has unfortunately been long forgotten by the press and players alike. It's a very good example of a game that comes across as very generic but subverts your expectations.
You play as Alex Mercer, a man seemingly infected with a virus that allows him to shapeshift and consume people. He starts out having amnesia and for the first half of the game comes across as extremely edgy. The characters and dialogue are very hamfisted and the scenarios the game throws at you are ridiculous to the point of being absurd.
However during the second half the writing starts to become more clever. The protagonist has a very noticeable character arc that I grew to like, and the general progression of the game from this seemingly pristine city to a demonic hellish Manhattan really gripped me a great deal. This weaved very nicely with the gameplay.
Prototype isn't a game that aged very well, and was pretty antiquated even when it first game out. Realism is thrown completely out the window as you regularly fly across cityscapes, run into npcs and absorb them into your body, and grow giant swords out of your arms to destroy tanks. It also hasn't aged very well graphically. However the controls are very flowy and I greatly enjoyed exploring the world. I also enjoyed how the player's powers upgrade gradually as you consume more people and found it appealed to my very morbid sense of humor. It also features a neat New Game plus mode.
Regardless, I recognize a lot of what I like Prototype for is very subjective. Objectively it's a very average game, and not one people are going to really remember 10 years from now. But it's still a game I like, and if you can find it for very cheap on sale you'll find a very charming sandbox game. Not the best but certainly not the worst.

Rush for Gold: Alaska is not the first game in the franchise. The first game in this franchise is Rush for Gold: California which is available for free from Microsoft's store. I would suggest that before you purchase Alaska, even at it's cheap price, that you give the free California game a play and then if you like it go ahead with purchasing this game.
AINSLIE'S LITTLE PEARLS
This is a cute little task orientated game where you are out to help your family all the while improving the little town in Alaska. The drive to help keeps you wanting to complete the next task. I enjoyed sending the workers from one task to the next, discovering gold, scaring off the wildlife and meeting new people who help improve the town.  The graphics are quite basic, but add to the charm of the game. The interaction and game play mechanics are quite simple but this makes for ease of task completion and game progression.  I believe you could complete this game quite easily if you are a competent gamer, for a new gamer it is an easy starting point.  It is a game I will to back to as a fun little break or escape time.
Rush for Gold: Alaska is a charming little casual game that is suitable for all ages and audiences. It's perhaps a little too basic for experienced gamers but a good entry point for those new to video games.

I bought this alongside Xcom 2 (Although didn't use it for that game). So here is a rambling of some thoughts after having it for over a year.
Quicknotes:
- It can be as simple or complex as you like to configure.
- Countless customisation options, completely unrivaled in that aspect. If you can think it, you can probably bind it (not limited by buttons, can have layers of controls).
- Frequently updated with more options and fixes
- Requires Big Picture mode unfortunately
- Controls feels light but weighted well by batteries in each handle, very comfortable in large hands, accurate and pleasant anologue and touchpads. (Feels and has proven to be durable despite light plastic).
- LOUD. Clicking things is loud with this controller, but it is a small price to pay.
I mostly use this controller for emulators (you will not find a better control for emulators), there is nothing better thanks to its practically unlimited options. You can bind it any way you like. I also used the game for Dark Souls where the paddles were great for quick actions and allow you to avoid moving thumb for face buttons in a lot of games.
Gyro is great fun for racing and shooting. Swiveling around on your deskchair to line up a sniper is incredibly satisfying. Gyro is altogether a fantastic feature.
I don't use the controller all that option since I play competitive shooters a bit, but when I do I wholeheartedly love it.

This is a controller for PC gamers. If you're the kind of person who doesn't like tweaking things around, if you only like simple plug and play, you won't like it. Go back to your console stuff.
Now that all those people who've never built a PC in their life are gone, let's talk about the Steam controller.
It's a little odd at first, but I got used to the steam controller in no time playing Dark Souls 3 with it. You just have to find the configuration settings that work for you! The customization is exactly what I look for in a controller for PC.
This thing is even great for emulation once you set the emulators to launch from steam and program the controller inputs to be from a 360 controller. You can do this using the built in steam controller configuration. You can do control profiles for each individual program, allowing you to play everything with no work after the initial setup!
It's a good controller and I suggest you give it a try.

I understand that after time Hartman would have wanted to move onto new projects, but in its current state the game feels almost incomplete. I want to recommend this game, as it was a personal favourite once-upon-a-time, but it's now a poorly managed mess.

After hours and hours of playing, I've changed my mind. This game is definitely worth $20. It has it's flaws but when compared to Sim City it really does shine in a way that forgives it of it's problems.
=== The GOOD ===
- Real traffic, real pedestrians, and their AI actually calculate's their travel all over the map. You don't have to wait in an area to see the traffic and pedestrians build up. You can zoom into a neighborhood and immediately see all the traffic. The city feels extremely lively. The masses feel real.
- Beautiful game.
- HUGE cities.
- Lots of detail.
- Great frame rate.
- Satisfying.
- Extremely unbalanced. But that's ok because you can use the "Rule Editor" in the Tools menu to change the capacity of all the vehicles, change the break down times, change how fast they are fixed in the repair shops, how many residents the city has, EVERYTHING. So you can re-balance your game however you like.
- I increased the city population density by 500% and it was awesome! You need to have an extremely good PC because the game calculates each and every person's commute. I increased the capacity of trams to 200 people per tram (more realistic) and 600 people per metro train so it's more realistic and the whole game just got so much more fun. I had 2,000 people waiting at my busiest transit stations. I was so happy. It was everything sim city should have been.
=== The Problems ===
- My game crashes every hour. there's no auto save. But it does not crash on my brothers computer.
- You can't upgrade current roads, you have to bulldoze them and when laying down the new road, if you curve or are off by 1 pixel the buildings around will be destroyed and you can't get them back.
- There's no "undo" option. So if you accidentally destroy a building or are having trouble with rail connections (and you will a lot) you have to bulldoze everything and start over.
- Trams can no longer do U-Turns on avenues like they used to.
- The addition of depots is extremely limiting. ALL buses, metros, trams must start out and end at the same depot. So no more little bus routes.
The team worked really hard on this game, and the assets are top notch. I feel like just 2 more years of development and this game can be fleshed out into a serious Sim City Competitor. If you have problems with the umbalanced gameplay, low vehicle capacity, short break down times, just change the stats in the Rule Editor and game on.

New players beware. This game has no ranking system; so you're not going to be dropping into your first battle with other newbs, you're going straight into the meat grinder with all the YouTubers and pro gamers whose videos made you want to play the game in the first place. You will get stomped, you will die, and it is going to be infuriating when you spend a long time grinding your way through match after match to work up enough c-bills to buy that mech you really wanted just to have its center torso blown out from halfway across the map as soon as you cross the first ridge.
If you're thinking to yourself, "Gee, Beiro, I think you just suck. I could probably learn from my 30 second bursts of playtime between loading screens and maybe even accidentally get a kill once a month!" then I've got to burst your bubble. Not only is the game completely unable to accomodate new players in any way, it is also riddled with bugs. What could be worse than your favorite mech getting chewed to sawdust as soon as you come within line of sight of the enemy (if you're lucky enough to even see them)? Respawning with the mech select screen stuck, making you either a juicy target for deathmatches, or a useless weight on your team for objective games. Either way, you're going to be bored and frustrated while waiting for 3-15 minutes for the issue to resolve itself (because despite it being an issue for over a year, there is still no actual fix for it), or for some good Samaritan to come by and put you out of your misery so that you can try to respawn again (and pray that it doesn't happen again).
If this still sounds like something you want to play, go for it. It is a great looking game, and the mechs are beautiful. The mechs and the weapons feel like multi-ton death machines with horrifying amounts of firepower, which is exactly what you want in a MechWarrior or BattleTech game. However, because of the glaring issues facing new players with low-end machines and standard internet speeds, I'll be sticking to YouTube videos and Hare Brained Schemes BattleTech Beta for my BattleTech itch.

I am posting a "recommend", but with a big caveat, which I will discuss at the end of the review.
The plus side is that Endless Space has the elements of  a good 4x, turn based strategy game set in space.   Ships are customizable to large extent, though without any visual customization;  it can be argued that this is only cosmetic, so having no impact on game-play.   Many choices are available for star system development and a few for individual planet development.   Combat is a variation on rock-paper-scissors with both long/medium/short range choices and missile/beam/kinetic weapons - while the combat takes place in four stages with set-up and long/medium/short combat resolutions.   So there is some "action" to be pondered during combat.  There are many discoveries to be made while exploring and deciding on where and how fast to expand.   The research "tree" - it is actually more of a "web" - leaves many choices that make reasearch interesting.    Empire development allows for setting tax rates which impact global and local happiness;   each star system can build either planet specific "explotations" or system wide choices.  Heroes are also available and can be leveled up in different ways as either planet admiinistrators or fleet leaders.   In short, there is a lot to play with in this game that is fun and the choices are meaningful.
Now for the caveat.   The tutorial, though necessary, barely scrapes the surface of what to do.  It basically just shows a quick run through on the interface.   Further, to get these hints you need to set tutorial mode on and then blunder into a situation where the game deems it necessary to explain a new part of the interface.   You can play a long time before this happens - and of course you will then say, "wish I knew about that earlier!".   Oh well.    The biggest caveat I have, however, is the research.    As you try to learn the game you can mouse over various choices to read about what is research item is.   However, although you will then get a name of the research, a list of items unlocked by pursuing it, and a description of the research, these three items very seldom give you ANY idea of what the research does.  The textual explanations are just gobbledegook that explain nothing.  For example, from the start you will want to know what to research to improve happiness.   You will get zero help even after spending a ton of time mousing over choices.   You can try searching for a tech, but I found this to be of little use.  You have to know the name of  a tech that you won't know in order to find it.    Now, you can get help by using google and reading hints by people who have figured things out the hard way.    Still, I found the whole business very frustrating.   And I have to ask how hard it would be to actually make the tech descriptions useful, using words like "happiness" or "kinetic boost", etc. instead of useless garbage, and allowing searches for such words instead of just titles that you don't know.
So in summary if you are willing to put in the effort to overcome this limitation there is a decent 4x space game here. If.
-----------------------------
As seen in the discussion below, there is considerably more information available on research than I originally indicated by my review.     Simply zooming in on the research screen shows the game effects of each research node.    And I noted that this fact is suggested in the manual if one takes the time to read it carefully.    Thus the "major caveat" becomes a "minor quible" as the "flavor text" is still useless and the reseach titles are still misleading.   Nevertheless the game is far more playable than I suggested.
And I am now playing  and having fun with this title.   Mea culpa, and thanks to MTB-Fritz for correcting me.

Endless Space is a a very satisfying entry in the 4x genre.
In generalities of 4x - it's a turn based genre where you explore a grid, find juicy spots to expand your empire, research new technologies that can do all sorts of neat things. And of course there are up to 7 other races/species/civilizations doing the exact same thing and when you come into contact there can be peace, trade, and friendship - or lasers, bombs, and death.
What really distinguishes Endless Space from games like Civ is a more dynamic and challenging AI. The AI is aggressive, but rational. You can generally tell almost exactly when an AI is going to declare war on you just using common sense - they spot some sweet weak spots in your territory, they're running out of territory and you border them (and are weak), and so on. And the AI is very challenging, but fair. Some games like civ cheat during the game to keep the AI competitive. So for instance if you're far up on technology the AI will simply start granting itself new technologies for free to keep up. You won't see that in this game. The AI on higher difficulties gets boosts to his rates of production, but otherwise plays by the exact same rules as you. This opens up lots of fun and dynamic possibilities. For instance advanced ships require various sorts of unique materials for production. Cut off an opponent's source of this material and you can bring his military industrial complex to a screeching halt.
The big downside of the game is in the combat system. While ship design and fleet organization is a lot of fun and very interesting - combat itself comes down to picking from some relatively uninteresting cards which come down to a frustrating and boring system of roshambo or paper, rock, scissors. Another small issue is a lack of polish. The in game skill tree for the heroes is incorrect and outdated, and there are various little annoying bugs. For instance if you alt-tab in the game, the game will consider alt as being constantly pressed. All you need to do is press alt again to fix this, but the lack of polish here and there really adds up.
That said I think this game has already overtaken Civilization and there are many ways it could be greatly improved and expanded upon. I'd strongly recommend this title and I expect to see more great things from this series with Endless Space 2.

A very interesting game that this is, but as often as these kinds of games are, it is a grind.
First and foremost I want to say that is that this game is great for those who have an interest in wanting to either learn about guns and how they function or people who want to learn how to disassemble and reassemble them. I have to give props to the devs for amount of effort that they put in to get all the little things about each gun in, giving the name of each part, and showing how much is into each gun. I imagine that it was a lot of research and experience that went into this and that the devs put a lot of care into fully replicating each gun.
I also do like that the game has more than just disassembling and assembling guns. I like that you are given a regular field strip of each gun, Operation and seeing how each gun operates and even giving inside and slowdown looks of how it works, to also quizes testing your knowledge of gun models and a puzzle where you are given 2 guns and have to match parts to the guns. For someone like me, this is a bit of a challenging game as I know nearly nothing on how guns work outside of loading and shooting them.
Now for as basic as this game is, it does a great job. However, I do have a few complaints about the game, some are nitpicks. First is that this game, for someone like me, can get boring fast. Honestly I don't think that there is anyway around that. Again, if you have a faciniation on guns and how they work and how to take apart and put them back together, this game won't get as quickly as boring as quick as it did for me. Granted that there are vehicles and skeletons to change it up a bit, but that leads to one of my nitpicks in that I find it weird that for a game called "World of Guns: Gun Diassembly" there are cars, motorcycles, tanks, and skeletons. I won't know why they are there, the devs know, not me, but it's just weird that they are there. Another thing is that just like with a lot of Free-to-Play games, this game is also a victim to grinding. While for some guns it can be very fast to get them, some will feel like an eternity. Granted that there are quizzes to help speed this up, but you'll be going through a lot of disassembling and reassembling to get some guns that are your favorites or want to try. This also leads to the credits. I get it, this is a free-to-play game and devs have to make some money somehow from this and in this case it's access to some guns, all guns, and credits. There are ways to earn credits in game, but it's a 1 per gun basis and unless you are really smart and fast, good luck getting the one achievement from each gun that nets you one single credit. There are some other things you can do to earn at least 20 of them, but that's just 20 and it's also a one time for your account. I would like to see some alternate ways to get credits, like login for certain amount of days or something like a random chance a day to get some credits. It is a minor thing though given how many more guns there are that you don't need credits to unlock.
In all it is hard to recommend this game especially with how fast it can get boring, but in the end this game isn't going to fit to everyone's taste just like every game and this game definitely will appear to some select tastes. Here's how I would recommend this game. I would recommend this game if you are really into or have an interest in guns, want to learn how they function, and/or want to learn how to take them apart little by little and put them back together. I know that I said that like 3 times during this, but what else could I say? Although keep in mind that depending on how much you are interested in guns is how much you'll enjoy this game and how fast it will get boring to you. This game is great for those people and it does what it does right. I can also somewhat recommend this to people who want to learn about vehicles, tanks, skeletons, and motocycles since this game does have them for an odd reason. I honestly can't recommend this to anyone outside of that.

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly surprised me. This is not a traditional game in any sense of the word. You are tested on memory and knowledge of guns here. How quickly you can disassemble and reassemble a variety of firearms is the main appeal, but the leaderboards help keep things competitive. The addition of X-ray, cutaway and slow-motion options greatly enhance this game and are incredibly detailed and fun to utilize. With a wealth of features and guns available, the only downside(s) I have found so far are that the UI is a bit cluttered, but this is an easy fix as you can hide the friends list and side bars; and the fact that there are so many guns that I am not able to get yet because of the high cost to get all of them.
Definite recommend if you are interested in firearms, curious about how they work, how to build or disassemble one; or just want to check out something very different than your atypical game.

When I play a videogame (regardless of genre), I expect it to grab me by the arms and drag me into it's world. I want to be fully engrossed in it's universe, story, and gameplay.
Personally, 8BitMMO did none of this for me.
Now, I realize I didn't play this game for very long. I plan to play more of it in the coming days, to really give it a fair shot. I also realize that the focus of this game leans more towards user created content then a narrative-heavy experience. I GET that. But what 8BitMMo is supposed to do, it doesn't seem to do particularly well. It just hasn't made a great impression so far.
PROS:
--Somewhat clever sense of humor
--Relatively empty servers
--Easy to pick up and play
--Does not require an email address to play
Cons:
--World-building, an already slow and unintersting affair (and unfortunately the whole point of the game), is made more difficult via microtransactions.
--Gameplay is fundamentally oversimplified, and not very interesting as a result.
--Quests lack challenge and variety
--Performance issues-notably server lag.
It's just hard to reccomend an MMO like this when there are so many better experiences available.

This is mainly my own opinion but I will try to make observations that will help new players understand what the game is like.
First, this game is magnificient for many reasons:
-PROS-
-Movement physics are extremely immersive (Especially if you're playing on a bigger screen) and I often find myself leanign my entire body over in real life while trying to make in-game maneuvers. This thrill doesn't wear off, it can sometimes almsot tricks your body into thinking that you are actually skiing.
-Weapon physics (minus sniper rifles and some of the weapons with fast bullet speeds) are really fun and there are a variety of physical variables that come with each weapon.
-Team playing and communication are usually great, there is a easy-to-use library of voice chat keyboard shortcuts to alert teamates to enemies or objectives.
-Maps accomodate both the high-speed freedom of movement and close-quarters combat in some areas.
-Equipment is balanced compared to other games: All weapons have pros and cons, and someone who's payed for all weapons isn't automaticlly good at the game. Skill is more valuable than equipment.
Now, there are a few things that make the game not as amazing as it could be...
-CONS-
-The class system sometimes seems like an "Easy, Medium, Hard" setting, since heavier classes get more health and damage. While lighter classes have more speed and agility, it is easier to get more kills and whatnot in heavier classes if one does not have very much skill. This casues many players to play as heavy only because other people are playing as heavies and killing them in 1-2 hits whereas lights take at least 3 or 4 hits to kill a heavy. However, it does make the light class more rewarding as skills develop.
-The amount of health that the heavy class gets compared to other classes is worth mentioning again on it's own. But that's just my opinion.
-People with extreme accuracy (whether it is their mouse equipment or possible cheating) can use the "hitscan" weapons to get kills for far less effort than with other weapons. These are mainly just the sniper rifles. I don't mind them as much because I find it fun using the stealth pack to sneak up and melee kill them, but many players find them annoying and I hear lots of compaining.
-The mechanics of the game are unique, which is what makes it so good. But because not as many people are playing now, most of the players are extremely skilled. This makes getting accustomed to the gameplay difficult, as noobs wil find themselved being killed easily even in servers with a level cap. DON'T LET THIS STOP YOU FROM PLAYING THIS AWESOME GAME THOUGH! It is still very rewarding when you get the hang of it.
-There are very few servers left. It makes me fear how much longer the game will be able to stay around.
I say 9.9 out of 10 because there's so many little tweaks that could optimize the experience, but it's still already one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.

The steam controller is perfect for playing many games which are traditionally "mouse required" games on the couch.
I've been a PC gamer for my entire life. I didn't start playing anything on consoles until about the last 4ish years... but I've gamed on PC for as long as I've been alive. Because of this, while I am quite comfortable playing games with a controller, there's something about playing with a keyboard and mouse that makes games feel more "real" to me.
Well this controller has managed to extend that "real" onto the couch. The mousepad-like joystick control makes me feel like I'm using a mouse, all while fitting in the palm of my hand. The haptic feedback also makes it really feel like you're moving some mechanical part around.
I would highly recommend this for traditionally PC gamers who want to play games on the couch. If you've played console games most of your life, it will take a bit more getting used to, but there's still no better way to play games like Civilization on the couch.

I remember when I first got the steam controller and booted up the Tomb Raider 2013 reboot and hated it. I almost wanted to refund it but I gave it some time.
After a month using it I got the hang of it, then after 3 months I started liking it. Now having the controller for about 5-6 months it's legitimately my favorite controller.
Let me get some of the cons out of the way:
- Steep Learning curve
- The build quality feels a bit cheap with all the plastic and hollow clicking sounds
- The shoulder button have an uncomfortable design
About 85% of my PC gaming is on this controller, and I play at my desk where KB/M is readily available. The amount of configuration is astounding, and there's only a few small features missing for more advance users.
The games I don't use it for are anything competitive, whether it be League or Overwatch. You can use it, and I've seen great configs, but the learning curve of it on top of a competitive game is too much for very little gain, if any.
I also don't use it for any game that NEEDS a solid dpad, usually a lot more retro games where I get a lot of mileage out of my Wii U Pro controller's solid Dpad.
Every other game i use this controller for: RPGs like the witcher, racing games, 1st and 3rd person shooters, etc. It's also a beautiful controller for Wii and DS emulation, a lot of the motion controls/ touch screen map perfectly to it, I was able to make a super optimized config for the Metroid Prime Trilogy that feels better to play than the original game.
The back paddles / grips are another major selling point for this controller. Being able to map 2 extra buttons to where your ring finger and pinky rest is amazing. It allows for you to aim and move while retaining some functionality of the face buttons (or whatever you map it to). This means you can move, jump, and aim all at the same time for example. Even if you just want a regular controller this works great because other controllers with back paddles/grips are very expensive like scuff controllers or the Xbox One Elite Controller.
The steam controller is the heart and soul of PC gaming. It's a controller that lets you go beyond the boundaries of what the original game developers created.

Score: 6.75 Naruto runs out of 10
Oh boy, another Naruto game. Where to begin?
INTRODUCTION (oh, there...)
As someone who has been an avid fan of the Naruto anime series and most Naruto games (mainly the Clash of Ninja series of Naruto games), I thought I'd give this game a try. Naruto has never failed me before, so why would it now?
STORY (potential spoilers? Read at own risk.)
So if anyone has played through the past Naruto games or even paid attention to the Shippuden series, they would understand a few things.
This game starts WAYYYYYYYYY in the past of the lore, then jumps WAYYYY forward into pretty much the end of the Shippuden series. Naturally, that fact right there is enough to veer people away. Don't be afraid of that! Most things missed sure are great to, well, not miss, but that doesn't make the story any less interesting. Hell, I hadn't even known how the series ended myself. The story to someone new to the series is not the greatest, but to an experienced consumer of Naruto content, it's like a pipedream.
CHARACTERS
What's the big problem with them? Well, it's more of a pet peeve of mine, really. THEY GIVE YOU TOO MANY CHARACTER FROM THE VERY BEGINNING! Honestly, they basically handed you the game with like 95% of the characters unlocked (not including the plethora of OTHER characters you can get from the DLCs). I checked even before opening the Story Mode because knowing I could earn and/or purchase characters from playing the game always appealed to me. I was appalled to be honest, and almost turned off by the game entirely. I went a step further, in fact, and looked at the store to see what was available there too. The Items available via the shop were all seemingly worthless vanity cards and in-game "ninja tools" that don't attribute much of anything toward the actual game. Big disappointment to me. I moved on to the game disheartened but still excited.
GAMEPLAY
Because I'm like any NORMAL person playing a Naruto game, I went to play the Story Mode before even learning how to play the game from tutorials. I was too excited to play and, to be honest, the tutorial was too hard to even locate at first that I didn't even care to try it after I found it. So there I was, first mission of the Story Mode, and I was already enamored with it. It started out hard as hell, Madara constantly kicking the ever-living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me for about 20 seconds. I was lost. At that moment I picked up my controller like any good player of fighting games and spammed buttons wildly. eventually I was able to discern what buttons did what for the most part and defeat Madara. That was when the game threw me into yet another battle fighting as ♥♥♥♥ing monsters n♥♥♥♥♥♥ While it made sense in the story, the game kinda got boring there, in that battle. That started a trend for me.
It got super repetitive sometimes, and not in a good way. The gameplay was ♥♥♥♥ing fun, don't get me wrong, but it felt a little lackluster compared to previous Naruto games I had played. Some parts of the story had me full of excitement, while other times I was practically combo-locked by the enemy. Speaking of locked, be careful when attempting to attack enemies, because getting out of those attack animations [that take ages] will often get you attacked instead. Those moments turned playing into an infuriating task that was made even worse when pressure of wanting an S-rank on every mission was on the back of your mind. This game also deals with chakra and other staple functions of Naruto games in a way I'm still not entirely used to, and that was a turn-off too. Not to mention, with only one attack button things got stale fast.
No wonder they threw so many characters at me.
One final gameplay problem that practically everyone notices in this game is the lack of in-game performance over 30 Frames per second. It is honestly a disgusting thing to have to deal with, as it makes the game seem sluggish and easier to be caught in a situation where you know you're screwed but have to sit through it for longer than you'd like. I know I don't have the best rig, but this kind of issue should still not happen in EVERY SINGLE MATCH.
ADVENTURE MODE
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ from a lore standpoint, this was an amazing idea. From a gameplay standpoint, it needs lots of work. Let it be known I have not played all of the chapters or whatever they're called in the Adventure mode, but from what I could see it had many good things and even more bad things to be said about it.
PROS
- The idea of post-story mode just makes you wanna scream with excitement
- It's semi-open world
- You can destroy♥♥♥♥♥♥br>- You can perform side-quests and main-quests that add purpose to destroying those ♥♥♥♥ing birds and stealing their sweet coinage
CONS
- Many quests end up being tedious attempts from the Devs to show off the world of Naruto
- LOTS of backtracking
- It's like 30 FPS PERMANENTLY, meaning that even while running you look like you're in slow-motion
- Most of the quests are less interesting than just breaking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of boxes and barrels
- Flashback Fever (though I guess Naruto is like, 30% flashbacks anyway, right?)
- Voice actors only say one or two words per speech bubble. For instance: Naruto says "Hinata, why the ♥♥♥♥ do you keep stalking me you creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥?" What the Naruto voice actor says "HI! :D"
I don't think I could ever convince myself to return to the Adventure Mode.
ROAD TO BORUTO DLC
Keep in mind this is DLC, so it'll cost you extra. It's worth it.
Though it suffers similar problems as the rest of the game (30 FPS WHY), It makes many practical improvements so I don't constantly grit my teeth and desire the slow, warm, and yet still inviting embrace of death. This "mode" is basically a mix of Story Mode, Adventure Mode, and the fighting portions of the game. They somehow made Adventure Mode's layout bearable. Though I move slow as♥♥♥♥♥♥ there's plenty to do while exploring the world where it doesn't feel like a forced field trip through the Village Hidden in the Leaves. Boruto is a ♥♥♥♥ing idiot, but still somehow likeable. The characters are overall well represented in the expansion, and the fighting is still mega fun. I just wish it had more Boruto stuff in it to be perfectly honest, but maybe the Devs are planning a Boruto standalone game?
ONLINE PLAY
I've only ever played with a friend, but DAMN WAS IT FUN! It was fairly easy to start up a game and subsequently invite my friend to play. The game was often times impossible to understand what was going on, but I guess that kinda added to the excitement. It felt very VERY different from squaring off against CPUs in Story Mode. My biggest (and possibly only) annoyance with Online Play was that as soon as you and a friend whom both have working microphones join a game together, they automatically turn on in in-game chat. As someone who engages in conversation with most of my compadres in an external VOIP like Discord, this displeased me. I was unable to find out how exactly to turn off the in-game voice chat, so I kept hearing my friend once more than I'd have liked to whilst we were exchanging competitive banter. It wasn't terrible though, but it had certainly altered my experience to a less pleasurable one. If there is in fact a way to turn off that function, it's WAY too hard to locate and turn off casually. I hope that somehow changes if possible.
tl;dr: This game is ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful and you should buy it, even though it does have a handful of problems with it. Both old-school AND new Naruto fans can enjoy easily.
Final Rating: 6.75/10

I have been playing MWO on and off since the Closed Beta Phase, having taken a substantial break from the game I recently made my return thanks to a friend.
The engine which the game utilises is far from perfect. It is capable of delivering reasonably nice graphics, however, it is a resource hungry engine.
Steep learning curve. MWO offers an incredibly deep experience which isn't well explained ingame. The tutorial explains some of the basic principles in relation to movement, shooting and some of the basic mechanics. The tutorial is far from exhaustive and fails to convey critical information, it simply gives you a push into the deep end.
Match making. MWO has two game modes, "Quick Play" and "Faction Warfare". Quick play utilises a match making system which often fails to provide balanced matches, the match maker is still being worked on by PGI and they are attempting to improve it. Faction Warfare does not use match making as it is intended, primarily, for units (Clans/Guilds).
Balance. The balance within MWO is less than perfect, part of this is a result of the source material / era which the game is set in. At present the game is set during the Clan Invasion when the Inner Sphere were at a technological and martial disadvantage throughout the majority of the conflict. The table top iteration of Battletech (MWO's progenitor) was balanced asymmetrically but this hasn't necessarily translated into MWO. At present balance is the best it has been for quite some time and with the prospect of The Civil War timeline jump on the horizon, this may bring a more balanced game.
Community. As with all games with an established community, the community within MWO can be daunting and at times outright unwelcoming. There is a group within the community which often convey an elitist mentality. This is NOT exclusive to MWO. There are also many members within the community who are incredibly welcoming, there are numerous open voip services where players can interact and find groups etc.
Progression. Like all F2P games you accrue ingame currency and exp which is used to purchase various items in game and "skill up" your mech of choice. Personally I feel as though this progression is quite reasonable, however, it is heavily dependent on your performance.
(Personally I think the system in MWO is better than in many other games but this is just personal opinion.)
Unlike many games, MWO offers a truly deep and rewarding game experience. The combat within MWO is simply one aspect of the game. Once you have purchased your own mech you can begin to delve into customising the load out and making use of the "skill tree" which will allow you to further customise the mech to the way you play.
Choices. MWO offers, at times, an overwhelming array of choices. These choices are one of the best things about MWO. To begin with you have the choice of 4 weight classes (light, medium, heavy and assault), from there you can then figure out which chassis fits your playstyle. If you fancy a Scout you can pick up the fast and agile Locust. If you want to use the equivalent of a good old Sherman tank then you can pick yourself up the Hunchback 4-G. Alternatively if you want to be the spear tip then you can grab yourself the iconic Atlas.
Teamplay. This is what MechWarrior Online is all about. Teamplay. MWO has ingame voip and a comm rose, something which is often overlooked.
Community. I know that I've listed this twice but I feel as though it is worth stating under the positives too. The community supporting MWO hosts various leagues and tournaments, it also plays host to niche options which have been supported by PGI in the form of a "Stock Mode" where players run mechs with standard loadouts. The community also plays host to a wide array of resource sites where you can find suggested builds and also numerous YouTube channels offering gameplay, builds and an array of other content.
PGI. The developer. This is possibly a divisive statement but in many ways I view PGI to be one of the better development studios out there. While they have their faults PGI have and continue to work towards implementing numerous supporting features to the community. They continue to add new content and, most importantly, they communicate. While this communication could be improved in certain regards, they at least take the time to engage with the community and to try provide explanation (where necessary) for upcoming changes and alterations.
Like all games MechWarrior Online has its faults but the positives far outshine the negatives. This game is not for everyone, it requires an investment of time, dedication and perseverance. It has a very steep learning curve but if you look in the right places there is a welcoming and supportive community.
MWO is a team based tactical shooter which offers a deeply rewarding experience which is often completely missing from many titles which could be considered competitors.
This isn't a game for everyone but if you're looking for a shooter with depth and you're willing to spend time learning the ropes, this might be the game for you.

I initially dove head first into this game and played it like it was a drug. The first few levels are very easy to progress through and the amount of garage space you get to work with allows you to make substantial progress unlocking new tanks and upgrades right out of the gate. After that, this game falls off a cliff.
First off, the multiplayer is unbalanced as ♥♥♥♥. I counted 14 games in a row where I was matched with people playing at a higher tier than my tank at one point, and only 2 out of maybe 20 games where a majority of players were actually within my tier. My tanks were NOT fully upgraded, but for some ♥♥♥♥ing reason I was CONSTANTLY pitted against opponents with higher level tanks than mine
Second, there's no 'ranked' mode where people can actually test to see how good of a player they are for lower tiers. There is a ranked mode at level 9 and 10, the highest in the game, but you'd have to grind for an absurd amount of time to get there, assuming you dont infuriatingly lose your patience well before then the way I did. Your stats are completely dictated by how your teammates do, a vast majority of whom prefer to hide in a bush and snipe from across the map rather then try to take objectives.
Third, Single shots from higher tier tanks almost ALWAYS will knock out your tracks or your engine, completely ♥♥♥♥ing marooning you in the middle of a field where half the enemy team take turns pounding you with fire, usually while my teammates are nowhere to be seen. There are consumables you can buy for instant repairs, but they hardly do you any good because some other tank will fire one shot at you and accomplish the exact same thing. This issue is amplified if youre unlucky enough to CONSTANTLY BE MATCHED WITH HIGHER TIERED TANKS like I was on a regular basis.
Fourth, the chat in the game is infuriating to use. Theres a character limit on what you can type meaning you cant point out where youre getting shot from or what the strategy of the team will be, and at the end of the game when im staring down a 2v5 because my teammates are all dead, the chat will quit on you and not let you type anything even when you open it. It simply opens and closes until the next match begins which only adds to the infuriation of this game. Not only does the bull♥♥♥♥♥♥hit you via matchmaking and gameplay, you cant even type anything about the bull♥♥♥♥♥♥either.
Im sure this game gets tons of praise because its free, simple, and great graphics, which I dont deny nor dispute, but the other aspects of the game are simply infuriating which in a game designed to be completely multiplayer are simply unacceptable and intolerable. The game starts out great but then becomes horrendously unbalanced, with fine layers of other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t layered on for ♥♥♥♥ knows why.
Give the game a try if you want, its free after all, but I dont recommend playing it because the game prevents individual skill from impacting how you do in the game. Its all dependent on the tier youre matched up against (Almost always higher than you), and the performance of teammates (who dont follow objectives).
