My first impressions of this game were mixed, but only later did I realize, that the game was good, and I was the one with the issue. Now I would just say this is a good game. Endless space is a 4x game where you explore the galaxy, and build an empire. The game actually does a great job of simulating something that countless science fiction writers have worked on for years. It presents the concept of a vast galaxy where your galactic empire is just that an empire. In an empire, your decisions as emperor determine whether your race succeeds or is wiped off the face of the galaxy. You may lose a battle, sacrifice a fleet, or even give away a planet, but in the end you are working for the welfare of your people and with practice you will prevail.
The game is hard, so start in the very easy modes at first. After you have a clear understanding of the game, each playthrough will be something unique and a place to experiment with. The game gives you the option of creating a custom faction to play with your own selection of skills and starting parameters. This allows you to really role play the content of this series well.
Honestly the most epic part of the game for me is when the player begins to transform worlds form barren dead worlds and eventually transform them into terran, or ocean paradises, for your citizens benefit. Nothing fixes their attitude more than turning a dead world into Eden.
I found myself chaffing a bit with some of the win conditions in the game, only to realize, you can chose which win conditions are active and which are not. In my case, I do not like having a final turn timer mechanic. I want a clear victory through expansion, domination, science, or diplomacy... though these are not all the win conditions available, I am able to select just these for my playthroughs and it makes all the difference, and at times if I want to just watch a galactic empire expland... I will play a last  standing game.
Take  the game slow, and take your time, and this game will give you countless unique runthroughs to enjoy.

Well for the most part.
Now this review is by someone is currently in the middle of a third playthrough of the game, so some of these critiques are based more on replayability than core-design.
I suppose I should answer the simple question first: Is it better than the original?
Answer: Highly debatable.
But what does the game get right? As a whole, the game is more open-ended than your normal game on Steam, so that's definatly a plus. I definitely think the game will offer those satisfying moments where you feel like you solved a problem intelligently As well, I think the atmosphere will be inticting for first-comers(I'll get more into that later). The art-style is a somewhat debated topic within this game, but in terms of most designs, it looks good. I definitely have to give props to the music, especially the Main Theme(Icarus). They really knocked it out of the park with most of the music, and I'd say some of it rivals the original. As well, I liked how they made hacking more complex than just clicking a hack button in the original. The story itself can be debated as being either good or bad, but I don't think I can deny that there are some high points to it, especially in the beginning. The game certainly has the conspriacy feel that Deus Ex games are known for(though not to the same extent as the original). I'd say the main characters within the story are compelling, such as Sarif, Pritchard, and Malik, as they all do feel like they have some degree of personality to them. As well, the hub cities are quite neat, and I do like how they have multiple levels each with their own secrets and items that can be useful later on. The augmentations themselves really do help make the levels more accessable in my opinion, which I think shows that they are quite useful. Exploration within this game, while not as good as the original, still feels enjoyable. I really think the game has a degree of enjoyment when you can just hack random computers and read emails that either flesh out the world, provide useful codes, or are just plain funny at times(though they do use stale memes for the most part). And in terms of how clever the game gets, I think that it has some good moments. I definitely think the theme dealing with Adam getting to terms with his augmentations in the beginning does represent what it's like to get them.
However I did say that the game doesn't fully live up to the original, and I wasn't kidding. To begin with, the game really promotes a more power-play mentality than the original. This is caused by a few things, those being the following: (A)Simplifed RPG System, (B)Rewarding for certain playstyle, (C)World being designed to benefit a certain playstyle. The simplification of the this game compared to the original is hard to deny, you no longer have skillpoints, updgrading is easier, and instead of using lockpicks, hacking, or multitools to access certain areas, you now just use hacking. It really does make the game feel simplier at times, espically in the hub cities. In the original Deus Ex, there were many ways to access a path, all of which required either using lockpicks, multitools, or hacking, and it made the game feel more open and big. In this game, every single compartment, apartment, and room, can all be accessed by hacking. I really wouldn't blame anyone for saying the game feels simplifed from an exploration standpoint. It becomes a lot more clear early on in the game that hacking is the way to go, and as such it makes the game feel less unique, as you can access all areas by the same solution, rather than having to think of different solutions like you did in the original. Also the weapons in this game feel far easier to use, which I guess if you didn't like the gunplay of the original Deus Ex, it's a great thing. And despite having improved the gunplay, the game still doesn't like it when you use lethal weapons(IE most weapons in the game). You get a higher bonus from using non-lethal. Building off of that, the game rewards a stealth playstyle more than anything. You get sneak bonuses for going stealthy, and also for hacking. Even if the game gives you an access code, just hack the console, it rewards you with XP, money, and hacking viruses for later on. The game essentially rewards you for sticking to a stealth playstyle only. This really goes against the philosophy of the the original, where you were never forced to adapt a certain playstyle, and you wouldn't get anymore rewarded for one playstyle, than you would for another. It was about what worked for you, not what worked for the game. And alongside gameplay, the immersion of Human Revolution isn't as strong as the original(Though I think this becomes more of a noticable problem during replays of the game). While I did say the art-style was good for the most part, I do think some aspects of it break the immersion more than it does to benefit it, especially when you get these really nice sceneic views that you never get to visit(like the Upper City of Hengsha). This is much more on the nitpicky side, but I really needed to talk about the character interactions, and the details of it themselves. Because of the weaker immersion, you will start to notice that the character models are reused a lot. There are only about 1-3 faces per each gender and race of the game, with just different hair and clothes. Trust me, you will get tired of it. And I really can't forgot the dialogue interactions. They really start to feel like a chore eventually. The thing that I noticed in my replay of HR, was the talking animations. Not only do they feel unhuman and a little unimmersive, but they are repeated multiple times within the conversation. You can not unseen those animations, and it really can impact immersion for some people. And If I am being honest in hindsight, the dialogue system itself feels a little gimmicky. It seems like they have gone for a Mass Effect style dialogue, with more clear choices and an option to ask questions(similar to the Investigate option in ME). The problem is, that unlike Mass Effect, this system isn't as much in-depth. There's no Paragon/Renegade system that gives you benefits and punishments for making certain choices. In fact, there really aren't as many important choices to make in this game than there were in the original. There something in this game called "Social Boss Battles", which are basically Mass Effect style arguments with characters, where you have to decide what will convince them the most to agree with you. The issue that some people have noted(and I begun to notice myself), is that some of the choices are eerily similar, to the point you wonder why they are considered seperate from each other. I understand this might be made to make the game more difficult, by making it more detailed, but it works in such a way where it's the kind of difficult that isn't productive. If you really dislike the social battles, you can install a social augmenatation that allows you to basically mind-read your opponent, and figure out what they like. Another thing that really annoyed me was how this game was beginning to have RPG cliches that the original Deus Ex was avoiding. The most infamous case for me was the sidequests. I really hated some of these sidequests. In the orignal Deus Ex, the "sidequests", were more like secondary goals, which you would discover whilst exploring, and as such didn't feel forced upon the player, which both helped further build the world, and actually had a relation to the plot of the game. This game however, suffers from having fetch quests and unrealted sidequests, that feel like a chore to complete. I don't want to be using that word in a Deus Ex game. Of all games, I'd argue Deus Ex should be the least associated with the word "chore".(Check comments for continuation).

Wow. What an experience.
The graphics look a little dated, but of course this was released awhile ago so that's understandable. One of the things that blew me away about this game is it's ability to transport you into this world and make it so realistic. Future-world politics using scenarios that very well could happen someday makes this game seem more believable, and the lore behind it is very interesting, it's very obvious a ton of thought went into it. The role-playing is excellent, as is the story. The cyberpunk theme fits well with a narrative that's usually very bleak, but oddly hopeful. The dialouge is great, the characters are great, the choice moments in the game are great (not as far reaching with consequences as in a game like Mass Effect but they were still good), and the combat was great. I played through the game on normal difficulty and I have to say even that provided a bit of challenge. When you got cornered in a fight, you REALLY were cornered, as most of the AI knows how to flank and use different means to get closer to you, which keeps you on your toes. To me, for 2011, the year the game originally came out (I believe), this is very innovative, as not a lot of games during that time used that type of programming well. The stealth gameplay was also great, I really felt powerful sneaking into an enemy base and slowly taking out each enemy one-by-one using whatever means I felt necessary. It just felt awesome. I also especially loved that there were many ways you could approach a situation, whether it be with stealth or it be with guns-blazing, using your vast arsenal to kill anyone anyway you felt like. Should I stun this guy with my stun gun or obliterate him from existence with my grenade launcher? I loved the fact that the game gave you that choice. And holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game has a lot of content. Side missions feel useful and even can give you rewards, as well as tie into the main story in ways you wouldn't expect. I know that many people may say "you think THIS game has a lot of content? Have you PLAYED Skyrim????", but I didn't think I'd get 30 hours out of this game, and I still enjoyed it.
The only real gripes I had with the game was the boss battles and some of the more extensive levels. The boss battles didn't really feel like boss battles that much, and weren't really as hard as I thought they were going to be. Most of the characters you were fighting weren't hyped up at all, so the only reason you had for fighting them was just because the game told you too. I would've liked it more if the boss characters would've had more of an over-arching reach in the story than just being these individuals that you had to fight to progress the story. I will admit, the very last one kinda did, but the three mercanaries? I can't even remember the last two's names. I felt they DEFINETLEY could've been done a lot better. Also, some of the stages seemed to go on forever, and I began to wonder how big could some of these facilities possibly be? The longest ones tended to drone on for a long time, and I felt myself getting bored after more than a couple of hours of them.
Other than that, though, this is by far a game I would recommend to for anyone that likes Sci-fi, roleplaying, action, and questioning their existence as a human being. 9/10

If you're planning to get this just to have a controller on PC: don't. This controller isn't meant to replace the usual Windows and dualschock controllers. And the job it does serving as one shows that. The d-pad and right analog stick being replaced with touchpads, isn't good for playing games that recommend using a controller. Sure the trackpad is more accurate than a joystick (if you can learn to use it, and can bother to take the time to adjust the sensitivities), but it isn't enough to replace an analog stick. In my opinion, if Valve wanted this controller to be able to compete with other Windows compatible controlelrs, they should have made the controllers modular in some way, so you could switch in a proper d-pad that isn't useless in every situation where it tries to be a d-pad, and you could use a regular analog stick, and maybe rearrange the whole face of the controller.
But, if you're planning to get this to try playing games not meant to be played with a controller, with a controller; well that's its job. This controller isn't a replacement for regular controllers nor the usual keyboard/mouse combo, but instead an alternative to a mouse and a keyboard, so you could enjoy games with no, or partial controller support, with a controller. Designed for the living room, not to replace desktop peripherals.

Its a unique game with a steep learning curve and a lot of customization.
If you dive in with zero research of mechanics and mech builds you are likely to get frustrated, fast. If you do a little homework you'll have a much better experience. Once you understand how things work, its a blast. No other game has combat like Mechwarrior.
There are multiple game modes but most play out like TDM. One life per round so tensions are high. The bigger your mech is the more you'll be expected to contribute. You either drop solo against solos or drop as a group against other groups.
You have full customization of your mech by using the mechlab. Double edged sword for new players. If you don't know how to build a mech properly you can waste c-bills(in game currency) and pretty much lose the match before you even start.
If you can avoid the noob pitfalls by doing a little research and enjoy giant robots you'll love this game. Most of the negative reviews are people who didn't understand the fundamental mechanics. Don't be like them!

I can honestly say after many hours playing this game; don't bother.
The issue is a combination of salty community and a matchmaker that for all intensive purposes does not appear to actually try and balance the individual matches. My impression is that balancing individual matches is difficult so the current match maker really just tries to alternate stacking teams to win/lose in an effort to promote 50/50 win lose rate. This is not perfect as people are hard to predict but you do get a sense after a while playing that after you have couple stomps in your teams favor you are about to get stomped a couple times. From a developer perspective I can see how this would be tempting to create for a situation. A player that always loses is likely to quite the game, and a player that always wins may not feel the need to get the next shiny thing. The issue is that it starts to make the game feel like it's on the rails and frustrating when you are placed with potato teams and even when you face a potato team if you are actually looking for a good match.  I think this may be part of what creates the salty community is these repeated unbalanced matches. Obviously this is only an issue if you are playing quick drops with the matchmaker but the salty community carries over to other modes and one would have to have the time to devote to group play to try and escape this.
Can you have fun still? Yes but I find for quick play at least it's usually in the off hours when there are less players online and it is harder for the matchmaker to actually do its thing. Ironically but to my point in my experience the matches at these times are usually more balanced than when the online player base is larger. Theoretically this would not be true since the matchmaker needs to balance tonnage etc. from the available mechs and more players should give it more freedom to balance by player skill rating as well.  So either the matchmaking system is just horribly bad or.....
To add injury to insult the missmatches and matchmaking times generally get worse the higher tier you go. I am fairly sure that this is understood among the player base so you will often end up with matches with AFKs or suicide charges. My guess some of these are players trying to keep their PSRs (player skill rating) down to avoid the horrible slog of unbalanced teams that awaits a player once they reach the upper tiers.
It is also important to state that this is an online competitive game with no anti-cheat measures really at all. The only semblance of this is that when a player dies they can if they want spectate another player. So often you will see players that appear to see through walls or are very accurate in the start of a match before others on their team die etc. It can all be very frustrating when you put the whole thing together. I Still play when I can find it tolerable because I have always really enjoyed the Battletech universe and I have become invested in the game from a time perspective and some purchases. At times though I feel like a hostage and I wish I had not tried the game. As far as purchases go I find that if I ever am having a good day and start to consider purchasing something with RL money  I just play 5 games in a row to check if I still feel that way. Since implementing that strategy I have spend $0 on this game and it has made me realize some of the short comings of the game more clearly.

World of Tanks Blitz is a ripover of the original World of Tanks, where you go 15 versus 15 in a map sized well enough for any kinds of purposes. When World of Tanks Blitz came out, I was hyped that I could finally play World of Tanks (kind of), but on either phone or later on, PC. After 3 months of the release on Android platforms, I was super excited because it was the time for me to roll out on the battlefields and use my wit for a good purpose - fight with knowledge that comes from the original World of Tanks and quickly farm up on tanks. My first months were all fine, I quickly got addicted to the tank and I was a great performing player, about 60% winrate. The game was without a question fun, but as I played more it got stressful because of my opinions pointing that either this or that is unbalanced. However, I could still give quite a beating and make profits and deal enough damage to satisfy myself, ignoring either if it is a defeat or a victory - all I care is how I performed in battle. A defeat with over 3k damage in tier VII was a victory, a victory with less than 1k damage is a defeat for me. Almost a year, I have a lot of tanks, premium account going on, still doing good. Phone got damaged over time (LG G2) because I was super addicted to the game - I would plug the charger into phone and keep on playing, the game was quite evenly with phone's performance, I wouldn't have lag but the phone would overheat and it would get slowly damaged over time. At the time the phone was done for, I was still a competitive player. However because of phone, I had to move on. The game was implemented on PC too, a phone World of Tanks Blitz available on PC - that sucks you know, there's already a World of Tanks game on PC: It's the original WoT! Anyway, playing on my 11-year old laptop took me about 2 weeks to get used to, but when I got used to the computer experience I could perform as well as I did on phone, slightly better of course because of how easy the controls are now. As I kept playing, I've grown a regret for playing on laptop because I felt this isn't the correct platform to play the game on - the game is meant to be played on either iOS or Android. The game was unstable with computer (and it is still), I decided to go on with the damaged phone. I  started playing back with it, but it didn't last long because I would perform poorly now. I tried to struggle a bit but I never could be as good as I was when I started first. It went like this, but only to last a very short period of 1 month. Later on, forced to play the game with laptop.
With the equipments update, the game got ruined, So horrible to play now, I was forced to play the game because the performance demands were so low and the game is still at least a percent of World of Tanks. The problem of view range imbalance, bush physics not being as good as it should be in World of Tanks, graphical bugs on PC and similar problems like that, I stopped my premium account, having about 40 days until it ends, I kept on playing. When my premium expired so did my fun with it. If I am to play the game, it'd only be for fun, which I can't have anymore because I can't make a difference alone. Cities in Motion 2 is pretty good. It definitely is true to purpose. It's a satisfying mass-traffic, public transport simulator and management game. I legitimately feel like I should be in an office building wearing a suit while I play this game, which, if you're interested, is probably exactly the kind of thing you're in to.
It has a map editor. It has a rule set editor. Both of these allow you to customize the game surprisingly effectively. I, personally, went through the effort of looking at Google Maps images and remaking my home city and then proceeded to play that map with my friends.
Road building is easy once you get the hang of it. Alternations of click and right-click allow you to customise the shape of your tracks and roads effectively. There is a lot of information available, so there is a bit of getting-used-to time required in order to navigate things correctly, from, for instance, lines to depots to buying vehicles. Timetables are important and there's a lot of micromanaging of vehicles and time required to ensure optimised routes and service. I would recommend starting with a standardised timetable (say, one vehicle every hour) to get the hang of it.
You need to connect to direct IP to get multiplayer to work reliably. Using a VPN such as Hamachi is a good idea for this.
All of the game's issues can be described as annoyances, which is an improvement on game-breaking issues, which many games have these days.
To cut to the chase, the game has the following issues:
- Multiplayer desyncs eventually, meaning eventually you and your friends will have different city economies, income, won't see certain things the others do, etc. You can fix this by manually getting them to replace their save file with yours, which can be tedious. It can take a satisfactory amount of time before this desync happens though, so multiplayer is still functional on a short-medium term basis.
- Many additional vehicles are DLC. It's money grubbing, and it does have some effect on the game, but you don't need the DLC to enjoy the game to the fullest extent unless your enjoyment comes primarily from seeing differently coloured buses and trains. You can modify the game's rules to make your vanilla vehicles have the same or similar functionality to DLC vehicles. No particular loss, just annoying.
- Changing ticket prices can be tedious, but there is a mod to help combat this (available through steam workshop).
If you are reading reviews on this game, you must be interested in some sort of a city management game. This is a public transport management game. It has some city management elements, in that the city's growth is directly affected by the success of your public transport system, but it is mostly a business management game, the business being specifically a public transport system.
I recommend it, you should try it, if you wanted to manage the busses and trains in a SimCity 4-esc city, whilst the city manages itself, and it is very good at doing that.

Lets see where to start? I will say that while I'm not a big fan of the level of micromanagement that the game goes to, it was well implemented in my opinion, not only giving you a strong feeling of control over the types of productions your planets can excel at but also how you want to specialize your ships for space combat or invasions and everything in between.
The combat is undoubtbly the weakest part of the game, which is a shame since they seemed to have put a good amount of thought into the customization of ships. There isn't any real-time fighting, rather you pick a type of strategy from a list for each phase and then the ships fight until one side has been destroyed or all three phases have passed. The fights usually turn into constant metaing or a rock-paper-scissors match with one side or the other choosing to spec their ships to fire whatever the enemy has the least defenses against. Personally I think they should have increased the number of ships allowed in each fleet so more diversity of ship roles could be filled without decreasing overall effeciency. Oftentimes I usually just had a fleet of high defense ships that repaired and no weapons up front to soak damage while I had high damage dealing ships in the back to destroy everyone. The limitations of the combat shows when you have more than 20 weapon slots on a single ship but it was to waste it's whole slavo on just one ship instead of targeting multiple ones. The combat is just not managed well and really felt more like a numbers game than applying any real tactics to win.
The pace of the game can somtimes be incredibly slow, as making first contact can sometimes take forever, ships traveling can as well and researching can be an ordeal if you don't focus enough planets on researching science. I played my first game on the easiest difficulty and I was more bored by the general pace of the game than how it became to crush the AI once I researched the right things and specced my ships the way I wanted to. Basically if you want a sci-fi strategy game with lots of managment and don't mind a soul-crushing slow pace of things then this is for you. But the combat is lackluster and the game doesn't offer enough interesting things on a turn-by-turn basis to keep things interesting.
If you want to be confused by overly-complicated strategies, buy this game. If you wish for confusing micro-managing, buy this game. If you want to have fun, buy Civ 5.

Quick Summary: Top down car shooter with a cheesy story but fun gameplay. You should definitely use a controller for this game instead of keyboard & mouse.
You play one of the Renegades, a kind of special ops team under the command of General Bryant who is trying to stop the evil Inferno from launching missiles at innocent people and generally causing chaos. The story is told in motion comic style, and the dialogue is like an 80’s action movie with everyone trying to act/talk macho, but it’s fun and frames the gameplay well.
You get to choose from about 7-8 different characters, each with their own “special move” such as temporary invulnerability, heavy firepower, or airstrike. The specials are on a cooldown timer so you can’t spam them but they’re definitely must haves for some of the tougher enemies. Each character levels up independently, and while leveling up doesn’t increase your stats, you get skill points that you can use to buy passive upgrades (such as faster cooldown or better armor). Other than the special moves, the characters are generally the same and all use the same machine gun + whatever secondary weapon you find during the level.
Something to note (and it’s actually really annoying) is that even though the game is played in top down perspective, you can very easily flip your car as you’re driving around. Seriously it’s like driving a Halo warthog while viewing from the top and constantly flipping or hitting things that you don’t see very clearly. The end result is that the vehicle is much more difficult to control than it seems and if you’re playing with a keyboard & mouse you will get frustrated very fast (especially when you’re flipped on your back and a dozen guys are shooting at you).
Pros:
+Very nice graphics and huge maps full of enemies.
+Fun cheesy story with a “MUHAHAHA” type villain.
+Co-op multiplayer is available
Cons:
-The car controls can be very annoying since a lot of the areas are very close quarters (such as driving through canyons or villages).
-For someone like me who is not used to shoot’em up or bullet hell games, Renegade Ops is rather difficult. You have a limited number of lives for each mission, after which you need to start over. You can grind for levels by replaying missions, but like I said earlier your stats don’t increase, so the game doesn’t really get “easier” even if you’re max level.
Overall it’s a fun game, and if you like a challenge you should definitely give it a try.

The unboxing of my Steam Controller was very satisfying. My hands were oriented to the feel of an Xbox One Controller so my first time use was not pleasant. It took me awhile to get used to the changes as it should. This controller is very different. It has different modes as well. PC mode where it acts as a mouse and partial keyboard; the Video, Music, Big Picture mode which is very fluid and easy to use; and the in-game mode which can be customized for each game. This surprise a.k.a. "icing on the cake" was when I found out it had a gyroscope. I have found many unique usages for it. It is very easy to configure as well. As for things I do not like about it; well, that right side axis stick for open world 3rd person games is pretty important. The touch pad makes it a bit hard to aim but I wouldn't take that touch pad off for the world. It is what makes it a PC controller not a Console controller. I also had hoped for a headphone and microphone port on the controller like Xbox and ps4 controllers have; it could remedy issues where only one headset can be used via a single PC.
I rate this controller 5 out of 5 stars. While it is not good for some games; it has made others amazingly easy and interact-able in ways that you just have to see for yourself to understand. Looking around just by moving your hands around; it is a great controller. Things I would like to see in future versions are rechargeable batteries, a 3.5mm stereo+mic jack for headsets, and more sound options not just on and off sounds.

I will admit, while it was a bit hard to get used to the controller at first, the learning curve was worth it. There are so many ways to play with the controller that fits for your liking. To this day, I consider this my favorite controller.

“Jack of all trades master of some”

The Steam controller is a real head-turner. With it’s sleek black body and unconventional shape. It really makes an odd first impression.
Closer inspection reveals the controller is very similar to the old Xbox 360 pad. The two peripherals even share the same face buttons. So all the in-game button prompts will still work with Valve’s controller. The four face buttons are also too small and cramped for most games. If you play fighting games like Tekken 7 you will often miss button inputs. And don’t even talk about the flat d-pad. It’s akin to playing the game using a plastic dinner plate. Lucky the controller has a left analogue stick to save the day.
Instead of a right analogue stick you have a thumb trackpad. Just like the trackpad on your laptop the thumbpad does OK but it will never replace a mouse.

The Steam controller is fully customisable so you could in theory create the ultimate control method for playing Tekken 7. Maybe you could rig up something using the shoulder buttons? You can create controller profiles for any game in your Steam library or download pre-made ones from the friendly Steam community. Customisation can be painstaking or fun depending on how you feel about it. Personally I’d rather just play my game.

Ergonomics wise the pad is awkward in the hands. The front “feet” of the controller are quite bulbous. Initially it feels as if you are holding the controller backwards. But in time your hands adapt. It's not what I would call comfortable.

The controller has some adorable startup and shutdown sounds when it pairs with your PC. So I can never stay mad at it for very long.

I give the Steam controller a thumbs up with a funny expression on my face. It’s such an odd design that’s oddly appealing to a gamer like me. It’s truly a jack of all trades master of some.

If you do pickup a Steam controller please let me know what you think of it. I recommend you play the game Refunct. It showcases the Steam controller in the best possible light. You might just fall in love.

The E3 demo looked like a uninspired corridor shooter with canned and long finisher animations that take away the momentum from your movement. The public beta was only for multiplayer which felt like it didn't know if it was an old-school arena shooter or Halo.
So when the game was released I wasn't expecting much. Fortunately, it turned out to be one of the most pleasant surprises of 2016.
The Glory Kill finishers looked like they were there just to look cool for trailers in the pre-release footage but they turned out to be pivotal in some brilliant game design.
Low on health? Instead of hiding behind cover to regen health or scurrying off from combat to find medkits hidden behind some crevice, this game urges you to keep fighting. If you want health you need get close to the danger and kill some demons. You turn into an unstoppable force and RIP AND TEAR through everything.
Want a power fantasy? This game has it in spades.
Even the story is surprisingly well done which is pretty unexpected for a Doom game. If you don't care it won't get in your way. But if you do check the journals there's some well written lore there,
Add in a superb dynamic soundtrack that makes those special moments even better, excellent visuals with great optimization (id Tech 6 is significantly more matured than id 5) and you got probably my favorite shooter in a decade.
I don't often have particularly strong reactions with games but this one always makes me happy.
I see a screenshot, hear a snippet of the soundtrack or just talk about the game and it just brings a smile to my face and when I sit down and actually get to play it - it's pure bliss.
Thanks id, you have redeemed yourselves in my eyes in an absolutely gloríous way.
An addictive experience.

Trucker is truly a masterpiece. It's inovative control scheme is beyone most people's mental capacity. The brilliance of using the arrow keys to move a truck and have it always drift when you turn while having the a and z keys shift up and down for you is quite frankly ground breaking. The AI's mental capacity rivals that of machine learning algroithms in its genious. The AIs mental capacity to not care about driving rules and randomly go to the other side of the road for no reason, unexpectadly stop, or get in car crashes with other cars. The physics in this game also withhold the best standard ever witnessed by man. If you hit a wall/fence at a slower speed you will only damage car not destroy it and lose the race. However, if you crash into the wall at a higher speed you will lose the race. You may be saying what if you barely skim the fence while going fast. In that case your whole car would obviously explode and you would die. Except wait! With these ground breaking  game physics you don't get to witness the amazingness of your car crash. It leaves it up to your imagination which has the best graphics you've ever seen. The amount of levels this game has is quite frankly amazing and all of the levels this game has are so distinctive. All levels have grass and road and generally the same style which results into the distinctive amazements of these different levels, but also gives the game a unique style. Modern games do not grasp this clasic masterpiece. With modern games, players are rewarded for damaging/destroying any cars/enemies. However in this game you can quickly lose money by crashing into stuff/being reckless. Modern games don't value true skill and the original down to earth racing expirience of the simplicity that crashing = bad and driving good = good. This game also has some amazing features such as adjustable volume which you will want to use because the music in this game is decent and the cars are loud compared to that at most times so you should lower the game volume but keep the music volume up. Also the game has remapable controls, so if you are playing with a controller, you can select a control imput from the start screen and then map it afterward. While most simpletons will play Euro Truck Simulator 2, it is clearly too easy and has too good of physics. Whoever plays this game has over 9000 IQ. Whenever I hear that someone is smart, I ask them how many hours they have in Trucker. Usually they correspond. I am trying to get 9000 hours in trucker so that I will have 9000 IQ and be able to solve quantem mequanics. Please by this game and truly expirience this true expirience of a mechanical Masterpiece.

Gather around little ones and I'll tell you a tale of an excentric trillionaire and nasty neighbors. A tale of generousity and betrayal. Allow me to tell you a tale from Endless Space.
I started this game with the only race who really seemed appealing. The Horatio. The Horatio are clones, narcissistic clones of the original Horatio who genetically altered himself to create the 'perfect being' and now wants to make the universe more perfect by filling it with himself. Fans of Red Dwarf will suddenly be reminded of the episode in which Rimmer, an equally narcissistic character, did the same thing with Rimmer World. Hilarity ensued.
So we start of with a bunch of scout ships being sent in opposite directioins about the ring of the galaxy, eventually encountering the other sentient race who on this occasion were the Vaulters. Now since I've never played this before, I knew nothing of this race and so I promptly left them be. Eventually setting up outposts on wormholes to the east and west of them. Relations were fine at first and trade routes established but trying to appease them proved almost impossible as they appeared to really dislike having neighbors. Eventually I get a request from them asking to open borders. This struck me as odd since they were anything but friendly towards my people. So I declined and carried on learning the finer points of gardening and economics. Then another request to open borders. This time it dawned on me and a big grin formed across my face - I had boxed them into a corner of the galaxy because I had colonized the only two wormholes out. After the 4th declined request to open borders they finally declared war on me and stormed through the wormholes with a moderately impressive fleet. But due to their hampered development they were unable to conquer any planets as their defences were too good. So they blockaded them instead and denied me the profits of those worlds. When I called for a cease fire they didn't return home either, they continued to blockage the systems so a game and cat and mouse ensued as they'd sometimes wander from system to system setting up blockades and I'd move manufacturing around to compensate. After galactic war 3 I finally got sick of them and forced a peace-treaty with a very generous donation of technology and a per round donation of Dust to appease them. Did it work? No. They just couldn't be apeased so the peace turned to a cold war and the cold war turned into outright invasion. Only this time, they'd used my generous donations to create several fleets of impressive power with heroes heading each one of them. Since most of my time had been spent focussing on the sciences and expanding the clone army across the stars my ships were totally unprepared for this. A brutal retreating battle of attrition ensued as fleet after fleet of clones were thrown at this Vaulter Armada created using our own funds. Eventually war ended and I suggested a cease fire - but little did they know I had a plan.
With so much invested into the sciences it was easy to suddenly develop ships capable of standing up to this new threat and within next to no time I broke the cease fire and caught all of the Vaulter fleets offguard. When the last one was destroyed I looked to the diplomatic menu, expecting to see the negative consequences of a broken cease fire agreement. What did I see? Bonus points of respect from the Vaulters who were impressed by the might of my new fleet?! Oooo....kayyy.... then.... Suddenly understanding that our neighbors were complete nutcases who loved nothing more than a good fight I promptly dispatched my own fleets to blockade every single one of their planets and suffocated any of their efforts to build anything more impressive than a knife and fork. A scientific victory followed as the Horatio achieved the next plane of digital existance. My only conerns now is that without the need to return to our corporeal worlds the Vaulters are now free again to go rampaging through the galaxy looking for the next good fight.
Now then, why was it nessersary to tell you this tale for a review? Well.. because these are the events which took place but it took over 20 hours of gameplay to happen and none of it is as impressive as it sounds. Endless Space literally has you spending most of your time looking at menus. All of the drama described really only happens when you sum up events in your head. It's like reading a book. It's nothing more than a bunch of words and page after page of more and more of them, but with some imagination it becomes alive. Endless Space is like that. It only works with imagination because in reality it looks very, very dull. The learning curve is also incredible as it isn't really clear what you should be doing most of the time and only with some pre-reading of guides are you going to get any enjoyment out of it.
Can I recommend it? Not really. I've seen other 4X titles and they really do give you some visual feedback to how your empire is progressing and ES just doesn't really do that. Having more dots on the starmap in your colour just isn't very interesting and doesn't give you that sense of achievement needed to keep you moving forwards. The 'exploration' is limited as you are essentially on-rails due to the cosmic string and wormhole limitations. When you discover new planets there really isn't much variety to what you can find there. Quite often the game falls completely flat as you need to take several turns before you need to do anything else. Numbers are moving behind the scenes but you just don't get the nessersary feedback you need to understand if you have made good choices or bad ones. Maybe ES2 will address these issues and I certainly hope so because there is plenty of potential here for a rewarding experience once some changes are made.

is an interesting learning tool for anyone curious how guns (or specific guns) work. However, the "game" aspect of it is lacking. You're scored largely on how quickly you can strip and reassemble a gun, with a significant bonus for only clicking a part that can be "activated." This would be fine if the game were consistent as to what constitutes a "part" (for example, sometimes each pin has to be removed before the parent part can be removed; sometimes the pins are considered the same part, and the whole assembly can be removed in one click) and how to tell when you're allowed to remove or replace a part. On the AK-47, for example, the accessories case has to be removed before the buttstock, and the buttstock has to be removed before the back plate can be removed. I can tell you from experience that that is not the case in real life. The game also forces the magazine to be first out and last in, which, while it is a good practice, is not mechanically necessary. These decisions make the challenge more about memorizing the puzzle as the developers have created it than knowing how the gun actually works.
All in all, it's not bad as a free toy, but I can't recommend dropping any money on this "game."

In my opinion, the Steam Controller is the best controller on the market today.
First of all, it is the most comfortable controller I have ever used. Some people disagree with this, and believe that it's for people with larger hands, and that might be true. I would consider my hands to be small to average size, however my mouse of choice is the Zowie EC1-A, which is marketted to gamers with big hands, so I might just be a bit weird.
Other than ergonomics, the sheer number of options in using the Steam Controller is its greatest asset. Thanks to this, I can now use just one controller to play all of my PC games, including those on emulators. For instance, Mupen64 and PPSSPP always give me trouble with the triggers on an Xbox controller, but with the Steam Controller I can remap the offending keys while still using the Xbox controller emulation, rather than mapping the buttons to keystrokes.
Also, since the right stick is a haptic pad, you can remap it to the mouse for more precise control that works properly, unlike, say, Antimicro, which although it is a wonderful piece of software, it can only register up to 8 directions for a mouse. Of course, I still use a mouse for games that require the utmost precision, but for my money, an emulated trackball beats an analog stick any day.
The oddness of this controller might put some people off. To me, it seems like it was designed to mostly use the haptic pads and 6 index, middle, and ring finger buttons. I have found that for some games, Dragon's Dogma for one, I prefer to map the actions I use most to these, and leave the analog stick and ABXY buttons for more ancillary functions. I actually like this because my thumbs stay on the movement and camera controls at all times, but others may disagree.
The one true drawback to the Steam Controller is the fact that you have to have Steam running in order to use it. I personally don't like the idea of having to use Steam to launch my non-Steam games, but thankfully since I'm a Linux user, the open source community came to the rescue. If you are a Linux gamer, I highly recommend you check out SC Controller on Github. It's not 100% there yet since it can only emulate keystrokes and an Xbox 360 controller so far, but it works without Steam, has a nice GUI, and lets you not only switch control schemes on the fly, but also lets you assign control schemes to certain games, just like Steam does. Unfortunately, SC Controller isn't available for Windows yet, but I believe the devs plan on fixing that one of these days. I believe there is at least one alternative that does Mac and Windows, but I can't speak for its quality.
With all that said, I'm really happy with my purchase. If you're in the market for a new controller, definitely consider the Steam Controller.

It doesn't have many explosive setpieces or dramatic fights, and it doesn't have to, because the thrill of "ghosting" through the level or finding a well hidden path is much more exciting. It also sets up a world that's not just a background for Adam Jensen's Wacky Adventures, but a place with own social, political and ethical problems - all of which you can uncover, if you read e-mails, e-books and newspapers scattered throughout each level. 9/10. Square Enix, if you're really going to cancel next Deus Ex game, I'm coming for you.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Directors Cut is a cyberpunk RPG with heavy emphasis on its story.
The year is 2027, the city is Detroit, and the overall feel is quite gloomy as there have been 'debateable' breakthroughs in human augmentation. You are Adam Jensen, an ex-SWAT that became the security chief in one of the biggest experimental biotechnology firms, Sarif Industries. Almost immediately after getting into the game, the firm's HQ is under attack by heavily augmented commandoes, that wreck havoc, killing many, destroying most labs and leaving you to die.  By the order of your boss, you are put on the surgical table and receive many top-grade augmentations. After a while, you are called back to action and your story begins!
Human Revolution has many great and interesting features, however, the one that intrigued me the most, is the ability for every objective to be approached with many ways. You can beat your way into a facility or you can sneak in totally undetected, or a mix between! Each way will reward XP equally, so because you are not killing or incapacitating, it doesn't mean that you'll stay behind in levels. In certain missions, you can even talk your way into or out of many situations. The majority of the gameplay happens in semi-open world environments, that, each, is big enough and will keep you occupied for quite a long time, especially if you want to explore it thoroughly and find potential hidden rewards! Each area contributes to the story by housing a part of the main questline, but you can find several side quests available, that offer rewards and XP. Additionally, you will encounter several boss fights, each unique, and each having more than one way to beat it.
In terms of progression through the game, besides the levelling system, that translates into augmentations, that either make your life easier or allow you to use new skills, there are several pieces of gear to find and use. From consumables to various weapons, with each weapon being further upgraded by various kits, that besides improving its stats, can add special attributes or features to it!
While the game offers the player quite many choices, in the grey area is the fact that you can quick save/load, and pretty much do so to either correct mistakes or even get the best reward, trivialising bad or wrong choices.
The atmosphere and the general feel of the game is great, as the level design fits the theme and is complemented further by the music. Additionally, the named story NPCs you can interact with, have quite a lot of depth into them. Making certain dialogues more intriguing than expected! It's safe to say, that the majority of the characters are not easy to forget! Additionally, if you want more, you can activate the Directors Cut feature and listen to the commentary.
However what surprised me the most, was the depth the developers have put into the idea of human augmentation. You will encounter several NPCs that are both pro or against it, and many times they may even comment why! While I was inside a flat, there was a dialogue of a couple arguing about it, and I was stumbled enough to stop what I was doing in order to hear the entire conversation! Overall I felt that the game allowed me to shape my own opinion on the matter!
The negatives are that the graphics are noticeably outdated. The hacking can be random and frustrating due to the random chances to be detected, and finally, while the AI will stop you from e.g. hacking a police computer, you can build walls with various environment items, such as boxes, to disrupt their line of sight, allowing you to do whatever you like.
Overall I give Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Directors Cut a solid 9/10 as I enjoyed every bit of it. If you like RPGs with deep story and options and don't care much for graphics, this is a must play! There are also many achievements to satisfy completionists and steam trading cards.

This game is neither good nor bad. It's definitely in between. I would recommend doing some homework before you consider buying it (especially at full price). If I were younger (pre-teens to teens) I would most likely be all over this game. The redundancy of simply running here, getting civilians then blowing this up can really turn a gamer off. Some gamers however, do like games where you simply make things go boom. The
is actually quite decent and may pull some players in. I know the local co-op will definitely raise a few eyebrows.
The game follows a top-down format in which you drive a car. The
overall isn't that bad. The left stick drives the car while the right stick shoots (shooting in the direction you are pointing). Different cars have differing abilities. Gordon Freeman (from Half-Life) is a feature character on the steam version and his ability is to dispatch 3 headcrabs which attack enemies. Roxy has the ability to deploy airstrikes which is quite effective. Armand has the ability to use shields (yay how exciting to play defense). Diz is able to literally shut down enemies with her EMP ability. Gunnar has the ability to use a heavy cannon that deals a good amount of damage (however he cannot move while using this ability). Gunnar is pretty cool but so far Roxy and Gordon and the most fun to play with (in my opinion of course)! On top of having these abilities, players are able to boost with A. This is a nice addition as going from one side of the map to another to pick up civilians or to make a time limit can be tough without this ability. The game likes to deploy weapon drops that add an additional weapon to your arsenal. Some of these weapons include a flame thrower or a limited amount of rockets that deal a decent amount of damage.
In addition to basic abilities given to characters, there is an RPG element to the game. Players can choose from three categories to upgrade their specific character : defense, offense and tactical. Each character has slightly different upgrades. In general, defense deals with upgrades such as spare parts (that spawn health pickups when your hit) or doubling up on nitro for a quick get away. In general for offense, some upgrades include starting off with consumable weapons (such as rockets or rail guns), auto-reload or ammo surplus. In general for tactical, cool-downs for specials can be reduced, things like ram-plates can be added as well as counter-shots. You need to cause some mayhem to get some ability points!
Missions generally consist of either defending or attacking certain targets while attempting to extract civilians. It's almost impossible to go off course unless they give you a secret path to follow. Some missions will have you get into a helicopter and start attacking from the air. I think it's really cool that the game attempted to mix things up a bit and give the player a different sense of control. The problem here for me is some of this becomes redundant and is a complete deterrence for my friends and I to continue playing. I'm glad they at least added the ability to drive into houses and knock them down. Adds a little more to the atmosphere.
The
are pretty decent. Nothing less than ordinary or extra-ordinary. The helicopter graphics I feel could have been a lot better. The
are decent as well and do not go over and above. The dialogue is okay but can get corny at times.
Overall, it's not a bad game. I have tolerance for a lot of games but most friends I have played local with neither dislike or like the game. More dislike than like the game. I will recommend it but with a big "BEWARE" sign.

ES is all in all not a terrible 4X. You have different races, turn based gameplay and a large tech tree as well as quite a few weapon and module variations for your fleet and ships. However, from my limited time with the game I also have too many more or less negative points I'd like to list:
- Faction differences sometimes seem a bit minor. Pretty much all the races play similarly. Ok, with one race you get bonuses for continuously and constantly winning battles. From another race you can't flee in combat. These are all details though and don't really change the general gameplay completely imho. One exception might be the "Harmony", the race introduced with the addon, who don't use "Dust", one of the resources in the game, and get actually punished for using it. That's a cool concept. Apart from that all other races use exactly the same sort of weapons, modules and ship types. The differences seem mainly in the numbers. Visually the ships look distinct, but they all fulfill the same roles: Corvettes, Destroyers, Cruisers, Battleships and Dreadnought as well as colony ships and fighters/bombers.
- The tech trees are too samey. Ties in with the above point. Even though every race HAS some unique technologies, they don't seem that interesting compared to the huge tech tree. I don't feel diverse enough to be honest. Speaking of the gigantic tech tree. This is divided into 4 sections, I wonder, however, why stronger and better ships require research into a completely different tree than military. Basically you can either invest in better ships or better weapons, but of course you also need research from the other 2 sections to make something even halfway worthwhile. I feel it would have been better to more clearly differentiate the trees into: military (ships, weapons, armor, modules), exploration (engines, wormhole travel, scanning, etc.), colonization (how to make different sorts of planets colonizable, how to improve the living conditions on those planets) and planetary improvements (highways, supermarkets, things adding to production of any resource in general).
- The "exploitation" mechanic is finicky, if you have to constantly change it for every planet, but can't even see on the overview which planet is being exploited in what way. Maybe I'm just blind.
- The fleet battles are generally a mess. These are divided into 3 main sections: long range, medium range and short range. For every section you can choose a "battle card" (more can be unlocked via research or your heroes), the effect of which is totally random, since it can be countered by the enemy fleet. Since nobody knows what cards the opposite faction is playing, this is pure luck and can either win you the game or ♥♥♥♥ you over completely. Not to mention that the game doesn't do a good job of actually explaining what the different ships do, how to properly equip them, etc. There is just no feedback in the game. Suddenly your Dreadnought got destroyed by a cruiser with half health and 4 scouts...SCOUTS!!!! And you have no idea why or how that is even possible. So, that's annoying.
That is a problem the game has in spades. Since there is no in game wiki, you have to basically look up everything online. Compare this game to Civ 5, in which you have a progressive (albeit boring) tech tree. You can pretty much look at that for 1 minute and know what you're going to do, since everything has a purpose and leads to the next thing. You can leave tech out and focus on what you want to do...either military or economic or cultural or just plain old money or space race. It's easy to get into. Endless Space's tech tree is just a big mess and a beginner has no idea what a good research route looks like. And that doesn't even include the rest of the gameplay, where your empire suddenly collapses, because you have expanded too much and your people are annoyed, and the tech to pacify them is light years away.
So, to conclude: ES is decent enough I guess, if you have the time and dedication to spend at least 50 hours figuring out all its internal mechanisms. I hope ES 2 is more newbie friendly and perhaps introduces the individual races in a sort of "endless" campaign like they did with Endless Legend. ES 1 just feels to samey for me to invest more time into it and the combat system is too arbitrary for my taste. I want more variation in ships and weapons. Why does a completely organic race use the same weapons as a fleet from Earth or technologically advanced researchers? Why are beam weapons just laser blasts and not actual beams? At least change the colour of some weapons...and give different races different support craft. Maybe organic suicide bombers. Spore launchers. And also boarding torpedoes. The sky is the limit.

Cities in Motion 2 - a disappointing upgrade from the original.
In the Cities in Motion franchise you take control of a public transit company, and attempt to meet the transportation needs of various cities.  You are given specific goals from the City and from other people in the city as 'side quests'.
The campaign mode in CIM2 is very disappointing compared to the first game.  In CIM1, every senario starts in a completely different situation for each city included, and had many tasks to be completed for each one.  So even though you may play in the same city more than once, the situation changes enough to make it interesting.  In CIM2 there are only 5 cities in the campaign, which is not a big problem, except how those cities are used makes it disappointing.  First, each senario typically only has one mail goal, which is usually pretty simple, such as attain a certain level of coverage, or company value growth.  The real problem comes when you return to a city later in the campaign, you are playing in the exact same city you left, with everything you already completed still there ready to go.
There are some good things about this game.  The graphics engine is definitely improved, although the overall user interface is not really improved.  Cities will grow and change over time.  For people who really enjoy micromanagement, you can set very specific schedules for each line you create.  You can also create custom metro trains for each line, however I do wish there was a method to save each custom train for easier purchasing and managing.
The game is still fun to play, but I would only recommend buying it when it is on sale.

A couple things:
1) Every game is in some way a Grind, but this game goes beyond GTA levels of Grind (What I view as the basis of grind that makes a game garbage. There are over 200 mechs in the game with roughly 70 unique styles. The game rewards heavily for completing a full set of one mech series. However, in the amount of time I've invested into the game, I've purchased three mechs total - the bulk of which was from my tutorial money, which is the only real time you will be getting any decent cash in the game.

As I said, way too much of a grind.
2) I keep hearing a lot of people who invested real money into this game complaining about being screwed over when items they paid for were removed from the game - primarily in a manner where they recieved practically nothing compared to the value spent on the item. Overall, I enjoyed the game... enough. It was no Hawken, but Hawken is dead so it's not like it matters. However, I give it a not recommended because the negatives just horribly outweigh the positives for this game right now, and probably will continue to do so, as this is a free to play game, and when haven't free to play developers been greedy in recent memory?

So this game isn't even close to as good as the "old school" NES games that I grew up playing.  After the first or second level I still had a mostly positive look on this game but as I continued to play it and got deeper into the “experience” my opinion of the title quickly did a complete 180.  Bosses that are just nothing but extra life stealers masked as damage sponges and tend to have a large array of weapon projectiles that can kill you instantly even while trying to avoid their fire.   Common enemy types of all ranges are very damage spongy while you are not, your vehicle’s inability to take any kind of fire even on normal is pathetic and an artificial difficulty addition that is unwanted and poorly designed.  Larger enemy types can literally one shot you from across 2 full screens and you have zero ability to know where the shot will come from because YOU can not see the shooter.  Projectiles are some of the most broken that I can remember in recent memory, more then 50% of the enemy types have homing projectiles which will follow you for literal MILES and turn along with you as you attempt to break the lock which is impossible, all you can do is ride it out and hope you survive long enough and avoid getting stuck in the game’s horrible level geometry.  Later levels have you pitted against flame thrower enemies, which normally you wouldn’t worry about.  In this “game” however fire units do INSANE damage to you and perhaps the best part is it’s also damage-over-time, something that an “old school” game like this should never have.  It sure is “FUN” when you’re pitted against multiple of the harder to kill flame thrower vehicles and you’re just killed by DOT rather then the actual hits, that sure is FUN and BALANCED right?  On top of everything else hitting you, splash damage is a significant threat as 80% of the projectiles fired at you have more then 90% of their damage go to you should the shot miss and impact next to you.
The vehicle handling is something out of......god I don't even know how to categorize it, it's awful, never knew an OLD SCHOOL game could put the player in so many situations where you literally roll over, and before you say anything yes I am using a 360 controller.  If you thought Borderlands or GTA4 had some of the worst driving controls in history think again, this title by far takes the gold trophy for flat out being the worst handling vehicle and driving mechanics in any game Period.  You will get stuck on every single surface and all while being shot at 99% of the time, the game takes far too long to spawn you while your sitting there on your back like a turtle getting your stomach shot off only to be spawned 1 inch from your current position and be shot at instantly.  You either get stuck on OR you careen off of the side of the many cliffs and mountain sides because, again, your vehicle handles so poorly and unwieldy that you will have to fight your game to retain control, NO proper “old school” top down shooter has ever had this issue.  One of this title’s biggest sins is the one that a few games do and that is making the player fight the controls rather then the enemies in the game universe.  If you want to turn your vehicle around you need an entire city block’s worth of room.  While using a controller is useful and somewhat better you may be better off sticking with the keyboard and mouse since you have the ability to use what the game calls “tank controls” which helps the crappy driving controls a bit but if you’re using a controller you are stuck with the horrible controls.
Level objectives range from ok to just plain ridiculous, oh and be ready for more then 50% of your total mission objectives, per mission, be timed because nothing says old school like totally arbitrary and pointless mission failing timed mission objectives.  OH yeah and having to watch the same cutscenes over and over and over and over without any ability to skip.  Later missions last upwards of up to 20-40 + minutes and should you die multiple times due to bull crap enemy sight lines or just unfair numbers/projectile spam then have fun REDOING the entire level over for an unknown amount of time until you get lucky and finish it.  There are no checkpoint systems or in game save functions that any normal PC game would have, since this is a poor SEGA console port you get none of the most basic PC game functions.  Speaking of cutscenes the voice acting is quite over the top and after a while grinds on you, normally cheesy lines are funny but really the voice actors are trying FAR too hard to make this title sound serious.
While on the subject of having to replay the same mission over and over and over and over and over, the later missions namely 8-9 have some of the steepest balancing curves that I’ve seen in a game labeled “old school”.  The difficulty spike isn’t even fair it is a cliff face there is ZERO progression and you slam your head against a wall of every single difficult enemy in the entire game thus far AND you are in tunnels and small rooms with zero room to maneuver your horribly controlling vehicle and will die to impossible to avoid fire by everything.  Level 9 is quite literally a battle of attrition as it is only a matter of time before you run out of lives after being killed 5 times (on Normal) by honestly bull crap enemies and rooms that simply have you pitted against impossible to avoid fire and odds.  Then later after you’re down to your last life or two you’re expected to do a battle royal in a small disk shaped elevator while the enemies get progressively more and more impossible as the “ride” progresses.  Since your vehicle handles like complete garbage and you have very little effective ordinance compared to your enemies, which by the way you LOOSE every time you die so enjoy trying to beat some hard miniboss/bosses with your starting gun.  Perhaps the best part about dying is that unlike harder games like Ikaruga that give you back your weapons within a timely manner after you die this “old school” game does not, in fact after you die you may not even SEE a single upgrade.  Unlike almost every single old school and wanna-be old school shooter worth its salt you can not gain extra lives through score/coins whatever so have fun just having 4 or 5 and a 6th if you’re lucky enough to find the 1UP in only a few levels, they aren’t even in every level.
There is an RPG like leveling up system but you level up so slowly at least once you pass maybe level 10 that it becomes moot.  The items that you unlock are not all that useful and more then half of them are disposable, which all RPGs fall into the trap of having 1 or 2 good skills and the rest being filler for the skill tree.  Since it takes you so long to actually get anything useful you’re also halted from using more then 1 or 2 until much later in the levels so you’re even limited on what you can bring to the fight which is not saying much quite honestly.  The developers expect you to try all of the other vehicles which for me is around 8 or so but it’s large amount given the fact that your skills and levels DO NOT transfer over from character to character so have fun being on the lowest level if you decide to play with another character.  I honestly can not say that I’m looking forward to that especially since I’d have to go through the entire game over again each time with each character.
The coop that this title offers is really nothing to write home about, rather then following basic SMART design choices the devs chose to allow teammates to hit one another with their vehicles. Along with that you and your team do not share pickups so if you see a weapon upgrade you’d either grab it first or watch as all 3 of your teammates tries to get it first, this design flaw also encompasses health pickups as well.

The game certainly seems fun in theory, but I can rarely get through a whole level before it crashes and loses my progress. This seems to be a common problem, and the fixes/workarounds are hit-and-miss at best.

I played Endless Legend before I played Endless Space and I think that more than anything is why I don't care for ES as much. The one aspect that I really enjoy a lot more is the tech, in that it's much bigger and more varied and their is more to change and customize on your ships than the units in EL. That said the tech tree is also a hurdle as you either have to play several starter games to get a feel for it (like almost every other aspect of this game really) or sit and read through dozens of tiny tool tips to figure out what everything does and where you should be focusing your research. I find both games lack in diplomacy a bit. I found Endless Legend's tech tree to be easier to understand and better paced. I felt like I knew where I needed to be at a given point in the game while in Endless Space there is just too much to really know how and where to focus my research, though given enough play throughs I'm sure I'll figure it out.
Also, the ability of enemy fleets to just appear in the middle of your empire due to warp jumps is a bit of a strain. It might be an interesting tactical crisis occassionally, but I prefer a game that lets me plan ahead, rather than having to garrison everything.
Also just as in EL, the restrictions on army size are annoying, but seem worse here as there doesn't appear to be a way for armies to reenforce one another. So if your enemy has tech giving him a larger fleet size, you either can't fight him, or you have to watch fleet after fleet die just to weaken his fleet enough for one of yours to beat it.
Lastly, just as in EL, the tactical battles are a draw back for me. I much prefer the sort of abstracted combat of other 4X style games. I don't need a battle mini-game to drag down an already long and slow genre.
Over all, I recommend you go for either Galactic Civ 2, or Endless Legend instead of this. The former because I feel it does space 4x better, and the latter because it's basically a clone of Endless Space that does everything better.

I like the Steam Controller but it is really hit-or-miss as to whether or not it will work with any particular game. That is even the case with games that fully support controllers. If you are patient enough to really dig deep into the many layers of settings you can configure for the controller, you will be able to dial it in and optimize your experience. The problem is that Steam is constantly updating the software for the controller so the settings you dialed in one week might not work the next. In fact, any particular setting you might be accustomed to using could be removed or altered at any time.
It's also possible that any given update will just break the compatibility with a game that you had no problems with before. I've been playing Fallout 4 for months. I had the controller dialed in so that I could use the gyro for precise aiming. This was working really well. Aiming was very natural with the configuration I was using. But then, without warning, the gyro became extremely twitchy. It was completely dysfunctional. There are some setting you are supposed to adjust to removed the twitchiness, but I've moved through the entire range and have not been able to get rid of it.
I mostly use the touch pads for camera and movement control. I set the left thumbstick to serve as the D-pad. This might seem weird but it actually works well for me. It allow me to keep my thumbs in a natural and relaxed position the entire time I'm playing.
However, without the functional gyro for precise aiming, this controller looses much of its utility. For that reason, I can't really recommend it.

I personally think that this controller has potential. The controller itself has functioned well for me ever since I bought it though the usb cable it came with was way too small, and broke pretty fast since it had to bend
There are a lot of features, but overall I think the design itself is fine except for a problem with the Left Bumper, and right bumper buttons. Maybe my hands are too small but they feel way too stiff for my liking, and seem to require stress on your fingers which can lead to pains after prolonged use. It could just be I have small hands though (the furht back trigger buttons are fine, and I had no issues with them).
All of this aside I don't think I would recommend this controller right now. I believe it used to be 40 dollars, or less, but now it's 50 dollars, still 10 dollars cheapers than your strandard controllers, but this controller seems to be trying to fit a niche market that doesn't even exist. Who is this meant for at 50 dollars? Why does it take batteries? Why does it have to be a touch pad? Why do we have to use big picture mode, and get rid of the convenient overlay that doesn't make games lag, or have trouble loading? There are some serious design flaws with this controller that make it unecessarily restricting. A controller that's about customization in it's software doesn't change the fact that many, many, many games are simply better with a controller that has 2 analog sticks, or a mouse and keyboard. It takes far too long to understand how the software works effectively, and steam isn't making sure that it works with a lot of games, or games start supporting it. Why make a 50 dollar controller, and not even back it in any of you titles? I could ramble on, but I think my point is made.
To not be completely negative I would like to make some suggestions. My biggest one would be to find a way to make the touchpad interchangable with with another analog stick. This wouldn't require a complete change in controller design, it simply makes the controller work for more games, appeal to more audiences, and could improve the experience as whole. I would even for as far as to say it would be better than most normal controllers if there were a way to interchange the touchpad. Also adding a built in battery pack should just be common place at this point. They work better, last almost as long, you don't have to turn off your controller every time to conserve battery life, you don't risk damaging the controller over time by having to take it apart to put in batteries, etc. I'm not sure how people still even defend batteries anymore. It just seems like a ploy to help keep battery companies in business when they are required for controllers. And that is about it.
Overall conclusion: The potential is there, but is simply not useful for anything besides a few nice features it has as extras. It has cool ideas, it has customization, and shows how it can be used effectively. This controller is definitely the next step for controller design in general, but the forced use of a touchpad simply doesn't make sense. I have never seen someone want to use their touchpad on their laptop over a mouse, or controller. This is leaps better than most trackpads, but doesn't mean it still isn't inferior to most other forms of controls out there. Other companies should take note when designing a controller from now on, and things like software to customize your controller, extra buttons for hot keys, gyroscopes, haptic feed back, etc. would make your controller stand out a lot more. Just as long as your don't make it a touch pad as a tradeoff.
