This game is half amazing, half meh. The meh is that the developers have very little veriety in their game mode arsenal: its 12v12 deathmatch (skirmish), 12v12 capture and hold bases (conquest), or 12v12 king of the hill (domination). Escort is basically a game mode where you follow around a slow as dirt assault mech with no weapons and no sense of self-preservation around the map, either blowing it up or using your entire team as meat shields are your only strategies to with, really. The newest game mode, which I can't even remember the name of right now, has one stupid exploit that players take advantage of. Faction Warfare is a joke, either choose Clans or your going to get completely wrecked.
Make no mistake, I absolutely love mechwarrior games. I own MW4: Mercs (considered by many the best in the series) and MW3, which is my personal favourite. I like this game as well, but some of the mechanics are a it meh. For instance, the amount of C-Bills you recieve per game is basically based on how useful you are during the match, combining damage, scouting, capturing bases and so on. The problem I have is that some of the people who play this game play like they don't know that it is a TEAM GAME, and that certain mechs have certain areas that they are best suited for.
Take Assault mechs for instance. Their big, bad, slow as dirt and can pack weapon configurations of pure annihilation that can melt the face off of other mechs with a single alpha-strike. Why the hell would you then buy an assault mech and fit it out with Long Range Missiles?!? LRM's are meant as support weapons, not main weapons. They are more useful on medium or heavy mechs, as their overall payload cannot reach that of an assault. Assaults are tanks, they are meant to be in the front and in the thick of the fight, not sitting in the back holding down the fire button and yelling at everyone to hold locks. In higher tiers, missile boats are virtually useless anyway as the players have learned how to avoid locks, making you nothing but a waste of space on the team, good only for drawing fire.
My advice for new players is to save up c-bills for a mech in the medium to heavy range, going for one that has high-mounted weapons. Avoid relying on LRM's and Don't buy a mech and then sell it a few games later because it sucks, even the worst mech in the game is a force of nature when piloted correctly and you will only learn to drive it right with practice. Keep your engine rating in the 250-300 range for a while, as those engines require no external heat sinks and are by far the most versatile, and whatever you do, DO NOT SELL THEM. Having the engines in stock means you dont have to waste hundreds of thousands of c-bills re-buying crap. Engine ratings lower or higher are for specialized builds, something new players really shouldn't worry about.
There are a few tricks too, like jump-sniping, constant movement and, the most important, torso twisting. Jump sniping is a little hard these days due to cockpit shake from jump jets, but the shake stops when you begin to fall back down to the ground. This tactic is only viable for light mechs though, and watch out for leg damage. This is not meant to be a static game, or Turret-Warrior online as some would refer to it. You need to constantly be moving with your team or you are going to be out-manuevered. The best strategy that works overall is to keep close to the assault mechs and protect them from light mechs until they reach the front, then follow them into the fray. That does not mean give them a back rub. If youre entire screen is filled with the back of another mech, you are too close. You can kill your own teamates by blocking their retreat. Dont be that guy.
The last is Torso Twisting. spreading damage is crucial to stay alive. With a standard engine, your goal is to twist your center torso away from the enemy. The damage spreads to all components hit instead of dumping into just one, so instead of taking 9 damage from a Large Laser to the Ceneter, you get 3 damage on your Center, 3 on a side torso, and 3 on the arm. It is entirely possible to survive while your center torso is stripped of armor and completely red just from torso twisting. Be careful though, as some mechs with long profiles can over-twist, becoming larger and easier to hit targets. You also want to conscider what direction to twist depending on the mech and your loadout. Some mechs like the Hunchback have the large majority of their weapons in one component or on one side of the mech. If that component is destroyed, you lose all of your firepower. It also goes for large amounts of arm-mounted weapons, as a destroyed torso will instantly destroy the arm it is connected to as well.
Extra Light engines, refered to as XL engines, are different. The XL engine takes up more slots, spreading into the side torsos, but is several tons lighter. The only ways to blow up a mech with a standard engine are to blow off both the legs, destroy the cockpit or, the most common cause of death, destruction of the center torso and, therfor, the mechs engine. Since the XL spreads to the side torsos, losing either torso is fatal to an Inner Sphere mech. Clan mechs require both side torsos to be destroyed for their XL engines, so keep that in mind. I would suggest to new players to stay away from XL engines for a while, as they are very expensive and you need to have a grasp of torso twisting to be effective with them.
I hope this helps anyone that is truly interested in playing the game, and follow the number 1 rule of all games: HAVE FUN!

Battletech used to be this thing id see alot of or hear about as a kid in the 80's but never really got into (i was a D&D person myself) But I got to play a few games based on the IP over decades and often found them overly complicated and somewhat 'tricky' to play, i was just a kid after all and things like Mechwarrior 2 scrambled my teenage brain (granted any sort of simulator did that back then).
We'll a few years back a friend got me to download and play MWO Online, and like my old experiences with other variants based on the IP i found it tricky. But after a short but steepish learning curve I got into it and now find it quite satisfying in its genre and well worth a go for anyone that likes the idea of a game where you pilot multi ton robots around a battle field shooting weapons at each other.
Its a little grindy when it comes to getting the ingame currency to buy mechs, but they have regualr events that give you c-bills and items, even mechs and mech bays without the need to sink real money into the game. Any new player should give the Inner Sphere mechs a go first, they are generally weaker (which is not true) by concensous compared to Clan mechs but they cost ALOT less and havent had their weapons nerfed radically over the years. Ignore the people who say Clan mechs are OP, IS mechs are just as compedative if played to their strengths (quirks) and ive been wrecked by IS just as much as by Clan while piloting my Clan mechs.
Above all MWO is a team game, if you work with each other, play cautiously, call out targets in Voice Coms and co-operate you'll stomp a team who doesnt 90% of the time. You have to watch the battle flow and move with it to succeed.
Recently PGI has taken alot of flak from veteran players to their new Skill Tree and the recent drop in the ratings on Steam are because of these minority 'whales' rage reviewing or changing their reviews to negative. Most complaints from the veterans are from refunds for in game currency and the 'chore' of reskilling 100's of mechs they might own... which for the majority of players like myself isnt a problem and is also something you can do casually and over time. Antoher complaint these 'whales' use its is to complicated, when infact its a simple web skill tree with values that can be take and previewed in a mechs loadout before commiting with the occasional gate node, basicly anyone who would find the Skill Tree complicated might find Mechwarrior Online too complicated in the first place.
The old skill system comprised of leveling up around using mech Xp to activate 8 generic performance boosting basic skills on 3 variants of the same mech chasis (which you had to buy even if you onnly wanted to use teh one mech variant), then leveling up around 4 Elite performance boosting skills (one of which was basicly pointless) on the same 3 chasis which would double the base 8 skills values and then let you get an extra module slot for the Master skill after doing so.
So yeah... Its a good game, that takes a little investment in time and effort to master and 'get gud' in but is still fun when you do.

Excellent game! I bought this maybe a year or so ago and it's quickly become one of my most played on Steam (probably second most played).
PROS:
* Really good building system
It's really easy to build huge elaborate structures and environments with good considerations for physics (you can't place floating blocks etc). There's a vast amount of bricks and colors in the base game to choose from.
* Great modding scene
There are so many mods for the game from new bricks and colors to whole new scripts and gamemodes.
* Online play
Despite what other reviews say, there's still a pretty huge online userbase. Of course it depends what time of day you play but normally when I play there's around 30 players on the top 6 servers and then 6-10 on the rest. The community is far from dead and the massive variety in gamemodes allow for repeated play.
The servers themselves vary in the gamemodes from freebuild (just building whatever you want) to minigames like team deathmatch, racing, roleplay, mining etc.
* Support
Although the developer doesn't release regular updates any more (the game is over 10 years old after all) there's still lots of support and resources available on the blockland forums.
* Programming
The game has a built-in event driven programming engine that lets you program blocks to do different things. For example you can program a block to show a message on-screen when it's clicked. This allows you to create amazing complex builds which really expands the amount of things you can do.
CONS:
* Toxic community
This is a term that's thrown around a lot about most games but unfortunately this is the case for blockland too. The community, on the whole, is quite nice but of course there's always those few people who ruin it for the rest. Since interaction is optional you don't have to talk to these people, you can just play the game and ignore chat or play singleplayer.
* Server Staff
Since each server is privately owned there's on universal set of rules to follow. Due to this, and often the young age of certain players, rules can often seen strange and you can get banned for what seems to be no reason. Being banned only stops you playing on THAT server however and does not stop you connecting to other servers.
Overall I would 100% recommend this game. It's one of the better building games and with the community and servers it makes it all the more fun. At the time of writing, I have close to 200 hours and I've barely scratched the surface of what's possible!

Ignore my hours, I've played this game before it was released on steam. For 10 years to be exact.
Before I give an example as to why you shouldn't buy the game as is, let me give you a quick disclaimer that everything the trailer shows is possible within the game. But note that the trailer is heavily showcasing multiplayer servers with unique bricks, addons, and colorsets. You can obtain these through the forums or through blockland glass but please don't go into the game thinking you can jump into any of the servers shown, because as of today you can't.
Part 1. General Gameplay. It's like legos on the internet. That's honestly it. You can go alone on your own server, build and event to your hearts content. There is a brick limit but chances are you won't be hitting that on your first day, least your first month of playing. You can join multiplayer servers that host a veriety of minigames that you can join ranging from mini empires to deathmatches. The quality of the server depends weather the host actually put any time or thought into their game so please don't expect a quality server on your first go. There are also a number of custom addons available to you to download and enhance/make building easier. More on that later.
Part 2. Servers. Mentioned above, servers allow you to create and host a server for others to join. If you don't know how to port forward then you're in luck because blockland happens to use a handy little feature called universal plug and play which allows your friends to connect even if you haven't port forwarded. Keep in mind this feature doesn't always work.
Part 3. Community. Oh boy where do i begin. To summarize this, just stay away from the forums. You don't need to be there unless you're viewing other people's builds, downloading addons, etc. Don't make an account and don't post. You don't need to, you're not missing out on anything special, just don't. Trust me.
Part 4. The state of the game and it's future. Now here's the part where i tell you about the legacy that was V20, but first a little back story. Blockland has had several states or versions which have significantly changed the way the game looks and playes. I'd say the best playable version that was available throughout the years was V18-20. Those versions specifically hit the pinnacle of what this game and engine was capable of and what we achieved within it. Back then there was an easier way to download addons and talk to friends. Think virtual steam for blockland. This was known as RTB or Return To Blockland. It was ran by a guy who's name is too complicated to spell. One day he had enough claiming he put more effort into blockland than the lead developer named Badspot did. The two manchildren fought and it resulted with RTB service being canceled and the developer for RTB being banned? (Can't remember if he was banned, or left. Either way he's gone for good). There were many attempts to substitute an RTB for the longest time but it was useless as there were so many that it cluttered and divided players up until 2015-2017 with Blockland Glass, a suitable RTB replacement. Kinda. Anyways that was nothing compared to the ♥♥♥♥♥torm that was "V21, the Shadows and Shaders update". You see, before this update blockland was at a point where players were content with the state of the game. We had a consistent playerbase and a slew of maps to play on. Oh yeah i forgot to mention that part, you could create your own custom maps and enviorments for the game at that time but the shadow and shader update got rid of maps completely, and opted for the "♥♥♥♥ you and your maps, stop being lazy and build♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; route. It's ironic considering bad spot wanted to make the game prettier but he get's mad when you compare it to any other sandbox title in terms of how the game looks vs how the game plays. Anyway back to the subject, shadows and shaders. This update was teased some time after (let's just call the dev of RTB, RTB guy for now) RTB guy left. Players were happy to see their game getting a much needed face lift but players were also VERY displeased because this meant that maps had to go. The community split and players left. Soon after V21 many players slowly started to leave, and many of those players were content creators so you can imagine what happened next.
Part 5. Here and Now. We're slowly starting to turn those gears again content wise and builds (that people spend a good amount of time on) have never looked better. But the playerbase is still substantially low. I wouldn't recommend this game anymore in it's current state and it doesn't seem like we'll be getting any new updates...at all...

I love this controller. I think the negative reviews are too harsh. The design is different, but like any other device (i.e. keyboard and mouse) you have to adjust to it's feel. I've used this controller for a while now, easily over a year, most of the crashing bugs HAVE BEEN FIXED.
Pros:
+ Endless configuration options - You can have practically unlimited keybindings on the controller, especially thanks to action sets.
+ No need for a right joystick - mousepad > stick
+ No need for a D-pad - It can be bound however you want
+ You can play ANY game with it, I haven't found one incompatible game yet.
+ You don't need to get up to do anything more than type in your PC password.
+ The built in keyboard is the next best thing to an actual keyboard.
+ Doesn't even need to be used on games, controls everything about the PC.
+ I bought this controller for 30$, used. No issues, and can still be bought at this price. Try finding anything better for cheaper.
There's a long list, but these are the main points.
Cons:
- No preset controls for individual games. It would be nice to launch the game and have it ready, you can always download another person's configuration while in-game, it should start with the most popular configuration (personal opinion). Otherwise just configure it yourself and save it.
- Controls get deleted every once in a while... this can get annoying if you don't save your controls.
- Saving controls online doesn't work well, I've stuck to saving controls locally.
- Big Picture mode can be annoying, can occasionally cause your game to unsync it's controls and force you to reboot the game. Not nearly as common as it used to be though, keep working on it.
- Should be able to open keyboard without steam open, or even when I'm typing in my password to the computer.
This is truly a full list of the cons, I wouldn't complain about anything else.
It's also good to note that setting steam to always run as administrator fixes most other issues. (i.e. unable to click certain things outside of games)

This is a difficult review because it depends on the type of gamer you are.
I have three of these controllers, and have tried VERY hard to love it, but alas cannot recommend it for hardcore (LONE) gamers. I say lone because if you use Steam strictly for couch gaming, then you will enjoy having a few of these laying around far more then someone who wants a controller to play first-person shooters, strategy, or action games MORE SO if you play them competitively.
This controller is best compared to the original Wii controller. While it's terrible to use when you want to kick back and relax to your favorite game (as it feels like a little TOO much work for half the results of mouse and keyboard or even PS4/Xbox controller.), it's a great controller to have a good time with a couple of friends (as that frustration will translate in a much more positive/fun light when couch gaming.), especially since most couch games available aren't about quick precision aim and tuned reflexes, but more about creative gameplay and an arcade feel.
I will say that the frustation felt using this hardware may be less the controllers fault, and more that 90% of games out there are not made with trackball controlls in mind. It's kind like trying to unscrew a phillips head with a flat head screwdriver, while it IS possible, you'll find it more of a hassle to do so then just picking up the proper tool.
While I understand that there is HUGE amount of customization available for the controller, ranging from various sensitivity tools all the way to a gyroscope, no matter how many hours I spend trying to get the feel JUST right it always manages to feel off and clumsy. Most of the time when I sit down to game using this, I spend more time in the menu adjusting settings then actually playing the game itself.
All this stated, I'm going to continue holding my finger crossed, hoping that the kinks will be ironed out eventually as this has the potential to be many steps above a console controller. When that time comes I will change my review to a thumbs up, as of right now I can't recommend it solely based on a dying breed of couch gamers. Especially at the current price tag.

Cities in Motion 2 (CM2) is published by Paradox, so that should tell you three things: first, it has a steep learning curve; second, it has a horrific UI and mind-boggling design decisions; and third, it will take something mundane and make it addictive. CM2 really has a problem with the second of these. For example, the victory conditions of the campaign maps are "Have x% coverage". Unfortunately for the player, "coverage" means nothing like the English word "coverage," and its precise meaning is never explained. This makes the game artificially difficult. Despite these gripes, the game still is entertaining.
While entertaining, and definitely worth the $5 I paid for it, I can't bring myself to recommend this game. This is due in part to the designer's attitude towards DLC ($5 for more busses?) and how its patches focus on niche markets (Mac-only issues, Linux compatibility) despite persistent and well-documented bugs that affect everyone.
TL;DR: Engaging and entertaining, yet buggy, has awful UI, and is worse than an EA game for DLC.

Yet another gem in my Steam Library.
In case you should have a god complex, this game is made for you -
If you don't.. it still is!
Basically you slip into the role of the more or less anti-hero Alex Mercer in the city of Manhattan that was infected by some kind of Virus and is now being controlled by Elite Soldiers called "Blackwatch".
Once you hit the button "Start new campaign" you get thrown right into the Open World with just a few background infos concerning the upcoming story. All you know is that you are Alex Mercer, who has been shot down and fatally wounded and later on got infected by a virus that somehow revived you and gave you shapeshifting abilities and superpowers.
Now he is trying everything he can to find out how all this happened, where it will be going, and how he could possibly end all this by "interrogate" the ones responsible.
Making your way through the story you get sucked in by a good load of interesting twists, challenging bossfights and tons of upgrades for Alex that make him the toughest enemy "Blackwatch" will have to face during the whole infection.
There are plenty of Sidequests to be done - some of them nice and some of them just to keep you busy finishing the game 100%. But if you focus on the Story Quests alone its possible to finish it within ~12 hours on a medium difficulty.
It can be frustrating at times (not just because of the AI) but because of overpowered attacs or wrong set "Mission Failure" parts, but once you've beaten the game it feels really satisfying even without Steam Achievments or cool costume unlocks for Alex Mercer. The gameplay itself is (to me) almost flawless and the possibilities endless due to Alex' powers and the maybe best looking armor in 2009's video games.
With this being said I'd like to leave you the decision if you should get this game on a sale for 5 bucks or just let it be, all I can do is just highly recommend it to everyone who loves a good classic and a game by 'Activision' that is not "Fast and the Furious" nor "Call of Duty" but actually a GOOD game.
A point some people might find interesting- the graphics are not horribly bad but neither outstanding for 2009...something in between should describe it precisely. If graphics don't bother you its a perfect game for a casual afternoon when you are off work and just want to relax..in case you do love good graphics take a look at Prototype 2 ..it has all the features 1 has to offer and even more - will write a review to part 2 aswell once I finished it on Steam.
*Note* I wasn't experiencing any performance problems on my nvidia card but I know that there are massive problems with all AMD cards... and they wont ever fix it I believe so in case you don't have a Nvidia graphics card you might want to play this one on a console.
As always I hope that my review was helpful and written understandable and made it easier for you to decide to buy a game from 6 years ago that is still more foward than todays releases...

The Internet is filled with tons of great free-to-play games these days but a vehicle combat game by Piranha Games Inc. called Mechwarrior Online stands tall above the rest. It is based off the Battletech strategy game universe.
Players each pilot a single BattleMech that they outfit themselves and take into battle in two teams of 12 per side. The arenas seem large and varied, two favourites are: Polar Highlands and HPG Manifold. Polar Highlands is cool because it’s such a wide open landscape for sniping with many trench-like pathways to move into flanks. HPG Manifold is a gigantic moon base satellite designed for close range brawling that is just an awe to behold.
BattleMechs typically weigh between 20 and 100 tons, and fall into one of four weight classes: Light, Medium, Heavy, and Assault. Depending on the hardpoints available for your ‘Mech, you can equip a dazzling area of different weapons configurations and this is where MechWarrior Online really shines. Weapons are split into three major groups: Ballistic, Energy, and Missile.
Ballistic weapons deal instantaneous kinetic damage but require careful consideration due to their reliance on ammunition. Energy weapons consume no ammo but generate significant heat that must be monitored to prevent overheating. Missiles come in both long and short-range variants, and are capable of striking out-of-sight targets with targeting support provided from friendly units.
Battling 12 other ‘Mechs is difficult as is but there is also an internal battle going on at all times with your heat level — when weapon systems run too hot you run the risk of shutting down or even completely detonating. Some trick builds equip the largest alpha damage into one giant blast and it’s very satisfying to just launch incredible damage at an arm and watch it explode right off, or one-shotting an enemy ‘Mech outright.
If any of this piques your interest check out TheB33f on YouTube, he specializes in total ‘Mech destruction — the enemy and himself. Sidenote: I’m proud to say that during this review of MWO I was killed in one alpha strike by TheB33f, maybe it will make a replay highlight.
In the current meta the strongest builds are Laser Vomit and Dakka. I personally prefer auto-cannons and there are two Battlemech’s that really take advantage of the four ballistic hard points required to pull it off.
The Warhammer Black Widow is a heavy Hero ‘Mech that costs real world dollars (approximately $50) but it can equip two AC/5’s and two Ultra AC/5’s. What this translates into is standing and blasting enemy face for about 30 seconds straight until heat becomes a serious issue. It’s basically like peeing lava on someone. The Kodiak is a 100 ton assault ‘Mech that can run a similar but much heavier setup and is a real ‘blast’ to play.
Just because light ‘Mechs are small doesn’t mean that aren’t enjoyable to pilot. Scouting and ECM electronics warfare is also an integral part of the game. In the final minutes when only a few ‘Mechs remaining a single light can dance around the enemy and do precision work with lasers and machine guns. It’s a frickin' spectacle.
MWO has been available since 2013 but recent patches have brought more game modes, and a new skill tree system online. The graphics and sound are both incredible and top-notch and PGI really takes advantage of the CryEngine. From my extensive 1000 hour review I have discovered a small handful of problems with the game.
1. Unstable servers are prone to disconnecting you or not working 100 per cent of the time.
2. The lack of melee is very frustrating. Why can’t a 100 tonne ‘Mech just punt a light ‘Mech like a football? ‘Mechs with hand actuators should be able to punch or wield axes and stuff
3. Intimidating complexity makes this game mostly for ‘nerds or people with patience.

Well this is an unusual game.
You take guns apart down to the last spring or screw and then put all the pieces back together. There are some challenges that make it a game, like doing it as fast as possible or putting the pieces back in the right order without mistake. And then there's the really tough stuff, like puzzles where you have two guns and their parts, and you need to guess which gun each part belongs to. You REALLY need to know every little part in detail to succeed on that one!
There's also shooting ranges, where you can fire some guns and try to complete accuracy or speed challenges.
The game also has interesting features, such as cut-away or x-ray views that let you see the inner workings of the guns as you reload or fire them.
The catch is that you have to really enjoy studying the inner workings of guns and learning about each of their little pieces. I was hoping that the game would make me enjoy that somehow, maybe with some captivating game mechanics, but it's fair to say that you actually have to enjoy this stuff already before you play the game. It's a very niche game for a very specific interest, so if that's not your thing the game probably won't entertain you very long.
But for those people who enjoy guns and studying their parts and mechanics, this game is VERY well done! Every little part is there, the game gives you all the tools you need to study how the guns work, and as I said there are some game mechanics around these things to keep you entertained.
It's really not for everyone, but those who like that sort of stuff should really enjoy it.

This "game" is terribley awkward and counter intuitive in a few ways.  There are two control schemes:  cardinal directions where up is up, down is down, etc., and "tank" controls where up is forward and steering is reletive to the car.  I'm not sure why it's labled "tank" because that's not how a tank works.
Aiming is much easier with the mouse because you can aim directly at a target and there is no spot you can't hit.  With the stick you have notches and gaps that leave dead zones between where your shots go.  If you park in one spot and rotate the gun stick there are spots you can't quite reach.  As a result, you have to try and balance dodging enemy fire with lining up your limited shot lanes.
Then there are the objective markers that don't seem to know where they're going.  They sort of aim you down the road, but suddenly change direction.  It woulsd make more sense if they just pointed at the objective itself rather than try to follow the road.
I suppose if I really worked at it I would eventually get the hang of it, but it's just so annoying and frustrating that I lose interest very quickly.  Just like I could probably eventually learn to ride a bike by sitting bacwards on the handlebars, looking in a mirror, while juggling with one hand.  But that's a lot of effort to learn such a limited use skill set.
Maybe if there were more games like this it would be worth it to learn, but this game alone isn't even very fun to begin with.

There have been multiple reviews that have said it best: the steam controller is weird. The grip can take some time to get used to and the touchpad/ d-pad circles aren't the greatest among controllers. But, after playing with it for some time, I can say that it's grown on me a bit. I've always had a preference for "couch gaming" all my life so sitting at a desk playing video games isn't always the most comfortable/conducive to my enjoyment of PC gaming. With the steam controller, I can lay on my couch/bed/whatever comfortable surface I want to play all the games I love without having to sit at a rigid desk for hours.
The only alternative I like to the steam controller is the Xbox One controller, and the Steam controller scrapes by on its sheer scope of customization. Being unable to play certain games due to the lack of controller support really discouraged my use of the Xbox Controller, but the Steam Controller allows me to keep playing those keyboard-heavy games like Civ 5, Castle Story, Elite: Dangerous, Factorio, and so on.
Another central aspect of my gaming career has been personalization; I love it when a game isn't tailored to a specific demographic but instead allows the player to choose how they get to interact with the game they're playing. Being able to map controls to my liking when the devs or community come close but not quite my style is very appealing to me, and getting a scheme that fits just right is heavenly. All in all, the steam controller is great for the "couch gamer" in you. If you go anywhere near competitive games with this controller you're going to be so disadvantaged against keyboard and mouse, but if you're hanging out and playing games with friends or just low-intensity games then the steam controller may be a good fit for you.

First off, Kudos to the developer for two things: Coming up with an original idea, and not using a demo RPG Maker town as a base for this spammy achievement game.
The Quest for achievements sees you drawn outside of your house, away from your computer, to hunt down sentient Steam Achievements which have gone missing from your favourite games. It starts quite originally, reminiscent of the old text adventure 'Imagination' on the C64. And from there, it quickly goes south, and all of the devs Kudos is stripped away.
The Quest for Achievements is an achievement spam game. You get literally hundred of achievements - over a thousand in fact - for opening chests and chasing steam icons down on the overhead map, with a smidgeon of real time combat thrown in for good measure. The thing is, you don't have to spend scores of hours chasing them down to reach the games goal of getting 999 to open the portal to the final boss: There's a cave in the Scorched Earth zone you can go into, open a chest, and retreat from, again and again and again. Every time you do this, you'll get ten achievements.
Once you've hit 1004, look for a flashing beacon in each of the four zones and walk up to it - that'll take you to to 1008. Then enter the final zone and kill the last enemy, leave through the portal and that's your final two cheevs.
Now, uninstall, and cry gently as you wonder what your life has become playing such absolute garbage as this, in order to raise an arbitrary number on your gamer profile, which only you care about.

Take on the role of Alex Mercer, a man who has no recollection of what’s happened to him or why, or how he came to acquire the shape-shifting powers he now possesses. Find the people who’ve done that to you and make them pay.
The game -action, adventure, open worldish- sounded fun and looked fun, and I was very hyped to play it. I was also very disappointed when I finally did. Controls, though a bit wonky, are not difficult. You can change your body “at will” to attack enemies and destroy things, and when I say “at will” I mean you only have so many things you can change into. I think the most fun aspect of the game is the fact that you can ‘consume’ random people and then turn into them, and run/jump your way around pretty freely.
I’d say the graphics are dated, but it’s an oldish game, so it gets a slight pass for that. What it doesn’t get a pass for, however, is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ performance. For a 2009 game that should run like a charm on my computer, it sure worked like crap even at the lowest settings, lagging worse than Assassin’s Creed III - and at least that one had a reason to lag (no “low” video settings, hey). I’m also not particularly fond of the reddish/orangeish filter they use on later cinematics and gameplay time, I find it bothersome to look at.
Your character is overpowered, which is not bad in itself if you like an easy game, but it does make things boring after a while as it’s all the same; to tell the truth, it reminded me a little of God Hand for some reason, only that one was actually fun to keep playing. With Prototype, I did the first few missions and was bored out of my mind - that along with the slightly eye-hurting graphics and slight, random spikes of lag made the game truly disappointing.
The gameplay is pretty repetitive otherwise. Fight a bunch of bad guys, have them call in tanks and an airstrike, be chased, shake them off, rinse and repeat with a moderate variety of enemies and mutants to fight against.
It’s not a completely unplayable game, mind you. If you’re extremely bored and want to play something that doesn’t pose a huge challenge, it’s not a bad game and could even be considered entertaining. I liked the city, the chance to explore it some, the general idea of the game was good (though the story was a bit hit and miss with me), but the execution left a lot to be desired.
Perhaps if the game had lagged a bit less I would have enjoyed it a bit better.
I wouldn’t recommend this game, but I would certainly not tell you to steer clear from it either, as I feel it could be a lot more fun if you can actually play it sans the lag.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a cyberpunk, stealth, R.P.G. developed by Eidos Montreal and published by Square Enix. Set in the year 2027 you are Adam Jensen, an ex-S.W.A.T. specialist who has been handpicked to oversee the security of one of America's most experimental biotechnology firms, Sarif Industries, and it's your job to safeguard company secrets. However, things quickly take a turn for the worse when an elite black-ops team abruptly breaks in and kills the very scientists you were hired to protect thus changing everything you thought you knew about your job. During the assault, Adam is not only critically injured but the woman that he loves is also killed in the process. Adam soon awakens to find that his life has been saved but at a tremendous cost as most of his body has been replaced with highly advanced cybernetics leaving Jensen to ponder the question..."Am I man or machine?". Determined to bring justice to those responsible for the attack on Sarif Industries...Jensen hits the pavement tracking down one clue after the next in his pursuit of the villains.
Aside from the excellent story, one of the best features of Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the fantastic gameplay that consists of a first person shooter with heavy R.P.G. elements. Fear not for just because this is a F.P.S., that does not limit how you proceed through this game. Instead of kicking down doors and running into every room with guns blazing one could choose the non-lethal stealth approach and actually go through the game from start to finish without killing a single person. Whether you decide to kill or not, the stealth aspect of this game alone is just incredible and is also where the gameplay of this title really shines. Choosing just how to play the title, as there are always multiple paths to success, really is up to you. As a dedicated R.P.G., Jensen is awarded experience points as tasks are completed during the narrative which can be spent on a vast array of character augmentations and upgrades for your cybernetics that unlock a number of new abilities. Fighting prowess, hacking, stealth...these are just a few examples of the many skills that can be enhanced for Jensen. Ultimately, it's up to you to determine how you want your character to evolve based on how you want to play the game. Speaking of the narrative, always remember that choices are at play as you must face the consequences of your actions as one decides how the story unfolds for Jensen. There are many points in the title where you must make heavy decisions with far reaching implications so decide wisely.
Graphically speaking, I may be a little bias because I love all things about cyberpunk so naturally I completely enjoyed the look of this game. Deus Ex: Human Revolution has at this point been out for a couple of years and the game still looks great to this day. It does a fantastic job of immersing you in a futuristic vision of the world with the gorgeous set pieces such as the vehicles, buildings, tech and even the clothing that the characters wear in the game. Also, the dark colors and subtle tones really help to flesh out the cyberpunk environment of Deus Ex. And since this is a Square Enix title, the C.G. rendered cutscenes are of course spectacular as they always are in Square Enix games. The sound quality is top notch as is the phenomenal soundtrack which I listen to quite often. In summary, Eidos managed to really paint a beautiful picture of the not too distant future for this game.
This title had been available for quite some time before I finally got around to playing it and I regret waiting so long to try it because I absolutely loved Deus Ex: Human Revolution from the beginning to the end. Jensen is just so freaking cool! Going down the list...the story keep me on the edge of my seat at all times, the action and gameplay mechanics were excellent and the soundtrack was fantastic. Like I mentioned before, you could go through this game on a killing spree and given what happened to you that would be completely understandable or one could take the more zen approach and choose the non-lethal course of action so the replayability of this title is very high. There are also quite a few Steam Achievements, some of them hidden, and Steam Trading Cards to collect as well. Deus Ex: Human Revolution is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED as it just does so many things right in so many different genres. You should..augment..your Steam library with this title immediately...see what I did there?! Aww shut up that was funny!

I have spent a lot of time on this game, possibly to much and for the most part have always found it enjoyable. The only negatives I have found is some of the prima donnas on the forums and a minor group of old school players who for some reason hate all change but even though I disagree with them they show the community is passionate about the game :-)
There has been a lot of crying since the most recent patch because some people feel like their favourite mechs have been nerfed or they are being forced to grind credits to get skills etc.
On mechs being 'nerfed' some of these people are probably unlocking the wrong skill points - pouring everything into fire power muwahahaha MORE POWER and then wondering why their mech has the agility of rock or the armour of a wet paper bag. Others may have a legit moan but this is a first release of a major new game mechanic PGI have already said that the skills are likely to be tweaked but this will be based on data from the game not forum rants. Yes folks they will base changes on facts not alternative facts / opinions - just because 20 people agree with someone on a forum thread doesnt mean they are right when you look at actual data.
In regards to the credit grind you no longer have to buy modules or three variants of a chassis in order to master it. that is a massive credit saving. Yes you have to pay credits to unlock skill points but PGI had to have some cost associated with skills because of removing the modules and the x3 requirement. We all like free to play but they need money to keep the game going and some of this comes from people buying premium time. Its common sense that they needed to do this.
For example, I purchased 8 mechs in this weekends sale at a cost of approx 35 mill credits. Before the patch I would have needed to spend another 70 mill credits to get the additional variants needed to master them.... that is a lot of grinding for a casual player. The 70 mill 'saving' is enough for about 1500 skill points without even considering the cost of modules and speccing the additional unwanted variants I would have previously had to buy with DHS, endo etc to make them even vaguely competitive.
Basically 'evil' pgi have made it cheaper and quicker for me to buy the mechs I want and then they allow me to tweak them how I want... the inconsiderate bstards...
With the skill tree release and the upcoming new tech people should almost consider the game to be in beta again.  The game as of this patch release isnt perfect but it is damn sight closer to where the majority of us as opposed to the vocal minority want it to be.
So do I recommend this game, hell yes, come drive and shoot big stompy mechs with us :-)

As of 5/20/2017 - After seeing a lot of negative recent reviews I think there is a lot of misunderstanding, to try and clear things up.. TL;DR at the bottom.
Non-premium new players will struggle to meet 100,000 cbills/match & 1000 xp/match not counting 'first win of the day' bonus and events.
Want to try out Faction Warfare mode? this will deffinitely interest you, as a drop deck requires 4 mechs (4 respawns worth) that must meet a max tonnage cap.
The cadet bonus that you can do by playing 25 matches in provided-for trial mechs gives you a total of 12,500,000 cbills and 48,000 GXP ('G'lobal experience points you can spend on any mech)
Weapon modules are unique in that they're 'levelled up', 3600xp~ total to do so. Onto the potatos;
Pre skill tree patch:
To obtain a mech you like and to max it out you would need to;
- Buy 3 UNIQUE variants of the mech you like (some 'unique variants were sub-par/frustratingly inferior ie World of Tanks DW german heavy)
- Level all 3 to minimum Basic (14,250 XP)
- Level your favorite one further to Elite (+21,500 XP), which doubles Basic bonuses, then Master (+21,500 XP) to unlock its last module slot. All up it is 57,250 XP.
- Modules (little slot-in items that boost something by 10-12% or add a feature) can set you back the price of a stock light/medium mech, between 3-6mil cbills, to fully module said light/medium mech could easily cost a fully fitted mech two/thrice fold (12-18mil~ - heavies and assaults, particularly clan mech can set you back around 10-16mil on their own). Many newer players could only afford valuable modules like Radar deprivation and Seismic sensor (both 6mil cbills each), then have to constantly swap those around on mechs they wanted to play.
Post skill tree patch:
To obtain a mech you like and to max it out you would need to;
- Buy the mech you want
- Out of the possible 237 total skill tiles to invest in, pick up to 91 in a descending chain in 7 different 'trees'.
- The numbers for this is each Skill Point unlocks 1 tile. 1 Skill point costs 45,000 cbills and 800xp.
To max out a mech will set you back a complete total of 4,095,000 cbills and 72,800XP.
- Modules are now non-existent, they have been factored into the skill tree itself and acquired through investing in their respective trees. Fully mastering a mech will now only set you back the aforementioned amount (4.095mil cbil/72,800xp) Modules and their exorbitant prices are not a thing anymore, they are part of that price.
(TL;DR) Onto the meat;
Knowing this..
Pre-patch would see you grinding a full CW drop deck (4 mechs worth, either for CW or regular play) at the price of around 20-32,000,000x4 cbills and 57,250x4 + approx another 62,000 XP for levelling modules. Not including price of extra variants for mastering favorite mech picks for your deck. Levelling was heavily stepped and distributed across 3 mechs too.
Post-patch would see you grinding a full CW drop deck (4 mechs worth, either for CW or regular play) at the price of around 10-18,000,000x4 cbills and 72,800x4 xp. The XP is dearer, but the cbill investment is -significantly- cheaper. Levelling is now a gradual process, individualized on the one mech too.
Many returning players who have previously invested heavily in modules have come out at a distinct advantage in having mechs maxed out, some having atleast 3,000 HSP (mastered mechs pre-patch were given this currency to re-master them again post patch) which would cover them easily for the next 32 or so mechs, not counting cbill returns from consumables and modules bought after december 3rd.
I won't lie about the complexity of the tree though, its a lot to go through, in my experience so far the lines of progression are very reasonable but with some perseverance you'll come to understand it. I would highly suggest letting 'the dust settle' before judging.
As for MWO itself;
- Good game, bit faster paced than World of Tanks, far less grind. Some events are great, most could use work for newer/less time restricted-players.
- Complicated skill tree will take a while to get use to, but is not unlike many other 'talent tree'esque styles you see in titles like WoW or Path of Exile - instead of flat 5/5 3/5 1/1 etc stacked bonuses its incremental. Still, overwhelming initially.

- Worlds finals premiered last year, slated for this year too. MRBC, BFM (competitions) etc regularly provided too. Player scene stagnated a little particularly for oceanic, but ranked queue coming this year may revive it.
- Not too much strategy involved outside of competitive scene, but deep mechanics in controlling your mech lend a lot to dynamic gameplay in how you approach a fight. Lots of options in mech customization, now moreso with skill tree.
- Several game modes, some more popular than others.. New ones being introduced/others changed over time.
Worth giving it a shot, particularly since the grind has just been shortened. 7.5/10.

I'd been wanting a
since they were announced and received one as a gift in February 2017. Here's my running review.
It has a pleasing visual aesthetic. Overall shape is interesting in that the handles are bulky and rounded compared to some AAA controllers. In that regard, I wonder if it could cause finger or hand fatigue over prolonged periods of use. My typical play sessions last two hours. Thus far fatigue hasn't been an issue.
I'm pleased with the number of buttons, bumpers and paddles on the device. It's a fair number and variety of inputs. The paddles on the back sound a bit clicky when pushed. The buttons, bumpers, triggers and analog stick all actuate very smoothly. Using the left track pad as a directional D-pad is not preferable to the analog stick. It doesn't respond as well as D-pads on conventional controllers. Fortunately the joystick works perfectly for this purpose.
The sensor trackpads work well enough to consider forgoing mouse + keyboard inputs, especially in the intended living room scenario, on the couch in front of a big screen running Steam's "Big Picture" mode. For typing (a primary intended use of these touchpads), the device works surprisingly well! Obviously not as fast or efficient as texting on a smart phone or typing on a keyboard, but I'd say more than acceptable in a pinch. It does fulfill the advertised purpose, albeit slowly.
As for whether the unique input enables control schemes and features for a controller that would normally be exclusive to mouse + keyboard, I've yet to play any games that test that claim significantly. The games I've played thus far mostly are small, action indie titles with very simple interfaces and play modes that don't require much in the way of advanced controls.
Familiarizing myself with the UI of Big Picture mode on Steam is an ongoing process. Working out how to customize, optimize and fully use the controller from one game to the next is an ongoing process. Mapping buttons in game (if said game supports mapping at all) is very convenient. I haven't messed much with controller settings for Steam itself yet.
Wireless connectivity remains 100% stable throughout my usage to date. I'm usually seated at my desk, one or two feet away from the wireless USB receiver.
The controller plays well with games such as
. I was able to keep up with my friends who all used either mouse + keyboard or Xbox controllers.
The fact that they got this sort of functionality on a controller at all is kind of a remarkable feat! The value here really comes out in the proprietary Steam features, the utility of trackpad input and the limited mouse + keyboard functionality on a controller. The extent of that value is still very much to be determined, personally speaking. It is the aspect that I will be focused on most as I update and eventually finalize this review. For now, thumbs up. #1 recommended controller for PC gaming.

First of all I really, REALLY like the idea of this game. As I noticed this game on Steam Greenlight I was really wow'ed and I tried instantly to get in contact with the developer to tell him how I much love his idea. Getting "ingame-achievements" to unlock real Steam Achievements is something new on Steam and that got my attention in the first place!
The plot is simple as that. First of all there is a small intro-level; just go south and go through the portal. Then you're starting in the main city called Starcrest City. There are three areas in this game to explore and to hunt for Steam Achievements.
You have to "catch" (ingame-)achievements with blue catcher-balls which you can buy(*) in the main city - in the middle of the city. If you actually catch one of them, you unlock a real Steam Achievement. Another way to unlock Steam Achievements is to find a chest in one of the three areas in the game where you get ten achievements - respectively - ten Steam Achievements. There are also chests in some caves throughout the three areas. The third ingame way to get Steam Achievements is to find one beacon in each area. You just have to open your eyes to find them - not really that difficult.
In the world of "The Quest for Achievements" you can find several weapons to kill enemies. There are some different kind of swords and other weapons. You also have unlimited "fireballs" as a standard weapon to hit and/or kill enemies. You cannot hurt enemies with catcher-balls; they are just meant to use for catching ingame-achievements. If you kill an enemy you will get coins(*), mostly 50 coins for each killed enemy. With the collected money you can fill up your life points if you got hit and/or you can buy new catcher-balls! You will have to find a shop to fill up the hearts in the main city.
There are some different kind of enemies like trophies, spiders, marshmallow-looking ones and some more you will encounter. In the most ways the enemies aren't hard to kill. You just have to get close to the enemies and hit them. You need to hit them between 1-3 times to finally get the kill. With every kill you raise a hidden bar (there is no one!) to get more hearts as life points. Unfortunatelly I still don't understand the system behind the way when and how exactly you will get more of these. At the end of the game I have had 22 hearts and I started with 10 if I am not mistaken.
If you have exactly 999 ingame-achievements - you cannot get more than 999 - you have to get back to the main city and head north there to reach the the final and forth area where you have to enter the portal. After that you are in the hell-themed area and you have to kill the last enemy - the boss. You need to hit the boss about 5 times. After that ... ok, I won't spoiler it. :)
In my opinion this game was needed for Steam where Steam Achievements actually get they "own game". And I have to admit that I really had fun playing it for hours. Unfortunatelly some things are went wrong so horrible. The potential was wasted so much that I can understand a little bit the negative reviews on Steam. BUT on the other side everyone has deserved a "second chance". Maybe we will see a second part of this game with a much better converted potential. :)

Before i go into an in depth review, I like to say that this game is well worth your time and money. Now, on to the in depth review and me trying not to spoil much of the story.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution takes place in the not so distant, 2027 (25 years prior to the original Deus Ex), Cought between the Paradise of revolutionary scientific descovery and the devastation of the people inevitably left behind. Protagonist Adam  Jensen becomes swept up in a globle conspiracy hinging on powerful, yet dangerous, human augmentation technology and is on a quest to unravel that conspiracy.
The story is well paced and very engaging, presenting the player with twists and turns along the way. Which in turn, prevents the story becoming stagnant or predictable. Another positive would be how well optimized the game is. It runs smooth, looks nice and is not system heavy for a 2011 game. One minor complaint would be, that some characters voice acting may appear dull or stiff, which can deliver some plot points without any/much impact.
9/10
The very core of the Deus Ex series' visual substance is Cyberpunk. The main visual form of the cyberpunk genre are futuristic anticipation, intense cluttering, the new creeping over the old, fog and smoke, information overload, corporate branding, cybernetics, transhumanism and many others became the staple of Deus Ex: Human Revolution's design, in order to create a proper cyberpunk feel.
From a technical standpoint, Human Revolution isn't doing anything special graphically. However, it has some of the best production design and art of most games in 2011 or in recent years.
8/10
In short, Dues Ex's sound design is excellent. From the pop of gunfire, to the sound of the environment around the player, blends togeather to create a truly memorable hearing experience. Coupled with the fact that the game has a phenomenal soundtrack. One minor point would be some of the awkward voice acting with some of the characters.
9/10
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an action role-playing (ARPG) game with elements of first-person action and stealth mechanics. Players take the role of Adam Jensen, a man equipped with mechanical cybernetic implants called augmentations. The game's environments, range from open world hubs to more scripted/liner environments. In these environments, players can find non-player controlled characters (NPCs) that will advance both the main story quest and optional side quests. Completing quests, along with other actions such as combat with enemies, rewards the player with experience points, which raise his experience level. Also accessible are black market vendors which supply equipment and weapons for Credits (in-game currency). Interactive objects within environments can be highlighted, although these options are either turned off on the hardest difficulty or can be turned off in the options menu by the player.
There are a variety of ways to approach the game's situations: players can use a violent approach and shoot their way through environments while using cover to hide from enemy fire. Alternately, the player can take a stealthy approach, avoiding guards and security devices, again using cover to avoid enemy sight lines. Taking down enemies while in stealth mode also has lethal and non-lethal melee options, in addition to weapons that can both kill and stun enemies. While in the game's environments, the player finds terminals and computers that can be accessed either with a password or through hacking. When hacking, the hacking screen is presented to the player, which shows the pathway through a device's security system to access the information.
At multiple points within the game, the player partakes in conversations with NPCs related to main and side quests. When talking, the player is presented with three different conversation options that affect the outcome of conversations.
In short. Deus Ex: Human Revolution establishes a gameplay vocabulary and rewards you for learning it and is insanely flexible and highly rewarding. Not to mention, that it gives the player an almost, complete freedom.
10/10
Practically demanding multiple playthroughs to achieve the multiple endings and achievements, Deus Ex: Human Revolution will take you anywhere from 25 to 40 hours on your initial run. This includes the main and side quests.

Ok, so I finally downloaded MWO after all these years, I stalked the development and beta for years and forgot about the game. As someone who played MW2 on PS1 and all three MW4 games on PC with a joystick and a MW tabletop player I can firmly say that this is a great addition to the MW universe.
Pros
-Amazing gameplay
-Mech design is spot on and cool to look at
-F2P, not P2W
-Tons of mechs and variants
-Lots of team players online
-Well designed and interesting maps
-Lots of customization options
-Beginner friendly, they have an awesome tutorial and give you a nice amount of starting cash to buy a couple of mechs, you have to play to get that extra cash thogh, which is good.
Neutral
-New skill tree, I started playing the day of the new skill tree release, that being said I like the way it is laid out, but I know  older players hate the update for various reasons. Regardless, I'm happy that I don't have to fill my mechbay with 3 of the same mech just to master it, so good on the devs, but bad for some people.
-Limit of 4 mechs in mechbay, you can buy more mechbays. The fact that it is F2P and that you can at least get one mech of each class is awesome though, you have to thank the developers for that.
-Maybe we can see some melee weapons? Also, press ganged industrial mechs perhaps?
Cons
-Can be a bit grindy, getting enough C-bills to buy that mech you want can take some time
-No tutorial for the menu, it is daunting at first
-Missing some mechs (like Uziel), this is partly due to the timeframe the game takes place within, roughly around the time of the clan invasion. They do plan on shifting the timeframe forward, which will bring more mechs with it!
All in all a great MW addition and a game I can see myself spending maybe 5 or 10 dollars a year, definitely when there are sales. That way I can buy more mechbays and some cockpit items or paints.

As of the May 16th patch (new skill tree), this game has become much more friendly to new players since it is a lot less grindy. Let me explain, statistically a tier 4/5 pilot (novice/beginner/noob) without premium gain on average ~119000 money (CB) per match. This was stated by the developers themselves so I'm not pulling that number out of my♥♥♥♥♥ Anyway, a new mech typically cost around 10-20m in my experience.
Now, before, you had to purchase 3 of the same mech (variants) to master it. That meant that if you purchased a Hellbringer for 15m like I did, you had to spend an additional 30m on 2 other Hellbringers to master it. Plus, if you wanted modules such as Seismic Sensor (6m IIRC), you had to spend additional million more.
All of that is gone now, a single mech will be sufficient for you to master it and you don't have to buy modules anymore. Instead you spend your money and xp on a skill-tree for that particular mech. Generally, it takes 1-2 matches (for a beginner without premium) to get 1 skill point, which means you will have a constant pace where you improve your mech. To master it, you need 91 skill points. This means it will eventually cost you 4,095,000 CB to master you mech. Which is VASTLY cheaper than with the previous system.
I think this new system is a big improvement from a new player's perspective and this is definitely a good time for trying out the game.

The Simple Science of Effective Triceps Training

There are a lot of theories out there about how to best train your triceps.
Some people say you have to focus on high-rep training and really feel the burn.
Others say you should be training them several times per week.
Others still say you don’t have to do triceps exercises at all and should focus on compound pushing movements instead like the bench press and overhead press.
Well, I’ve tried all the above and more, and I’ve worked with thousands of people, and here’s what I’ve learned:
1. Most people need to train their triceps directly to get the size and definition they want.
Heavy chest training will build the triceps but it’s rarely enough to build enough size and definition to satisfy.
2. Heavy compound movements are best for adding strength and size.
High-rep sets and cable and machine exercises can be included in your triceps workouts, but they can’t replace heavy free weight movements.

When your training emphasizes heavy weights (80 to 85%+ of 1RM), optimal volume seems to be about 60 to 70 reps performed every 5 to 7 days.
This not only applies to the triceps but to every other major muscle group as well.
Now, in the case of the triceps, we have to take into account the fact that they’re heavily involved in your pushing.
If you’re doing, let’s say, about 60 reps of heavy chest pressing per week for your chest and about 15 to 20 reps of heavy overhead pressing for your shoulders, then an additional 60 reps of heavy triceps training is going to be too much.
If you drop that to 30 to 40 heavy for the triceps per week, though, you’ll find that it stimulates additional growth without causing issues related to overtraining.
That said, every so often I run into people whose triceps are very stubborn, even when bulking properly, and I have them do the following each week:
9 sets of heavy (4 to 6 rep) chest pressing plus 3 sets of triceps exercises in the 8 to 10 rep range.
3 sets of heavy overhead pressing a couple days later.
6 to 9 sets of heavy triceps training a couple days later.
This slight increase in weekly volume isn’t a “magic fix” by any means, but it does help break through stubborn muscle growth plateaus.

If I were to do just one triceps exercise, it would be either the close-grip bench press or weighted dip.
They both emphasize the lateral heads of the triceps and also gives a little boost to your chest development.

The key isn’t just doing exercises–it’s progressing on them.

That is, increasing the amount of weight you can move over time.
The reality is if you want any part of your body to get more muscular, the best way to do this is make it stronger.

This one didn't really click for me.  The expansion/colonisation parts are okay.  The initial game was interesting, expanding my reach and butting up against other empires.  But once I got into military planning and combat, things really started to fall apart.
Combat is realtime and is always limited to a "long range + medium range + melee" three-phase system, after which it just ends, even if there are still ships alive on both sides.  As such, it can take several turns to actually wipe out a fleet, even if you dramatically outclass them.  There's also no way to use e.g. stand-off tactics that don't involve diving down into close-range combat.
There's little rhyme or reason to either the AI ship designs or to the tactics they use in combat, and strategic movement is fast enough that you can easily get ambushed, so it's very difficult to plan ahead.  Even if you've already fought a particular class of ships, there's no way to see what their stats are, nor is there any sort of intelligence / spying system to see what an empire is capable of (e.g. what techs they have).
Even if you could see their techs, it wouldn't really make that much of a difference.  Weapon and defense techs are really just a three-tier system with very little personality to each.  Compare this to, say, the old Master of Orion, where ship technologies were numerous and varied, there was no guarantee of getting any particular technology, and there was a tendency for an empire to focus and rely on a particular weapon type, making it easier to design against them (if you had the tech to do so).
The victory conditions are also pretty wonky.  By the end of my first game, I was stomping all over the galaxy, taking over every system and controlled well over half of it.  I was notified that I was well on my way to both the expansion victory (75% of systems) and the supremacy victory (controlling all faction homeworlds).  Yet despite clearly being on the road to inevitable victory, I still lost because the other major empire happened to reach the annoyingly arbitrary economic victory, by making 720k dust over their empire's lifetime.  (Granted, you can turn each victory condition off if you don't like them, but they're all pretty arbitrary to begin with, and not individually customisable.)  There also wasn't any sort of end-game summary with graphs etc. so I could see what I could've done to stop them.
The hero system is okay, but it doesn't give you very many over the course of a game.  It would also probably be a lot better if the heroes were distinctly separated into two separate pools, one for running systems and one for commanding fleets.  As it stands, you can quickly run out of skills to add to your governors — and yet the skill tree is completely hidden from you, so you often have to pick combat skills (useless for a governor) in order to get to more skills that might actually be useful to them.  The only advantage of the current system is that you can level up a planet governor by having them run a fleet or vice versa, but it doesn't seem worth all the extra mess.
I may come back to this after trying some other modern space 4X games, but I doubt it.  Doesn't really give me what I want out of a 4X.

A neutral review, it's a good game that sadly gets monotonous after awhile. Replay value is moderate, if anything it'd be to just try out the other factions. Definitely worth it on sale at 75% ($7,) higher prices don't justify the content to cost.
It is a good game, the empire building is fun and complex, diplomacy/AI are very competant as compared to the other 4X game AIs, albiet still not perfect mind you.
Sadly the biggest draw back is the replay value, there really isn't much of a replay value as compared to other strategy 4X games. As strange as this sounds despite maps being somewhat large and randomly generated, the maps are very limited to where you're able to go - the star system and planets are always in different locations but the map is always the same. All you can do is basically follow the dots and your empire building essentially becomes a game of connect the dots, it's like this for all games. The lack of movement and diveristy of maps is the major con of this game.
Empire building, AI are the best features of the game. The Empire building is complex at times by having a difficult balancing act between Food Industry vs Dust and Science (FIDS) along with population happiness.
Combat is a matter of personal taste, personally I'm on the fence about it. There's no "real" interaction and the scenes are always the same. However the amount of customization you can add to your ships (no cosmetic changes unfortunately, if there were cosmetic changes it would be amazing) and your selection in cards help offset the boring battles which often results in just auto-resolving to save time, sense manual combat all you get to do is watch (and change cards if you need too.)
- In the end, it's a good game with both strong postive features and strong negative features.
EDIT: Ah, and the factions are worth a mention too. There is a very limited amount of factions but they're unique in all aspects with an interesting lore which the AI actually sticks too. Unlike other 4X factions where a religious AI ends up going war-like, the AI in E.S. ends up sticking to what you'd expect from that faction; either warring, expansive, economic or generalized. The lack of factions however can be made up by creating your own factions with a TON of options. Sadly you have to choose from one of the faction skins for your ships. Again, this is another example of strong positive and strong negative features of this game.
Overall the positives outway the negatives but im firmly in the meh category.

Cities in Motion 2 is a well made game. The city grows dynamically with night/day cycle but no weather.
You're in charge to develop and maintain the various cities public transportation. In game this includes: Buses, Trams, Trolleys (Busses with overhead electric lines), boats, and trains(metro which includes subway). Each individual in the game's world is given a category among others: pensioner, businessman, student, tourist, white collar worker and blue collar worker. Each of these categories has their own public transportation preferences and different service level expectancies. So you try to cater for their different needs while trying to make the company profitable to further expand your services. All in all it's quite a detailed game. This controller will ONLY work through Steam. This is something I wish I had known before purchasing it, but it's such a ridiculous limitation that I hadn't even thought to check. Although it installs its drivers upon being connected, it doesn't respond as a generic controller as you'd probably expect. Instead it acts as a mouse and is not detected as a controller by any software outside of Steam. It's very disappointing, since the right touch pad is very nice and works well as an analog stick alternative.
Until this controller functions without Steam running in the background, it's going to be that much more inferior to every other controller available.
Some people may suggest launching all of your software through Steam to get around this limitation, but not all software plays well through Steam. And even then, it's a step that should not be necessary.
For this reason, I cannot recommend this controller.

If you enjoy shows with fun, childlike exteriors while also having some surprising depth behind the scenes, I can't recommend this show enough.
If you find it hard to look past poor animation, aren't a fan of shows with a tone of childlike innocence, and/or absolutely abhor moe and animal girls though, you should probably look elsewhere.
Kemono Friends was the black horse of its season. Nobody thought an anime based on the same concept that a since shut-down mobile game was, made with 3DCG, and with a budget approx. 1/6th of a normal shows could be good. But here we are, and Kemono Friends ended up as one the best shows.
Personally I have seen this show twice, once while airing and once again with friends. So my hours here are representative of my 3rd or higher viewing.
Why this show works is largely due to the careful balance it holds between its fun, playful exterior (hence all the tanoshii~ and sugoi~ memes) and its surpringly dark undertones, from the ED which shows footage of a long since abandoned amusement park to the clear signs that there's something that has happened to leave Japari Park as it is (for example, as a minor spoiler,
).
While nothing in the script would be called exceptional, it comes together nicely and creates a fun-yet-ominous tone that carries the show.
Let's not beat around the bush here, the animation is not very good. That said though, there is something weirdly... moe, or charming, about how you can tell the animators tried their hardest with what they had (excepting some examples in the first episode, where they were clearly still getting their sealegs).
The voice acting is a mixed bag, but as with the animation still holds a certain charm. Kaban is voiced by Aya Uchida (Kotori from
, among other smaller roles) and her moderate experience shows in her relatively nuanced role as main character Kaban. Kaban's traveling companion, Serval, is voiced by Yuka Ozaki, who's only other main role was in
, and her inexperience shows in voice acting. That said, her lack of nuance is almost a blessing in disguise, as it really helps play up her energetic optimism (the tanoshii~ and sugoi~ memes are from her voice characters constant use of these phrases).
The side characters are generally okay, nothing standout of exceptional, but they get the job done.
I absolutely adore Kemono Friends with all my heart, but there's no denying that it's also flawed at times. It's for that reason I have to give it a 7, which to me means "Enjoyable if you can look past the minor issues". None of the 3 friends I've showed this to have enjoyed it as much as I did, and there reasons were seemingly that they couldn't hit the mental state where you end up charmed by this show trying its best in the face of a terrible budget, rather than just annoyed at its flaws.
This is a show about animals who are also friends. This is the correct thing to make a show about. But maybe you think it doesn't seem good? Wrong. It is good.

I will say this now:

Just kidding, there's a lot more to that.
Now this show may seem simple, and a bit rough around the polygons, but Kemono Friends is the anime that really changes the mood of most of what we get from the anime world. You typically have all those action/drama/intense BS battles where every character acts like they're one step ahead because everyone is apparently a situational genius, but Kemono Friends dares to go somewhere else.
It is a much simpler time where the cast is much more relaxed and innocent, and oftentimes clueless. A lot of characters are ditzy and adorable, but that's what makes them so great. Every animal girl is unique in their own way and they all have their little specialties and quirks, as well as weaknesses, which is addressed in each episode. You're not overwhelmed with characters that are way too big for real life and you're not overwhelmed by intense action that never ends for no good reason. This anime was meant for those who just need to grab a good fluffy pillow and sit down somewhere to relax and enjoy these adorable animal girls.
This anime was also meant to serve a better purpose. It's not just a mindless slice of life, or some over-the-top action show. Believe it or not, it actually has a pretty nice plot. In each episode, you get at least 2 interviews with real zoologists and animal experts that tells you real facts about each featured animal, which I thought was pretty nice as well. On top of that, my girlfriend told me that due to the popularity of this show, the Japanese Government had decided to take this opportunity to revert the focus back to Parks and Zoos, which have been dwindling in annual attendance.
I truly believe that my purchase of this show, even after watching it for free, is going towards a good cause and a very good anime. I totally recommend this show for all of you out there who need to break out of that typical mold of anime that has caught us in all these mindless tropes and repetitive premises of hero vs. villain, or the dregs of circling around your daily life.

Endless Space is a 4X strategy game (eXploit, eXpand, eXplore, eXterminate), developed by Amplitude Studios.
The game revolves around the legacy of an ancient sentient race known as the Endless, and the technologies they left behind when they went extinct. Many centuries later, factions of different kinds and species are locked in a battle for control of the galaxy, and control of a substance the Endless have created, known as Dust.
If you have played other 4X strategy games, such as Civilisation or Master Of Orion, then Endless Space will feel familiar to you: You start off on one planet in a system, and by researching technologies, colonising other systems and managing your resources and military power, your rise to fame takes place.
The game's soundtrack is beautifully sublime as well, consisting of slow-paced electronic music with Middle-Eastern instruments mixed in, all composed by FlyByNo.
The only flaws I can think of the game are perhaps the tutorials. While they explain the basics of the game rather well, I feel they do not go in-depth enough about certain elements of the game to allow the player to fully understand a certain research capability or how to stockpile resources.
Regardless, Endless Space is an amazing game, and one that is highly recommended for any tacticians out there. If you have never played a 4X strategy game before and want to get into it, this is where you should start.
