Renegade ops belongs in the twin-stick shooter genre and a controller is recommended. It takes a while to get a grip on the shooting because movement is physics based. This brings an element of randomness to the driving which can lead to unintentional crashing and rolling over. Same rules apply to enemies as well and the game is mostly just a beautiful chaos. Weapons are powerful enough and sound like they mean business. Enemy variation could be higher since the same ones repeat over and over again but personally i got so much out of the destruction that i wasn't bored.
Player takes control of a single vehicle from a selection of 5 (+2 with DLC). Each of these has a special ability and look different but mostly operate on same way. You can pick up better weapons and health from fallen enemies and since these are random you can either be really lucky or stuck with your crappy level 1 machine gun for a long time. Any experience you gather is automaticly saved which is great since it makes failing a bit easier to swallow. Upgrade system lets you choose a bit of what to focus on but doesn't make a huge difference. You can only use 4 skills at a time and for example i liked Gordon Freeman (yes, the) because of his antlions. 4th upgrade slot opens at level 30 and at that time i allready had all of the skills a liked. So from 30 to max level of 45 i used the same skills.
Graphics are colorful and great. Scenery changes often depending on the mission so there is plenty of variation. Frame rate stayed solid even though at times the action and set pieces are just insane. During my 8 hours (of which about 2 was with DLC missions) with the single player the game crashed once but otherwise worked without problems.
I have no problems with the overall lenght of Renegade Ops. What i do have problems with is the lenght of individual missions. Normally a single mission takes about 20 minutes to complete and there are no checkpoints in the game. Especially in a game that puts the player on the mercy of a physics engine this is at times really frustrating. Missions starts with (depending on the difficulty) 3-5 lives and you can get one extra from a skill. You can also find extra lives but most i managed to find in a level was one. Casual mode is also available but it disables upgrades and other good things about the gameplay.
On medium lack of checkpoints is no problem but on Insane it takes one little mistake and few bad respawns to lose 3 lives in 30 seconds. I suspect that insane difficulty is meant for co-op which i didn't have the possibility to try out. It's for 4 players and if it works as well as single player it should be a blast with friends! It should be much faster to complete the game in co-op so take that into consideration.
I got a suprising amount of enjoyment out of a game that i though i'd get bored in half an hour. Renegade ops is stupid fun and i liked it a lot!

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly (WoG) is essentially a catalogue of exploded diagrams for various firearms, except instead of two-dimensional isometric drawings, the component parts have been meticulously modelled in three dimensions.  What’s more, the component models can be manipulated, both individually and as assemblies.  The camera controls (e.g. pan, tilt, zoom, track, etc.) allow fly-throughs of the models from any perspective, even those that would prove impractical in reality.  There are also cutaway views and several levels of x-ray views, in addition to the lovingly rendered photorealistic finishes.  What’s more, the actions of each model have been animated, and the animations can be run at normal speed or a number of slow-motion speeds, with any of the views!  This allows study of the ingenious mechanisms (e.g. springs, levers, cams, index wheels, gas porting, etc.) at a level simply unavailable anywhere outside the digital realm.
The game aspect of WoG involves dismantling and reassembling the guns, with challenges based on speed and accuracy.  There is also a shooting range, although only a few of the guns can be used for target shooting.
Some of the models allow alternative parts to be fitted, such as different size magazines and custom grips, and some allow you to mount accessories such as suppressors and scopes.  There is also a paint mode, where budding graphic designers and modellers can create custom skins for the models.
The firearms catalogue is quite extensive and growing all the time, with community voting used to decide which models should be developed next.  The majority of the catalogue is not initially available, being unlocked with experience points earned by performing tasks with the unlocked models.  It is possible to purchase the entire library, but I would not recommend doing so immediately, as the higher complexity models will be very daunting before developing some familiarity with the system.  It appears that there are also other, non-firearm models available for purchase, such as automobiles and animal skeletons, but I have not explored this.  There is also a significant body of community-created content available via the Steam Workshop.
I recommend that anybody with even a remote interest in firearms or mechanical engineering download and try WoG.  The price is impossible to argue with, and there is a chance that it will prove fascinating.

Alright so this is kind of important to pay attention to if you want to buy this product.
When it comes to 3rd person action games, strategy games that don't require a whole lot of quick rapid input, and games that require intuition and intelligence rather than precise aiming, this controller is absolutely fantastic. Want to play Witcher 3 with this thing? You'll have no problem. The movement stick on the left feels nice on your fingers and responds well. Even has a click function just like its Xbox controller counterpart.
But when it comes to things like FPSes, some fighting games, and games that require quick rapid action this controller falls short for a very specific reason: The touchpads.
See the touchpads can be adjusted for sensitivity but ultimately they are an inaccurate and imprecise form of movement. For camera movement they work great but when it comes to trying  to line up that epic headshot you'll be out of luck. The gyros help but they can't make up for the fact that a physical analog stick or a mouse make for a better aiming device overall.
The huge benefit of this controller though is all the programmable buttons and the fact that it can be used even in games with no controller support. There's like a million buttons on this dang thing and they can all be customized to your liking and done so quickly too. I found it kind of awesome to play games like Dead Rising which has spotty controller support and just set it up the way I wanted. Instead of having to go through some complicated controller install to set up an emulated controller, I can just plug in my steam controller and play. No muss, no fuss. Rocket League also plays well with this controller because the custom design and extra buttons can make setting up shots easier. Heck, you can even set up buttons to do specific combos so you can play a fighting game and have your character's special abilities lined up for use at the touch of a button. That's pretty wicked.
So in the end, I'd say look at your library and decide for yourself if you want this thing. If you want to play some games that don't require precise aiming you'll be absolutely in luck. Its a comfortable and customizable controller that will suit your needs.
However if you're a big fan of shooters or things that require precise aiming and control, this is most certainly not the controller for you. This is a bowie knife, not a scalpel. Useful for a lot of things, but precision cuts are beyond it's abilities.
Either way I'm going to reccommend it. Because its usefulness outweighs its potential problems. For me at least.

Deus Ex? Deus Ex. Now that was an adventure! And a fun one at that. And fairly long too. Playtime: 64:19 hours; played offline mostly so Steam didn't track the time. Non-lethal, completionist on hardest difficulty. Didn't go for all the achievements though. There's a lot to be said, so let me just get onto it.
Story. I usually have a hard time describing how was the story or whatever the flaws were, 'cause over time I tend to forget details and I also am guilty of actually having fun while playing video games which often leads to something as simple as taking everything at face value - this especially being the case with fantasy settings. Here, the story was fairly easy to follow and had a certain flow to it that... made sense. I often catch myself checking questlog to see what the hell was I supposed to do to progress or what exactly did they ask me to do - none of which happened during this playthrough. All was laid down nicely, your mission is clear. Solid, engaging plot that near the end took a slight dip - that doesn't mean it's suddenly terrible. It was more linear than not, yes, but that was only for the better. The game still offered a lot of freedom to play around - but about this later. It all left me with questions some questions still unanswered and some new ones emerging - personally I wouldn't take it as a negative, all the more reason to do another playthrough and catch on/connect dots previously missed.
Sidequests were very well done. Surprisingly even, I'd say, considering how many games just throw those in to artificially extend playtime that way. Written and introduced in a way that - keeping Jensen's background and general attitude in mind - they made sense for him to do them. Majority also had additional layers, depth, that made them even more interesting and offered multiple ways to complete that weren't straight up abandoning if it didn't fit what you'd do. And the best part is, only one of the bunch was a traditional fetch-quest.
Conversations and general dialogue was definitely a highlight and something nice to see. The challanges to convince someone to give out information, give access somewhere and other similar actually required some thinking on how to act and what to say. What makes it even better, it's all doable without the social augmentation. Just wits and proper analysis. Definitely a welcoming change from a bunch of titles that required certain amount points into certain skill which afterwards unlocked new options that might be actually successful in opposition to default ones.
Now, gameplay part. Deus Ex is an action game - an action game you can entirely stealth through. I stealthed it all as much as I could and it was damn satisfying and well done. There is no wrong way to play it and whatever you choose to do, game gives you the means and ways to do so. It REWARDS creative thinking - like obscuring turret's sight with boxes so you can pass through to the next room or taking objects from the other end of the city just to stack them on each other and pass to another area. There are many more examples of this; it really did feel satisfying to see an unorthodox solution work in the end.
The AI, while not the smartest, was very perceptive. Enemies could spot you from very long distances - same goes for turrets and the like - and would force you to act fast. There was no room for sitting in one place for more than few seconds, no matter if in the open to scout the area better nor if moved a bit farther away from cover for whatever the reason could be. From playing 'Dishonored' a lot I got a habit of trying the get the higher ground, mainly because NPCs rarely look up - here it was the opposite. You could get spotted very high up by a guy that walked a bit farther away on the ground. Those guys also looked behind - now that's something.
Boss fights. There were four boss fights in the game, although I'm not really sure if I should count one of them. Those were interesting. There was a bunch of enviromental stuff one could use against them, areas were big and gave a lot of room to move around. My main complaint would be how easily exploitable they are, what (un?)fortunately makes them easy to beat. I am not used to boss fights in stealth games - what made those probably harder than they would be, aside from being a terrible shot - and the fact that I could get the boss stuck in a behaviour loop and shoot him to death was... dissapointing. The final fight is also very lackluster comparing to the previous ones and incredibly easy. It took a different approach but it was very much 'meh'. Not really feeling like the final fight should.
City areas were big and well designed. They allowed player to go pretty much anywhere, uncover little secrets, learn a bit on daily lives of people - and not only. There were quite a few missions happening inside them and the freedom to come and go, maybe continue story stuff in short bits without getting punished for 'leaving the quest area' was damn good.
Graphics were alright, nothing mindblowing nor necessairly bad either. Only thing that struck me as awful was lip sync and facial expressions - or lack of them, rather. They definitely took an interesting art direction, moving away from the regular blues and grays of cyberpunk and using goldens, yellows and browns, giving the game warmer palette. It could also be linked to the idea of the story revolving more around the rich and powerful - thus giving golden all the more reason to be a main theme, being generally associated with those circles. As much as the main cast varied in terms of clothing and looks, regular civilians were as boring and as regular as one would expect. Maybe with exception to punks and gang members but I'd say even they weren't all that different once you've seen a couple.
Final verdict? Damn worth grabbing. I'm not sure how would one enjoy it as a regular action game, but as a stealth fan it's a must. It had it's flaws but not strong enough to take enjoyment out of the game and it was definitely an experience worth having. I highly recommend it to anyone that happens to be a fan of cyberpunk or stealth games - bonus enjoyment points for both - and at least giving it a go if one finds it's concept interesting.

Genesis Rising: The Universal Crusade is the only tactical space combat game I know of which uses the idea of organiform spaceships which is even a rare topic in Scifi literature. There is only one catch - you have to get it working on a modern OS. After an hour of testing I succeeded in getting the game running on Win10_64 Pro in 4K. I set the compatibility for TestApp3230.exe and GenesisRising.exe to 'Disable display scaling on high DPI settings' and 'Run this program as an administrator' in the bin subfolder of the SteamLibrary. Good news is the game is already patched  to version 1.0.44 which seems to be the latest. After clicking away the dozen error messages at start up the game starts and runs without issues for me.

Let's get this straight, if you aren't a fan of Naruto or at the beginning of watching the series you probably won't be able to enjoy this game as much as others and may end up disliking it.
Naruto Ninja Storm 4 is a game taking place at the very end of part 2 (Naruto Shippuden) of the series. It will have confusing characters, strange abilities and lots of spoilers for those who are only a little bit into the series or who have never watched the series at all. For you guys, I would reccomend watching the series all the way through before getting this game.
That being said, the gameplay itself is amazing in an "Easy to learn, hard to master" arena-style fighting game. The character's attacks and moves are unique, and the added in abilities of leader changing and chakra infusing make this game stand out from both other Naruto Storm games and fighting games in general. Fans of the series will really enjoy being able to fight as the characters from famous battles in the Naruto Shippuden series.
Overall, a great game and a must buy for long-time Naruto fans, however if you are new to the series I suggest watching at least halfway through shippuden before buying.

In this extremely annoying top-down shooter your drive an armored vehicle through a series of levels, plowing through buildings and blowing up waves of enemies on the way. The problems with this concept are obvious from the first minutes: first of all, your field of view is very limited due to the perspective. This means it's difficult to drive at speed, you're constantly taking fire from off-screen and you have to keep shooting at the edge of the screen in anticipation of enemies. With all the explosions and chaos it's especially difficult to spot and dodge enemy missiles, as they get covered up by the completely ineffective enemy machine gun fire. The whole concept feels archaic and I can't think of a way the game wouldn't be improved if it used a standard 3rd person camera.
Secondly, all of the main mission objectives are on a timer, which only actually appears on the screen 2.30 before time is up. I assume this was supposed to keep the pace fast, but in practice it's to easy to get caught up in optional secondary objectives and run out of time, which means replaying the whole mission. You can't explore the maps at your own pace, and the timer is infuriatingly even ticking down when you're fighting a boss. It feels like a completely pointless punishment. The same can be said of the old-fashioned lives system, which forces you to retry to whole stage should your run out of lives.
Lastly, the controls are quite imprecise with a keyboard and a mouse, plus you can't rebind them. That's a nail to the coffin for a game that requires a constant slalom amidst enemy fire. Unless you have a supreme control of your left pinkie, it's also going to be really hard to boost (left shift) while steering left with A.
All these issues make Renegade Ops a nuissance insead of light entertainment, making it hard to recommend.

This game is incredibly rich, robust, complex and deep. The learning curve is immensly overwhelming, especially for first time entrants into the 4x genre. Even those who have had experience in 4x games of days past will be challenged by the sheer number of options available to you from a variety of different perspectives. The end game is to be able to carefully master and manage the delicate coexistance of four core dynamics of the game - Food, Industry, Dust and Science. Successfully micromanaging those will yield significant advantages over your opponent but it is only one spoke of the wheel and you must manage other aspects of the game just as carefully if you are to be vicotrious in your endeavours to rule the galaxy. Faction and hero stats and abilities play a massive role in swaying the lead and turning the tables, as do control over a variety of other resources. Of course keeping your people happy is also a top priority while you balance all these other mechanics. In the long run, it is a game that you can easily sink many many hours into and compeltely forget where you are and what time of night it is. Better set your alarm, because once you get into this game - it's really hard to come out with your sanity intact. There's definitely a "just one more turn" notion here, something that drives you to want to better your playstyle and learn as much as you can so that you can do even better in your next game. The visuals are not stunning but they don't need to be. The game is immersive enough as it is, and with the stellar soundtrack it's all the more a world you'll want to enter and never want to leave. Tutorials gently ease players into the game while more hardcore 4x management staples will challenge even the most seasoned of strategic geniuses. I highly recommend trying this game if you like any manner of strategy game, but especally if 4x is your cup of tea. Things to Research:
Creating Artificial Atmospheres, Utilizing Perpetual Motion Machines, Harnessing Dark Matter for Manufacturing, Black Hole Mining, Quantum Processing, Inorganic Biology, Negative Mass Mechanics, etc.
Making Colonies:
Earth-like planets, all metal planets, gas planets, hollow planets, lava planets, also settle on asteroids.
Factions to try:
Humans, not-humans, robots, religious robots, half human-half robot, mysterious crystal beings, parasetic race of insectoid robots, and Ameabos!
Review:
The descriptions for the various research alone is enough to keep you occupied for a while... the science-fiction in this game is well thought out, perhaps most of it can even be refered to as speculative science. Since this game takes place in a thousand years (as of this review) the game lends itself credibility by applying current theories and ideas into it's gameplay.
If your interested in quantum and theoretical physics, this game has that... if finding out more about exotic biology and ecological systems is fascinating- this game has a whole tech tree dedicated to just that. If researching various ways on exterminating entire armies and fleets peaks your interest, this game has many flavors of science and technology just for that purpose. And of course there's an entire section of diplomacy and trade that you can explore if you prefer to take the non-barbaric route of your empire.
Combat is simple, so is creating units... it also wont take 2 hours for a conflct to resolve (infact it usually ends within a handful of turns). Expanding is also really easy, being able to do something is really easy in this game, the difficulty comes from the fact that other players can do a lot just as easily... what it comes down to is who can make smarter decisions.
This game is not for everyone... 9/10

Featuring a large supporting cast of interesting and unique Friends whose personality traits match with the animals they are based off, our heroines seek out ‘the Library,’ where they hope to discover what kind of Friend Koban is! To get the Steam Controller working on Apple OSX, one way is to use a third-party program called Karabiner (see the following
discussion page). Karabiner is a remarkably convenient and capable program for remapping keys.
Karabiner uses its own names to refer to the "events" that the Steam Controller sends. To find out the Karabiner names of the various events that your Steam Controller sends for the various keys of interest (the Shift keys, the Control Key, the Option/Alt keys, the Command keys) one way to do it is to map one of the Steam Controller buttons to whatever key you're unsure about in Big Picture's "Base Configurations" -> "Desktop Configuration".
Then select "Launch EventViewer..." from Karabiner's square icon in the OSX menubar.
When the mouse is inside the "Mouse Area" of the EventViewer, you'll see the events being listed, since the Steam Controller is sending "desktop events" and Karabiner can now see them.
They have strange names, for example, the left option key turned out to be
"KeyCode::DANISH_DOLLAR"
on my MacBook Pro running OSX, and the left command key turned out to be
"ConsumerKeyCode::POWER".
But anyway, here's the file that I'm using as the "private.xml" file in Karabiner's
"Misc & Uninstall" tab, under the "Custom Setting:" button called "Open private.xml" (right-click on it, and choose "Open with TextEdit.app"), then paste in the following contents. This will do the trick for games like ProPinball Ultra Timeshock, which depends on both left and right shift as its default configuration. So now you'll be able to use the same configurations as you use on your PC, without having to have a whole separate set of configurations for your OSX machine.
One has to wonder what they're doing at Valve if cross-platform support for their own in-house designed controller isn't one of their top priorities, especially as it's one of the least expensive wireless controllers with a gyro and dual trackpads. They don't even support it in their "Steam VR" virtual reality launcher program either, which is disapointing as it's feels superior to the HTC Vive controllers for things like web browsing and playing videos. Perhaps Valve plan to extend the Steam Controller software to allow the inputs on the HTC Vive controllers to be similarly configurable.

I got to tell you, this controller has been beyond bad♥♥♥♥♥ I love how I can program it for any of my games, and I like the sometimes people have already done the ground work for the controller. Hell, I even love that I can use it outside of Steam. The truth of it all, is that not everyone likes using a controller for gaming. I bought this because, after looking at it's feature set, it looked really cool. I knew everything would ride on the accuracy and precision of the track pads. When I finally got it, I decided to test it with 2 major games - Dark Souls 3, and Doom (2016). It performed extremely well in Dark Souls 3, and in many ways actually outperformed the 360 controller I was using. Being able to rebind the reverse buttons (the ones on the back) to the X and B keys, made important combat actions much more fluid and easy. This did not require much set up at all either, which was good. The touchpad performed admirably, although with lock-on targeting it was not really required all that often. Doom initially had some problems, but after setting up the touchpads to my needs, it again performed extremely well. Not as good as a keyboard and mouse, as they will always be king, but miles and miles above my 360 controller. While I would definitely not play a competitive FPS like CSGO with the controller, it is definitely good enough to reliably play any single-player or coop FPS without missing a beat. I would highly recommend it for all but the most fast-paced competitive FPS games. I was expecting it to not be so great for FPS games, since most controllers are garbage for first person shooters.
Another test was playing Descent: Freespace. This allowed me to test multiple things. Firstly, it's a non-steam game, secondly I was launching it through a launcher program, and thirdly it had no controller support at all, forcing me to emulate a keyboard and mouse. While it did require a lot of initial set up (there is no existing community one), I was able to get a very nice configuration set up going. That highlights one of the best parts of the controller - it is extremely customisable and extremely flexible, allowing many games which may not even support controllers at all to feel like they are natively controller-based games. The only real problem is there are no on-screen prompts, or if there are, they reference keyboard keys, but this is a small price to pay. I was able to run GZDoom through steam, and the controller works fantastically there. I have not tried it with the Dosbox version of Doom available on Steam, but I assume it will work admirably based on how it has performed in other old games. It's fascinating that a device from 2016 can play a game from 1993 so seamlessly and easily, feeling almost like the game was designed for the controller.
I would highly recommend this controller. It has a learning curve, which makes it seem less fantastic than it really is when you first start using it, but with some practice, you should have an absolute blast with it, both on your PC and on your couch, for both modern and old titles across a large range of genres.
It is a real shame that Valve is not pushing this controller as hard as they could be, and it is also a shame that so many people, including prominent YouTubers are rejecting it out of hand without putting in any time to practice and learn the control scheme and how it works, because this device is extremely innovative, and console manufacturers would do well to learn from it in the future.

I purchased the Steam Controller with cautious optimism, and I have to say that I am pleased overall.  It is comfortable and flexible, if a little light.  The biggest gripe you'll see online might be the ergonomic placement of some buttons/functions; but this is small concern for those willing to map functions themselves through the easy naviagation menu and transform the default arrangement into something more intuitive, personal and unique.  If you believe that a controller should be a carbon copy of a console standard, then you will be initially disappointed.  This is different by design and pairs the function of the keyboard and mouse into a handheld format-it isn't Xbox or PS4, and if they're your interest-they already do their own job really well!  Your enjoyment of this device will vary based on your desire to take the time to arrange the set up and practice until muscle-memory kicks in.  It isn't work, but for the institutionalised console gamer, it is a step BEFORE truly enjoying the gaming experience fully.  The drawbacks for the controller itself would be shallow bumper buttons and gloss surface (easily addressed with some decal).  The greatest positive is the flexibility of input and ability to map for titles traditionally not compatible with controllers.
This is not a pad for everyone, and it is use-oriented rather specifically.  Am I going to use this for every game? No.  This is a unique tool that you employ for certain tasks and I'll certainly be using my xbox360 wired for FPS or Arkham/Assassin's Creed style gameplay.  However, for desktop or couch gaming with titles like Civ, indie titles, Elite or emulatiors there is no comparison.
Hope this helps!

Deus Ex? Deus Ex. Now that was an adventure! And a fun one at that. And fairly long too. Playtime: 64:19 hours; played offline mostly so Steam didn't track the time. Non-lethal, completionist on hardest difficulty. Didn't go for all the achievements though. There's a lot to be said, so let me just get onto it.
Story. I usually have a hard time describing how was the story or whatever the flaws were, 'cause over time I tend to forget details and I also am guilty of actually having fun while playing video games which often leads to something as simple as taking everything at face value - this especially being the case with fantasy settings. Here, the story was fairly easy to follow and had a certain flow to it that... made sense. I often catch myself checking questlog to see what the hell was I supposed to do to progress or what exactly did they ask me to do - none of which happened during this playthrough. All was laid down nicely, your mission is clear. Solid, engaging plot that near the end took a slight dip - that doesn't mean it's suddenly terrible. It was more linear than not, yes, but that was only for the better. The game still offered a lot of freedom to play around - but about this later. It all left me with questions some questions still unanswered and some new ones emerging - personally I wouldn't take it as a negative, all the more reason to do another playthrough and catch on/connect dots previously missed.
Sidequests were very well done. Surprisingly even, I'd say, considering how many games just throw those in to artificially extend playtime that way. Written and introduced in a way that - keeping Jensen's background and general attitude in mind - they made sense for him to do them. Majority also had additional layers, depth, that made them even more interesting and offered multiple ways to complete that weren't straight up abandoning if it didn't fit what you'd do. And the best part is, only one of the bunch was a traditional fetch-quest.
Conversations and general dialogue was definitely a highlight and something nice to see. The challanges to convince someone to give out information, give access somewhere and other similar actually required some thinking on how to act and what to say. What makes it even better, it's all doable without the social augmentation. Just wits and proper analysis. Definitely a welcoming change from a bunch of titles that required certain amount points into certain skill which afterwards unlocked new options that might be actually successful in opposition to default ones.
Now, gameplay part. Deus Ex is an action game - an action game you can entirely stealth through. I stealthed it all as much as I could and it was damn satisfying and well done. There is no wrong way to play it and whatever you choose to do, game gives you the means and ways to do so. It REWARDS creative thinking - like obscuring turret's sight with boxes so you can pass through to the next room or taking objects from the other end of the city just to stack them on each other and pass to another area. There are many more examples of this; it really did feel satisfying to see an unorthodox solution work in the end.
The AI, while not the smartest, was very perceptive. Enemies could spot you from very long distances - same goes for turrets and the like - and would force you to act fast. There was no room for sitting in one place for more than few seconds, no matter if in the open to scout the area better nor if moved a bit farther away from cover for whatever the reason could be. From playing 'Dishonored' a lot I got a habit of trying the get the higher ground, mainly because NPCs rarely look up - here it was the opposite. You could get spotted very high up by a guy that walked a bit farther away on the ground. Those guys also looked behind - now that's something.
Boss fights. There were four boss fights in the game, although I'm not really sure if I should count one of them. Those were interesting. There was a bunch of enviromental stuff one could use against them, areas were big and gave a lot of room to move around. My main complaint would be how easily exploitable they are, what (un?)fortunately makes them easy to beat. I am not used to boss fights in stealth games - what made those probably harder than they would be, aside from being a terrible shot - and the fact that I could get the boss stuck in a behaviour loop and shoot him to death was... dissapointing. The final fight is also very lackluster comparing to the previous ones and incredibly easy. It took a different approach but it was very much 'meh'. Not really feeling like the final fight should.
City areas were big and well designed. They allowed player to go pretty much anywhere, uncover little secrets, learn a bit on daily lives of people - and not only. There were quite a few missions happening inside them and the freedom to come and go, maybe continue story stuff in short bits without getting punished for 'leaving the quest area' was damn good.
Graphics were alright, nothing mindblowing nor necessairly bad either. Only thing that struck me as awful was lip sync and facial expressions - or lack of them, rather. They definitely took an interesting art direction, moving away from the regular blues and grays of cyberpunk and using goldens, yellows and browns, giving the game warmer palette. It could also be linked to the idea of the story revolving more around the rich and powerful - thus giving golden all the more reason to be a main theme, being generally associated with those circles. As much as the main cast varied in terms of clothing and looks, regular civilians were as boring and as regular as one would expect. Maybe with exception to punks and gang members but I'd say even they weren't all that different once you've seen a couple.
Final verdict? Damn worth grabbing. I'm not sure how would one enjoy it as a regular action game, but as a stealth fan it's a must. It had it's flaws but not strong enough to take enjoyment out of the game and it was definitely an experience worth having. I highly recommend it to anyone that happens to be a fan of cyberpunk or stealth games - bonus enjoyment points for both - and at least giving it a go if one finds it's concept interesting.

Meh. I keep buying these space sims, expecting something that actually attempts to simulate a spaceship. This is really a naval combat game without the water. It's 2-dimensional (the graphics are 3D but the actually playing field is not; you can only move in 2 dimensions). Say what you want about Homeworld not NEEDING a 3rd dimension; at least it had one.
Having said that, this is a pretty unique naval RTS. When you kill another ship, you get to harvest it for both health and abilities for your own ships. I've only played the first couple missions but the mechanics seem solid and the ship customization is very intuitive. Once you've killed a few enemies, it's very easy to customize your identical ships into specialized individuals.
For example: on the second tutorial mission, I loaded all my beams onto one ship, all my short-range projectiles onto the second and all my long-range missiles onto a third. What started out as three ships with two pea-shooters each quickly became a useful unit with very distinct roles.
Haven't played far enough to say how the story or mission variation is but just based on the core gameplay elements, I recommend Genesis Rising.

Football is one of the most popular sports in the world. American's call is Soccer but for all intents and purposes you could ask anyone in Europe what the #1 sport is and the answer would usually be football. If you have ever sat down and watched professional games you'll notice one distinct fact about the game however and that is most of the action takes place in the mid-field where the chance of scoring goals is minimal. This is why most football games end with each teams score being single digits. When you compare this to games like basketball you will also see that there is a connection between the amount of points scored and how far the players are from the goal. Why am I talking about sports? Because MechWarrior Online plays like a football match. Allow me to explain.
Regardless of the gameplay mode you take part in, the pace of the game is the same. It has more to do with positioning of the players, holding ground, looking for ways to outflank the opponent. It's a slow process and just like football it results in a great deal not happening for the majority of the game but then there is a break in the defences and for a brief moment excitement kicks in as one team desperately tries to recover their composure.
Like football this will appeal to some, but not others and certainly not to me as I would prefer not to keep waiting around for 10 minutes before something interesting happens.
There is a learning curve but it won't take you more than a couple hours to figure out enough to become competant driving the mechs but then there is the time needed to understand that MWO is a game about positioning and little else. You will spend most of your time driving from one strategically advantageous point to another and then sitting your 100 tonne mech on that spot like a giant metal chicken as you settle into a slow and tedious game of peek-a-boo with other players who have also chosen their camping spot.
With mechs being simply superior to other versions in terms of efficiency you do have the potential to be at a disadvantage simply because you didn't buy a premium mech or saved up enough in-game currency. So in some ways strategy is thrown out of the window and victory becomes due to superior technology rather than skill.
But in the end, this is a game where you would really only get enjoyment from it if you are working on a well coordinated group and appreciate the depth of teamwork that the game affords. But if you're just in some random PUG then MWO becomes more like a walking simulator than a strategy game. Namely lots of travelling around with nothing happening interspaced with the occasional bit of actual gameplay.

Here is the not so heroic journey of trying to open one friggin' stubborn mayonnaise jar, presented as a clicker game full with sarcastic achievements. Uhm... Okay. I won this game in a giveaway and tried it out of pure curiosity to begin with, which doesn't serve me right most of the time. Writing a review for this one will be a challenge. I really should appreciate the way developers' mind work here. Even now I'm trying to get my head together to think about something imaginative to say about a mayonnaise jar, and as absurd it may be, some people managed to make a whole game out of it!
Ehm...
is a clicker game - and aside not really being the most absurd one that I've ever seen in the market either, has a weird sense of humor targeting a selection of pop culture references wrapped in a vintage display. There is really nothing into it aside clicking on a mayonnaise jar while listening to the repetition of the same pesky 40s advertisement jingle tune. After a certain amount of clicking, you unlock short and absurd story paths for your mayonnaise jar and given the opportunity to dress it up in various accessories. As being the mission of any and all clicker games, your primary motivation here is to kill some brain cells while looking at your screen with empty eyes, silently drooling and clicking with your mouse to fill the illusion of you are actually doing something. Well done! It takes 10.000 clicks to collect all that there is within this game, never to visit again. If you are a strict achievement hunter and got it for an easy completion; sure, this is your game. You might consider running a script rather than actually clicking it through anyhow though.
Could I recommend it? Sure, why not if you strictly know what is it that you are getting here? I, myself prefer games with actual stories but also know first handedly the mindless therapeutic relaxation of being able to not think anything serious as a long time player of
.
is a perfect medium for that. The game deserves some appreciation for being humorous without being imposing, obnoxious or promising false depth anyhow. While we ponder on the philosophy, the boundless ethical and existential conflict hidden behind a mayonnaise jar, we keep clicking. Will we ever grasp the enlightenment?

Blockland may not be as 'good' as it once was according to its long time fans, but nevertheless I enjoyed revisiting this after about a two year hiatus.
Blockland, at face value seems like it could pass as a Lego game, however Blockland allows people to do more than just build like you would in Lego - people can meet up online and enjoy either a fast paced Team Deathmatch, a roleplay, a freebuilding session, battling against a boss, kart racing, the list goes on! Of course, that is all thanks to the people running all of these online servers everyday - some are even dedicated (meaning they never go down, even if the host leaves - but it stops when the host decides to close the program which allows this.)
To make all these enjoyable servers happen, though, hosts take the time to learn how to script events. With events, you could make a single 1x1 block explode like a nuke, send you flying upwards, sideways, etc., and even kill your character instantly. You can even make a block dispense a weapon like a Rocket Launcher, a sword, or a Spear. On the subject of dispensable items, you may notice that your selection of items is a bit lackluster in the core game - sure, you have a gun.. dual guns.. a broom that pushes people away... basic tools... that's cool and all, but where's all the cool stuff? Where's the laser blasters and lightsabers and sniper rifles and TF2 based weapons?
Well, that my friend, is where Add-Ons come in.
Blockland has a massive Add-On community - in fact, there's a forum for Blockland with at least 3700+ posts / threads in it's Add-On section, and about 3500+ posts / threads in its Music section! To make things even better, getting add-ons into your copy of Blockland is incredibly easy - all you have to do is open the game's files, go into the Add Ons folder, and place your newly downloaded addons into there!
I must say though, while I do really enjoy this game, there are several things that may hinder your experience online. First of all, while there are amazing coders and 3D modellers showing their stuff off in the Blockland Forums, the actual players are... well... there's a reason why earlier I said 'people' earlier and not 'kids'. Most of the actual players of Blockland are some of the most immature people on the Internet - people with atrocious names, people who are pure toxic, the list goes on. Granted, not everyone is like that on servers. Sometimes you can find people who can make a joke but are able to hold back any urge to be immature.
Secondly, and this one is easy to notice - Blockland looks outdated graphics wise. Animations of player characters are smooth in the core game, but body parts look a bit rough around the edges - it could be argued that it's natural as this game is called Blockland where you control customizable Blockheads.
Thirdly, and speaking of customizable Blockheads, the amount of things you can customise on your character is very limited - a small amount of colours to choose from, a limited amount of options on the hats you can wear, same for shoulderpads and things to wear on your back and only two types of feet and hands. More customisation options would have been better.
All in all, I believe even though Blockland is definitely flawed and isn't really in it's golden years anymore, it's still a fun game to me nonetheless, and I will recommend it. If you have a kid who wants to play it, though, do everything you can to limit them only to Singleplayer before they go online.

This is one of the few 4x games I own. When I bought it, I was primarily looking for an entertaining space-themed game with cool battles, which is exactly what I got. It is worth mentioning, that I don't play this game on the higher difficulties which means that this review might not reflect the experience of those who do play on higher difficulties. I do believe that the game can become a bit boring in the mid- to lategame unless the focus lies on military expansion. The boredom will, however, be mitigated by learning technologies that allows for further colonization of different planet types. Furthermore, wars can, in my experience, become tedious since they easily become very focused on production and the mangement of damaged ships.
On a final note, I want to mention a couple of positives. Besides from the beautiful combat cinematics, there are two things that I particularly enjoy about the game. Firstly, it is the advisors. These people, of all species, will aid the empire they are working for with their special skills and they can be specialized according to the players prefference. Secondly, I found the different species and the customization to be a fun factor. Mostly because it feels like the species are played differently from each other, and that they often have noticeable boons, and in some cases even drawbacks. I like the ability to create a new species, but the customization options are somewhat limited and it often feels like it is restricted to what already exists.
In the end, I'd probably recommend this game, especially if it is on sale.

Endless Space is easily the best space 4x I've ever played.  The diversity between factions is broad enough to allow for interesting replays without being so different as to be unbalanced.  Planet management is on the complex-but-reasonable side.  Ship design and development is fantastic and detailed, yet not micromanagerial.
The integration of the components of the rest of The Endless series gives this a compelling universe as a backdrop, and you can easily imagine how an escape pod from one of your fleet became the explorers in Dungeon of the Endless or how one of the uncolonized planets you uncover could be the one you're developing in Endless Legend.
Highly recommended as long as you don't mind spending hours playing "one more turn."

I honestly haven't done reviews in ages, and when I did I was a ridiculous kid running a website beyond his control reviewing, and distributing anime. If that gives me any merit with you continue reading.
I got this games in the hopes of re-establishing control over my account. It had been so long since I made a Steam purchase that Steam was beginning to limit control over my account and the features I could use. Needless to say making this purchase did not help me, but what was discovered is priceless.
Maybe I am in the dark here but I haven't encountered a game layout like Galaxy Admirals. The unique, almost boardgame style of it's maps are casual, yet engaging in strategic warfare tactics. The "revolving star system" you control your units in gives a style of gameplay similar to Chess and other boardgames where critical thinking, and foresight are key.
The game is very colorful for the most part, if not leaning to the "Blue" spectrum a little too much. I would like to see different backgrounds for maps to offer a "relief" in tones. The graphics the game utilizes reminds me that of a Android game as well as it's control interface which in fact, can't be a bit quirky with the mouse. It almost seems like a game that should be native to Touch devices.
The AI Campaign offers some fun, some frustration, and in the end satisfaction on completion. Giving you a boost to move into multiplayer and dominate the scene... however this is where I hit somewhat of a roadblock: Not many people actually play online yet. As a early access game with very little exposure you won't encounter many online yet. I hope this will change with more reviews and Steam-based promotion.
In summary, I do suggest this game to other users that are fans of boardgames, turn based strategy games, and science fiction. Great job JetDogs Studios.

This is rather a unique game. If you like this style of game, it certainly seems to be set at a bargain price. Basically, it's a turn-based tactical combat game set in a small, moving arena. Through the first dozen-odd levels, it seems to be constituted by a small but carefully balanced array of different spaceships; each ship is good for something, but no ship is absolutely dominant. The best ship is very expensive and can be quite readily be destroyed by a range of well-used, cheaper ships.
However, once one gets even further into the campaing, one realises that there's a whole other array of weird and complicated ships to play with. Honestly, for me, at that point it started to feel less like a strategy game and more like a puzzle game. Understanding all of the different abilities of all the different ships, trying to keep track of what will happen with the movement of the arena in the next turn, and predicting the moves of the enemy, feels quite "brain burning", or conducive of a state of "analysis paralysis". So, for myself, it became less fun and more like work. But if you like tactical puzzles, these seem very well designed and they certainly give you a lot to think about!
Finally, I think the multiplayer would probably help to make this more engaging... but in my experience of it so far, there never seems to be anyone else on when I am. So, a cautious thumbs-up... just be aware of what style of game it is you're getting into.

Pros:
+ Controller with touch pads!
+ Per game configs
+ Desktop/non-steam game config support
+ "Easily" reconfigure controls on the fly
+ Uses AA batteries; Easily changeable.
+ Large feature set to choose from, especially for the touch pads, the joy stick and the shoulder pads
Cons:
- Must have steam running to use controller
- Uses AA batteries; heavy controller. PS3 controller: 179g, Steam controller: 279g, WiiU controller monstrosity: 484g
- Must use BigPicture mode to configure controller
- Configure software kinda sucks
- Missing some complementary config features, especially the ability to turn OFF the gyro if (and only if) a touchpad is used.  (The feature to turn it ON exists.)
This is a great device. I use it daily:
I use it when I casually browse the web.
I use it when I need a remote for my youtube/mplayer videos.
I use it for all those flash games has keyboard movement but mouse menus.
Sometimes, I even use it for steam games.
This device has freed me from some of the back and shoulder pain resulting from constantly leaning over a keyboard and mouse.
Whether this device can be thought of as a gaming controller or not I leave up to you to decide; Regardless of which, it is a great device, that fills a need that no other controller can.
While the controller itself is great, the software (specifically "big picture mode") is sometimes buggy, and not power user friendly. There's no option to copy/paste parts of a controller config, which gets especially annoying if you're creating a multi-layer config with multiple "action sets". Sometimes, it feels like every option you need to change to create that perfect config seems to be 4 levels deep in menus upon menus.
You also need to have steam running in order to use the controller. While this is understandable for steam games (the primary focus for the controller afterall), having the user-specified desktop config installed as a default on the controller itself would've been a really great move, freeing up the controller to be used even on OS'es and machines that have no steam support.
The linux support on the controller is great; Apart from some issues with the on screen keyboard when outside of steam, and some big picture overlay issues in-game (possibly due to me using XMonad as my WM) I don't have any issues. And since the controller is run via steam, there are no driver issues.
When it comes to the actual hardware, the only downside I can see is that the buttons sometimes are a little hard to press. I guess this means that the controller will last longer, but e.g. the l1/r1 buttons (in PlayStation terminology) are hard enough to press that I seldom use them. Still, my hands feel better from using the controller for an extended period of time than they do from using mouse and keyboard.
All in all, it's a great input device/controller thing with a lot of uses both as a gaming device and a general activity device.

The Steam Controller is a great piece of hardware. It is comfortable and responsive. But the software part is poor. The SC drivers only work through steam so you can't use the controller outside of Steam and they have removed the option to use the Daisy Wheel keyboard which is superior to the "standard" keyboard. I can't recommend it because it has no native windows/Linux driver support.

The Steam Controller is to a regular controller what the Spy's Butterfly Knife is to a regular knife. If you're willing to commit to learning the ins and outs of the Steam Controller, you'll find that it's a precise, multi use tool that goes beyond what a conventional controller could ever possibly do, but if you're just looking for something that you can plug in and hit play and not have to worry about bindings or sensetivity, you're probably better off picking up a standard console controller.
That being said, I do still recommend picking up a SC, particularly if you can find it on sale. There are bindings for damn near every game on Steam, and a quick Google or Youtube search will lead you to recommendations for games that will help you adjust with less frustration. My only real issue at the moment with the controller really comes down to the fact that while not connected to the internet (Be it through offline mode or simply not having WiFi or an ethernet connection), you cannot make any changes to bindings. You can apply previously created templates, but any attempts to adjust any part of your bindings on the go are discarded upon backing out of the config screen or trying to export said changes.

This controller admittedly has a bit of a learning curve,  BUT once you learn a bit about how to take advantage of all of its many, many features, you can recognize just how well-engineered this controller is. One of the best purchases I've made regarding gaming, the steam controller is incredibly useful as both a controller in-game, and as a mouse/keyboard combo for navigating my computer.
I can't recommnd it highly enough. I love this controller, and I think it's worth the $50 they're asking for, but if I were you I would wait for it to go on sale which apparently it does quite often.

I have been playing this game long enough that I have a Founders badge.  It is amazing in so many ways.
Pros:
Mech Gameplay that is slow enough to involve strategy, but fast enough to not bore you to death.  Most quick play matches are less than 10m of your life
You will rarely get one-shotted unless you are standing still in a light mech.
Communications in game are great and PLEASE use them
Weapon balancing is good.  It changes and breaks the meta often enough to keep it from getting stagnant.  There is currently no one super mech that wins every time.
Faction play is finally improving where the matches take less time to form, and scouting FP is a great addition for quick small games.
Cons:
Ok, this game is "free" but if you are new, I seriously recommend playing for a week with the trial mechs, finding a chassis you like and buying the full set.  Once you have a few mechs you are good with, you can use in game currency to get going, but that initial start is rough.
Faction Play is a bit one-sided still.  The clanners get the best units 9/10 times.  The mechs may be more balanced, but the units that are top are clan currently.  Hopefully with the new IS gear coming out soon that will change, but I know I watched 3 great inner sphere units collapse after the clan mechs were redone and made too powerful and it still has not recovered from that.  The mechs are balanced, but the playerbase has not come back to the IS.
Heat Management is still weird.  If you fire too many of the same weapon type you get "ghost heat" to prevent people using too many of one weapon.  this makes sense for large weapons like PPC's, but for med las, sm las, and srm's I think it is silly.
I highly recommend the game.  I still fall back to this game every time I finish anything else.  I have a lot of hope for the faction play and eventually feeling like we really make an impact on the game world.

There are pros to the game: The potential for an awesome city-transport simulator is there. It is quite detailed in this respect.
However, the gameplay is severely lacking. Construction can be an expensive endeavour that will leave you frustrated and wishing you'd saved. You could easily blow 50% of your (easily obtained) budget because you built something different than what you wanted. And there's no undo button, so the easiest is usually just to reload if you make a mistake during construction. This is worse if you accidentally delete something critical in the infrastructure and essentially have to start over.
Transport Tycoon had more variety in transportation in one form alone, but this game requires you to buy DLC to get variety (seriously Paradox, stop it with the DLC).
The campaign missions are bland. The maps are different, but the goals are essentially the same. Establish coverage. Build a number of good lines (reputation is pointless, just build something that will cover as much as possible), wait until you have more money or take out a loan, and build more lines. You don't have to think about where people are going. You just need to cover everything until you reach your goal, then move on to the next coverage mission. Growing cities is just a matter of waiting until you have enough money.
Metros in this game are of the Danish variety - no one knows how to build them underground, so the most effective ends up being floating them 8-12m above the city streets. Even if you did build it underground (which is possible) you can't build stations underground, so again, just build them floating.
For these reasons, I would not recommend this game, although it is a fun little game. I certainly wouldn't pay more than 2-3 euroes for it.

Endless Space deserves some praise for being one of the few games that has lost very little of its appeal over time. It has a simple and elegant design with no apparent flaws, an efficient management system and a good ship design platform.
For someone who likes Master of Orion series, Endless Space is an upgrade. In my opinion it beats the latest one of the franchise, even though it was published several years prior. Even Stellaris, the recent creation of Paradox, known for high quality strategy games, doesn't put Endless Space to shame.
What little improvement it would have benefited from is a quest system or some event chains that where applied in a later Endless Legend.
There's a sequel coming to Endless Space. If it'll be an improvement to the original, we could be talking about a real gem!

tl;dr: Watch this show. Stop being butthurt about the CGI already.
Kemono Friends is the undisputed anime of the year when it comes to BD volumes sold, reaching 200,000 copies for vol1-3 as of May 25, with episode 1 having more than 8 million views on Nicovideo. This happened despite that it came in as the underdog of Spring 2017 with little fanfare. For that matter, the west has largely treated it to a lukewater reception at best.
Kemono Friends Project came about as a collaboration between Yoshizaki Mine (Sgt. Frog) and Kadokawa Comics Editor in Chief Kaji Masa, and the anime was a part of a trifaca of a franchise that would have manga, anime and the game. The game project was produced by Nexon, and it received a poor reception. By the time that the anime aired, both the game and the manga had both ended their runs, and the franchise was nearly unknown in Japan.
The anime was produced by Yaoyorozu Studio (Tesagure!, Minarai Diva) who specializes in CG productions. Their first exposure to Kemono Friends project came when the studio was approached to develop the promo video for the game, and they were then asked to produce the anime. The process took around 500 days due to the studio being quite small (with only 5 animators in all) and that the anime was put on the back burner.
The Director of the anime fortunately received near free rein on the anime, and he worked very closely with Yoshizaki Mine and the Kadokawa chief to make the show. Although the initial idea was to make a show that aimed to be child-friendly, the anime never received a prime-time airing slot as they got assigned the 1:30AM slot. As such, the anime's main audience would be adults.
The show follows Kaban (Bag), a girl who woke up in this abandoned gigantic integrated Sarafi zoo known as Japari Park without any memory as she seeks out what animal she is. Her co-protagonist and companion is the Serval Cat who was the first 'friend' that she ran into. The sidekick assistant is this robot called 'lucky beast' who strangely wouldn't talk to anyone except for Kaban, yet it is known by all the humanoid denizens of the zoo as 'boss'. The mystery of Japari Park slowly builds up throughout the course of the story, but it's never presented in a ham-fisted infodump to the audience.
The animation quality is not the strength of Kemono Friends at all. However, the tight execution, the attention to details, the subtle worldbuilding, the amount of hearts that the production team has put in and the dynamics of the characters really made the show into something special. The characters mostly don't fall on the cute animal girls trope in order to sell themselves, and instead lean to being representative of the actual animals.
It's not everyone's cup of tea, but do give it a try.
Truly a modern masterpiece. Kemono Friends saved anime and my life.

In
(hereafter: '
' for short) you're Adam Jensen, the chief of security for a company that deals in technological augmentations for the human body. The company gets raided by a group of people who are opposed to augmentations and its consequences. You see, society is divided between people who are for augmentations and people who are against them. This leads to tension, protests and full-fledged riots. After the attack on your company, you're heavily wounded and the only way to save your life is to turn you into an augment. After that, you're dispatched to investigate the attack, to find out who's behind it and to stop them from repeating their destructive actions against the company.
The game puts you in a futuristic world that's utopian and dystopian at the same time. Technologically it's a very advanced society. But socially, it's in shambles. The developers of
managed to create a world where you feel both at home (you're not on a different planet or in a magical fantasy setting) and out of place. The technological advancements you see are impressive enough, compared to the time we live in. It's not just the main idea for the game i.e. the technological enhancement of the human body. The futuristic atmosphere is also created by means of small details like computer screens have no visible edge and they project an image that can be seen from either side of the screen. It all feels 'near future', making it a believable setting.
I have to point out that for me personally, the first part of the game that's set in the city of Detroit, felt a bit generic and started to bore me after a while. I even considered quitting the game to play something that's more fun. I'm glad I stuck with it though, because from the last part of Detroit until the end credits rolled, I had tons of fun with
. I'm not sure why I got so bored with Detroit. The city feels large but a bit empty. The decor is repetitive: a dozen garbage cans and news stands in every street, a bunch of 'civilians', 'punks' and 'police officers' you can't really interact with, and a lot of buildings of which you can enter only a few. Maybe I still needed to get into the game or maybe it was because Jensen doesn't have a lot of augments (skills) yet at that point. But whatever the reason was, the game got a lot better after Detroit so you may want to know this, in case you feel the same during the first part of the game.
is a first-person stealth action game. But you can play it as a first-person shooter, too, if you decide to take the more aggressive and harder route.
Don't get me wrong. Gun combat in this game is certainly enjoyable. There are different types of guns (pistol, revolver, stun gun, assault rifle, sniper rifle, laser rifle, rocket launchers, ...) and there are a few skills to enhance your shooting skills and your defense against opponents. Also, you can systematically upgrade your weapons to really give you an edge. However, in the first part of the game you won't be equipped to survive more than 3 seconds of actual combat, so you'll automatically turn to sneaking and sneak kills, at least partially.
The whole sneaking system, which is pretty much the essence of
's gameplay, is exciting and fun, although it can get a bit repetitive. You watch the opponents' patrol routes, pick out one of them, sneak behind him and then push a button on your keyboard/controller to eliminate him silently. You then drag the body out of sight of any remaining patrols or security cameras, move on to the next group of opponents and repeat.
Besides sneaking and/or shooting your way through the game, you'll spend a lot of time hacking computers and electronic locks. I think it's too bad the hacking minigame is based on pure luck. You can increase your luck by investing skill points but it always remains a minigame based on luck. There are some consumable items that can make hacking easier, but you'll want to save those for the really difficult hacks. So long story short: you'll be reloading a lot. I would have preferred a minigame that relied on logical thinking or on dexterity to one of pure luck, especially since you'll be playing the hacking minigame a couple of hundred of times.
People tag this game 'RPG'. I do not
disagree with that but it wouldn't be one of -say- five tags I'd put on this game. Yes, you gain experience points for doing stuff but your character doesn't gain levels per se. Every time you accumulate a certain amount of XP you just get a point to spend in a skill tree but you'll get plenty of skill points and it's abundantly clear which skills are good and which aren't, so everyone will end up playing the same character. There is only one personality skill and it's completely superfluous.
You're offered some dialogue options during the sporadic conversations in the game, but mostly the result is exactly the same and storywise your choices make no difference at all, nor do they impact what the game world looks like. During the conversations with side quest givers, you can even go through all the conversation options e.g. be a complete prick and ask for a reward from your dead ex-girlfriends' mom for looking into her death, and it changes nothing about the quest,  its reward or the quest giver's attitude towards you.
I guess it depends on your definition of 'roleplaying game' but in my book,
is a game that may have some vague RPG elements but where 97% is about action and/or stealth. From what I hear it's comparable to Mass Effect 2 & 3 in this regard. If you consider those two games an RPG, then you'll feel that
is an RPG, too.
The graphics are quite nice. The characters' faces look decent and the animations are lively. After a while though, the techniques that are used to achieve this (like the nodding of the head when any person is talking) become very obvious and the initial feeling of being impressed starts to fade a little.
Surroundings and objects are detailed, except for objects in the far distant background (e.g. the city's skyline when you look out of a window) which are low resolution images and look just ugly and out of place. Other reviewers mention this was not the case in the original version of the game, making this even stranger.
The voice acting is top notch. Piranha Games has done an amazing job with the BattleTech/Mechwarrior franchise here. MWO plays a lot like a "tank" simulator requiring every pilot to consider range, heat management, hit loctaion, ammunition depletion, weapon payload, and many other details when preparing their mech "build" or dropping in to combat.
The gameplay reminds me of a mix between Ghost Recon 2, World of Tanks, and Operation Flashpoint: Dragon Rising. I feel like for the casual tactical simulator player, MWO can be pretty punishing. I also think this is one of MWO's many strengths. To be a successful pilot the player will need to be co-opertive (most lone wolves aren't gonna make it), understand good mech build practices, and watch the changing meta-game so as to inform them on those mech builds.
MWO is amazingly a Free-to-Play game. Yes there are many things a player can spend their money on, camos, warhorns, special mech types, BUT unlike WoT, Hawken and other F2P (pay-to-win) models, buying a specialty mech rarely affects actual performance on the battlefield. The MWO devs have done a spectacular job balancing this game.
The specialty mechs do appear on the battlefield, and they perform generally well, but rarely will they outperform a variant chassis with a good build.
MWO is one of those game it is easy to jump into walk around in your mech and shoot at other mechs.... that's easy. Performing at a high level requires practice and good judgement on the player's part. This is a great game and although I'm not great at it, I am getting better.

For all the legitimate issues people have the devs, and wanting new maps, and wanting updates, at it's core, the game IS really good. It's my go-to "I want to play a couple rounds for 30-40 minutes" game.

The Steam Controler is pretty  unconventional with it's use of just a single left-hand joystick, and two track-pads replacing the Right joystick and arrow-pad. However, this exchange works out pretty dang well with a bit of fine tuning. In FPS scenarios, this controller can be mind-blowing, and only slightly loses out to a conventional mouse and keyboard. Even then, it might just be a matter of bias and practice time.
This controller is fully loaded with features. It has a gyroscope for toggleable motion control, and paddles underneath. It's also fully programable, with variable key bindings, and plenty of room for tuning. This means that you can set the controller up exactly how you want it to be. Of course, this means you'll be tempted to spend time fine-tuning everyting. But, if your into that, then that's another plus.
Long story short, I really like this controller. It's well-enough built, it's confortable, and it's customiable. If I had to say one bad thing about this controller for the sake of it, I'd point out how the screw holes on the bottom, plus the awkward seam where the top and bottom halves meet, seems a bit chintzy at first glance. But even then, at least the fit-and-finish is clean and consitent.

Settings menu also bugs out and forgets your changes if you don't back all the way out of the settings after each individual change, Even still, sometimes the controller fails to be recognized when leaving the settings, and your character gets stuck because the controller refuses to work until you enter and re-exit settings again. Track pads work poorly as a mouse, and even more poorly as an analog stick, making attempting to use it as either suboptimal in either case. I played around with the controller for at least 10 hrs attempting to get some sort of functionality out of it but every option i tried felt lack luster. Buttons are cheaply made and click loudly. Cheaply constructed with lightweight, flimsy feeling plastic, no heft whatsoever to the controller. Feels incredibly small in your hands, and given that the two track pads are exceedingly close to the edges of the controller, makes holding it and interacting with the track pads very awkward. Returning it ASAP

Probably the best single player FPS out atm. Alot of love went into this game, so if you've been sitting on this and not playing it for fear of it ruining the series, you've nothing to fear. Plus its optimization is godly and it can run on any potato or toaster
The level design tries to harken back to the originals and succeeds for the most part. It gives you reason to backtrack and explore your enviroment yet keeps you forward focused enough so as not to break its own pacing unless the player chooses to do so.
The gunplay is also extremely solid. You can even set the gun to sit in the middle of the screen instead of the side. That said, every weapon feels powerful and useful. They allow for approaching different situations  in whatever manner you want and manages to avoid pigeonholing them. They really do an amazing job balancing the feeling of the weapons being overpowered, yet actually aren't, as well. There's also no janky animations in reload and moving that make the guns feel disconnected from the character
The only con I'd have for the game is the enemy spawning. While is isn't always true, It basically locks you into fighting arenas and you kill them as they come in. While I suppose this gives control to the developers on how each situation might play out, it just doesn't feel as good as seeing things naturally existing in the world and removes a bit of fun in randomness or strategizing a more in depth way of approaching a situation. Although, they handle it in a way that makes sense - you don't just feel locked in because it's the games mechanic, but rather that it's a natural thing to occur.

DOOM has beed rebooted successfully.
It's really intriguing what id Software will do with the franchise moving forward, but if they're going to build on this game and improve, count me in.

This is Blockland, the game that introduced me to the Internet, Memes, and lots of other things.
I decided to do a review, since it was 10 years since the retail version of Blockland came out.
It was also 10 years since I played it for the first time.
This isn't the Blockland I grew up in.. The Blockland I grew up in was back in 2007-2012 where it was in it's glory days.
Blockland started out as quite a small community, but it was a good community, a community where if you go and look for a server, there wouldn't be an empty server, and of course not to forget that it had lots and lots of add-ons made by many people.
Now here is where I talk about the maps, if you're a completely new player in Blockland, then you probably won't know what I'm talking about.
Back then maps in Blockland were unseperable, it was a known feature of Blockland where it kinda made the game unique.
Coming with the game, you would have a good amount of maps that you can choose from, and if you wanted, you also could've added custom maps to the game, and there were LOTS of maps, ranging from interiors to terrain maps, ranging from full cities to whatever's imaginable. It wasn't like right now where it gives you ONLY slates.
As Blockland progressed in the years, it started releasing more and more updates, and more and more people started to join as well, then RTB got introduced, RTB is an add-on that lets you download add-ons without going in to the forums and manually installing them.
That add-on installs add-ons while you're IN the game, and put them automatically in to the add-ons folder.
This thing blew up, so many people downloaded this amazing add-on, and using it was comfortable.
At this point in time, the game was getting bigger but the community was still creative and friendly as always.
The game got updates along the way, Renderman was added (A Blockland version of Slenderman) in Halloween..
And then...
Update V21 was released.
This update is what killed the majority of the community, and again, if you don't know let me explain that to you.
As we all know Blockland had maps, but those maps were an unseperable part from the community.
Every player in Blockland played in those maps, and gained a connection to them.
When that update came out, most people just decided to quit the game all together,
As that update removed all the maps, and now all you got is a customizable slate, shaders, and a Day Night cycle, and maybe a few gamemodes that were added.
That's it.
Then the game was released on Steam where it got more people in to the game, but they were a threat to the community as they were trolls that enjoyed ruining people's fun in the servers, from what I've been hearing
After a long time when the game was on steam, RTB was hacked and shut down, which made even more people quit.
And now, as far as I know, nothing is left but a small number of players, empty servers, and a memory of lost community.
Imagine if they hadn't have removed the maps for those pesky shaders, Day Night cycles and customizable slates.
If only they had done a better job as including them all together, who knows what we would have today?
The same community as ever but larger. Maybe?
We can't know for certain.
This my review, I recommend Blockland, but not THIS Blockland. The Blockland from the old days.
