There are pros to the game: The potential for an awesome city-transport simulator is there. It is quite detailed in this respect.
However, the gameplay is severely lacking. Construction can be an expensive endeavour that will leave you frustrated and wishing you'd saved. You could easily blow 50% of your (easily obtained) budget because you built something different than what you wanted. And there's no undo button, so the easiest is usually just to reload if you make a mistake during construction. This is worse if you accidentally delete something critical in the infrastructure and essentially have to start over.
Transport Tycoon had more variety in transportation in one form alone, but this game requires you to buy DLC to get variety (seriously Paradox, stop it with the DLC).
The campaign missions are bland. The maps are different, but the goals are essentially the same. Establish coverage. Build a number of good lines (reputation is pointless, just build something that will cover as much as possible), wait until you have more money or take out a loan, and build more lines. You don't have to think about where people are going. You just need to cover everything until you reach your goal, then move on to the next coverage mission. Growing cities is just a matter of waiting until you have enough money.
Metros in this game are of the Danish variety - no one knows how to build them underground, so the most effective ends up being floating them 8-12m above the city streets. Even if you did build it underground (which is possible) you can't build stations underground, so again, just build them floating.
For these reasons, I would not recommend this game, although it is a fun little game. I certainly wouldn't pay more than 2-3 euroes for it.

Renegade Ops; A name that explains itself and explains the game at the same time, an underrated little masterpiece that’s jam-packed full of chaos, anarchy, weapons of mass destruction and all in the form of cars and trucks.
To call this old-school or retro would do it something of disservice, it’s essentially more original than that. Renegade Ops takes the old classic, then moves them to a modern level with co-op, persistent character and tremendous graphics. The camera angle is familiar with a style of zooming around a large map in a distinctive style to Desert Strike, but a little more intense.
The campaign has an interesting climax to it with a dry sense of clichéd humour and cheesy one-liners as you complete primary and secondary objectives. As you play, it is liberating and anger relieving to blow-up tanks and cars, run yourself through building, and turn infantry units into road-kill.
Renegade Ops offers various ways of controlling your car through a game-pad or keyboard, whatever suits your style of gaming. Overall, it’s a great example of a really enjoyable game based on a simple idea that is executed with care and attention to detail.
Altogether, a great single player and co-op game you can play with your friends.

A great game after the like of Galactic Civilizations, but with a bit narrower focus. It's a turn-based game of exploration, colonization, and occasionally combat that is not unlike Civilization in space. As you scout from your starting system you find additional solar systems connected by jump lanes, and you settle the planets in these systems and build upgrades on them to increase your resources and influence. Like GalCiv, the combat is a largely un-interactive rock-paper-scissors affair that has been expanded since the original release to allow a bit more flexibility. You customize your ships with a few categories of weapons, defenses, and other bonuses; ideally you create fleets that counter the technologies being fielded by your enemies. The progression is much like other turn-based strategy games, and victory can be achieved by expansion, conquest, or research. The pace of this game is generally slow, and it is well matched with an amazing soundtrack with ambient instrumental songs.

Lots of options for what to do with systems and planets you own, from terraforming to population control. AI/relations with other factions is pretty straightforward, perhaps a little more competent than Civ5, as least in regards to how alliances work. Ive never had an ally backstab me or drop relations for no reason, which is nice. The UI is simple and polished imo, if you've played any other AMPLITUDE Studio's game, then you'll recognize most controls since its very similar to their other games. Overall a solid 8/10 game that you can easily dump many hours into.

"Even if you don't think you'll like it, just spend the 2 dollars to buy it. It is worth WAY more than the 2 dollars it costs, and even if you don't like it, it's only 2 dollars that you wasted!"
-Original Review
Alright, I decided I should put more effort into it. This game is better than all other turn-based space strategy games because:
*Doesn't do too much behind the scenes, so using the highest quality setting won't affect performance 90% of the time, and means most computers that aren't 5 years old and slow as ♥♥♥♥ can run it with no problems, even at the highest quality setting.
*Is innovative in the sense that the whole board moves, or 'orbits', around the center. This may not seem like that will make any difference. However, at corners the rings closer to the center end up moving farther than the rings on the edge. Because of this, you have to plan ahead to how things move to make sure you move/aim things in the right position/direction.
*Costs only two dollars! Because of this, if you don't like it, it doesn't matter that the money spent on this game was put to waste.
Anyways, that was my first REAL review on a game, if there are any errors in the review, please tell me so. I hope you enjoy this game!

Honestly, this game isn't bad at all. It's actually very innovative. It's a strategy, in space, with a twist. The map's hexagonal fields rotate every turn, simulating an orbit, and giving you something extra to think about in advance when planning ahead.
I got it during a weeklong sale, wanting to get rid of spare change in my Steam wallet. Since it had positive reviews, I decided to try it, and well, for the price, it's pretty enjoyable.
It's got a little singleplayer campaign that kinda teaches you what each ship can do, and gives you a strategic challenge, it's got your multiplayer, where you invite someone from the lobby, and you get to duke it out in space, and with its sandbox mode, you can mess around or play against another player locally, or against the AI. With the multiplayer, and sandbox mode, the game feels replayable. You can generate a nice map with ease, you can choose the amount of asteroids, crystals, and other features, however you want it.
There are two races, each with a number of similar (but not exactly the same) ships, each filling the same role differently. The variety of the ships is large enough to give you a plenty of strategic options.
The music, while repetitive after a while, is pretty nice to listen to during the gameplay, the sounds are just fine, and the GUI is pretty simple.
It does have a few flaws, yes. For example, right now, you connect to the Lobby automatically, and people who are in the lobby as well can spam you with invites. Thankfully, the people that were online while I was trying this game out were considerate, and only sent one invite. When they got declined, they didn't send another, so I guess unless there's a braindead spammer among the players, you won't be bothered much, or at all.
Some reviews also say the game feels like a mobile port, and well, I suppose that's true as well. That alone doesn't feel like a flaw to me however. If this were a game for mobile devices, however, it would be wonderful.
I think the game is worth trying. It's cheap, and for an early access game, it really feels like a finished product. If you enjoy strategies, you could probably enjoy this. It's simple, yet complicated, and it can probably kill a few hours if you get into it.

Wow, this game is fun. Basically I had some money in my steam wallet and this looked interesting, so I picked it up, at first glance the UI looks like a mobile port, but the game works fine with mouse and runs really smooth on my PC, looks pretty good too when you have the graphics cranked up.
Gameplay: This game is a turn based strategy game set in a solar system, unlike a lot of turn based space strategy games this game has no extra fluff, no CCG elements, no 4X style campaign mode, just a simple to learn, but suprisingly complex strategy game. The twist with this game is that everything on the map rotates around the center, although it seems like this wouldn't matter as relative positions would stay the same, that actually isn't true, because everything orbits at the same speed things closer to the center go around faster than things on the edge, these rotations really add new depth and it takes some time to get used to, but the devs have really taken advantage of this with delayed attacks and timed bombs that can take advantage of the orbiting system.
Content: At the time of writing this review (5/13/2016) there are 2 races implimented into multiplayer, 1 campaign (combines humans and aliens, no story just kind of a tutorial and extra ai battles), 9 Human ships, 9 Alien Ships (kinda ten b/c aliens have a ship that can build nanobots), and a sandbox for you to test out new things or play hotseat on the same computer with your friends.
There are some gameplay mechanics that I didn't go over like the resource system, but you can figure that out once you buy the game, oh, and by the way, BUY THE GAME.
My ONLY major complaint is this game doesn't have enough players, so it can be hard to find a match online, but it's more fun to play against your friends and family anyway, so personally, I dont care as much, but if you want to be MLG and wreck everyone online, you might be a little dissapointed with the amount of people that go online on any given day.
If I had to rate it with 5 being an average game, I would give Galaxy Admirals a 7/10, and that will only go up as the game moves further into development with the planned 3rd race coming out and further UI improvements. Good Luck Devs!

When the first Deus Ex was released, it was heralded as one of the greatest games ever. After Invisible War fell short of expectations, the franchise was put on hiatus and ion storm eventually died out. After Eidos was swallowed by the Square Enix juggernaut and a reboot was announced, nobody expected it to live up to the original. That all changed when the cinematic trailer was released, several people changed their minds and to this day no trailer has ever surpassed it.
The game itself lives up to the Deus Ex name easily. The original had great atmosphere and complex mechanics, but you can't get away from the fact that the gameplay was quite clunky and buggy. Human Revolution kept most (but not all) of the RPG elements, but the gameplay far and away surpasses the original. Of course the number of options you had to customise JC in the original were far more extensive but Human Revolution doesn't seem dumbed down - just streamlined a bit. The game now has a cover system, which may put some people off but to me it's very welcome and in no way a bad thing. Just like the original, this game has impeccable level design with open-ended, numerous ways to tackle objectives. I also didn't see a single bug, so that's always a bonus. Overall the gameplay is great and I see no problems with the updated mechanics.
The presentation is ridiculously good. The weak point of the original Deus Ex was its graphics, which are sub-par even for a 2000 game. Well Human Revolution has no problems in the graphics department. The detailed textures and flamboyant art style have a great atmosphere, despite what people may say about the weird yellow tint in most of the environments. The voice acting is really the best you're likely to hear, and Elias Toufexis's performance as Adam Jensen is astonishing. The distinctive voice that made him sound like he gargles with concrete every morning made him a really memorable character and the Clint Eastwood personality comes across really well. But the unsung star of this game is Michael McCann, the soundtrack composer. I know most people think that the soundtrack to the original Deus Ex was unsurpassable, but I disagree. I think that this game has the best soundtrack of any game ever. Most people will disagree, but I really think that without such a great soundtrack, the atmosphere would not have been so palpable. Also, the Icarus theme is the best song ever composed for a game.
The story can be difficult to follow at times, but it's still engaging and if you spend enough time thinking about it, everything will be clear to you. The writers did a good job tying this in with the original and you'll hear a lot of names like Joseph Manderley or Versalife. Overall I think this is a great return to form after Invisible War and a worthy entry to the sequel. I'm just glad Mankind Divided didn't go too overboard on the yellow the tinting again.

If someone tells you this game is bad, they're bad, their mech is bad, and they should feel bad for talking this way about the game.  The epitome of team work and balance, a tactical game where knowing key map points and the weaknesses of mechs is impertive, if you're looking for a game that's immersive and balanced almost to the point of stupidity, this game is for you. Pros:
- Extremely balanced.  Because all mechs in their respective factions pick from the same pool of weapons, you can't blame something for being overpowered unless you're just approaching it from the wrong angle of attack.  Everything has a weakness from not being able to aim at certain angles, to being slow, to being a large target, to being extremely squishy in certain areas, to not being able to turn fast.  Over time you learn what mechs can and can't do well, and you can exploit this.
- Huge variety for customization to suit every play style from people that like tanks and huge damage to people that like stealth and fast jabs at enemies.
- Lots of mechs to choose from, each with their own strengths and weaknesses.
Cons:
- Huge learning curve.  Your first 10 or so games you will do less than 100 damage, perhaps a bit over 100 if you're in an assualt, and after 50+ games you'll be happy if you get 400 damage.  A damage amount for a skilled player is anywhere from 500-1000, and over 1000 for long games.
- Sometimes you get matched up with people that don't communicate.
- Poor optimization.  I've got SLI 1080 ti with a 6700k OC to 4.8 and in some moments I drop down to 40 fps.  Turn down settings if you have issues.

My first thought when I saw the cover of Renegade Ops, was that it looked like G.I. Joe. The impression was made stronger with the game's plot and its FMVs (which are all rendered in comic panels). What kind of game is Renegade Ops, though? It's a neat top-down shooter, in which you control a combat vehicle around large stages, fighting infantry, buggies, tanks and the other forces of the evil C̶o̶b̶r̶a̶ ̶C̶o̶m̶m̶a̶n̶d̶e̶r̶ Inferno.
To accomplish this, you have your trusty primary weapon (your machinegun which can be upgraded with powerups collected from the stages), a choice of secondary weapons with limited ammo (rocket launcher, railgun, flamer) and your speed boost function which can help you reach your destination faster, but also makes your vehicle harder to control. Before you do all this, you have to select one of the characters that the game offers. Each character comes with their own combat vehicle, with each of them differing in speed, toughness and general handling. What they do have in common is a very nice sense of weight, in that what you're driving is really a buggy/jeep/4X4/whatever you want to call it, rather than a bloody motorbike or spaceship. Aside the aforementioned differences, all characters have a unique ability to help them in combat (such as Riz who can use an EMP to disable all enemy weaponry, or Gunnar who can ground his vehicle to the spot, effectively becoming a turret that can dish out huge damage), and their own unique upgrades, which either enhance an attribute of their vehicle or their unique ability.
Of course, to upgrade your stuff, you need to obtain upgrade points. You obtain upgrade points by levelling up. You level up by increasing your high score within a stage, and you increase your high score by, you'll never guess it, blowing stuff up... and it's glorious! Michael Bay would be so proud of this game. But, I was only saying half the truth above. You can also increase your score by completing objectives and in almost each stage, you are given a secondary objective, which you can choose whether to do so or not. A factor that can make the completion of secondary objectives a bit hard is that primary objectives are time-limited and if you fail to complete them within the alloted time, you have to restart the whole stage, which can be quite annoying, as some of those stages can last well over 20 minutes. You'll also have to restart the whole stage if you lose all your lives (you can't save in the middle of a stage), but the game isn't really that hard on normal (this only happened to me once during the final stage), for this to occur regularly.
Despite the long stages, the game doesn't really last, though, clocking in under 5 hours (even with the DLC campaign). Still, playing it with a different character and in multiplayer can certainly give it enough replayability and the flaws I mentioned above, weren't enough to prevent me from really enjoying the game.

When Early Access games hit a low point in quality, Galaxy Admirals, a turn-based strategy game developed by Jetdogs Studios brings some hope in my heart for Indie companies developing rather under budget games.
For the get go Galaxy Admirals separates itself from the top down turn-based strategy games with its unique mechanics. The game is played on a hexagonal map  but what makes this game unique is that the map rotates at the end of each turn around a “Blue Star”, placed in the centre of the map. This may not seem like much but this mechanic adds a lot of depth to the combat as the player needs to adapt to the situation, plan ahead and outwit the AI to achieve victory.
The objective of the game is to destroy the enemy base while protecting your own by using your fleet of ships. The ships are unique and have their own properties which fit their design. Crystals are consumed to make ships. Each player gains a crystal on their respective turn and crystal fragments which are placed on the map can be harvested by specific ships.
There are 15 missions in the campaign mode and the game can also be played in multiplayer mode, where all the fleet ships have been unlocked before-hand. A sandbox mode has also been added where you can test your abilities against the AI.
Speaking of the AI, it is surprisingly good though it can be predictable at times as it focuses more on the objective than your ships it is good nonetheless.
Each map has a fixed amount of objects that spawn to match its theme, so the placement of objects is not always the same when playing a specific map again. This is actually a nice touch as players cannot rely on the same strategy when replaying a map.
The visuals and soundtrack are actually quite good for a game of this price, though the animations are simple. Players can also choose the resolution and graphics quality when they start the game, which is a nice addition. The game also has achievements and trading cards which is a plus.
Honestly, the only mechanic that I do not like about the game is that while playing campaign mode you get logged into the multiplayer lobby, while playing a single-player mode. This is annoying and sometimes frustrating as other players might spam invites for a multiplayer match while you are trying to focus on the campaign battles.
In the end Galaxy Admirals offers what it has to for its price and there is little chance for a buyer to feel robbed of his money considering the cost of this game. Galaxy Admirals is a great game for any strategy genre lover and casual gamers.

Blockland is a great game, in my opinion.
I know that most of the veteran community disappeared, due to the update (v21) which removed maps, and terrain. It was devastating for them. But new players may not understand how maps and terrain meant everything to them.


Another thing: Barely anyone plays Blockland anymore. Back in 2009, 2010, or 2011, you would find thousands of servers and people on at once. The last time that happened when thousands were online, was on Thursday, June 26th 2014. 1843 people were online then. It went down over the next few days, but that was about it. If you want to know how much servers there were, guess what. On the exact same day there were so many players, there was 600 servers online. Not kidding. 2014 was the only peak high year that Blockland had post-map-terrain-update. Nowadays, there's only 100 servers! 500 servers less than it was in 2014.
Blockland was born in late-2003, and was created using a 14-year old game engine: Torque Engine. If you want to create addons, you'll have to learn TorqueScript and some Blender. I'm not gonna lie, most players have created some *really cool* content, if you look in the trailer. Although, not really anyone hosts these cities or whatever anymore.
Blockland is barely updated anymore, so don't expect updates. Badspot only does REALLY tiny updates, and I really mean really tiny updates. If you want to see it for yourself, check it out here:
As you can see, there were only 3 or 4 fixes.
The community is pretty alive and well, but most of the new community are just unpleasant. Take a look at this locked post, for example:
If you are a fan of sandbox games with a Lego-style to it, then Blockland is for you. If you're not a fan of 14-year old game engines, it's not for you.
It's fun, yeah, if you're still intrigued by the "wonders" of your childhood LEGO sets. Derailing from that, you're in no luck if you're not in the mood for tedious sessions of building.

Galaxy Admirals is a solid turn based strategy game.
It got its own unique gameplay style where each turn the field is getting rotated and things aren't the same as the last turn.

Galaxy Admirals is a turn-based strategy game.
The objective is to destroy the enemy base by protecting yours with your own fleet in a middle of hexagonal tile board that rotates each turn around a star.
This is the main attractive of the game, the placement of the objects changes randomly each turn so you must adapt your strategy to the movement of the tiles.
You build ships spending crystals and you gain one crystal every turn that must spend to build ships.
Each ships has its own cost, its own properties and different range of movement, amount of  shields and power to attack. So you must plan carefully your movements depending your resources, the distribution of asteroids and mines, and your opponent ships.
You can play in three modes: Campaign (AI is so correct), multiplayer or sandbox, where you could define the size of the map , the number of the different objects that appears in it and the type of the opponent.
Graphics are well detailed, and each ship, asteroid and mine have a very look shape.
Music sounds like techo chill-out and sounds are very basic, some shots and explosions but the game doesn't need more.
The game has achievements and trading cards.
This is a different game from Jetdogs Studios that you have to play if you like strategy board games.

Although I can understand why many people may have a different opinion to me, I believe this is easily one of my favourite games ever. The universe you are thrown into seems rich and developed yet not linear as every game of Endless Space seems to throw something new at you. The artwork and sound design is some of the best I have ever seen in a game and I personally find the UI beautiful and easy to navigate throughout however some may disagree with me here. The complexity of the game mechanics seems to find the perfect divide between being to simple and overly complicated allowing for an experience which is enjoyable to both new and veteran players. The only two downsides I see to this game are the combat system and part of the AI behaviour. Although the combat system has a few cool features such as the ability to select fleet formations, admirals, ship targeting behaviour and others, these features are built around a card based battle system which feels a bit like an underwhelming complecated version of scissors paper rock. The AI although I personally found to be one of the better AIs of 4X strategy games, seems to play an extremely aggressive expansion strategy in the early game every single time. Although this makes the early game fairly predictable, it also keeps the player on edge and competitive with the AI. Overall, I would highly reccomend this game if you enjoy 4X startegy games similar to Sid Meier's Civilization V and I really hope Endless Space 2 lives up to the great name this iteration of the Endless Space series has created. Also lots of sync-bugs prevent you from playing the multiplayer properly. I really enjoyed the coop mode, but you always only have a very limited time to play before the game totally craps you up.
WARNING: If you play this game in multiplayer over a longer period of time, you'll always get out of sync without any chance to get back. Your coop-partner may build lines but you don't see them and also other important data (like the time of the day, your money, your company value and your weekly income) is totally off for you and your partner. Saving and loading the game again does NOT help to fix this! (Edit: Turns out you can manually end the game, let the host send you the savefile and then load it again to enjoy another few minutes of synced multiplayer gaming until it gets out of sync again. It's still very annoying though, you kinda have to spend half your playing time to manually keep the game synced...)
Do I recommend this game? If this was a beta version: Totally yes! Unfortunatelly the options and variety of this game are very limited and it's totally bugged (at least the multiplayer) and there is very little chance that there are any updates still being made to this game, so it's not really worth its price.
All in all: Great concept, great ideas, bad implementation.
Stay away from this game and eventually hope for a sequel to make a better implementation of this great game concept.

If you’ve played any Dharker Studio visual novel before then you already know what to expect from this. I had experience from a couple and found myself positively surprised by Club Life.
+ Clean, decent art style
+ Simple but enjoyable story
+ Girls stand out from one another
+ Developer provides restoration patch
+ Skip button works perfectly so replay is easy
+ Going back on text is easy in case you missed something
- Several grammar mistakes
- Poor plot writing in certain places
- Main character’s speech font is very bulky
☆☆☆☆★★★★★★
6/10 - Above Average
Relatively short visual novel with a nice art style. There isn’t much variation in sprites but the expressions manage to be even endearing – I found myself liking this game more because of that! Music is simple and repetitive, not distracting but also not memorable in the slightest. The game is short and relatively easy to 100% if you care about achievements. The game has a restoration patch that will include few additional lines of sexual content and artwork, but even without that you’ll know when characters are gonna have sex.
In Club Life the player takes control of Sean, a social recluse who is pressured by his math teacher to join two student clubs or she won’t write favorable recommendation letter for him. There are three clubs to choose from, each with a romanceable girl and two mysteries to uncover. Sean himself has some emotional baggage, which he can either work through or keep adding to.
The plot isn't complicated, mostly just slice of life type of dealings that won’t keep you on your toes as most of it is predictable yet manages to be fairly enjoyable. The writing does have some hiccups, the most cringeworthy content coming from “sex education seminar” part of the game. Nearly all of the others are in one girl’s route as her mysteries seem much too ambitious for this visual novel; the other is highly unsatisfactory as it simply introduces a huge plot element that is never addressed! The other, more realistic mysteries, unfold much like you expect them to and feel complete. When it comes to grammar, this game has multiple glaring mistakes ranging from words being misspelled to general grammar problems ("Was you looking for something?”).
As stated there are three main girls, and whichever two you pick will have interactions with each other as well. I found that to be a nice touch, even if the interactions are extremely cliched. All girls are very different from one another, none of them feel like copies.
Quirky, bubbly and inquisitive. Her influence can really pull Sean out of his shell, but
. She is the type of girl you’ll either find adorable or infuriating, I personally landed in the former category but I can see why it would be easy to dislike her.
Meek, frank, and studious. Her actions can get the more protective side of Sean to emerge, and because she is a fellow loner she feels like the most suitable companion for him.
Abrasive, determined and bold. She has history with Sean unlike the other two, and it was made clear that Sean held no fondness for her in the beginning. Thanks to this it can be difficult to fathom the two of them having a relationship.
Additionally:
It feels as if
is meant to be the “real end game girl” because she gets two good endings while the other girls get one.

Very fun and energetic VN that can be finished in a very short amount of time. I'm a fast reader and skip text I've already read. With that being said, I finished in about 2 and a half hours. A lot  of the text overlaps, but it's nice because it doesn't waste your time if you want to read other routes. There are three girls to choose, each with their own unique story line. A bonus fourth girl is thrown in, but it's not as involved as the other three.
This story features a male protagonist (Sean) who has become a recluse following the rejection from a fellow student three years ago. His teacher Ms. Nevara tells Sean he needs to join two school clubs in order for her to give him a good recommendation for college. In his final year, Sean is unoptimistic about making friends, but decides to join two of the three clubs anyways. Your choices are the swim club (Janet), tennis club (Melissa), or newspaper club (Kylie). Because you can only pick 2/3 clubs, you can only ever see two girls at one route at a time.
I enjoyed the fact that they've chosen names for characters that are more "North American." It appeals more to me as a reader and doesn't have me mixing up the girls or forgetting names as often. Each girl is very different, and they all have their own appeal - even the ones that you like slightly less than the other ones. It has it's mix of fanservice of sexual innuendos but it's a fairly tame story overall. Lighthearted, and very enjoyable to read. A fairly easy read too. The gallery images feature the girls in skimpy clothing, but there is no full on nudity involved. The game is colorful and features nice music.
I'd recommend this to anyone who likes Dharker Studios works, or who enjoy VNs in general. This one is very much in the style of other Dharker Studio workings (such as Beach Bounce), including the writing and art style. The game is relatively short though, however, so I'd recommend getting this on sale. 13.99 is a bit steep.

This is a visual novel pretty similar to what Dharker usually release both content and length wise even though it was one of the weaker to me. Part of that is because there are three different paths, each being similar but with one heroine missing and my first run was without the most interest girl. Maybe it's because they use this same artist in multiple of their games but it really felt like I already saw the girls design.
Without spoilers, Melissa and Janet both are not really interesting early on but develop a bit to make their story at least enjoyable. But it's Kylie that add a lot of humor and energy to the story and she even spice up a bit the other two girls when you take their path with hers. While the path with only the two other girls they barely interact at all and brings nothing good to either.
It is nice that you can pick two girls instead of only one at a time but since it barely change the story it would have been better to work on a story with the three of them at the same time. It add replayability but you get a lot of the same scenes with very few differences so you have to read again or skip one girl's scenes while trying to go for the one you missed the first time. Despite that, the artist's work is always nice to look at and Kylie's path make up for the other two being a bit cliche and standard.
Since Steam only allow two ratings, I will recommend this game but only to those that are looking to enjoy more VNs while having done most of them already. Visually it is great, I honestly don't notice music that much in VNs but it was there and the story is partly entertaining and not bad.

This is a fun little visual novel. It stars Sean as a senior trying to get through the year and into college. Unfortunately, his advisor wants him to broaden his horizons, and makes him join two clubs in order to gain a recommendation. Depending on which path you choose, you can meet three girls. Melissa and Janet are in the athletic clubs, while Kylie is in the newspaper club. Depending on how serious you are in those clubs, you can end up being able to ask one of the girls to prom. And if you have done the right thing, they might even accept and begin a relationship with you. There is also a chance that the teacher advising you, Ms. Raven might... be interested in you, too.
There is an explicit patch, but most content is at the end of the paths (there is one CG on one path that might also be affected). I'm not really sure it adds anything to the story (though being a visual novel, and the most explicit content is after the final choice... I guess it is a guarantee that you will live happily ever after with your chosen girl).

Did you like Tribes? Did you like Tribes 2? Did you like Tribes: V- hahahahahah, no one likes Tribes: Vengeance. But you might like Tribes: Ascend. The fundamental mechanics(especially after the latest pair of patches) are very much Ye Olde Tribes. You pick an armor weight, you pick a weapons-and-gear loadout, you spawn, you use your jetpack, you ski, you eat a spinfusor to the face like thirty times before you remember that Tribes isn't like other FPS games.
But then you get your first Air Mail or Blue Plate Special(mid-air kill), and suddenly you're having fun. Because suddenly you GET it. You get into five-minute duels with others, you grab the flag at 300kph(or stop a capper going at 300kph) and you GRIN, and suddenly it's 2am and you have to make an executive decision whether to go to work with five hours of sleep or play Tribes for another three hours and calling in sick.
The only thing holding back Tribes: Ascend is really a few balance issues(Beowulf tanks are currently a bit pitiful and Shrikes could use a mild nerf) and some map design issues(on some maps, generators and base assets are very vestigial indeed), but you should still play the game, because on the good maps, you're really going to be having a LOT of fun once you get the hang of it.
Plus, you know, the damn thing's FREE. Kind of hard to beat that price, especially since they stripped out the grinding aspects that usually come with F2P games.

Mechwarrior Online is the latest iteration to the series, before Battletech and Mechwarrior 5 hit the scene in the coming months. Its gameplay consists around, you guessed it, piloting giant mechanised machines of war and blasting your opponents in the face.
What makes this game so different from the generic shooter? the necessity of Strategy, communication and cohesion is imperative is you don't want to be stuck in the lower tiers. Ever since the games conception and early design back in 2012, it has come quite far in terms of appeasing to the player base, though shrinking due to PGI's valiant efforts to avoid community feedback, thus nerfing all the weapons to appease our clan-loving horde.
Saying that, the game is always changing and being tweaked here and there, even if to the Inner Sphere's detriment.
In of itself, you get to pick how you play the game, as there are 4 weight classes that adhere to a certain playstyle and ability to customise, but does take quite awhile to understand how the game works for the newcomer. Weapons, engine sizes, modules, armor/structure types, cockpit items, camo patterns, colors, etc. As a F2P game, it gives you plenty to work with without having to throw actual money at the game, a decent tutorial, a "cadet bonus" that allows you to learn and earn at the same time.
--------- EDIT: As of 16th May, MWO had a "skill tree" overhaul, which incorporated a system wherein you must now spend XP and c-bills on adding quirks to your mechs, as before, certain mechs as certain quirks dependant on their loadout; Players will now have the option of spending 4-million c-bills in order to "master" a single mech, unlike before the patch where the player had to purchase 3 variants of 1 mech in order to master it and gain more usefull skills, like speed tweak.
There will not doubt be ALOT of naysayers about this new update; these will mainly be people who either don't understand the new system, ♥♥♥♥♥ about "ugh, so many button clicks!" or the fact that missiles actually have a purpose to this game. prior to selecting skills, mechs will be at their base stats; base armour, base weapon ranges and cooldown times, etc. etc.
Personally? I hoped this update would help the game flourish as it adds alot more customisability to the game, if not very grinding without premium time, but im so glad about the update because now, players no longer need to commit to a specific mech and it's variants in order to master it; you get to play it how you want, and if you want a new mech for a different playstyle, your more than welcome to.
Bottom line of this game? It's a fun little strategic shooter when your not getting missiled to death, but I recommend diving into the universe of Mechwarrior to truly get a sense of how big the world truly is; play the older iterations within the series; Mechwarrior 3,4, Mercenaries, Mechcommander, most of them, if not all.
P.S: Don't bother with buying supply caches unless you like spending premium money for already purchasable weapons.

I love Mechwarrior in general. Most of the games have been great, and it annoys me deeply that you can't get the earlier games very easily anymore. If they had earlier mechwarrior games on Steam, I'd likely own them all.
Mechwarrior Online isn't quite the same. It's a player vs player game. Think World of Tanks, with Battle Mechs.  This is mostly a good thing.  The interface is a bit clunky, but the game seems to run well, and it looks pretty.  I've played this game for hundreds of hours before it hit Steam, right through the early Betas.
There are many, many mechs to choose from, both clan and inner sphere designs, and a reasonable number of maps. The wait times are comfortably tolerable, and the match-maker's not too bad either.  Unfortunately, you have to vote on maps and game styles upon queuing up, and without fail the majority seems to choose the same damn maps... so while they have a good selection, in practice you don't get to play on all that many.
Also, many of the mechs are behind a pay-wall. Not all by any means, but a lot of the really nice ones. It doesn't quite get to the level of Pay To Win, but it runs close. Patch after patch they bring out new monetisation in the form of new mechs, but not a lot of other content.  This can be deeply frustrating.
Equipping your mech is fun. Lots of fun. There are a great deal of options available - though unlike many of the earlier Mechwarrior games you can't just throw what you like on your mech up to the wieght limit. Certain slots are limited to projectile weapons, or missiles, or energy weapons, etc.  I can understand why, but it does cut down on the configurability a bit. You can get different variants of the same basic mech, which does help mitigate this a bit.
There are down-sides however, and a lot of that is to do with how the game has ultimately developed.
Back in the earlier days, the matches felt a lot more epic. Mechs seemed slower and heavier, and each could take a real pounding. You could almost feel the tonnes of metal lurching around, being blown off, etc.  More recent updates seem to have put the emphasis on action. Everything is a lot faster than it was, and I think this is a shame.  You don't quite get that visceral *thump* of steel hitting steel anymore, and everything feels a bit more cartoony as a result.  Also, your mechs come apart a lot faster.
There are no missions, it's all arena play. The arenas themselves are various sizes, but generally quite big, with lots of room to maneuver. However, unless you have your own "platoon", you'll find the random matches tend to involve people not really working together... which is a real shame.
In short, it's not bad, but it's not great. If you don't want to send money on it, it's also free. Got to recommend it just for the big robots.

Not too sure what to write about this game so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

This is what Doom 3 should have been: a slick, brutal romp that takes to hell and back- literally. Doom is an insanely polished game, fast-paced, intense, and surprisingly smart. The level design takes a range of forms, from the tight, dark corridors of the UAC facility, to the extremely vertical industrial facilities, and finally flying across the wide, winding canyons of hell. On top of the astounding level design, the game is just gorgeous, never sacrificing looks for functionality, nor the other way around.
All the weapons feel satisfying to use, and more importantly, remain viable throughout the entire game, something that many modern FPS games miss. The addition of runes (perks, essentially) allows you to tailor your abilities to your playstyle, but they always encourage to rush in head-first, there's no crouching behind cover every 10 seconds to wipe the stawberry jam off your eyes in this game.
The single-player experience was everything I could have hoped for and more, which only makes the extremely mediocre multiplayer that much more disappointing, seeing as it was made by a completely different team. It's slower-paced, less mobile, and the level design was rather uninspired. But then again, you generally aren't playing Doom for its multiplayer anyways, which made me all the more baffled at the fact that all the post-release content was for the multiplayer.
TL;DR: Fast-paced, brutal, polished, Doom is everything you could want in an FPS, with the only downside being its multiplayer.

Let me start by saying that while I do recommend this game, the Steam version has given people some problems; some say they have had errors on trying to launch, which I have not had, and others have said they have had some in-game oddities such as ships not loading, which I did encounter and initially kept me from advancing past the 2nd map.
The steam version is missing a couple of folders. It is silly but adding these empty folders resolves some of the problems such as the ships not loading. Click Read More if needed to see the fix.
--
Go to your Steam directory.
In Steam\steamapps\common\Genesis Rising
Create three new folders called 'replay','temp', and 'save' (without quotes)
Then in Steam\steamapps\common\Genesis Rising\data
Create a new folder called 'scripts' (without quotes)
--
[Many thanks to Future2012 who originally posted this fix.]
Other than that I didn't get any errors on Win7 64-bit when launching it so I don't know if compatibility mode would help or if it is an OS or driver issue. When I did the above fix I have been able to play through several missions without incident.
All that said, the game itself is really good and has everything from voice acting to cutscenes and a story with some deep religious undertones if you care for that, and if not then you still get to blow lots of stuff up and capture enemy ships and bases. In fact there are countless decisions you get to make about how you want to set up your ships and even which ships you want to take. Moreover I pose that you have likely never played a space game quite like it, as it has elements of RTS thrown in and on top of that your ships are ALIVE and can be genetically modified to suit your desires, and changed on the fly to boot. Plus the music and visuals are quite appealing, so if you can get it to work then it is easily worth $5 or more. Good luck!

Club Life is an anime visual novel from Dharker Studio in a high school setting. It includes adult themes.
In Club Life, you play Sean, a loner student in your final year at school, just trying to cruise through doing your own thing. Your nosy home-room teacher, the rather attractive Miss Nevara, however, throws a spanner in the works by saying that she'll only write good things about you in an important recommendation letter if you join two of the school's clubs that year, as socialisation is big on her list of Important Stuff.
Graphics are nice. Character portraits are excellent, but few and far between, with only the love interests shown at all. They are very pretty with some nice outfits, though. Backgrounds are also well drawn, but again, are relatively limited in number.
It's a shame there aren't a few more characters included, even if not a core part of the story, and the backgrounds could really do with some overlays in different situations showing some of the other students and teachers; the school seems deserted for the most part, with only five people inhabiting it.
There are no graphics options, but that's okay; you don't need any.
Music is so-so; sort of typical for this sort of VN, and I can't actually remember any sound effects, although they may be there. Unfortunately one great thing about a lot of these anime VNs is the Japanese voice over, and Club Life loses out there: it's only text, with no voices at all.
Club Life plays like most modern anime visual novels: there's a basic story with multiple endings that you can reach through a number of major choices in the game. There are also a host of minor choices that don't change the ending, but allow for more interest during multiple play throughs, as they change one or two sections of the story each time. I didn't count all of the many choices available here, but there are six endings: one 'bad' ending where you don't get the girl, one ending for each of the four love interests, and an extra ending for one love interest.
The story is typical of the genre, with the player character being a late teen male and the aim of the game being to get the girl, or in this case, one of four girls. Club Life has essentially three major story arcs: one for each of the swimming, tennis, and newspaper clubs. You can choose any two clubs each time you play, so there are at least two play throughs required in order for you to see each major arc at least once, but if you're interested in Steam achievements or the characters in the game, you'll probably want to play through six times to see each ending. This is made much easier by the excellent high-speed 'skip' function, which skips through any text you've already read.
Most of the writing in Club Life is actually pretty good, though, with excellent grammar. I can imagine high school kids saying and thinking a lot of what they do in the game, and other parts of the story obviously intended to be tongue-in-cheek. Even the sex scenes, which some other reviewers have criticised, seem like they're reasonably written to me when you consider that the text is supposed to be what a teenager is thinking or saying.
Club Life also has a free adult patch available from Dharker Studio's website, or you can patch the Ren Py files if you know what you're doing (it's not very difficult). From what I can gather the patch makes the sex scene graphics a bit more 'hard core'.
Pros:
+ Attractive characters with different personalities
+ Excellent writing and a reasonably interesting story for the genre
+ Reasonable replayability, thanks to the multiple endings
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- No voices
Club Life is a solid entry in the crowded anime visual novel genre. The story is well written and the characters are attractive. The free and easy to obtain adult patch is also a nice addition given Steam's rules on adult content, if you're into that sort of thing.

Probably the one controller I was always searching for.
Best couch controller to access movies, search online from the couch or bed, but playing with this... waw. A whole new thing! I love the precision of the trackpads, I even used the steam controller in CS:GO competitive (but I still need to improve my aim).
The steam controller shines in every games I played. If not, it just requires to configure the SC (steam controller) but let's talk about this configuration!
Just like Xinput for other controllers, here you can customize EVERYTHING on your own or download the config of someone else (which is great in the beginning, so you don't get lost and understand all the mechanics). You can configure double tap, long tap, combos, different "mods" (which is great for Arma, so you have different config for Walk, Land Vehicle and Flying) and let's not forget the gyro which make FPS / TPS a great experience once on couch or even at the desk. I surprise myself to only use the keyboard for talking or some RTS which requires lots of shortcut (but I know I can use the SC if I really wanted).
Talking about the keyboard, you also have access to a small pop-up keyboard from the desktop (or from games). It's a very intuitive, responsive keyboard (or keyboards since you have two ways to write: keyboard or daisy wheel! You should try them both).
As much enthousiastic as I am, I have encountered a few "problems" (which can be very minor) I am sure it will be fixed in the next SC release:
-A better shape: Somehow, this controller isn't as comfy to have as an Xbox 360 controller, I was so surprised after a few months of use when I had to use a 360 controller at a friend's house only to realize how well it was in my hands.
-You will not write an essay with this controller: if you think about ditching your whole keyboard and replace it with this controller... nope... at least, I didn't manage yet ;) it's still great to fast reply on facebook / discord / steam chat or even right long comments. But here, I am using my keyboard to write the review as I type faster.
-Better shoulder buttons: somehow, I dislike them, they aren't as responsive / clicky.
-Missing small bumps in the center of the pads, which would make aiming better sometime :) just having a place for my thumbs to rest
-Shiny plastic getting smudgy
Voilà! Really, if you think those are big problems, they aren't, those are just wishes for the next SC.
In conclusion, if you were hesitating to buy a SC, thinking it would make your life greater for desktop / couch playing or couch / bed internet and movies.... You can buy it!
If you wanted a SC but don't know when the new SC is coming... then buy it!
If you wanted to wait for a discount and it's on discount... THEN BUY IT!
If you heard of a new SC coming and people say it will be better... wait for the new SC and look for reviews ;)

CTF was MADE for this game.  Unlike most other games, it seems like 99% of the time both flags are taken.  It's odd at first, but as soon as you understand the way Tribes works you'll fall in love.
There isn't any other game on the market like Tribes.  It's a great addition to any gamer's library, AND IT'S COMPLETELY FREE!
One last thing to mention is that I HIGHLY recommend looking up a video on YouTube about how to Ski.

First of all, this game is suited only for people who are Naruto fans and have watched the entire series. The story mode here re-tells the events of the last canon episodes of the Naruto Shippuden series, so you need to be up-to-date in order to enjoy this game fully. If you're a Naruto fan but haven't catched up to this point, not only will you feel lost but you will get the story spoiled for you. If you're not a Naruto fan, don't even bother with this game.
Like i said, this is a game for Naruto fans. You'll experience the last canon episodes of the Shippuden series, fighting the main battles. Contrary to past Storm titles, the story mode here is shorter and more limited since there's fewer characters involved. But since it has to closely follow the story, i understand that it needed to be done that way. What i hated was the lazy cutscenes using (bad) anime frames with generic animations. Since the story was shorter, there was no excuse for this. Not all cutscenes are like this though, and the ones that use the in-game engine are really good, because this game has an excellent animation work, with plenty of details that will delight the fans. Speaking of animations, the facial expressions are simply amazing, with anime quality. When you're finished with the main story, there's an adventure mode, but that's mostly filler content with main and side quests. It isn't that bad, and it'll take some time to do everything, but it isn't very interesting. The world navigation is also a bit limited. The standard battles are mostly like the past Storm titles, but with a big addition: the ability to swap the main fighter with the support fighters almost anytime. They share the same stats, but this adds combinations and freshness to the combat system. The roster is also huge. Sure, most of the content is recycled, but if you want the definitive 3D Naruto fighting videogame to play standard battles, this is it. Don't expect a lot of online activity though. I will also write briefly about the DLC packs: they aren't terrible, and add more content, especially the Road to Boruto expansion, but they're a bit expensive considering the amount of content added. This expansion also lacks playable characters from the Boruto movie, which is a bit disappointing. If you want the definitive experience, then grab them. Recommended if you're a serious Naruto fan who watched every episode (excluding filler, of course) and also the Boruto movie.

TL;DR: Proceed to summary.
I would describe this game as an arcady shoot'em up.
In a top-downish view you control a vehicle freely in a set area and shoot the hell out of your enemies while crashing through buildings. You obtain objectives to progress and occasionally sidequests. If you take too long, ignoring the main objective, the game starts a 3 minutes countdown. No need to become desperate as in my experience no mission takes more than 2 minutes.
Killed enemies may drop pick-ups. Those are
Harder foes are introduced through progress in the campaign. You need different approaches to beat them. It ranges from kill before they fire to circling around them. It also depends on which character you have chosen as the special abilities differ much.
If you die you lose any picked up upgrade. If not ending up on the wheels, the game resets your car and you won't lose anything. If you get stuck somewhere or sink in water, you will respawn, again without loss. The game has no checkpoints. Losing the last life requires to rebegin that level, nonetheless any earned XP gets accounted.
There are
levels and 5 different characters/vehicles you may choose from (excluding DLC, see below). Every car has another special ability which can change the playstyle a lot. Points you earn while playing are also accounted as XP towards your chosen character. By leveling up you earn upgrade points and unlock additional perk slots. You can use those points to unlock perks from 3 single-pathed skill trees: Offensive, Defensive, Tactic. Off and Def are the same for all, only their order varies. Tactic perks boost your special ability. Reaching max level every perk is unlocked.
(Side note: I only played on hardcore.)
It took me the first 2-3 levels to get used to the game and achieving consistently good results. It still was a challenge though. The final level is a bit tedious
You can view them in the main menu and while pausing the game. Unfortunately you can't remap them. Even though the game recommends a controller, I had no problems playing on keyboard & mouse. You move around with [W], [A], [S], [D]. Press [SHIFT] to drive faster in return you won't be able to fire. [CTRL] activates the handbrake so that your car won't roll by itself (down a ramp). Use [SPACE] for the special ability and [E] to switch secondary weapon (giving up the current one). Tap [TAB] to show a semi-hollow map which will be displayed in the center of your screen. It shows the locations of your current mission.
The mouse is used to move a reticle on your screen. It marks the spot you will shoot at. [Left Mouse Button] fires machineguns. [Right Mouse Button] fires secondary weapon. If you target something above (e.g. helicopter) or below (e.g. down a ramp) you, the game adapts automatically.
The default movement emulates a d-pad, giving 8 possible directions. I recommend to enable "Tank Steering" as it allows you to move freely. [W] being forwards, [S] backwards, [A] for steering left, [D] steering right. Keep in mind that "Tank Steering" won't apply to the helicopter which is no problem as you won't encounter many obstacles in the air.
The story is straightforward and foreseeable, nontheless it's good enough to attract your attention and wanting you to learn more. As the store page already states, the main plot line is "In Renegade Ops you must defeat Inferno, a madman intent on global domination."
The cutscenes are presented in comic style. When the story/mission goes on while playing the game displays a single panel at the top right, not disturbing your view. Subtitles are fit in the pictures and don't break the comic art style.
Available settings are resolutions, anti-aliasing (none, x2, x4) and v-sync (none, 60).
The game ran smooth on my machine and I never encountered lag or drops in framerate.
Settings: 1920x1080, AAx4, no v-sync.
Specs: Intel Core i7-4702MQ 2.2GHz, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 850M, 8 GB DDR3.
The game is nice to look at while cruising through the well designed areas. The levels vary and you will encounter different environments and textures. Water and most important fire effects are an eyecandy. The explosions are a blast and even though most entities are quite small, they are detailed.
You won't really pay attention at the music except for the intro/menu/cutscenes as your concentration focuses on the action and the sound effects will predominate. As far as I was able to listen to it, it fitted well. Outside of fights it keeps subtle and turns more intense while fighting, adding the feeling of action. As everything is about firing and explosions the sound effects are a blast. The audio never annoyed me in except for one thing: Driving at max speed keeps looping the sound of the car, including shifting etc.

Galaxy Admirals is a little strategy game, turn-based, that can be played solo or in multiplayer. The goal is to destroy the enemy base by protecting yours with your own fleet. Each turn will grant you a crystal that can be used to build different ships: support (gathering crystals on the map but also repairing anything that will be suffering damage), missile carrier, etc..
The twist is that the hexagonal map is turning, making the field different each time, mainly with the asteroids that can block your path suddenly (but the enemy's too). I suppose that more obstacles will appear along the way as I'm only at level 4 in the campaign.
Because of the twist, you need to be careful and try not to be blocked, though you don't know how the field will change.
The visuals are simple as it's a top-down map but they're also neat. The soundtrack is correct.
Not being a strategy fan, I've an hard time to think about my fleet and with the field changing each time, I'm not really at ease. It means that Galaxy Admirals is not my cup of tea at all. Yet, I'm pretty sure that fans of the genre will see in it a relaxing game compared to the blockbusters of that kind. I suppose that the multiplayer can bring more fun.
For the price, you will not be robbed. So, go for it if you're a fan or if you want to try the genre.

Mechwarrior Online, at an initial glance, seems to be a continuation of the Battletech franchise. After all, that's what it bills itself as. However, when you take a close look at the game, what it really boils down to is a giant robot combat sim that borrows some names from the B-Tech universe and some very basic mech designs.
Using the Inner Sphere vs. Clan theme, there are supposed to be two technology types. In all previous renditions of the game (including table top), Clan was always superior tech wise. However, thanks to the very venomous and rabid community, PGI has decided to nerf Clan back into the stone age and buff IS way beyond what it should be. Clan is now ultra fragile technology while IS has become the tankiest of the bunch. PGI has tried to reason this away in an attempt to appease the crybabies of the community instead of making other changes that could have addressed this in better ways.
To top it off, most of the player base is very toxic. The most vocal of these are those who prefer to meta a game to death and look down their noses at anyone who doesn't play according to their ideas of how it should be done. If you post something on the forums that these self appointed "elites" disagree with, they'll let you have both sawed off barrels. In game, if you make a mistake, take a loadout they don't like or anythine else, you'll get verbal abuse like you can't imagine. The moderators are not much of a help either.
As someone who has been playing  Battletech since the late '80's, I'm very distraught over the direction MWO has gone. If you're a die hard fan of the universe, a lover of the lore and everything that made Battletech great, stay away from this game - especially if your allegiance is to any of the Clans.
If you are a lover of generic giant robot combat sims, someone who doesn't give a care about the B-Tech universe, is someone who only wants to meta a game to death, and is someone who has a very toxic personality, then this game is for you.

It's hard to really say what hasn't already been said about DX:HR. Having played both the original and the directors cut I think it's fair to just comment on my feelings about if this re-release improves the experience or not. Beware of SPOILERS ahead.
On the face of it, there isn't much added except the DLC with its extra chapter and some new items like the auto-hacking devices. First of all, theres the new chapter. In the original game the transition from Hengsha to Singapore felt jarring. You're told that you've been off the grid for days and yet there is no reason why. It just seemed like Jensen had been in a stasis pod for that time and had only just been revived. Now we know that he was at the Belltower facility which provides the storyline nessersary to explain why the Hyron project had women strapped inside and why there was indications of kidnappings happening throughout the game. I genuinely get the feeling that the game was originally supposed to have this DLC content but it was cut due to deadlines. As for the chapter itself, it is hit and miss. It is split into two sections. Firstly is the ship and then the second act is aboard a Belltower facility.
The ship itself is a very unique environment in the game as it feels chlostrophobic and more tidy than the cluttered offices and grimy streets that the DX series is fond of. So that was a refreshing change. The fact that your augments are disabled ramps up the tension and really makes you notice just how valuable they were since prior to the ship you've no doubt reached a point where you have a wide range of abilities.
Moving on you have the facility itself which is unfortunately very generic and has a painful amount of backtracking. It feels like the developers didn't have the time to truely flesh the environments out and chose to have the player going back and forth through the same areas again and again. The voice acting for this section is also cringe-worthy and if it wasn't for the fact it fills a nice plot-hole I would have never said it added anything to the game.
The Directors Cut remixes the boss fights to cater to players who have been focussing on their stealth skills over combat. However you can tell that they didn't plan for this as the 'solutions' are really a trivial case of reaching a control room area and turning on gas/turrets/bots and then letting the boss wander into these hazards. The AI for the bosses is really revealed as lacking due to these additions as well. The addition of the DLC auto-hacking devices will appeal to the players who don't want to bother much with their hacking skills but are really not placed in the game where they are needed most - namely the early chapters. By the middle of the game a combatant will now have started to invest in hacking skills anyway and yet this is where you start being bombarded with these tools. Again a design choice that feels half-hearted and poorly thought out.
All in all, DX:HR - Directors Cut is worth taking if you want to have the storyline to make more sense and carry additional weight but not if you are looking for it to offer a totally new experience compared to the original. The revamped boss fights haven't received enough attention, the new items don't offer more varied gameplay and the additional chapters gameplay is average at best and tedious at it's worst. I'll go with recommending it myself however as I truely play the DX games for their storyline.
(as a personal gripe; I attempted the non-lethal play through and somehow, somewhere an NPC got killed and I got the blame.  Devs really needed to add a way to know when a achievement was lost so I could have reloaded an earlier save and correct whatever happened to cause the death)

Having just completed the video game DOOM and looking for a new shooter to get way into, I came across the new Deus Ex: Human Revolution game which comes from the company Eidos Interactive's Montreal Canada branch. The book the game reminds me of most is "Stranger in a Strange Land" by Robert Heinlein. Incidentally, the company is also the maker of the women's adventure game Tomb Raider, the thought of which I find very interesting
Deus Ex is mildly fun but I guess the word that best describes it is "milquetoast." The main character, Adam Jenson, is no James Bond, that's for sure! The guy is a weenie. He and the guys he works with are part of a company which is involved in corporate espionage of the most dastardly variety against an enemy company that seems to be staffed by Navy Seals. Perhaps it is a banking, multinational, fortune 500 or life insurance firm. In any case, the main character follows an enemy Navy Seal / Blackwater bodyguard type who is part of a small team of terrorists that go through public, government, & private office spaces hating & shooting everybody in sight. He has to zip after those guys & try to either join their team or take them down, one or the other.
General style: Deus Ex doesn't introduce anything new to the genre or anything like that - on the contrary, it is sort of along the lines of the original Counterstrike but with slower & more humble pacing. That isn't necessarily bad, as the whole hacking thing is kind of neat and the character development thing is fun. The male character interacts coherently with a girl who is a helicopter pilot and the two seem to get along nicely, even kissing at one point and getting each other coffees. The dialogue does seem to be campy & seems stilted, so that is a minus. Everybody wears fairly expensive designer clothing, which is a plus. There is a threatening individual who is featured prominently in the gameplay of Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Things are too serious in this game, which is another minus. A poor & desperate unemployed country person is a character in the game.
Unlike, for example, the original arena combat FPS Unreal Tournament 2004, this is a shooter in an office/city setting. That is a concept that has been done to a more successful degree in the new-ish game Crysis 2. Just to avoid accusations of being unfair to the game, I will say that it is pretty OK even if many of the things in it have been done before in a better way in different video games. That's not such a bad thing. I'm a fan of the first-person-shooter genre in any case so I enjoy the ride even if it isn't "GROUNDBREAKING NEW-AGE STUFF."
Final rating: 6.2/10, which is a C-. Sort of on the line of not worth buying or else worth buying but only at a steep discount. NOT a top-tier shooter game, in my humble opinion. "mean & hostile" interaction format. The FPS is not for kids, as there is sexual violence, bad language, betrayals, hostility, & other "Rated M for Mature" themes going on in it. No doubt François Lapikas, lead developer from Eidos Montreal, is slightly embarrassed about this sort of mediocre-to-bad title
Not to cut this game out right off the bat, but if you want to play a groundbreaking, sort of trend-setting FPS game that is indisputably GOOD, I would suggest you check out Metro 2033: Last Light Redux. It is about the same vintage & came out at about the same time but is a real classic of the genre & is much more inspiring & heroic.
I must reiterate that I do NOT want to be unfair to the game Deus Ex: Human Revolution! It is a good game that works & there is nothing hackneyed or trite about it. Just because there isn't what seems to be a bulldog on the cover, that's not a cause to make fun of the game.
Regards,

I've enjoyed this game quite a number of times on my Xbox 360 and have had a great playthrough on PC as well. Game appears to have been ported very well, though I imagine by this point your PC would have to be several years or more out of date to have any technical issues here. I suppose due to prior experience, I found I had a better time using a controller over a mouse/keyboard setup, then again the game feels designed for a controller. Though combat being somewhat limited, save for a handful of mandatory flow breaking boss fights, control preference won't be much of a difference in gameplay, so it's up to you on that one. As for the story, nothing ground breaking but it does feel like it does the Deus Ex universe some justice, though I'm to understand there are a small handful of conflicting plot elements from the first title, but nothing to crazy.
When it comes to gameplay, exploration and finding different ways to reach or complete objectives is key. Though as mentioned before, this is completely broken by mandatory boss fights which seem hamfisted into the game, breaking the exploration and stealth entirely. In some cases, such as a no kills playthrough, this can hurt some players, as they may not have a lethal weapon or hardly any ammo to make it through a boss fight forcing almost game breaking instances. Luckily, Deus Ex: HR has an autosave system which if you ask me, autosaves far to often, giving that unseen crutch for people save spamming their game in the first place.
There is a modest amount of story and dialogue which can be entirely missed, some of it very easily in the two hub cities you find yourself in. If your a completionist, it pays off to search every nook and cranny and check around NPC's for goodies or hidden or otherwise missed objectives. That said, the story is nothing to be amazed by, as Jensen (the character you play as) comes off as a kind of a kook. He's likeable on some levels and his motiveations are in place. But he never comes across as relatable. And considering how much time your going to be sending as Jensen and the amount of dialogue he has, it's hard to relate as he keeps replaying the "I never asked for this" card, as if being a victim would add to his depth, if anything it hinders to his growth and almost goes against the grain of his personality. If anything, the story development must have been off. Several writers or cut dialogue and sequences during the games final development. It's difficult telling.
As for combat and stealth, well, killing really doesn't seem to effect the games outcomes at all, 'nor does a no kills playthrough. A few things will be different here and there, but most of the consequences barely seem to differ at all, only serving as another funky plot point to keep the train rolling. So when it comes to stealth/no kills or combat/lethal kills it doesn't really matter and amounts to more of an aethestic choice of the player in how they'd like to carry out objectives and levels. However, stealth never seems as rewarding as it could, as with the ridiculous amount of upgrade points you get in the game turn you into a regular futuristic James Bond from Detroit. The balance of some skills and there uses seem forced. Some upgrades being completely useless and others being so ridiculously useful you effectively turn the games difficulty down.
In the end, without spoiling to much (SPOILERS WARNING) I have to mention one detail of the games lackluster ending.
You get stuck with basically five choices of stock footage and expostion, none of which reflect your deeds in the game in the least which is rather disapointing. That's all I'll say there.
Overall, I had a lot of fun in spite of some funky bits here and there. I'm sure you'll have a good bit of fun too, especially if you catch this on sale, it'll be worth the price. Exploration is rewarding, the combat and stealth is enough to keep you entertained and the story, though it could have used some work, is engaging enough in a dialogue in human civil rights and attempts to reflect modern social and economic norms which adds up to the old saying, "The more things change, the more they stay the same."

Kylie, the newpaper photographer/conspiracy theorist, is the best character even if you're not romancing her, and the fact that
only makes things funnier, in my opinion. The real disappointment was Ms. Nevara's ending, which I left for last. Okay, so... Here's the thing. Although steam only says I have 1.3 hours in this game, I have a total of roughly... I don't know, I don't feel like doing math. Let's just say I play an hour to three hours of this five-six days a week, roughly, and have been doing so for the past year.
I grew up playing Mechwarrior IV Mercenaries and the Battletech Tabletop game. And I loved both. MW4 was fun as hell, even if it completely screwed canon. There was not really a "learning curve" to it. And that's not even going into the arcad-y shoot 'em up that was the Mechassault series.
So, Mechwarrior Online is interesting. It's the closest to tabletop rules a Mechwarrior game has gotten to in recent memory. But it's player versus player only, undoubtedly a loss or turn-off to a lot of people.
And there's a hell of a learning curve to it, seriously. People play a few matches, freak out because they die every time, and give up, leaving a bad review before even actually getting to play. To like this game, to get good at this game, you have to put in the effort. You have to grind for experience-not in-game currency/mech experience, *Actual* experience. You have to know your mech, you have to know your role, you have to know the maps. For as much of a "Thinking Man's Shooter" as this game used to be, it still is, even if people say it's not (And they are wrong.). You *NEED* to use teamwork. You *NEED* to communicate. Otherwise, your team gets rolled, and it's a slippery slope when you try to get out of the hole you dug yourself and the rest of your team by lone wolfing it.
Don't let the nay-sayers get to you. This really is a great game, but you have to be willing to learn to play it. About a 7.5/10, in my opinion, and it's slowly getting better for me personally even now, especially with the upcoming Summer updates.
