PAYWALL: No. There isn't a paywall, it's not P2W.
Let me elaborate: When you first create an account, your first twenty missions each will reward a buttload of cash. More than enough to buy ANY mech in the game of your choice off the bat. After your first mech, the boost goes away which does lead into a grind, but that's in any game. For instance, a match on average gives you 100,000 C-bills. Most mechs can range between 6million to 14 million depending on the faction and its weight ratios. These are daunting looking numbers, but they're not as bad if you managed to get your favorite mech with your starter money.
In my personal experience, being a big fan of the Timberwolf from previous mechwarrior titles (Mad Cat) I saved my noob bonuses until I had enough to buy one. I was beyond words with my excitement, and found myself forgetting an economy even existed. Why would I care? I got my favorite mech. Naturally I started looking at other mechs, and by then I had played my Mad Cat so much that I had enough C-bills to buy them. So yes, it's a grind. But they give you some lube by letting you choose a mech to start your grind with.
They even have "starter" mechs which are builds the Devs make themselves that you can use free of cost. And they're by no means bad, either. Edit: Not entirely true. As someone pointed out to me, the trial mechs are builds created and voted on by the Community, not the devs.
Moving on from the noob experiences, gameplay is actually quite fun. It's intense enough to have you on the edge of your seat but simple enough to where you can actually take your time and enjoy it. The learning curve isn't as rough as other games, and Mechwarrior is easy to sit behind in terms of actually piloting the mechs.
Enagements can lead to being fast, agile light mechs attempting to weave between the armored titans and strike at their weaker rear armor to playing the massive skulking titans and delivering devistating volleys into your enemies. Keep in mind, however, that it is a TEAM game and that the biggest may not always be the best mech for the job unless you're working with your team.
Customization on the other hand can be daunting, so I suggest maybe watching a quick guide if you're planning to play.

The game goes out of its way to give a bad first impression --
if your graphics card is half decent/recent, the game will get confused and think you can only do ridiculously low resolutions. So you fix that by installing some stuff.
Next, the sound is ridiculously quiet. So you fix that by installing some stuff.
Then, the game drops you into a scene with no background or context, which is bad in itself, and the visuals are really pathetic at that point (I think it's because there are many yellow cabs in that scene, and cars are the single most♥♥♥♥♥♥♥looking things in the game) -- which is misleading, as all in all, the graphics aren't great, but serviceable and quite acceptable for a game of that vintage. Oh yeah, and you can't pick your character, so you're stuck with one who looks like a dork (all of the time) and acts like an♥♥♥♥♥(half of the time).
So, the first big challenge then is to make it past the first 30 minutes. After that, it's good fun for a good while. An open world and Awesome Powers(TM) go a long way, and the game is good fun for a good while. Eventually though, the missions get a bit repetitive, and starting about 2/3 into the game, it's usually not the missions that are the problem -- getting to the mission is (travel basically implied the choice of not using powers, in which case you'd get swarmed by zombies, ragdolled by soldiers using rockets and artillery on the zombies, and it would generally take forever, or you'd use your movement powers to speed things up, in which case you'd probably get detected, and take just as long trying to shake off those pesky strike teams. It sounds like a good, "realistic" idea in theory, but in practice, it was nothing more than a nuisance).
That said, it's not a bad game if you can get it really cheap, but one that overstayed its welcome a bit and would have benefitted from having 1/4 - 1/3 of its playtime cut. (Or, as the more expensive option, have that additional playtime be made more varied and interesting -- something that largely succeeded in Prototype 2.)
Pet peeve: The protogonist doesn't have that many voiced lines; he (as well as his sister) has a unisex name, depending on whom you consume you may run around as a woman anyway, and pretty much everybody else calls him "it" anyway (on the grounds that he's an evil infected commie mutant), so their dialogue wouldn't even change. At that point, they might as well have vastly improved the game by giving you a choice of character, at the cost of adding character creation, and a few dozen voiced lines for the protogonist (much more easily so than in P2, for a start, which has more story, and more dialogue -- even so, Saints Row IV, which rips off Prototype mightily, runs circles around both installments in that regard, just like SR3 ran circles around GTA).
SO, DO I NEED TO PLAY THIS FIRST IF I WANT TO PLAY [PROTOTYPE2]?
You know, I can't say with certainty. While P1 is summarized at the beginning of P2 (incompletely, and colored by the agenda of those doing the summary), you'll need P1 for the full story -- while P2 has a new protoganist, it continues the same story in the same setting, and certain key characters of P1 return. As P1 feels like it has a simpler, slightly less engaging story than P2, with less "story per hour", it's hard to say whether it'll be worth it when you really just want to play P2 and are only playing P1 for the additional background. That said, if the P1/P2 package deal is cheap once again (making P1 £2 or so) and you actually have the time for both, give it a shot -- if you really hate P1 two hours in, you can still fast forward to P2.
THEREFORE,
Qualified recommendation for the B- list P1 (decide whether you can stomach the somewhat retro look), recommendation for the A list P2 (whose only faults are that you have no choice of protagonist, and that it plays a somewhat cliched evil-corporations-and-uncaring-government plot straight, if rather better than P1 did).

Absolutely a phenominal game. The best story in any shooter I've ever played, with philosophical themes ranging from what it means to be human to questioning the price of progress. The game also covers many contemporary thoughts about social equality, wealth inequality, corporation rights vs the people's right, what life is like in a police state and what happens when a few men without morals control the outcome of an entire generation. For gameplay itself you can approach it stealth style (metal gear solid esque) or go rambo and try to kill everything in sight (this usually ends in failure though). There is quite a few different weapons for each approach, for example tasers and tranqs for stealth, machine guns, rifles and rockets for rambo. You can upgrade most of them with items you find for exploring areas or sometimes upgrades you can buy at blackmarket dealers. There is also an upgrade system for you character which allows you to do things such as sprint faster, get more armor, hack computers easier etc. Overall this work of art gets a 9/10 from me, if the shooting mechanics were a little more unique I might give it a ten. Definitely worth the sale price and possibly the full steam price if your into near future style shooters. (btw my first review)

This review is based on my time with this games Multiplayer part, and from playing with a friend.
The first hour of the game was exciting, me and my friend having a good time figuring out the basics of the game.

Do you want a game to burn some time? Do you want a game where the point is to ship people from point A to B and back? Do you want a unmoddable, unexpandable(as of now 12/1/13, there are no known expansions other than the monorail.), and generally generic game?
Well, here you go, a city transport game in full 3D with a handful of vehicles to haul people and NO goods or other transport-worthy stuff. However since this game is a people transport game I suppose I can ignore that fact. However I cannot ignore the fact that after you plop the stations and watch the buses go... there is nothing else to do... I have played OTTD (Open Transport Tycoon Deluxe) and I can be on it for hours, mainly due to the fact you have TRAINS. In CiM2 I play with some metros which oversimplify the game generally. Also, you'd have to pay at least $5 more to get a decent amount of trains or verierity, since the regular game has just 2.
This puts me into the main problem of the game, the game lacks a worthwhile amount of content. You get about 11 vehicles in total (14 or so if you preordered like me) and probably 150 props and buildings. Thats it. The devs are working to cram more vehicles, but only if you pay $5 for 5 vehicles. It is unknown if the devs want to make a building pack as well.
Something I can give it credit is its road system, it has a really  flexible road system which includes from roads, expressways, and one way roads
Graphics:
Odd, the graphics/color sceme might not be for everyone, I had mod it in order to suit my tastes. Modeling and texturing are fair but not world-class.
6/10
Content:
As I said before, there isn't much beyond the 150 buildings and props, and the handful of 11 vehicles in the regular version, the DLC adds some  20 more but the cost of that alone can buy the game probably twice.
4/10
Gameplay:
Gameplay is well, like it is, you place a line from point A to B, and hope to make as many stops as possible to make more money. It generally thereafter is just making sure you have sufficient vehicles and depots to store them. Making grids with the roads is a hazzard, since the roads don't snap with each other in order to make crossings, thus resulting in you making grids road by road until you have a grid. After all is done and said, there is pretty much nothing else to do.
5/10
Rating:
5/10

My Final Opinion:
Don't buy this at full price, or better yet, buy CiM1, you'd have more fun than this dead end game. Maybe if you wait a year or two maybe the game gets better. Right now, its not worth the $20 (+ $27 DLC).

I love love love my steam controllers... great for using in desktop mode and I love being able to play almost any game from my TV.. I mainly just use community templates for the controller for different games, but I have made my own in a few more indie games that I play. My only gripe is that I've had the controllers about a year and a half, and one of them got killed by battery acid :(

+ Works out of the box with Steam games on Linux and Win
+ Very customizable
+ Feels sturdy
+ Can be used as a mouse and kb
- Wireless requires AA batteries
- Not good for twin stick shooters and games that require good d-pad

Overall I have had a very positive experience using the Steam Controller. However, this is not saying that it does not has it's issues. Just going to lay it all out!
-The controller simply feels great in my hands. Easily the most comfortable controller I have ever used. I feel like most controllers are just way too small for my hands.
-Ridiculous amount of customization. This by far is the greatest part about the controller. You can change and adjust everything on it. I can play games without moving my fingers off buttons at all. It is simply amazing. If you are playing a game and something feels a little too tight or loose, you can adjust it on a slider somewhere. Definitely takes some time to figure everything out, but the sky is the limit when compared to other controller hardware.
-The trackpads are great. However, it is going to take some time to get used to using the Steam Controller. It took me months, I am over a year in and I still feel it is a little odd sometimes. Once you get the customization tools down and the use of the trackpads, you can do A LOT without having to move your fingers to other buttons. I also find the accuracy in FPS games (when dialed in and trained) is superb to that of an analog stick. The Mouse to Joystick is just amazing. However, I had had some issues playing twinstick shooters, as the trackpad is very large compared to an analog stick ... I often lose track of where my finger is, which makes gameplay frustrating at times.
-Non-Stop Beta, every day. There are constantly updates to the Steam software, and you really should be using the beta client if you want the most compatibility out of your hardare. I find the constant updates tiring and have seen them break a few things as well.This is infuriating at times when something has worked the day before, and is completely broken the next. I would have hoped the software would be more nailed down by now.
-Compatibility issues are another issue I have had on a number of products. Many of these problems stem from other input devices I have connected to my HTPC, but I have also had games work, and then never work again (Kalimba for example). It is frustrating when you have issues with the controller, and is definitely MUCH different in that respect to console gaming.
-No D-Pad. This is probably my number one issue with the design. I use a controller for side scrollers, platformers, and games that should be played with a controller. If you are playing an FPS game with a controller ... just stop. The clunkiness of the left track pad doesn't make up for this in the slightest. Would love to see a modification or improvement to this.
-Rechargeable batteries are hard to get out. They must just be slightly larger than normal AA batteries. I am not sure. But both my Duracell and Energizer rechargeables are hard to get out and end up getting damaged occasionally when trying to eject them. I hope this is improved on a new version.

First off, let me preface this by saying that Endless Space is one of my favorite 4x games and one of my most well-loved games. I have decent experience with 4x games and many are bad, while just as many are good. At its base, Endless Space fits into the 'good' category, however it is plagued with numerous glaring problems that I would recommend playing another 4x game.
Endless Space is a space 4x strategy title developed by Amplitude and you know that already. The gameplay consists of building an interstellar empire, balancing economics, research, military, and diplomacy, like most 4x games. The largest problem that Endless Space has is that these mechanics either do not play well together, or are almost entirely broken. I want to draw attention to the positives of the game before I delve into specifics as to why I do not recommend it:
First of all, it is fun, usually immensely so. Games can take anywhere from 1.5 hours on the fastest speed to around 10 hours for the slowest, meaning it has a playtime per game comparable to other 4x games. There are some imaginative factions, from involuntarily ravenous insects to sentient stones, and the most of the default factions can be considered balanced. There is a custom faction creator, a staple of 4x games. The graphics are stunning for a strategy game, especially considering that it came out four years ago (though not as breathtaking as Endless Legend's), but despite this, the game still runs on most machines I've tested it on with Fantastic graphics. Even on the lowest graphics, though, the game definitely still has formidable aesthetic. This was Amplitude's first game, and you can see the charm of an 'indie' title in it, if that sorta thing appeals to you. All-in-all, it's a rather generic 4x strategy game - it's probably the closest thing to "Civ in Space."
Now, as much as it pains me to do so, I will explain why I cannot recommend this game.
The first, most glaring problem, as I mentioned, is that the various 4x mechanics do not work very well together, at all. Scientific playstyles are, without a doubt, the most overpowered/easiest way to win. This is mostly due to the fact that overdeveloping a tall empire gives many more benefits than a wide empire would, resulting in end-game tech at the beginning of the mid-game for all other players. Space combat isn't difficult when you have end-game weapons put up against low-intertia slugs. Diplomacy is absolutely broken, half the time completely invalidating the need to have a tax rate above 0%, by way of simply offering open borders/peace in return for a large amount of that empires' dust per turn. The other half of the time it is exceedingly useless - AI that feel 'Very Close' to you will declare war within the first 50 turns, regardless of empire proximity, score, expansion, etc. The diplomatic relations and treaties are mostly useless - why even include a button to allow AI to trade planet if the AI won't trade a single system for *everything* in your empire, including your 20+ systems? Making an empire focused on dust production is almost entirely useless unless you're trying specifically for an economic victory, and even then, it's not likely that you'll have a fun time of doing it. Combat (and sieging by extension) is the absolute worst combat I've ever experienced in a 4x game, basically boiling down to a phase-based CCG. Ship building seems cool at first, but it's really a snapshot of the original Master of Orion ship builder - you start with 3 classes of ships and can research up to 4 more, then add various modules to decide exactly what role the ship will play. This sadly boils down to stacking obscene amounts of weapons on very cheap ships, scout ships not even being built, and colony (settler) ships being far to cheap if they're modified at the beginning of the game. Heroes are extremely useful as governers and next-to-worthless as fleet admirals. Finally, the game has quite bad problems with micromanagement, like the majority of 4x games. Turns will end up taking up to 10 minutes to complete by mid-game. There is an AI governor mechanic, of course, but it's about the same as in every other 4x game that features AI governors - they will ruin absolutely everything you planned for. Custom factions, while quite fun, are sadly much too overpowered to have balanced play with AI.
Moving on from problems with game mechanics (which is, honestly, a trap that most 4x games fall into) there are immense bugs. The game is UNPLAYABLE on multiplayer due to a well-known desync problem that the devs seem to have forgotten about - if you can make it to turn 100 on multiplayer regularly without a perpetual [End of Turn in progress...] then I envy you, and also don't believe you. Array Index errors, common with the Unity engine, are more prevalent than any game I've played previously on the engine. Most of them, around 70%, are absolutely harmless and mean nothing whatsoever. The remaining are game breaking, resulting in anywhere from no input being accepted to the entire GUI failing.
All in all, this mostly means that Endless Space's multiplayer is unbalanced, and broken in more ways than one, and the singleplayer is either frustrating or a faceroll. There are simply better 4x games to play. Endless Legend, the developer's next 4x strategy game, is mindblowingly good. Endless Space 2 is currently in early access and it is looking to be shaping up and taking care of most of these issues. For a single player 4x space game, I'd recommend Galactic Civilizations 2, while recommending Endless Legend in all other cases.

I've tried playing this game through on several occassions over the last couple years and I'm not sure that I've made it ot the end of a game more than maybe once.
From a UI perspective, the game simply leaves one in the dark far too often.  One is navigating themap and finds a fuzzy line instead of a sharp line.  What is that?  Nothing gives you any clue.  Why can't I move along it?  Nothing gives you any clue.  One finds a planet with a resource.  What is that useful for?  Nothing tells you (you have to perform an exhaustive search over the entire tech tree to find out what it is used for).  You built a ship - great!  Where is it?  Well, hiding in a dock on some planet, of course.  There are abbreviations and icons in various places in the tech tree that are often difficult to figure out what they mean and how they are relevant.
From a strategy perspective, I've found the game to be one-dimensional.  It always boils down to who has the biggest fleet.  So one has to push for command points to get a bigger fleet, larger hulls and better weapons.  The rest is just window dressing.  I've had entirely too many games simply become unplayable because some faction got a large fleet and it is simply unstoppable.
Given that military is the only viable strategy, the game mechanism for combat and weapons tech are too simplistic.  It is all glorified rock, paper, scissors.  It is more important to guess what card the other side is going to play and play the countering card than what the card itself does.  Three weapon systems with three matching defences, and the tech tree only gives small, incremental changes to both.  Planetary defense is more or less non-existent in the game, making fleets the only issue of importance, and the fleet mechanics make fleet size the dominant factor.
Even terrain ends up becoming more or less irrelevant fairly quickly.  Initially, one can only travel along the connecting lines between systems, which gives rise to chock points and and least some interesting decisions about the relative imporance of defending various systems.  But the tech that allows one to free travel is fairly early in the tech tree, which prety much eliminates the importance of the travel lanes early in the game.
I come back and try to play this game periodically, hoping that I will find something in the game that I missed previously, but so far I keep finding myself unable to play a game all the way through due to lack of interest.

I bought this game because I played Dungeon of the Endless and it was a lot of fun, namely because it was unique.
I played this game for many more hours and I liked it. But there are much better 4X games out there.
=== The Good: ====
Simple and fast gameplay that's relatively easy to learn for a 4X game.
Great graphics.
Good music.
Awesome stories.
Good random events.
Great simplified combat and interesting cinematic view. -- Wish there was a speed-up option.
=== The Bad: ====
As this is a thumbs down review, I will need to explain myself.
1) The races are very similar and it's usually not that a good idea to specialize too much in tech.
2) The UI is simple, but too simple.
3) The game plays more like a board-game, this is also a double-edged sword.
1) Races and the Tech Tree:
- The hero pool is shared. The way they develop and grow is identical.
- The races grant relatively small stat bonuses that don't seem to affect the gameplay too much; you can win in almost any way with any race without too much trouble.
- Races do not modify the tech tree with the exception of the starting couple of tier-1 (basically free) techs and the locations of a couple various other technologies.
- The tech tree balances everyone's research, which basically makes every empire the same even as the game progresses, making specialization sometimes even harmful:
a) for bigger military fleets, you must research diplomacy;
b) for new combat ship chassis, you must research colonization;
c) for more combat tactics, you must research architecture;
d) for more armor against one kind of weapon, you must research a different kind of weapon;
e) for more heroes, you must research 10 other technologies;
f) if you resarch enough of one weapon, you can research high levels of another weapon without researching its preceding levels.
I'm sure that there are more examples, but these are the main ones that I thought seemed too illogical. I think that the tech tree should be more linear. Whatever you want more/better of, that's what you research. Also, certain races should have exclusive access to entire branches, not just a slightly earlier tier-4 missile.
2) The UI is Bare-Bones Simple:
This greatly helps find the important information you need right away. Also, perhaps the game is trying to lower its learning curve, but it makes it hard to get the information you need to get your most out of your empire without going online.
- You can't know too much about certain fleet stats until you're in certain situations where they are directly applied, for instance, invasion/bombardment stats.
- You can't see clearly what a ship is equipped with or what abilities is has.
- You can't see what a class is designed with without going in to modify it.
- You can't really see what enemy ships have (even ones you've fought) without fighting them adn watching the cinematic view.
- By-turn math for resources seems mostly transparent and listed out quite plainly, but they often don't add up right. That hero's ability isn't reflected in the score correctly, or that +50 dust bonus isn't showing in the system or in the universe as it should, or that operator that you thought should be multiplied was maybe added. I think it's good that they try to show everything, yet it doesn't _quite_ show everything and it makes me uncertain whether it's bugged or if certain things just aren't shown or whether the description doesn't match the actual effect(s).
- The specific effects of many facilities are unclear from their descriptions. After building them (see above), they don't seem to add together right according to what the description(s) made me think.
- Trade routes are undisplayed (as far as I can tell) in the UI yet there are so many abilities and facilities that deal with them so they are probably quite important. Values that seem to be purely integers have percentage modifiers that can be applied which doesn't really make sense.
3) It's a Board Game:
- With similar fleet layouts, whoever has the higher battle rating wins mostly unharmed, so a wealthy empire has no way of swarming (and beating) a much smaller yet only slightly higher-tech empire.
- Countering card types is more important than actually paying attention to what a card does, so the content of your fleet and the compatibility with the card is not very important; instead you'll find yourself either guessing what the AI will probably do or just start save scumming if it's a close battle.
- Some of the random events are too random, too powerful, or scripted poorly. Need 1000 dust to save your homeworld from an attack of 5 large pirate fleets but you only have 34 dust? Not a problem! -- Did you just spend 34 dust and basically wipe out 4 empires? Lucky! -- Did you wait five turns investing (resource) to unveil some Endless secret but never get a message? What a pity!
- You can't micromanage ships very much, you can't customize ships very much, you can't rename ships, you can't choose how you renovate ships. It's literally as if they're fixed game pieces on a board. There's a very finite number of ship chassis (6) to work with that offer little in the way of diversifying.
- All the planets develop mostly the same way, by building one of each of the same buildings on them. I prefer the facility limit method where you have to pick which ones you want yet you can repeat certain ones to create mega-factories that would starve without outside food. Yet, you can terraform planets to specialize planets. So that almost balances out this situation.
- There are literally 3 weapons and 3 armors. You are playing adaptive rock-paper-scissors.
- Heroes are all the same between empires, options are limited with how they interact, hero development follows a fixed perk tree, it plays out exactly like a board game. A more RPG, free-growth stat style (optionally, with perks) would be more immersive.
If you like fast, very balanced, simple gameplay, being like a board game is a feature. I would rather not need to focus on rules and ideal build orders as much.
Final verdict:
This is a pretty, story-tastic quick bare-bones 4X that meets the demands of the genre and stops right there. If you're new to this genre, this is a great way to get into them. The combat mechanics are simplified, rule-oriented and even a little card-y. The sides are quite balanced, too. If you like Risk, you will probably like this game.
I want to feel like I'm leading an intergalactic empire in a very asymmetric universe. This game is a little oversimplified for me and the limitations of the UI alongside the general lack of options make it feel very unimmersive.
Hope #2 is more complicated, it certainly looks that way in the previews.

Since the game is by the same folks who made the Just Cause series the cheese in its extremely simplistic story is ever so present and adds to that with its very comic book style cutscenes and dialogue. One thing that gripes me though is that the "cutscenes" in the game where the game just stops for dialogue aren't skippable at all. Luckily there weren't enough for me there to be discouraged to replay.
The sound in-game is a little underwhelming where the noises from the explosions, vehicles, and gunfire are pretty a bit too "equal" in volume and don't quite entirely sound like they show off much of an impact.
The game doesn't take very long to finish and it may perhaps be faster too with other people but I wouldn't know about that part because the multiplayer is pretty dead and I don't know anyone I'd play this with.
It was a bit surprising to find that I was controlling vehicles and not people. It took a little while to learn how to properly handle the vehicles I was using, especially when making turns, but it didn't take very long to get a feel for it. Personally I find that performing seemingly skillful fast & smooth drifts and turns to avoid oncoming rockets and mortars and whatever the like whilst simultaneously shooting the enemy is the most satisfying part about this game.
Though the game will always say "a controller is preferred" or whatever when starting the game up I think it all just comes down to preference with this game since they both work. Playing with a controller makes driving a lot more smoother and satisfying however your aim in shooting is merely reliant on where the right thumbstick is pointed. On a keyboard & mouse there's a little bet less control when driving but aiming to fire should be significantly more precise thanks to the crosshair you move around with the mouse.
You get a choice of some characters with pre-selected vehicles to use before any mission. Everyone uses the exact same standard machine gun that can be upgraded to a maximum of 4 (or 3 I wasn't counting) that can be fired simultaneously. Along the way you'll also acquire other secondary weapons such as the flamethrower, rocket launcher, and rail gun that can be dropped from the bigger enemies for you to pick up & use. All machine gun upgrades and pick-ups are kept for the current mission or until you die. Each character I think controls the same though they have their own "special" weapon/abilities for your preference that can be activated with the press of a key/button.
Each character may also level up upon use which then rewards you with a sort of "upgrade points" which are used to purchase a selection of upgrades currently available. You earn EXP for leveling by simply destroying hostiles though the more you combo up your kills the faster you level and even if you fail the current mission you keep your current levels and EXP. As you keep purchasing upgrades you'll be able to purchase more newer and possibly better ones. Unfortunately the number of upgrades you are able to equip is incredibly limited even at max level. You first start out only being able to equip one but as you level up the character you unlock more slots with the maximum being 4. Though the challenge and encouragement of the extremely minimal strategy when it comes to choosing is nice it seems a bit odd for the game to present you with all of those nice boosters only to let you use such a low amount per mission. And you're only allowed to equip & unequip upgrades when choosing a character.
There are 9 main missions in all with maps sometimes being very linear and others being a little more open.
Almost each mission contains one optional "secondary objective" that are merely there to give you a bigger high score and/or achievements for completing them. Plenty of these you don't really pay much attention to as you finish them along the way in the more linear maps however there are a few that have you driving off around the map a bit but again they're optional.
The primary objectives are simple and bluntly pointed out via the dialogue and a waypoint indicator thing for the most part. If you plan on roaming the map a bit for those secondary objectives you'd have to be weary of the three-minute timer that will eventually set if you take too long not completing the current primary objective. If you can get through each mission without getting a game over they go somewhat fast.
The difficulty settings range from Easy, Normal, to Hardcore. The game being arcadey as it is, it uses a lives system which I think works well here as it adds a bit more tension to the possible challenges it sets, at least in Hardcore mode where you take crazier damage and you only have 3 lives and wasting them all means you'd have to start the entire mission all over again. Easy mode gives you an unlimited amount of lives and the only thing you'd have to worry about in this setting is the timer that would eventually come. Normal gives 5 lives.
It's a simple game with simple objectives and simple ways of getting through them where it's all done pretty alright.

I've used the steam controller quite a bit and appreciate the design and capabilities.  My one major gripe is that there is only one stick.  I mean, if you're going to have a thumb stick at all, go with two.  If it was to be trackpad based, there should have been only trackpads.  What I've experienced is a negative impact in fps games because the right trackpad just does not compare to a stick in regards to accuracy and muscle memory.
**** Important Update/Tip ****  go into the right trackpad config for joystick mode, under advanced, and A.)  Increase the center dead space radius, as well as B.)  Increase the outer dead space radius out towards the edge of the trackpad.  These two important changes solve the trackpad issue fairly well!  Note that this advanced function was designed into the product by the great folks at Valve.  The Steam Controller truly continues to impress me.
I recommend this product overall, but for fps games it is not perfect.  There is a subtle slowness with trackpad vs thumb stick under the right thumb.  Those milliseconds (of thumb positioning) mean you lose!  You can work past the issue with practice, but prepare to die a lot in the process.
You can also enable gyroscope aiming, which allows you to sortof "micro adjust" your aiming in FPS.  It's pretty sweet and makes for a fun challenge.
All features are top notch and far outweigh any negatives.  It's so good that I own two!  As well as two Steam Links.

This is a very fun and well desgined Hidden Object Game (HOG). With various mini puzzle games and loads of loads of objects to use. The game has a fun story and plot and it takes longer to complete then the average HOG game. Portal of Evil: Stolen Runes is a must play for any HOG fan!

I have played my fair share of HOGs, and Portal of Evil: Stolen Runes ranks just above "awful in every way".
Story-wise, it's the same mumbo jumbo as always in these games, and I'm always laughing at how the protagonists are OK with time portals, beasts from beyond or whatever you throw at them. So there is no fault for doing that again, but this game brings absolutely nothing new to the genre.
The ending of the game, though, is just that. You work hard to crack all the puzzles, and it suddenly just ends. Even the tacked on extra chapter, which is clearly there to call this game a "Collector's Edition", is just a simple continuation of the story, that still brings no ending to the story.
Production values are below average: Decent backgrounds, but awful Poser models with the most lifeless looks I've ever seen. While the dialog is bad in itself, the voice actors sure aren't helping: They. Read. It. As. They. Were. Rehearsing. For. A. William. Shatner. Role.
The mini-games are of the worst kind, were you have to rotate a thing to get another thing into the right place and have the right color at the same time. One of these types of games are usually fine, if annoying, but over half of the mini-games are these types of games. It's just lazy design to stretch play time.
There was a decent amount of Hidden Object scenes, and I liked the "reverse HOG", where you have to put objects into the scene, instead of removing them.
The map was also useful as it provided fast travel, which should be a standard for all HOGs nowadays.
All in all, it wasn't a good game, and there are plenty of HOGs on Steam that will provide much better entertainment.

This review comes from someone who had never heard of Dog Mendonça and Pizza Boy before this game, which I got in a bundle on HumbleBundle. At this time, I have therefore not read the comic books or any other related media.
As it says, this games consists of either 2D cutscenes (some requiring some input) and point-and-click sections where the player has to solve a puzzle or small puzzles in order to solve a bigger one. There is no game over or death in this game (even the conversations cannot go wrong), so you can go in with a cool head and enjoy the story. Personally, I found that the conversation options did not reflect what was exactly going to happen when they were chosen, but that's subjective.
This game has nice voice acting, which is very important for this genre. However, this did not prevent me from skipping some of the dialogues as I had enough time to read them just to know what would happen next (the whole text appears before the voice acting). The graphics are nice and in HD making it pleasant to look at and the scenes are really vibrant (to look at, even if they lack things to interact with). The game is accompanied by an ample amount of dry humour, good rhymes, and jokes that break the 4th wall. At times, it wasn't that obvious what had to be done and I ended up using a walkthrough, just because the story was so intriguing and I wanted to know how it develops and I did not want to waste time figuring the puzzles out, which is actually a good thing screaming ''top-notch storyline''. The right way would have been to interact with everything and talk with everyone to figure out what needs to be done as they provide a lot of hints, even if some of them are subtle.
Sadly I found the main character's face expression lacking, in well, expression. Also, there was no animation for running, which is not that much of a bad thing when playing the game, but however at one point -in a brief cutscene- you'd expect the character to run because of the emergency, but no ... just regular slow walking. Running would have been appreciated in the point-and-click sections too, as it would allow to go along a scene you are just going through feel less tedious, but it's not that frustrating, one just has to be a little bit patient. In very few written dialogues, there is a slight discrepancy or typo compared to spoken dialogue, but nothing game breaking.
In short, it's an okay point-and-click game with an 80s detective show vibe with a great plot and personally slow to get through according to my taste, even if it took me only 5 hours to get through the game (with some help from a walkthrough). If you like easter eggs and references, this one is full of them if you know where to look; I particularly liked the ones about Doctor Who and Bioshock. To that effect, there are also some interesting case files to look at on the desk (main menu). However, keep in mind that there is a slight element of violence in this game (
).
And frankly I keep saying game, but with a walkthrough, it was more like an interactive story for me (that I completed in around 4-5 hours) as I did not exactly try to figure everything out by myself. But that's how I played it, how are you going to play it?
Note to self: The visuals are great but I wouldn't recommend myself getting this at full price as I am not into this kind of games that much. Maybe when it is under $5. Hey wait, I did get it under $5. Hypothetically, I could have gotten it as soon as it came under $10 if I was into this kind of games. Hey reader, still keeping up? The note to self is just an in-game joke thing in the aforementioned files. Wink wink.

I received this game as a part of a bundle and it was nice playing an adventure game for a change, which isn't usually my genre. All in all I had some fun with it but would not recommend it as a go-to game. Besides the great art, I found nothing particularly intriguing about this game.
The original Dong Mendoça and Pizzaboy was a comic series and the artwork and atmosphere of this crowdfunded game are accordingly fantastic. There are issues with the writing and the characters however. For instance, there are 2 side kicks (the gargoyle head and the girl) which may be important in the comic but here they could have simply been left out as they never amount to anything. The dialogue also frequently breaks the 4th wall just for the sake of doing it.
I won't complain about the logic of puzzles as bizzarre logic is part of the genre, and perhaps the appeal. Luckily, the game has 2 inbuilt help functions that ameliorate the frustration of being stuck so often present in earlier adventure games. The notebook that the main character carries with him keeps track of objectives and can even directly tell you the solution to a puzzle.All interactive objects are also highlighted when you hold down the right mouse button. Unfortunately the game never tells you about this!
All in all an OK-ish but not excellent game.

The art is gorgeous and the music is pretty great, but many of the puzzles are either hinted at so heavily that I felt like the game was trying too hard to hold my hand, or so poorly hinted at and so unintuitive that even with a guide, my most frequent reaction to reading a puzzle solution was "How was I ever supposed to have thought to try that?"
The game does have a system to help with puzzles, but instead of hints, which would have been much appreciated, it just gives the solution to the puzzle in exacting detail, which completely ruins the puzzle and gives me a choice between either struggling to figure out an unintuitive puzzle with trial and error, or having the whole solution given to me.

Game had great graphics, rather interesting story and was even pretty funny.
But to continue the story, you had to do several illogical things that without any guides would have taken ages to figure out. If you won't happen to slide cursor above a small object, you can easily miss it and be stuck untill you happen to find it by accident, or if you just give up and check a guide. Also using certain items on objects didn't make so much sense and I would be still stuck if I had done this all without help.
I had to use guides till the end, of I would have got totally frustated and never finish the game. That is the reason I can't really recommend this game, at least with this price. It's fun little story, but it's in most parts unplayable.

Humans and machines are becoming one. Obviously this is going to create conflict, so for some reason it's up to you, the head of security at Sarif industries to set the world straight.
Pros:
--Best Illuminati based storyline you're probably ever going to play. Seriously, Assassin's Creed doesn't hold a candle to this.
--Level design is top notch. Multiple paths to complete nearly every quest, and multiple ways to go about those paths.
--Graphics still hold up incredibly well, and it's pretty well optimized.
--Huge variety of weapons and gadgets with an actual smart inventory system so you won't have to♥♥♥♥♥♥around for hours organizing things (I'm looking at you Resident Evil.)
--Multiple endings for you to muse over for hours.
Cons:
--No way to stealth boss fights, at least they added that for Mankind Divided...
--Speaking of bosses, they're all pretty easy, even on the highest difficulty.
--Common enemies have terrible AI, which makes stealth a little too easy/rewarding.
--At some point your character just becomes crazy OP and you're basically a silent ninja death dealing (or nap inducing) ghost.
In any case, this game should definitely be bought and played by everyone who enjoys a good story and good FPS'.

If I had to describe this game in one phrase it would be "difficult to learn, fun to master". I bought this game about a year ago and after getting absolutely stomped by the AI on easy mode several times, I dropped it to go back to 4X games whose mechanics I understood. However, after playing the absolutely superb Endless Legend from the same developer, I decided to revisit Endless Space. After consulting some online tips and running a few games on very easy mode, I became comfortable with the game's unique resource system and asymmetric factions. Speaking of asymmetric, it really is incredible how differently the playstyles of the game's 12 factions vary. The factions of Endless Space aren't simply separated by buffs to certain resources, but rather by drastic and often game-altering differences in resource mechanics that somehow manage to maintain a semblance of balance against all odds. While this game doesn't have the replayability of a game like Galactic Civilizations 3 or the visual style of its successor Endless Legend, it can offer massive amounts of fun and satisfaction to those willing to learn the ins and outs of its gameplay. I'm currently dominating in normal mode with my custom faction and thinking of moving up to hard difficulty, and I recommend that any fans of strategy games give this one a try.

The game goes out of its way to give a bad first impression --
if your graphics card is half decent/recent, the game will get confused and think you can only do ridiculously low resolutions. So you fix that by installing some stuff.
Next, the sound is ridiculously quiet. So you fix that by installing some stuff.
Then, the game drops you into a scene with no background or context, which is bad in itself, and the visuals are really pathetic at that point (I think it's because there are many yellow cabs in that scene, and cars are the single most♥♥♥♥♥♥♥looking things in the game) -- which is misleading, as all in all, the graphics aren't great, but serviceable and quite acceptable for a game of that vintage. Oh yeah, and you can't pick your character, so you're stuck with one who looks like a dork (all of the time) and acts like an♥♥♥♥♥(half of the time).
So, the first big challenge then is to make it past the first 30 minutes. After that, it's good fun for a good while. An open world and Awesome Powers(TM) go a long way, and the game is good fun for a good while. Eventually though, the missions get a bit repetitive, and starting about 2/3 into the game, it's usually not the missions that are the problem -- getting to the mission is (travel basically implied the choice of not using powers, in which case you'd get swarmed by zombies, ragdolled by soldiers using rockets and artillery on the zombies, and it would generally take forever, or you'd use your movement powers to speed things up, in which case you'd probably get detected, and take just as long trying to shake off those pesky strike teams. It sounds like a good, "realistic" idea in theory, but in practice, it was nothing more than a nuisance).
That said, it's not a bad game if you can get it really cheap, but one that overstayed its welcome a bit and would have benefitted from having 1/4 - 1/3 of its playtime cut. (Or, as the more expensive option, have that additional playtime be made more varied and interesting -- something that largely succeeded in Prototype 2.)
Pet peeve: The protogonist doesn't have that many voiced lines; he (as well as his sister) has a unisex name, depending on whom you consume you may run around as a woman anyway, and pretty much everybody else calls him "it" anyway (on the grounds that he's an evil infected commie mutant), so their dialogue wouldn't even change. At that point, they might as well have vastly improved the game by giving you a choice of character, at the cost of adding character creation, and a few dozen voiced lines for the protogonist (much more easily so than in P2, for a start, which has more story, and more dialogue -- even so, Saints Row IV, which rips off Prototype mightily, runs circles around both installments in that regard, just like SR3 ran circles around GTA).
SO, DO I NEED TO PLAY THIS FIRST IF I WANT TO PLAY [PROTOTYPE2]?
You know, I can't say with certainty. While P1 is summarized at the beginning of P2 (incompletely, and colored by the agenda of those doing the summary), you'll need P1 for the full story -- while P2 has a new protoganist, it continues the same story in the same setting, and certain key characters of P1 return. As P1 feels like it has a simpler, slightly less engaging story than P2, with less "story per hour", it's hard to say whether it'll be worth it when you really just want to play P2 and are only playing P1 for the additional background. That said, if the P1/P2 package deal is cheap once again (making P1 £2 or so) and you actually have the time for both, give it a shot -- if you really hate P1 two hours in, you can still fast forward to P2.
THEREFORE,
Qualified recommendation for the B- list P1 (decide whether you can stomach the somewhat retro look), recommendation for the A list P2 (whose only faults are that you have no choice of protagonist, and that it plays a somewhat cliched evil-corporations-and-uncaring-government plot straight, if rather better than P1 did).

First off, let me show pros and cons in a fair review; then I'll explain why the whole "downvote" thing.
Cons:
- Opressive microtransaction system. (Seriously, you can't even 'breathe' without them getting all up into your grill about spending $$$. You cannot even resupply ammo without having to keep a careful eye on the gold button....)
- Unbalanced sortie (Some of the tanks are unfairly over-armored, lacking sufficient drawbacks to make them fair and balanced. Also, there's obvious bias towards and in favor of american and swedish tanks, whereas the japanese tanks lack even half as much love and consideration...)
- All that glitters is definitely gold (The "good tanks" can only be gained by being purchased with real world money, or by purchasing crates in order to reduce the grind. Otherwise, yer gonna be growing grey hairs before you get that Maus. Additionally, tanks that you buy with $$$ are pre-equipped with max-tier gear, and give you bonus credits with every victory. Pay-to-win, anyone...?)
- Moderately poor mapmaking (A lot of maps have subtle advantages to one side or the other, making most matches against the favored side a dicey situation at best....Also, placement of concealing terrain is in such stupid places, no one would ever 'actually' wanna hide there, rather than just relying on camo to hide in plain sight.)
- Magical camo of vanishing (Enemies vanish into thin air if your view range isn't sufficient, even if they're in plain sight. Not even camo can excuse this, guys! Come on now. I'm sure you can do better than that.)
- Limited maps (Seriously. You'll be fighting in the same couple of maps several dozen times before finding the miniscule number of more advanced maps which are more or less the same thing....)
- Bad community event organizing (For example; The Mcragge's thunder event was designed with the full intent of it being a month-long event. HOWEVER; Steam users only got informed of it once there was ONLY A WEEKS WORTH OF TIME LEFT. Thus making it impossible to succeed without chunking in a hundred dollars to get two tanks. ONE HUNDRED. DOLLARS. Let that sink in for a moment.)
- Intentionally-hobbled revenue gains (Unless, of course, you wanna pay a hundred dollars a year to renew yer premium subscription, in which case it doesn't matter HOW much you suck, cuz you'll feel like a winner 24/7. They know full well that credits are earned agonizingly slow; that's why, for just 20$, you can 'enrich' a tank, causing it to recieve bonus credits for every battle. Rrriiiight....)
Pros:
- Fun timesink (Seriously though; it is an incredibly fun way to spend yer time while, say, waiting for a dentist appointment, or while waiting for an update to install, or whatever. While waiting for something more important to happen, it's always fun to just kick back an' blow stuff up.)
- Easy to learn, easy to play (The controls are VERY simple. even a 3rd grader can to really well.)
- Simple rules and simple maps (You can develop strategies in seconds of glancing at the map. Also, it's basically JUST capturing control points or deathmatch. There's literally no other objectives or game modes. Just a mashup of KOTH meets deathmatch, or a mashup of 3-hill KOTH...with deathmatch.)
- Low specs (It can run on a modern phone. So obviously it's got low spec requirements. Perfect for people who wanna play world of tanks, but lack the specs to play the real deal. It's also okay to run a buncha background programs as well. I've run a full scan with windows defender, and had a web browser open with a youtube video playing in one tab and a social media site open on another tab, and yet not even a single frame of lag was detected.)
- Nice looking maps (Beautifully scenic. Ya know, considering. It's like TF2 level graphics here. Almost.)
- Really pretty tankies (The tanks are usually very nice looking. Except for a few problems here and there... *coughcoughthewholebottomflooroftheMarderIIismissingcoughcough*)
Ultimately, I rate this game with a 4 out of 10, below average. Bearing in mind that it's free-to-try-to-play, AND that it's a cell phone game, those two facts have cut it some slack. It would've been a 2 of 10, if not for those two reasons. Sure, the graphics are real pretty, but in the end, all this game is is just a pathetic excuse for a cash grab. And after playing world of tanks blitz, I have reconsidered buying world of tanks original, and will instead chunk that money into TF2 cosmetics. Heck knows a hat that doesn't do anything but glow and shine is a much better use of the money. xD

Blockland is one of my favourite PC exclusive games. It was pretty much the only game I owned on Steam back then that would run for me! Lets review it.
Blockland has gave me 50 hours (and counting) of fun gameplay, in what seemed like so little time I had alreay indulged myself into the many servers that the game has (my favourite being the PvP) until at one point I decided, "Why should I keep playing OTHER peoples servers when I can make my own?" not only does this statement show that servers are hosted for free but it also shows that the community made me feel welcome so much I wanted to let them into MY places. So off I went! My natural instinct was to start some sort of RP server as I knew this would only mean basic building so I could slowly get to grips with the games controls and its compelling and complex "Event" system that allows players to code/link things up to other things that does things? As you see I haven't delved into that but I know you probably will!
Blockland has a very unique art style within the character and models area, essentially creating a virtual Lego experience! The option for shaders* is there and the latest patches automatically enables them if your graphics card supports it! Overall nice, rich textures and unique model style never seen before.
Your basic Blockland controls consist of the regular WASD keys for movement and spacebar for jumping. It's all fair and well saying this but there IS a learning curve to this game (not a curve that will take ages to learn, just some basic memorising). The key curve to this game is the building mechanics, the building has its own keybinds! Hurray! Fortunately there isn't MILLIONS of keys that make the brick move 1cm of a brick however it does consist of the numpad section. For some people the thought of this could be quite daunting however I assure you that you will learn. Jetpack as well so thats awesome, right?
As this review has got quite long I believe it may be time to wrap this up. So overall I'm going to rate this game 9.8/10! This is by far one of the most precise ratings yet for me however the 0.2 is just for the unfortunate loss of playerbase now - it appears to be steadily decreasing... Overall awesome game. Must have for any person who is a fond fan of Minecraft and/or other sandbox based games.
I hope you enjoyed my review (if you read it that is)!
*For those of you who don't know, shaders basically add shadows to the game and other visual effects that overall make the graphics look MUCH nicer.

This point ‘n’ click adventure game tries a bit too hard to be the next Monkey Island, even though it lacks the length and the strong enough main character for it. Nonetheless, it is an admirable attempt and one that should entertain any adventure game fan for a few hours.
The creators of the Dog Mendonça & Pizzaboy comics admitted that they wanted to make something akin to Monkey Island—except here, Portugal takes the role of the Caribbean, and the pirate theme is replaced by another classic, the Universal movie monsters.
Dog Mendonça himself is such a monster: a sleazy, lazy werewolf private detective who tries to maintain the fine line between monsters and humans. This is important to know beforehand, because this Interactive Adventure tends to assume that players are familiar with this world; also, because Dog is actually missing for about 90% of the game.
Our actual lead is the Pizzaboy, Dog’s kind of sidekick, who spends the game trying to find his missing partner and unravelling a serial murder case that may or may not involve a gypsy curse. His main problem is that he is not an interesting character, yet the rest of the cast has barely any screen time to counter that. The dialogues luckily fare better, although sometimes they rely too much on breaking the fourth wall and inside jokes.
To continue the Monkey Island parallel, the game uses ancient point ‘n’ click mechanics: find and use items in the most colourful adventure game logic. Nowadays it can be tiresome, especially with such a price level, but the short (3–4 hours) game time makes it bearable—even recommendable, if you crave something old-school.

It's 2027, and the world reaches new heights in technology with every day passing. New innovations arise, such as augmentation implants that allow people to achieve an higher level of body prowess such as thinking faster, move faster, and act faster.
However, this apparently incredible technology is hiding a terrible flaw: in most of cases people bodies do not react well with their mechanical parts, causing excruciating pain and suffering to their owners.
Many industries in the world are trying to obtain a new type of augmentation that can solve the issue, without the need for augmented people to take on drugs in order to relieve.
Sarif Industries is very close to achieve this, however soon before the research is completed the structure is savagedly attacked by a team of mercenaries which seem to murder every scientist in cold blood.
Adam Jensen, the playable character, head of security in Sarif Industries, is involved in the attack and suffers severe body trauma, almost dying from it. However he turns out to be still alive when medical aid comes, and the only way to save him is by implanting augmentations on his body.
After six months spent recovering, he decides to take on himself the investigation about the slaughter:
eventually he will find himself in something way bigger than he expected, involving governments and corporations worldwide.
The game, which is a prequel of the first Deus Ex, is strictly loyal to the original, featuring many different ways to solve missions, which the player will discern based on his/her playstyle.
Many easter eggs about the first game are present, which add a well thought touch from the developers.
Worth noticing are the game's length and focus on the plot: the story results interesting and the characters' development is to be praised as well.

For many years, PC gaming has been home to the hidden object genre. While these games do sometimes make their ways to handhelds and consoles, the bulk are on the computer. With so many to choose from and more coming out each day, it can be hard to decided which title to play.
was in my backlog of games and, at random, I decided to give it a shot. While it may not be the most memorable or groundbreaking HOG on the market, I enjoyed playing it quite a bit. It’s a good game for veterans and new players to the genre and offers a fair amount of challenge.
Players assume control over a young woman named Vanessa Helsing who receives an invitation to St. Peter’s Cathedral in Italy in regards to information about her missing grandfather. However, once there she becomes mixed up in a secret order that her grandfather was a part of and a mission to stop a gate from opening and releasing evils upon the world. The plot is pretty generic and straightforward, there is a traitor amongst the order who stole the magical runes that held the gate locked so Vanessa can trust no one. But there aren’t many other characters in the game and my first guess on who the traitor could be was right from the beginning so any real sense of mystery is minute.  The story also ends very abruptly and you don’t even get any resolution unless you play the bonus chapter.
Gameplay is pretty standard for a game of this nature. It’s all point and click so you’ll only need a mouse. You have an inventory system and a map for easy teleporting and backtracking. The game has a good mix of hidden object scenes and puzzles, though I wouldn’t have minded a few more of both actually. You’ll be visiting most scenes twice, however. This isn’t so bad because the game offers two types of gameplay for the scenes. One is the usual list of items in word form, you search the scene to check off items from the list. The other is you’re given items and you have to find where in the scene the item goes, an example being you’re given a glove then you find another glove in the scene and put it there. I enjoyed this different take on things. Most of the games are your usual fair though they do offer a decent challenge as do the hidden object scenes. A small complaint I have is the item menu, it’s at the bottom of the screen and there was no way to lock it so that it would stop minimizing. I know this feature isn’t always in every game but it’s one I like, I like my item inventory always visible.
Graphics were good, very pretty scenery that fit the story of the game. Colors are bright when they need to be but dark and unsettlingly as well helping to bring Vanessa’s journey to life. The items in the hidden object scenes were well rendered, not too hard to find. I found some to be a bit tiny or just too obscured by darkness, however it was so infrequently it wasn’t a big issue. The cutscenes are well animated, lip movements may not match the lines being said but again, it’s not a big issue. All characters are expressive. The music sets the atmosphere well and there is also full voice acting. The quality of the acting is passable, not the best, but I’ve certainly heard worse.
I would say
is a good game, a bit middle of the road but still better than a lot of other hidden object games I’ve played. I found it fun and enjoyable, I liked the story and I felt satisfied when the game was over. There are Steam trading cards and achievements as well. Older reviews say that two of the achievements are broken, this isn’t the case anymore. The issue was fixed in an update so no need to worry. I fully recommend this game, I think if you enjoy hidden object games then you will also get a good experience from this title, just as I did.

If you liked TTD (Transport Tycoon Deluxe) back in the days, you will most likely like this game as well. The goal is to transport people across a city in multitude of ways. The real challenge comes from efficency and you can really grind down in to the details. You can change the layout of the city by creating new roads (one way, avenues, with or without sidewalks or bus lanes) or you can adjust the individual time tables (frequency, what type of vehicle, times etc.) of busses and other transports.
It's a good deal of fun, and the simulation is really good. I can only recommend for those who liked TTD.

Even if you're not a fan of the transport simulation subgenre, CiM2 will keep you entertained for hours with its city builder aspect. I've never found any game in which you can create such detailed road and rail networks (including highways).
If you like creating cities, well this one is a must have.

The Steam controller has easily proven to be one of the most noteworthy gaming purchases I have made in the last five years.
Though I don't exclusively nor constantly use it, it is definately a "must own" for living room couch-centric PC gaming, enabling a much more compact and ergonomic option than mouse and keyboard. It's become my default in the living room for non-twitch gaming that would otherwise be mouse or hotkey dependant. I frequently use it for side scrollers as well. It lives alongside my XBOX One controller, my Logitech bluetooth keyboard with integrated trackpad, and the occasional mouse and keyboard combo (which I usually reserve for my non-living room computer).
The haptic feedback feels right, the default control profiles usually work great (and there are tons of community profiles and tweaking options out there if they don't), the battery life seems good, range seems reasonable, Big Picture integration is well done, and the controller sits well in my larger end of medium man-hands.
If you're skeptical like I was, pick it up on sale (like I did). I grabbed my first one on sale, loved it, then picked up another one the next time it went on discount.
My only minor complaint? Not enough color options. I'd love a white one to match my newest gaming build!

I enjoyed the game for it's story, characters and dialogue. The voice acting is solid, the art style is nice but the gameplay is lacking, sadly.
It reminds me of the The Wolf Among Us title from a few years back. It is about a detective who is a werewolf but unlike TWAU, Dog Mendonça is more akin to Inspecter Gadget, with his sidekick Pizzaboy filling the role of Penny. Although it is based on a Comic Book from Portugal and published in the US under Dark Horse Comics.
If you like the sound of that but in more of a traditional point and click game style, then you may enjoy this too.
It is however far from flawless, the puzzles do not require a lot of thought behind them. I only got stuck on one and it wasn't because it was difficult to solve but actually due to the object I needed, not really being all that visible.
There also needs to be some Red Herrring objects in the game, as everything here that you click on, is an object you are going to need to progress. There's not much in the way of just silly observations made by Enrico, when clicking on something that has nothing to do with the story. Which in a game like this, it really should have. Everything has a purpose.
It is also very short and at £10.99 it may seem a little on the steep side. As much I want to support these guys, I think that price tag is not going to help them out. I have 6 hours recorded but actual game time is more akin to 5 hours, as I often would leave the game to do a few non game related things.
Overall it is a good game, funny at times and worth a look if you like P&C games. Play it for the mad story, not the puzzles.

English review:
(Polska recka niżej...)
I have a certain problem with the point and click genre: while  they require the logical thinking to complete  puzzles, at the same time the authors seem to expect  me to suspend the logical part of my brain from questioning the fact that the only way to push the narration ahead is painting a pot of petunias blue, combining them with a honey badger and finally using them both on the protagonist’s nutsack. And while I might be exaggerating slightly, I only do so to point out how arbitrary and obnoxious can sometimes  a point and click puzzle be.
Okay, enough complaining. I have finished Dog Mendonça without much regret. Perhaps, because the game is short. Still, I must say that the puzzles in this game, while being logical for the most time, are also pleasantly creative. On the other hand, the game is hardly challenging, each chapter consists of only about 3 or 4 locations, and a handful of characters and items to interact with. Whether that is good or bad, I leave up to each player to decide.
Good things first: the game is superbly drawn and written. Furthermore, it’s world is interesting and the protagonist is likable. I must admit that for the first three chapters of the game I could not shake off the feeling that this is exactly how the Telltale’s “Wolf Among Us” would have looked like if it was a classic point and click adventure. And, while I’m not going to spoil anything, this game could pretty accurately be described as a mixture of detective noir and a lighthearted comedy taking place in a world where humans live (mostly) at peace with various monsters and mythical beasts. The music is pleasant and always fits the events currently happening on the screen. The voice acting is a mixed bag though.
Speaking of the problems with this game, there are a few. First of all, there is no quick travel on double click – and the protagonist often walks so slow that crossing the third part of the screen takes him several seconds. There is a hot-spot detection (Quite surprisingly, under the right click…) but it doesn’t always work. And while I realize that this game is rather short, I wish there were more than 3 save slots. Finally, a quite significant problem: the final chapters seem rushed and the ending is extremely clichéd, short and weak.
To sum up: perhaps the most significant reason not to buy Pizza Boy is the price tag. 15 euros for a game that can be completed in 4 hours, and that lacks a certain final polish, is much. On the other hand, the moment I’m writing this review, Dog and Pizza Boy can be bought on Steam at -75% and that is what I recommend you to do if you are a fan of point and click games.
Polska recenzja:
Mam pewien problem z point and clickami. Polega on na tym że wymagają ode mnie logicznego myślenia żeby rozwiązywać zagadki, a jednocześnie ich twórcy oczekują że powstrzymam logiczną część mojego mózgu przed zakwestionowaniem faktu że jedynym sposobem popchnięcia akcji do przodu jest pomalowanie na niebiesko borsuka, połączenie go z doniczką petunii a potem użycie ich obu głównemu bohaterowi na mosznie. Ok, celowo przesadzam odrobinę, ale tylko żeby podkreślić jak bardzo naciągane bywają niektóre zagadki w przygodówkach.
Dobra, bez narzekania. Skończyłem Dog’a Mendonçę I nie żałuję. Może dlatego że jest to gra krótka i raczej prosta. Dodatkowo, zagadki które tu się pojawiają nie sprawiają wrażenia wydumanych - wręcz przeciwnie, przez większość czasu pozostają logiczne, a mimo to przyjemnie kreatywne. To duży plus, jednak z drugiej strony każdy z rozdziałów gry to około 3 - 4 lokacji, tylko kilka postaci i przedmiotów. Czy to plus czy minus zadecydujcie sami.
Z dobrych wiadomości: Pizza Boy jest fenomenalnie narysowany I napisany (choć nie po polsku…). Dodatkowo mamy tu ciekawy świat I bohatera którego da się polubić. Muszę uczciwie przyznać, że przez pierwsze trzy rozdziały gry nie mogłem pozbyć się uczucia że tak właśnie powinien wyglądać “Wolf Among Us” gdyby był tradycyjną przygodówką. Nie będę oczywiście zdradzał szczegółów, ale wydarzenia gry mają miejsce w świecie gdzie ludzie żyją w całkiem przyjaznych stosunkach z wszelkiej maści potworami I mitycznymi bestiami, które - w przeciwieństwie do dzieła Telltale - wcale nie mają zamiaru ukrywać swojej obecności. Opowiedziana historia zgrabnie balansuje pomiędzy detektywistycznym noir’em i radosną komedią, a trafnie dobrana muzyka wpada w ucho I umiejętnie podkreśla wydarzenia na ekranie. Voice acting jest taki sobie.
Skoro już jesteśmy przy problemach, gra cierpi na kilka. Po pierwsze nie ma tu szybkiego przemieszczania się pod dwuklikiem, a bohater potrafi wlec się tak niesamowicie że przejście 1/3 ekranu zajmuje mu kilka sekund. Wykrywanie hot-spotów jest (pod prawym przyciskiem, nie mam pojęcia dlaczego… ) ale nie zawsze działa jak należy. Dodatkowo, zdaję sobie sprawę że jest to krótka gra, jednak chciałbym więcej niż 3 miejsca na zapis. Dużą bolączką jest też to że dwa ostatnie rozdziały są znacznie gorsze, a zakończenie boleśnie przewidywalne I zwyczajnie słabe.
Podsumowując. Możliwe że największym argumentem przeciw jest cena. 15 euro za grę którą spokojnie można ukończyć w 4 godziny, a która dodatkowo cierpi na kilka irytujących problemów, to zdecydowanie za dużo. Jednak, w momencie kiedy piszę tą recenzję, można Dog’a kupić na Steamie w -75% I fanom przygodówek dokładnie to polecam zrobić.

Point-and-click adventure games will always have a tough time appealing to me, purely because the Monkey Island games exist.  They are the gold standard in the genre.
I tried out The Interactive Adventures of Dog Mendonca & Pizzaboy (TIADMP), which I received as a gift from a friend as part of a Humble Bundle.  I was willing to be forgiving, with the gold standard set so high, but I quickly came to a conclusion...
I didn't like the game, and I couldn't recommend it to others.
THE VOICE ACTING is a shambles.  It is wooden with no sense of comedic timing.  Worse than that, the voice actors often went off-script (or the written dialogue was changed after the voice actors had finished their work).  Worse still is that in one instance a line of dialogue was READ BY THE WRONG CHARACTER, with Pizzaboy offering himself something and thanking himself for it.
THE PUZZLES are spoiled by the notebook kept in Pizzaboy's inventory, which gives 'hints' that are far too specific about what must be done.  If you decide to persevere with this game and you want a reasonable challenge, don't read the notebook.  Unfortunately, every clickable item is meaningful.  There are no red herrings here, which makes puzzle solving simpler than it should be (even without consulting the notebook).
THE ART STYLE... is actually ok.
THE DIALOGUE falls into a similar trap that LA Noir did.  Let me explain...
LA Noir invested a lot of time, talent and budget on acting (not just voice acting) and mapping those looks of guilt, annoyance, fear and disinterest onto characters' faces in-game.  The aim was to have meaningful questioning of suspects and witnesses and read their reactions to determine whether they were lying, not giving you the full story, or being honest.  The problem LA Noir had was that the player was given options that described in only a few words what kind of approach you would take, without actually seeing what question you were about to ask if you chose any given option.  These short descriptions were bad at representing what question would follow, which often ruined your careful line of questioning.
TIADMP has similarly vague and misleading descriptions of potential lines of questioning you can take with a suspect.  There is no need for this.  There is the entire width of the screen going to waste while our questioning is summed up as 'empathetic' or 'tease', for example.
In LA Noir, if you got the questioning wrong, there were no second chances, but in TIADMP if you choose the wrong approach to questioning, you are given the chance to try again.  Sounds ok, right?  Well no, because now you have options that don't matter at all, since you just stab at options until you find the right one.
There are more aspects of the game that could be reviewed here, some good, some bad, but the points above were the main factors than led to me abandoning it without finishing.
TL;DR - Don't bother.  The voice acting is a shambles, the puzzles are spoiled by the notebook and pose less of a challenge than they should, the dialogue offers choices that aren't really choices, but the art style isn't bad.

Portal of Evil: Stolen Runes [CE*], is a HOPA* game, developed and published by 8 Floor Games
*CE - Collector's Edition
*HOPA - Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure.
Since this is an collector's edition game, it comes with some extra features, that aren't available in the regular edition game.
I want to mentioned that the visuals for this game is nicely done. The visuals can be adjusted in the option menu.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only three difficulty game modes to choose from: Casual,  Advanced and Expert.
Diary Notebook it keeps track off all game's objectives and tapes.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations. But it isn't immediately given at the start of the game.
All of the hidden object scenes consists of traditional word lists, placing items back with little or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them. Some of the puzzles can be replayed in the game's extra content section.
There are fifteen collectible messages from the main character's grandfather. They're scattered throughout the game to find.
There's a bonus chapter, but it can be access, only after the main portion of the game is fully completed. The bonus chapter is the direct sequel to the main story.
There are twenty different achievements that can be unlocked from playing the game. Each of these achievements do has some requirement before they can be unlocked.
There's a built-in strategy guide for the game. It can be access anytime during game play.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

Playing the HO scenes only twice is a good thing. Even better is that one scene is a classic HOS and the other one is a 'use item' HOS. However, I would argue the 'use item' HOS are more like 'find a match' HOS: you need to place an item on the scene, f.ex. coins in a purse, instead of actually using it. Sometimes they feel a bit tricky but at least the approach is new.
If you are accustomed to Artifex Mundi's minigames, this brings a nice variation. Some of the puzzle types I came across for the first time which added a little difficulty in a positive way.
Despite all the positive points, the game manages to get a clear 'not recommended' from me for one single thing: broken achievements. To me this is unnacceptable. If you do not care about achievements, I would recommended giving this HOG a try.
