What's this? A really good hidden object game that
come from Artifex Mundi?!
Shocking! But true.
There isn't necessarily anything ground-breaking about this game - it doesn't reinvent the hidden object wheel or introduce anything innovative, or even all that especially memorable, if I'm going to be completely honest - but it's as rock solid as they come in delivering something that's fun, is just the right balance of challenging without being a pain in the *ss, and lasts long enough to be satisfying without wearing out its welcome.
The story is standard hidden object fare so you all know the drill by now... young woman has lost some old geezer and goes looking for him but there's ancient evil forces at play so she has to find a bunch of items to go about banishing it back from whence it came and yadda, yadda, yadda. But at least the narrative allows for some gratifying wanderlust as you travel through a portal to various different times and locations (and even the afterlife) which offers a lot of variety in settings to mix things up nicely rather than being tied down to one place.
The art is at the higher end of the quality spectrum, even if the voiceover and story are as mediocre or cringey as ever for the genre. The hidden object scenes feel mostly fair and the puzzles tickle the old grey matter just enough to stimulate without feeling like banging your head against a wall at any point. I don't know whether it was because I was enjoying it as much as I was, or because I didn't hit any real roadblocks with the puzzles at any stage, but it did feel maybe just a liiiiitle bit on the short side, and the ending felt somewhat abrupt, even with the extra bonus chapter. But in this particular instance I'm perfectly fine with that, and it just meant I was able to play more great games instead.
Like I said, unless this is your first time with these types of games, it's hardly going to blow your mind, but between the price, the amount of game that you're getting, and the fun that you'll have, I can hardly imagine anyone having a bad word to say about this and could easily point anyone in its direction for some quality hidden object larks.

Graphics: 4/5- Very pretty areas with unique themes. As the title indicates, the MC travels through different portals to different areas so there is quite a variety of nice scenes to travel through, my favorite being the Mayan ruins.
Anything else: I think that this game attempted to stay out of the trap that many HOGs fall into, at the end, the puzzles are simply auto solved, the HOGs are limited to none and most of the time is spent running around areas only to carry the new item back to halfway across the map. This game does a decent job of avoiding that pitfall but I still felt there was that rushed feeling at the end of the game.

It's years late and on a different product version than the original release, but this game deserves a positive review enough that it's better late than never.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a prequel to the original Deus Ex, taking place almost 30 years before the events of that game and about 10 years before the creation of the primary antagonist faction in that game. Mechanical human augmentation has changed how people view humanity, leading to the revolution of human ability. However, corporations that are more powerful than governments vie for dominance and secret societies try to have their way with the masses. Adam Jensen, an ex-SWAT that now works for a biotech corporation, is forcibly augmented by his employer after an attack that leaves him wounded and many of the scientists he was meant to protect dead. In trying to find why his company is being targeted, Jensen begins to unravel a global conspiracy to control augmentation technology and humanity itself.
Human Revolution brings about a number of changes to the Deus Ex formula to bring it closer to what the audiences of 2011+ expect from games, such as regenerating health and bioenergy (to an extent) and a 3rd-person cover system. But it's still Deus Ex at its core, allowing multiple solutions to almost every problem. You can sneak past almost every enemy using cloaking and alternate pathways, fight them with a variety of lethal and non-lethal methods, hack security systems, or try to talk your way out of problems.
A few flaws to point out: In the original 2011 release, boss fights required you to use combat to succeed (and the 4 original bosses will die even if you try to be non-lethal). This version introduces a few new ways to succeed, but not every build will be able to access these alternate methods, so be ready to have 3-4 tough fights, just in case. In addition, the integration of The Missing Link into the full game means that you'll have your augs reset near the end of the game. You'll get back your praxis points (and a few extra), but it can be jarring to those used to the original release. (Be sure to grab your gear before ending that mission, after you get your praxis back, or it will be lost!)
The story of the game focuses on transhumanism just as much as the conspiracy, and brings up a lot of important topics that are gaining relevance in our own world. The story examines what it means to be human when people can replace their flesh-and-blood body parts with better, mechanized versions. The conspiracy and its primary members will be familiar to those who played the original game, but there are enough new faces to keep from confusing new players with the call-forwards to Deus Ex. While the story often leaves the player begging for answers just as much as Jensen is, much of the conspiracy is explained, either in the story scenes, ambient conversations, or emails. The game comes to a final confrontation with the conspirators in a climactic ending level, though the final boss fight isn't built up very well (even with the additional plot hooks in The Missing Link). The endings are ultimately canned monologues based on who you sided with in the final level and your playstyle (lethal, non-lethal, or mixed), but they cover a number of important philosophical themes relating to the game.
Lovers of modern FPS or RPG games, or anyone who enjoys cyberpunk, Deus Ex, or the "immersive sim" style of solution-finding gameplay should find something they enjoy in Human evolution. With 15-25 hours of content (depending on optional objectives and playstyle), there's lenty of game to play. A worthy first game in the revival of the Deus Ex series.

I'm going to recommend this game because it has some unique ideas for an Hidden Object Game, but it is very, very repetitive.  Instead of the standard list of words, in this game the object is to find matches of two or or sometimes three identical items.  The puzzles vary from the standard static HO scenes to ones where the items move around and ones where the items are layered on top of each other and the player must move them around.  In between some of these HO puzzles are a few memory match games, jigsaw puzzles and strip puzzles to do.  While there is technically a story involved, it is just told to the player inbetween the various HO scenes and looks to be the story that one plays through in "Fall of the New Age" which is also by the same developers.  Honestly the story has nothing to do with the HO puzzles and just seems to be there to break up the game so that the player isn't just playing one HO scene after another (which he is anyway) and the story could have been dropped entirely from the game and it would not have made any difference to the gameplay.  All the HO scenes use pretty much the same pictures over and over again, which gets tiring and makes this a "meh" HOG at best.

BattleMechs do not stand still. In live combat if you are standing still you may as well paint a giant bullseye on you. In short the tutorial does not prepare you for the riggers of war in a Mech.
2: Mech Builds
Within my limited knowledge never have I seen in Battletech, MechWarrior and MechCommander has anyone ever decided for you how you will build or set up your Mech. Before M.W.O. your only limitations were Tonnage, Heat, Defense, Offense and Utilitarian. Now with M.W.O. you have to deal with what you are allowed to put where on YOUR MECH!!!
3: Pay walls
Where as I follow the philosophy that nothing is truly free and few people can truly be trusted MechWarrior Online is the absolute epitome of pay to play. You can’t get a mech that does what you want it to, you can’t open a cache, you cant have items in your cockpit, you can not change the color or pattern on your Mech, you can not run a Unit successfully without cold hard cash and for some of us that is just not a possibility.
4: Be it BattleTech, MechWarrior or MechCommander there has always been a story to tell. In MechWarrior Online there is no story to tell and that bothers me.

Cities in Motion 2 is a worthy successor in all regards. The city is now 3D and can be tilted in any direction. Most importantly the city development is now dynamic so less easy to predict and it also doesn't get quickly too boring unlike the first part where you basically repeated the same steps over and over again for the same result. The interface has been improved immensely and it's quite a lot of fun to develop the transit system. On top of that CiM2 was quite cheap, compared to the first part, however it comes with its downsides.
Yes, CiM2 is much cheaper (about half the price of its predecessor) however time is now being calculated in weeks and not in years anymore. As a result period vehicles have been abandoned and you are stuck with the vehicles you get from the beginning (3 busses, 2 trams, 3 trolleys, 2 waterbusses and 1 metro, as far as I remember). Everything else is DLC content, though quite surprisingly not all as expensive as with CiM1 (I probably was just lucky as everything but the bus/tram pack was on offer).
CiM2 obviously - who would have expected - comes with quite some bugs (as the first one did), most importanly, it has a multiplayer, but we couldn't get it to work. We had to bypass the multiplayer problems by using Hamachi. Obviously not a solution. Many tiny but annoying issues with the interface, i.e. going underground still shows the overground streets, as a result a metro track under a street is basically unclickable. The usability suffers a bit, however has still greatly improved. Another issue seems to be the dynamic growth of the city, as sometimes three or more buildings of the same type are put right next to each other, which doesn't necessarily make sense (3 opera houses in the middle of the industrial zone).
A massive improvement is the fact, that streets can be built, especially streets with bus lanes and many many more options which greatly improves the way you can build your tracks. This includes bridges and tunnels, metro now looks like the CiM1 train tracks and can be build over- and underground by simply using PAGE UP and PAGE DOWN, entrances for the stations are build automaticaly and off you go watching the people walking around like crazy popping out from one stop into the next one.
Everyone who liked CiM1 should definitely get CiM2, despite the hickups and bugs and little annoyances - it's a great game. And though you might say "damn DLC" - the game can be played without the DLCs. Yes it's nice to have a choice of 2 metros instead of one, but in the end, you don't need it. Tell the game to send out a subway every 10mins instead of every 30min and you can compensate for the heavy usage. If you still would like to have the DLCs, check Steam for sales (only Bus DLC at the moment) or currently the other vehicles (Tram DLC, Waterbus and Trolley DLC) are cheaper in the Paradox store (however, you need to use Steam Wallet for that, which ones more makes nore sense, but they promised to make the rest of the DLCs available in Steam asap as well).

Maybe not so much as a review as much as a possible "design flaw"? TL;DR at end.
I play a lot of rocket league, and, comfortably, I have assigned boost to the right bumper. Now due to the frequency I push/hold the bumper, an internal component broke. So I opened it up and found the weakest connection of plastic in the entire controller in position of a major function. No problem. I used epoxy to glue it back together and it worked like new.
Week or so passed and it broke again. Imagine the piece that broke to be about the length of these dashes: x--------o-
It is glued at the x now, and pushes the actual internal button at the o. Now the problem with this is where the bumper puts pressure on the piece of plastic. When you hold it down, the bumper pushes right in the middle of the two spots. And because it does this, it snapped in a different spot, at the "v" shown: x----v----o-
I have taken this controller apart twice to repair it, but I presume that no matter what I do it will just break again. I feel this could have been easily avoided had the pressure on the thin piece of plastic just been moved to the end where it actually clicks the button or even by a centimeter closer.
Long story short: A small piece of plastic on the interior controls the bumpers. This breaks easily with consecutive and constant usage. I can't use the right bumper now.
Other than this, I have had no other issues. Great controller.

I'll start by saying I've never heard of these characters or read the comics upon which they are apparently based. I actually picked this up as part of a bundle and was mostly just after another game. I was able to play through this entire game in one day as it is very short, and enjoyed it quite a bit. Normally I don't play through these types of games and review them, mainly because the solutions to puzzles are either so outlandish you would never guess them or you simply have no idea where to go or who to talk to. Most of the time these games are just nice to look at and often lack in gameplay. That being said I've had experience with Monkey's Island, King's Quest, Deponia, and Night of the Rabbit and this game was probably the most fun I have had playing a point and click in years. Anyway, there isn't much to this one, if you're looking for a low-stress interactive experience pick this one up on a sale. My short list of pros and cons is below.
Pros:
-Absolutely fantastic hand drawn artstyle. It's just eye candy the whole game.
-Fun characters that each have a different personality.
-Short. Some might disagree here, but I thought the serving size on this game was just right.
-An interesting enough story that keeps you intrigued.
-Funny and at times politically incorrect.
-Solutions aren't so far out there that you have to resort to a guide. I never had to use one while playing. In fact the game gives you plenty of clues, even going so far as to give you notes on what to do, but not where to find what you need. That part is up to you.
Cons:
-Easy. I think this is just an innate trait of the genre, but this one seemed easier than others I've played, especially considering the guidance they give you.
-Hard to know what you can interact with in the environment. Everything blends together so well that sometimes you have to mouse over every little object until a description appears so that you can interact.

This is my personal review about the game (3 hours of actual play and counting. Edit: Finished in 5.5 hours without cheating).
I will say this at first, if you're really into slow paced novel like/point and click games, you might like this.
If you aren't a big fan of playing slow paced point and click games in general, you might find this one boring.
That being said, i will summon up some key elements that appeal me the most within this game.
First let's talk about the graphics and the music. Both are very well done and match perfectly impo.
Secondly the story and the pacing. Both are okay, however it took some time to getting used to in the beginning because the story isn't that interesting nor that clear at the start, and the slow pacing surely isn't it's greatest strength either so give it some time because it really does get better as soon as you're past the first 2 - 3 chapters.
The humor is at times silly, and at times you'll laugh out loud, but mostly it's those jokes you've heard somewhere else before and also better or more convincingly.. Thus, it's okayish without ever becoming bad, but don't expect greatness in this department okay because honestly you'll probably end up getting disappointed by it afterwards and impo that shouldn't be the case here (it all works just fine).
Thirdly, the actual value/length is something i think should be somewhere in the middle and therefore i can recommend you to get this game at a 50% discount or through a purchase at an official games site where they might also offer it at a bit cheaper price, even during Steam sales etc. (i have done so anyway, and i haven't regretted it one bit)
Lastly, to conclude:
The game is good if you're really into it, and i do mean that but it's story wise not nearly the best i've played by far. However i'm honestly glad that i did and i'll make sure i finish it because i'm currently at the point that i really want to know what truly happened etc.. I don't do spoilers here guys, it's entirely up to you to explore the game on your own.
(one small hint i will happily reveal is, for those old school fans that have watched movies like Gremlins, Back To The Future etc, there are references of many movies included such as these throughout the game..)

Honestly, this is probably one of the best open world games made to date. Even though the graphics are slightly dated it doesn't detract from the experience at all. You play as Alex Mercer, a man who woke up in a morgue with little to no memory of who he is or what happened to him. The entire story isn't handed to you by playing through the main missions, in order to fully understand what's happening to you and New York, you will need to seek out certain key people marked as Web of Intrigue targets. Hunting these people down and consuming them will give you pieces of the story, this method of storytelling is pretty interesting and made me want to keep searching just to figure out what the hell happened. By consuming powerful enemies you add new powers and abilities to your arsenal. I don't think there are many other games that can make you feel like an unstoppable badass that leaves a trail of death and destruction wherever you go like Prototype does. Just to clarify, you won't be so overpowered that you'll never have a challenge. As you progress through the game, the military will adapt and start making things a bit more difficult for you. They have viral detectors that can see through your disguise, supersoldiers that can match your strength, and there are times when your cover is blown and you'll end up fighting multiple tanks and strike teams of apache helicopters, so it can get pretty hectic if you don't know what you're doing. However, if you manage your powers pretty well and know what situations to use them for, even if♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan and you're under attack from all directions you can still come out on top fairly easily. Especially with the use of devastator attacks that have a large area of effect and can quickly turn the tide in your favor.
TL;DR version: You're a badass with a lot of powers and you can do a lot of cool stuff.
Overall I give it a solid 9/10. I highly recommend you get it if you see it on sale.

The visual engines of both Prototype games behave in a strange manner:
1. They need to run at 60 frames per second on 60 Hertz to have smooth motion, were it not for the insane amounts of stuttering. This stuttering looks very much like an extremely severe case of microstutter, yet I only run a single GPU setup (1 x GTX 780 TI).
2. Running the games beyond 60 fps (either through disabling the vsync or running at higher Hz) make them look like a 30 fps game. It looks like the engine repeats every frame even though any framerate counter will state that the games run smoothly at any Hz rate the monitor is set. (eg. 100 fps on a 100 Hz display, but it looks exactly like running a constant 50 fps on 100 Hz.)
Both engine faults give me a headache when I try to play the games.
I've tried every "fix" I could find on the internet (including disabling all HID devices, running at the lowest in-game graphics settings, adding command line parameters, setting processor affinity, using the resolution fix .dll, etc.) and none worked for me.
So I know this isn't much of a review of the game itself. It might be good, but I never got to experience it myself because of these technical issues which I admit being sensitive to. Therefore, I can hardly recommend the game, now can I? I did, after all, not have a fun time playing this game.
As such I feel I need to not recommend it. You might not have issues with it however, so keep that in mind. Yet, I still wanted to write these words of warning to those few people who might have issues with this game if smooth motion is kind of a must for them, or to those who loathe bad PC ports in general.

Portal of Evil opens with Vanessa Helsing discovering that her grandfather Abraham has gone missing, and quickly thereafter learning that her family is part of an ancient order tasked with protecting the world from a demon invasion through the titular doorway.  This quest takes her first through the bowels of the fake Vatican, then to a series of ancient times, where the door's seals have been spirited to by a mysterious villain. It's a great premise, and the game makes good use of it, switching from time to time and location to location, ensuring that the player will never have a chance to get overly familiar with a given location.
Now, how about some Hidden Object Criteria?!
Criteria 1: To what degree do the puzzle screens look like a thrift store vomited on my monitor?
Oh god, it's bad. Really bad. The first screen I came across was set in the garden of the almost-Vatican, and it was just a mess. Random, out-of-nowhere objects tossed on every surface, hanging off of walls, seemingly hovering in mid-air. Throughout the church location, there's screen after screen of items that have no reason to be together in places that shouldn't be messy, dropped on the screen to create a completely arbitrary obstacle. The game does much better with its historical locations, keeping anachronisms to a minimum and developing much more logical item placement. Still, it's about as mixed a bad as one can get.
Criteria 2: Are the searches justified by the premise/story?
It's all standard 12:1 gameplay, I'm sorry to report. The screen might be well-drawn, but the developers haven't done a great job of giving me a reason to go scrounging through them. Even worse, its features an object placement screen for every HOS. While I can understand the appeal of these screens in theory, they just don't make sense within the world of the game. Where did I get this armful of items I'm placing with others on the screen? Why on Earth am I doing it? Maybe someday a game will combine these two types of puzzle screens, and have me pick up 12 random items on one screen and then use them to complete 12 broken items on the next, but until they do, I'll keep judging these screens harshly. It's called the HOG genre for a reason, people, and it's not because I'm supposed to be putting angel statues together.
I don't know why, but the angel statues turn up a lot.
Criteria 3: How well do the various puzzles and object searches meld together to form a coherent whole?
It's actually a fairly well-structured narrative. While I may have been hard on some of the HOS design, it's all in service of a good story that moves relatively quickly. Likewise, the puzzles all fit fairly well into the story - Vanessa moves exclusively through ancient hideouts and secretive enclaves, so the elaborate traps and locks all don't come anywhere near stretching believability. Also, the game features two of the easiest puzzles I've ever encountered in the history of Adventures. They're so easy they barely count as puzzles. It's actually quite remarkable.
Portal of Evil offers a strong story with acceptably solid gameplay to support it. The HOSs could have been tighter, and a couple of the puzzles are a little more finicky than I'm used to, but the hint/skip button recharges quickly enough that it's never really a problem. The problem arises in a puzzle that turns up in the bonus chapter - which by the way, isn't really a bonus chapter at all, it's really just the end of the story. I can't stress enough that this game's story, without the bonus chapter, is not complete, and releasing a version of the game without it would just be insane. Back to the problem - there's a keypad-based puzzle that's flat-out broken. Vanessa encounters two halves of the code, but when she enters them into the pad, they don't do a thing. I entered them half a dozen times, but couldn't get a reaction - sure that I'd done something wrong, I finally skipped the puzzle, only to discover that I'd had the right numbers in the right order - the game just refused to acknowledge them for some reason.
It absolutely a decent game and I have no problem recommending it, but don't be afraid to use the skip button here and there.

The variety is good but I feel like there were too many “rotate these things to match” puzzles. Point & click aspect is great! You can move around the world quickly as the transitions from screen to screen are quick. There are lots of items for you to collect and use. There are times where you need to backtrack to find a HO puzzle that wasn’t there before. However, you have a map that will show you where an action is available and you can even fast travel there.
I would recommend playing this on “Expert” difficulty. The only thing that changes is the removal of the little sparkles showing you where things are. I initially started the game on “Normal” but found that it took away all the fun to be shown where things were at.
Art, environments and music in the game are very good. Each world is detailed, sharp and has a feeling of uniqueness. No world feels like another.

For the most part, "Portal of Evil: Stolen Runes Collector's Edition" is a decent casual adventure Hidden Object Game (HOG).  The graphics and actual HOGs are fine, and the voice-acting is only moderately bad.  I found the game to be weak in two areas.  First, the story is senseless.  Sure, our heroine has to find the stolen runes or bad things will happen.  So, that's reasonable.  The problem is that there's no reason for the bad guy to have stolen them in the first place (I can't see that he'll get anything out of the situation) and once stolen, since only a van Helsing can travel the portals, there shouldn't have been any way to put them where they were.  The second issue is that the puzzles swing wildly between ridiculously, trivially easy, to bash-my-head-against-the-desk hard.  I'd have much preferred more HOGs and fewer puzzles.  But, that's a personal issue.  Anyway, I got 7.9 hours of decent gameplay out of it (6.3 hours in the main game, 1.3 hours in the bonus chapter, and an additional 0.3 hours getting my final Achievement).  So, I'd say the game is worth it even at its current list price of about $6.

Story: Vanessa Helsing, grand-daughter of Abraham van Helsing, receives an invitation to come visit Father Bendict in Viva, Italy.  Since her grandfather is missing Vanessa goes there for information.  She is also having terrible nightmares and day-mares and hopes Father Benedict can answer those questions too.  Father Benedict explains her family and ultimately she is a part of the secret organization, the Order of Light.  It is the organization's task and hers to prevent demonic evil from entering this world through a gate door.  Vanessa embarks on a quest to return the four runic seals stolen form the door and to find her missing grandfather who was/is chasing the traitor thief.
Gameplay:  This plays very well with amazing cutscenes.  There are ultimately 5 areas with subareas which break down into 8 chapters, plus the epilogue bonus chapter.  The first area is the cathedral from which 4 other areas open via a portal, and another area for the bonus chapater.  Warning: while searching for the grandfather's letters (scrolls) make sure to find all of them in a given area, since once the runic seal is found Vanessa is instantly teleported to the gate door and there is no longer access to that area.
The game is quite a bit point and click, with some different puzzles types from the standard fare (several quite difficult slides in that "keeping track of where the pieces are supposed to go type" of way).  The HO scenes are of two types: 1) the normal list with a use object (highlighted in red on the find list) and a sub/hidden HO scene with more objects (highlighted in blue on the find list). 2) A reverse list called "It goes where?"  In this HO the gamer puts the clue items (pictures) on their "list" into the HO scene.  For example: A glove on the list would be placed next to its mate to make a pair.  A very different type of HO perspective and the reverse of a standard find.  Note: the reverse HO scene (placing objects into a HO scene) does count toward the Eagle Eye Achievement (find all clues in 1 minute or less).  {Much discussion about this achievement in the threads, and I am unsure whether or not all achievements are possible in a single playthrough.  I personally cannot do this the first time nor do I try to ever get this particular achievement the first time.}  I think every scene gets played twice first as a reverse scene by adding objects then secondly as a straight clue list find.
I think the cutscenes are excellent.  There are quite a few, especially when meeting and talking with the characters.  The game is slightly interactive in that regard since the characters give exposition as well as clues.  If a character is there click on them, and in one case where the character does not leave click on them at least twice to get all the information and clues needed for that particular area.
This is fairly difficult and relatively long Hidden Object game.  The only real difference when playing on "expert" mode is the lack of sparkles on the HO scenes and the skip feature on the puzzles.  There is an in-game strategy guide so there should be no problems if the gamer gets stuck.  The no-penalty fast travel map comes in handy when looking for missed non-sparkling HO scenes.  There is back and forth travel between the portal world and the real world while figuring out how to get that area's runic seal.
The only extra find are grandfather's letters in the form of a scroll, 15 in total.  The scrolls are easy to locate and are not "hidden" in the least.  As I warned before find all the scrolls in a particular portal area before leaving by taking the runic seal since portal areas lock at completion and cannot be reentered.
All in all an excellent game to play.

Overall problem with the game
Gameplay dynamics are short sighted and unoriginal.
its a pc game based on a tabletop game, but most of the older renditions of this game have vastly superior mechanics.  Here are a few glaringly obvious problems that can easily be fixed.
1. Match mechanics suck.  Guard the VIP? most people dont even bother they just go for the kills, in fact that's usually the tactic of all of the match types on Quick and Faction.  Get kills, win match.  Why is this a problem?  Well it's actually really easy.  1 life matches mean people are either aggressive or passive (passive usually end up being "snipah's")  If every match you play earns you CB or XP based ENTIRELY off of kills and damage done... chasing down objectives in light mechs is sorta boring.  You can earn as much or more CB from losing and doing high DPS and getting kills than winning in a light doing objectives.  There is NO incentive to do otherwise for most players.
2. One match / One life quickplay.  Again... quickplay matches are where fun goes to die.  Why?  because you either have a team that works together, has the right mechs for the map (snow maps with a NARC light and a few LRM boats... its horrible to be on the receiving end of that), and the right mechs for the team.  Imagine having 3 Direwolves on your team, and they have 3 Pirates Banes.  Most pugs simply leave the Direwhales in the rear, and "usually" every match has some slow Assault mech getting his♥♥♥♥♥chewed up by a pack of zippy lights.  Direwolves arms shoot very low, which means that if you have a team of mechs with only a few Pokers or pop tarts, it means that your heavies have to put their entire torso and core into view to fire back.  Trades become lopsided and when the "battle" ensues your bruisers are far more abused then theirs are.   With only 1 life, you have only 1 chance to have a good game or a bad game.  Once you die, thats it you have to sit there and watch your team.  The end usually ALWAYS has 1 team chasing down the other teams last light mech around the map.
3. Objectives are the "last ditch effort" to win the game.  Sorry but this is why your gameplay mechanics suck so much balls.  If the teams ONLY care about the objectives as a second thought, you failed.  I mean consider this.  IF you have an assault match, 2 flags... you can either attack or defend.  Imagine which of these outcomes is "mostly" successful?  Doesn't take a genius to figure it out.  I have had MULTIPLE matches where both teams sat back hoping the other team would attack.... for 8 minutes or more.  Sitting around doing a little trading.  Its ♥♥♥♥ing boring.  You dont care about the objective, you just care about the outcome of whatever the team is doing.
4. Mechs Meta's are ♥♥♥♥ing lopsided as hell.  This is really the most trivilized part of the game.  Its trivial to PIR, and it shouldnt be.  The table top game, yes i played it, isnt anything to write home about.  It's like playing Dark Elves vs Khorne knights in Warhammer... One side can field anything, the other side has to field the perfect army or get wrekd.  Ditch the damn tabletop♥♥♥♥♥♥and focus on mech mechanics.  Clan omni mechs have huge customization capabilities, and even if you dont "master" a mech, you can get a fairly desirable outcome with builds.  IS mechs are locked into Meta builds.  Heat, tonnage, DPS, Engines and speed are customizable, SURE... but you don't see XL Assaults with massive loadouts stunting DHS and FF... its just not possible.  You trade... speed/DPS/defense.  XL Engines for IS are... well... almost suicide.  You do it for speed and firepower.  which means that the mech better HAVE the hardpoints and speed to make that concept work or its a ♥♥♥♥ing death sentence.  This is what I have the MOST problem with.  ITS THE CRYENGINE... look at what games like Star Citizen and other "mechanized" game play mechanics are doing with their game tech.  This game is seriously lacking in the area of "breaking the mold" for 50% or more of the mechs available.  What do you do with a MX90?  DAKKA.  What do you do with a Timberwolf?  ♥♥♥♥ man, PICK SOMETHING.

Hi everyone!
It's me, Ivan. I am a huge BattleTech fan and experienced in all MechWarrior titles so far. Yes even the ones in the pre Pentium Prozessor age. "Fine..." I think. Lets buy a light mech. Store, store, ah! Up there, ok. So I need something in exchange for a Battle mech. Some numbers occur. Seems like a currency. Lets google again...
Aha, the blue one is called "ComStar Bills" and the yellow one is claled "MechCredits" after some random clicking I find out that I can buy the yellow one for money. Whether I can earn it somehow? I don't know. Thats not explained anywhere. Ok, so no BattleMech for now. I have build up enough trust issues till this point, that I am not willing to throw money in this weird menu which is mocking me with its dialog boxes and non explained features.
Lets go and play a quick match. Seems like I can still choose between some BattleMechs. I am basically going to a Battlefild with the property of someone else? Well.... ok. Now some tiles with pictures of landscapes appear.

The match begins. An what a feast of battle that is! Awesome! I like that a lot!

TL;DR, they give you extra money for your first 25 trial matches that will allow you to buy basically any mech in the game as your first mech. After that, it's a grind, only made bearable if you really enjoy the combat. But hey, it's free - give it a shot.
FULL REVIEW
It's a decent game. The community is one of the better ones out there, as you might expect from a niche genre with a small playerbase. It's a little tough to pick up if you haven't played anything similar before, and there are lots of stats and numbers to look at to optimize your mech builds. Most of the fun comes from playing with the configuration of your mechs and trying different combinations of weapons. If you're the kind of player that MUST HAVE ALL THE THINGS you will hate this game. There are ten billion different mechs to choose from, only a handful of which rank amongst the best. The rest collect dust, only being taken in to matches due to personal taste and lack of caring or understanding of the metagame. The game has two primary game modes - Quick Play and Faction Warfare. Most of the review focuses on Quick Play, as it is the basic game mode.
The maps range wildly from lots of fun to complete garbage, and you head in to each match not knowing what map you will end up on. This means that sometimes, you drop in with a short ranged build and get picked apart by the team with better long range weapons, or you pick a long ranged build and end up on a map full of buildings and cover where everyone ends up brawling. If you try to hedge your bets and build something with variable ranges you just end up being terrible at both.
Once one team loses two or three mechs to the other team, the game is pretty much over and the team with superior numbers will stomp through the rest of the weakened enemy. Only about 1 in 10 matches end up being close. You can, however, leave the match with no penalty after you die and immediately queue up for another match as long as you are willing to play a different mech. Mechs are locked in their matches until the match ends.
For me, the strength of the game is the combat. Each mech is made up of several individual components - Head, Arms, Legs, and Left/Right/Center torso. Each section takes damage individually, and some sections are expendable while losing others is fatal. This means that with practice, you can influence where you are getting hit in order to "spread" the damage you take over multiple components, greatly increasing your effective life total. It also means that if you get good at noticing where enemies are damaged, you can take them out of the fight quickly. This creates an interesting dynamic where you may be critically wounded, but as long as you can avoid taking hits to your key, damaged area, you may be just as much of a threat at 50% health as you were at 100% health due to still being able to contribute firepower for your team - but if you can't spread the damage and lose your center torso early, you're just out of the fight and your team is down 1/12th of its firepower.
A lot of frustration for newer players will come from positioning. Some of the mechs are incredibly slow, and if you accidently walk in to the open or in to the enemy team early, you're going to die before you ever even start moving backwards. Generally, the more firepower and armor you bring in to the fight, the more effected by positioning you will be. Unfortunately, good positioning requires knowing the maps, and that just takes time.
FACTION PLAY is the other way to play the game, but unfortunately despite years of iterations it has never felt like the massive, galaxy-encompassing war mode that they seem to want it to be. At best, it's quick play with three respawns per player, which unfortunately just tends to mean that the stomp just lasts longer for everyone. It can be fun when you're winning, but when you aren't it's just a brutal slow loss.
The faction play experience (and indeed, the quick play experience) is greatly enhanced by joining a unit and playing with a large group, but that's up to you. The game itself doesn't offer any good way to find one.
I've enjoyed the time I have spent playing MWO. It isn't perfect, it's certainly a grind sometimes, but it's a fun niche game that's definitely worth a shot. I feel like the devs have been pretty generous with the amount of currency that they give to new players, and at some point in the game's life cycle the "trial mechs" you can pick from at any time got updated to actually be pretty good(they used to have completely crap builds and came with a -30% currency earned penalty or something). Pick it up and give it a try, you may end up being a fan.

It's a pretty good game apart from a few substantial flaws.
Pros:
-good combination of strategy and skill makes for interesting gameplay
-many diverse mechs to chose from, at least half of which are viable.
-good communication at higher tiers (rank)
Cons:
-Pay to win elements
-Terrible soloq team balance (even worse in group queue)
-Relatively little weapon diversity (most weapons are either not viable or too much like other weapons)
-very grindy (unless your a rich sucker)
I am critical of MWO and the main reasons are the first two cons. I really don't like pay2win elements of any sort. For example you can buy cooling boosts (cool shot 18) that essentially give you free damage when you would otherwise overheat. You can get a lesser version with in game currency but it's not practical since you would spend around as much as you make in a match if you used the inferior free ones anyhow. The best mechs in the game are often real money only (hero mechs) the one i want for example is called spirit bear and costs about $50 CDN for the single mech (there are dozens). P2W is currently the biggest problem in the game and so far every time i've looked up top scoring players in youtube or their stream they are using p2w strategies.
The matchmaking is the other major problem. about 90% of soloq games are a massive stomp where you have almost no power to sway the battle. I have spilled a drink causing me to miss the first 3 minutes and when i was ready to get into the fray (i play slow mechs) my team had already won 11v12. They balance the size classes of the mechs so the problem is clearly that they are completely unable to measure player skill. This is made obvious by the thing called tier creep where bad players will naturally gain tiers even if they perform terribly due to a bad ranking system as well as the imballanced matches where they will get carried regardless of how poorly they do. In the end it breaks down to
10% fun matches where you feel your performance was a major factor in winning or losing.
30% decent matches where your performance was some factor although it seems unlikely you could have actually changed the result from win to lose or vise versa, but at least you get to fight somewhat fairly not 1v6.
60% games where one team absolutely steam rolls the other, if it's your team winning you are relieved to at least get the win and money rewards so it's not terrible. If it's their team winning it's a complete waste of time. If you try to be aggressive you will often find that no one else on your team is even trading they are just hiding behind hills and terrain the entire time. every time you peek a corner or hill 3+ will shoot you since they have no other targets. If you play cautously they will just kill your hiding teamates one at a time until you have no team and then roll you 6+ vs 1. In these games which happen often (many people report 10+ in a row in forums) you just completely waste your time. Your only purpose is to give the premium players on the other team target practice and even more free c-bills on top of the 30% boost from p2w mechs and the massive boost from being premium players.
Overall it's a relatively good game with some pretty big flaws. It became a lot more fun when i joined a unit and I became more forgiving of the p2w aspects after getting a lot of free stuff in the lucky charm 3 event.

My Name is Mayo is a clicker game.
There are no skills needed to play this "game" (I use the word "game" loosely here, because it is not what I would normally think of as a game).
All you need to do is to continuously click on a big picture of a jar of mayonnaise.
There are various achievements, all of which involve clicking on the big jar of mayo.
You need to activate most achievements by clicking on the relevant achievement icon, which will change the look of the mayo jar, and you then click away for the prescribed number of times.
I had heard that this "game" was all about clicking on a jar of mayo, but I felt sure that there had to be something more to it than that - well, I suppose the inclusion of some achievements gave it something more, but it certainly wasn't much more.
To finish all of the achievements for My Name is Mayo, all you have to do is click the right number of times on the right picture of the jar of mayo, and then do a few thousand more clicks. All up, it takes 10,000 clicks to finish.
The only reasons I could think of for playing this game are:
1) You intend to write a review of it. (I can tick that box).
2) You are really really really bored, with absolutely nothing else to do.
3) You want to get some Steam cards; either to sell, or for a new badge.
4) You are a "stat wh*re", wanting to raise your "Avg. Game Completion Rate" on Steam.
5) You are an odd person with a psychiatric problem (like some sort of masochistic disorder, or Munchausen syndrome) who wants to get RSI.
The odds are if you play this game too much, you will end up with a repetitive strain injury.
Unless you fall into one of the above 5 categories, don't buy My Name is Mayo - even if it is on special.
You have been warned!

After much thought I have to go against recommending this new entry into the "point and click" game library.  While it's worth playing I would only play it if I had nothing else in the "adventure game" category to play.  It is actually the reason why I bought it and played it.
The game has a lot going for it but it lacks a few things which bring it down the rungs against newer indie point and clicks and the classics from the old Sierra/Lucas arts days.
Its easy to see that this game wasn't originally meant to be in English as some of the phrasing and speech acting doesn't flow so well or has the wrong intonation for the particular phrase.  It feels like most of the actors just read lines for sound samples.  That isn't a dealbreaker however but just something to keep in mind, there are other adventure games that may not look so pretty but the voice acting is better.  I have a feeling it might be to do with the translation and the odd dialogue progression sometimes, ala LA Noire, that the whole thing feels a bit confused and rushed.  It makes sense it just doesn't flow quite right.
The artwork is perhaps one of the best features about this game, bringing back the old hand drawn feel of some of the later adventure games such as the original Broken Sword but in such rich detail and clarity.  The problem is there is a bit too much of it with no ability to interact with anything even if it's only just for humorous intent.  Some of the detail just doesn't make sense for where it is and just gives a feeling of cluttering the scene.  Also some wonderful scenes are only just briefly shown  when they could've made up another scene for puzzles and info, it feels a bit of a waste.
The animation is great in some areas of the game but oddly sparse in others, there's also the feeling of being a little lazy in some of the animation with certain things moving slightly  just for the sake of  moving when they could either be still or be a bit more animated such as people swaying.  This gives the feeling of there trying to be more "action" than there really is.
One of the great things of this game is the easter eggs and details relating other classic movies and adventure games, the bad thing is in some scenes  there is a bit too much of it and not enough original content creating a bit of a feeling of riding on the legacy of older games and movies.
It is very short, it really feels like half or even a quarter of a game due to the plot being crammed into the scenario.
There are a lot of really fresh things in the game in terms of plot, dialogue and humor, some great injections of fresh thinking even if sometimes it doesn't work e.g.  The "Jacket inventory" which is a great idea but unfortunately blocks some things if you're not far enough to the right.
It's worth giving it a go but if you're a fan of adventure games perhaps when it's on special.

As an adaptation of the somewhat popular comic series, The Interactive Adventures of Dog Mendonça & Pizzaboy works exceedingly well. It has all the atmosphere and all the humor and all the gorgeous art. It is a humorous take on the "underground paranormal detective" trope done with a lot of love for the point and click adventures of old.
As a game, it has some shortcomings: the environments could be more interactive, the descriptions more detailed, the puzzles less straightforward and the length of the adventure... well, longer. But even with this shorcomings, the game is a nice one, fun and interesting, with some innovative takes on action (sort of QTE sequences for fighting and interrogation loops to go through).

Tribes is back.
I started playing Tribes: Ascend during the open beta, having toyed around with Tribes 2 a little bit in the past and playing a fair amount of Tribes: Vengeance well after its time passed. This game was amazing at that time. There is still no feeling like hitting that clutch midair or getting that long-range spinfusor kill. The speed and skill in this game drew me in once I got over the admittedly steep learning curve.
I loved this game for a long time, even when they added items I didn't like (and it seemed no one else did either). I was there when they added the game to steam, hoping it would bring in new players in spite of the high skill floor. I only quit when the latency for every server suddenly became 200 ms and I couldn't play anymore. I held on as long as I could.
I heard about the update a month or two ago and hoped it would be enough to bring this game back. I fnally got a chance to play it today (I had to troubleshoot an outdated authentication tool that wouldn't uninstall). I didn't get the instant gratification I hoped for after being away from the game so long. I kind of expected the thrill to come back right away and was disappointed when the game felt obtuse and clunky.
I kept going, though, remembering how hard this game is and hoping to get at least one nice blue plate special, and then I started to hit a few shots against grounded targets, then I started to find them on targets against walls, then I hit someone with a disc from a mile away after guessing their travel time and path correctly in a split second and I remembered how much fun this game can be. I felt the joy of making crazy things happen returning to me and played like I meant it. In my third game, I got four blue plates and made the accolaides board in three categories at the end of the match. At that point, I knew I had been sucked in again.
This game is awesome and it's more tractable now than it ever has been. The technical issues, especially the latency problems, have been largely cleared up. Warning to new players: you will get demolished for a while, but it does get better and so do you. You learn to avoid explosives and hit your shots and ski well enough to keep your speed and ration your jetpack fuel and suddenly you just go off and the game makes sense. It won't be for everyone, but everyone should try it because this game is capable of more than any other game I've played. Give it a try. It is worth it.

I've only played this game for a short amount of time for a 4X game.  And I can thoroughly say I enjoy it.  I played without the tutorial awhile ago, and it seemed complex and difficult. I played with the tutorial this time.  I hate reading long texts on how to play a game because I usually forget most of it.  But I found the tutorial truly enlightening.  It wasn't complex and it actually revealed a game that has a lot of autonomy linked to it.  You build your own units, you decide which way to take the game, and the victory options aren't limited to the usual 4 options of victory.  The "civilizations" are also diverse and interesting.  If you know the game well enough, you can even make your own.

Starting with newbie difficulty might be slightly boring, but it really shows you how your games can work, and if you make mistakes, you will know and be able to recover from them easily.  For example, I tried to start an invasion of a planet without invasion units.  I thought I could simply do so over ships with overpowered weapons.  Not so.  I learned from my mistake and carried on.  I paid the price for it, but it wasn't game breaking.  It is my personal opinion that when starting a new game with entirely new mechanics that you should be given the option to fail without letting it destroy your game.  It was effective in Guitar Hero, Braid, and a diverse amount of other games.  Of course, the option should eventually be taken away.
Overall, I found Endless Space to be an entertaining game.  I could not reccommend this game enough.

Endless Space
The Basics: Turn Based 4x Space Strategy Game
Previous Time Spent: 15 minutes
Expectation of learning Curve: medium
Why I bought this: Super-cheap steam sale, reviews, art style
First Impressions: Endless Space has lovely art and interestingly thought out factions full of intelligent beings of different mindsets and abilities. I found myself lingering over the various sliders that come with starting a game, including galaxy size, relative connectivity of star-systems, and the age of the galaxy. I was also taken aback by the differences in the groups, and found myself settling on "The Cravers," a group of cyborg-insects, which bore a strong similarity to the Borg, and seemed like an interesting start. Everything looked cool, and the first few turns seemed to provide interesting choices and goals.
My 3 hours: I spent my first hour with Endless Space trying to learn, following through in-game tutorials to make sure that I understood the systems involved in the game. I played as the Cravers for my first hour, and spent some time tooling about the galaxy and focusing on trying to colonize other worlds. I had set up the galaxy so that spreading out was fairly challenging, and my ambitions of spreading like cyber-locusts and darkening the skies of the entire Galaxy were ended when a heroic space pirate set up a blockade around my home system, effectively preventing construction and further growth. With that, I scrapped my first game, and first hour within the game. Overall, I found myself liking the feel of the game, and finding the basic systems well-described, but frustrated by a lack of external benchmarks for my performance.
In hour 2, I excitedly restarted the game, this time taking on the role of some kind of birdlike warrior race (think Goose-Klingons or something), and I ended up in a less doomed starting position, but ultimately not getting very far. This came down to the barren galaxy I had chosen  to set up, and what seemed to be a relatively non-transparent system for colonizing. There are a variety of technologies needed for colonizing non-earthlike planets, and I focused too much energy on learning how to colonize fairly exotic planets, instead of covering the basics. This led to the area around me getting taken over by more pragmatic aliens, and a lot of lessons learned.
In hour 3, I restarted once again, this time as a species of friendly space Amoebas. My goal here was a focus on mostly peaceful expansion throughout the cosmos. I knew the systems far better, and was this time able to concentrate on gaining the ability to colonize actually useful nearby worlds, creating a small foothold in my galactic neighborhood. I also experienced some mild conflict with my neighbors here, without ever escalating into a declared war.
This allowed me to see the way the game handled combat, which I quite liked. When a battle is about to commence, you as the player don't get to control your fleets directly. Instead, you have something like a deck of tactical cards, built up by your technology and other special abilities, and play one card per combat phase, which generally dictates what your assembled fleet will do. There's a bit of a rock paper scissors match to this, with some cards effectively countering eachother at various phases. I'd like to see this in more detail in the later stages of this game, with higher technology and fleet sizes, but for the scale I saw it in, it was satifying.
My Highlight:  Testing out if an opponent would be willing to declare war after I chose to destroy one of their scout vessels that had been trespassing far into my territory and threatening an area I was eyeing for colonization. I got to feel some legitimate fear as I entered combat, crushing their ships, and waiting for a diplomatic response. Realizing that my foes were too smart to be baited into war by one hostile act was exciting to see.
My Verdict:  Endless Space is a game with a lot of character, and some great writing. But, ultimately, I don't see myself returning to it in the near future, as once I had the basic systems down, I more or less felt like I was clicking through turns, waiting for things to happen. I think if I had more time on my hands, my verdict might be very different, but for now, it's not for me.

I haven't been playing a good HOG, without the signature of Artifex Mundi for a while. Following the advice of a friend, I decided to give this one a go.
is a HOG from 8floor Games - which I've never heard of, before - and one with the most beautiful artwork that HOG genre is capable of presenting us. Yes, I am pleased.
It all started with an ominous nightmare and a knock on her door... Vanessa Helsing was pretty much oblivious to the world of mythical beasts, powerful artifacts and mysterious doors leading to other realms, just a couple of weeks back. Her grandfather, Abraham Helsing disappears mysteriously and Vanessa receives an invitation from an archbishop Benedict, to the St. Peter Cathedral in Southern Italy. Growing up with the major mystery of her grandfather's job, Vanessa accepts the invitation and hits the road to discover her family's legacy. Unbeknownst to her, she is about to be the sole hope for a perilous matter that centers a certain door which connects the Hell to our mortal realm.
The first thing that I'd like to declare is that the artwork is marvelous! I usually try to restrain myself from using such adjectives for this genre, but when I found myself taking a cartload of screenshots and just taking a pause to watch the light moving over the scenery more than once, I make an exception. Developers really gave their best in environment design, with a strong renaissance theme. Cinematics weren't exceptionally good, but they carry a quality that we stumble in adventure game genre, not HOG, so even that is a bonus.
Gameplay didn't carry any revolutionary elements. It is your millionth HOG, with generic but beautifully illustrated puzzles. HOG sequences were okay, and wouldn't give you much hard time. Your map is interactive with a teleportation feature, and an available action indicator, so the obscene amount of backtracking wouldn't cut you off from the story. Story itself is pretty much generic also, with some pretty details scattered around. I'm not going to spoil it for you, but the ending - a common downside for the HOG genre at this point - would leave you with a "seriously?" face and wonder if the game really did end there. Oh, and voice acting is horrendously bad.
Nothing award winning,
would give you a lazy evening with some really beautiful scenes to watch. Considering I got the game in sale, as part of a bundle, I got my money's worth and added some backgrounds to my wallpaper collection. Win-win.

I remember playing Jackal in the arcades.  You run around in a jeep, shooting stuff, and rescuing prisoners of war.  Renegade Ops is an updated version of that game with graphics, music, and comic book style cut scenes.  This isn't a bad thing.  Renegade Ops takes a simple formula and makes a decent game.  One problem it has though, is the missions have a time limit.  You will be having fun blowing stuff up, and suddenly have to abandon that to complete the mission in 3 minutes or less.  The biggest problem is the controls.  The game is compatible with an X-Box 360 controller, but I don't have one.  You can play it with a keyboard and mouse; but controlling your vehicle is difficult.  I managed to program my controller for the game, but aiming with the second stick was also difficult.  In the end, I had to drive the vehicle with the controller, while shooting with the mouse.  This wasn't too big of a deal, but I want to try it with an X-Box 360 controller to see if I can have better results.  Renegade Ops was definitely worth the $3.00 I paid, but certainly isn't worth full price.  But it is fun and a great timewaster.

I've purchased this game so many times across multiple platforms, and I still find myself coming back to it. It's been a while since I played it, but I can still offer my opinion. Spoiler alert: it's fantastic
Another one of those games you'll remember in 20 years. Like deus ex 1, Human revolution gives you freedom unlike no other. You no longer have skills, but augmentation choices are more meaningful, and they're split between passive bonuses, and tools that you can use in the gameplay sandbox. Melee weapons are also absent, but they don't really hurt the game, since you can just use takedown moves on an enemy. I found that annoying, of course, but I quickly got used to it. Not a huge deal.
Instead of the massive, sprawling fortress-like areas of the original, HR puts you on a semi-linear path, but rewards you for exploring and finding alternate ways of accomplishing your objectives. I prefer the original, but HR is just as good. It's just my personal preference.
I found the plot to be a good addition too, but it suffers near the end, and the ending was laughable. It's still riveting stuff, though, and you even see a few characters from the original DX.
It's a great prequel, and it's exactly what you'd expect a modern version of deus ex to be.
I'd definitely recommend this one, but please play the original first.

Don't even think about starting MWO.
If you love the lore or story you started playing a long time ago, for all others this game just falls flat.
The grindwall for new players is gigantic, even if you pay for exp-boosters in this F2P game.
If you decide to spend money in this game the return per buck spend is very poor. Mech packs or Exp-Boosters are very expensive, the cosmetic patterns are chassis specific and you even have to pay for the colors (account wide) you'd like to use.
The lore (and playerbase) prevent all adempts to balance or enhance the gameplay.
Because of the small playerbase and to reduce wait time, the matchmaking system doesn't take any skill into consideration but only matches similar tonnage of mechs.
This means as a newcomer with a standard mech, no modules, no map- or timing-awareness you WILL match against the best players this game has in their completely outfitted, optimized Mechs.
There are different game modes like Capture the Base or Conquest, but 90% of all games end with killing off one team, making them essentially all team deathmatch on a limited set of maps.
Faction play, supposed to be the serious end game, is played on a random map/game mode with 4 mechs for each player.
Additionally to the flaws in Quick Play the matchmaking here also pairs random groups with 8+ player premades resulting in lots of games being spawncamps starting after the first wave of mechs.
With your limited (not optimized) mech pool as a new player there is no chance to get into serious organized group play in a reasonable amout of playing time.
Edit: As discussing game balance in a game review is pointless I striked the balancing part of the review.

I love visual novel and choice stuff. Here's my summary of this game.
1. Story, I kind of like this story at first. Intriguing plot. But it's more like a novel than role-playing novel. For one thing if you're writer for this kind of game, you shouldn't describe how your character feel(which is too many lines for this). You should describe what your character see, taste, touch, smell and everything. You let player feel all emotion and moral consequence themself.

Portal of Evil has a great concept and beautiful visuals, but it cannot keep up the interest after the first few scenes. It is a good hidden object game, but nothing makes it stand out of the crowd.
Portal of Evil: Stolen Runes is the kind of game which starts great. The introduction video, the design of the first few scenes and the basic premise all sound and look exciting.
The plot is fairly basic: the protagonist discovers that her family is part of a secret order, and now it’s up to her to gather four mysterious artefacts before an unexplained evil enters our world. There is some attempt for a few twists with the introduction of a traitor, but apart from the very end, the story pretty much disappears after the starting area.
Initially, most hidden object scenes and puzzles feel fresh, exciting. Then you slowly realise that just like in the story, most ideas were used up in the starting sequence. They are good, don’t get me wrong, but get repetitive really fast.
Also, a note for completionists: two achievements are bugged and never unlock in the game, despite the numerous complaints.

A nice game with a good enough story. The puzzles could be a bit harder sometimes.
A bit more background would have been a nice touch - what did the traitor intend with the seals? What will happen now that he escaped? (Bonus Chapter, teaser for a Sequel?)
Aside from the standard puzzles there is a hidden-object minigame where you have to PUT items into the screen. A nice idea, but sometimes annoying - logic is subjective, just because the developer thought it's obvious that X goes to Y, doesn't mean it's obvious for me.
(Basically the same problem you have with object names - is "bat" the animal or the club? Is "club" the weapon or the card suit, etc...)
What I absolutely loathe, though, is the ridiculous shaky-cam in the cutscenes. I'll never understand why the camera has to shake when two people talk to each other (standing still)...

Exceptionally well designed and beautifully presented adventure with hidden object passages. The gameplay is not too hard although some mini games will get you scratch your head a few times before you arrive at your personal Heureka!-moment. Since the map lets you jump to previously visited places, it'’s easy to get in a flow of “just one more puzzle!”. The cut-scenes are nicely rendered, unfortunately the characters’ facial animation is straight from the uncanny valley, but that’s really minor criticism.
A special shout-out to sound and music. Every object has its very fitting signature sound and every scene its own environment sound which really sets the atmosphere with the gorgeous renderings, the icing on the cake is a symphonic soundtrack perfectly capturing the mood and mystery.
As for the story, it seems I have played, read and watched a number of variants of it before, but it gives you enough motivation to carry on puzzling and never gets cringeworthy, thanks to the solid voice acting.
All in all it’s apparent how much effort went into that game as is obvious on all the little details: There are cobwebs swaying gently in the wind, ants crawling on rocks in the wild, particles dancing in the air and each interaction with inventory items has a fitting animation: You can watch nails getting hammered in or doors getting pried open. On top, every single UI element is lovingly placed and animated. In short, this game has its visuals, sound and gameplay polished passionately.
If you have any interest in adventure games, puzzle games then Portal of Evil is a quaffable and formidable experience. I enjoyed it a lot so far!

is, in my opinion, a very well designed hidden object game. The amazing artwork and the great soundtrack, combined with an interesting story make this game one of the best of this genre.
The story itself is pretty lengthy (around 6h) and quite captivating. An ancient evil threatens to break through the weakened portal to our world because four of the gate’s seals have been stolen. Vanessa, our main character, is asked to help the secret order of light that guards the gate to find the missing seals and to secure the gate once again. In order to find the seals she travels to several worlds of astonishing beauty: some darker and other brighter, some mystic and others demonic.
The artwork is centered on angels/demons, several scenes having influences from the Renaissance period. The lightning in some of the locations is simply breathtaking. The atmosphere is perfectly completed by the powerful and heroic music, very fitting for the whole angel/demon theme.
There are two types of hidden object scenes in this game: the classic ones that we’re already used to, in which the player has to identify the objects from a list and find them in the scene;   however, there’s another type that I found really interesting: the player is given the objects and he needs to put them back to their places; it’s like a reverse hidden object scene.
Aside from the normal Hint system, you have a complete walkthrough together with the solution to the mini games and the HOG/HOPA scenes available in game – this is very useful for people that prefer to play with a guide nearby, since it spares them from tabbing out of the game. But even if you’re an expert HOG player, you might find yourself in need of peeking a bit at the walkthrough because some of the puzzles are really difficult to solve. However, most of the mini games are of easy / moderate difficulty.
The only aspect that I didn’t like about the game was the abrupt ending; it left me hanging, with a lot of questions.  There is no explanation about what exactly that ancient evil was or what its plan was. Or how was it helped by some of the suspicious characters that you encounter throughout the story. I thought that the bonus chapter would shade a bit of light upon this mystery but even after playing it, I didn’t receive the expected clarifications. Maybe they will release a sequel; in this case I am looking forward to it!
Portal of Evil comes with achievements that are obtainable in a single playthrough, if you play on Expert difficulty. Note that two of them are currently bugged; however the developers promised that they will be fixed in the next update.
Bottom line, I consider
to be a must-have for all the HOG fans out there. It is well worth the money, even at full price.

This game is not great, in fact in my opinion it isn't even good. I wouldn't say I'm a die-hard 4X player but throughout my life I've put anywhere from 600-700 hours of 4X gaming into my life. Endless Space only accounted 6 hours of that, which is rather small.
The reasons behind this are simple, too.
1- The User Interface is horrifying in my personal opinion. The tutorial goes over the majority of it all, however it's just- ugly. Descriptions of tools and buttons are paragraphs long, the colors are dull, and the panels to access key game elements don't stand out, as if they're hiding from you.
2- The Music. I didn't have any problems with it at first. The music was unique and entertaining to listen to, for the first 10 minutes or so. Afterwards it's extremely aching to the head. Constant and useless noise echoing through my ears is what I remember of it.
3- The Battles. Endless Space is like no other 4X game that I've played. The battles are won by cards and luck, and they're cinematics rather than the player controlling the battle himself, on top of that they get very tedious after the first four or five times.
4- The overall lack of immersion really kills it for me. I'm big on immersion. Whether it be Arma, Stellaris, or even Mario Kart on the Wii, I always want to feel as immersed as I can be. Video games are meant to shift your mind into a new world, with new experiences and activities. Endless Space does not do this, in fact it does the opposite. For me, playing Endless Space wasn't immersive at all. When I played it felt like a chore, me pushing to WANT to enjoy the game. I hate doing that, and it ruins the overall vibes.
5- The lacking of any strategy was surprising and a big reason why I haven't clicked the "Play" button on this game since July 2016. I get it, I explore systems with no diversion other than the color of the planets surface and size, colonize any available worlds, and expand. This is natural in any 4X game, yet when I do it in Endless Space I grow, well bored. There is no real reason to choose certain worlds other than their size for maximum population, and when interacting with other nations I feel as if I'm playing Civilization 1. It's the typical bland diplomacy system with a few various options. In the end, you'll almost always go to war with all of the nations anyway, so you might as well forget diplomacy entirely. AS I've said before, the combat system is also extremely dull.
6- The map of the game and even the game itself feels dull. I'm not certain how to describe something of this nature other than the fact that it's missing something most other 4X games have. I don't know, maybe replayablility perhaps?
Overall, the game works well, and the developers put there time and money into this game, so I'll be nice and recommend it. But in the end, most people won't put more than 50 hours into this game. In fact, haven't even gone over 10 yet.

This is the definitive twin stick shooter, featuring 2-player local co-op and 4-player online co-op.
As with most shooters, the main gameplay mechanics involve moving and shooting; the greatest shooters of all time use these mechanics together to make an interesting game (like how Quake 3 uses fast movement and jumping mechanics with a variety of weapons to make great arena combat, or how Rainbow Six uses slow movement and deadly weapons to make combat deliberate and tactical).
The vehicles in Renegade Ops are fast and manueverable, though some are faster than others, which encourages the player to see and dodge enemy attacks, and find better positions to attack from. The fast driving also makes navigating the environment really enjoyable. I especially love using the boost on narrow roads; the dust cloud and vehicle handling makes me feel like a rally driver.
The combat is flashy and explodey, with no qualms about its comicbook inspirations. You're supposed to help save people while you actually end up destroying most of their village.... The basic machinegun gets upgraded quickly during missions through pickups, and you can pick up one of three secondary weapons. Each vehicle also has its own special ability; using these in tandem with co-op partners adds to the strategy. From there, tech trees allow you to customize your abilities depending on your playstyle.
Finally, this game is not very demanding. I am able to play it on high graphics on my mainstream laptop (A8-4500M, 8GB RAM). It's a blast to connect it to an HDTV and play with friends.
