The Steam Controller is an oddly shaped controller offering near limitless customisation in terms of controls and functionality. You can use it to browse the internet from your couch, you can play any game you can think of, and you can make it suit your needs very easily.
Offering 2 touch pads (1 including an incorporated D-Pad) you are able to mimic similar mouse funtionality. Both have the option to be used to click, and have a nice feel to the overall trackpad response.
In an unusual place, down the bottom - middle of the controller you find the AXYB buttons, and a movement joystick. Finding these buttons and thumbstick without looking can take a bit of mental rewiring, but I was able to quite quickly remap my mindset on their locations.
Unlike most controllers you will also find two new paddles on the back of the controller, nicely located offering seemingly mindless additional controls.
I have messed around with the controller through playing a First Person Shooter (Takedown: Red Sabre in this case) messaging teamates instead of using voice chat, as well as being probably the same skill level as I would usually be. After a few minutes of mentally mapping the buttons I would need and where they would best feel on the controller - I found that a lot of controls were already setup in a basic format that would work. Yay, not too much remapping required. After a few tweaks though, I was ready to go and kill some extremely overpowered bots.
Next up was playing the FPS, Adventure, Survival Game- Osiris: New Dawn. This game took about 10 minutes to get some controls I was comfortable with setup. But I figured it all out.
I am able to quickly and easily swap to different weapons using the rear paddles, Zoom in and snipe aliens with my Assult Rifle that can be easily reloaded and unequiped. On top of all this, I decided to play like I usually would, and so ran into a problem! There were too many keys necessary for complete control of the game. Not to fear, I simply assigned a button to open a virtual keyboard. I can then use the not so prominent keys needed quickly and easily by opening this keyboard and closing it just as easily.
Speaking of the virtual keyboard, you might be wondering how well that works. Surprisingly, very well, and much quicker than any keyboard you would ever find on a console. It works very well and I am frankly enjoying it alot.
So to shorten all that...
It is very easy to use, has a weird shape that seemingly works, and there was not a problem I could find among a few games that could not be solved quickly and easily within the moment.
Now to whether or not you should buy one.
1. Do you play a lot of console games? Well if you do, I am not sure I can recommend it. It can be annoying to remap your mental thinking manner to a new controller layout. (Switching between PS & Xbox can be a little confusing every now and then for some people..)
2. Do you like trackpads? I don't- but the controller somehow makes it work for me, so I guess its just personal preference.
3. Can you afford the $50 USD or $89 AUD? I could, and it seems to be worth it so far. I imagine it will replace my PC Xbox controllers.
Overall Review -
Controller doesn't feel the same as an Xbox or PS controller. It does feel cheaper, but certainly not a bad form of cheap. It could be because it feels so light weight?
It is comfortable and nice to use.
Very easy setup, and configuration. (Plugged in wireless USB, a few seconds later Steam tells me - If you're using a steam Controller, switch to Big Picture Mode. This is for a firmware update, after that you dont need it. Then it was ready for use!)
I think I will have this permanently sitting on my desk now, and then connected to the Steam Link upon setup of that.
9/10
(The extra point is reserved for any issues I am yet to find)

2012: the year many tribes fans were dissapointed by the thought that Hi Rez didn't have the money to support this game further, and more so by the thought that SMITE was the real money maker. some folks thought that they were abandoning the game to milk the MOBA genre for money...
in some ways, they were right. in others... well, that's the story of today.
yesterday, the game had the aptly named "Out of the blue" update, which was being made behind the scenes with help from the Tribes community being the testers for... and oh man is it a doozy. everything is fine tuned, or changed up, aside from the maps, which only have the addition of 3 more to the roster, but they're still the same aside from the tweaks that affect the game with the update.
the main thing you need to know is this: the old classes got kicked out. instead, it's simplified to 3 armor types that can pick and choose weapons and gear from thier weight class... if this sounds familiar, that's cause you're a Tribes vet. each of the 3 armor classes have thier upsides and downsides such as the tradeoffs of survivability vs speed, as well as what weapons and gear each class can use (heavies can't bring snipers, and lightweights can't bring heavy weapons or use spinfusor discs or discos/fractal nades). in addition, you can bring 3 weapons, but with another hitch: you are limited to bringing one of each weapon class. (heavies can bring 4 weapons total instead of 3, btw).
TL;DR, this is the best chance to possibly get back into tribes, and give it another go... and before you think of it being P2W... the weapon upgrades are gone. when you unlock a new thing, what you see is what you get.
PS: any exp and gold spent has been refunded, and if you have gold, you will have access to the entire armory.

well the game look good, and decent, using direct x10 technologies, the vechicles and enviorment are very detailed and the shooting and exploding effect are great, there is nothing to complaint about, any low to mid range gaming pc would be able to handle the game with no hassle.
✪ gameplay:- now here is where a game like this shines, the game suppports 60fps and resolutions up to or even higher than 1440p, the mechanics of the game are smooth and natural, driving the car around is pleasant and doesn`t feel weird, the gameplay is fast paced and keeps you on your toes, so u have to keep moving and shooting no matter what car you are driving. overall your gonna be addicted to it for a while especially if you playing with someone else. ( get to theat in a min)

you get 5 charecters to choose from, each with a different car, it`s all about the cars not the one driving them so each car has a special ability to use, so no matter what you choose you are always left with strengths and weaknesses.
you have upgrades you can buy with points you earn along the game, upgrades slots are divided to 4 with each slot is dedicated to a certain strength, one of those slot is your special power, which is you want to keep upgrading to get powerful. and trust me you will have to finish the game more than once to fully upgrade your charecters.

*As of the time of this review*
There is only one character slot and no option to buy more so you have to choose between male or female--but you can change this later on at an appearance vendor.
The controls are decent and use the same layout for all classes so you don't have to memorize anything different.  The combat isn't as smooth and flowing as something like "Blade & Soul" but it doesn't feel clunky or heavy.
You don't level up in the traditional sense of experience points, instead you have to invest in-game resources of credits and 'Knowledge of the Enemy' into your Cathedral and Tower of Knowledge respectively.  The problem with this is you're only able to invest those resources so many times a day so it limits your progression into new areas, since they have higher level enemies and you can't level up to match them.  Your level is refered to as "prestige" which confused me very much at first.
You start off with 3 classes:  Cryomancer (ice mage), Paladin, and Lightbinder (support).  To unlock other classes you have to invest 25,000 Sparks of Transformation which, as you can imagine, aren't collected very quickly.  It's slow to get up very many of these completing some missions only reward 500 at a time.  So you're stuck with these three classes for a very, very long time.
There is no traditional healing in this game either.  Most of your health regain will be in the form of light orbs after you kill enemies.  The support classes only buff and protect others--the few healing spells that exist are expensive to cast and have a very long cooldown.
There is no swimming in this game!  If you walk in waist high water you will die!  Ironic since your player character is an immortal.
It's decent for a starter MMO but if you're a veteran you'll probably get bored with it.

It's hard for me to find anything bad to say about Crimsonland, for a number of reasons.  One of them is, I'll admit, I've been playing it off and on since..around over 10 years ago?  I don't remember when it came out, but a buddy of mine showed it to me and we played it constantly.  So there's some nostalgia and attachment there for me.
But I'm honestly surprised that, as old as it is at this point, it still has received updates in the past few years.
Crimsonland is a top-down shooter, fast paced and at times brutal, but in a fun die-click-repeat-die again till you win kind of fashion.  It's one of those great time killer games, where maybe you want to play something cool, but don't have time to fire up something as cool as The Witcher 3 for example, and just need to get in a quick fix.
There are several modes to choose from, plenty of weapons and perks to unlock, and for what it's worth, there are leaderboards, but I don't pay much attention to those personally.  The music is decent and fits the game, though I usually opt to put on something from my personal collection if I'm gonna go a few rounds, which suits me just fine.  Some modes I don't really care about, but to each their own.  Survival is by far my favorite.
Give it a try.  It's worth the modest asking price.  It's cheap, fun, and addictive.  If you enjoy this, I'd also recommend Neon Chrome by the same developer.

I now play on PS4, I have not played PC Loadout since.
The PS4 came with a campaign that was inculded in the Loadout Campaign beta that I played on PC. This brought a whole bunch of changes. Adding a campaign made the game feel like it was supposed to be serious, but in reality, from previous experience of the pre-campaign era of Loadout, I would like to say that this was originally not the case. While I can recommend the game to new players as the system is a bit more well rounded, once you get to level 10, you kind of hit a barrier. It is the barrier where you discover "this game just got seriously stupid with its logic" and the price of weapon parts go to a level where you don't get to play a match and get a weapon part through in-game currency straight afterwards. Now it's play 2-5 matches before you can afford that weapon part, and there is no buying parts for previous levels, meaning you can't buy that 2200 part that now costs upwards of 5000.
Previously, before campaign, there was no leveling system, and the parts were on an equal playing field for becoming acquired. There was no seriousness to the game other than teamwork. No grinding countless hours just to get the parts you want, only to realize that now that you have the blutes (in-game currency), you have leveled up, so you can't afford the several dozen parts you wanted to acquire. It was not meant to be serious in another location relating to blutes being awarded at the end of the match in an almost equal fashion to everyone, with winners receiving 500 more blutes (doesn't matter everyone got 2500 anyway). Now it's like this: You win and get 2500, you lose and get 1500. What happens if both teams have no co-operation and someone on the other team has a gun they have spent days making shows up? Fifteen-hundred blutes and a really long and boring match.
I really wish there was a yes/no selection to reviewing. I can't exactly recommend this game to veteran players anymore, and at the same time, can recommend it to good players. It doesn't feel right to play this game as it used to be, but if you have never played this shouldn't be a problem....until you hit level 10.
10/20 would level character to level 10 again, just to make the gun I want. (20 is level cap)

Probably the coolest and most realistic MechWarrior to date besides their upcoming game announced at Mech Con.
Pros:
- Lots of customization
- Pretty to look at
- The devs constantly give free stuff away by way of in-game events (currency, parts and entire mechs)
- Can obtain everything by being completely free to play (buy to play mechs are only available in such a capacity for a limited time before their purchasable through the in-game currency)
Cons:
- No tank tracks for legs like the Armored Core games (used to be my personal favorite)
- Public groups sometimes get stuck dealing with 8-12 man premades
- There's no Co-Op campaign or any other sort of campaign period

It really is free to play.  The rate you earn C-bills (the in-game currency) is high enough that with some minor grinding you can get yourself some really decent 'mechs.  Your first twenty-five matches also pay out at a much higher rate, letting even beginners gather enough money to own at least one good 'mech.  It is monetized, so payng real money is a much faster way to get the 'mechs and accessories that you want - and some 'mechs and options are ONLY available for real money.  Still, it's totally possible to play free; those who spend money on their builds don't have any automatic adantage over pilots who don't.
The gameplay revolves around a really outstanding player base - an older crowd, not the bunch you find on COD.  And the developers, three years later, are still heavily involved inupdates and making new maps, gamemodes, and balance adjustments.  All in all this is a great game; it could be improved with a single-player campaign mode, but that is a fairly minor complaint given how free and how enjoyable the game is overall.

I've been playing this for over 2 years.  The developers are continually adding new content and improving the game...sometimes its a step back before 2 steps forward.
It's not an easy shooter.  It takes effort to get good (knowing the meta, learning different chasis and their weaknesses, positioning and targeting with different weapon systems, etc...).  One must also learn that working with ones team is vital.  Even the best players are easily taken down when isolated from their mates.  MWO is also about strategy: which mech you bring, how you build it, when & how you engage, which weapons you fire, etc...
This game is already a first class shooter; It sets the standard for stompy robot shooter games.  It has a rich lore in the Battletech universe.  But, it has potential to be much better.
However, it falls short in the meta game...the game really offers nothing beyond shooting opponents in different styles of mechs.  The community warfare mode needs a lot of work.  The war between the Inner Sphere and the Clans fails to engage.  Even to the extent that teams can make a minor impact, the fruit of these efforts are largely meaningless.  Individuals fail to reap any tangible impact from their efforts.  That combined with battles that are often one-sided as skilled teams drop against randomly grouped pugs...and the mode can quickly become discouraging...even for a top tier player.
Overall, I enjoy the game.  I am critical because it could be great!

The review turned out longer than I expected, so I will include a summary of my thoughts at the bottom.
Like alot of people, I remember Crimsonland from back in the day. I first encountered it on a demo disk that came with a magazine I used to buy. With only the first chapter of the Quests mode being playable, I remember replaying it over and over again. Some years later, I discovered the Internet and what it had to offer, so I managed to obtain the full version of the game, finally being able to play through the entire thing. Rediscovering it again on Steam was quite a surprise, with a new look and a tempting price tag. However, having found out that perks are no longer present in the Quests mode, I decided against buying it.
Forward a year later, and what do you know: Crimsonland is on sale, 80% off. Not only have
re-added Perks into the Quests mode, but the game now comes with the classic version from 2003. It was a steal at the discounted price and I immediately bought it.
A few weeks have passed since then and after playing through the game and going for some of the achievements, I'm happy to say that Crimsonland has not only retained everything that made it great (and a tiny bit frustrating at times), but has also managed to slightly improve upon it with a couple of new weapons, perks and game modes.
Quests mode is separated into 6 chapters, each one having 10 levels. There is no story that follows these, but they're all thematically different from one another. They also have replay value as you unlock difficulty levels and achievements.
You start each level with a pistol, and pick up different weapons and powerups as the level goes on. You can't however switch between weapons you've picked up, but are instead stuck with the last one you did. Kills earn you XP which can be used to select perks that can help you through the current level, as they reset at the end of each one. Beating a level will unlock a new Survival game mode, weapon or perk. Everything you unlock will then be present in Survival mode, as well as future Quests levels.
Speaking of the Survival mode, it is devided into 6 other modes, each with its own set of rules. For example, Blitz is just like Survival, but sped up, with an increased number of monsters and powerups. Nukefism on the other hand has leveling and weapons disabled, allowing you to only use powerups if you want to survive.
All  game modes provide a good challenge. The powerups and perks feel usefull and make a notable difference. Some weapons may seem underpowered, but each has its benefits in a specific situation. However, the randomess of it all, accompanied by some difficulty spikes may give the feeling that the game relies more on luck rather than on skill.
Even though all of the game modes are playable co-op with up to three other players, and each survival mode having its own leaderboard, there is no online play.
The game has a very clean look to it, so you'll be able to tell whats happening at any given time. Over a hundred monsters can be on the screen, with particles from your weapons, perks and powerups flying all over the place, the bits and blood of the monsters you killed clearly visible on the terrain for the remainder of the level. All this while the game manages to run smoothly all the way through.
Although the graphical update of the new version boasts has plently of advantages, I feel as they didn't go as far as they could in some, and at the same time, could have toned it down in other places.
The only purpose for the maps may be to provide a background for all the carnage to happen on, but they could have greatly benefited from a bit more detail, which would add to the atmosphere as well . Something I feel the classic version did better, as it had more robust visuals and a muter color palette .
All of the weapons unfortunately still share the same model, something worth changing that carries over from the classic version. This is one of the best games I have played in a long time. I would go from marathoning it for hours on end, quiting to take a break, then jumping back in after 5 minutes away because I needed more. The gameplay is very fast paced and will get your adrenaline going (especially in the late levels).
I found the story interesting though I know some others called it a bit thin. I would definitely recommend "grabbing" the random historical story bits you come across (green things) as they offer an interesting recollection of what happened previously. Not the best story I have experienced but definitely not the worst.
As I said the gameplay is some of the best I have ever come across. It is very fast paced and the music helps to amp you up even more in the high pressure situations. The guns fit the fast paced gameplay perfectly with many different ways of taking down the demons you come across  (you will likely use all within the same situations at points). Which brings me to the glory kills: hell yes. The glory kills are great and do not slow the gameplay down at all. Instead they make it feel more smooth as you go from shooting every demonic thing you see to doing an epic kill then back to running for your life and trying to survive.

This has an amazing campaign (coming from a person who doesn't necessarily enjoy campaigns) and an equally great multiplayer brawl with it. The game also incorporates the mods within the community to an extent where I haven't seen any other games that have done the same.

The first, biggest and most important thing to note about Mechwarrior online is it will be a grand test of patience. Both the matches and the advancement in this game are slow processes filled with careful decisions and deliberation. For people used to a game with a much faster pace and dislike a shooter that requires caution and patience, I would reccomend Hawken instead.
Second, This game is based on the Battletech universe, but it is not a canonical battletech game. People expecting a true mechwarrior game like the classics might be disappointed to find that the designs, stats and some features are changed to better suit balance for a multiplayer mech shooter (However I for one love the new reseen mech designs).
Third, The learning curve is a big one and difficult one. I remember first starting this game before it's steam release and struggling to fight other players when I could barely control my mech's torso and legs at the same time. Since that time the tutorials for the game have gotten far better and alot more is done to help prepare new players for the real game. A process that used to consist of getting stomped many times until you figured everything out the hard way is now alot less painful, but you will still need to expect having to climb that first hill. Fortunately, the game does include popular tried-and-true 'trial' mechs for newer players that are high quality and let players try new playstyles and mech types, excellent for deciding what sort of mechs you'd rather pilot.
All that said, I personally don't mind the lack of canonicity- it's close enough to battletech and still awesome.
For people not familiar with mechwarrior games, the game consists of, most of the time, two teams of twelve players each divided into three 'lances', or four member squads. There are simple objectives in each game mode such as capturing and holding points, king of the hill, escorting a VIP, or assaulting an enemy base. There is also a larger scale invasion game mode that involves defending or attacking a critical location, and a small scale scouting game mode.
You pilot a Battlemech and have a very large variety of mechs and mech variants to choose from. Mechs are divided into four weight classes (Light, Medium, Heavy and Assault), and can fill a number of different roles (Fire support, Brawling, Spotting, Sniping, etcetera). The mech models are heavily based on models and variants in the actual battletech universe. Combat consists of destroying armored segments on an enemy mech to expose critical systems, destroying them cripples and potentially destroys the enemy mech. You only get one life per match (With invasion as an exception where you get four), so despite the game's slow pace, matches tend to be short. It also emphasizes caution and strategy- losing even one mech can change the course of the fight. Truly amazing fights in MWO take place between two well coordinated groups attempting to outmaneuver and outsmart the other.
If you play alone, those matches are a rare jewel, however. Most solo games will have you in uncoordinated teams in a test of raw skill rather than strategy, and players may not listen to anyone who issues commands. I reccomend finding and sticking with a unit (Clan of sorts) to play with or finding a group of friends and joining a group, the game becomes much more fun this way and really amplifies the difficulty and intensity.
The community is mostly a quiet bunch in solo, and it has a fair share of both small numbers of loud toxic people and coolheaded supportive types. That sort of thing is to be expected with any multiplayer game.
Content in this game is amazing, you are free to take apart and build your mechs however you want. New mech models are released every single month, and the list of usable mechs has grown by alot. There is no such thing as a 'bad' mech, only popular ones. Tweaks and balance changes are constantly being done. I don't know about other players but I spend about 2/3rds of my time in this game trying to build the perfect mechs, and I find it as much fun constructing them with love as I do actually in game. If you like variety in your death machines, that will be something to love in Mechwarrior online.
I will say this game is absolutely not for everyone, it's a certain kind of person who enjoys a slow paced thinker shooter like MWO, negative reviews from people who didn't enjoy the game are understandable. But as a free game, I think it's definitely worth the oppurtunity to find out if you'd enjoy playing it or not.

I wanted to like this so much. It is almost painful to give it a thumbs down. There is so much in this game that is so close to making it really good, and really this is not so much of a thumbs down as it is just not a thumbs up.
So, where to start...
This is, as you should know, a 4x space game but there in lies one of the first problems with it. It is a 4x game "light" IMO. The game takes the approach of making many aspects of a 4x game and automating them. The combat is completely automated, there is mostly no colony management outside of setting a tax rate and building que, there is no real desicion making in research other then to just get it all, there is little to no diplomacy other than war/peace, and there is no espionage.
Overall, while this makes the game a bit more casual and easier for newer players to understand, after multiple games and hours of play time everything just kinda falls flat. And honestly, I wouldn't have minded all this so much if the rest of the game was there as well. This is not a bad game, by any means. For what is there, it is polished, beautiful, the music is nice, the lore is interesting and the game does a great job of pulling you in and making you want to play it. But once you get past that intial love, you realize there is not anything else there. It is super shallow and after a few games it becomes very repetitive.
The worst offender in the game and what possible pushed it down for me was the combat mechanics. Let's face it, most 4x games result in lots of combat and this one is definitely no different. However, the mechanics of how they work in this game make them very uninspired, bland, and does nothing to reward the player for being smart or playing better. See the main problem with the combat is all combat is done through ship fleets. A fleet can have a certain amount of "Points" of ships in them. The bigger the ship is the more points it is. You can gain more point maximum per fleet through research and racial traits. Actual combat is all done 1 fleet vs 1 fleet at a time and is all automated, winning is simply a numbers game that compares fleet defense number vs enemy attacking number. So what this boils all down to is the empire that can have the most points of ships in each fleet has a huge advantage simply because they have more of everything. Since combat is all automated there is no tactical advantage for smaller faster ships or ambushes or any battle tactics whatsoever. It is all just a numbers game and who can have the biggest number. Unfortunately, this carries over to the rest of the game because what this means is that once you get past the initial exploring part of the game all you will ever do is build ships non stop and throw them at the enemy and whomever can build them fastest with larger fleets wins.
This is also exactly all the AI does as well. So once war is engaged, and it always will in most 4x games, it becomes a sluggish slog that becomes very boring very quickly. This is were the rest of the shallowness starts becoming very apparent as with other 4x games you may be able to start other tactics, whether diplomatic, espionage, etc to help move the combat and war along. Unfortunately in Endless Space there is no other tactics, and there is no other option other then to just slog it out, or simply stop playing. Which was what I did.
As with so many 4x games in recent memory, Endless Space fails to build upon earlier games that were far superior. The developers, for whatever reason, failed to learn what made those games popular and whom, by many, are still considered the best of the genre, even some 10-15 years later. Yes, the graphics are better, the sound is better, the ships are cooler, and the lore is engaging, but 4x games require more then that. So I cannot recommend this game, there are just simply better games out there of this stype and style.

As a game- this makes a good puzzle game. At one time there was sort of an offline support. And now there is weird offline support, as based on pervious statement only the game becomes massively glitched.
Detales are on the externally visibal parts, meaning internal parts are undifined gray or black shapes of the actuall parts. No big deal to me, as I don't know much about video game texturing
As an educational tool- It's ok. It shows every part that goes into making a gun whole, but sometimes it can be lazy as it doesn't show how to properly remove and/or replace various parts. My best example for players is the Beretta 92's clip release. This one stands out to me because I took apart my own Beretta out of bordom(it did need a little cleaning too) and accidentlly popped the clip relase out.(and by popped out I mean nearly hit me in the face. So I didn't see how it came out) It took me a few minutes to figure out how to replace it because unlike what is shown in game, it doesn't slide in and out. I've noticed other parts that seem to just slide in and out of other models as well.
There are also a few skeleton models, not sure why. Cars, which seem cool.(I'm a free player) Two military vehicals, also seem cool. And a single plane for now.
As for the shooting ranges... meh, basic FPS style, but it hard for a game to depict a trip to the range. also only a few ranges to use not a wide variety.
And finally, the biggest turn off of this game, the few things that ruin this.
The microtransaction DLC(?) packs- 1 or 2 of the pack are 100% FREE, as they are in the free version of this game. Others are mostly free as only a couple of the guns are credit locked.(why would I want to pay $10 for something thats already offered for free???)

I am 100% about this game...
... Which is ironic because I really wasn't sure if I'd like it or not. I'm pretty positive that I got this from a bundle of some sort (HumbleBundle, I'm looking at you), and so kind of tossed it in my never ending backlog pile. It was buried so deeply, in fact, that I can't even tell you how long ago I added it to my library.
What I can tell you is not playing this game sooner was a total mistake. Although Crimsonland might look like your stereotypical top down shooter, it's far from it. 10tons LTD puts their own spin on Doom-inspired mechanics and themes, and really takes the top-down genre to a whole new level. Sure, Crimsonland might not be the most graphically impressive game, but trust me - this literally does not matter whatsoever. The mechanics of the game run as smoothly as a hooker covered in lube. Or blood. Or something ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
The basis of the game is simple - you start with a pistol (and yes, it totally packs a punch!), and in the early levels you encounter only handfuls of enemies. As you play, powerups and different guns are dropped (which, by the way, you unlock a wide variety of new ones as you play through levels). I'm not going to lie - the powerups in this game are absolutely amazing, and range from freezing enemies in ice to freezing time. A certain amount of tactical prowess has to be applied to each different level, as this isn't any simple top down bullet hell.
Last but not least, the game modes must be mentioned. There's a "quest" mode in which you unlock all the available powerups, guns, etc. Annnnnd then there's the "survival" modes, which offer a bunch of different and unique flavors of the game. Amongst these are a typing mode, an actual survival mode, a powerup-only mode, an AK-47 only mode, and a limited ammo mode, as well as a la mode. Wait, no, I lied about the last one. That's for pie and ice cream or something :D
Gory, gritty, and intense, Crimsonland draws you in with its fast pace, delicious mechanics, and lots of zombies. If you enjoy top down shooters and don't own Crimsonland, you should. If you do own Crimsonland, then stop hesitating. It's worth the time investment, I promise.

I usually stay away from wireless controllers. I prefer wired controllers for many reasons. Latency, battery life and durability. The wireless ones that I have use have been lack luster. IMO. My kids however love using them. They've used Logitech Gamepad F710, XBOX Wireless Controller and Kycola GC21 Dual Vibration Wireless Gamepad. I did not like these at all. They got me the STEAM controller as a gift on my birthday. I've been regularly impressed by it. My family games on Linux (Ubuntu Mate, Linux Mint, Lubuntu, Manjaro and Arch) and this controller has been at the center of our gaming experiences on our HTPCs and on my main gaming rig for over 1.5 years.
I've imported my gaming library from GOG, Itch.io and Humble Bundle to STEAM to use with this controller and for games like the SNK 25th Anniversay series, Flat0ut and many others this controller has been the king.
The only draw back that I can point to is a recent STEAM update (few months back) in which the controller did not work without an edit to the udev settings on Linux. You would only notices this if you had the controller for a long time and updated through the years. If you installed a distro right now, it works fine.
The battery life is excellent. I use rechargeables and I game daily for at least 1 hour or more. On the weekends, I have HTPC gaming time with the family (we now have 4 STEAM controllers - sold the other wireless gamepads online). I am usually recharing every month and a 1/2.
The durability seems to be OK. We've not dropped ours, yet (knock on wood) but the gamepad feels hefty and sturdy.
I've yet to see any latency issues with fast games like Skullgirls and even with racing games like Dirt Showdown.
Programming this control pad to work with games that don't support gamepads is easy. It's a great feature to have inside of STEAM. As a gamer that's been using gamepads with computers since the late 80's - it would require a 3rd party program to work with and save profiles. Getting rid of the need for a 3rd party program is great but only if you import your non-STEAM games to your STEAM library.
Highly reccomend it!

Like it but I had some very bad first experiences with it. First I will address the layout of the controller. It definitely is not the standard as you know. I can appreciate that they are trying new things, and while I will say that this attempt is not bad, I wouldn't go so far as to say that this attempt is above what is currently the standard with the DS3 and XB1 controller. By standard and I am referring to the layouts of the controller and the use of conventional thumbsticks.
Now what is exceptional about this controller is the amount of configuration that you can do to it. I will discuss this more in depth further in the review. First I would like to talk about plug'n'play. This controller does it and does it well. I had a large problem with this initially because of conflicting software (MSI Afterburner, more on it later as well). Immediately upon plugging in the device (provided you have Steam open), Steam will recognize the controller. It will notify you that it is best used with Big Pictured mode and likely request you to enter that mode so that it can update the firmware. Not a problem.
When you launch a game, if it is a more popular game, such as GTA5, The Witcher, or Rocket League it will load up what the developers consider the optimized controls for that game. This is a very nice feature, but it is more or less in line with same expectation I have with plugging in a standard type controller as well. Obviously the default controls may not be to your liking and this is where the controller really really shines. Just press the Steam Button on the controller and enter the configuration menu (one of the first options). From there you can on the fly, browse, download, and apply custom made community configurations all within a few buttons. These configurations are voted on by other Steam Controller users, so the top ones are generally very good. Should you not like something you can customize whichever configuration however you like. For example, you could make it so the left haptic pad works as joystick, mousepad, direction pad, trackball, whatever can be thought of can be done with a ridiculous amount of options that are easily presented.
I would consider the ergonomically feeling of how the controller sits in one's hands to be superior to the standard DS3 and XB1 controller. I would say that the Steam Controller definitely win in making it comfortable. Now using the haptic pads and the buttons is another matter. I would not say it is bad. I would not even say that it needs work. It is just a different experience. Not necessarily a bad one, but just different. It can be compared to using a regular mouse versus using a trackball. Neither one is better than the other. They are different things. Its a different layout that standard and when one goes to play a game that is definitely something that will be noticed. At first it feels a little wrong and it feels overly sensitive or under sensitive with regards to the haptic pads.
When it comes to the buttons, this is what I consider to be the weakest area of the controller that could use work. ABXY aren't bad, they aren't great, I would call them mediocre. Definitely subpar to the DS3 and XB1 controllers. There is less resistance and it slightly reminds me of pressing a worn out, but more raised original PSP button. It could definitely use some resistance. The Start, Select, and Steam button are even worse than that. They have a horrible gummy feeling. If I had the option to change the springs in them or whatever I would. I hate the feeling of them.
Now onto the Triggers, RB/LB, and the joystick. The triggers remind be of the PS3 controller. It operates like a dynamic trigger, the more you press, the more your car accelerates or whatever. Once you depress it 75% or more it enters the second stage which is like when you fully depress a firearm trigger, just with less force. There is a noticeable (not annoying) click. I don't mind the triggers. They are just different like the haptic pads. I hate the RB/LB buttons. Whereas the other buttons went with too much softness, these ones were clearly designed by someone else and went with much too much stiffness. I also feel like the positioning of them could have been done better. They are large and pushed further out that the regular controller. I would say they are definitely worse than the XB1 Controller, and only slightly to mildly worse than the DS3 controller. The amount of force you have to use to push them down is just too much in my opinion.  Now regarding the singular joystick. I like it. Its more like the DS3 joystick than an XB1 joystick. It has a nice tight feeling. Very tight to no deadzone and I believe it will last. Maybe a little too much force required to push down on it to click it, but not bad.
The back buttons are great. Probably my favorite thing along with the easy customization of the controller. If there are two reason I would recommend someone to buy this it would be because of the back buttons and the ease and superiority of customization versus the other competitors.
Now I will talk about my technical problems with the controller. I have a over clocking and overlay program called MSI Afterburner that starts with my computer. The controller did not like this one bit. It would work in 50% of the games and in others it would not work whatsoever. It would not apply configs and the default scheme was completely broken. I was about to say the controller I received was just defective. Steam needs to make it more apparent that third party overlays break the functionality of this controller more. I would say just have a nice informative screen when you first plug it in that includes this information, other helpful things such as use of Steam button and of course recommendation of using Big Picture Mode.  For those that are wondering Nvidia Shadow Play appears to work just fine. Only Afterburner has warranted this reaction thus far that I have seen.
Now would I recommend this controller over the XB1 or DS3 controller. Thats a very difficult question. On one hand, those controllers are much more standard and it feels more "right" per say. Another plus of them is that because they are more standard the default configuration of them is likely to be better and more games will have a default configuration. However, with that said, the moment you throw in the ease of customization of the Steam Controller I would say it blows the other two out of the water in this regard. The primary problems that this controller has, I feel is just that it is not the same as the others. It is a different experience and is very difficult to put into perspective what it feels like to use it. If you are interested in it.
Here is my simple answer, yes, buy this controller over the others. But, try to buy this controller at a retailer that will allow you to return it in the event that you regret it. Some people are going to love this because it is ground breaking and all that nonsense. Some people because it is unique. I stand more in the middle it definitely is different and I could see this as primarily a hate it or love it product.

Loadout is a fun free-to-play game that is just chaos in every match you join. There are many pros and cons to this game and I want to talk about some of those pros/cons.
The first and one of the best pros this game has is the weapon crafting system, it's a system in the game that's lets you craft many weapons of mass destruction like a gun that shoots 6 rockets or a gun that sprays fire all over the place.
You can also give you'r character different clothing like a leather jacket with shorts and nerd like glasses. You need to spend real life cash to buy these clothing and I feel the choice to make it so that you have to buy these items in real life cash is stupid and dumb because those clothing don't give you any boost in the game and is just there to make you'r character more pretty and cool.
Even tho it takes a long a$$ time to find a match, once you do get in a match, it's will be crazy, fun and amazing. There are differnt game modes like capture the flag but instead a flag, there's a giant hammer that you need to take back to you're base and maybe along the way back, you can crush you're enemys with the hammer. Another mode is when one person from each team is a collector and has to pick up certain items that are spread out on the map and has to bring them to one of several points. There's another mode that each team must fight over and hold a certain postion that is somewhere and everytime a team capture one of these spots, their team gets points and the spot is moved over to a random location.
Since this game has no story mode and just leans on the multplayer, there isn't alot of content in this game besides making you're own guns and killing other players. Even tho there is just multiplayer, this game's multiplayer is (in my opinion) better than most FPS online.There is a  feature in the game that I love is that when taking damage, you're character change like when someone headshots you, you'r head blows off and you are still alive and you can now see you're tiny brain and eyes and if you get shot in the chest, there is a high chance that a giant hole will form that will make you see you're ribs,lungs,guts, ect.
In my opinion, Loadout is a great Free-To-play FPS but I feel like this game lacks content. I give this game a rating of 7/10. It has a great weapon crafting system great multiplayer but lacks content and most of the servers are dead. You might have fun with the game but might get bored with the game in a week or 2.

Endless Space is a complex, and beautiful 4X strategy game that draws natural comparisons to games like Sins of a Solar Empire (Endless Legend, possibly Civ). If you don't like having to spend possibly hundreds of hours exploring tech trees, managing morale, supply lines, and configuring ship outfits this game isn't for you.
My one gripe (with most 4X games for that matter) is that the pace is often (intentionally) slow. Even after learning the mechanics; skirmishes against AI will take multiple hours. This is fine if you plan on casually playing a game over the course of days/weeks/months (which I'm told many people do), but in many cases the larger strategy (i.e. any of the 'X's) will largely overwhelm the rest of the game, to the point that most tactical aspects will feel mechanical, which leads to a lot of largely unfulfilling early games (which will burn 10-50 hours).
If you appreciate the zen of turn-based strategy, you'll love this--and for the money, playing this game is effectively identical to Endless Legend (which I believe is currently more expensive).
A fun game with long matches and a steep learning curve. Cool ship designs, Love the multiple upgrade paths.

Prototype has its ups and downs, but more downs that ups.  The main character has some super fun super powers that allow you to do some really crazy things as you fly, jump, or run (horizontally and vertically) through the city.The game also looks pretty good.  The story seems really fascinating as well, but that's about where the good ends.
First off, the city gets pretty boring pretty quickly as there is nothing really unique about the city that makes any part of the city look any different from another part.  I found myself just following the quest markers on the mini map and not trying to learn the city at all.  I never knew where I was unless I pulled up the main map.  There are lots of cool powers, but when the fights get going you are so busy running around trying to stay alive and kill that you never really get any time to really bask in the fun of watching a cool ability when it is triggered.
The main negative is that it appears that the controls for the PC port didn't translate properly.  The keyboard presses are super sensitive.  I've been using this keyboard for a few years and dozens of games, so I am comfortable with it, but I never had such problems with the keyboard in any other game than I did with Prototype.  To top it off there was no sweetspot for mouse sensitivity either.  Either it took HUGE hand sweeps to turn left and right, with the mouse, or my camera would go sitr crazy at the slightest twitch when trying to adjust the sensitivity.  Also y-axis sensitivity was way more sensitive than the x-axis.
As a result, I could barely control my character as I bounced off walls, hitting things, or attacking things except the actual mob I had selected as my target.  My character looked cool going bat crap crazy all over the fight zone, but if this game had been real life, the people I was fighting would have thought I was an idiot as they easily gunned me down, which is what happened during game play very often.  I eventually got so ultra♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at the lack of character control that I finally quit and removed the game from my system.  Experiencing the story wasn't enough of a draw to make me spend many frustrating hours getting killed constantly and wander through a boring city.  I'll read the story on Wikipedia or something.

For years I've been only listening to the game's soundtrack, which in itself is a masterpiece, well done and thank you Michael McCann. While I tried to get into the game a few times, I always felt like I'm missing something and never had the motivation to return to the game the next day.
Now in 2017 I played through the first Deus Ex game after 16 years. When I first tried it after release in 2000 I didn't really like it so I never got past the first map or even to the end of Liberty Island. Now I gave it a chance and I have to say even today the first Deus Ex is a great game. It's not pretty and it feels a bit empty sometimes, but still I really enjoyed it.
After I was done with it, I had a quick look at Invisible War as again I tried it on release, but couldn't get into it. I may play it through one day, but this time I moved on to DXHR, since this was my aim from the beginning. And this time, I got into it and I didn't let go until I finished it.
I have to say that it wasn't entirely what I was expecting. I mean I played it before, done the first mission and strolled about a bit on the streets of Detroit, but that was it. But after listening to the music for years I got a bit different picture in my head about the world of the game. I expected it to be a bit more sci-fi environment-wise. I mean the setting is sci-fi enough, only the atmosphere is a bit different like what I was hoping for. This is a good game, don't get me wrong. A really good game, even a great one. But something is missing for me.
I cared about the story, although there are some loose ends, but I guess it is because we get back to them in DXMD, which game I will play when it is done and all of the story is available... So in DXHR I enjoyed the interaction with NPCs, and with the environment, and the controls and weapons felt too good to not use them and kill 80% of the enemy populace with them :P My favorite is the silenced 10mm pistol, and at the end I found that the combat rifle is quite handy too.
I'm a completionist so I hacked everything, read everything (well almost everything, I hate/am lazy to read), done everything, (at least I tried because according to the achievements I apparently missed some things) and this game provides the same interactivity as the first DX game, or even more. It provides you with choices, different paths - although I explored all of them - and an interesting protag who was even funny sometimes although not on the same level as Mr JC "heh heh" Denton. The ending though. It is weaker than that of the first game, in other words dumbed down. It may have a reason to why it's like that, I don't know. A hidden message perhaps. Gameplay-wise though... not satisfying.
Just like the first one, this game was thought provoking too. It had enough missions and wasn't overwhelming like some RPGs with their 100 quests at once. The game simply has you have things to do at all times and to me that was enough.
If I had to rate DXHR I'd give it a strong 9 out of 10. I personally didn't find a single bug and the mechanics are all well thought out and well done. Maybe the animations and lip sync during conversations are lacking but it's not a biggie. The story was good - the ending could be better though - and the length was fine as well. It took me 46 hours according to steam to beat it. As I mentioned I expected something a little bit different, but if I forget about that, to me this game is perfect.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I was introduced to Artemis SBS by a friend last year and now I mourn the years before I knew what this game is about. This game is unlike anything else I've played. Getting together with friends to fly a starship, fight enemy ships, and complete challenging missions as a team has an energy and an appeal all its own. More than that, I've discovered that there is a robust community around this game that embraces the team experience and continually pushes the bounds of what is possible through game updates, custom missions, mods, and even hardware.
At its heart, this game is about the people playing it and group roleplaying a starship crew. The mechanics pull you in and set the stage for grand adventures and lots of shouting, as others have noted. Note: Please disregard playtime. I've bought this game twice, once on here, and once on the official site(which is more friendly for modular and local play), and would do so again in a heartbeat.
This game is a true platform, able to fit a wide variety of gaming niches. It works equally as well for casual party play in a living room with friends and family using their personal laptops, as it does for a fully purpose-built touchscreen bridge setup in conjunction with LARP away teams. It's a must have for any fans of Star Trek, Battlestar Galactica, or Babylon 5, and anyone who wants to experience the thrill of teamwork on the bridge of a spaceship.
This is a game that can be played by as few as 1 person(who has to run the entire 6 station starship by themselves!), to as many as *88* (8 ships, each playing a carrier that holds 5 starfighters) on a single server!(To be honest, I don't think this has ever happened, but it's possible!)  With the right scripted mission and Gamemaster support, the number of people that can participate in a mission across multiple servers is *unlimited*, as we found out during the 2017 Artemis Armada Convention.
In the multiple years I've owned this game, I've had ever increasing amounts of fun with it. The developer(just one guy!) is constantly adding new content and functionality, listens to feedback on the official forums, and honestly just wants people to have fun playing his game. There are other games out there that might look 'better,' offer VR, or have some bip and bops that this game might not, but there truely nothing that can beat the immersion of sitting behind the weapons screen (your own, real life screen!) of a cruiser, watching enemy ships come into range on the main screen (just a few feet away, in real life!), and asking (or yelling for) the Science officer sitting nearby to give you the frequency your beams should be set to.
This game does not have any sort of dedicated server support, so while plenty of groups do play over the internet, it's up to each person to find people to play with.  I do not feel that this is a flaw, however, and this game works best when you have a ship's crew in the same room.
The communities that have sprung up around this game are, while secondary to the game itself, absolutely excellent. From the official forums, to the modding and mission scripting folks, to the yearly convention in Cleveland, OH, to the many, MANY groups worldwide that run their own events, this is a game built by the players to be whatever they want it to be.

This is what Star Trek games should be.  This is a pretty simple take on  the concept but one that makes it fun and easy to play.  A great recommendation for groups and LAN parties.  It can however be a challenge to play solo.  Even though it is not part of the official franchise Star Trek fans will like it.

The paying aspect of this game is to buy gold and upgrade to a premium account for a specific amount of time. Special tanks can be purchased with gold but they can not be advanced or built upon. Premium accounts just earn you 1/3 more credits and experience each game and there's plenty of ways to obtain premium account status without paying. Renegade Ops; A name that explains itself and explains the game at the same time, an underrated little masterpiece that’s jam-packed full of chaos, anarchy, weapons of mass destruction and all in the form of cars and trucks.
To call this old-school or retro would do it something of disservice, it’s essentially more original than that. Renegade Ops takes the old classic, then moves them to a modern level with co-op, persistent character and tremendous graphics. The camera angle is familiar with a style of zooming around a large map in a distinctive style to Desert Strike, but a little more intense.
The campaign has an interesting climax to it with a dry sense of clichéd humour and cheesy one-liners as you complete primary and secondary objectives. As you play, it is liberating and anger relieving to blow-up tanks and cars, run yourself through building, and turn infantry units into road-kill.
Renegade Ops offers various ways of controlling your car through a game-pad or keyboard, whatever suits your style of gaming. Overall, it’s a great example of a really enjoyable game based on a simple idea that is executed with care and attention to detail.
Altogether, a great single player and co-op game you can play with your friends.

In a single year this became my favorite game of all time. When I first heard of it I thought it would be terrible, and only gave it a shot because there was nothing else quite like and, well, it's free. And I'm very glad I did that.
The gameplay is really good, with a lot of depth and customization. It features hundreds of different 'Mechs variants that can be customised: loadouts, cockpit items and camo patterns.
Some 'Mechs and weapons are inferior to others, but overall the game is pretty well balanced.
As for the F2P aspects, there are C-Bills, the common currency earned in every match, and MC, the premium currency. The best things that MC can buy are premium time, that increases C-Bills and experience earned in every match, 'Mech bays, that increased the maximum number of owned 'Mechs, and Hero 'Mechs, unique variants with a 30% C-Bill bonus.
The Hero 'Mechs are not overpowered (some are actually worse than their C-Bill variants) and so players that spend money on them have to rely more on their loadout, skill and teamwork rather than the type of 'Mech they own.
One of the biggest problems with the game is the lack of more advanced tutorials. The in-game tutorial only teaches the very basic concepts, and for everything else I had to watch tutorials on Youtube.
The performance of the game, while not terrible, is still worse than it should be, especially for a F2P game.
That being said, Mechwarrior Online is a really good game, albeit with some flaws. It is the only game I never get tired of,  and I can't wait for the new content planned for 2017 (new weapons, equipment, 'Mechs and skill trees).

First...I've only been playing for about 6 months. (We'll come back to that in a minute).
This game is a "Stompy Robot Shooter" game. Basically an FPS but with robots of varying size and abilities. In some ways it's like Hawken but less of a 'video game' and more of a simulation. Which is what attracted me after getting burned out from COD (especially it's new Infinite Gymnastics release). So...if you're an FPS guy....this is a good FREE TO PLAY robot FPS. 3 out 5 stars right there with no othere considerations (see below) and it's free...you can spend a LOT of money in microtransactions but you don't have to if you just want to play it casually.
Now...If you are a Lore-♥♥♥♥♥ then this game could be bad or good depending on how you want to view it. Yes, it does have some non-cannon parts. Yes, PGI can sometimes play fast and loose with mech design and weapons....but....you can't go from tabletop to video without some changes. I, personally, like the changes.....but those with OCD might not. (More on that in a minute).
So...the game itself is pretty much like a lot of FPS games. You have teams. You have certain modes (TDM, Escort, Dom,o etc). Your weapons, while futuristic, break down into beam, ballistic, and missile. The mechs go from small to large. With the smallest being the fastest with the least armor and arms, while the Big Boys are slow but are walking bunkers.. The maps are, mostly, open so you can engage at range. (though there are some tight maps too).  If you are an FPS player its  an easy transition. You do have to watch your consumeables. You do have UAVs, System Cool Down Shots, Air/Artillary strikes...so it does have a more 'thinking' aspect to it than some of the other FPS games.  You can drop into random matches...or...join "Faction Play". Faction Play is currently a work in progress but has already, in my short playing time, gotten much better. You pick a side and either defend or attack to win all the planes in the games universe. You have the 'clan' (human descendents who are invading) or the "Houses" (star kingdoms ruled by a family or official who are defending from the clans). You'll need to read onlin and in game...LOT's of info.
Now...let's talk about the community.
I have met many awesome players and youtube posters who love the game. I've played with a few and had an absolute ball. One of the things (some) players talk about is how great the community is. For the most part it is....but....
DO NOT GO INTO THE GENERAL FORUMS...STAYIN THE NEW PLAYER FORUMS!!! >>>> There are a large percentage of 'older' players who are NOT happy with the game. They're called "Bitter Vets" and they can be really mean and ugly. Most because of lore...some because they don't like the way it's morphed into more of a mainstream FPS game. but mostly because the tabletop lore is not the same as an online game. (NOTE: there were PC games in the MWO genre from the 80's and 90's and some can't understand why we can't have that kind of gameplay on MWO now...so still Lore ♥♥♥♥♥s but from a different generation of players).  Many of these "Bitter Vets" really really want this game to crash and burn  because they are so offended. Many of them have spent thousands of dollars to get every mech and they expect that the game should cater just to their needs.
TLDR Rating?
4 out of 5

Cons:
* F2P MMO, so yea, it's a thing.
* Game scripting, well, I've seen worse, but that does Not make it good.
* Very, very, VERY grindy to do certain things. (Like unlock more classes, grrrrrrr..)
* Non-combat animations, character possession clipping, and outfits are clunky/detract from the game's visuals.
* DLC are bloody crazy-expensive for what they are, unless on sale of course.
* Classes have a very small range of skills to use. (Small enough the only choosing is what key they are bound to.)
Pros:
* The world-graphics and combat animations are breathtakingly beautiful.
* The class and level system is fresh and different, and there is actually a variety of mechanisms to increase the power level of your character, which you only need one of, ever, to enjoy the wide range of activities possible.
* The free Steam DLC is a great starter pack to get you going, and the Outlaw/Gunslinger class is a /lot/ of fun.
* The (optional) storylines, after the intro trash of course, is actually pretty decent and well written. Have yet to see any typoes or improper grammer that tend to plague most F2P MMOs as well.
* The pathfinding is crazy-good, I was actually seriously impressed by it. (Look at a quest objective so there is a lil popup thingie, hit your action button, and you will run to it via the shortest path without ever getting hung up on anything.)
* There is a wide variety of interesting game mechanics to discover, from having a city map that you can pull up and upgrade buildings to make tyou more powerful, to random limited-use weapons from a selection of types with appearances and animations particular to the mob that dropped it, and yea, LOTS of other stuffu too.
Murder Immortals:
* Yup, I'm an immortal in training to be a goddess. How do I train you ask? Well, first I kill things, then I save people by killing things, then I recruit followers (hey, I have over one-thosand thus far!) by killing things, then I go collect herbs for some guy's healing potion by killing plant things, then I do community service by going to the beach to clean it up by killing eggs AND killing the things that leap out of the crushed eggs attempting to claw my face off, then I go to a secret research facility to supervise an experiment and kill the things that come out of the gaping hole in reality when things go wrong, then go for a stroll through a beautiful and serene to relax and kill starved/ravaging/infected/agitated/cautious possibly-rabbie-slobbering natural widlife. And hey, I am REALLY good at killing things, so it works! And a lot of fun too, no puzzles, no over-thinking, just plain simple go kill things in an amazing number of ways.
Edit:
* So as to be perfectly clear, in my personal opinion this game is in no way Pay To Win. All of the cash items are either cosmetic or purely convienence, there is nothing you can get with cash that you are unable to get without, with the exception of garments which have no stats attached to them. In addition, only a small ammount of the in-game currencies are available for cash, and are available in ample supply simply by playing the game. Finally, you also receive the "cash currency" in small ammounts simply by playing.

tl;dr great game but there's a couple of jarring technical issues that have tedious solutions, get this game on sale
Despite the feature being present in Storm 3 and Revolution - and despite this game has been out for over a year now - you STILL can't mute yourself or mute the other person in game.
Wanna play a game with some randos while talking to your buds on VOIP? Nope, you'll talk in-game and that stranger will listen to everything you say and there is NOTHING you can do about it.
Wanna play the game and not listen to your opponent like you rightfully should? Nope, you'll have to listen to his vacuum cleaner and heavy breathing through his Wal-Mart mic as you're playing.
Wanna talk on Discord/TS3 with your friend while 1v1'ing them? Nope you gotta talk in-game instead through the terrible sounding codec.
There is ZERO way to work around this, I have not seen a single person find a solution to making it so you can mute yourself or the other person. Bandai ONLY considered consoles when they created the majority of the game's UI and technicalities, knowing that using Xbox One and PS4 party chats can prevent these issues. What do we get for PC? Absolutely nothing.
Aside from these mic problems... there's also crashes, menu scrolling problems at 60 FPS, the requirement to have your FPS set as the same as your opponent before fighting them (so people with relatively better computers have to downgrade their FPS to play against their friends with bad computers) and probably more.
As a game though, it's still great (esp the story). I love Naruto Storm and all the previous ones, but this one simple problem actually makes the game almost unplayable for me and my friends.
In terms of technicality, this game is absolutely terrible and shows how Bandai can be so stupid at missing the most painfully obvious menu and utilities in their games (this includes their other titles as well).
Get the game for cheap during it's sales, or hope to god that Naruto Storm Legacy has this trash figured out when it's released.

Trying something new in the clicker game genre ins't easy, My Name is Mayo does so by giving you tiered achievements tied to a few different story bits or random fun facts and different "dresses" for your clickable jar of mayo.
Yet for all its trying the game doesn't stray too far from others and is, at most, a brief and forgettable distraction.
-the various story bits and random facts are somewhat interesting
-some of the mayo dressups are quite funny
-very easy to 100%
-once you're done with the story bits the last achievements require a few thousands dull clicks
-very short
-price tags on clicker games are always a bit of a gamble, and this one doesn't do much to justify it
Just as you start having fun with My Name is Mayo the game is basically over as after about 4k clicks you'll have seen all the random facts, story bits and mayo types: the rest of the game will require you to click a few thousand more times with little to show for it and you might aswell just macro it.
Even the funny bits are quite forgettable though and in fact the game doesn't do too much to stand out from other (and better) clicker games: it was gifted to me as a way to cheer up after a bad day (and it worked <3) and it is indeed a funny timewaster but it can't be considered much more.
Nothing really stands out enough for the game to justify even the very low price tag imho: sure there's some fun to be had and it's an easy 100% (if that matters to you) but it's overall too simple and forgettable to earn a recommendation.

While the game is entertaining, my largest complaint is content. The tech trees are are very similar, and there really just isn't much to the game. I expect my 4x games to last 30-40 hours at the very least for each playthrough. Games in Endless Space are usually over in a matter of hours, even on the largest of maps. The battle system is extremely boring and not very tactical at all, so after the first few playthroughs I would just select my cards and auto resolve the battles.
Having bought it on sale for a steep discount, I can feel that I got my money's worth out of it, but it just doesn't hold my interest the way other 4x titles have. It simply just doesn't have the content to compete with other titles in the genre.

Let me just start this by saying I don't like arcade shooters (I am into 4X and RTS at the moment) - and I thought this was going to stay on my HD for only a few minutes - how naive.
It is a twin stick top-down shooter, the graphics are quite nice, apart from the occasional fire effects that don't look a bit squarish. The game itself brings me back to the arcades I used to go to in the 80's and the games I used to play - crazy stunts, powerups, some timed missions (don't worry they are very doable) and lots (I mean lots) of explosions.
HIghly recommended.

We had a lot of trouble configuring this to work over various firewalls, but once we did, it's quite a good game.
We weren't all in the same room, and used TeamSpeak to communicate, and the game played pretty nicely with four people.
It would likely suffer quite a lot if you didn't at least have three.  You can actually play it solo by running it twice on your own PC - a server and a client - but it's not really designed to work that way, so expect it to be awkward.
It's graphically average, with weird glitches and stuttering popping up every now and again, but nothing game-breaking. It suffers a bit from effectively being on a 2D plane, rather than a full 3D environment with a Z axis, but it more than makes up for all of this with being a hell of a lot of fun if you've got the right group of people.
That's the key, really. You need a good group of people you know and get along with. People have organised 'pick up games' of random players, sure, but without a lobby and built-in networking, that can be frustrating and annoying.
We also had a few crashes, where one person would, for some reason, get kicked and not be able to get back in. That can be a game-breaker. It didn't happen often, but just enough to make us a bit nervy about it during longer games.
I have to recommend it, because if you've ever wanted to play Star Trek with all your mates, this is as close as you're ever likely to get. Issues aside, it's priced relatively nicely, and while it's a nuisance to set up it's definitely worth the effort once you can poke a few holes in your firewalls.

This game is a dream come true for any Star Trek fan who ever wanted or dreamed to be on a starship bridge to participate in whatever task is required for the ship to function. Artemis divide this in 3 primary roles and 4 secondary roles of which the former are Helm, Weapons and Engineering and the later being Captain, Science, Communications and Fighter Pilot. All 7 stations serve a critical role on any given ship and while you could technically fly a ship without the secondary stations it would certainly greatly impact on the overall efficiency of all the primary ones.
After all this have been said and done, the core of the game really resolve around communication between the crew to resolve problems. Only Science and the Captain actually have a full view of the "outside world" on a global scale and while the Helm and Weapon officers also have a short range view of surrounding space, the communication officer and especially engineering have absolutely no clue of what is going on. It is thus critically important that every station report their own info/problems to everybody else to be able to perform about any task in an efficient manner... Just like it would/should happen on a real starship bridge!
My primary concern when I bought this game was that I would not be able to find anybody online to play along. It was a very valid concern at the time because you do need at a minimum 4 players to have an efficient ship and I had nobody else in my friend list interested in playing the game with me. With some digging around forums and such I discovered two groups which are not only present but extremely active and really friendly to newcomers as well. The one group which I strongly recommend for new players is the United Stellar Navy (USN) which can easily be reached and joined on their discord server and who also are responsible for maintaining the
which display publicly when the next planned Artemis game is going to happen. A quick visit on that page will show you all you need to know about Artemis players activity: there is a game planned for every single day on the week and that won't stop anybody from creating an impromptu game on the fly if enough player bust in at the same time and make a request for it.
In conclusion, I must say that this is clearly one of the best game I ever purchased in my life. Period. about 8$ for 200 to 300 hours of pure fun and no sign of me stopping any time soon? What more can you really ask for?
See you in space. :)
