Day 1 through 6 I really hated the thing, but I finally sat down and learned what all of the options did and came up with a great base template for the mouse pads that worked. That's really the key because the base settings are likely going to feel like garbage for you. I cannot deal with the trackball ON setting at all and smoothing made all the difference between dumpster and belonging on my coffee table for the rest of it's life.
Now, I've used this for 4 months and some change now and have come to the conclusion that it has a permanant home in my kit that consists of a 360 controller, a DS4 controller, a fight stick and high tech keyboard/mouse. I like PC Gaming because of all the options and when I'm playing 4x or strategy games on my big screen this is the only option for me. DS4 for most other gamepad oriented games, because honestly if the game already supports gamepads, this just isn't going to replace a better gamepad. As an actual gamepad it's not that great. We all know mouse/keyboard is the jam for highly competative FPS/moba etc so don't expect me to try argue with that because I can't.
This controller is a labor of love and you can get seriously deep with some of the settings, particularly the overlay that allows you to macro up to 16 things to the touch pad. The customization is insanely deep and the community of people making profiles usually has a great starting point for me to make my own profile. That's really the thing though. If you put the effort in, this thing is dreamy, but if you just want a plug and play gamepad, then buy a DS4 or if you really need those triggers that I love for racing games, a 360 pad. Or you know both since you can do that with a PC.
Darkest Dungeon, Stellaris, Civ 5/6, X-com 2, Cities Skylines and all similar games on the couch with this controller are all extremely enjoyable for me and just won't work well with a regular gamepad (with the exception of X-com 2 of course), There's a few in-between type games like Factorio that I've made work, but get a bit sluggish. You trade comfort for ultimate perscision in a lot of these games unless they have some really sexy developer made profile like Civ5/6 where it almost feels faster to be playing with the steam controller since game flow really adapts to it. I'll trade a fraction of my speed for laying back on the couch all day long where it makes sense. So again this thing is more of an option than it is an outright replacement for anything. Essentially it's the Red Mage of game controllers. Jack of all trades: master of nothing aside from letting you be lazy.
Also: Battery life is freaking amazing. My DS4 lasts maybe 6-8 hours before it's whining about needing charged. I've had the batteries that came with the unit in it since Xmas and they are still going 4 months later.
TLDR: Only recommend for people that wanna play light m/k games on the couch without being tied to a m/k setup. It's wasted if you are sitting at the desk with a m/k or a better gamepad in front of you. Even for pure gamepad games, the gamepads are better. HIGHLY rtecommended for 4x/Strat gamers that wanna move their long sessions to a more comfortable setting.

First...I've only been playing for about 6 months. (We'll come back to that in a minute).
This game is a "Stompy Robot Shooter" game. Basically an FPS but with robots of varying size and abilities. In some ways it's like Hawken but less of a 'video game' and more of a simulation. Which is what attracted me after getting burned out from COD (especially it's new Infinite Gymnastics release). So...if you're an FPS guy....this is a good FREE TO PLAY robot FPS. 3 out 5 stars right there with no othere considerations (see below) and it's free...you can spend a LOT of money in microtransactions but you don't have to if you just want to play it casually.
Now...If you are a Lore-♥♥♥♥♥ then this game could be bad or good depending on how you want to view it. Yes, it does have some non-cannon parts. Yes, PGI can sometimes play fast and loose with mech design and weapons....but....you can't go from tabletop to video without some changes. I, personally, like the changes.....but those with OCD might not. (More on that in a minute).
So...the game itself is pretty much like a lot of FPS games. You have teams. You have certain modes (TDM, Escort, Dom,o etc). Your weapons, while futuristic, break down into beam, ballistic, and missile. The mechs go from small to large. With the smallest being the fastest with the least armor and arms, while the Big Boys are slow but are walking bunkers.. The maps are, mostly, open so you can engage at range. (though there are some tight maps too).  If you are an FPS player its  an easy transition. You do have to watch your consumeables. You do have UAVs, System Cool Down Shots, Air/Artillary strikes...so it does have a more 'thinking' aspect to it than some of the other FPS games.  You can drop into random matches...or...join "Faction Play". Faction Play is currently a work in progress but has already, in my short playing time, gotten much better. You pick a side and either defend or attack to win all the planes in the games universe. You have the 'clan' (human descendents who are invading) or the "Houses" (star kingdoms ruled by a family or official who are defending from the clans). You'll need to read onlin and in game...LOT's of info.
Now...let's talk about the community.
I have met many awesome players and youtube posters who love the game. I've played with a few and had an absolute ball. One of the things (some) players talk about is how great the community is. For the most part it is....but....
DO NOT GO INTO THE GENERAL FORUMS...STAYIN THE NEW PLAYER FORUMS!!! >>>> There are a large percentage of 'older' players who are NOT happy with the game. They're called "Bitter Vets" and they can be really mean and ugly. Most because of lore...some because they don't like the way it's morphed into more of a mainstream FPS game. but mostly because the tabletop lore is not the same as an online game. (NOTE: there were PC games in the MWO genre from the 80's and 90's and some can't understand why we can't have that kind of gameplay on MWO now...so still Lore ♥♥♥♥♥s but from a different generation of players).  Many of these "Bitter Vets" really really want this game to crash and burn  because they are so offended. Many of them have spent thousands of dollars to get every mech and they expect that the game should cater just to their needs.
TLDR Rating?
4 out of 5

Recommend: "Yes" with caveats.
All things considered, this game does a significantly better job representing the board game than most people it credit for.  Most weapons are designed in a way that effectively translates the benefits and downsides from the board game into an online game (for example, PPC's have a  hit penalty in the board game and are difficult to use effectively at close range in this game) and each mech handles fairly well.  The visual effects are fairly immersive: the 3D cockpit, sound design, and feedback make piloting a mech feel more like you're driving a walking tank much better than other competing games and any previous Mechwarrior game except debatably MW3(although the MW5 trailer looks like that game will do the job better).
Overall they got the mech combat mechanics "mostly" right. That's the most important part of the game.
Mixed:  Pay schedule.  Although the game does a fairly decent job of allowing free players to contribute meaningfully with most mechs being available for in-game currency only, some limited edition mechs and all customization options are locked and not easily obtainable without spending real money.  The biggest problem here is that the prices on most in-game content are absolutely absurd.   While some packs are decently priced most are absolutely insane with prices reaching as high as $20 for a single mech.
Balance: Great effort on PGI's part, but they're clearly inexperienced at this sort of thing. They generally do a poor job of taking non-numerical factors into account with mechs (like hardpoint location, hitboxes, etc).  For the most part they favor nerfs instead of buffs for balance which frustrates players who purchase item with real money.  Pre-ordering content is not recommended because of the risk of a post-launch nerf that outweighs early adopter benefits.
Bad:  The game's scope is fairly limited.  There aren't enough maps for this type of game, not enough variety of game modes, and not much to it other than arena based PVP.  It offers both a freeplay mode and faction-based modes.  however in faction games there isn't much in between either the casual friendly "scouting" 4v4 matches and the "invasion" matches where every players has a deck of four mechs and consequently strongly favors hardcore players and/or organized groups.
The game's great at one thing, but it's also a one trick pony.  It does what it does well but doesn't even remotely touch into what's possible with the Battletech setting.

This is my all time favorite twin-stick shooter! I have played the original back in 2003 (which is included) as well as the re-release.
There are several game modes, the main mode is called Quest Mode and it offers 3 difficulties. You are placed in the middle of the map while enemies are storming at you in waves and you have to defend yourself from a top down perspective. Weapons (shotguns, rocket launchers, plasma rifles and many more) and powerups (for example bullet time, fire bullets, shields) are randomly dropped by dead enemies. While you shoot your opponents you will gain experience points and level up. Those levels offer special perks you can pick and they range from faster reload times to poison bullets. Each stage in Quest Mode has a distinct layout and starting weapon and by completing them you unlock new perks and weapons. The more you progress the more difficult the stages become.
Of course there is a Survival Mode, where you have to survive as long as you can as waves of enemies come after you. It features all perks and weapons that have been unlocked in Quest Mode. Or you try the Typ’o’Shooter or Rush mode. The game also offers local multiplayer of two players on the original and up to 4 on the re-release.
Crimsonland's Quest Mode and multiple side modes offer enough content to have you entertained for hours. Each round feels different, depending on the perks you pick and the random weapon drops. I tend to play the game in short bursts, you can easily drop in and out. It controls fine with both mouse and keyboard or gamepad. Tech-wise Crimsonland only shows age in terms of graphic options, the overall look and mechanics have aged well.
The price tag is a bit high, but it's not spectacular overpriced. If you like action games with light RPG mechanics, give this one a go!

It took me ten minutes to find out what was wrong with this game. Now, I am never playing it again. Allow me to list my problems with the game. Note that I have nothing against games with 8bit or 16bit art styles, as I actually own several true 8 and 16 bit games.
1. Your character has two sprites, one as an idle sprite, one for walking. This means you will never know which way you are facing.
2. These graphics just seem lazy. The charm of 8bit is taking that limitation and making something beautiful out of it, not going HELLO LOOK AT ME IM SUCH A NOSTALGIA JUNKIE LOOK ITS 8BIT SEE SEE. That doesn't stop your game from looking like crap. Take an example of another game that uses an 8bit artstyle, the ever popular Shovel Knight. The difference between these two games is that one looks good, and actually has different sprites for which direction your character is facing, as well as the simple fact that it actually looks like a game from the time period it's trying to emulate.
3. Whenever you walk against walls, everything kind of jerks around and I have no idea why.
4. The music is like someone took a generic dubstep loop and gutted it of anything that might have made it good.
5. The game tries to be cool by breaking the fourth wall in really dumb ways.
6. User created dungeons are rarely a good idea.
7. Don't even bother walking under any sort of ceiling. The effect is not pleasant.
8. The first mandatory dungeon is a LOLcats reference.
9. There is no point to any NPC humor whatsoever. This lead to me skipping so much of their dialogue.
10. Stepping up onto another block makes the camera jerk around.
Don't support these developers, and don't play this game.

This is not a very good roguelike. I mean at least it is a roguelike: grid-based, turn-based, procgen dungeons, permadeath, but sorry, it is very bland and annoying.
There's a weapon slot and an armour slot but you start naked with no weapon. The first thing you notice is that you have to hold down keys and use the autorepeat because you miss a lot and it takes a lot of hits to kill a single monster. I'm talking like 15 hits is not uncommon to kill a trashy, normal monster; one of the ones with visible armour on can take 50 hits. You're holding that button down, trust me.
The only thing that stops you getting completely mobbed by mobs and killed on level 1 is the fact that mobs don't pursue you like in most roguelikes, they just sort of move about randomly unless you're right next to them. The tactic is to kind of move round them and avoid them as much as possible, looking for the exit.
And that brings me to the map. There isn't one. No mini map, no 'm' for map.
It's just all rather simplistic. There's no field of view, you can just see everything; mob AI seems really primitive; combat is hold down button and watch your hp and enemy hp go down. The dungeons all look the same at least as far as I got (level 6?). [edit: slightly different wall graphic, I noticed]. You get different looking enemies but I didn't notice them doing anything different to each other. There's supposed to be 3 abilities you can get but I never got one.[edit: got one, see later] You can carry one potion which gives you most or all of your hp back.
Graphics: They aren't bad but they aren't great. There's no animation. The pixel fonts have anti-aliasing on them which looks awful.
Sound:  They were obviously aiming for retro 8 bit "chunky" sounding samples like old arcade games but the sound effects aren't that good. There's a few little snippets of speech which aren't 8 bit so maybe they weren't going for 8 bit after all, or maybe they just wanted the speech samples to be intelligible.
Controls: 4 way movement only. You cannot rebind the controls, it's cursor keys or gtfo. R to rest, e for potion, 123 for abilities (Finally actually got one recently but seems they are limited use).
Iti's just-- why would you play this when you can play a better roguelike game for free off steam with more depth, variety and fun? There's loads, from dungeon crawl stone soup to brogue, angband, sil, - there are tons. If you have to be on steam then get curse of yendor- same price, much better game.
I seriously do not recommend you play this game, even if you got it for free.

Ignore my playtime. I spend a lot of time playing this at various cons.
If you're looking for an accurate representation of what running a spaceship would be, this isn't exactly the game you're looking for. It's important to know that going in.
What this game really is a bizarre game of telephone, with numerous (hopefully) intoxicated players that don't have a complete view of what's going on trying to achieve missions in space. The captain wants to attack the enemy vessels attacking DS3. That's great. But that helmsmen has to get you there, and he has no idea where it is. So the captain gives him coordinates and vaguely describes what to do. But you're going too slow, so the captain orders engineering  to cut the shields before you run out of power. You arrive, but the enemy vessel is shielded. The captain orders Science to scan the vessel, and reports their weakness is shield frequency D. The captain hears this and relays it to weapons, and... you're about to die because the captain forgot to remind engineering to raise shields. So you flee, leaving a path of missiles flying behind you while Comms tries desperately to find a DS that can replenish your nukes. You find one, but you have to n navigate a minefield and asteroid belt to get there while enemy homing missiles track you down. Rinse, repeat.
And that's the game. People chaotically passing along information that's often jumbled or incorrect, trying to make a starship function in an uncaring universe. It's half Next Generation, half co-op Mario Party. And it's a thing of beauty.

They say that gameplay is more than story. Not for this game. This is a marathon. This is about endurance. This is about knowing that your name is Mayo and that you need to know that Mayo is who you truly are deep down.
White.
Easily moved.
You can relate to anything.
You make up your own story.

What do we do now?
Have you ever been stuck in life, feeling scared to do anything because you're afraid of failing? And when you know you have to do something but instead of doing something, you keep asking yourself "What do I do now?".
Well first of all, you should feel scared of failing, failing is scary and it's devastating. But that's normal, everyone is scared of failing. Second, you shouldn't keep problems to yourself, it's just like math, more people you share with, your problems will be less hard.
Sharing success with others is easy, but sharing failure and asking for a hand is not so easy. You probably feel uncomfortable showing negative emotions to others, most people keeps them to themselves and only try to show the positive part. I mean why would you burden someone with your problems? But sometimes a problem is too much to handle by yourself and when you are faced with that kind of a problem, talk to someone. And when you see someone with that kind of a problem, don't step away from it. Even if you're uncomfortable, go talk to them.
Now you know what to do when faced with a problem, but how do you start? Well "My Name is Mayo" is a game that explores the habit of hiding one's self to others. And hopefull this game will encourage you to be more open about yourself.
"My Name is Mayo" -just like it's strange title- is kind of a strange game. You start with an ordinary jar of mayonnaise, and as you progress through the game you will unlock stories of the ordinary jar of mayonnaise.
At first glance, these stories seems like nothing but a joke, at first glance this whole game looks like nothing but a joke.
But after completing the first playthrough and you take a second look into each story, you will see that this game is far from just a joke.
There are four stories of
, four very different kind of stories(which I wouldn't go into much detail about, because unlocking the next part of each story is something you should experience for yourselves). All four stories deal with the same idea, that we should be more open to others. Whether it's in a relationship, with your parents or with your friends, you should always feel comfortable sharing.
As seen in each story, not being open to others have consenquences. You might break up, you might get into fights or you might lose someone important to you.
So why keep a problem to yourself? You gain nothing from it, and you won't lose anything from sharing it. After you played through this game you'll know, whenever you ask yourself the question "What do I do now?" just open yourself to others, open a jar of mayonnaise.

Outside of Steam, I don't even know how much time I put into the game. I played for a few years.
The cons are:
There is no variation in gameplay. Almost all gameplay is peek shooting, mexican standoffs behind obstacles until someone runs out and gets shot, and going behind the enemy. The way capture and hold styled modes are implemented is contrary to how combat works in the game, and it's very telling that they've still not properly worked out how to implement it as a gamemode without making it “broadly ignore the points because doing anything near them makes you a sitting duck for want of cover, and try to kill the other side”.
The cycle of adding overbuffed mechs in grab bags, then nerfing them a month or two later in line with everything else after the burst of outrage from people who don't like to spend money on the game. It happens every game update, every time they add something that can be sold. 
In public games, you can tell which team will win simply from what they're using. In private games, you can still do it reliably, but the margin of error increases slightly.
Not every mech is good. You will see newer players blundering about in certain mechs and getting picked off, and more experienced players gimping themselves by using them for fun. The catapult's the fan favourite example for this, because it's been in the game for long, and it's the worst choice if you want to play a heavy mech because the hitbox and speed impediment isn't balanced at all by greater firepower or utility.
Old mechs are just trash. The catapult's hitboxes are still absolutely awful. And it's unwarranted. You're not doing any more damage than anything in the same weightclass, you're no more of a threat, you're simply far easier to cripple for the very simple reason that the devs can't play their own game. And we've seen that every time they try to play.
Piranha also have a fondness for adding overbuffed mechs instead of fixing old ones. Another example of that, is that for the longest time, a Mad Cat was just a better Cataphract, now it plays (vaguely) differently.
The game's also horribly programmed. No matter how good your computer, it'll randomly lag on you, because it still has assets from your last match loaded that it needs to get rid of or something else silly's happening inside the game because they rushed to complete it. Can you tell if the community hates Piranha yet? I remember when they fired someone to try and save face. pfft
I couldn't think of any pros. Well, one is, it's fun at first, when you don't know what's horribly wrong with the game. The more games you play, the more irked you will become. Unless you're the whaling type, who can spend oodles of money on something just because you like the intellectual property and Piranha might one day not be awful. This game is enjoyable, beautiful, and will run on a potato at 60fps, but if you like 4X space games I can't honestly recommend it over the Galactic Civilisations series. Combat  in Endless Space is a very uninvolved tactical endeavour, and the empire management becomes easy mid-game. Even playing on the harder difficulties, I feel like the game isn't challenging enough. If only the developers made a Brave New World-style expansion to give players more to do in the mid game. Maybe the multiplayer is more enjoyable than the lacklustre AI.

Endless Space is a 4X Strategy game you can choose between a number of races and victory conditions depending on your play style. Like many games of this style you conquer, colonise and generally expand your empire in order to be better than everyone else. I will briefly go through the good and ugly below…
Good; Depp strategy elements, with a good amount of micro-management. Nice set of ways to win other than your standard kill everyone else. Nice detailed tech tree. An “ok” diplomacy section with races not always either agreeing with your or out to kill you because you sneezed a nice balance if you like. Like other endless games you have a nice set of heroes with some minor RPG elements. OK’ish graphics and sound/music.
Ugly; Tutorial was ok but could have been a little more detailed for those not used to these types of games. A major gripe is the combat which is more akin to a card game or none complicated game of rock/paper/scissors than your typical strategy game. Later on in game micro-management can become very time consuming.
Overall I would give it a thumbs up, worth a look on sale maybe not full price considering what you can get nowadays in the same genre.

Crimsonland surprised me with how much fun it actually is.  It is an incredibly simple game in terms of gameplay. Simplicity is a double edged sword, it can be a great element or a terrible one, it all depends on the execution.
Crimsonland is  a twin-stick style top down shooter.  You spawn in a square map, enemies appear from all over and you must kill them all or die.  Simple as that.  There is more added in the form of unlockable weapons, “leveling”, power-ups/drops, and perks.  During each round you kill enemies, gain experience, level up, defeat all enemies, rinse and repeat.  Each time you level you can choose a perk.  Playing the “quest” missions steadily unlocks additional weapons and perks.  Both the weapons and perks are enjoyable and are a meaningful reward for the completion of a level.  There is enjoyment to be had from trying out each new weapon and perk.  Additionally during combat power ups will drop, these are things like temporary shields, health packs, temporary fire/damage boosts, speed boosts, etc. The perks do not carry over from level to level, which I kind of understand.  I think eventually if they did carry over you’d be far too OP.  The drawback is that it can be a bit jarring to go from a level where you’re powered up (and much faster than normal) to suddenly back to zero.  I died a few times on some levels readjusting.  It’s not a major problem by any means, and was the only real issue I have with the game.
Although Crimsonland is ostensibly a generic and basic game, the extra touches in the form of tons of weapons and perks elevate this game above it’s generic base. I highly recommend Crimsonland. It’s a great deal of fun. I would however recommend waiting for a sale. Not to disrespect the devs (in saying they’re hard work isn’t worthwhile) but $13.99USD is far too high a price. Pop Crimsonland on your wishlist and wait until it’s $5USD or less. Crimsonland is great, and worth a purchase, just not at it’s normal asking price. Good luck, may all your games never crash. :D

The combat might not be rock-solid and the individual levels might be smaller than the original Deus Ex.... but all the parts of this game add up to an all-time classic..... albeit one with a tad too much yellow in the color scheme.  The story has enough pull to where you REALLY want to see what happens and where things are going and there are quite a few "Oh ****" moments where things take off in a direction you wouldn't expect.  Some people complain that the lead character is a bit too monotone and flat... but I rather liked him.  A dry but witty sense of humor and a complete bad*** without being tacky or steriotypical.
The game itself is essentially a large number of equations that must be solved and you are given a TON of tools in which to solve them.... but you won't have ALL the tools at your disposal until VERY late in the game.  In the meantime you must carefully pick and choose which upgrades and augments you wish to unlock.  Through Praxis Kits, which can be found and bought, and through gaining experience for your actions and accomplishments, you gain "Points", which are your currency for upgrading your character.  There is cloaking, enhanced jumping ability, enhanced armor, ability to fall from extreme heights, resistance from EMP/electrical damage, silent movements.... etc etc.  In this regard it is very similar to the original Deus Ex.  There might be a few more items in the toolset in the older Deus Ex (Not Invisible War, though.... where you only get the choice of 5 augments out of a total of 15 options) but in the older game you must find SPECIFIC upgrade packages for SPECIFIC abilities.... example- to get Enhanced Jumping you must find a kit that allows you to unlock Enhanced Jumping.  This system means you might not be able to get certain abilities until late in the game.... one of the things I LOVE about Human Revolution is that you simply earn points and then can use those points to unlock ANY Augment/Ability you choose.  If you want to unlock Invisibility first- you can do so.  Or Enhanced Jumping, or Enhanced Strength, etc.  I've played through the game 3 times, 2 on PS3 and once on PC... and have had very different experiences each time.  With different abilities I've been able to find many different ways to get through each part of the game.... my first playthrough I didn't unlock Jumping or Strength until the very end of the game- my last playthrough I unlocked them both as soon as I could- and found shortcuts, secrets, all sorts of cool stuff.  While I found those 2 abilities in particular to be quite useful- each ability can be quite useful in the right hands in the right circumstances.  Some are certainly MORE useful than others, but all have their uses.
This is also quite a long game, especially if you explore, read people's computers/emails, search through the game's hub areas, talk to everyone, do side quests, etc.  My last playthrough was 43 hours and that was with me going all rambo-kill-everyone in the last few areas.  I probably like this game about as much as the original Deus Ex..... if that game's graphics were better I'd put that one ahead by a little bit- I'm not a graphics snob but when it comes to First Person Games I feel graphics are more important than in most cases.
In short- this is a TERRIFIC game.  Great story, very good gameplay, an amazing suite of tools in which to work through the game in wildy different ways.  The combat isn't super-smooth but it is still quite good.... the combat is much improved in Mankind Divided, though.  More and cooler augments, too.  On that note- don't worry about all the people slamming Mankind Divided.... it was a bit sluggish when playing on Ultra- but plays wonderful on Very High and High with the anti-aliasing turned down a few pegs.  Prague is an AMAZING hub, too, perhaps the best I've ever seen in a game.  Many of the complaints about Mankind Divided are from people that, when you distill their comments, are upset that they had to turn their graphics down.  That, or that they don't like some of the DLC offered.  Just read through some of their comments and you'll see what I mean.  I'm only about 12 hours in on Mankind Divided and it's been 12 of the best gaming hours I've ever had.  Unrelated to Human Revolution, I know, but I'm just so frustrated that the current rating for MD is "mixed"- but most of the complaints have nothing to do with the actual quality of the game.  I'm just worried that this will chase off sales and thus hurt the chances of another Deus Ex game.

Highly recommended stealth-action cyberpunk game set in the near future.
The game doesn't outright punish you for going on a killing-spree during a mission, but rewards you for taking a more covert approach. And don't worry about not being able to use your awesome upgraded weapons. You can try them out during the bossfights. Speaking of, the bosses are WAY too easy, even on hard. You can beat most of them within a few seconds.
The director's cut adds a whole new level, introducing a ship and platform for you to sneak around on.
If you're too impatient to sit behind a crate and study patrols, you can easily find vents to climb into that will bring you silently to your goal (and reward you with items and xp)
The diversity in weapons is a little lackluster though, only having 1 in each category: 1 pistol, 1 revolver, 1 machine gun etc, but if you spend your time sneaking through the game you won't really cry out for more anyway.
The soundtrack and overall atmosphere is great, each suiting their level appropriately.
There are also a lot of computers you can hack into and read people's emails, adding to the immersion, as in vampires: the masquare bloodlines.
Actually, this is very much like vampire set in a futuristic sci-fi setting, with even a few parts of the soundtrack reminding me of the aforementioned game.
Overall a very rewarding experience if you're into stealth, cybernetics, conspiracies, and vents (!)

I don't usually play RPGs (the only other one I've played in any reasonable capacity was KOTOR 1, which I still haven't finished), so I wasn't expecting this game to hold my interest. But, 12 hours later, I had spent 10 of those hours completely immersed in the world and story of this game, sneaking through air ducts in an effort to put the entire staff of a police station into a peaceful, collective slumber. Coolglasses McCool (better known by his common name, Adam Jensen), my frighteningly effective (or ineffective, depending on whether you judge by the end result or by the dozens of reloaded saves it took to get that result) corporate loss-prevention agent, made a private laughingstock of the station's security and its officers with nothing but his righteous fists -- at one point even going up against five officers at once. May they sleep in peace. They should all wake up soon, none the worse for wear . . . except maybe that one guy who was dragged headfirst into an air duct. Hopefully someone hears his cries for help before he starves to death. Anyway.
Coolglasses McCool seems to have an addiction to superpowers -- having gone so far as to sell all his weapons save for a silenced pistol so that he could buy more upgrades, and laughing maniacally to himself every time he got another. He may be ever so slightly insane. Still, if buying the ability to jump like you have rockets up your butt isn't the equivalent of buying happiness, I don't know what is. Flinging yourself into the air repeatedly is quite therapeutic. You should try it sometime. Even if you don't have rockets up your butt (although they do enhance the experience).

Crimsonland is an action-packed top-down twin-stick shoot-em-up. You, a single human (or more if playing co-op, which is even more fun),  must face off against thousands of bloodthirsty enemies at once. With the aid of game-changing perks and screen-shaking weapons, you will conquer the levels, only to do it all again on the next difficulty up. And after that, there's an impressive variety of unique survival modes to hone your skills. Crimsonland is one of those games where a level may take 5 minutes, but a gaming sessions last hours.
- Crimsonland 2014 (which has been updated so it's now a 2016 version) is an impressive overhaul of the freeware game Crimsonland. The graphics are scrumptiously HD and there's delicious new graphical effects. Killing the hordes of the enemies results in juicy crimson splatters, which permanently stain the environment. The permanent splatter and corpses allow for an incredible aftermath experience that most games can't even fathom. The glowing plasma is splendid and the ion weapons are stunning. The glows and explosions and colourful effects all add up to make a visually pleasing experience. Amidst all the effects, the actual graphics quality though is fairly mediocre to today's gaming standards. The background environments are vast but bare and bland, and the enemies are uninspired and indistinctive. The visuals of Crimsonland play a vital role for the action, providing a colourful experience, but still lacks in quality.
- The audio in Crimsonland is awesome. As soon as you start the game, you're greeted with the rock (I don't know genres, but I'm sure it's rock) music in the main-menu. The music is intense and gets the blood pumping, puting you in the mood for the massive hectic slaughtering of the impending onslaught. The sound effects provie solid feedback, from the gunshots to the projectile impacts. All guns sound unique, which makes them all stand out. However, the explosions lack proper oomf and the avatar's death sound is hilarious. Enemy deaths are appropriately satisfying and do a good job of letting you know you've killed your foe. Overral, the audio aspect of Crimsonland is pretty good.
- Crimsonland is gameplay-centric. There are many different guns ranging from blowtorches and shotguns to plasma miniguns and missile swarmers. Bonuses drop during gameplay, and these temporarily buff you with speed or fire bullets among others. Beating levels in the campaign unlocks perks and weapons which can drop in any game mode. Contrary to the store page description, there is actually 6 survival modes (the Typoshooter gamemode added in version 1.1.0). Having 6 different forms of survival really improves this game's longevity. However, the classic survival mode is probably the one you will play the most. Crimsonland also includes global leaderboards so you can show off your skills (or your hacks) to the world. This game's massive variety of survival modes is really awesome, and more games should follow in the vein of Crimsonland for this aspect. Survival mode is arguably the prominant feature of Crimsonland, however I believe the campaign is the best bit. The manually crafted levels offer unique scenarios for you to battle through, but even the same level will be a unique experience for different plathroughs. This is due to randomized weapon and bonus drops, and the almighty perk system. Kill enough enemies and you get to pick from 3 perks. They can improve and massively alter the gameplay but they only last for that level. Perks range from standard fire rate increase and reloading time speed, to bearing a contagious disease that slowly kills off enemies. You can get multiple perks per level and there's a massive amount of perks that allow for unique game experiences. Some perks are even multi-tiered, so that means you can get a seperate perk that improves a previous perk. The amount of perks and perk combos means you will be always experiencing new and exciting gameplay styles. Overral, the gameplay of Crimsonland is hell of a lot of fun, and local co-op opens up opportunities for even more fun!
- N/a
- Crimsonland has a couple of graphical settings and minimal options. This game is highly optimized and runs very smoothly even with thousands of enemies on screen at once. I am glad to see this game still receive attention even after its initial release in 2014. Overral, Crimsonland is a perfectly functional game.
If you're looking for crazy top-down shooter that you can play with your friends, then I highly suggest Crimsonland. This game will give you plently of fun and offers many gamemodes for different playstyles.
I give Crimsonland a 6.5/10, great hectic fun, but offers nothing substantial or innovative.

I don't usually play RPGs (the only other one I've played in any reasonable capacity was KOTOR 1, which I still haven't finished), so I wasn't expecting this game to hold my interest. But, 12 hours later, I had spent 10 of those hours completely immersed in the world and story of this game, sneaking through air ducts in an effort to put the entire staff of a police station into a peaceful, collective slumber. Coolglasses McCool (better known by his common name, Adam Jensen), my frighteningly effective (or ineffective, depending on whether you judge by the end result or by the dozens of reloaded saves it took to get that result) corporate loss-prevention agent, made a private laughingstock of the station's security and its officers with nothing but his righteous fists -- at one point even going up against five officers at once. May they sleep in peace. They should all wake up soon, none the worse for wear . . . except maybe that one guy who was dragged headfirst into an air duct. Hopefully someone hears his cries for help before he starves to death. Anyway.
Coolglasses McCool seems to have an addiction to superpowers -- having gone so far as to sell all his weapons save for a silenced pistol so that he could buy more upgrades, and laughing maniacally to himself every time he got another. He may be ever so slightly insane. Still, if buying the ability to jump like you have rockets up your butt isn't the equivalent of buying happiness, I don't know what is. Flinging yourself into the air repeatedly is quite therapeutic. You should try it sometime. Even if you don't have rockets up your butt (although they do enhance the experience).

This game is cute, and definitely has it's pros, but overall I don't recommend it.
The pros:
1. Who doesn't love a trying-to-look-old super pixely game?! I find it adorable, personally.
2. The music just adds to pro #1.
3. The quest-giver dialog is entertaining and worth reading.
4. It's free.

The cons:
1. It's super laggy. I'll click a teleporter and won't go, so I'll think I missed it, move closer and click it again and suddenly I'm thrown into the new world and then back again because I accidently took the teleporter back.
2. Building. It's terrible. I (very accidently) spent 200g on blocks and somehow am still able to walk through the walls of my "home."
3. After the first few quests all you're doing is trying to build, exploring random towns other people have built (good luck figureing out which blocks you can walk on and which you can't), or trying to memorize player-made dungeons so you don't keep falling into the same hidden spike traps.
4. There's other people running around, but other than talking in chat, I haven't found any way to interact with them (ie forming a group to do quests or explore together?). I'm not saying it doesn't EXIST, just that I couldn't figure out how.

The chief theme here will be broad strokes, which is what Prototype has. It's got the framework of a bunch of cool stuff, and it works to an extent, but there's ample room for improvement in everything. Take for example, the movement. You can climb and jump around most anything, and going in a single direction feels awesome most of the time, you can glide and dash and leap to your heart's content. But, if you're trying to get a tricky collectable from atop an antenna or building, Alex will often tweak out and flip over and around everything in sight, and it's quite a job to wrestle him into precise movements. Want to turn left or right? Hope you've got a few seconds cause unstoppable forces don't turn on a dime. Another example: Do you hate collateral damage? Don't even, cause there is nothing you have that won't wipe out a 90 degree arc about 10 feet in front of you at least. You're going to be smashing civvies and other innocents all the time, and the game gives you a nice running total of how many families you've ruined after each fight, so good luck sleeping I guess.
The actual in-game storyline is, nyeh? It's okay, it gives me an excuse to destroy all this junk, and it joins up all these events just fine. There were a couple of standout moments, but ultimately it was pretty by the numbers. It does tend to wrench control out of your hands to show you things during missions, or straight up transport you across the map afterwards, which can be annoying. The Web Of Intrigue though? That's some good stuff right there, loads of dropped hints and filling in the gaps, much speculation and other really cool junk. I spent ages just cruising the city looking for targets cause they were so interesting. Word of advice though, never skip a target movie, cause good luck remembering the name and then finding it in the hundred-something strong web.
Combat: Losing relies chiefly on some very dubious things: Unavoidable chip damage, homing attacks, and super-damaging stunlocks. It's not that it's not challenging, cause you will die if you're not paying attention, but it's really going through the motions of action/reaction to the above three. Some cooped-in boss battles can make the game feel hard, and especially early in the game when you're not very powerful. Oftentimes you'll find yourself cheesing fights by staying on the move and chipping at stronger foes from range, because moving in for actual damage provides them with too many opportunities to stun/grab/hit you and it's not worth the risk. It makes fights more of a chore than fun sometimes, and that's not so great. Health is relatively easy to come by, by grabbing and eating mooks, but it makes every mistake another chore, since everything big hurts you so much you'll have to find and consume 2-3 of the little guys safely before you can re-engage. It skews the pacing and atmosphere of fights quite a bit, and it's often more advantageous to just bug out. Unless, of course, you're doing a scripted story mission or event that requires you to clear an area, in which case hunker down for the long haul. The AI isn't very smart, not at all, but they are numerous and widespread. It's not about outsmarting them, it's about outsmarting the group and learning to play the way they work to your advantage. Stealth isn't, really, but it does what it needs to and works within the larger framework. Many of the stronger enemies are niusances rather than challenges, but again you gain the powers to gib them or to lose them fairly early on, so it's not really too big of a deal.
Speaking of powers, those are pretty cool. You get a bunch of different arms, some defensive stuff, some supports, and they all have a use. You'll probably find yourself favouring one or two though, since there's quite a bit of redundancy between them. I'd have liked to see some more differentiation, but only a small fraction are mandatory so I guess not having everything must be allowed for. There's lots of stuff to spend your money on, special moves for each power as well as ones for plain old fisticuffs, movement and health upgrades, super moves, the store really does overflow with stuff. The movement too, once you figure out how to do it right, it's a joy to traverse the city and the challenges become simple matters of route rather than speed. You can fly and dash and grab walls and leap and dive, there really are a lot of things you can do and that's great. Also, when you enter the power radial selection everything slows down for a second to let you pick, and that's awesome.
While it's not perfect, Prototype has one excellent quality: Not many other games make you feel this powerful, this badass, all of the time. You have a couple of dozen ways to destroy the dude that's ineffectually pinging at you with his rifle, and you have so much health that you can afford to decide. If he brings ten friends, it still doesn't really matter cause you can just nab one and chuck him at the others and then elbow drop the rest before zipping up a building and being five blocks away before backup even thinks of arriving. If some tougher guys decide to chase you, you're stronger and faster than them so just hit them with a ventilation unit and disappear, because you can. It broaches on God Game territory sometimes, but you're running around on the ground being all-powerful, and that feels really good.
+
Fun as all hell
Oodles of powers and upgrades
Feels godlike, man
Options, options, options
-
Poor PC controls
Combat can be cheap at times
Showing it's age graphically
In the end, Prototype was worth the time I put into it, and despite the above tirade, the good outweighs the bad. Much of it is just frustration about what could have been great but ended up being just good. But, that still leaves you with a good, fun game, with tons of things to do and stuff to see, and a lot of extra storyline junk for those interested.

I'll start with the positives.  The ergonomics are great.  The hardware is great and the design is great.  The inclusion of a gyro is great.  The built in mapping software could use some improvements, but it's pretty good and you can map the controller to most games quite nicely.  If the controller lived up to all this promise without any downsides, I would be singing its praises from the rooftops.
Here's the bad: the driver support.  Valve's usual poor quality code with the steam really shows when it's trying to do the job of a driver.  And make no mistake, they are indeed having their 250MB RAM eating, webview laden cow of a game download client, pull double duty as a hardware driver here.  If you quit the steam client, the controller reverts to default mouse emulation with no mapping support.  They could have built mappings into the driver.  They could have given you a standalone GUI app for loading up controller mappings.  Anything to avoid  a quarter gigabyte RAM footprint being mandatory for an input device.  But nope.  Valve don't care.
This would be annoying but tolerable if this behemoth omni-software running the spectrum from device driver to web browser were good and stable.  Oh, if only it were that easy.  The steam controller amplifies the various quirks and bugs in steam's overlay and big picture UIs tenfold.  Let me enumerate some of the bizzaro world bugs I've had to contend with:
- the overlay randomly crashes, forcing me to restart a game before I can use my controller mappings again
- the overlay still works, and I can *look* at the mappings, but they mysteriously don't actually work (falling back to the default mouse emulation mappings) until I restart both the game *and* the entire steam client
- the steam overlay mixes up focus, and sends my keystrokes to the game when I'm typing in a steam overlay text box, making it impossible to chat without screwing things up in game, until I restart both the game *and* the entire steam client
- the steam overlay mixes up focus, as above, but this time keeps focus while dismissed, so that when I try to play my game, it gets no input and instead I hear random steam overlay bloops despite the overlay not being visible.  Until, of course, I restart both the game and steam client.
- the controller firmware hardlocks, so that restarting the game, the steam client, the computer, the dongle, etc, don't matter, until I actually pull the batteries from the controller and boot it back up
None of these are freak occurances.  All five things have happened to me multiple times and across multiple games.  None of this has ever been an issue with any of the other controller mapping software I've ever used, because none of the other controller mapping software relies on a monster internet-connected GUI client and requires a buggy DLL-injection-based in-game overlay to do the simple job of translating inputs to mouse and keyboard actions.
There is nothing wrong with the hardware, and I would love to recommend it whenever the software supporting it is no longer trash.  So far, though, Valve has had plenty of time to demonstrate that once they have your cash in hand for the hardware, they aren't concerned if it works.  There is an open source third party driver in development, and I am eager to be able to revise this review if it becomes mature.
Look I don't know how to be nice.  This has been production hardware for 4 months.  Some day maybe I will recommend the hardware, after third party community efforts re-do a lot of the work Valve should have done themselves, but everybody involved should be deeply ashamed about their willingness to keep collecting so much money for hardware while not caring if it can be stably used.  Only gamers are treated like this.  I don't know where else you can find a product where the driver regularly crashes and makes you restart other programs, and it stays on the shelves.

I received my Steam Controller as a gift, and I really enjoy using it.
The Steam Controller has a relatively long breaking in period. By this I mean that it takes a long time to get over the initial "Ewwww!" that comes with using the device. The trackpads really do feel much different to any controller input method that I have used and feel quite strange.
The haptic feedback feels peculiar due to the fact that it is a little itchy bump type feedback rather than the over the top vibration that comes with other controllers. It is jarring not to have this feedback from a controller as your brain expects there to be a bone shaking vibration coming when you complete an action.
I have no issues with the button placement unlike many other reviewers. I like how out of the way most of the buttons are which means that pressing a button is a deliberate action as opposed to what is sometimes a haphazard mistake. I would like to say however that the buttons feel mushy weak. I refrain from properly mashing them in QTEs as I think that I am going to break them.
The batteries supplied didn't fit, I had to get some other ones instead.
You need a USB 3.0 connector on your computer in order to get the most from your controller wirelessly, if you don't have one then using a wired connection is also a good bet. I haven't noticed any latency issues with my controller.
Configuration is a mess. It is really difficult to configure the face buttons, trackpads etc. I just use a prebuilt config and just tweak it a little.
All in all, the Steam Controller is a fine gadget and I would give it a solid 8/10

After I became an adult and joined the US ARMY (11B) I got more serious about my collection. It was not until I started my own company and could start buying seriously expensive firearms that I really took off.
I ran into a dilemma a few months back. I had my Fully Automatic Browning M2 .50 and I could not get the charging handle to move all the way to the rear. I tried my best to ask around but nothing worked. I was about to throw in the towel and take it to my local gun smith when I remembered that World of guns existed. After going through the in-game play, I found out that it was a simple two-inch piece of metal that I had not put back in the proper place. After talking to the local gun smith. He told me that the repairs would have cost me almost $2,100 because of how much time it would have taken him along with the peace being ordered.
World of Guns is so detailed and in-depth. The developers really went to full lengths to make it as realistic as possible. They must have the actual firearms in the studio to get the attention to detail that they have. I salute the developers for going the extra mile and giving us firearms fans something to be really excited about.

My Name is Mayo isn't great.
I didn't expect much from this game, but for less than a dollar (when 40% off), I bought it hoping for an interesting game with a fairly good story. Unfortunately all I got was half of an interesting game without a good story. The game did make me laugh at some points with it's strange visuals, but the good story I was hoping for? Nothing. All I got was a silly, forgetable bunch of nonsensical stories that didn't intrest me in any way. I think the reason why I feel this way is because I couldn't connect with the character.
In a game about clicking a jar of mayonaise, I found it difficult to conect to the main character, Mayo.
It may sound strange, but have you ever played a story game for the gameplay? I'm sure about 85% of you will say no, you play a story game for the interesting and memorable characters, for the detailed plot. A plot about a horny, philosophical jar of mayo? No. A plot about a criminal named Larson Hoover who discovers he has lung cancer, so he spends the his last 8 months trying to right his wrongs and reconnect with his family? Yes. That's what My Name is Mayo was lacking, a good story.  Does Mayo have a family? Does Mayo have an occupation? Does Mayo have a secret? Nah, he/she/it's just an admirer of bikinis and a nut for philosophy.
So that's my thoughts of My Name is Mayo as a story game. what about as a clicker game?
Awful is the only way to describe it. It adds nothing new to the clicker games. I fact, It took away the only few things that made the clicker games good. All you do in My Name is Mayo is click a jar of mayonaise, and that's it. There are no upgrades, no temporary power-ups, and nothing changes. A good example is Cookie Clicker. For those of you that have played the game, you have probably discovered the "grandma incident". I remember when I got to that moment, all I could say is, "Holy ####, what the #### is going on!?" In My Name is Mayo, nothing like that happens. You just click away and get frequent hand cramps with no changes in gameplay whatsoever. It's boring.
So after ######## about all the bad things, because I'm a glass half empty kind of guy, lets talk about some of the good things My Name is Mayo has to offer.
The game isn't so bad that I want to lock myself in a glass box in front of a kindergarteners and suffocate to death. The visuals and story gave me a small chuckle every now and then and the random facts were fun to read. And I rememer marveling at the amount of time people put into this game to get on top of the mayo clicking leaderboard. That was fun. And... um............ yeah, don't buy this game. Get a gumball with your dollar or something. This game will leave you feeling robbed and unsatisfied.

How does one start, and where do I begin...Well...Lets try the more honed points.
Skyforge is an ARPMMOG (Action Role Playing Massively Multiplayer Online Game) It features relavent playstyles to that of a cross between TERA Online and Riders Of Icarus, two other titles I've played. Both of which feature a non-target locking system and smart spell casting layout that put a lot of stock into hand-eye-coordination and combination abilities. Safe to say, if you have tunnel vision or lack of your surroundings this game may not be for you, but it is pretty forgivable in that sense, so if you have trouble in that area, it's a good game to get training in.
Skyforge features all the works of an MMO and a little bit more; All in all, I gave it a pretty good run and didn't find myself wanting anything more. The Allods Team did a good job with this one.
+++
--PvP/PvE
--Open Area for grinding and questing
--A Campaign and Story
--Several Unique classes, and unlockables
--Free To Play
--Grind isn't overtaxing
--In-Game Store and Cosmetic Items
--Dungeons & Raids
--Guild Leveling System
--Character Leveling System (Might) The more you get, the higher your strength.}
--Multiple Weekly Events
--Garrison type Loot System
--Individual Loot System, No MORE ROLLING!!!
--Great Community and friendly players that benefit from helping others.
--Daily Loot Boxes, Turn-Ins and Bonus Quests
--High repeat-ability
===
--PvP is a bit imbalanced with the item restrictions. Some pieces of a gear are a little silly for certain classes.
--PvP is very skill based, There is always a player who knows more.
--Dungeon Q'ing is non-existent, you will have to find players with the same quest or type LFG (Abbreviation for zone goes here to get invites)
--Some players are Elitist and want quick clear times and don't wait for players, You might want to invest your Argents into a fast 18k Mount.
As a starter player for this game, obviously you are reading this Steam Review, I recommend you get the "Steam New Players Kit" which is a great starter kit, It gives you a bit of premium time which helps you accelerate past the first 30 prestige levels with ease, Prestige is your overrall character level which is gained from collecting items, completing quests and might. Try to be patient with your playthrough and enjoy the wonderful scenery with no framerate drops.
I don't like to tell people too much about the game in the review because it sours a flavor. So I will just pop up and say that this game deserves a bit more attention for it's well organized system.

Skyforge might not appeal to some, but may appeal to others. I came from a MMORPG with many flavours. Jumping puzzles, dynamic events, fractals, raids, etc. and SkyForge, if they continue adding contents to it would be my third major MMORPG. Playing this game for approximately 30+ hours now at level 30+ and here's my initial assessment to it.
// THE PROS
On-demand class switching -- One thing SkyForge caught me is how your character is able to change class on-demand. This is a very interesting feature and in my opinion, it's the best selling point of this game. Instead of creating another alt character, it lessens your time, effort and money to create another one.
Stunning Graphics - I believe the developer has put a lot of efforts on developing the cosmetics of this game. From environment elements up to weapon details are superb, especially with how did they design weapons like the chainsaw greatsword of the Berserker class with fine and elaborate details to it, I'd say they did best here.
Combat effects and animation - one thing a game turned me on is how my character deal skill animation to its opponents. The feeling of the skill hitting the enemy and how both react on that effect. It's not overdo neither underdo. For me it's flawless and has an elegant punch to it. My favourites being the Paladin and Berserker combat animation effects.
Story - I havent heard of SkyForge having a story line-up in it. However since i am new, maybe they've added this recently. I’m surprised how they did the story, it's not as superb but very decent in my opinion. I'm currently in the "Pundits" story chapter and I'm very excited on finishing it.
// THE CONS
Content - The content may seem pretty standard for an MMORPG like this game. I wish in the future they could add some more features that a player can enjoy and have more time to spend with other than "kill here kill there". Other casual features can be added for those casual gamers that dont like too much blood or fighting in the game. The story line is a big start and hoping for continous content addition to this.
Too much repetition of quests - Since in my opinion, maps are limited at this time, SkyForge utilizes the same maps and environment for quests. Though of course, they tweak playing mode my adding flavours to each repeated map/quest with different things to do or get.
Duel Mode - My previous MMO removed this capability and instead auto-balanced the equipment and status in PvP zone. This is to remove abuse of those high level players from those lowbie ones in engaging duel battle. I encountered one or two in the game like they were twice as much levels from me. My wish is for SkyForge not to remove it, but at least equate and balance the level/stat on-the-fly on both players when a duel is initiated, this would give the lower level player a fighting chance on said challenge.
Pay to Win? -- notice the question mark. Some reviews indicate this is a pay to win game. Some say this is a pay to fast progress game. I tend to agree on the latter. Since this is a free game, it's our way as players to shed a few bucks in order to support the developer. They have families too to feed, or bills to pay too as well. :] And imagine those taxes, net fees, etc. In addition to paid voice overs too.
Final Thoughts -- I think SkyForge has lots of greater potentials. The ability to incorporate modern touch and high-tech stuffs to a usual MMO is a big plus for me. Most MMOs are medieval and old fashioned and all of them in the end game would be grind no matter what, but SkyForge has managed to make a non-traditional MMO combined with both worlds in it, and I like it. -- my initial lowbie player review.
Edit:  I wish there could be flight in the future.

MWO is a very enjoyable game - but it is not a perfect game.  So, let's look at the pro's and con's shall we?  (Also, I played on the original launcher and have only recently moved over, so add roughly 150 hours [over the course of about two years] or so to my 'Time Played' count please)
It is a F2P game with good graphics, a stable engine and solid game mechanics - though note that the "Faction Warfare" gamemode is still fraught with problems but is still an enjoyable if sometimes taxing on your sanity.
It is NOT a BattleTech game - though if you don't know what BattleTech is then you might not care.  I care, but it is still a good game regardless of this VERY important misstep.  The game struggles very much with the technological disparity between IS and Clan machines and equipment - this 'struggle' comes from the artificial 'balance' between the two rather than using the already well-established BattleTech rules that this game is based upon.  VERY important misstep.
The player base seems to consist mostly of people who are looking for fun and are willing to help as much as they can rather than to fall under the "Internet is for a**h***s" standard of user base.
The game does rely on microtransactions, packages and other bits of the game that require real money to be used - HOWEVER - I personally have yet to notice any real "Pay to Win" - but the so-called Hero 'Mechs are certainly "Pay for Variety" and "Pay for BattleTech" - in the case of the Yen-Lo-Wang for example.  NONE of this a bad thing, however, as it is almost solely used to pay the company, expand the options for or allow access eariler to players who are willing to pay for that, but does not allow access to things that give the "wallet warrior" any appreciable edge during gameplay.
The META is REAL! - Real BattleTech is better.  I play BattleTech in here, it makes it harder but also gives me satisfaction to use that and kill META users...hehehe.
While the basics of the gameplay are easy enough to learn (keyboard and mouse), they are a bit more complex than a run-and-gun shooter.  More important than twitch shooting (see above for that) is your ability to read situations, plan ahead and keep awareness beyond often what you can currently see.  It WILL take time to learn the how/when/where of its combat, but it is well worth the struggles earlier on.
The best and worst parts of a multiplayer game are the players - what else is new.  No, this is not a contradiction to what I said earlier.  Both are correct and it was worth mentioning twice.  This is a team-based game.  Leave your team or get left behind, and you're life expectancy will drop drastically.  And yes, you will have bad teams, bad luck and bad timing - no honest person will tell you life (or death) is fair.
If you like the idea of using a giant walking tank to shoot up other people in giant walking tanks with guns, lasers, missiles, countermeasures, electronic warfare, positioning and maneuvers - and of course are willing to accept its faults (which you really should IMHO)...
PLAY THIS GAME!

A game that i'd recommend to anyone who likes blowing stuff up.

Now then, where to begin:
TL;DR: get the console versions, the PC port is not good at all, but the game is good.
The PC port is not optimised, so the frame-rate will chug when smoke &/or particle effects are going on, there is no option to play it in windowed mode and the timers in the PC version seem to be lowered for no apparent reason. Many cheap deaths as well from enemies you couldn’t see doing huge attacks. Also the lock-on system is garbage since it only shows priority targets one should remove first rather then what the player wants to target.
All that said the game is good. The different attack styles one can use to kill enemies are really visceral. But what I will praise to the end is the movement system. If you play this game you will feel absolute joy just running amok on Manhattan Isle, mainly just running around like a mad Sonic the hedgehog killing NPCs as you please.
I will say now I haven’t finished the final boss battle. The last segment of the battle is timed and because the timers are lowered on the PC version you won’t have enough time to actually finish it.
So get the console versions: either the Xbox 360 or the PS3 version. The PC I don’t recommend either way. But it’s worth experiencing the pleasure of the movement system alone for the game.

I had a love-hate relationship with the limited inventory space mechanic, and always found myself hoarding grenades, painkillers, and energy bars I never used. The augmentations were so cool that I just had to attempt the game for a second time (in + mode) so I could get more upgrades and try them all out.
If I had one complaint, it would be with the map system. Maybe it's just me being bad at reading maps, but the maps weren't very helpful in my attempt at navigating the hub worlds.

8BitMMO, created by Robby Zinchak aka RobbyZ is a old school styled Free Roam Rpg. 8BitMMO is a game that takes inspiration from many games such as Minecraft, Legend of Zelda, and even Mario. In 8BitMMO you start off waking up in a man's house who is completely aware that he is in a video game by breaking the 4th wall. He sends you off to complete quests in order to just get you out of his house, he references that he has done this multiple times and that strangers waking up in his house has become a common problem for him. This snarky dialogue made me enjoy my first 10 minutes of the game, as it reminded me of dialogue coming from games like Saints Row. I love it when games make fun of the fact that it is a game. Unfortunately after the tutorial this dialogue seemed to cease and enjoyment of my gameplay experience began to decrease more and more. The combat in 8BitMMO is simple enough to play with one hand, with occasionaly reaching for your mouse. Only having the WASD keys for movement and the space bar for attacking made hunting quests and fighting off enemies a bore after the tutorial. There is also another element that makes 8BitMMO a little more entertaining; the ability to build. You are able to build a houses and environments like a top down Minecraft or Terraria. The building can become tedious with blocks stacking not the way you want them to and having a lack of tools to do anything truly spectacular. Although I didnt enjoy this feature, I did see many interesting and cool user created homes and even areas that put the building and combat to good use. The music is probably what I enjoyed most from 8BitMMO, it had beats that went along with the art direction and it had the convenient feature to skip the current song as if i was using Pandora radio. The game does have a leveling system like most other MMO's that encourage you to rank up in order to get certain items or get to certain areas. I have to completely honest and say that I didnt have a great time with 8BitMMO. It is free on Steam and does offer microtransactions, BUT doesnt flash them around begging for money. The game might be fun with a few friends looking to make your own quests and adventures but playing alone is just plain boring.
Overall:
8BitMMO has a lot of great ideas that just dont work out yet. After sometime and update the game can be great. The music fits in with the world perfectly and the combat is a little bland. In my opinion I would like to see RobbyZ create either more content for this game or make more games with the same amount of snark and wit that the tutorial of this game had. I loved the original dialogue and was set to play a game that knew how to make fun of its self but instead, I got a bland and lifeless world that could and should be improved dramatically. And could be alot of fun if your bored with nothing new to play or if you find a group to play with.(Roleplaying could be fun in this game)

Keeping this review really brief...because writing any more about this review is a waste of time.  Game really doesn't have much depth or multi-layered depth.  An example of a game that has multi-layered depth (combines different gameplay/game-mechanical features) is warframe.
Positives..
+Has a good UI for customizing mechs
+Graphics for mechs and Cockpit are done well
+Game runs well
Negatives
-Developer doesn't seem to know what to do with MWO.  They changed Faction play into quickplay mapsmodes, some of which are horribly designed to work for Faction play
-No Salvage system like in other mechwarrior games
-No AI, except for static targets
-Game favors rewards based on kills/damage dealt, versus completing missions.  I thought mechwarriors was suppose to be more than this?
-mission payouts are too low
-very repetative gameplay
In relation to the comments for further reading, more indepth reasoning for the negatives...
Salvage has been in nearly every mechwarrior game in some fashion.  Winning a battle and being able to salvage a mech or being able to salvage parts for a mech could have great feature added to the game.  It might have been outside the scope of the intial developement, but you do get salvage credits at the end of every match.  They could be instead be used for further depth into MWO

Overall when i played doom, both the singleplayer and multiplayer, i vividly enjoyed the experience i had with the game, though it wasnt without its issues like most games.
Pros(singleplayer):
-towards the later stages of the game the enemy variety and count was incredibly enjoyable making many different fights enjoyable to run around dodging claws and plasma
-again towards around halfway to 3 quarters throguh the game the weapon variety left nothing to be desired, especially when unlocking the chainsaw and the BFG
-the modelling and texturing was on point for the game, making everything look great (or bad but in the 'good' bad way) aswell as the gore and dismemberment making the game all that much more satisfying when killing
-in correlation with the gore and dismemberment the different glory kills, mostly, felt satisfying and meaty, especially when later on you can make such things easier or faster meaning you cna just rip through crowds of enemies
-the variety of the challenges and secrets that were scattered through the levels were thoroguhly enjoyable to find and collect, if your someone who enjoys scouring every inch of a level for the last secret you cant find, its for you (though there are also upgrades that help with finding them
-checkpoints are fairly forgiving, so you dont need to replay an entire level if you screw up one jump or decide to give a mancubus a hug
-probably one of the best parts of the game that made it so bloodpumping and enjoyable, the sound design and music of this game made every shot feel ncie and meaty while the background music got me bobbing my head all the way through
-with the addition of arcade runnign through the levels trying to beat your own, your friends and other peoples scores is fairly enjoyable with a few different thigns making it a bit of a different experience to playing the regular game.
Cons(Singleplayer):
-the start of the game can be quite slow due to lack of weapons and enemy types, if it werent for secrets and challanges i wouldve probably had a very boring early game
-if you arent like me and replay levels to find missing secrets and collectables or try to complete all challenges n such, the game can be quite short compared to a lot of other similarly priced singleplayer games
Pros(Multiplayer):
-similar to old games feels very nice and fast paced, spawns being fast (based on gamemode in some cases), running around is a great pace and the maps are really nicely scaled for the pace of the game
-nice variety of gamemodes, though many of them are the basic ones you might find in most other online shooters
-nice variety of maps, in the time i did play th emultiplayer i never particularly got sick of playing any of the maps or got them time after time
-character and weapon customisation is really nice and in depth, though its ashame it uses basic characters for multiplayer
-they recently made the multipalyer dlc free for everyone, so youre no longer locked out of content, thoguh it didnt really give those who had paid for them before hand much compensation from what i remember (though i dont specifically remember everything)
Cons(Multipalyer)
-small playerbase compared to many other multiplayer shooters
-althoguh i dont massivly mind the loadouts for the multiplayer, it would have been nice to have map spawns for weapons instead of them, some people might mind this more than me or not
-i found atleast for multiplayer, there were only really a few different weapons that were worth using, based on the how much range you could get fromt he maps, the rocket launcher and shotguns being one of the most common weapons i saw, seeing very little else
Overall id say that this game is wholeheartedly worth buying for th esingleplayer alone, i mostly view the multiplayer as a nice little bonus though if i were to choose id definately choose the style of much older shooters like the original dooms, quake and unreal tournament as some examples. if i were to give this a number score out of 10 10 being perfect, id probably say a solid 8, could be better but still an amazing game and thorouhgly enjoyable.
