Good idea on paper but the lack of proper support kills it.
To be honest it reminds me of the dark days of gamepad support on PCs before Microsoft standardized it with the Xbox 360 controller. Before that came along there wasn't a common way of doing things on PCs. For example, on screen button icons never matched anything and had generic icons like "1 2 3" that didn't match your controller, configuration was a pain, features like vibration rarely worked, analog input rarely worked etc. Once X360 controller became the standard on PCs, things magically started working. On screen icons matched, analog input worked, every feature that worked on consoles started working. Controllers not working properly on PCs was one of my major problems with PC gaming and that was a thing of the past.
The reason I mentioned "the dark days" is because Steam Controller reminds me of how bad things were. Since almost no games have official support for it, you either mimic an Xbox controller or you go through community made configurations. The fact that you have to this annoys me a lot.
Being able to map it to KB+M sounds neat in but you have to memorize the configurations because you have no way of telling what's what once you're in the game. You pick a popular configuration and go into the game. You start and the game tells you to "Press Space to Interact". You won't have any clue unless you happened to memorize what mapped to the space key.
Let me try to sum it all up with my experience on trying MGS V with it:
- Default configuration mimics the Xbox controller. I started the game and noticed that aiming with the right trackpad is mapped to an emulated right analog stick. It was too slow to aim and way worse than an actual analog stick. It was unplayable.
- I exited the game and checked out user made configurations. There were some that mapped it to a controller and some that mapped it to KB+M. I picked a popular controller config. The aiming was still terrible.
- I exited the game once again and picked a KB+M config next. This time aiming worked the way it should have worked. However, now the analog stick was mapped to WASD. It was not an analog input anymore. Also, in game interactions showed icons like "Press Space" and I had no idea what mapped to what. I'd have had to memorize which buttons mapped to which key to be able to play the game.
- Next, I browsed to see if it there were any configurations that used analog gamepad input and mouse aiming. There were none, because the game doesn't support it. Even with an Xbox controller if you touch your mouse in game the on screen icons converts to KB+M immediately. The game doesn't support a mixed input mode. Basically you either have to sacrifice aiming or analog movement if you want to play it with the Steam controller.
I haven't tried out many games but it seems to me like most official configurations are basically Xbox controller maps.
It actually pains me to see how much effort Valve put in themselves. I've tried CS:GO to see how a Valve game fared. They actually mapped out a pretty interface just for it. What pains me is the fact that no one in their right mind would actually play CS:GO with this controller, because there's no way they could compete against KB+M players because aiming with it is nowhere near as good as a mouse.
I also agree with common complaints people have like the lack of a dpad and an actual right analog. I also think the placement of ABXY on it is bad. It hurts my thumb if I use it for long.

10/10 would buy again.
Although Joy-Stick mouse emulation needs to be worked on so it feels natural for games that do not support simultaneous MKB and Controller input like Skyrim.

Actual controller:
The design of this controller still feels like a prototype. The size of the controller is just a bit too large; I had to adjust the way I hold it in order to get a comfortable grip so I could reach the “shoulder” keys. I’d say I have fairly average sized hands.  The addition of the two grip buttons on the back is a unique addition and works quite nicely. The XYAB keys feel just a bit too small. You can tell they aren’t exactly the focal point of the controller, and I think the Steam Controller suffers by putting them in an awkward area. The right touch pad feels comfortable and smooth. Left touchpad is...it's certainly an enigma. In practice, it feels quite awkward to use. I tend to bind all my less used functions in that area. In honesty, it’s the least appealing part of the controller, and I feel Valve wasn't quite sure how to integrate a D-pad and a touch pad together. When using it, you’ll definitely feel that confusion as well.
Haptics were a big letdown for me. They can be set to three different intensities, which goes from a sensation of light ticking, all the way to rumble. However, it simply doesn’t feel good. Those who are used to haptics on their phone are in for a nasty treat, because that subtle “clean” feedback isn’t present. The audible clicking made by the haptic feedback makes it sound like the controller’s plastic is creaking. The unsavory noise along with the odd origin of the vibrations creates a less-than-stellar result.
The Steam Controller uses x2 AA batteries exclusively. On one hand, it feels like a major step back compared to other modern videogame controllers. On the other hand, there’s never the issue of charging. Also, the batteries last a very long time. No other controller comes close to the battery life here.
Compatibility:
Steam Controllers won’t work outside of Steam games (curiously, you can use it on the Windows desktop and browse the internet with your controller). That’s all there is to it. Personally, I find this a major mark against the controller. Maybe the powers at be will change this in the future, but I’m not counting on anything until that announcement comes, if it does. Be prepared to shell out more money for a second controller if you want to play a racing game on Origin, for example. A bit of googling shows that workarounds can be made with varying levels of success. However its not something Id factor into this review, and it’s likely something you want to spend time thinking about if you want to use a controller outside of the Steam ecosystem.
Configuration:
Almost every game will NOT be Steam Controller ready (meaning, the developers don't have Steam Controller configuration uploaded). This burden falls on the community, where a user can choose from different popular configurations created by others. Luckily, it's easy to browse configurations, see their popularity, usage, and layout. However, every community configuration I've used needed some tweaking to accommodate my playstyle. It's safe to say that you’ll spend a fair amount of time adjusting controls before your specific configuration is modified to your liking. This may also happen over the course of a few hours or days as you play test your design. For kart racing games like Sonic All Stars Racing Transformed, setup was only a minute or two due to the simplicity of the game. For Grand Theft Auto V, the process was about two days as I used it to perform online heists on high difficulty. For Cities Skylines or Civilization games, its servicable but ultimately painful. Some games are always going to work better on keyboard and mouse. The Steam Controller doesn't win any groundbreaking awards in that department. Finally, controller configurations are saved to the cloud, so ideally you’d do this once per game and never again.
It’s also worth mentioning how useful gyro settings can be in some games. You can use your right thumb to flick yourself in the right direction, and then use motion control to fine-tune your aim(in the case of a shooter game). It’s one possibility of many. To further my precision, I have gyro sensitivity to about 1/3 , and only have it activate when a certain button is held down. But again, you can adjust this due to the near infinite amount of settings. Valve really nailed the gyro design. It adds a layer of feedback and control to games, but more importantly, it remains practical to use on a daily basis.
Ultimately, the Steam Controller in its current form will never match the ease of use and simplicity as an Xbox controller. With the former, there is much more tweaking and testing involved. The latter has the added benefit of having identical controls to console games, and “just working”.
Conclusion:
With all its warts, I enjoy the Steam Controller. It's certainly a unique offering by Valve due to its near infinite customization, gyro, and insane battery life. While the software end of the controller is well done, the fact it's limited to Steam will disqualify it immediately to some. Furthermore, the requirement to initially configure (and likely adjust) the controller configuration for each game will turn many away. And finally, the appearance and physical quirks of the controller still scream “prototype”.  That all said, I’d recommend this controller to someone who is keenly aware of its faults, and is willing to play their games in a new and exciting way.

With three games played and considering a fourth, something about it has me hooked, so I guess that's recommendation enough. This game is feature complete and isn't a platform for 4+ years of continuous overpriced DLC, so there's that too, I guess.
This game is the definition of what I think when I hear "Civilization in space," and is just about the same as Civ in how much of a repetitive slog to inevitable victory it is despite its shipbuilding & combat systems, and SUPERBLY crafted factions each with unique art/units/style, backstory, and game mechanics; I fell in love rather quickly. Sadly, as time went on and the veneer of starry-eyed wonder wore off, I discovered that the game ultimately lacks depth, as you end up rushing the same buildings & tech, and falling in line with the same battle strategies regardless of enemy or faction.
The Pros?
+ The Factions. As stated above, it's clear a lot of time was spent to make them all different, with detailed artwork & backstories, unique models for all faction ship classes, and game mechanics. I'm not just talking superficial changes in how they play, either: unique improvements, tech (and a mixup of where certain tech is in the tree), different specializations on your different ship classes, and a specific set of game rules - not just modifiers, but actual mechanics - endemic to each race that attempt to steer you into a particular playstyle with that race.
I mean, this alone makes me start up new games with factions I haven't played.
+ The shipbuilding, the real meat that sets Endless Space apart from many 4X games. The ability to personalize every part of your ships' systems and loadouts really adds a personal touch to your empire, and made me feel (rightly or wrongly) that any combat failures were my fault, that any overwhelming/surprising successes were my doing, and not some dickery of the game. There is no inevitability of overwhelming enemy numbers: as the supposed "weakest" empire in my first game, my 9 little gunboats held the border against the entire enemy armada from the empire with more than double my score, simply by hardcountering its build.
+ The aesthetics. The music definitely fits the whole "intergalactic space empire vying for supremacy" thing, and the map, artwork, ship models and planet models are all still a glory to behold, even after all these hours. It's pretty, I guess.
The Cons?
- You can - and eventually will - be dicked over by the galaxy generator. That's just the nature of the beast, sadly. A crafty player can overcome a bad start position, at least, but if you're looking for a quick game, you'r ebetter off just surrendering and restarting. The AI has deep difficulty in overcoming bad starts; I'm talking entire galaxy arm with less than half of their planets colonized by turn 120 (on normal speed).
- Every faction plays the same. "But what about those different mechanics you talked about?" Yeah, forget it. Notice how I said the different faction traits "attempt" to steer you into certain play styles. Ultimately once you've found your groove and know what works, you'll rush the same techs & improvements every game, regardless of pressure from the game itself to play differently...because there is an optimal way to play, and it just simply works best regardless of the faction.
- Combat is dull; you'll want to just autoresolve about 95% of it when you learn what you're doing. Sure, you can pick formations (which determine what your enemy shoots at) and strategies (which determine what you shoot at), and you can select from certain tactics cards to give an edge in a nearly "rock-paper-scissors" fashion...but ultimately, "manual" fleet control proves useless in a game where combat is just two fleets colliding into each other with no maneuvering, and really only has a use in changing your attack strategy to "guillotine" or "nosebreaker" when things unexpectedly go♥♥♥♥♥♥up and you try to get as much damage done before inevitable defeat. Even battle tactics become trivial after the early game, as you unlock ones that are just objectively useful in all situations.
- The tutorial is objectively♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's pages of text overlaying screencaps of the game, talking you don't understand when you first boot the game. It's 2 hours of reading for an info/text dump that'll just leave you vaguely confused; you're better off finding a friendly FAQ/guide online somewhere...or do as I did, and stumble around in your first game learning as you go.
- The shipbuilding. It is vital, a necessity to know what you're doing with ship loadouts in order to survive, & WILL be the cause of you losing your first games. Also, hard-countering your friends is fun. Being hard-countered yourself is not fun, and will will be the cause of much raging and quitting when your entire armada is slaughtered by 9 piddly gunboats.
Yeah...I think that's about it. Probably forgot something, but that's what I remember off the top of my head.

There are games that you play for fun, and there are games you play for the story. DX:HR is both, offering both an entertaining stealth-based experience and a deep, complex story that examines many social issues and humanity, with intricately written sidenotes (emails, Ebooks, pocket secretaries) that offer a much broader scope of view into the game world than what we see through Adam's eyes. That is the beauty of DX:HR.
Though the endings seem a bit put-together due to the lack of in-game perspective and observation of the ramifications of Adam's actions, they still manage to capture the difficulty of the choices our wearing-sunglasses-at-night protagonist has to face. Deus Ex Human Revolution along with Mass Effect are the two games that change and define my life and my story-writing, world-building know-how.
Gameplay-wise, I have seen and agreed with the mentions that the gunplay doesn't quite stack up to the stealthy approach. What brings out the best of the game is the multi-route, non-linear directions which you can take to accomplish something, which makes the results and consequences of your actions feel both satisfying and devastating. However, the one thing I am absolutely ADORE is the conversation (or more precisely, Persuasion) system. With extremely well-written dialogues, great voice acting and the complexity of how the character handles his conversation with Adam truly show how much effort the game devs and writers truly put into making their final product a true masterpiece.

I’ve been playing Skyforge since it launched on PS4 in March of this year (2017) & have played the PC version (pre-Steam).
When I started playing Skyforge, I can honestly say while it was very fun & addictive the game was an absolute mess. You would be forgiven for accusing the game of being purely Play2Win. However, I must applaud the developers for the improvements they’ve made within the game the past few months & I hope to see it continue.
I started playing online-RPGs as a kid, when Phantasy Star Online was active on the Dreamcast. No game since has scratched that itch in quite the same way. Skyforge comes close though!
A lot of what I liked about the original PSO is present within Skyforge. The simplistic approach of a main lobby or 2, selecting a quest either solo or with a small party, completing the quest & then returning to the main lobby. A selection of classes to choose from & the classes being easily identified by unique features (in the case of Skyforge, it’s the weapons).
The storyline is nice enough. There is a main quest line to follow and additional optional “seasons” that you can do along side it or after that fatten the story up a bit. There are also “open-world” areas for those who like to roam & gather (although the open-world areas are not extensive).
End-game is when the fun really begins (I don’t want to spoil anything so I won’t go into much detail) & the developers try to keep the game fresh with “invasions” that change every 6 weeks or so. There are also 5 & 10 man dungeons as well as a satisfying PvP mode.
Instead of standard experience points – you gather various currencies to upgrade various aspects of your “towers”, fight bosses for equipment upgrades & garner followers on your adventures. This will in turn amass prestige which dictates your character level (it’s not as complicated as I make sound, promise).
Your character build can be altered depending on what “bastions” you choose & what additional abilities you unlock while going through the post-story content. You will likely find a class that will suit your play style but I have to say this is where the game hits a bit of a lull, the class system.
First of all you can change class at any time so long as you’re not in combat (literally, even mid-quest). This is handy for if you’re soloing or in a small party of 2 or 3 players & hit you a wall. You can try a different class to see if that gets you past where you are stuck. However, it causes problems in 5 & 10 raids. You can select your “role” before entering but there’s nothing to lock-in the role you chose! This means you can be in 10 raid full of tanks for example. There are no true healers in the game, the support classes largely providing shields & buffs but they are still as vital as healers in other RPGs There are a couple of “mage” classes that should really have their own category but are shoved in “attack”. They should either be in support or the devs should add a “crowd control” role. It can also be extremely tedious to gather the currency to unlock classes (although you can buy class packs – I don’t see this as P2W personally, it simply unlocks the class).
The combat is fairly straight forward but unfortunately you can’t customise your own palette & some skills are exclusive to soloing or in PvP.. Quests will unlock in difficulty the more you do them.
The P2W aspects really lie in being able to buy the in-game currencies which can be used to upgrade the afore mentioned “towers”, which will in turn level you up. With that said, it’d need to be a HELL of a lot of money & the way the game is designed it’s not really worth it & you’d be more worthwhile going premium, which gives extra currents for killing enemies and completely quests. Therefore, it’s not purely P2W as some folks claim, everything CAN be done in game for free & there’s no real way to “catch up” with those who’ve been playing years or months regardless of how much money you put in the pot.
Skyforge certainly has it’s faults but it’s a nice game & it doesn’t take a powerful PC to run it. If you’re looking for a modern PSO-style game then give it a go.

For a free MMO, this game is damned impressive. The graphics are beautiful, and the gameplay is very action-oriented, containing a lot more depth than hitting hotkeys in a rotation. The story isn't really anything new and exciting, but there's a lot of lore packed into it if you're willing to take the time to look around and read up.
Perhaps most rewarding is the fact that there's no Pay-to-Win structure in place. You can earn just about anything you can buy for real money in-game. You might have a bit of a grind involved, but if you're enjoying the game, that really can't be counted as a negative. The game even liberally hands out 3-day terms of its Premium status for completing various objectives. There are a lot of classes available, and they all play pretty distinctly different from one another. You can also change classes whenever you please (except in combat), so if something isn't working out for the content you're in, you can switch it up and try another approach.
Skyforge is also very solo-friendly, allowing you to complete most missions and quests on your own. There are instanced dungeon-type areas, as well as large open-world maps where you can complete new objectives as you make your way around. You can take the dungeons solo or with a group, and the open-world areas allow you to meet up with other players as you play, so you can play however you want to.
A lot of people will spit venom about
or Allods (a previous game done by these developers), but having played Allods a lot back in the day, I really don't have anything bad to say about them. If you're willing to put time into the game, you'll be able to get whatever you're after and enjoy yourself.

Two years have passed since I picked this up and took a break. I returned to a complete disaster.
Lets take a look at what has changed.
The most apparent change is the abscense of the Ascention Atlas. The one true way to customize your character.
No longer can you focus on attributes that increase your survivability or go all out on critical chance. Your character is as plain as everyone else's.
Speaking of character customization, do you like hunting for items with the perfect stats to match your build? That's a shame if you do, because all items are the exact same this time around. The only difference is the values.
Class customization was considered too complicated as well. Half of all abilities were removed, while others got restricted to use in PvP only. Unlockable class passives are naturaly gone with everything else.
Unlocking new classes wasn't the fastest before, but it didn't rely on uncommon drops that provided 100 resources towards the 25,000 requierment for a new class.
One of the positive things is that the rebalance everyone wanted back then happened... but it's a mess.
No longer you are at the bottom of the food chain and get one hit killed by the weakest of enemies, but instead destroy boss enemies within 10 seconds of a fight, so long as you play Lighbinder, the support class. Yes, the support class has more than double the damage output of any DPS class.
Progression is a complete mess as it expects you to tackle all kinds of content, including daily directives. Problem is, when this travesty occured, half the playerbase up and left. It takes a significant amount of time to find a group for the easier stuff to outright impossible for raids.
At the moment of writing, a demon invasion is happening, which affects what content you are expected to do. Unfortunately for someone starting fresh, this means running missions tailored for max level players. The developers suggest that you join a guild and get carried through it. Maybe I can make a bot to farm credits for me to automate the entire game following that logic.
Out of the completely new stuff that I tackled, there were two zones at the last province which you revisit constantly to progress Bastions (one of the ways to gain pseudo-exp) and they are awful. Giant, empty with a total lack of mini missions found in all other open areas. It feels like these places exist for the sole purpose of forcing you to buy mounts.
Nothing is more pathetic than playing a god that has to rely on some sci-fi scooter to get around.
I know I sunk a lot of hours in despite the state of the game. I'd attribute it to nostalgic value, but I'm dropping this the first chance I get.
P.S. I forgot to mention that one thing actually remained unchanged since then. The notorious bugs such as the audio dieing out and then blasting your ears with random incredibly loud sounds and the good old "fell through the world after loading" hijinks.

A simple sentence to describe this controller perfectly:
Not recommended for FPS games, but pretty good with everything else.
There's a steep learning curve if you want to use the Steam Controller for FPS games like CS:GO, CoD, and even L4D2. There's hardware utilities like the gyroscope and the back triggers that can help you aim and play better, but personally I didn't enjoy playing FPS games with the controller -- even though I've played quite a lot of FPS with it.
The controller works perfectly for any other type of game, though. This includes strategy, roleplaying, simulations, plataformers, sand-boxes, sports, point & click, you name it. I had an amazing time playing games such like Transistor, Bastion, and Dirt 3. Other favorites include X-COM, Binding of Isaac, and Enter the Gungeon (just to name a few).
The controller is built in a way that it allows you to have a firm grip on it without straining your fingers, allowing you to play for hours on end. The two touch pads are absolutely soft to the touch and can simulate a real mouse perfectly. This controller is perfect for couch gaming, no questions asked.
Here's the crux of the controller: The amount of customizations you can choose from. You can simulate absolutely any key in a keyboard with any button in the controller, allowing you to create your very own controller configuration for any game of your choosing. This is not just regular 'key-binding' for a controller, the amount of settings you can bind to a single button is just overwhelming. There's also community templates for the controller settings in case you don't feel like creating your own.
All in all, it's a good controller. Personally not recommending it for FPS lovers. Price tag is reasonable due to the fact of the broad freedom you have when it comes to customization.

This provides absoultely no in-game assistance, but is merely a convienence tool to boost progression (I myself use it as a full time student also working full time with generally only 5 or so hours a week to play the game). Any other core content can be earned. If the childish playerbase took the time to learn the game, understand the fundaental mechanics, they would see the fruit of the game design and enjoy it: the primary antithesis of this is the same as all multiplayer games - the community is short tempered and have a severe misunderstanding of the game. The game mainly focuses on standard "Go here, shoot this stuff" objectives, while also giving you secondary objectives.  There's a balance between completing the secondary and the time-sensitive primary ones.  Also you can play as Gordon Freeman and summon Antlions.  It's not exceptional, but if you like twin-stick shooters, it's a lot of fun.  Protip: Play with a controller.  It's more difficult with mouse and keyboard.

TL;DR:
- If you do random decisions and are unwilling to learn in advance... do not even start this game.
- If you are willing to read all that is below and much more about game, then it may be for you.
- - - -
Disclaimer:
Instead of telling you all the good and bad stuff, You should decide for yourself.
MechWarrior Online has:
- 2 "sides": Inner Sphere, and Clans
- Each side has separate modules and weapons preventing you to install "IS" weapon/module into "Clan" mech
- > So study your 1st mech wisely before you buy it
- There are 2 general types of mechs: Battlemechs, and Omnimechs
- > Battlemech allows player to optimize Everything there is to it except types of weapon slots available on each part of mech (Including Engine power/size, armor type, inner construction material, ...)
- > Omnimechs on other side comes almost allways with most of basics stuff predetermined (Fixed power/size engine, fixed armor type, inner construction, ...)
- > But Omnimech offers ability to take any mechanical part from other variant of given mech (except main torso) and use that. So You can have more Laser slots as you take arm from other variant with lasers instead of rockets.
Progression:
- For playing matches you get reasonable amount of credits which can get you anything and everything in game
- You get XP spendable directly on mech you are playing in match (Unlocks bit higher speed, cooling, rotation rate, ...)
- > Mechanics: Each mech has several "Variants" of chasis with different weapon/equipment slots. 1st Tier of unlocks is available to every mech. 2nd Tier of unlocks becomes available only after you have 3 "Variants" of same mech with all Tier 1 unlocks purchased. Same goes for Tier 3.
- You get tiny bit of global XP used to unlock global pilot skills/mech modules
- > warning: Clan skills are not compatible with IS mechs, so if you go for Clan increased laser range, it will not fit into IS mech with lasers
Size/Speed/Weaponry:
- Huge "Assault" mechs are very slow to move,to turn and can't aim at their feet = Tiny mechs which get to their back up close can eat them if they are not protected. But they carry a lot of armor and often a lot of weapons.
- "Heavy" Mechs are often nearly twice as fast as some Assault mechs in all ways. In some cases they can carry nearly same weaponry as Assault mechs. But always come with lower armor.
- "Medium" mechs are kind of odd in most cases. Even lower armor than Heavies. Speed is often not that much better. Lower weight limit to carry weapons.
- "Light" mechs on other hand are more often than not very fast and hard to hit. This benefit is paid by low armor and light short range weapons.
= = = =
Most important thing:
- 1st steps in game:
- > You read about "IS" vs Clan mechs incompatability. About Omnimechs vs Battlemechs difference. And about need to have 3 Variants of one mech Chassis to fully unlock all passive upgrades for mech.
- > So how to pick 1st mech?
- = > Game offers ability to preview all mechs in "shop" and as you select them, you can go and click "View in Mechlab" where you can completely remove all there is from mech to see how many Tons you have for gear/armor/engine.
- = > You can check what is locked and what is customizable.
- = > You should look at other variants of same mech to confirm that they will be up to your different weaponry/play style choices (as you'll need 3 variants to unlock all 3 passive skill tiers to make your mech awesome as possible).
- > How to buy 1st mech?
- = > 1st 25 matches on account give you credit bonus which is quite nice and this bonus is moltiplied by premium time which You'll get 24hours of at account creation. This gives you 8~12M credits in total.
- = > Basic Training completition gives you additional ~2.5M credits right at start.
- = > Each completed match gives you credits based on your performance/team play and game mode selected. Usually between 0.1M and 0.25M credits.
- = > So after 25 matches you'll have plenty to buy 3~5 variants of Light mech. 3~4 of Medium Mech. 2~3 Variants of Heavy mech. Or 1~2 variant of Assault mech. But that depends on your spending during those 25 matches on different weapons, engines, modules as that can be so expensive that you only got 1 mech and a lot of weapons you can't use at same time. So spend wisely.
- = > Or you can buy Mech for real world money to support game.

- Buying mech for Credits in game is instant. Buing for real world money from steam/webstore gets you your new mech on full hour. So buy 12:05 and you'll get your purchased mechs on 13:00.

The game's objective is easily outlined and aptly described by its title:
You have a gun. You take the gun apart. You put the gun back together.
It begins with a field strip. Then a disassembly. Then a reassembly. The game holds your hand at that stage, so you get a rough idea of where you're going.
Then, after getting a run through how to work the gun, you get the Game modes, playing against the clock and your own ham-fistedness, trying to achieve a high score.
New guns are unlocked via experience points, which are effectively available infinitely, and with credits. A single credit is earned when you first reach the top spot in the leadboards for a gun. This means that there is a finite amount of credits to be had, and their spending should be well-considered.
Of course, there's another way to get credits and EXP, and that's where the microtransactions come in. I've not personally done this, but you can buy credits and EXP for real money. It is not, however, necessary.
As for the gameplay itself, it is for the most part fairly solid, though often overly particular about which bits can be taken off the gun at which point in time. Figuring this out is solely a matter of repetition, yet often a source of frustration. It's an incredibly grindy game, no two ways about it.
And I, personally, adore it. After a while I decided I'd be a good little blighter and give the devs some money as a show of support, so I bought the car pack.

I bought this game since it was on sale for $5. After playing it for about an hour, I really like this game. It has a GTA-ish vibe to it since it is set in NYC. It features several Landmarks bubbles that when you collect, give you points to spend on decking Alex out with upgrades such as sneak cloning and a huge defense shield. Although this game is really fun to play, I do have some cons: To start off with, when trying to be stealth you're not exactly disguised as police officers and such will act "suspicious" several times my cover will be blown and then I have to run away for a short amount of time. My only other con is that Alex sometimes can move a tad too fast as if you try climbing buildings and such, you can fall off by accident due to how fast he is. Still this is game is a HUGE pickup since it is for sale at the moment. I always want to mention, controller support is AMAZING. All you do is plug the controller in and you're good to go. Someone asked me if this game is hard to run. My answer is NO. My fav game so far. Very nice gameplay and balance between mechs. It's not just about twitch reflexes and tactics. You also have to strategize a bit. There are four different mech categories ,namely light, medium, heavy and assault. They all offer different playstyles so you can really find your particular one and enjoy it.
This game is not pay to win, infact the best competitive mechs are of the standard versions that are grindable ingame for free. There are plenty of events that reward players with random items, c-bills and even MC, all year round.There are five game modes, domination, assault, conquest, escort and skirmish. There are also two additional game modes in faction play, scouting and invasion.
The game is so much fun once you master the workings of it. That might take a few days or a couple of weeks, there is a little bit of a learning curve but not too terrible. The matchmaker is pretty decent and it matches you according to your tier. There are five tiers with tier five being the rookie tier and tier one the highest. Depending on how good you perform in each game you will fill the tier experience bar and when it gets full you advance to the next tier. This takes longer the higher the tier is but it solely depends on your performance in a match, for example, even if the match is a loss you can still get positive tier progress. So the game does not punish you for having a fail team.

Skyforge like any other mmorpg would ultimately be a grind but that is to be expected. Its a struggle sometimes but the end level brackets (140 to 160 rank) do make you feel really strong and powerful which ultimately is all that matters. The reward is good at the end and you feel like the time spent getting there was well worth it.
The idea is to make friends, join a good pantheon and get youself to the top ranks where you can participate in the end game content. The end game invasion keeps rotating every 1.5 to 2 months so the content is always fresh. Well atleast for someone who is new. If you play through all the invasions and complete all the distortions only then you can say I have done and explored everything and now i can move on to another game. But for people writing reviews with less than 100 hours into the game are not giving you the full picture. Would you listen to the endless negative reviews or think about those of us who are still playing ?...some even more then 2 years.
This game can be played by putting zero dollars into it, the difference between a premium and non premium is only a little matter of time. Sure maybe the top premium rank person would be 2 months ahead of you....so what. If things were too easy then no one would stick around to stay. Besides that the game does reward a lot with events, you can spend a month farming your credits and then comes an event and you get easy rewards because you saved all the credits which were useless anyways besides putting them in events. Since i have joined, it has been over 4 months and I have collected a lot of freebies from events. So it doesnt make you feel like you have to purchase anything with real money.
The P2W elements are there somewhat but its more like a rich guy has to put an insane amount of money to get quick progress (There are limitations how much you can progress per day). You really dont need to progress that fast. Yes i have put money in the game and I am premium rank 8 as of now but i got my friend to start playing and he is a 100% f2p player and he reached rank 143 (max rank now is 160) in 1 month by focusing on prestige boosting activities only rather than wasting time in anything else. He even managed to save a lot of credits to complete one page of event and get all the rewards. So if a f2p player can do it then anybody else can.
Play and learn everything about the game, get better, master all the classes, get all the top gear and do the distortions. Without this, you havent seen skyforge.
Dont let all these negative reviews discourage you. Whatever it is, the game is surviving well and there are many players and we are doing a lot of stuff and enjoying ourself daily. So you decide, Play or Not your call :)

Endless Space is a pretty sweet strategy game. The gameplay options for customizing the maps, factions, and play style are plentiful and varied. One complaint I have about the game is that the games themselves are slow paced and quite lengthy. Also, in terms of the 'Emperor Edition', I'm not sure of it's value. Please don't buy this game, play it only for a couple of hours and then toss it with a bad review. (I almost did that) It takes a bit of learning... (probably not unlike the VERY first time you tried Civilization) But it's worth giving it a full playthrough as a race and then trying again with the same one. Once you get the basics, swap to another race and prepare for a whole new game. Each race has different perks and some have different improvements (not unlike Civ). But the best part is that the tech tree is slightly different for each race to capitalize on those perks.
For example, one race has a buyout bonus. Then through research they can gain money (dust) by killing enemy ships and build unique improvemnts that rake in cash. Then you can basically not worry about long build times because you can just buy everything in one turn!
The diplomatic system can be frustrating at times... not being able to declare war for a certain number of turns after a ceasefire or peace agreement. But the "Cold war" aspect is pretty neat.  Another drawback is that sometimes the AI will make stupid decisions. "Sure i'll give you the REST of my planets for a ceasefire..." or "I'm about to capture half of your planets in the next turn but ok... I'll accept this ceasefire for nothing in return."
The battles can be repetitive, but you also don't need to watch em...(there's an auto button that skips straight to the outcome... takes 3 seconds) And it's fun to watch the battles that you deem worthy. Watching 15v15 is almost as cool as watching 4v4 with capital ships!
In sum, it's a great game... give it more than just one shot. If anything it'll give you something to look forward to in the upcoming sequel!

Firstly, the context of my experience with this game. I bought the four pack for myself and some friends. My first playthrough was with one buddy and we played through all nine missions over two nights on the medium difficulty without much trouble. Next we will do the hardest difficulty and we will try the DLC which we immediately bought after our first playthrough. Eventually I will get two more friends on for this game and probably play through on solo as well.
Secondly, the positives. This game is simple fun. The basics of the game are: an arrow points towards your mission objective, you follow the direction the arrow is pointing and blow ♥♥♥♥ up along the way. The mechanics of the game make it easy to play so you can enjoy the action and focusing on not getting killed.
The story and cutscenes are hilarious and enjoyable. Never once did I find myself saying, "Oh no another cutscene." Infact it was the opposite. I truly enjoyed every single one. Bryant is a badass. The ending to this game is, in one word, AMAZING. Best ending ever? Probably.
Thirdly, some comments in general. At first I had some issues with the controls. The default controls are set up such that W moves you towards the top of the screen, S towards the bottom, A to the left, and D to the right. This is really counter intuitive. Luckily there is an easy way to change this. Simply turn on tank steering in the options. Once that option is enabled W moves you forward, S backwards, A turns to the left, and D turns to the right.
Some have criticized the mission timers that appear occasionally when you are playing. I am unsure why they find these unenjoyable. Firstly, through my entire first play through I think I saw a timer maybe 6 times. This game isn't about exploration. It is about fast-paced action. You get more points for doing more damage in a short period of time. You always want to be moving forwards to the next objective. Not to mention the fact that the timer isn't arbitrary. It is usually tied directly to a mission objective. IE Destroy the tanks before they reach the town. The timer was never a challenge for me, it was more of a reminder to get the primary mission done.
Finally, the negatives. I found the game quite easy. Dying wasn't really a punishment as you just respawn a short distance from where you died and lose some of your power ups which you can quickly reclaim. During my entire first playthrough I did not get a game over once and did not struggle at all to do things within the time limit. The game being easy had the benefit of allowing me to just enjoy the action and story of the game. In short it was a nice casual playthrough. I hope the hardest difficulty puts up a good fight.
Also, I would say the game is too short. I am not saying the game is not worth the money, far from it. I got my moneys worth out of this game. I just wish there was more. I wish there was more DLC and more missions. I wish this game wasn't over so fast. I wish there was more story and more Bryant. I would follow that guy into hell and back.
So that is my review of the game. I hope you find this helpful.

If you love puzzles, this is the game for you.
If you just love shooting things, this is probably not the game for you.
The basic premise of this game is simple... dissassemble and reassemble every kind of gun imaginable. From notable historic models, to modern military pieces, even a few vehicles, and some skeletons, this game has a lot to offer anyone who loves fiddling with intricate models, and looking at how things work.
It's got a few negative quirks, though. As others have noted, the game is very unforgiving to those who don't want to pay for microtransactions. If you're just a casual player wanting to look at all the different models, expect to pay a lot.
Even if you're really into the puzzle aspects, expect to throw down a few dollars on occasion for that really nice model you want to try out.
Another negative is the inconsistency between models. Some models will require you to pull apart every single little screw, bolt, flange, and spring. Others will do most of the detail work for you, dissassembling large amounts of items with one click. It can be especially frustrating when trying to get the higher difficulty achievements, to figure out just how much attention to detail a specific model wants you to have. Planning and memorization are key.
If you like puzzles, though, and aren't afraid to shell out a few dollars now and then, pick this up. You'll be engrossed pretty quickly, I guarantee.

Now then, where to begin:
TL;DR: get the console versions, the PC port is not good at all, but the game is good.
The PC port is not optimised, so the frame-rate will chug when smoke &/or particle effects are going on, there is no option to play it in windowed mode and the timers in the PC version seem to be lowered for no apparent reason. Many cheap deaths as well from enemies you couldn’t see doing huge attacks. Also the lock-on system is garbage since it only shows priority targets one should remove first rather then what the player wants to target.
All that said the game is good. The different attack styles one can use to kill enemies are really visceral. But what I will praise to the end is the movement system. If you play this game you will feel absolute joy just running amok on Manhattan Isle, mainly just running around like a mad Sonic the hedgehog killing NPCs as you please.
I will say now I haven’t finished the final boss battle. The last segment of the battle is timed and because the timers are lowered on the PC version you won’t have enough time to actually finish it.
So get the console versions: either the Xbox 360 or the PS3 version. The PC I don’t recommend either way. But it’s worth experiencing the pleasure of the movement system alone for the game.

I've been using an Xbox360 controller for several years and decided to go with the steam controller because I've never liked aiming with the 360 controller. Games like GTA5 and Watchdogs 2 I use the 360 controller for driving, but always find myself setting it down and grabbing the keyboard and mouse when it came time to get into a firefight.
I got the steam controller a week ago and like many people, I initially hated it. After the first hour of using it I thought it was a mistake buying it. The button placement felt akward. I kept hitting the wrong buttons because they were laid out so completely different from what I've been used to for years.  I couldn't aim much better with the track pad on the steam controller than with the stick on the xbox360 controller. It just felt completely akward. Like trying to write left handed when you've written right handed all of your life. After the first hour of using it I put it down and thought I would sell it. I didn't think I would ever like it.
A funny thing happened. The next day I picked it up again. It still felt akward. I still kept hitting the wrong buttons. I just plain sucked using it. I still didn't like it.  But I noticed after another hour of using it, I was getting a little better using it. I noticed that I didn't put the controller down to grab the keyboard and mouse during shootouts as much. I was still crappy, but already I could aim better than I could with the 360 controller.
The 3rd day I had it I watched several youtube videos explaining the software for the steam controller setup. The one I found most helpful is called  "Deciphering the Steam Controller Software (In-Depth/Very Long Video)".
It's about a 10 minute video that goes into all of the settings in detail and what they actually do.  I learned a lot about what this controller can actually do and how much I'd been missing.
With that new found info, I spent an hour just tweaking my settings for Watch Dogs 2. What an amazing difference. There is so much customization that can be done.  Being able to set up activators (multiple uses for the same button).  Long press does one action, double press does another, single press does yet another), gyroscopic aiming, mode shifting and so much more. It made a huge difference. Immediately I saw much better results.
So now, after a week of using it, I have played exclusively without using the mouse and keyboard at all in Watchdogs 2. Something I could never do with the 360 controller. I LOVE this controller now. I'm still getting used to it, but it's already comfortable to me and I'm miles better aiming with this controller than the 360 controller.  I'll start adding in other games as I get more comfortable.  Playing a First Person Shooter with a controller is now actually a reality for me. I'll be ordering a steam link next week so I can play from my couch on my new TV.
Bottom line thoughts:
If you buy this controller, it will feel akward, unweildy and clumsy at first. You WILL get frustrated. You WILL want to throw it against the wall. STICK IT OUT.  It's because you've been using other controllers for so long, you've built up muscle memory to that controller. Keep using it, learn the settings and tweak them to your preference and you will amazed at how much better this controller is than anything else on the market.  I HIGHLY recommend the steam controller for PC gamers.
Edit: So almost a month later and I have completely adapted to using the steam controller. I've now moved on to playing my entire library of games using my steam controller. Even first person shooters. It's fantastic!  I've bought a steam link and have been playing my entire library from my living room couch.

Crimsonland is a simple game. A topdown arcade shooter fending off hordes of enemies with all the old-school trimmings: weapon pickups, score modifiers, bonus powerups, and generally being pretty bloody difficult. I assumed that I'd pick it up for a few hours, get bored fairly swiftly and face a bit of a grind to reach the end of the game. Surprisingly, despite my general disdain for wave-based shooters and zombies, this didn't happen.
There are two chief game modes - Quest is the 'story' mode, with sixty missions varying in difficulty and enemy types, and the progression through the game felt fairly natural. It's worth saying that this mode DOES have perks; in all game modes, you unlock perks within each level as you gain experience via slaying and wanton destruction. In earlier versions of the game, they weren't present, but have since been patched in. The perks and weapons that you unlock are varied and random, which lends plenty of replayability to each mission. One run you might open up with a Gauss Shotgun and absolutely massacre the opposition, and the next you'll be sprinting away wielding your piddly Blowtorch. Add in different enemy types, three different difficulties and the added lure of completing each mission without being hit, and there's plenty of content there.
Survival Mode is the other chief enterprise, and other modes come under this banner too, as you unlock them. This is a true arcade experience - you're just out to live as long as you can, and take as many abominations as possible with you. It gets very difficult very quickly, and you'll need to be more than just a decent shot to survive. Strategically strafing around the compact map towards powerups is a must, otherwise you'll be cornered and devoured before you know it.
Ultimately, the visceral gameplay is what underpins everything, glues it together. The visuals and audio are bland, dull, functional; the story nonexistent,  But it's damn fun to use all the different weapons, to repeatedly (but not mindlessly) butcher wave after wave of meatbags. I found myself wanting to come back to play a few more rounds, just for the satisfying feedback I got from using the weapons - I feel like the sound effects must have played a decent role in this.
It isn't perfect, and it won't be for everyone, but Crimsonland is as fun as hell. Hardcore and Grim difficulties await you beyond the main quest, and you even get the original Crimsonland (dated, but still fun) to boot. Pick it up at 75% off or better, and you're golden.

Crimsonland have like 60-stages campaign, stages that are repetitive, but not mindlessly. Cruising through each almost identical looking level are teaches you the finer points of Crimsonland's brutal risk and reward centric combat, which can in turn be parlayed into its many score based challenges. At the end of each level, you'll unlock a new perk or weapon that can be used while chasing high scores on the leaderboards. You might want to jump right to the leaderboards from the word go, but that'd be a mistake. Everything you need to learn and earn rests in a campaign. This is awesome, since there's a reason to play everything.

AMAZING GAME. (Possible spoilers)
While this game has faults, all in all, it was amazing. A fun, gripping and thought-triggering game.
Some cons i found were:
a) There are no cons to sneaking or alternatively, no pros for going loud and murderous. For instance, the most you might get from killing a room of guards or the like would be a little bit of ammo.. which you already used to kill them.. So unless you want to release some pent up anger, going through vents and hacking into rooms are the most logical solutions
b) Incomplete character finales. What happened to that police guy who you gave a job to, or what happened to Megan Reed? She just buggered off to god knows where.
c) Low character depth with Jensen and the people he interacts with. I particularly enjoyed the interactions with Pritchard and Malik but hardly any of their character personalities were revealed.
d) Too many explosions and fights. Much like with the Bioshock Infinite game... there was just constant fighting... Don't get me wrong, i understand that it's a fighting game, however it would have been better to have deeper conversations. You can get the persuasion aug but that's just manipulation and you barely find out anything useful about the characters you interacted with.
e) The guns that were used for stealth take outs were... boring.. AOE cannon stun, tranquiliser or a stun-gun? Wow.. In this regard, and the stealth and no violence, i think it's alike Dishonored. Limited ways of no violence while really interesting ways to kill people. I found a Laser gun that was so fun and i upgraded my revolver to 1 hit everything besides bosses with explosive rounds... barely had a chance to use them unless taking out robots.. In the end, i just went ham and blew everyone up with my large arsenal of murderous weapons but it was just a lost oppertunity to do something spectacular with the creativity invested into this game.
d) The very expected twist at the end. Don't get me wrong, i liked it.. but it would have been nice if it wasn't so obvious after you listened to the news where Eliza interviewed Darrow how he came up with this too good to be true solution for global warming.. I loved the aspect of human nature constantly interwined with the story just.. it came off a bit... lame in the end...
e) The Irish dude and his hidden associate. Like.. what the fudge happened to them? They made the plot that was starting to go a bit stale, entirely swing back into "oh yeah i can probs play this game for about another 40 odd hours" and then they're never mentioned again.... Like.. ??????. I don't know if they are included into later games but that's really a let down.
Now that's done.. time for the pros:
EVERYTHING NOT MENTIONED ABOVE.
BESIDES THOSE FEW POINTS, ITS AN AMAZING GAME. FULLY SUGGEST GETTING IT. 8.5/10. I'm going to replay it again a few times after i forget parts of it and just go full serial killer and other things.

This is, without a doubt, one of the greatest games in existence.  Now, I don't know what's up with my playing time counter up there, but I assure you it's wrong.  While I've only played through the Director's Cut version of the game once on PC (also once on PS3), I played through the original at least half a dozen times.  It really IS that good.  The only con I have against it it is that, as good as it is, it's not as good as the original Deus Ex, surpassing it only in graphics.
Deus Ex: HR is a first person stealth/action RPG.  The key word here is choice.  Pretty much every choice you make has a consequence that changes how the story plays out (save for the endings, which are chosen at the last stage) and how your character develops.  The game pretty much allows you to play it how you prefer.  Whether you want to go guns blazing, move like a ghost where no one can see you or just knock out everyone you run into, you can.  Though there's no denying the game rewards slightly better a stealthy approach, anything is possible.
The cyberpunk sci-fi futuristic setting is gorgeous.  You play as Adam Jensen, an ex-cop whose body is brutalized in a terrorist attack and ends up having to be turned into a cyborg to survive.  Augmentations, as the game calls them, are both popular and hated among the populace, but Adam's are bleeding-edge tech that allows him to do stuff normal people can't, like punch through walls, turn momentarily invisible or be inmune to toxic gas.  I really can't say much without ruining the experience, so I won't.
If you've only played the regular version and want to know what the Director's Cut does, is this: it makes the previously terribly snuck-in boss battles being able to be won without the use of guns, it integrates all DLC right into the story and it corrects a few bugs, while very slightly improving the graphics.  It's the perfect DE:HR experience.

I just beat this game in it's entirety in the last half hour. My finger hurts, but I don't regret it. My Name is Mayo is a completionist's wet dream, but it's also decently entertaining.
.Premise.
This game is about a jar of mayo, as you're likely aware. The "story" is presented in a series of unlockable achievements, both in game and out, and there are a handful of different ones to click through. Fulfilling the clicking requirements for one
.Game play.
Click. Click for your life. You can cycle through the achievements in order to get more achievements, which also result in a Mayo costume change. Then you click some more. Both the costumes and the story itself are funny for their shock value and off the wall...ness.
.Soundtrack.
Eh... I didn't pay too much attention to it over the 'clink, clink' of tapping against a simulated glass jar.
.Graphics.
It kind of looks hand-painted, which is nice. And a few of the props actually moved around.
.Price.
For a game with absolutely no longevity, I'd say I can't complain about the $0.59 price tag at launch. 1.00USD is a little steep, but that's up to you.
Bottom line: it's amusing and clever and I'd love to see a less casual game from the developers. Definitely worth a look if you have some time to kill. When else are you going to see Mayo in such a sexy state?
My only complaint is that I ran out of funny story achievements and costume changes at around 5000 clicks, which left a solid 5000 clicks for completion without any added silliness.

Range Rover. Check. Mounted .50 cal machine gun. Check. Even bigger gun ready to spring out of the boot. Check. Driver's name is Gunnar. Check. Why hello there "Expendables, the game." , how are you today? No, I'm not confusing the games here, this is the game that the Expendables license should have been slapped on, it has everything you could possibly want. Big over the top villains, a thoroughly ludicrous story, a main protagonist so masculine that you will feel testosterone seep out of the monitor, and a crew who either should be skydiving, in jail, or both.
The game runs incredibly smoothly, even when there's a lot going on, and there's enough graphical whizzbangery combined with the over the top explosions (yes, everything blows up, and blows up spectacularly) that you'll feel like you just took a seat in a movie theater to be greeted by Sylvester Stalone and Jason Statham fistbumping. The music is nondescript, it serves mostly as a backdrop for the constant sound of your guns going DAKKA-DAKKA-DAKKA. The story is paper thin, but let's be honest, if you're considering this game, it won't be for the plot.
What's on offer here is straightforward, to the point, and does what it sets out to do with aplomb. It's entirely brainless and a great way to kill an afternoon.

I just want to disclose (primarily to the company) that I'm aware I don't have that high of rep with them after some words were exchanged between me and them . They could tell me repeatedly that this is the same game as the one that was greenlit and I still wouldn't believe them.
However, despite the relationship in question not affecting my opinion of the game, some of you will probably be aware I didn't like this studio's first game "Kimulator: Fight For Your Destiny" and to this date, I still believe it to be one of the worst games on Steam. Now my opinion of Zombitatos is a bit different to my opinion of Kimulator. There are parts of which Zombitatos improves on Kimulator and there are also parts of it which make it worse.
Gameplay is probably the worst part of Zombitatos, Zombitatos consists of 1 point and click segment which is about 5 minutes long and then the entirety of the 15 minutes of other gameplay is simply choosing from a list of choices to make. And yes, you heard me right, this game is only 20 minutes long. That means you can play it, see everything and still get a refund for the game for the £1.59 price tag on it. Say whatever you want about Kimualtor, at least it had more overall content than what Zombitatos has and it also had more variety, which is bad for a game that seems to promote it's self of being a "choices matter" game. The choices in the game consist of only 1 right choice and then the rest of the choices just lead to death and you have to sit throught these painful FMV segments over and over again, just to get back to your original point. Also, like I said before, the game only has 1 point and click segment and your only goal is to go into a room and pick up your password for your computer. BMC, a bit of advice, if you're going to make a point and click adventure game, add more point and click segments, what you have is a game with 1 point and click segment and the rest of it is a visual novel with some really bad jokes. The jokes are both bad and forgetable, and like what happened in Kimulator, an offensive joke is put in saying that at least their game was "better than 9/11." I'm not sure if it's just my style of humour or if people actually find that sort of thing funny, but I fail to see how 9/11 is funny, I also fail how to see how the holocaust is funny.
Also, even though you're making a comedy game, you still have to have some sort of actual logic to apply to what it is you're creating. Like I said before, you have to choose from different options and only 1's right and the others lead to death. Basically, because of the lack of logic shown to you of what might actually work, it's nearly impossible to get through the game without getting something wrong.
For example, one of the choices was "Sleep" or "head to a gaming convention" At the beginning of the game, it's revealed by the narrator that it's gamers that are affected by the zombie apocalypse. So by normal logic, the gaming convention would be a bad idea because it would be full of gamers (zombies) but gues what? That's actually the right choice. Sleeping, an innocent need that you have to fulfill leads to death, however heading to the outside of a gaming convention, possibly full of zombies/gamers leads to success. That's what I'm meaning about applying logic to your game, you need to actually have reasons of why this would occur in the world you're actually trying to create. If you're aiming to create a comedy point and click game, then do soemthing like what game slike Day of the Tentacle, Grim Fanfango and the Secret of Monkey Island did, create bizarre solutions to the puzzles that make you laugh, not necessarily laugh out loud but so that the writing of the puzzle is clever enough for you to maybe chuckle a bit. The issue that Zombitatos has is that the humour is forced and unfunny and always has a confusing centerpieces of the humour it's self and the only puzzle of the game is literally going into a room and picking up your password.
One thing that I'll give Zombitatos over Kimulator however is that it's at least consistant (or at least more consistant) than what Kimulator did and I believe that this is due to the decision to make the game entirely FMV instead of cutting to FPS moments. Now this decision has both good and bad things to it though. The thing with Kimulator is that the FPS segments was basically the only form of slight entertainment in the game. With Zombitatos, despite it being more consistant, is much more boring. At least in Kimulator you were actually doing things, Zombitatos is basically just a huge bore-fest.
The one full praise that I'll give Zombitatos however, is the main theme. It's annoyingly catchy and I couldn't get it out of my head, so music is pretty decent in it.
Overall, Zombitatos is an unfunny, forgettable and boring point and click game by BMC Studio.
Pros

Cons

- No logic to it
- Dead end choices
Final verdict: 2/10

This is my first Naruto game ever, and I have to say I enjoyed it quite a bit. The game has plenty of content, it was nice to relive the war, and the adventure mode provided some new experiences of the story. I did have a few issues with the game though, specifically slow downs due to FPS drops. I highly recommend that you check your PC specs with the one listed in the store page, prior to buying this game, especially if you want to play in the 60fps mode. If you do encounter such as issues, the common solution is to turn off aliasing in Naruto, and enable it via Nvidia Control Panel (or Catalyst). Make sure the game is running with GPU and not your iGPU, especially if your a laptop user. For desktop users, changing your 3D settings in Nvidia to preferring high performance, will be very beneficial for the 60fps mode. Other than that, lets get deeper in the review.
Pros:
•The story mode covers about 5-8 hours worth of gameplay, with very fun boss battles.
•Adventure mode adds a new variety with free roaming, questing, and allows you to experience things not seen in the Shippuden anime.
•VS has many options that will keep you enaged, from survival matches to local 1v1 multiplayer.
•Fluid controls and mechanics
•Tons of content
•Has different cinematics, from stand still images of the show in certain scenes, to recreated scenes via the game engine.
•Character interactions in a fight, is pretty entertaining, some character react uniquely to others.
•Has a huge roster of characters to choose from, and with team based gameplay, the amount of combinations is huge.
The game has so much content, that it would be difficult to blow through it quickly. The story mode allows you to relive the events in the anime, while the adventure mode brings you to experincing the Hidden Leaf and many other locations across the world. Across the adventure mode, you will find plenty of sellable items that are used to customize a character. For VS, you have the ability to enter tournaments, or survival matches, where you can choose your own team and go head to head with other predefined teams, or 1v1. However, there are some bad points to this game.
Cons:
•As mentioned earlier, this game does suffer from slowdowns if the fps drops.
•Performance isn't quite good to begin with.
•Lip sync is horribly off for dub.
•Like the anime, too many flashbacks. I wished Adventure mode would be new stories, but most of it was flashbacks.
Aside from that, the overall content is bountiful and the replayability is extremly high. I highly recommend getting the "Road to Boruto" dlc, as it expands on the Adventure mode, by offering more new stories and relives the movie.

Not going to lie- this is a pretty awesome game. At first I was skeptical due to the fact that you have to pay 50 dollars to buy all the guns unlocked, plus 10 dollars for the gun range. Because of this I thought the "free" really meant "demo," which after playing the tutorial I found out it wasn't a "pay to get more play" game. Instead, you gain experience from doing certain things to the original gun you get such as disassembling, assembling, and time trials. These activities merit you experience with which you can aquire more guns. The second gun you get, the Colt, is about 2,000 experience, so after you do a few tasks for the tutorial you will have just enough experience to buy the Colt. The unlocking in this game is sort of like a tech tree where as you can't unlock more guns until you unlock the previous gun, and as you get higher in the tree it branches off. For instance you unlock the Colt, then the MP5, then that branches off to the Bretta or Tech 9. After you complete certain tasks you gain the power to shoot the gun, customize the gun, and watch it in x-ray and slow motion to see all the working parts. To sum everything all up, if you love guns and love learning more about them, this is the game for you!

This is an extended review about Prototype, so before starting, let me sai it short. This is a very cool game, but full of bugs and glitches in the Steam version. I bought it on sale, and I suggest doing the same thing. Now, let's start with the extended review.
STORY/GAMEPLAY: This is a sanbox game. very unique in its kind. In spite of being the typical delinquent who wants to rule the mafia, the main character is a human infected by a special virus that allows him to absorb other living beings, and mutate part of his body. There are a great deal of "natural weapons" to use, and also the environment is pretty much destroyable, with the exception of building. The story in my opinion is the shining point of this game, and the funny thing is that it's not explained at all in the beginning, but it's revealet little by little through special events (that last far over the "main story", if you want to collect all pieces of it).
The free roaming is quite good. It's cool being this spiderman-like character, and desn't get boring over time.
GRAPHICS: Graphics are average. The main character and the cinematics are quite pretty, but the rest sucks pretty much. There are 10 to 15 "characters" in the game, so the world feels pretty monotonous and dull. The building are quite monotonous too, put together with a little variety. Despite this you can feel some slowdown when there are many enemies on the screen, even if you have a last generation video card.
BUGS: If I understand correctly, this is an xbox/ps porting, so it's full of bugs and glithces. Looking on the internet you can manage to fix pretty much everything, but still sucks having to "open new game > return to main meny > load saved game", or else the game crashes.
AI: Artificial intelligence just sucks. After just a couple of hours of game you can perfectly predict what will happen, even what moves your enemies will do. I think that you can pretty much expect it from a sandbox game, but the overall scarce variety of character is quite dull.
I think that's all. To sum up, this is a short list of pros and cons.
PROs:
- very good story
- feels incredibly cool
- complete it 100% is quite challenging
CONs:
- bugs
- AI
- graphics (i put in the cons because of the overall effect, and the slowdowns)
That's all. Hope this review is helpful.

"It's Star Trek, Jim, but not as we know it".
Don't go in expecting the full Star Trek experience because you will be disappointed (unless you get a game master). However, if all you're looking for is joining a Starfleet ship, this game exceeds expectations and then some.
What you see is what you get: you and a group of friends fly a spaceship, each member getting their own interface.
While some interfaces may seem daunting due to the amount of information displayed (particularly engineering), each one of them is well designed and surprisingly intuitive; you'll get used to the controls rather quickly.
The gameplay is rather standard as far as Star Trek flight sim games go (mostly combat), but it does deliver this sense of belonging to a rich universe (even if the map is the size of a single solar system)
Speaking of solar systems, the world objects (or rather the lack of) are the only drawback of the game. Maybe I shouldn't expect much from game that takes up a quarter of a gig, but a couple of planets and moons wouldn't go amiss.
Overall, it's a great party game for those who love sci-fi. Just don't be caught on dreams of grandeur.

Unofficially the official "totally-not-Star-Trek" Star Trek bridge simulator. You get a crew together and take command of a starship to valiantly defend USFP resources and interests. Ideally, you'll end up with a captain and five officers for the helm, weapons, engineering, science and comms stations. If you're short a player or two, fret not: you're able to man multiple stations if need be.
Simply put, they're not top-notch; the game looks and sounds both aged and basic even in light of its release date. That being said, its UI is thematic and fairly consistent throughout. Furthermore, it's still able to provide that awe-inspiring scenery where you look out into the vast expanse of space and just let your mind float adrift among the stars... and enemy debris, but mostly stars! The sound sticks right to the classical ol' space beeps, boops and bweens. The music's actually fairly good, limited though it may be.
As stated above, the UI is thematic and consistent. It's easy enough to navigate around it, though the controls themselves need plenty of explaining and/or pressing-stuff-to-see-what-it-does. I do highly recommend reading the manual and digging up the control configuration file.
Let's start with game modes: Solo (single ship, can still have multiple players), PVP (ship vs ship), Co-op (multiple player-controlled ships), and Scripted. To hone in on that last one, the premade scenarios can be lightly compared to challenges or quests. Players can make their own scenarios as well, in which a seventh player would typically take the position of GM and spawn in enemies and environmental hazards for the players to deal with. Whichever mode you choose, it's also worth noting that you can customize a lot of the settings from enemy and player ship stats to what kind of ships and environments will appear in what quantities. This customization, combined with the ability to setup your own encounters, allows you to effectively tighten down to the perfect mixture of difficulty and enjoyment. Speaking of enjoyment...
The game's always more fun with friends. Always. There's the issue of role assignment that makes role-based teamwork difficult at times, but once you're past that each position can provide a challenge. Yes, a captain gives orders for the crew to follow, but a
captain listens to input here and there while always ensuring that the crew has direction so they don't lose focus, get bored or feel useless. The helm officer goes where the captain instructs, but a good one is already coming about to bear on the next objective. Each role has room for improvement... even Comms has hidden levels of skill to strive for.
If you step back and think about the way the game plays, it doesn't seem like it should be so interesting: you fly around, kill some baddies, resupply then rinse and repeat until victory. Then... you consider the sense of tension and urgency created by that group environment. The captain spins their plan and tells the crew what they want, helm focuses intently on maintaining firing arcs while avoiding those of the enemy ships, weapons carefully targets the opposition's weapons systems with beams while loading and firing torpedo tubes, engineering constantly shifts power levels up and down to provide better performance without overloading systems, science keeps an eye on ship statuses and positions while providing beam frequencies for weapons to fire on, comms keeps an eye on station supply levels while directing allied ships and demanding the enemy's surrender. During this, each player is providing vital information to the other stations. Depending on your crew this can mean a loud mess, a constant stream of curt statements in a rotation, or the one thing feared most by all captains: total and utter silence from the stations. Autonomy's good, but silence rarely is.
I'll leave gameplay on this final and important detail: there are no offical dedicated servers. The community hosts either with their computers or through servers they run maintain/pay for themselves. In most cases this means you'll need to know about port fowarding and/or setting up LAN environments in order to play with other people. It's a sharp disappointment since the game is geared so heavily towards group play.
It's a blast if you're up to the task of organizing and operating a match. I've converted eleven people IRL to the cause so far; we LAN party it up just about every weekend. Get some friends, get to a guide on how to setup an Artemis server, and get to defending the galaxy from Kralien scum.

I like it. I used to do modding for the game (primarily additional bricks) but the lack of general interest in the game so did my desire in modding. In it's core it's a good game, but it's a game which stands on it's community to create the environment. Which is awesome, but smaller the community, the harder it is to get new people to play the game, which is unfortunate and I can't phantom there being any better times upcoming for the game.

The game overall is very fun at times, Blockland is basically a First-Person/Third-Person sandbox where you have the game world in your hands to build whatever comes out of your mind. With an environment editor, eventing system, a variety of bricks to choose from the game is pretty fun.
With mods, everything changes, the game is absolutely much more better when you have mods installed to your game, these add-ons can include new bricks, vehicles, clients, scripts, events, and so on. There's also a new dedicated service called Blockland Glass, a mod hosting service and chat service that is basically a replacement from the abandoned Return To Blockland.
The community is small, but you can find good people here, some are toxic, but that's what you'd expect from games. there's usually over a hundred people online every day, but at night around the US, it lowers. Numerous servers can be found though, and you have the ability to buy one from a community hosted service, or you are able to host your sever dedicated or non-dedicated.
The last pro is that the game itself has it's own forum, called Blockland Forums, here you can find many threads and topics that mostly relate to Blockland, except the off-topic. Add-ons are mainly released there, and you can find many discussions, such as help with the game, making add-ons, or generally talking about anything else related to Blockland.
The game is very fun in my opinion, and it sadly got it's last big update in 2013, when the game was released on Steam. Things have come and gone by then, but I'd assure that you'd have a good time playing the game when you have friends. My experience in Blockland so far gives me a rating of a 8/10.
