I haven't played this game very much, but it is very fun when you get the chance!
First and foremost, it would be unfair not to give the readers a heads up that if you don't have people you intend to play this with, it can be
difficult to get into a game. Teamspeak 3 helps immensely, but even there if you don't want to preschedule when you play, you really need to hope that there are others on the server. I recommend using extreme caution if you do not have friends to play this with. Don't expect this to be like most games that you can play at your leisure.
With that out of the way, the game is fun in much the same way a TTRPG is fun: it provides a memorable experience of a shared adventure (though at this stage, it seems more often akin to "battle"). I have not had the opportunity to try engineering or captaining as I write this, but of all the others I found that in order of easiest first to hardest, it goes:
1. Weapons
2. Communications
3. Science (for the most part)
4. Helm
Though to be fair, all of the stations I have tried so far are rather easy. The trick of the game has more to do with efficient communication. Everyone has something to contribute, but it all needs to be managed (generally by the captain) in a way where all the relevent information is being communicated in the right order at the right time. The interface/game element is actually extremely easy, though captaining appears to take more skill (in terms of identifying what the immidiate threats are and taking the proper course of action).
Weapons: Generally this is extremely straightforward. Leave beams on automatic (some prefer manual, haven't figured out why yet), listen to what to load and when to load it, time your firing properly, it is generally straightforward in terms of the game itself. Just click fire and load at the right times, have the right ammo loaded and set the beams to the correct frequency. From a communication perspective, it seems the important thing is to have good timing. Have an idea of what the captain means by "about 3 seconds." Make sure the captain has an idea how much ammunition you have, and it might be a good idea to remind the captain at times that you can convert energy to and from torpedos.
Communications: Probably the most difficult part is sifting through the relevant an irrelevant com chatter. I haven't yet figured out if there is a way to tell if the ships are trying to communicate with you directly, because messages not intended for your ship will show up too (I think). This ties in nicely with the communication element. The captain probably doesn't want to hear that a friendly ship is requesting permission to dock at a friendly base miles away. If two enemy ships are taunting each other and looks like they might fight or one is offering surrender, that would be very useful for the captain to know.
Science: The first game I played I doubled as science and communications. I had no idea that the frequencies are displayed as bars. The right frequency to use doesn't just appear as a letter. My teammates were also kind enough to tell me right off the bat that you will likely have to scan multiple times. Getting used to it I found much harder than getting used to any other position so far. Once you are used to it, though, you spend most of your time sitting around scanning stuff, and making the captain aware of what is going on long-range. You are effectively the eyes, more specifically the peripheral vision, of the ship. Don't let the others get caught up in fighting one ship and not realize that there is an ambush en route.
Helm: Definately the most tricky in terms of actual game elements. It uses what I will call, for lack of a better word, continuous steering which many find tricky to use. I mean this as a contrast to car steering or joysticks where you push it one way and it returns to a straight path. Steering here means that the ship will continue turning in the same direction as you first set it. This can frustrate many, but I was already familiar with that control scheme from other games. The most important element of communication to stress here is that it has the most urgent communication needs. You need your captain to tell you when to drop out of warp as you can't see that far out, but you also need to inform the captain of any difficulties you encounter immidiately after you encounter them, you can't wait. This seems to be a position that I would expect to challenge and perhaps frustrate introverted people that struggle to speak up. You must speak up without hesitation, and react quickly when given instructions for maximum efficiency. And then, of course, there is the means of steering to get used to.
Altogether, this is a fun game if you either have friends that you can organize a session with, or if you don't mind only being able to play occasionally. TS3 is a must if you are not playing with others in the room. I say TS3 because that is where you will find others online looking for games as well. The fun in all roles except maybe captaining come more from communication and hanging out than from the game itself. Will hopefully update with more information soon.

This is a game that combines some of the best aspects of Masters of Orion 2 and Galactic Civilizations 2.  However, it is also missing a lot of the personality both those titles portrayed.  It plays a lot faster, but in general is a lot less "involved".
Pros:
Custom Races
Multiple Tech Research Trees
More Streamlined With Less Micromanagement
Custom Design Ships
Strategic Resouces Really Matter
Easy Access Information VIA Sortable Charts/Tables
Can Manage All Systems From A Single Screen
Cons:
Very Little/Limited Diplomacy
Very Simplified Combat (blessing or a curse depending on tastes)
Not Very Immersive (most of your time is spent looking at data in charts/tables, giving it a less organic feel)
Travel Between Systems Is Too Restricted (does not have the open world exploration feel of typical 4x games)
The degree of control you have over governing your race and systems is brilliant.  You can micromanage as much or as little as you want.  Instead of individually micromanageing every planet, this is more system based.  Upgrades such as building improvements are system wide, yet you can still terraform individual planets and set a planetary focus.
Combat is very much like it is in Galactic Civilizations 2, but with some added tactic options that can be employed in each of 3 combat phases.  You do not individually control your ships, but instead issue a fleet wide order each turn.  This makes combat take a min instead of an hour like in Masters of Orion 2, yet you still have some tactical options that actually matter.
If you enjoy custom designing and controlling a space faring race with a focus on maximum efficiency, while having control over the degree of micromanaging involved and having turns and combat that don't take forever,  then this may be the game for you.  However, if you are looking for an immersive tactical experience with personality, you may wish to give this a pass.
I personally feel that it's a dencent game overall, but it could have been better.  It's nice to have a 4x game that is fast paced, but you sacrifice a lot of depth to get it.
Many positive traits. The space environment is interesting and inspiring. However, the cumbersome and rigid micromanaging spoils the fun the further the game advances.

The game is playable and enjoyable up to a certain point and then the limited parameters of the  clumsy tactical combat system lock you into an "Endless" war. Retreating ships cannot be fired upon???? Who came up with that brilliant idea???  The tech tree is almost undecipherable until you play the game a few times and is laced with pedantic and misleading verbiage.  There is very little room for diplomacy and you can't really engage in cloak and dagger shenanigans or black ops  such as assassinations or clandestine raids on outpost systems. There are no orbital battle stations or defensive systems (satellites or mines) which would discourage  multiple incursions into your space and free up your fleets to engage and repel the enemy. While on that subject you should be able to disengage a fleet from a system being besieged in order to protect or relieve another beleaguered fleet or planet. Planetary sieges are extremely boring  since there is no quick way to completely neutralize a planet or system by means of neutron weapons or biological warfare. Planetary defenses are visually nonexistent and dependent on simple variables.  Please note: I've only played this in single player mode so some of my criticisms may or may not apply to the multiplayer version .
There's supposed to be a sequel to this game and I hope they improve on the combat, diplomacy, orbital defenses and tech systems in order to make the sequel more immersive and rewarding.

Taimumari can be summed up as playing X (from Megaman X) in the original Megaman.  The mobility of the protagonist is excellent, but the levels and bosses are clearly not balanced.  For example, the Knight is a pushover, while Explosion Girl is aggravatingly difficult.
The greatest disappointment in the game is the lost opportunities presented by the story.  Rather than presenting a dynamic world in which time and space are slowly disintegrating, the uber-powerful forces commanded by the bad guys serve only as a backdrop for some fairly lame melodrama.  This game milks the "misunderstood villain" trope to the fullest, sacrificing excellent opportunities for a meshing of surprising gameplay and narrative in the process.  I mean, seriously, one of the villains disrupted the fabric of space-time so he could look cool for a girl?
I also should note that you shouldn't trust reviews from anyone with .6 hours on record saying this game is just-hard-enough.  They haven't reached the third stage of
the main villain's fortress.  The game was pleasantly difficult--and concurrently very rewarding--until then, at which point it seems as though the developer decided to design an entire level after Megaman's infamous Yellow Devil.
So why am I recommending this game?  A few delightful positives make it shine:
First, it's an excellent clone of
Megaman, and the added mobility of the protagonist (double jump, wall dash, wall climb) is not only great fun to play with but excellently utilized in level design.  The way levels motivate you to learn and use the protagonist's mobility is perhaps the best part of the entire production.  Kudos to the developers.
Second, there are segments in two of the game's four main stages that implement welcome changes in gameplay.  In one, you hang from the ceiling on a descending rope that you have clumsy control over, a la Battletoads, while in the other, the game becomes a Bullet-Hell shooter.
Third, the time slowing spell quickly becomes a go-to ability for the most interesting and clever parts of play.  The joy of laughing at your enemies while you dodge their bullets, get in some cheap-as-free hits, and jump-dash-jump through terrain that's supposed to be tough will motivate you to level up your magic meter just so you can keep laughing at them a little longer.
Despite its weaknesses, Taimumari is definitely worth playing.  The gameplay isn't consistently great, but there are enough tight maneuvers, rewarding challenges, and interesting enemies to keep me playing.  Now if I can just get through the third chapter of the final boss stage (the developer deserves a smack on the jaw for that one), I can find out if the ending was worth the wear on my teeth.
Instead of this, go download MegaMari. It's free, and it's a way better Mega Man clone.

A Mega Man fangame that leaves much to be desired.
Graphics are bland at best, embarrassingly bad at worst with some of the sprites (Warai, the penguins, etc.)  Most of it is outsourced from free graphics sites, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but nothing sticks out here.  There is custom anime-style art for the major characters, some of which is decent, but for the most part it's some medicore DeviantArt-quality stuff; looks like something from one of those teen girl American cartoons of the 2000s that tried to ride the anime wave.  The music ranges from terrible to decent.  Also of note 'aesthetically' is the translation, which is hilariously bad, which is definitely not a positive point but might give you a laugh or two with its overuse and misuse of commas and its bizarre dialogue style.
The gameplay is actually its strongest suit; things feel really 'cheap' and floaty, but it has better control overall than many other lower-end indie games of this sort I've played lately.  Nice mobility options including a doublejump, dash and wall climbing, as well as several powerful skills you can unlock like a huge shield against projectiles, slowdown and even rewind spells.  Several fairly powerful attack spells, as well as a very short-range but extremely fast melee attack round out what would be a nice moveset, but... the sad truth is, like I said, everything just feels terribly cheap.  Nothing has much 'oomph'.  You can easily get through the game with the default spell and slowdown ability and everything else feels superfluous.  There are various upgrades which barely make any kind of noticeable change except for your health and mana pools.  Everything just feels... flimsy.  Most bosses can be cheesed easily in varoius ways, and most areas can be bypassed easily with repeated air-dashes and the slowdown spell.
On top of all this, the game's quite short and very lopsided; the first several areas are hopelessly easy with one or two obnoxious sections, as well as every stage having at least one slow section (such as an autoscroller) so even trying to speedrun feels uncomfortable.  The last half of the game is the 'Wily Castle' of sorts, and it's weirdly super-difficult if you don't downright
your OP spells and abilities, and even then you'll lose many lives -- while the bosses of these areas are all, still, ridiculously easy and simple to play cheap against.  The experience simply feels strange and unsatisfying.
It's not the worst game ever, and for fans of action-platformers it might be worth a buck or two, but there are just so, so many better games like this out there.  In fact, if you like the idea of a Mega Man-ish game where you play as anime girls and can use either swords or ranged attacks try Rosenkreuzstilette and its sequel, they're far superior.
I recently reviewed a very similar type of game on Steam (a Mega Man-like fangame with less-than-professional anime character designs) called Metagal, and just BARELY gave it a thumbs-up; this one I'll just barely give a thumbs-down, as it's very similar in middling quality but Metagal felt like it had more heart and soul put into every aspect of it (if only a bit) and just felt like a much tighter game overall.  Taimumari just didn't make the cut.

It is so depressingly easy to take the wrong lessons from classic games. Mega Man 2, for example, is a master class in play control, graphics, sound design, and challenge. However, there were undeniably some enemies that were tuned a little too high, and some level segments that presented unfair challenges or could force a restart under some conditions. Taimumari is a retro platformer made by the sort of people who look at the laser beams in Quick Man's stage and think yes, this is the sort of thing we should be shooting for.
The enormous blocks of poorly-written text the game opens with explain that your magical world had a thingy that could make everyone divine but some dudes messed with it and now everything is disappearing. You play a young, inexperienced mage who gets the quest to save the world thrust upon her for unclear reasons. The pleasant, pastoral intro level eases you into your double-jumps, wall jumping, magic, and dash abilities before depositing you into the hub town. Here you can talk to people, buy upgrades with stars, or choose your next level to challenge.
For God's sake, start with Sir Fallenstar because his creepy-themed level is the only one that offers a reasonable challenge. All the others devolve into improbable arrays of bottomless pits and instant-kill spike platforms that will force you into Super Meat Boy-esque contortions to pass. Explosion Girl's stage has a long moving platform section where you have to keep perfect pace with your ride, and Roketto's stage (I swear I am not making these names up) has some Flappy Bird-style weaving through spike gauntlets. Passing these obstacles can take numerous attempts, sending you back to distant checkpoints for each retry.
This alone wouldn't damn Taimumari, because honestly the platforming challenges aren't all that much worse than those of the NES ball-breakers of yore. No, what kills this game is that you get exactly three tries to pass each level. Lose all your lives, and you get kicked straight back to the hub with a big, chunky GAME OVER. You can spend your precious stars on 1-ups, and most levels have one or two hidden away in particularly deadly spots, but that does little to ease the pain of losing your last life on learning a boss and having to re-do the entire 10-minute stage.
If the game was particularly polished or compelling you could almost make a case to stick it out, but Taimumari can't manage that either. The graphics do a lot of flickering all over, especially during scene transitions. Everything is oddly-proportioned, with a lot of long, uneventful walks and melee combat taking place at the very bottom of the screen between squat characters. The backgrounds are detailed but the foregrounds and characters are not, especially the larger ones. Weapons are poorly balanced, your sword has aggravatingly little reach, and enemies take a ridiculous number of hits to kill.
I feel like all the right intentions to make a good game were here, but the polishing and balance passes were overlooked or skipped altogether. Unless you like your platformers absolutely punishing, something is going to make you rage in this game. It might be the umpteenth nigh-unkillable enemy, it might be the thousandth death by corner spike, or it might be the laughably bad dialogue between the embarrassingly bad characters. And with a range of threats like that, you're much better off staying far away from this one.

Even though this game is relatively new it still holds up as being one of, if not THE best zombie game on the market. It's not only fun playing single player but it's hilarious when you can get three more friends to join in the zombie killing.
There's of course the standard Easy - Hard difficulities (Here being Easy, Medium, Advanced and Expert). So if you're looking for some mindless slaughtering to do you can put it on easy or if you and your friends is a tatical squad preparing for the zombie apacolypse this is a great way to start!
Also you don't have to play "Kimulator: Fight for your destiny" to get into this one, all the maps and more from Kimulator are in this one. Even if you want to play oldschool there is a mode for that. Speaking of modes, there's Versus mode which is exactly what it sounds like, you control both the zombitatos and the Pc master race in rounds. The one who ends the final map with the most points win. There is also a realism version of this mode which means the Pc master race can't see the green/orange/red glow around them as they used to.
There's also Survival which is aslo what it sounds like. Survive for X amount of time and you get bronze, silver or a gold medal depending on the requirments for the map you're playing.
Scavanger is the last major gamemode, here you play as survivor and infected and the objective is to fill a generator with gas. Who wins depends on which team's the fastest.
Then, finally, there's something called mutation. These are pretty much fun little mini modes. For example you have to try and survive an entire campaign on your own, you and all your teamates have katanas and can't get other weapons, you need to carry around a lawngnome to win etc.

One word - Phenomenal. If you are reading this and want a new controller, one that can replace a keyboard and mouse unlike any other controller out there, buy it right now! Easiest 10/10 I've given. If you want a few more details in a "mini-review", read further.
The controller is, in short, amazing. However, there are some design quirks. The left trackpad is a little too close to the Back button and possibly the analog stick for my tastes. I end up grazing the trackpad unintentionally sometimes, and if you set the trackpad to a non-click function, you will trigger it with a graze.
UPDATE - After getting used to the layout a lot more, I don't really graze the trackpad now. Like any controller it requires a bit of use to really get used to the layout, and since the design of this controller is so different than anything else we've seen, it will take a bit of extra time if you're coming from the standard Xbox or Playstation controllers.
It also has a learning curve in terms of using it (I'm not talking about the curve for programming it, which is higher.) The 2 new "Grip" buttons are phenomenal, but they trick my brain at times. I am used to having 2 triggers and 2 bumpers, so I end up freezing for a second when I want to push a Grip button. My first reaction is to pull a trigger. Weird, but I'm sure I'll get used to it.
UPDATE - And I did get used to it, even faster than the trackpad.
I think the X A B Y are actually great. I haven't pressed any of them accidentally yet, and the right thumb can access them easily. They feel good to the touch and the smaller button size means, for my hands, there is no reaching needed at all to comfortably push them.
The trackpads feel really good as well. The trackpads themselves are almost flawless in terms of control reactivity. You can do really precise things (mouse control, etc..) with the right settings very easily. The 'clicks' on each trackpad are very heavy-duty, "clicky" and satisfying, almost too much so. I found myself using the trackpad feature more as I really like how it feels and operates, but the operation of the 'click' functions are great as well. When you can add functions to the trackpad and then different functions when you click it, well, it just gets silly in terms of what you can do with this thing. The right trackpad as a mouse is *very* satisfying to use, and I find myself using it in Trackball mode as my main input device on my PC a lot of the time.
The triggers feel nice, too. They are as reactive as you want them to be, whether with just a slight pull or a full click. I find that a slight pull, not a full click, in a game where you have to click the left mouse to move is very nice. The analog stick works well and feels good, seems like a typical, high-quality stick, and all of the finer settings of the triggers, bumpers, grips, buttons, stick, trackpads and even the built-in gyroscope can be fully programmed and tweaked on a per-game basis.
Overall, I can easily say that it is hands down the best controller I've ever used, both in terms of the feel of the controller itself and the incredible level of function it offers. It's very high quality and well-built all around, and the Steam integration is excellent (programming it is actually much easier than it should be thanks to Valve. The built-in "software" functions impeccably, you can quickly and easy test your control setups and bounce right back to programming it. You can also do fun things like use the controller with your desktop, assign buttons to start Steam, close Steam, etc., and basically control your PC with it if you'd like. Cool stuff.)
There is a problem with it, though. The problem with this incredible controller is Valve getting people to actually use it. I'm nearly convinced that it could play any kb+m game comfortably with a little bit of programming (I've already built profiles for several old-school CRPGs that normally would require mouse and keyboard to play.) The thing is, since everyone will use it differently, have different comfort levels and feel with the controller, it's likely that a single profile is not going to work for everybody. So, you will likely need to program the games yourself, or at least tweak someone else's profile a bit to get it to feel good for you and your preferences. *Note - I am talking about playing old-school RPGs with it, PC strategy games and games that typically require a mouse and keyboard. This is why I bought the controller. Playing modern RPGs that have controller support will be a cinch. It's the older games you'll likely have to program the controller, or at least download someone's template and tweak it a bit to your liking. If you are cool with doing that, digging into it a bit, you will be very, very pleased. I didn't think you could actually get old-school RPGs to work on a gamepad, but like I said, I'm pretty much convinced now.
Again, they made it about as easy as possible to program while still maintaining high amounts of functionality and advanced settings. It may seem daunting at first, but after a couple hours of tinkering with it and you'll be flying around and setting up your own profiles in no time.
I mean, it's an easy 10/10 from me. The sheer level of functionality and well-built feel make it the best and most versatile controller I've ever had the pleasure of using. I really hope this thing catches on and Valve continues to improve it, because no other controller will be touching it for a long time. At least not for PC gaming. I'm almost certainly going to give my Xbox wireless adapter for my PC to my old man as I don't see myself ever needing the 360 controller anymore. This controller frankly makes other controllers obsolete.
Hope this helps you guys. If you have any questions, feel free to send them my way or join my Steam group (Fluent's RPG World) to chat. Ciao!

Generally, most people who turn up here are likely to be aware what ASBS is. In short, as someone else already put it, it's the Star Trek game you've all been waiting for.
Now, I'm just gonna get you riled up - I'm more of a Star Wars guy. I also friggin' loved this game to bits. Now, let's go over the important stuff.
What is readily apparent is that the game is a social game. You essentially roleplay a Star Trek style crew, so it's gonna take people. With a bit of creativity you can run it remotely but the game really comes into its own over LAN. Each player gets a specific role on the bridge, and they damn well better do it well. This is pretty much the core of it.
Now, it takes some effort to enjoy it properly. It takes setting up a bridge, and it's indeed ultimate nerdery if you can set up a whole faux spaceship bridge (which some people do). The game's more than just the software, and you always need to remember. The game is also your crew. A lot of it is when you raise a glass to the finest crew in Starfleet. A lot of it is when the engineer cuts power to the engines because the drunken helm officer is zipping around to blindside enemies. The visuals are not spectacular and the sound is a little tacky.
Which is sort of part of its charm - this is not an AAA title where you're a one-man army. Oh, your ship does most of the heavy lifting, but it's the crew that counts. You need to communicate for maximum efficiency. The imperfections of presentation actually make sense, as they give a nice retro feel to everything. And it's not exactly an excuse. That feel does evoke Star Trek, which is precisely the point of the game. It's not taxing on the hardware but it's precisely the point, as it naturally requires you to use multiple devices. Unless you are tech savvy enough to cheat around that (and considering you're a huge nerd, not saying it's bad, as you're eyeing it, you actually might be), but that defeats the point, as it's a true multiplayer game.
Make your stories, make your legend. You may not be Commander Shepard, you may not be Captain Kirk or Captain Jean-Luc Picard. But in this game you'll soon be boldly coming at them with your crew by your side and your pha... beams hot.

Tutorial consists of half a game manual copy-pasted into the game and presented one screenful at a time, telling you how a well-developed empire looks on that screen and what every single function is, much like showing every single tooltip at once and making it nearly impossible to figure out what you should be looking at right now.

There might be a good game somewhere underneath, but the first impression is akin to having invited a guest to my house who turns up naked and asks me to provide him with clothes. I am not such a close friend that I want to indulge such ridiculous demands on the first meeting, and Endless Space has not piqued my interest enough to make me struggle through the interface until I can discover the gameplay.

I have been playing this game on-and-off for quite some time now and conclude that I quite like it. For me, there is a bit too much micromanagement to make it super enjoyable, but is well balanced so that various types of players will still like it.
The pros is that the game is beautiful with nice art and spaceships that cool. You can customize your ships extensively to introduce strengths and/or weaknesses to certain weapon types. The tech tree is pretty good with some strategy needed to determine exactly what you are trying to accomplish.
The negatives are that the AI is not very good and cheats badly to try to be competitive. You will never have the feeling that you got outmaneuvered militarily and/or diplomatically, just that the 500% resource bonus or whatever will wear you down through attrition. The battle system is also needlessly complex - I understand they probably spent a ton of time building a beautiful real time fighting display, but you have such limited control that it just slows the game down. Even picking "cards" is annoying when the AI spams you with dozens of stacks of ships. I hope things will be improved with Endless Space 2!
Also, I did end up buying the DLC that I am torn over. The Harmony are a cool race with much different mechanics, but other than that, I feel that it is not worth the cost. It simply adds even more micro (troops, fighters, etc) to a game that arguably has too much already.

In the near future, you're a guy named Adam Jensen, working security for Sarif Industries, one of the leaders in the biotech business. One day, however, before a presentation in Washington, an attack occurs. The key staff is presumed dead and you're mortally wounded, however, with the help of advanced augmentation technology, you're brought back from death and are back on the job a mere six months later.
It's a successor to the original Deus Ex, and a worthy one, at that. It is not an RPG in the traditional sense. Your aim is not impaired if you're untrained in a weapon. There's no locational damage. There are no skills to upgrade, besides your augmentations. It's far more an action/RPG hybrid than the original Deus Ex, while keeping the spirit with large, sprawling, living environments, fleshed out sidequests and a fantastic atmosphere.

Yes, yes it does. And it is fantastic, one of the core contributing factors towards the atmosphere. It gets more energetic when it needs to, and keeps slow, fades out to the background when you're making your way down town, asthmatically jogging to your next point of interest.
This is one of the main gripes to be had with the game. The stealth is half-baked. No light levels. At all. You can be up in the rafters concealed in darkness, the AI does not give a damn. It's all line of sight. Some people find this acceptable, but as an officianado of the original Splinter Cell titles and the Thief series, I think it's inexcusable. The shooting is not great, either. The cover mechanics serve the firefights well, but unless you upgrade your weapons, a lot, you're going to be fairly useless by the end of the game. Oh and also, the close combat takedowns take energy and are cutscenes. Oh and also, you can't sprint for longer than 10 seconds, even if you're upgraded to the maximum possible for both your rebreather and legs.
Yes, and a very good one, in fact. The story is a complicated mix of higher powers controlling everyone, corporate warfare, street crime, news spinning and human evolution. Going into any detail would be an injustice towards the game.
To be truthful, everyone. It is by far better than Invisible War, the previous title in the series, and it has enough elements to bring new players in to the classic Deus Ex formula, keeping people hooked with the immersive environments and fantastic story.

Taimumari is a great side-scrolling, retro-style action platformer that uses a variety of magic, maneuvers and a sword as you collect things across a selection of five different levels. There's an equal amount of fun and challenge. The game is no pushover, but even the rough patches are no reason for frustration.
Its a game that oozes that retro style with great chip tunes and sound effects from that Nintendo era. The graphics fit for the most part, but they can be an bit immersion breaking with some of the ugly looking giant dragon heads and the giant boss pictures that kick off each level. The backgrounds and terrain look a lot better and have more detail than the moving sprites in the game.
Right off the bat, this is a game about great controls and an abundance of them. You have a double jump, a dash that rockets you forward whether you're in the air or on the ground, short range sword, wall clinging, long range spells that use mana and you can even charge your spells. The only downside is sometimes its tough to get away from a wall. You can drop, but trying to leap off to a different area is tough. Its best to play it safe and stay on the wall.
The story is simple, but I'm never one to read a story. The town is in danger, now you must go through four levels to defeat their boss before unlocking the fifth level to stop the true evil at the end. Its a formula that has been done before, but that's no reason to turn away.
Each of the five or so levels has a different theme and spell to find. A haunted castle, an aerial castle, a post apocalyptic wasteland, a frozen cavern, and so on. The levels keep track of your best times and how many items from that level you've collected so there's a reason to go back and speed run.
These levels are a healthy length and do offer a variety of different platforming action to make each stage feel more unique. One stage has a shooter section and after that you keep the wings to let you jump as many times as you want in the air. Another stage halts the action in two different rooms for you to dodge an array of arrows and another to avoid smashers. The ice cavern lets you ride ropes down to the bottom. It shows that effort was put into the game to make it more than just another platformer.
The brief tutorial level that spoon feeds you with text as you run through the level such as how to jump over a pit. Then the game opens into a town where you can purchase upgrades and head off to the next level. its a hub world and with every game over, you respawn here with everything but your score in tact. Its a forgiving game. Every item, star, ability and spell you've collected stays with you.
Continues are infinite and each one grants you three lives, but you can purchase more for forty stars. You can also find or earn lives as you play. Each enemy drops one or two stars and you'll need at least one hundred for any upgrade.
The merchant in town will sell you upgrades for your attack strength, health increase, spell strength and mana recharge rate. There is one passive ability to purchase that will let you attract items toward you like extra lives, hearts and stars. While none of these is a game changer, its more of a reward for your hard work.
Because you have attack strength and spell strength, that means the enemies take a while to defeat. You need to put a little effort into slashing a slime a half a dozen times. By effort I mean the sword will slash as fast as you can mash that button.
As for the spells, there are four of them. A simple shot that can charge into a bright blue beam. A triple shot spark that can charge into a shield of eight shots which then throw out in different directions. A bomb that charges into four bombs. Its a skill that feels lackluster. The last spell is the ice spell, which does... lava? No it is just a simple ice spell. The charged variant of it throws out three blades of ice forward and one behind you.
There is only a small variety of enemies. Knights will charge forward. Slimes just hang out and jump every so often. Ghosts fly in. Birds dive toward you. Flowers spit projectiles in three directions. Oh and spikes they are instant death traps, but this game goes easy on the amount of spikes, but it uses them well.
Then the bosses tend to be the ones with diversity. Each boss has a few different simple patterns and can throw a lot of projectiles. A lot of them will force you to jump to hit them and scurry away to avoid projectiles. They are a good challenge after a long level when you've run out of lives and health.
Taimumari makes you earn some of the collectible items and even hearts that give you full health. The items are found near pits or hard-to-reach places like just over a cliff. While its nothing too difficult, it makes you challenge yourself to get them. Once you have them, you never have to get them again so you can even cheat by just dropping into a pit after collecting the item. People looking for a challenge will avoid the pit.
I did find some minor issues, such as projectiles shooting backward. When new areas of a level would load, the screen would shift around. Its nothing that broke the game and they did seem quite consistent.
For the price, this is a great game even if the game can be considered short with five deep and diverse levels. Its still well worth the price for any issues that I have with the game.

Witches, spells, and the possible destruction of a world you become destined to save. This is what awaits you in the platforming game Taimumari. What better way to create a new world with such grand powers than in one of the most tried and true genres of gaming. This game will throw you for a loop, though. As cute as it looks, it is often very difficult. Proving that hard games come in cute packages.

Taimumari is a very weird mixed package. It's a satisfying and charming little indie platformer that gives you a lot of good gameplay for a very low price. It's also very frustrating at times with some incredibly questionable level design and it incentives grinding for upgrades above almost all else. It feels like a game that could be amazing if it was just a little softer on the player with instant-deaths and very slow money drop rates.
Also, the game is apparently Russian and it kind of shows. The translation is laughly bad, in a way that's actually sort of charming. Don't expect much of a story here though.
I'm giving it a thumbs up for now because despite everything that frustrates me about it I still find myself coming back to it. I might update the review when I finish the game though. It's cheap enough that i'd say it's worth buying if you're into hardcore retro-style platformers.

Even if you engineer the most effective setup you can imagine, you might find yourself reminded of those mobile games that merely simulate a joystick. Like a cheesy movie, you had the real power all along.
PROS:
-The clicker buttons on the back are excellent; I wish my regular controller had these!
-The joystick and most of the buttons are comfortable
-Seemingly endless nuances to the customizations you can make to the trackpads and every other button
CONS:
-The D-Pad functionality is a worse-than-♥♥♥♥ing-useless, oversized piece of garbage that somehow pales in comparison to the crappy D-Pads that most modern controllers have (pardon my French)
-The mousey circles will never be as good as a real joystick when you need a joystick, nor as good as a real mouse when you need a real mouse.
-You can get a good controller instead - such as the $30 XBOX 360 wireless controller for Windows - and still benefit from most of Steam's excellent controller customization features.

I picked up the Steam Controller back in  2015 when they first launched. When I got it I was super excited and had great time customizing the controls on my favorite games and trying new things that couldn't be done with the standard 360 controller I had been using.
Overall, I was really impressed. The feel of the controller was natural and everything worked great short of the random bugs and changes that would come up with BPM beta. Once I opted out fo the beta again it stablized and I didn't have to tinker as much.
No for the big problem. It is now March 2017, just about 1.5 years in and the thing has busted. The Right Bumper has stopped working completly making it a pretty fancy paperweight when it comes to playing my games. Maybe I have been spoiled by the tried and true 360 controllers which appear to be damn near indestructible, but having a button fail 6 months after the warranty expires just leaves a bad taste in my mouth. I reached out to Steam Support, who first merely replied "to send in a replacement hardware request." Tried that, warranty is expired so system wouldn't let me request a replacement. I replied to Steam Support yesterday and haven't heard anything back, I am assuming because it is the weekend. I will update if they find a way to resolve this, but my best guess is that I am stuck buying another controller.
If you want to try out a cheap controller with paddles and a tone of customization it may be worth it, but if you are looking for something that lasts, you may want to look elsewhere.
UPDATE: Steam Support got back to me and said they could put in the replacement hardware request for me, so it seems like they are replacing the controller (not in my hands yet). Also, since I figured I wasn't getting a new one I took a shot at repairing the bumper. The bumper buttons use these thin plastic tabs that are attached to the trigger assembly to depress the actual button on the board, these tabs flex when you use the button and eventually just snap. To fix it I just took the tab and used epoxy to attach it to the depressor guide that is actually part of the bumper itself (eliminating the interface with the trigger assembly). This seems to work perfectly fine and is holding for now.

This game is a little buggy, a little uneven, and does not feel like it's yet been fully realized. Having said that, I can still fully and wholeheartedly recommend it, but with  a few caveats that I will get to later. The bottom line is: this game is so much fun! Seriously, if you are into, or were ever into Star Trek then you owe it to yourself to get it. Artemis is a simulation of what it might be like to be part of the bridge crew on a starship like the Enterprise.
Here's how it works: You run one instance of the game as a server and then each player (up to six for a full bridge crew) runs another instance and those clients connect to the server. Each player picks one or more stations to manage (captain, helm, tactical, engineering, science, and communications) and each station gets its own interface needed to perform its functions to run the ship. So the helm gets a control layout to be able to fly the ship, engineering gets controls to manage power to various systems and mitigate damage, and the tactical officer gets to fire the weapons. The captain ties it all together, making decisions and issuing orders to other crew members. The captain has his own view which is a map with some basic information, or s/he can simply use the main view screen which is provided by the server.
The developer clearly intended originally that this game would be played by people all in the same room and the simulation lends itself well to LARPing and role-playing. An ideal setup would be all six players in the same room using their own machines and whichever machine is running the server (any one of the machines could run the server and one of the clients--you DO NOT need a separate machine and/or copy of the game to play) would be connected to a big screen tv to show the main screen. Thankfully, the latest version of the game allows for playing over the internet. My gaming group uses Skype for voice chat since the game provides no native voice chat. It works fine for us.
The server is what runs the actual simulation and it allows for setting up various scenarios in the game and tweaking all sorts of parameters to increase or decrease difficulty. The are various sorts of ally and enemy ships to encounter and bases to dock with and defend. The game has modes for multiple ships with their own crews that can go head-to-head or do missions cooperatively. One server can support up to 36 players (six bridges with each having their own crews of up to 6 players).
Each role has different things to do to keep the ship running smoothly. Admittedly, some stations are more fun to play than others. Also, some stations feel very heavy on the micro-managing and others feel like there's not much to do; many people complain about the communications station for being sort of thin in this area. I actually don't mind playing Communications Officer You can hail friendly or enemy ships, monitor distress calls from friendly bases or ships being attacked, demand that enemy ships surrender, taunt enemy ships into attacking, direct friendly ships away from deadly areas of space, order friendly ships to attack, prepare bases for docking to improve refuel and rearm performance. And most importantly, you have the button to set off the red alert klaxon. As Communications Officer, you may also get side quests from friendly forces which usually take the form of, "Dock with this base to download this data, then take it to this friendly ship and then come back and dock with use to get more energy/coolant/weapons/etc."
So once again, I do recommend this game if you have at least two friends to play with. You DO NOT need six people to play this game. At the very least, you need helm, tactical, and engineering, but personally, I like playing with five or six people. Also, as I said before, the game has no native voice chat if you are going to playing over the internet. Something else to be aware of is that the game does nothing for you in terms of matchmaking or anything like that. You'll need to have each player connect to the server via IP address and you'll need to set up port forwarding on TCP 2010 to be able to have any of the clients be able to connect. One other gotcha to to be aware that when you play over the internet, you won't be able to use the IP address of the server that is reported in the game. That IP will only work when playing over a LAN. You'll need your internet-facing IP address to hand out to the players for connecting to the server.
I bought the six pack and gave the five other copies to my gaming group. I've had fun playing this game over the internet as well as all in the same room. It's a lot of fun especially if you have a madcap gang to play with like I do.
I just hope the developer continues to work on this game. It's good already but it feels like it could go a lot farther.

Beyond the dodgy hit detection this is a game that loves one-hits that ignore health and defence. So enjoy clipping through the floor or drowning in knee deep water. There are achievments for that.
This is a MMO that actively discourages player interaction by isolating them in questionable coding. Play areas are set up for(and sometimes require) groups of 3, 5, or 10, but if you have any sort of story quest going on you are locked into solo play. Getting into pvp or grouping for a dungeon is so broken that players have to stand in the hub area begging for another 10 or more people to attempt to use the nonfunctional matchmaker and hope they are not the one left in the lobby. A ritual taking more than a halfhour on a good day. Five times I attempted to join the netoriously unbalance 'Battle of Golems' before I just started using one of the three freeium currencies to skip pvp assignments.
Now after spending weeks grinding along the endless tutorials that perminently bugged my menus on day two, I've hit a wall. There was some pacing as the base mission worked up to about lvl 55 before I unlocked divine form and the system decided I was ready for lvl100+content. Now I'm trapped at 60 indefinely. You need ingame money to progress, to buy exp, and I've been cut off. Now that the game is only giving me impossible to complete endgame tasks I can't grind up to at any sane rate.
It will be two more months of slow tedium before I can even consider attempting the lowend of their cheap trap ridden dungeons with their forced failule bosses.
I'm just done.

First off let me state that this is a Free to Play game.  You start off very limited but are able to build up to competitive levels without dropping a dime.
This game is for those that want an FPS multiplayer game that moves a bit slower.  MWO is wrapped up in the looks of the Battletech/Mechwarrior universe and tries to relate to some of the other game systems.  For those that don't know, Battletech is a tabletop game where this all comes from and Mechwarrior was the brand for the FPS computer games.  This IP has come out with tabletop games, video games, dozens of novels over the years and is steeped in amazing lore.
MWO doesn't have too much of the lore, even if you get into the faction play.  It is more the idea that you get into the Battlemechs and stomp around shooting other people in their Battlemechs.  MWO leaves the mech chassis customizable for swapping out things like engines, weapons, armor, etc.
So if you are looking for a slower FSP where twitch skill isn't as much of a factor and where you can customize a mech chassis then give this one a try.

It's just OK.
The gameplay isn't breaking any records, though it is a competent cover-based sneaky shooter. The ending is a disappointment that, for me, taints the whole experience. The gameplay flow screeches to a halt every time you melee someone or use a supermove so the camera can zoom out and show off a stock animation that is really cool the first couple times, but after a couple hours I wished it would just get on with it. Half of the skill upgrades are either completely useless, or very situational, or provide miniscule improvements. And the cover/combat system feels clumsy. This is NOT a nice clean RPG shooter. The Division's cover system and weapon handling are far better. Perhaps an unfair comparison considering the shooting--like the graphics and character models--have aged about as well as orange juice behind the fridge. And the icing on top is that Fullscreen Windowed is not an option. Normally I wouldn't care but this game hates alt+tabbing and it's sooo slow in between story missions I've got YouTube running on the other screen the whole time.
There's some good stuff though. I like how the inventory system works. I like how you mod your weapons as you progress, applying a new magazine you found here and a barrel you bought there. The hub worlds are well designed, and I don't think I was ever groaning over the commute between main missions. Side activites are... there; offering decent rewards that contribute to the main game.  The hacking is pretty cool, though it didn't set my crotch ablaze either.
I dunno, I'm just lukewarm to the whole thing. I recommend, but if there was a "Meh" rating I could give, it'd be that. It's perfectly functional, nicely polished and all, but it just isn't that interesting.

The Good: Excellent visuals, great controls with lots of action, nice variety of challenging enemies, fun four player co-op
The Bad: Gets repetitive quick, can be very hard, levels are too long, can only equip four upgrades, very short with only 7 levels
Twin stick shooters are running amok on mobile devices, but the best tend to be on consoles. Renegade Ops lets you choose from a variety of characters with a special weapon each. You can level up and unlock new upgrades while trying to mow down as many enemies to rack up a high score. The story is actually really cliché and stupid with a commando leader named Bryant trying to stop the evil Inferno from taking over the world. The cut scenes are drawn in nice comic book style stills, but the dialog is as cheesy as it can get. No matter how you try to kill Inferno he always seems to survive and it's just one of those "You'll never kill me Bryant! MWAHAHA!" type stories.
Besides the cheesy story the action is really fun with some great graphics and physics. You drive around your vehicle using the right stick to shoot with your machine gun. Along the way you can get pick-ups to make your machine gun stronger as well as secondary ammo pick-ups like rocket launchers, rail guns, and flamethrowers. There aren't many pick-ups which is a real bummer, but this is just the start of what else there isn't much of. The enemy variety is interesting with varying degrees of difficulty, but it leads to the game being very difficult most of the time. You start off with 5 lives per level and if you lose them all its game over. The levels are very long and you will be infuriated if you have to go through all that effort again.
My main concern about the game is that it gets very repetitive very quickly because all you do is drive around and shoot. The graphics are excellent so you could get some cinematic scripted scenes going, but instead you just follow an objective arrow around all over the place and kill everything in front of you. There are secondary objectives that lead to achievements, but they span the entire level and take way to long to complete. You are also timed on primary objective so if you don't get it done fast enough a 3 minute timer ticks down and if you don't complete it by then it's game over. This means you have to abandon the secondary and makes things just more frustrating. When you die you lose your machine gun pick-ups so you start with the weakest form and can die easier that way because it takes longer to kill enemies.
There is a lot of fun to be had here with destructible environments, and four player co-op which makes the game easier and more fun. The upgrades are disappointing because you can only equip four at a time and this leaves a lot of useful upgrades unused. There are only 7 missions so you will beat the game in less than 5 hours, but most people probably won't go through again due to the difficulty and repetitive nature of the whole game. Twin stick shooters should pick this up and rejoice, but don't expect it to change the genre.
~Score: 8/10

is a turn-based 4x strategy game similar to the popular Civilization series, which has been a long-time favorite of mine. To be perfectly honest, strategy games aren't really my forte, but I do get quite a lot of enjoyment out of them occasionally, often losing track of time and suddenly wondering,
The sci-fi space theme of this one really got my attention though because I'm so used to strats that take place planetside: land, sea and air.  Managing fleets of spaceships and star systems, colonizing planets and discovering artifacts of lost alien civilizations... Pretty amazing stuff!  But
isn't without its dangers....
++ Customizable Ships Builds
++ Nameable Star Systems/Ships/Fleets
++ Graphics
+ Decent Learning Curve
+ Music
-- No Campaign/Story Mode
-- Rock, Paper, Scissors Combat
- Disappointing Diplomacy/Trade Relations
= Room for improvement, potentially in a sequel?  Absolutely.  But it's far more amazing than not, and a must-have in the turn-based 4x strategy genre, especially for fans of the sci-fi/space theme.
--  Truthfully, it didn't take long to get into this game.  Based on the reviews that I read beforehand, I was very concerned about the learning curve and the lack of a decent tutorial, but once I started a match and began navigating its different menus there were detailed tutorial popups that explained just about everything I needed to know in order to play.  If you skim/skip through it to get to the action faster, however, then yeah, you'll run into that learning curve everyone talks about.  So read up!  Many Bothans died to bring us this information.... No wait, that was Star Wars.  But I'm sure a few interns had to fetch a lot of coffee and make burrito runs while the devs stayed up late just to make us this tutorial.  So if not for yourself, then do it for them!
One of the first things that I really came to love in Endless Space was its customizability.  You get to name your own star systems and fleets which is fantastic, but the best stuff is when you start creating new ships.  Want another ship type?  Then create one!  Put whatever modules you want on it (given you've researched the necessary prerequisites) and give that new ship design a name of your choosing.  Maybe the naming feature isn't crucial to gameplay, but I got a kick out of it at least.
The graphics are pretty stellar, especially for a game of this genre.  No complaints there at all.  The music is great too, but a little more variety couldn't hurt.  After a while, you may want to pop in your own Awesome Mix cassette to listen to while you're out getting into trouble around the galaxy.
--  There's no campaign mode!  I suppose these aren't hugely common in strategy games, but they should be.  Playing a standard match is fun and all, but it can get a little stale after a while.  Having a campaign mode, with varying types of missions that require different strategies to accomplish objectives, and (gasp!) a story that tied it all together??  Come on, that would be awesome.  And making a unique campaign for each race would be out of this world!  Unfortunately, no such luck.  Just your typical choice of race, map size and number of opponents -- ready, set, go....
Just as bad probably is the lack of any real strategy in combat.  Most battles/wars can be won with sheer numbers.  Researching the military tree and designing ships helps some, sure, and choosing so-called battle plans can potentially make a little difference, but in the end it really just comes down to "Paper, Rock, Scissors" and either a little luck or a lot more ships than the other guy.

Lastly, I found the diplomacy and trade relations with other races rather disappointing.  I wanted to feel like these were real, living beings that I was up against/allied to, with feelings or ambitions or bloodlust or a combination of different things, but they aren't anything more than pieces on a gameboard.  Other than a list of some numerical stats and an emoji (literally, an emoji), there's nothing to suggest your diplomatic actions, trade, or aggressive behavior affects them or your relationship with them, at all.  For me, its about immersion I guess, and the difference that a pop-up with an animated ambassador would make is significant.  If you don't care about that kind of thing though, then this point is probably moot.
--  I had zero trouble putting nearly thirty hours into this game right away, and I'll still put in more over the course of time.  Even though it lacks a campaign mode to sink your teeth into, the standard matches are still very fun to play, and there are plenty of races and ways to gain victory (not just combat-related) to keep you entertained.  Lots of amazing little details add up to make this one heck of a game, and even though it lacks in a few areas none of it is enough to bring it down.  If you enjoy turn-based 4x strategy games and sci-fi/space themes,
is a must have.

OVERVIEW
In Taimumari you play as Himari, a female wizard on a quest to restore balance to the world, in a challenging old school platformer. The game consists of 8 levels with a boss fight at the end of each one. There are stars along with other collectibles on each level, and you can use the stars you collected to increase your health and mana bars, and your physical and magic damage. There are a variety of spells to unlock in this game and they are all helpful and necessary to get through parts of some levels. There are three difficulty settings, and although I played on the easiest one, I still found the game a challenge and have gotten stuck on the second to last level.

PROS & CONS
Pros:
Unique bossfights and levels
Lots of spells, slow time down, reverse time, or summon a magic shield!
Lots of hidden collectibles every level for completionists
Extremely challenging, and certain achievements require beating the game without buying any upgrades!
Cons:
Getting powerups can be grindy
Some English translations were sloppy

SUMMARY & FINAL RATING

is a fast-paced, very well thought-off and balanced top-down shooter. The game is clearly based on the classic with the same name from 2003 - with the most recent major update, the original game is even presented for free when you buy
on Steam. Just as the original one, the new version is a no-nonsense game in which you get several different gamemodes which offer access to just the one thing that really counts: slaying monsters, aliens and zombies. And there are a TON of those, so you need some decent gear, don't you? Happily,
offers exactly that: the number of weapons isn't overwhelmingly large, but they are very different from each other and most ask for an appropriate playstyle to make the most of them. You'd better stay out of the melee with the Ion Cannon and take on the mob from a distance, but a flamethrower just wants you to get in there are clear a small ring of safety around you.
Thankfully, 10TonsLtd have also included a fairly large number of power-ups which appear during the fights and which come in most welcome when the crowds get bigger and bigger. Make no mistake: this is no easy-going game, and the going gets really tough towards the end of the different scenario's. Happily that's where the dozens of available perks come in: they offer a permanent of way of buffing your character, and allow for some degree of ever so slight character building, especially with regard to a playstyle which suits you best.
Graphically, the game gets the job done, but not more than that. Some extra effort and more visual appeal would have been welcome. Sound is pretty good though, with all weapons having a very clear identity of their own. Steam cards and a bunch of interesting - and some quite difficult - achievements make sure this game offers quite some playtime.

Tl;Dr: Comfy, good battery life, very customizable, feels cheap and slightly brittle. Best controller for couch gaming.
Review:
The Steam Controller is a fairly intuitive controller. The touchpads take a bit of getting used to, but once that's done you don't even notice it. Moving the camera around in RPG-style games can be bothersome, but it isn't a dealbreaker and is fairly comparable to using a mouse. Action maps, the Steam LED, and boot/shutdown sounds can be easily customized via Steam Big Picture.
The controller is
comfortable in the hand; it beats out the Xbox controller by a very comfortable margin. Triggers and bumpers are ergonomically layed out and require no effort to switch between the two sets. Battery life in my experience is better than any other controller I've owned, averaging 75 hours of playtime before sacrificing two more AA cells to the gods.
You can choose between wired and wireless modes. The connectivity via wireless is nothing short of spectacular, not even breaking a sweat when I'm downstairs on the opposite side of the house. The cable is 3-4ish feet, but it's a standard MicroUSB cable, if you want longer pick one up on Amazon for like $5.
THAT BEING SAID.
This thing is like 70% glossy plastic. Granted, it attracts fingerprints much less than the likes of a monitor bezel, but it still attracts them. From someone who has used custom controllers in the past, this controller feels very cheap. The two back switches feel very brittle, though whether they are or not is another matter. I wish the sole thumbstick was more grippy. The ABXY buttons are difficult to switch your thumb to if you aren't looking at the controller.
If you're sitting at your desk, stick with your trusty KB+M. They offer more refined control and it's safe to assume most of us know how to use them by heart. This controller really shines when used for couch and bed based gaming. It's an absolute joy then, and I regularly grab it instead of my capillary-bursting expensive 360 controller.
I feel like the $60 CAD price tag was worth it.

Sure, there is some story and a bit of a narrative... but it's mostly inconsequential and shoved aside (sometimes quite beautifully even in-universe), and is not annoying nor does it get in the way. Doom is about killing demons in absolutely hectic battles, and none of that soap story stuff. And this game does it beautifully.
id Software has lost their edge over the last decade or so, releasing game after game (and not even so many of them) that tried to improve technically, but forgetting what makes games actually good, and thus the results have been relatively "meh". Not bad, but not that good either. Just meh. However, Doom is a great attempt at getting out of that creative slump, and returning to the basics, to what id Software was formerly good at.

The game was perfect back in its 2003 release, now it is ruined by unnecessary balancing to weapons, powerups and perks as well as removal of perks from Quest mode. The stages are now marked with a star when completed without taking hits, but the game was not at all balanced to that and it requires tremendous amount of luck to perform in later stages, making the lives of the completionists amongst us extremely miserable.
As the old saying goes, if it ain't broke, don't fix it.

If you're like me and loved the original Crimsonland (from 2002), then I would NOT recommend this game. Sadly, it is nothing more than a watered down version of the old game. Several key features that made the game great are now missing.
- No perks in quest mode. This is HUGE! For some reason 10tons removed perks from main campaign mode. Which basically took all the fun out of the core gameplay.
- No weapon switching. You are now only able to have one weapon at a time, which not only limits your fun, but also your ability to win.
- No choosing when to take your next perk. There used to be a button for leveling up, which was very handy. It is now gone and instead the player simply levels up immediately via a pop-up menu. Not only does this detract from the overall strategy of the game, but it's also horribly disruptive. It will cause you to lose focus on the action, make mistakes, or even worse: accidentally pick the wrong perk. Because you have only one second to stop clicking before the perk menu pops up, you risk clicking on a random perk if you don't stop shooting.
- No timer on powerups. It's a small thing, but again, it takes away from the subtle strategy of the game. There used to be a small timer for each individual powerup off to the side of the screen. That has been replaced with a generic circle icon surrounding the player character. You won't know how much time is left on any of your powerups except the most recent one.
Without these features the game is, as one user said, butchered. It simply isn't as fun and doesn't contain the depth of strategy it used to. I'd recommend going online and finding a freeware version of the 2002 Crimsonland.

First of all, I would like to correct a common misunderstanding. You do not require 6 people to play. Each ship has 6 roles that can be filled with "up to 6 people". Having one person take care of one thing makes it really comfortable and this is the way, this game is meant to be played. But it is perfectly possible for 3 people to have the responsibility of 2 stations, and fly the ship with its full potential (in a single instance of game client). I have 4 friends that got comfortable with the game, and now we're running comparatively easier set games with 2 separate ships (3 and 2 people per ship). Sometimes I like playing the game solo, even though it's hard to do so and possible only under lower difficulty settings. I'd say having 5-6 people per ship is ideal, but with 3+ people the game is absolutely playable.
Second false information all over the place. You do not need a separate pc with its own copy of the game to be the server. Go in the Steam/Steamapps/Common/Artemis and run artemis.exe. First window should be set to server mode. Now run it again, and make the second window the client. I personally connect my huge TV to my laptop and become the server, use the TV for the server screen (which is also the outside view of the ship), and use my laptop screen for the client screen (which is the screen of whatever role I'm filling). Entering 'localhost' will connect to the server running on the same machine.
I realize that this is more like a troubleshoot, instead of being a review. But in the process of deciding to buy the game, I immediately recognized how awesome this game is. The questions I had were the ones I just described. You don't need this review to know that this game is awesome, it's already all over the place. What you need to know is that the most frightening part of the game (6 people minimum thing), is actually incorrect. Also; it is possible for up to 8 ships to play Co-Op or PvP modes. Talk about awesome.

I played this game big WoT brother for couple years already (still playing it from time to time with friends) and I can tell you that WoT Blitz is good.
Pros:
- Battles are shorter, about 2 mins: battles have more action, I practically don't see snipers sitting whole battle in the bushes, it's just doesn't work here.
- no arti.
- gold rounds has less damage (or less penetration in some cases), so you think twice before shooting it.
- +-1 tier is much better comparing to +-2 in big WoT
- no need to put any money if you are playing I-VI tiers
- this is not Pay-to-Win. You can buy everething with silver (ingame currency). It's pay to progress faster.
Cons:
- of course Wargaming wants to milk your money, so stock tanks suffer until you have 100% crew and open at least a second gun on it.
- the most of the tank trees are built to have a couple very bad tanks to stimulate you to spend money and just past it.
- maps are very similar... just hills. Very little difference in tactics - stay close, don't get yourself in crossfire, attack when you have advantage in numbers. Maps don't change that. Big WoT has a lot of maps that force you to play differently. A lot of progress needed here.
Suggestions to developer:
- tanks are officially blind, view range is VERY small. It feels very strange. I understand that it because of small maps, but it needs some kind of rework.
- please add some achievements and prizes for them. I like medals, but it would be nice to get 100 gold for Kolobanov medal or for first 100 destroyed enemy tanks...
Overall:
- Good alternative to big WoT
- Fun to play
- Truly free to play (at least for small tiers where you can be out of stock in 2-3 battles)

I've had 300+ hours of fun with this game and haven't paid a single penny for any of it. Not that I wouldn't, it deserves the support, but I didn't
, and that's what's important. Thanks to constant competitions, loot bag events, sales and other special events, I've been able to earn enough in-game currency to buy whatever 'Mech I want and do whatever I want to it; I've even won a couple of free mechs (A Cicada and a Centurion).
It's great fun, and if you like giant robots, lasers or team-based shooters, I highly recommend it.

Primer: If you play this, finish the Mech Academy and your first 25 games to get your cadet bonus C-Bills, save those and play the freebie mechs until you find a frame to your liking then spend your money. Mechs can take a while to grind out if you're not stacking premium time or buying them outright. Just a PSA
8/10
Good:
-Fun (no I mean that give that some thought)
-Mech game
-Quality Mechanics
-Quick Play isn't terrible
-VOIP (organize when in game and most people arent toxic from what I've seen)
-Connection is consistent (i average around 80-130 ping in NA servers where i usually play, its higher than some games for me, compared to Overwatch where the highest i see regularly is 60-70 but its a different game and you don't notice. Take that from a guy who's played twitch shooters for nearly 20 years.)
Bad:
-Not "Armored Core" (playful joke for those who know)
-Mech balance can be amazing to terrible depending on what just happened with the "most recent patch"
for more on that.
-Can soak up money like a sponge if you don't have good wallet control. (How many WoT premiums / time did you buy? yeah same thing here)
-UI is a mess, but its useable if you trudge through it for a day or so. Its not terrible, just not great.
-Has the same Meta shift most games like it do (again WoT) where whats good in one patch may be unuseable in the next or overpowered, the dice roll is real.
-Faction Play has no point (if that's the entire reason you're here, just don't)*
Extended commentary:
If you're looking for a Mech game this is about the best one I've played on PC if you enjoy even the most remote idea of tactics and teamwork, granted you're going to have to talk to other people and go out of your way to co-ordinate with them both verbally and with mech selection (makes the game better IMO) so know that going in.
You can solo que this up pretty good but the game shines when working with a team (of any number really 2 man squads all the way up to full 12's are fun when you can get them. The more people in each team that are organized the more fun the Quick play que is.
Mechs have strengths and weaknesses which should be obvious based on class / weapon location / speed / armor etc:
I'll say this as well MWO gets a lot of flack for PGI seeming to be a greedy company rolling out mech packs for sale / pre-order (just look over at
for examples) and i'm sure that can be easily seen as such. However to be fair they do produce consistent products on a semi regular basis for those looking to get more new stuff and they do, all be it sometimes ham fistedly, try to take care of the game.
*Faction play is not to be trusted, some enjoy it but I'm willing to bet they are a minority and it requires good teamwork and already having a decent stock of mechs in the garage, so it wont be where you start out.
In conclusion I have fun with this game and play a lot of genres that sometimes don't treat me so well recently, MWO hasn't done that to me. I've purchased a mech that turned out to be bad, sure, but it's still fun to build and take into the Solo que with different weapons and configurations trying to make something work. Afterall thats how you improve as a builder and pilot.
Not as boring as Chromehounds, not nearly as bleeding edge as Armored Core. MWO sits very comfortably in the middle as a tactical-esque arcade mech shooter that treats its players alright as long as they arent looking for hand outs.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution (DXHR) is the third installment in the Deus Ex series of games. This is a prequel to both Deus Ex and Deus Ex: Invisible War.
The previous games were set in the distant future (2050's) where human augmentation is a reality, the United States is no longer a major global power, mega corporations have filled the power vacuum and conspiracies abound.
Set in 2027, some twenty years earlier before Deus Ex, you portray Adam Jensen, chief of security of Sarif Industries, a mid-sized manufacturer of human augmentations and contractor to the United States military. Along with Megan Reed your former flame and chief scientist of the same company and CEO David Sarif, they are about to make a major announcement of a discovery that will potentially make human augmentation accessible to all. With the goal to enhance human lives, Sarif sees this as the start of the next stage of human evolution.
The story is relatively easy to follow and isn't going to intimidate you, definately not one for those wanting something deeper, however it does contain a fair bit of well researched science and futurism to create a credible future. Progression storywise is well paced, but felt a bit short towards the end, given the original premise. The Director's Cut commentary explains that some of what was originally planned for the game but had to be cut. The original DLC The Missing Link attempted to correct that missing chunk of story towards the end, and is integrated into the core game, with this edition of the game. Although I feel they could taken the extra time to also add further elements to further flesh out the story.
The aesthetics of the game are remincent of the Blade Runner or original Total Recall movies, which is a huge plus. Indeed, this is one aspect of the game that is an improvement over its predecessors. The music is beautiful and for me the biggest pro of the game. I was a little disappointed in the character animation though, specifically the conversation animations seemed to be rather limited in variation. This was probably due to time constraints as well as mentioned earlier.
Like the previous installments it is a first person shooter (FPS) with stealth elements and ability to complete tasks using different paths. This largely follows what was possible in earlier iterations of the series.
There are three styles of gameplay: the direct, indirect and stealth approaches. For instance to open a door you can take out a guard then take the code from them (direct), hack a computer terminal for the code (indirect) or just bypass the door itself via another route (stealth).
Combat likewise has varied options with melee combat (called a takedown), an array of short to long range ballistic, energy and chemical weapons as well as the option to (depending on the weapon of choice) lethally and non-lethally taking out your opponent. Almost all weapons can be upgraded to suit your style of play as well.
The core gameplay mechanic of the game is of course to aquire augmentations as the game progresses and allows you to essentially gain a variety of superhuman abilities over time. I won't go into specifics as this is what makes Deus Ex stand out from other FPS's. But they are well worth the wait as they add to the tools at your disposal, when completing the various tasks.
Overall the game comprises a healthy mix of a well structured story, game play, character development all set in a cyberpunk, distopian future. If you liked Thief & Hitman and a fan of Sci-Fi then I recommended giving this game a go.
