Deus Ex: Human Revolution is what brought my interest back to RPGs and first-person shooters. When I first heard about this game through a list of reccomended games I first had quite a few doubts about it, thinking that it would be another typical, overly-cliched, military-based first person shooter game, but boy was I wrong! To start off, this game's sub-stories aren't set in stone like most other RPG's, as when you're on a quest you're constantly given some choices you have to make, all of which affect what happens later on in the game, which adds quite a bit of mystery that makes you eager to explore the game. On a topic tangent to the storyline, you have a wide variety of skills to choose from as you earn XP's, in which the skills you choose have a consequence on your gameplay experience, so depending on you that may be good or bad, mainly depending on if you decide to be naive with your choices.
Furthermore this game doesn't feel too constrained in terms of it setting, seeing as how you're constantly moving around the globe from mission-to-mission. Lastly, this game has quite some great music to it. So ultimately, do I reccommend this game? In my opinion I definitely would to those who have a great sense of exploration and action.

This game has everything you would want in a 4x space strategy game.  Except for one key thing that imho is most vital in a 4x strategy game ... the space combat is absolutely, without a doubt, the worst I have ever seen in a 4x strategy game with the possible exception of MOO 3.  Its just a matter of seleting a few 'cards' at the start of the battle and click a button.  Thats it.  No strategy and no real planning.  Just hope you pick the one card that trumps whatever random card the AI happens to pick (If the fleets are evenly matched).  There is no way of possibly guessing or knowing what the enemy will pick based on thier weapon platforms (that I could tell) and ship design.  Might as well close your eyes and pick, its just as effective as anything else you might pick (tested!).  Than click a button and watch the ships slug it out (no fleet control) and cross your fingers!
This is most unfortunate because the rest of the game has everything you would want! Customizable races, heroes and fleets that level up, deep/rich/interesting tech tree, lotsa resources to Xploit, customizable ships... ect ect.  It seems the dev spent all this time in creating an awesome game then spent about 10 minutes implementing a combat system before release.
If you arent into the combat aspect of 4x games you would really like this title but if interesting/tactical/fun combat is something you are looking for in a space strategy game stay away from this one!

PROS
- Unique and interesting playable factions with a robust suite of options for creating your own.
- Great art design and graphics that still hold up well. Massive battles between fleets of ships are especially impressive.
- So many ways to be "hands on" with your empire such as building your own custom military units and battle plans.
- Very well thought systems for colonization and development of your systems and planets.
- An interesting tech tree that doesn't feel copied and pasted from similar games.
- A more exciting late game than a lot of similar games.
CONS
- Less than stellar AI. There are mods that make it a little more interesting but for the most part it's not amazing.
- High learning curve. Even if you've played games like Civilization before, there's a lot of different systems to learn here.

Prototype is an action-adventure open world game.
You are Alex Mercer, a man without memory armed with amazing superhuman powers and the option to go most anywhere you like and do most anything you want once you get there.
A virus outbreak has claimed Manhattan, forcing the island into a military quarantine. The infected citizens turning the population into mutants.
The main story path is entirely linear. The missions are a sloppy mix of poorly paced ideas. Long missions involve simply going from one end of Manhattan to the other, while some of the short missions are climactic sieges and battles. Missions can be brutally challenging, often because of the uncooperative auto-lock system. Boss battles are much longer than they need to be and more often test your endurance rather than your skill.
As you work your way through the game, you will earn experience points that can be used to unlock new and ever more exotic powers. Experience points are also the only thing you get by finding collectibles.
The graphics are not the best, buildings and environments are ugly, so the world is not a place you want to explore.
All in all, the awful boring and repeating missions and linear gameplay ruins the overall experience.

A different kind of cinematic hacking simulation.
Like the classic game Uplink, this is a "hacking" game where you play as a hacker as interpreted by pop culture.  But instead of the cinematic style of being an elite hacker of anarchy in trenchcoat, typing console commands rapidly with flowing green text on black background, in this game you play as investigator working in an intrusive cyber crime law enforcement agency.
Sure, you'll spend some time on some simplified magical console command, but you'll spend your time more in the ingame-windows-mockup, browsing with pretend-internet-explorer, checking your suspects' blogs, tracking paper trails of drug transactions and who uses which bank account. Hacking is a tool, the important thing is knowing what you need to get that arrest warrant. If you need to gain access to a site to get it, then you use your magic console command.
So far for me  this game feels both simple and complex. You'll overthink things and underthink things. The user interface feels strangely both overly simple and overly complex, using your magic console command to gain access to sites you're not meant to both feels too simple and feels too much busywork.
But either way, this is a quite a unique and satisfying game, where you do feel like an investigator in some corny Law and Order cybercrime spin-off, trying to track someone who's stealing the all city's IP Address using their GUI ICQ HTTP. I'm fully expecting to encounter a site with spinning skull animation later on.

Minecraft is a sandbox video game created and designed by Swedish game designer Markus "Notch" Persson, and later fully developed and published by Mojang. The creative and building aspects of Minecraft enable players to build constructions out of textured cubes in a 3D procedurally generated world. Other activities in the game include exploration, resource gathering, crafting, and combat. Multiple gameplay modes are available, including a survival mode where the player must acquire resources to build the world and maintain health, a creative mode where players have unlimited resources to build with and the ability to fly, an adventure mode where players can play custom maps created by other players, and a spectator mode where players can fly around and clip through blocks, but cannot place or destroy any. The PC version of the game is noted for its modding scene, where a dedicated community creates new gameplay mechanics, items, and assets for the game.

The gyroscope!

Overall i'd say it's a really good controller. But after 1 day i can already see it'll be replacing my xbox one controller for casual gaming when i don't want to sit at my desk and just want to relax. (i even played diablo 3 with it comfortably) The touchpads gave me much more accuracy than a stick, and combined with the gyro on right thumb pad/left trigger down it gave me the finer control of my crosshair that's needed for FPS games. It takes a while to get used to and while a bit clunky at first, it is a decent controller.
Highlights:
Personally, it's a bit too large, thus feeling a bit clunky. It feels like it needs to be scaled down about 10-15% and it would be perfect.
The touchpad is interesting and allows for a pretty solid control of the mouse pointer, although I don't recommend it for games that require fast aiming as nothing really beats mouse for precision aiming.
The curve of the back of the controller seems a bit uncomfortable. The controller feels like it's always sliding out of my hands, although this may be an issue with the controller's size itself.
Battery life is great, it does use 2 x AA batteries, but I haven't had to change mine in the past couple months.
The controller can be plugged in with the provided cable if you choose, but I use mine solely wirelessly.
The feedback and input of the controller are spot-on.
Final Thoughts:
Overall it's a nice controller if you don't already have one. My Steam Controller replaced my long-used 360 controller and after a brief adjustment period, I definitely won't be going back.

Renegade Ops, or as I like to call it, "EXPLOSIONS", is a top down action arcade type game from the guys behind Just Cause 2, and like Just Cause 2, the story is awful and the game is a blast.  You take control of one of 5 vehicles with an all-direction machine gun and basically roll around blasting every damn thing you see into a dazzling explosion.  A lot of the game is about racking up high scores, allowing for a little competitive gameplay with your friends list, but also offers online multiplayer to allow co-op play as well.  The story has 9 levels and takes about 5 hours to complete, but some will find replay value in the co-op and the ability to level the other characters as well.  It obviously can get a bit repetitive and frustrating to those who lack the hand-eye coordination to drive a car smoothly and fire a directional machine gun, but if you're looking for a fun, arcade-like challenge, you'll find this one well worth the $15 price tag.  Michael Bay would be proud.

Multiplayer is offered to too, so you're not going in alone and overall, RO is a great diversion from much more serious game types. I would strongly recommend a 360 pad for this game as it's much better suited than K&M for inputs.
The only nagging issue I have with the game is that at certain stages, the game suddenly decides that you have 3mins for example to complete the objective at hand. Often, this is not long enough - and tied-in with little in the way of a saved game feature - means that many frustrating replays can be had.
Still, it's a very good blaster. Well worth adding to anyone's Steam Library. 8.5/10

Prototype is what happens when you combine the urbanized open worldness of GTA4 with the plot of Crysis 2 (except the virus is a Left 4 Dead / Resident Evil-esque virus instead of aliens) with a protagonist that is essentially a cross between a biological human T-1000 and DC comic's Parasite (he consumes people to gain abilities, knowledge, skills, etc). The superpowered gameplay is definitely my favorite part, there are many ways to win the major story battles and sidemissions with the various moves at your command. As Alex Mercer, you can either pick up guns and rocket launchers or become a weapon yourself by shape shifting your body into claws, blades, bludgeons, whips and even a cannon ball move that launches you toward your target with enough force to blow up armored vehicles later in the game. Speaking of armored vehicles, you can hijack tanks and skyjack helicopter gunships (and this even looks exactly like that scene in T2 where the T-1000 gets on that chopper and tells the guy to get out LOL). When on foot and exploring Manhatten you use your augmented abilities to parkour the landscape, at full upgrades you can leap over 5 story buildings easily and glide / airdash through the air very similiarly to how mario from Super Mario World glides with the super cape. There is an element of Metal Gear Solid in this game too since you can shape shift into other people that you consume, ie soldiers or pedestrians in the street in order to blend in since the military is constantly looking for you. The story mode is pretty unique: your character wakes up having exactly the same knowledge the player does as to what is going on, and through a mechanic known as the web of intrigue you eventually come to understand the game's story and background on everything that is going on around you. As you explore Manhatten you will find people with the Web of Intrigue icon over their head indicating that they can be consumed by you to learn what they know in connection to everything that happened. This game features sidemissions that show up on the game's minimap that will showcase your skills with the various abilities you acquire and see how fast you can be parkouring from place to place and get bronze/silver/gold/platinum medals depending on your 1337ness.
I started playing this and finished it in about a week, making sure to get every sidemission completed on platinum. Because the plot is advanced through Web of Intrigue it is possible to finish the game without getting every bit of story out of it so I did a new game+ to find the remaining consume targets to get the whole story. For the most part the main story missions are easy with some tricky boss fights that really make you use all of your abilities to some degree, the most challenging aspect of this game is definitely getting platinum in every sidemission (think classic NES game level challenging). Overall I give this game a solid recommendation for its fluid gameplay (I love the parkour!) :)

Endless Space is a turn-based 4X strategy game, covering the space colonization age in the Endless universe, where you can control every aspect of your civilization as you strive for galactic dominion.
I like 4x space games, but I try not to play them that much because most often than not they require lots and lots of time, which I usually don't have. And if a game is good it turns into just one more turn, just one more turn, just one more turn, and then it's 3am and I have to go to work in a few hours. And that's how Endless Space treated me when I got to play it. Damn, the endless in the title is there for a reason.
There is no single player campaign to speak of, but you get a small/medium/large map with 1-7 enemies thrown in and just go at it. You can win in several ways, by waging war, trading, science, etc. Usual stuff. There are lots of races, lots of planet upgrades, lots of spaceship combinations (you build your own ships!). And everything looks quite pretty and is accompanied by nice music.
I liked:
* nice graphics
* huge map with 8 players is lots of fun
* lots of civil and military upgrades to toy with
* you can create your own race
* that just-one-more-turn feeling
I disliked:
* steep learning curve and the tutorials blow
* that just-one-more-turn feeling (I don't have enough time!)
* it's almost impossible to meet certain victory conditions
Get this:
* if you like 4x games
Don't get this:
* if you don't like 4x games
* if you're looking for a quick game

Top down shooter like Smash TV, Dead Frontier, Bunch of Heroes, GTA (1 and 2).  The graphics are okay for this type of game, but there is no music/sound if you just walk and aren't shooting.
The gameplay is too slow for me.  There isn't an option to skip through to the harder levels.  You are forced to play through the easy levels.  The game controls are simple, WASD to move and click to shoot.  Aside from the slow gameplay, the biggest problem for me was that mobs can spawn anywhere.  They do not come in off of the screen, so it's possible to die with full health because they spawn where you are standing.  You literally have no chance to move or defend yourself (this is the only way I was killed twice in the 30 minutes I played.  Level 2 - 8).  The levels appear to be static, so you can learn where they spawn and stay away from those areas, but I didn't like this aspect of the game.
The power ups appear where you kill a mob.  If you are skilled and kill mobs across the screen, due to your slow movement, there's a good chance the power up will disappear before you can loot it.  When a nuke drop (destroys all mobs close to you), you sometimes have to kill the mobs that are close to you to get to it.  By the time you can get it, there are no mobs to destroy with the power up.
There are spawners that pop up (think Gauntlet) which the mobs also spawn from.  I think the game could be a lot better if it had random spawning (off screen) or if they had pure spawners.  The only time I've had a slower runner was in Parasite Eve. :)

This is one I really wanted to like. Learn about the mechanics of firearms. (As machines go, firearms are pretty amazing.) Emphasis on detail and realism. Sounds perfect. Emphasis on "sounds."
And it would be, except it uses the painful Apple App Store model: you can earn unlocking points at a snail's pace (in this case, both "experience"
credits) or you can...you guessed it...buy 'em. Adding insult to injury, you can't unlock whatever model you want as you go. Nope, there's a
for some reason which dictates what guns you can unlock and when. Except we all know the reason, don't we? Sure do: money!
At the end of the day, when we're being honest with ourselves, progressing through the game without paying for unlocks isn't going to happen. You could devote the same length of time to going through actual gunsmithing training. So you're going to end up paying $50 to unlock all the guns. Or do the smart thing and wait for a sale.
Once you do buy your unlock, though, this game becomes incredible. Each model is highly detailed and exquisitely precise. It's not just about disassembly and assembly, either; in the Operation mode where you can watch the gun fire, you can select which parts you want to be transparent so you can understand the operating principles. While there are cookie-cutter "x-ray" views, this dynamic transparency tool is outstanding. Combined with variable-degree slow motion, you can really get a feel for how each part does its thing.
Were it not for the microtransaction bull, I'd be giving this one a thumbs-up without so much as a second's hesitation. Sure, it's pricey, but the level of detail and precision are worth it. So I'm going to recommend this game with one
caveat: expect to buy the all-access pass currently priced at $50, because if you don't, you'll be unlocking about two new guns every decade (and with ridiculous amounts of grinding) or you'll piecemeal buy everything eventually at a massive markup. So go ahead, get it, enjoy it, but prepare to pay quite a sum for a fully-working copy.

The Director’s cut for Deus Ex Human Revolution is better than the standard edition in some ways while it kind of takes a step back in another way. The experience in its entirety is improved overall, and it manages to be a solid entry in the series.

The gameplay is almost identical to the original Deus Ex released in 2000. It plays as an open area first person shooter with role playing game mechanics in the form of anatomic mechanical augments which are purchased using praxis points, Human Revolution’s version of skill points. In terms of the shooting, the controls can be quite awkward starting out, and is something that they could have tried to fix if they were revamping the game. The right mouse button is used for going into a third person like cover system which allows the player to hide and see what is around the corner, and also can be used to shoot somewhat inaccurately at enemies. It serves best as a means of scouting or cover melee takedowns. When shooting its best to stick to first person mode. Herein lies the next control quirk. Since the right mouse button is mapped to cover, aim down sights is toggled by pressing the middle mouse button, making aiming feel cumbersome. Because of this control scheme, it is hard to recommend taking an aggressive approach. It is best played in a stealthy manner, using non-lethal melee takedowns, headshots with suppressed weapons, or non-lethal weapons. One thing to note is that melee takedowns require energy cells. By default the player is given two and can obtain more through augmentation, however only the first two will auto recharge. In order to get a full charge on extended cells one must eat a freaking huge jar of protein powder or protein bars. The augment system is as robust as it is intuitive, and it lends itself exceptionally well to the open approach that is encouraged in pretty much every situation except boss fights. Boss fights are much improved from the standard edition and no matter what play style you choose, you won’t run up against any difficult walls. The second boss fight in particular was nigh impossible to beat without having the typhoon augment in the standard edition. That being said, with the typhoon augment the second boss is super easy. The inventory system consists of a bunch of squares; a beer or energy bar take up one square, whereas certain guns can take up to twelve. It is wise to decide what to keep and what to sell depending on how you choose to play. Inventory capacity can be expanded via augments if you really think you are going to use that huge gun. Hacking can be a huge part of the game for stealthy players and can be augmented so that Jensen will be harder to detect by the anti-intrusion software systems. Hacking is performed via a simplified abstraction of the real thing and is quite fun. To perform a hack, walk up to a door or computer terminal and select the hack option, if your hacking skill is equal to or greater than that door or computer system’s level then you are  given the chance to try and hack it. Once the hacking mini game begins, you will have to capture various nodes to capture the main node. All the nodes are laid out across a linear web like system with sometimes multiple paths to the main node. With different one time software items that can be used during the process the system becomes really fun, and it never feels tedious or tiring. Of course if you don’t develop the hacking skill, you can always just toss an automatic unlocking device that you purchased at that black market weapons dealer, and that is why the game is so much fun to play. You are given freedom to tackle problems your way, to a certain extent. You can also opt to be a smooth talker to get yourself out of certain situations, or convince somebody to let you into a restricted area, or to divulge information. Persuasion can be augmented to activate a pheromone system that analyzes an npc’s personality type as beta, alpha, or omega and will have a meter to hint as to which dialogue option should be chosen. The game play is just so solid and offers a wide variety of options making it some of the most robust and modular that you will see in the triple “A” space today.

Looking at the world of Human Revolution, it is split into different open areas that Jensen is able to explore. Any side quests must be finished before leaving said area or else they will not be able to be completed, even though you will return to two of the locations, which is nothing new if you have played the original Deus Ex. Each area is not that large, but contains many hidden passages and locked doors which give the player a lot of freedom to play according to their style. In Deus Ex the level design is not about quantity but all about how intricate and approachable any given scenario can be. All the areas in Human Revolution are metropolitan or industrial and give off a futuristic vibe that is very fictional but also seems very believable. All the areas are populated in the right way, with npcs and open areas where they should be. The world and level design is a very strong point for this game.

The story of Human Revolution takes place before the time of JC Denton, Deus Ex’s protagonist. At this time human augmentation is just starting to take off with scientists largely supporting them and seeing them as a means to the advancement of the human race. Others are strongly opposed to them. The protagonist of this story is Adam Jensen, who is more or less a one tone very boring dude. This does not hamper the story overall in any way, as it is able to deliver compelling and cohesive writing that is easy to follow and serves as an engaging action thriller. Jensen is thrust along one task at a time to unravel the greater mystery and players behind the shadowy and elusive factions that are vying for their own goals. The conclusion is satisfying and offers the player a choice of up to four endings depending on how many of the optional objectives are completed in the final area.  Delving into the side content there are a handful of very well thought out side quests that offer intriguing side narratives to help flesh out this world and some give a sort of side window into Jensen’s life before the beginning events of the story. In the earlier half of the game the optional markers make you feel a sort of urgency, it is something about the shape or size of the markers that beckon you in a strange way to them. The side quests in the first half feel relevant while the latter ones don’t feel as much so. One huge problem with the story’s pacing that also pours over into the gameplay lays in the inclusion of the Missing Link DLC into the main game. It happens about two thirds of the way into the story and kind of throws a wrench in what otherwise might be considered an amazing story. The main reason that it feels so out of place is that Adam Jensen loses all the abilities he has picked up throughout the course of the narrative, and the player is forced to start again from scratch until the end of that segment in which all the stuff you had is returned to you. This just feels so jarring and could have been done without. Because of this particular choice, instead of an amazing story the game has a great one.
If you are wondering if you should buy the director’s cut of Deus Ex Human Revolution, the answer is yes. It offers a healthy helping of great extras, a free and open approach to gameplay in part due to its great level design, the story is great, the graphics are passable, but the performance is great.

I have spent the better part of a year trying to convince myself this was a worthy investment.  And yet on the shelf it sits like many other products that unfortunately fall short of their full potential.  I actually use a 35$ Used controller in it's stead almost all of the time due to the harassment of using this product.
I have been so excited since I got this controller to be able to finally find a game I really, truly enjoyed using it with.
I so looked forward to jamming unconvential games like Dota, and other RTS's with this controller.  I've played first person shooters, DOTA 2, WoW, other MOBA's, and Emulators of various generations with this controller.
instead of enjoying the games it's meant to be playing.  If this product had half the intuition of an Xbone controller it would topple the controller market forever.  Unfortunately you have to rely on the playerbase, yourself, and an extremely complicated setup to get the true nature of the controller to reveal itself.  I have spent many more, and I do mean many, more hours playing with the damn program to set this thing up, than I have actually spent playing games.  It's not intuitive, FPS's don't automatically seek out a comfort level on sensitivity, you have to adjust settings both in-game and out of game constantly to find some type of appealing balance between a "natural" controller feel and to get any benefit of the high levels of sensitivity and control provided by the device.
I recently had the lovely experience of losing access to my steam account due to a phone loss.  Upon switching my account and attempting to utilize my controller offline, I truly felt some shame at the controller's offline capabilities.  I realized then that this is not a product intended for offline use, and I wouldn't even bother attempting to take it to a friends house to show it off, due to the excess of time required for setup and the lack of offline capabilities.  I could not use my configs, I could not load what I would consider "Default" configurations, and eventually, like most days, I myself defaulted to a controller that actually works when I plug it in without hassle.
The weight ratio is grand, as someone who suffers from chronic arthritis of the elbow, wrist, and fingers, it feels comfortable to hold, and the weight can be modified on the fly simply by removing or adding the batteries.  The shape is ergonomic, the pads feel fantastic, the haptic/tactile response is amazing.
If we all take a look back at the controllers that we grew up with, well, they all started out pretty shoddy and worked their way up to the excellent gaming devices they are today.
I am not a "console guy", I am a hardcore PC gamer who respects his own time investments and there are only two deep regrets I have with this product for that reason alone.
Don't buy the Steam controller because it's a good controller unless you're willing to suffer through an admittedly feature full configuration setup software that will hassle you without end.  I have yet to have had that plug 'n' play experience you wish for.   It begs you to play with the configuration software over and over again until you want to give up.  And I do.  I have submitted every time to this supposedly great controller.  I don't know any sensible person who would stubbornly bash their head into this product the way I have.
I pick it up time and time again to be disappointed with the results.  Which usually involve me staring at a configuration screen, my in-game settings, and a general distaste for fineggling with settings that I thought I left behind when my girlfriend threw down on a nice 700$ gaming PC we could play together.
I'm not that gamer who buys a game and sits it through.  I like to change games like some people flip through TV channels and this is the least condusive controller on the market for someone who likes to throw down at the drop of a hat. For someone who has a group of friends that enjoys a large variety of games and different experiences.  And someone who has chronic pain on one side and needs some quick relief from the mouse and keyboard so that I can be the Champion, The Hero, The Warrior, I was meant to be.  If you're anything like me, avoid this product and it's confuggling software man...  Still the nicest paperweight I own though.

Great game if you enjoy space games and more importantly team work..
Originally developed as a LAN Party game, it has been given some basic internet connectivity and works *somewhat well*..
Artemis puts you and 3-5 (recommended min 4 players - max 6 players) of your friends in command of a star ship.
Each person has specific roles assigned to them, the roles are:
- Captain (The boss)
- Helm (The driver)
- Weapons (Pew Pew Officer)
- Engineering (Must be short, scottish and unable to reach the control panels)
- Science (Sensors, Scanning and Voyeur)
- Communications (Intergalactic Receptionist)
You can easily condense Science and Coms into one role as they are the least demanding.
It is also possible to play the game with as little as 3 people but not as efficiently as with 4 or more.
Those with multiple screens are able to run a role on each screen simply by running the executable from the game folder, dragging the resolution dialog that pops up at the start to the screen they want and pressing start.
Multiple roles can also be handled by single screen users also via tabs that appear along the top of the screen.
The game is simple and does not have a huge amount of content but is highly enjoyable as one of those now and then small event/group games.
Grab a group of your friends you think might be into this type of game, fire it up, forward the needed ports (See guides) and have a blast or just sit back and wait for someone to make a silly decision, hit the wrong button or warp everyone into the middle of a mine field..
Also, if you are into lighting systems, the game actually has DMX support  so you can hook it up to DMX enable lights and program cues.

Some people compare Endless Space (ES) to the classics of 4X, say, Master or Orion II. I disagree with that comparison, and would say ES occupies a slightly different niche: a complex, but not /quite/ as complex 4X game, very pretty to look at, very good music, and plenty of fun.
Compared to MOOII, there's less to optimize, battles are played out faster, per turn you spend less time on giving orders, so I'd say it's overall slightly less complex, and a bit more "casual" -- but not by much.
So MOOII (and perhaps: Civ), and Endless Space on the other hand, fulfill two different kind of 4X needs, in my opinion: maximum complexity, but sometimes being a bit dragged out for the former, very enjoyable, easy to jump in and out, but a bit more casual, the latter.

So it's a "hacking" game, set in a fictional country that I suspect is based on the UK. The graphics are nice, with a particular colorful and pixelated style that's easy on the eyes. The sound is good, with understated music and occasional sound effects that make you think of "classic" computer systems. The writing is reasonably good, amusing and dramatic where it needs to be. The gameplay is much more in the realm of social engineering than "real" hacking; you poke around computer systems, read documents, guess the answers to puzzles, that sort of thing. So to my mind it doesn't really seem like an "authentic" experience, but it's pretty fun. There are definitely some clever moments, especially the final puzzle where...I don't want to spoil it, but you explore several computer systems in a clever way.

Overall I would said this was a fun little game.  Not too complex to require looking up a guide but complex enough to have me sitting and thinking about a solution for a little while on certain cases.  Story was decent.  That being said, I wasn't too satisfied by the final case.  The evidence required to solve it didn't quite make sense, IMO.

Solve cases by pseudo-hacking other people's accounts and look for contextual clues to the case at hand. Submit the suspect, location, and evidence pointing to the case to produce an arrest.
I just finished the 3rd case. I've had to look online for help in every case. This makes me think the game is poorly designed.
A few good ideas, but overall poor execution.
Good ideas
- I like the pixel art
- I enjoy the pseudo emulation of an older Operating System
Poor Execution
- there are seemingly several ways to try to convict a suspect, given the multitude of evidence pieces one can submit; however this quickly turns into trial-and-error. Given a suspect / location / evidence combination, you'll be graded right or wrong. Submitting a wrong answer does not produce a penalty. You end up submitting several combinations in order to solve the case. This becomes frustrating, as it's no longer a logic-based game, but one where you *think* you have it right, get it wrong, then submit all other logical combinations in frustration.
It's almost there, but not good enough for me to recommend.

TL:DR; Good game, short and to the point. Sometimes too easy but worth a buy, especially if found on sale.
Pros:
-Great Artstyle (If you like Papers, Please or Please Don't Touch Anything you will love this)
-Great Gameplay Ideas (would love to see other game with that Switching OS's idea)
-Later Half of the game does a good job of switching things up on you and making the situation feel a bit more personal
-The Mainline system did make me feel a bit badass at times (Possible a con for some, since the gameplay for it don't change at all through out the game, i was ok with it)
Cons:
-Game is too linear, just when you think you can explore a bit just for fun. You find out the devs never programmed anything that far. (Example: You might find a website or email address, and you want to look it up just for fun but the devs never made anything for it. Would be nice to have more side stuff to hack into or mess around with.)
-Difficulty to some might be level of hand holding
-You personally never feel really attached to anything as a player and the character you play as (You don't really feel like you or your character is a part of the world and everything going on in it, the later chapters start to sort of fix that but by the time you feel something the game is over.)
-Like i said in the Pros list the Mainline System is the main gameplay aspect used in this game (To hack, check IP address, download stuff, etc.) and it can get repetative since it does not change at all
This was my first foray in the Hacker-esque type of games. I had my eye on Orwell, Uplink, Hacknet, etc. but Mainlining hit the right spot with its artwork reminding me of Papers, Please (there might be people that hate that fact that so many games are in a sense "copying" that style but to me i can get enough of it, if done right).
Took me about 8 hours to beat but honestly i left the computer running during gameplay many times so i would say a leisure run through this game for me was really about 6 hours. Once over the game definitely leaves you wanting more but the aesthetics of the "papers' please" type of games always has that to it (Perfect example is the great game "Please Don't Touch Anything").
Difficulty was honestly easy, very easy, sometimes holding your hand easy...but for my first outing in this type of game it showed me what was possible with it and left me wanting a game developer to take advantage of it, so to say in short i kinda have a hunger for more games like this but I definitely need more challenge.
Gameplay mechanics and story was very well done, for a kickstarted game. It seems like the devs had a plan they wanted to execute, they just needed money and once they got the support they needed, they created it flawlessly. The only downside to that is the game feels very linear (Meaning i wish there was even more stuff i could hack it to just for fun, other peoples emails, websites, etc. there's to little in this playground of a gameworld once you really get into it.) but like i said its a kickstarter game so i have forgiveness for it, if it was otherwise i would have to say i feel like the game devs didn't want to strive for more and just wanted to create the bare minimum needed to call it a finished project.
All in all, good game, short and to the point. Worth a buy, especially if found on sale like i did.

Crimsonland is a very classic top-down arena survival shooter from late 90's (I seem to have a faint memory of playing the game back then) so it has come a long way since then.
I am reviewing the Linux version of the game as this is the one I played. the hardware requirements are ridiculously low, I played this on an old Acer AspireOne D150 netbook (1.60GHz Atom, 1½GB RAM, Intel GMA945) and it ran like a charm, even on a weird 1024x600 resolution.
The gameplay is simple. You control a guy from a top-down perspective and you have a crosshair you aim at different enemies and you shoot them before they overrun you. The game can get very hectic at times but there are weapon pickups and perks that give you a fighting chance against the onslaught of monsters.
The weapons are pretty standard, with some sci-fi ones added in to the mix, ranging from a sub-machine gun to a swarm missile launchers and plasma cannons. They do a good job in being varied while still being simple and useful.
The perks are pretty fun, there is a wide variety from faster experience gain to faster reload or having a poison cloud around you that damages enemies and other quirky things. You get a choice of a few random perks every time you "level up".
This game is deceptively addictive. It is easy to pick up and  play and it will keep you entertained for a little while. It is also good game for an older machine or a netbook to pass a few minutes on a break.
The €6.99 asking price is a bit steep, but If you can get this during a sale, get it. You will not regret it, it is well worth picking up for a couple of euros.

Crimsonland is a frantic top-down twin-stick shooter with multiple modes and dozens of unlockable weapons and perks. I found many of the weapons unbalanced, on both ends of the spectrum; I loved using some of them and relied on them whenever I could, and others I avoided at all costs because they felt worthless. On several occasions, I nearly ragequit because some of the levels seemed cheap and impossible to clear without the right (lucky) weapon drop. (To be fair, it's also possible I'm just bad.) Regardless, that didn't stop me from putting in 16 hours, completing all six chapters of the quest mode, and unlocking all of the perks. It was frustrating at times, but more often than not, Crimsonland hit that sweet spot between challenging and frustrating that kept me coming back and giving each level "just one more try."

For those of you who were old enough to remember its release, the original Deus Ex was (and still is) one of the greatest PC games of all time. This iteration of of the series has some pretty big shoes to fill, something it does remarkably well.
The game was ported to PC by the wonderful company Nixxes, the same people who ported Hitman: Absolution and Tomb Raider. Needless to say, the port has a very finished feel to it, and the devs threw in some extra graphical goodies exclusive to PC.
The game itself is a tactical FPS with light RPG elements. You as the player are given complete freedom to complete missions as you wish, with XP bonuses encouraging you to take the more difficult routes. The combat feels tight, and exploration really feels rewarding. The only weaknesses this game exhibits are the boss fights. They are clunky and frustrating, and the whole idea of "bosses" in this game feels a bit contrived. However, they do little to detract from the rest of the game. All in all, this is a game that truly shines.

I played through the game originally on PS4; just imagine my review with slightly better graphics.
There's not a lot to be said that hasn't been covered before, but I'll reiterate the consensus: DOOM is a phenomenal single-player FPS campaign that transcends genre preferences and should really be experienced by everyone. It's fast, aggressive, beautiful to look at and is weirdly well-written and humourous for something of its type.
The action has a tempo and viciousness to it that has the vaguest tinges of a Hideki Kamiya character-action game, coupled with that tried-and-true gunplay that id are famous for. It was probably the game I had most unironic fun with in 2016. I had a lot of ironic fun with Ar Tonelico Qoga as well, but that's a conversation for another time.
The multiplayer is fine, not offensive exactly, but it straddles a line between Quake and Call of Duty without really playing enough to the strengths of either game. It's a fun enough knockabout, but I kind of wish there was a LAN/splitscreen free-for-all option in there. I'm one of those weirdos who played a lot of Quake II on the N64.
It's fantastic at any price, but the fact that it's frequently so cheap means you absolutely cannot go wrong. Rip and tear (your credit card out of your wallet), until it (the purchasing of the excellent DOOM videogame of 2016) is done!

I really wanted to like Artemis - but it wasn't always easy!
I tried Artemis in a LAN setup with 5 friends. The setup was epic: 1 TV, 6 monitors, 5 guys and 1 spaceship we were all in charge of! There certainly were some high expectations going into the simulation.
The problems started right at the beginning. We started the game and had absolutely no idea how everything worked. There were no tutorials and no hints. Everything seemed alien to us and even downloading the game manual didn't help, because it was made for an earlier version of  the game.
Determined not to give up, we started googling for help. Luckily, some guy had made a 30 minutes long "short tutorial" to Artemis. Our captain watched the whole thing and each of crew members watched their own section. This was by far the easiest way to get to know the controls of the game. Once they were explained to you in youtube, it was not so complicated after all.
Spirits were high when we finally launched a random scenario and were able to defeat it. It was fun playing as a team and there were even some very nerdy roleplaying going on with our captain walking around with a coffee mug in hand giving orders.
However, the random scenarios were all kind of the same. You have to defend your bases and eliminate the enemies, that's pretty much it. We were hungry for some exploration and plot, so we tried to launch some of the custom scenarios.
The custom scenarios are a very nice idea - they allow people to create scenarios with plots and twists and turns for your delight. However, much of the scenarios were made for game version 2.0 and we had the newest version from steam (2.1.1) and I guess this is why all the scenarios had severe problems - game simply stopped running etc. Even after much trying, we couldn't get the custom scenarios to work.
Now I realize Artemis is a single-man project and it's awesome how awesome it is, even now. But you should be aware it is not really a finished game with good support. It's a single-man coding project with a small community that has made a handful of scenarios.
Right now Artemis is more of a simulator and less of a game - though it could change in the future. It's unique, however, and if you are really into space and stuff and have a couple of friends living close by who feels the same way, I definitely say it's worth your money to try it together (just don't expect everything to be perfect)!

Endless Space is a turn-based 4x game. You are the emperor of a galactic empire. You start off small and slowly through warfare, trade, diplomacy and exploitation you grow into a huge empire spanning hundreds of stars. There are a variety of empires to choose from ranging from a hive of robotic insects who wish to devour the universe to your standard galactic human empire and a gelatinous mass of cells who are peaceful and only wish to socialize. Another excellent point are the resources. There are your basic 4 resources Food, industry, science and dust (FIDS). But there is a wealth of others to choose from. There are 2 main types of these: Strategic resources which can be used in shipbuilding and luxury resources, which confer permanent or temporary bonuses on your empire. The tech tree is a mixed bag. It's HUGE. Now this may be a good or a bad thing. There is loads to research, almost too much. With many of the coolest ones at the very end. Even very important ones are locked away. Want an alliance? Well, you have to research about 3 techs to lead up to that. Found a new resource? You're going to have to research it. Want bigger and better ships? You need to research that too! This brings us up to the next point, ships. Ships are fully customisable. With about 6 ship classes and a wealth of add-ons and modules the possibilities are endless. Unfortunately, using the ships is a different kettle of fish. When engaging in a conflict you must pick 3 "action cards, " these come in a variety of formats, but basically work like rock, paper, scissors. But when the engagement begins you get to watch it play out like a battle from Star Wars. Its cool for a while, but it soon gets old. Taking all these things into account I give this game a solid 7/10.

As someone who remembers playing the original Master of Orion back in the early 90s, this game has come the closest to capturing the enjoyment of the original MoO and MoO2 experience of my youth.
It is not a perfect game, some people may not enjoy the more "cinematic" battles as opposed to controlling the fleets themselves.  Afterall, that's what made Homeworld such a fantastic game, was the minute RTS control of the entire fleet including the economy.
However, I found that the pace of this game, and greater focus on Empire building and Macro development to more than make up for the battle instances.  And while it took me awhile to appreciate how the "cinematic turn based" fighting occurred, I became a big fan of sort of "issuing a strategy" and then watching as missiles, lasers, fighters and bombers did their work on the opposing fleet.
While not quite as deep in ship design, as say, Galactic Civilizations, the interface is at least intuitive without needing to try to figure out "where to stuff something."  This ship design has X amount of things it can fit - and you fit what you want.
Most importantly - the ability to retrofit your units to more modern designs as technology becomes available is simple, and keeps the game moving smoothly, since you usually have a bunch of other things to take care of each turn.
In short, this is perhaps my favorite space-based 4x game I've played in the last decade.  And I really enjoyed the usual (Sword of the Stars and the like) ones, but for me this game has stood out.  It is not as complex as many of the games in the genre, but in my opinion really captured the spirit that I have not happened since I was a 10 year old sneaking onto the computer late at night to play Master of Orion until it was time for school in the morning.

Mechwarrior Online does a respectable job at emulating what it feels like to pilot giant 20 to 100 ton killing machines in the Mechwarrior universe. You start off with trial mechs that cannot be customized and earn enough currency (with their new player bonus) to purchase your first customizable mech of choice. There are many weapon, equipment and mech choices to choose from which can be overwhelming for the new players but it adds quite a bit of depth to the game. The matches generally consist of 12v12 with the except of the 4v4 Scouting mode in faction warfare. New players are advised to try the 12v12 "quick play" mode since that mode will match you against players of equal skills. In faction warfare, you'll likely end up fighting against veteran players with fully customized battle-tested builds as it is a no holds barred fight to capture planets in that particular game mode.
Other notable pros:
Graphics - The graphics based on the Crysis engine is generally very beautiful. Even the older maps in the game can be visually stunning.
Movement - The movement in addition to the aiming in the game feels very smooth compared to a number of other FPS titles I've played.
Other notable cons:
Hitbox - There are some invisible hitbox issues with the terrain in some of the maps.
Grind - The game does tend to get a bit grindy especially if you're aiming to buy some of the bigger mechs.
Other notes:
The developers have been heavily criticized for this but they have been making some progress as new maps and mechs are added. They are fine tuning the game modes to ensure they are fun and there has been talk of newer projects in development. I'm looking forward to a PVE coop mode in particular as this will not only make their faction warefare mode more interesting but also provide a proper experience for some of the more casual players.

MechWarrior Online is the next game in the classic MechWarrior franchise, a series of simulators that puts the player in huge, hulking fighting mechs. In many cases, a free-to-play business model is a worrying sign, since pay-to-win is always a possibility in these games. Fortunately, from what I've experienced, MechWarrior Online has a very fair business model, but I'll get into that later.
The game is essentially a multiplayer mech sim that pits two teams against eachother in a variety of modes, such as TDM, Domination, and Conquest. The players may pick and choose from a large roster of different mechs from four different weight classes; Light, Medium, Heavy, and Assault. These mechs all fill a certain purpose. For instance, light mechs are very maneuverable and quick, making them excellent for scouting. They can, however, also be used to flank and destroy heavier, bulkier mechs. In the hands of a good player, a light mech can circle around a heavier mech, always staying at their back, while dishing out heavy damage to their weak backsides.
Assault mechs, on the other hand, are sluggish, and move at a glacial pace. They do however, bring a devastating amount of firepower, and they're naturally very good at soaking damage.
The big gimmick of MechWarrior online is that all of the mechs are heavily customizable, the options ranging from weapons, jump jets, modules, and so on. Because of this, every player's mech feels unique, but they're familiar enough that you can still gauge how potentially dangerous they can be to you. Additionally, each mech has their own 'quirks', unique features that a mech benefits from. Some mechs may turn faster than normal, while others may recharge their weapons faster, and so on.
The game looks and sounds pretty great, while also managing to be quite well optimized. There does seem to be a lack of music in the game, which lends it that suspenseful simulator vibe. If you don't like that though, you can always put on the MechWarrior 4 soundtrack.
Now, onto the game's business model.
This game does F2P well. It doesn't gate the players by arbitrarily limiting their choices of mechs, currency is earned relatively quickly, and new players are loaned four mechs from each of the different weight classes (16 mechs in total). Additionally, these mechs are on constant rotation, meaning that they'll change over time. Players do have an option of purchasing premium time, which increases the amount of credits and XP that you earn.
There are also loot crates in the game. One of these are given at the end of every match, to a random player in the game. They require keys to open, but the currency needed to purchase keys can be earned ingame. The rewards range from credits, to actual mechs.
All in all, the game's fun, and I'll be continuing to play it. Since it's Free to Play, it doesn't hurt to try it out either if you're curious.

TL;DR: Only gameplay is poking (clicking) a mayonnaise jar. Is this art or junk?
It is unfair to regard
like a conventional game. Clearly it doesn't have gameplay as its main focus. It left me with a rather mixed feelings but having to choose, ultimately I'm leaning to the side of thumbs down.
Presented with a huge jar of Mayo (tm), you proceed to poke at it with the equally huge finger-shaped cursor. Click click click, poke poke poke. Is this supposed to be a thing? Since it's mostly sold in plastic tubes around here I don't have experience with real-life mayo jars.
There are no time limits nor arbitrary restrictions of other kinds: it's the epitome of casual.
It's basically an achievement dispenser. All cheevos have an in-game picture and associated text, which forms a short story or monologue, so they are integral to "the story". To see the whole story, highlighting the picture will add some detail into the mayo jar (like a bra or a simple curious animation) and story will proceed when you click it again a bunch.
Graphics are okay, music makes you hum along even if it's terribly repetitive. However, this extremely casual entertainment lasts only as long as it takes for you to click about 10000 times, so likely just 30 to 60 minutes. Leaderboards for the highest clickers is basically a tongue-in-cheek joke.
So is it a good game? Definitely not. Is it fun or entertaining? Mildly. Is there a higher meaning to all of this? It is slightly thought-provoking to the point of being pointless. Mainlining is a nifty little adventure game with a hacking theme that, unlike other hacking games available on steam, eschews the nitty gritty of command-line interface wizardry in favor of telling a succint story well within its means.  That is to say, if you've avoided other hacking games because they emulate real-world operating systems all too closely, you can relax - Mainlining's CLI is quite simple and doesn't require any foreknowledge of how command-line operating systems work.
Instead of bringing the hardcore keyboard thunder, Mainlining opts for funtional aesthetics.  When you first start up the game, you'll be looking at a pixelated mock-up of a WinXP-like desktop.  Though typing away in the CLI is a big part of the game, you'll only ever need three or four commands, all of which are easy to remember.  The rest is as you would normally navigate a desktop OS these days - with a mouse.  Throughout the game, you will load applications onto your start bar, read files on your desktop notepad, and browse a well-realized fake web, all the while using information you find to remotely hack into other systems.  Throughout several cases, you will follow a bread-crumb trail that will eventually unravel to reveal a story.
That story being you work for MI7, a sister org to the famous MI5, only its main focus is online activity facilitating real-world crimes, and the backdrop of all this is a new act simply called the BLU Pill.  While it never gets into specifics, BLU Pill basically enables the gov't to break into systems legally in order to fight crime.  Naturally, this angers a few people and they organize themselves into a secret hacking group to counter MI7's efforts.  The game makes no hard stance on the politics of such a law, but throughout the game, you're never quite sure if you're the good guy or the bad guy.
In any case, this is all handled with beautiful pixel-style art from end-to-end, from presenting you nostalgic mock-ups of popular desktops (WinXP, iOS, etc) to a whole database full of pixel faces of the citizens of wherever you are.  In terms of aesthetics, Mainlining really reminded me of Digital A Love Story, and it unfolds in a very similar manner.  As you read chat logs and other random files you nab off unsuspecting systems, you'll learn about the inhabitants of this world and the characters found therein.  Moreover, there are live chat windows on your screen that dole out large portions of the story and all you ever have are names.  You're not told who's who, but it eventually all slots into place.
While I didn't encounter any glaring bugs, the game doesn't give you a lot of options to go off-script, nor does it make any effort throw any red herrings at you so unless you're really trying to find ways to break the game, you likely won't have a problem.  At all times, I was patienly waiting for the proverbial Other Shoe, but it never really came.  As each day/case passes, you'll be told what you need to find in order to proceed and any previously-learned knowledge usually doesn't work again, so going off the beaten path doesn't really present itself.  You either figure out what to do next or you don't.
That being said, I completed the game in about 2 hours or so and never even so much as wished for a hint.  All of the challenges in the game are easily met and good segments of the game are just waiting around for some things to happen.  I can't really describe more since that would spoil it, but for the most part, it plays a lot like the old standard of cutscene -> gameplay -> cutscene.
All in all, I found Mainlining to be an enjoyable experience and a perfect entry point into the genre since it really does a little of everything.  Outside of some proofreading mishaps, the game is solid.

To start, I'd like to say that I got this game as part of the Humble Android Bundle (some number), and that I only got the bundle for Neverending Nightmares, so this was like a bonus.
I decided to try this game out this week while waiting for my card drops on it. Started the "campaign" (which is basically just some levels with different enemy placements and different enemy and weapon selection for it), finished it in like 3 hours or something. I don't really know if there was a story because I really didn't care, I just wanted to shoot some stuff and see some blood. And it worked. Starts slow with♥♥♥♥♥♥weapons and normal enemies, and gradually introduces new enemies, new enemy types, new weapons and perks (which are useable on the Survival gamemode). So yeah, it starts slow and builds up into something cooler quite fast.
Gameplay: Normal top-down, twin-stick shooter, with quite a lot of weapons and different perks. Not many enemy types, but they work in "races", like, aliens, giant spiders, etc. Enemy design is quite okay for a game like this, and the shooting is really solid. Campaign was fun but the Survival gamemode is what really shines here. Lost another 4 hours playing the different survival modes to try to get a highscore. The game IS fun.
Graphics: Well, it was a 200mb download if I remember correctly. There aren't many different scenarios (they are just like a board of dust and sometimes some grass or some urban hangar stuff), which is something I didn't like that much. Enemies have cool designs, wouldn't say "original" but they're cool, you can see the difference from each one. Your character is quite simple and the animations are just fine. Overall, acceptable, though could have some more stuff in scenarios.
Sounds: The menu song made me instantly turn all sounds off because I didn't like the mixing in it (quite low quality), but won't say anything about game effects because I just wanted to kill stuff listening to some prog/death metal.
Story: heh.
Overall: 6/10. Cool game, can easily get you to waste some time of your life playing it and it is fun. Get it for the gameplay if there's a discount and you think this might be for you. Was quite a surprise for me.

Artemis is a great game, arguably the best Star Trek game that never was.  It is a team-based game, requiring 6 people to play at maximum effectiveness, though you can do it with 2.  The 6 stations are: Captain, Helm, Weapons, Engineering, Comms, and Science.  Each of these stations must work together to defeat any enemies encountered.
You and your friends are in command of a spaceship, usually dubbed "Artemis," and are out to defeat the alien hordes.  There are several game modes, with version 2.1 adding 3 additional modes.  You can also create custom scenarios.
The big thing I dislike about it (not nearly enough for a no-go) is the strategy is very simple.  EMP a group of targets, then nuke them.  When you're out of nukes, head back for more.  Rinse and repeat.  Other than that, this game is a blast, especially when you can get 2 or 3 ships working together to accomplish the goal.
This is a great simulation game and I believe it is also a great team building excerise.

After a few hours of playing and emerging in this game, i have to say: it definitly is a nice game, allthough it has some severe flaws.
1. Resources: The FIDS system is pretty much forward and allows to manage your empire on a very easy understandable, but yet not so easy to master level. The decision too whether transform a gas planet up to terran/jungle/ocean or not e.g. isn't as simple as it seems first - provided you do not have all improvements unlocked yet. But in the end, this has a feelable impact on your overall resources. Another thing i really like is the fact, that you have to gather stratigic resources to be competible. So in this department i can clearly say, the devs did it right.
2. Diplomacy: Okay - this is one of the bad parts of the game... I really had a hard time to understand, why this game was delivered with a subpar diplomacy system. Okay - you can choose how far to bond with the other factions (from only beeing at peace, over trade relations to full scale alliances), but still it seems a bit to simple in the given options. Another offset is the - IMO - strange diplomacy rating towards your faction. I still don't get, why some of them really hate me, although i play these extremly harmless, but cute Amoebes... - perhaps it's because of the amorph appearance - who knows...;) The only thing it's good for is to gather strategic resources and gain some money and research from your traderoutes.
So in general diplomacy isn't a real strenght of this game.
3. Combat: Yeah, some of us still remember the good old Masters of Orion games. At this time i loved the combat mechanics. The cool thing about Endless Space is, that i am somewhat reminded of these glorious times... :D
Guys and Girls: Do NOT only stick to the general rating of your fleet! in the end it all depends on your fleet setup, skill choices and knowledge of the enemy. I've easily won fights against a higher rated fleet, just because of a few bombers on my ships and the right battle action choices. The manual fights are - compared to the rest of the game - a bit of an eyecandy, but pretty useless and timerobbing at least. After about 5-7 fights i started to stick to the automatic mode - it'll do the job ;)
4. Planetary Management: This is the spice and flavour of the game! I really liked the micromanagement in the first to second third of the game. As in every good 4x game you sometimes have to think twice, when managing your colonies. Maximum research output, although some planetary bonuses are more cropfriendly? Standard situations in managing your systems/planets. This is something Endless Space gets right! I really love the fact, that a lot of improvements solely depend on your planettypes, the resources and percs of them. It does make a slight difference just to have a moon, special resources or anomalies. Last, but not least the graphics are quite nice... ;)
5. Races: Yeah - this is the section, where the devs got it right. Good balanced and nicely designed races and the ability to costumize your own races. I simply love this one.
6. Longtime Motivation: A 4x game must have a high replayability. Given the extremely high level of customability, this is a yes for this game!
7. Hardware: One really big backdraw is the unbearable long time to load advanced sessions... This is something i can't understand, if compared to other titles. This is definitely a thing to improve on!
Summary: Yes, i recommend this game. If you like 4x and SciFi, you'll have a good time playing Endless Space.

The lack of a proper directional pad makes this awkward to use with fighting and retro games. The lack of a right analog stick makes this awkward for first person games that require fast reflexes. Fans of this controller claim they can make this work with first person games by using tilt controls combined with the right touch pad, but that requires lots of practice to get used to.
I totally get what the devs of this controller were trying to do though. The dual touch pads are awesome to use when you are simulating mouse movement. This allows you to play point-and-click games on your couch, and you can even navigate your Windows desktop with the controller, which is pretty awesome. Overall, this can't compete with a traditional Xbox or PlayStation style controller, mainly because I prefer retro games and aiming with a traditional analog stick. Racing games are just fine at least, since you won't have to bother using any of the trackpads.
If there is a will there is a way though. If you explore the community options to optimize controls for specific games, you can find clever work-arounds to get used to this. I'm going to keep this controller around for those specific types of games I previously mentioned, but this definitely isn't the "universal controller" that I was hoping for.

Finally, something that can compete with mouse and keyboard. I've long used mouse+keyboard, even on the couch, but the steam controller works well enough to replace it on the couch.
The one big negative is that it requires big picture mode to be running to get full functionality. This is stupid. Big picture mode is a resource hog, and it doesn't make a ton of sense to use if you have a mouse handy.
The other (smaller) negative is that while the right touchpad does an excellend job emulating a mouse, it does a somewhat ♥♥♥♥♥♥ job emulating a joystick (because a joystick will spring back to center).
Valve could fix this by adding another joystick (so 2 touchpads and 2 joysticks) or having a modular design. Ultimately, it's not a huge deal, because there's a good chance you have another gamepad lying around for the occasional game that requires a lot of fiddling to get comfortable.

Steam Controller Components:
Joy Stick – The joy stick on the bottom left corner feels very nice. It’s easy to get a solid firm grip on the joystick. The size of the joystick is perfect and the responsiveness is amazing. You are able to click down on the joystick just like a 360 gamepad. I have exactly zero issues with the joystick.
Trackpads – There are two trackpads on the top left and right of the controller. This is where the learning curve comes in. For a lot of games, you’ll use the right joypad to control camera angles in a 3D environment. Initially, I had mostly negative things to say about the trackpad, but after an hour or so playing Dark Souls, I got the hang of it. It’s an adequate and in many cases a better replacement for a joystick primarily used for camera controls. The most interesting feature of the trackpads is the haptic feedback. The controller sends a little rumble to the position of your fingers on the trackpad. This allows you to know where exactly your fingers are on the trackpad.
D-Pad – The left trackpad duals as a D-Pad. This is no replacement for an actual D-Pad. Pressing down on the D-Pad requires more force than a traditional D-Pad. Due to its size, it’ll take longer switching between D-Pad buttons on click. However, you can set the D-Pad to not require click. For an example: if your finger touches the upper part of the trackpad, it will trigger the up button. If you use this mode, you’re sacrificing speed over accuracy. Switching between D-Pad buttons is much faster, but you’re not guaranteed to get the accuracy you want. Because of this, using D-Pads in a fighting game where both accuracy and speed are paramount will be extremely difficult.
Face Buttons – There are four main face button located on the bottom right on the controller. These face buttons are smaller than most traditional gamepads. The buttons are also closer together. I personally like this as I can quickly jump from one face button to the next with ease without losing accuracy. There is a steam button which launches steam settings if Big Picture is enabled as well as two  “start” and “select” buttons.
Bumpers – There are two bumpers located on the very top of the controller above the triggers. The bumper positioning is a little awkward. The trigger button is more diagonal than straight. Resting my fingers on the bumpers felt unnatural at first. As far as actually pressing on the bumpers, I have no complaints.
Triggers – This is where the steam controller shines. The triggers are very sensitive. It only takes light pressure to press allowing you to easily adjust without any strenuous effort. When you press all the way down, you’ll feel a very light satisfying click.
Grip Buttons – There are two additional button located on the back of the steam controller’s legs. These are great additions to the controller that allows you to map more buttons for games with complex control schemes (e.g. Splinter Cell Chaos Theory, MGS V).
Gyro – Much like the DS4 and Wii controller, the steam controller has a gyro function. You can map certain controls to the movement of the controller. This has great uses in FPS and racing games. You’re able to use the controller as a wheel with tilt gyro functionality.
Software – The biggest drawback of the controller, in my opinion, is the front end software (i.e. big picture). Big Picture is great if you’re primarily playing games from your couch, but not so good when you’re playing games from a desk while running other programs.
I will go through a list of some of the games I played on steam controller. I’ll do a quick comparison with the 360 controller.
Dark Souls: SC beats 360. Setting up the steam controller for Dark Souls is a snap. After I got use to the trackpad to adjust my camera angle, everything fell into place. I was adjusting the camera with so much ease that I did not have to think about it. One drawback of the 360 controller in Dark Souls is the awkward hand placement when sprinting and controlling the camera at the same time. Since sprinting can be mapped to the grip buttons, this is not an issue with the steam controller.
Super Meat Boy: SC slightly beats 360. This game is best used on the joystick instead of the D-Pad. I find that steam controller’s joystick is slightly more comfortable than 360’s control stick. The face buttons allows for quick reaction since the buttons are smaller and closer together on the steam controller.
Metro 2033: SC beats 360 by far. First person shooters on a joystick feels awkward and aiming is less precise. The trackpad and gyro precision allows for better aim. However, since you use a mouse with your entire hand, a mouse will always beat the accuracy of a trackpad or a gyro.
Injustice: 360 beats SC by far. The D-Pad on the steam controller is the stuff of nightmares for fighting games. As horrible as the 360 D-Pad is, it’s still much more usable than the Steam Controller for fighting games. The D-Pad on the steam controller is all about sacrificing accuracy for speed and vice versa. In fighting games, you must have the best of both worlds. The steam controller simply doesn’t provide that. I can do combos and special attacks by clicking the D-Pad, but it takes much more time. If I put touch settings on the D-Pad, then it’s nearly impossible to perform any combos or special moves.
N64 Emulator: SC beats 360 by a lot. The Steam Controller is a match made in heaven for N64 games. The C-Buttons on the N64 works well with the right trackpad and it feels much better than a joystick. The Z-Button feels more natural mapped to either grip buttons.
GameCube Emulator: SC beats 360 by a lot. The strong point comes from the mapping of the C-Stick and customization of the joy stick. Playing Mario Sunshine and Metroid Prime with a steam controller feels so natural. The C-Stick on the Gamecube pad is different than a regular joystick. The positioning on a C-Stick is more discrete than a traditional joystick. Having a trackpad as your C-Stick feels much better than a joystick. There is an added accuracy bonus for FPS games like TimeSplitters 2.
SNES Emulator: Varies. All SNES games uses the D-Pad, primarily for movement. Because you’re constantly having to sacrifice accuracy and speed for steam controller’s D-Pad, you’ll want to use the joystick in directional mode meaning your joystick will behave as a D-Pad. This is great for platforming games, but iffy for bullet hell games like Gradius and Contra.
I DO NOT Recommend this Controller If You:
* Mostly play fighting games like Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat X, and Injustice
* Want to just play the damn game. Configuration for most games take 5-10 minutes, but if you only have a few hours to play a game a week, then wasting 5-10 minutes may not be worth it.
* Mostly play SNES, GBA, GameBoy, Sega, etc games. SNES controllers are four times cheaper and works great for every game.
I DO Recommend this Controller If You:
* Want to play non-competitive FPS games from your couch. It won’t replace mouse and keyboard as far as precision goes, but it’s the next best thing if you just want to relax and play FPS on a couch hassle-free.
* Play racing games, but don’t want to drop cash for accessories. The steam controller does racing games really really well thanks to gyro capabilities.
* Play emulators on fifth+ generation consoles. The level of customizability combined with the controller’s unique layout will give you a better experience on emulators rendering 3D graphics.

The one down side is the boss fights, they really phoned those in. There are 3 bosses in particular, heavily augmented soldiers, who you can only kill - there is no non-lethal option. Fortunately if you're going for the Pacifist achievement, killing the bosses doesn't ruin it. Best advice for those bosses though - hit em with the stun gun repeatedly and you'll get past them easy on any difficulty. So yeah, the bosses are kinda broken. But every other aspect of the game is top notch.

OK, but not great.  I came back to play this one again, and found I didn't care for it as much as I had on first impression.
The mechanics are ham-fisted and arbitrary.  Metrics like "approval" are illogical in the game context, and simply there to slow down the player's rational march toward victory.  Example: citizens on planet 1 are rioting because you colonized planet 7 in another system.  Why?  There is no rational reason within the fiction of the game.  It is not like overpopulation on a single planet.  And there are actually good logical reasons for people to be proud, like any other civilization in history.  Yet the designers want to slow you down, since you will obviously want to Xpand, which is why you came to play this game.  So you either take the hit to an empire-wide reduction in output, which is self-defeating, or you pause to build expensive infrastructure on every single star system in order to magically make people happier.  Oh, and don't forget that you have to first lengthily research the arbitrary technologies to build the  happy places.
There are some interesting features here, but they are overwhelmed by the chores put in place to slow your rational progress down the 4X path.
