The game allows you to do almost everything the leftists in your country won't (in my country PT - Partido dos Trabalhadores/Worker's Party). As a gun enthusiast I can say it's the best simulator in the genre that I've seen, it's an almost real experience. If you're looking for a random FPS don't download it, probably you'll find it boring, but if you wanna learn the mechanics or practise the disassembly of some of the most known and reliable weapons it's a must in your library. It has a greater educational value than entertainment value, however I do find pleasure on this kind of knowledge.
Modes are: field strip, disassembly, assembly, operation, game, super game and hardcore game, each has a description at the beginning. There are also achievements for each mode and world leaderboards for all 3 game modes. If you liked in the first 10 minutes, chances are you'll play for 10 hours in the first day, so I don't have to say it's replayable and addictive. You use the mouse to interact with parts and control the camera, you can also use keyboard for some actions but I don't recommend. Sometimes a different part is selected in game mode and in some modes the camera moves against your will. In most modes you have to wait for the end of the animation to perform an action, that's annoying in timed modes. RMB is a good and quick way to zoom a specific part. Controls could be more precise.
Models are very precise and some even include a bit of visual external wear (mechanic wear would make a nice DLC), however they only look like plastic. Options are very limited, but they're not very relevant on this game, you can identify any part at all times, and if you don't, there's a caption in the lower centre of the screen for each part selected. There's native AA support and fixed frame rate at 60fps. The game is windowed by default. In general the models look like any good directx 9 game, I believe it's playable even with integrated video cards. Menus could look better. The game hasn't crashed yet.
There are several models of handguns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, SMG's, etc. You start with an AK-47 and afterwards a Colt 1911, the other guns you will have to buy, but you can unlock many more with your exp. points. You get exp. completing achievements and logging in everyday. As if it wasn't good enough, you can also disassemble skeletons (got the highest score of the day :D) and vehicles, which I find amusing. In addition there are shooting ranges, quiz and information about the weapons. Models are downloaded the first time they're used.
All in All

After trying out the controller on a variety of games in my library I've found a few issues. First, the design isn't very ergonomic. It would feel more comfortable if the buttons and analog stick were moved closer to the outside edges of the controller. The overall design feels too wide and the three triggers on the back and top of the controller feel spaced far apart. Second issue is the sensitivity of the touch pads. I had very high hopes for this particular feature and it's the primary reason I wanted to try this controller. There seems to be very little adjustment available for the sensitivity which at times feels too sensitive, while in other situations it feels too slow. Third, game support. I'm surprised that some of the games I own that don't have any issues utilizing a 360 controller would not work with the Steam controller. Games I purchased through Steam. I assumed this would have been addressed while designing the controller and software. Overall I think the design holds promise, but I feel it needs some fine tuning. It's not the worst controller I've used but considering the price, coupled with the flaws, I can't personally recommend it.

You can play this game without ever spending a penny,  and you'll be on the same playing field as someone who spent $100. All the microtransactions are for indirect things. Like paint-jobs on mechs, or bonus experience gains. You can't just pay money and buy the best mech in the game.
That's the beauty of it too. There are no best mechs! It's so balanced in terms of gameplay, that no one mech is better than any other. Each mech has its role,  and it's pros & cons, none of which give any mech an unfair advantage.
It's what I like to call "a thinking man's shooter" because it's such an involved game,  that you really have to think about what you're doing as you play.
Really the ONLY negative thing I can say about it,  I'd that the community for it is too small. I'd love it if the game had a massive community, like a big Triple A title game has, I feel like it could benefit greatly with a bigger community.
I love this game to death,  and would recommend it to anyone who loves mechs, mechwarrior/battletech, and shooter games.

A friend bought me this game as a joke, having no idea what it was before hand. My first reaction was 'is this I am Bread 2'? But I could not have been more wrong. Upon opening the game I will admit that I was not impressed. "It's just a jar of mayo," I recall myself saying, "There's not even a main menu." But I soon realized that there wasn't any need for that. The game in itself was all it needed. What followed was, in my experience, was a few minutes of me clicking on the jar as I figured out the various achievements I could get while said friend watched on my broadcast.
Within ten minutes I was dressing up my mayoanaise jar. Within twenty I had unlocked all of the achievements other than the ones to do with click number. And that's where my story began, the true journey of self discovery. As my friend laughed, I continued to play and click until my muscles hurt and it felt like my finger would fall off. But I was determined. I watched the number rise. 5000... 6000... and so on until I finally hit that glorious number.
10000
And what I realized about myself changed my view on the world completely. If I hadn't given this game a chance, I wouldn't have these precious memories. And so, I say, give things a try even when you're hesitant to. Or be like me and be addicted to clicker games.

Mainlining is a game that is generally worth a try, even though it is pretty simple to beat and quite short (I spent 4.3 hours beating the game). The gaming time vs price ratio is therefore average at best, with no replay potential.
About the games, contrary to other reviewers I have not been annoyed by bugs. The plot is nice even though it gets sometimes confusing, which is probably something the devs wanted.
The thrill of discovering things in someone else's computer is nice but unfortunately there is little things that have absolutely no link to the story. It is disappointing that everything seems to have a purpose. I don't believe that the same should be filled with dozen of useless files but it would have be interesting to have some sorting to do between the useless stuff and the stuff that is actually useful. This makes you feel that you are just pulling a string that leads you to the end. There is very little occasions where you actually have to think to get through the case. For example I am very disappointed that there is no decryption challenges (hidden in pictures, fileinfo, enigma...)
The arrest system is badly designed as you have to use exactly the good file and therefore make a lot of false arrest that has by the way absolutely no consequences.
So the game is a generally good experience and it is enjoyable to go through the story, but the whole thing is only dedicated to the story and this lack of content does not serve the game's potential...

The basic idea of the game is really cool, but the amount of bug and bad UI design makes it really unpleasant to play.
Most of the game is spent writing commands in the console. You would think that the console should have been a well designed thing in this game, but no, its terrible. Anyone who has used a real command line before will want to pull their hairs off when they use this.
Typing "too fast" makes the game not register some keystroke.
You can't easily edit the thing you write into it.
Pressing the up arrow will bring back the last command you wrote into it, but only one.
You can't copy/paste thing from/into the console.
Sometime the console will just bug on you and make some command not work.
The error message aren't clear so you don't really know if you made a mistake in the command, if the website doesn't exist or if the console is just bugged.
And the list goes on, and that's only for the console, there is still so much more about the rest of the game
Placeholders in the text
Bugged window that won't come back into focus
Bugged window that won't let you write
Story bugging and not letting you progress so you need to restart the whole mission from scratch
Game settings not working (fullscreen setting not being applied correctly)
Game not playing sound
I really was enjoying the game at first, but after a few level it just became really anoying to play.

A decent enough game at first, this 4X game really only has 3X's. The X it lacks, is eXtermination. Technology research, colony management, exploration, and spaceship design are all comparable to other space 4X games. You don't really know what is missing until you start fighting with the other races. There is absolutely no way to win consistently in space combat because battles are basically just a comparison of fleet size and strength with some modifiers thrown in based on the results of a pre-combat game of paper, rock, scissors. Forget all the other 4X games out there where you can command individual units and beat the enemy fleet with strategy and tactics. You pretty much just pick 3 tactics from a list and then passively watch the battle happen.
The computer is an amazing empire manager, so even on normal difficulty, you will find yourself at a distinct disadvantage in terms of technology and military strength when you encounter the enemy races. Once the galaxy gets divided up, wars are slow, boring, and repetitious processes of attrition. The end result is a game where any way the human player can gain an advantage by using their brain has been removed.

Artemis is a bridge simluator where friends can get together and become the crew of a starship.  Although the game was designed for all members to be in the same room, running this with something like Teamspeak will allow you the same feel over the internet.
One person starts the server.  Then others connect to that server and choose what stations they want to control on the ship.  You can choose multiple stations on one computer, but these are all active stations and can get too complicated if you choose the wrong combo to work.
You can control Helm, Weapons, Engineering, Science, Comms, or Captain the ship.  Each station has it's own screen and working in conjunction with the other players you make the ship function.  There are strange occurences, enemies, space monsters, etc out there to explore and find.  The world is also customizable, so you can set difficulty levels and overall content to suit your crew's abilities.
The person who starts the server CAN play at the same time.  All you need to do is copy the shortcut from your library to your desktop and launch the server off that.  Then launch the game through steam as a client and you can connect and play a role.
Note that as the server, the game will give you the IP addy of your PC for others to connect to.  If you work through a router you need to open port forwarding to 2010 and the IP the router gives you.  Then give your crew your actual IP that you should be able to get in your router properties.  There are some guides on this in the forums if you need help.
Overall, it's a blast to play with a crew.  We played with only 4, doubling up captain and science/comms, and the game was great fun.   If you ever wanted to get on the bridge of a starship, this game is worth it.  Just remember it's not designed for single player.   You need at least 3 to play smoothly, though you could probably do with just 2, but would be difficult to fight on higher skill levels.

I was genuinely surprised by this game.  It's a pretty simple concept:  Correctly disassemble various firearms while trying to beat your fastest time and maintain accuracy.  The nice thing is that this game can be completely F2P.  You unlock new weapons with EXP, which is gained from disassembling and reassembling weapons you currently have access to.  There is also a Quiz mode that you can redo every 30 minutes.  During this quiz, you are given a picture of one of the weapons in the game and 6 choices; all you have to do is identify which one it is.  You do this as many times as you can until you either get one wrong or run out of time.  If you run out of time, you get 200 EXP for each weapon you identified (granted, you gain nothing if you miss one).  You also gain EXP for logging in every day.  Consequently, it isn't quite the grind some have suggested.  Yes, you could just disassemble the AK a few hundred times.  Or you could start with unlocking cheaper models, learn the quiz, and remember to log in each day.
Personally, I chose the route of picking up one of the access packs while it was on sale, as I play this pretty casually and just wanted to have a few guns available at the start.  I already feel as though I've received my money's worth.  I haven't had any issue gaining EXP, and still have a surplus of weapons to learn.
As for the game itself, it plays smoothly.  If you're at all gun or engineering savvy, you'll run into a couple of occasions where you'll think "Wait...why can't I take that part off before I take that other part off?", but this is the only real limitation I've seen so far.  It's great if you're like me and just want what amounts to a more interesting puzzle to mess with while watching TV.  If that sounds like you, I highly recommend checking this out!

Very accurate models, and some fun game modes.  Can be challenging to compete against other peoples times.  Can be helpful to learn more about real world firearms, especially those you may own.  Can be downright facinating to disassemble some of the more complex weapon systems you'd never have a chance at seeing in real life.  Some aspects of the game play can be frustrating (e.g. you have to wait for a the full animation of the part removal to complete before proceeding, not just for it to "look like" it's been remoed, etc.) but it's pretty minor in the grand scheme of things.

My number one complaint and the only reason that I do not recommend this product is that there's no joystick or controller drivers for this thing for Windows.  It can function as a mouse/keyboard in windows, but without steam, this thing is not a video game controller.  The unconventional way that the hardware is handled also creates an array of strange problems, for instance, GTAV cannot regain connection with the controller after it's been lost (afk timeout, battery failure, etc).
I've been the owner of 2 steam controllers for a bit more than a year I think..  Now, both of their dongles have ceased function and one no longer powers on.  They're video game controllers, so I can't say that they've been treated with the utmost care, still, I've never had an xbox controller give up on me.  Maybe one?
If you're looking for a very customizable piece of hardware, strictly for use with steam games, this is the controller for you.  The platform really could be awesome.  If someone is dedicated enough to basically program their controller for perfect function per game, this thing could compete with mouse/keyboard, theoretically...
If you're looking for a controller that you can just plug in and play games with, steer clear.
My conclusion is that this thing is the worst of both worlds in the marriage of PC and console gaming philosophies.
Addendum to conclusion, it could really be a great piece of hardware, with the right support.  Steam, we get it, you basically invented PC game DRM.  You're awesome for that.  If licensing or proprietariness is what's keeping you from supporting this thing outside of steam, GTFO.  This thing could be awesome, but it's so community and user dependent that you really have to let it go.  You can't pirate a piece of hardware, right?  get these things in as many hands as possible.  Make em work with everything you can.  All it would take is one high level gamer releasing a config for one high profile game.  Create the scandal, "is using the steam controller cheating?"  Let people play overwatch with it.  Battlenet games, origin games, who cares, disconnect your controller controller from steam, let that thing be called directly from windows.

before beginning, to provide a reference point, I've owned and used every PlayStation controller (always, save for one, Sony brand), 360 controller, and for several years exclusiving used a gaming mouse (Logitech G5 then G500 when that wore out) and keyboard (most recently a Das Keyboard S Pro Silent).
It's a "do anything" controller, though it does some things better than others. I got my first one (I now own two) via pre-order in August 2015. Good thing too since my 360 controller died on me, and my wrist had been giving me serious issues with KB+M. For some games, it outshines everything. These tend to be 3D ARPGs like Blades of time and Divinity 2. For others, it is somewhat poor. These don't fall into any particular genra, but to give examples, I find Skyrim and Mass Effect 1 to play poorly with the SC. Most others are somewhere in the middle, preforming about as well as the better of KB+M or controller.
In summary, YMMV but it usually is as good as other input methods.
As for build quaility, in comparison to my 360 controller and DS4, I can't say it's better or worse. I can say it was cheaper, even when it isn't on sale. I find some buttons hard to press such as the touch pads, face buttons, and shoulder buttons, where as others, like the second stage triggers, are too easy to press. Overall the button layout decent. Nothing exceptional. I play wirelessly about 25% of the time (which is considerable), and have not noticed any delay. This is coming from someone who complains about double digit pings in League of Legends. I have been told that I am over sensative to responsse delays, so chances are you won't have a problem either.
In summary, compared to other controllers, the SC has comparable build quality and ergonomics, and there doesn't appear to be any reasonable amount of delay in controller input.
The only real downside is that you either need to customise the controls yourself, or rely on someone else's. Personally, I don't care much for most of the community control schemes, which is fine since within an hour I'll have scrapped half of even the ones I like.
As an afterward, even with Steam API applying to the DS4 now, this still is better for a lot of things, though it isn't a solid replacement. It is a solid replacement for KM+B about 95% of the time. Also, as far as having to use Steam...come on. Unless you are trying to play a Windows-only Steam game that is actually teathered to Steam (not all are) with Wine or CrossOver (do you even know what I'm talking about?) this will cause you absolutely no grief. Unless you hate Steam/ValvE in which case you won't buy one of these anyway.
In summary, while the DS4 is suppior to the Steam Controller in some case, it can (and I do) be used as a drop in replacement for KB+M. The sole exception being if you want to play a Windows game that has Steam DRM (which not all Steam games have) on a non-Windows OS.

This game is grinding. You can't get around that even if you paid real money. That also means there really is no reason to put real money on the game until you are familiar with it. I repeat, please give it two weeks before committing your currency.
You have 4 mech bays at the start, 0 mechs, but with an army of trial mechs (you are unable to change weapon configuration on those). New players will get bonus cbills from start fights to provide them quite fast their very own mech. The web is full of tips how to use those first cbills and I strongly advice you to read guides before blowing all your starting bills to a single mech like I did.
There are often events with additional rewards, even mechs. Within a year, I managed to get 20 mech bays and them occupied. All this without giving in more than my time.
Game modes and maps are limited, and you would think this would make the game dull, but different mechs with different setups give you lots of diversity. At first you are just conserned about getting the enemy into your aim, soon you realize you have to take account your distance, your level of heat, ammo conservation, facing of the enemy, position of your allies and position of the target allies. Can I even hit him? Should I even shoot? Should I realign before I'm surrounded.
It should be also be noted that as the matches are only 15 minutes tops, it is also easy to enjoy it in small amounts.

Great game, has some really interesting gameplay mechanics and a good storyline which doesn't get boring.
I've tried other hacking games and they may be nice, but they have their problems (no story - only hacking, overcomplicated or have timed events), and so far Mainlining is the one that I've actually enjoyed. The difficulty balance is great as well - puzzles are logical, and the game thankfully doesn't punish you for making wrong decisions so you don't have to start over.
Other reviewers have complained about bugs, this is why I've decided to write a review - I haven't encountered any bugs in my whole playthrough. I'm not saying there are no bugs, but at least I think the situation is not as bad as other reviewers describe it.
If you like hacking games, I do recommend it.

When I first discovered Tribes:Ascend, I wasn't a huge fan of first-person shooters. They all seemed to be exactly the same, no real skill needed. But then this. This game. This gem.
I played this game for hours on end, every day after school. I recommended it to everyone, because it was so phenomenal. It wasn't so hard that it was impossible, but you still needed considerable skill to play properly. The community was wonderful: the right mix of "WHAT AN ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" and "PRAISE THIS MAN." I made so many friends playing this, and I don't recall ever having so much fun playing anything, let alone an FPS. Tribes: Ascend is quite possibly my favorite game, period.
About a year ago, I uninstalled it. Why? You know why. You've read the news, the comments. Hi-Rez dropped this game to favor Smite, a much more profitable venture. They left it here to rot, full of bugs and glitches that ruined the experience.
Why, then, am I recommending this game?
I'm hopeful.
That's right, they're picking up where they left off. I'm not saying they're going to make this game perfect, and I'm not saying that they won't completely ♥♥♥♥ this up. What I
saying is that Tribes deserves our attention, even if Hi-Rez doesn't deserve our trust.
I'm recommending this game based on the fun I had forever ago, and also on the tentative hope that Hi-Rez won't let us down again. Don't give up just yet, guys. They heard us, and they've answered. We still have a chance.

This is easily one of the best space-themed 4x games out there, and it has a ton of really neat ideas. Sadly, the game falls pretty short in execution (with AI opponents at least). Several in-game systems just don't work in practice.
The diplomacy aspect of the game is probably the most aggregious offender of broken mechanics. Computers will violate or end treaties willy-nilly even when it benefits you and hurts them. The computers appear to suffer from mass technology trading (to your detriment) like older Civ games did. Additionally, the game will often kill treaties for nonsensical reasons. On multiple occasions I've had alliances and cooperation aggrements auto-cancelled by the game because I lost a resource, even though the resource was never involved in the trade. Amusingly, this even sometimes happen in error when the game somehow thought I had lost a resource.
The combat system initially feels neat; however, it gets tiring quickly. For some bizarre reason the designers thought it would be a good idea to incorporate an arbitrary time limit before you can resolve any combat. It's possible this is some weird technical reason because of simultaneous online/AI play. Regardless, it's dumb; it gets old extremely fast. Additionally, the computer seems to play their combat cards randomly. You can reload and replay the same encounters 10 times and you'll get 10 different sets of cards played by the computer. Often the cards the computer plays makes absolutely no sense. Also, the combat system will often say you have an (often large) advantage with combat, you can counter multiple computer cards, and yet somehow still lose your fleet without killing a single ship. This isn't a rare occurrence; it's frequent. To make matters worse, I've found that the fleet design system seems to work really well if you just let the computer design ships for you based on your best components. When prompted, the computer will always pick one weapon and one defense piece and use only those pieces. Finally, there doesn't appear to be a way to examine the makeup of an enemy fleet until you click the combat button. Once you've clicked that button there's no way to cancel it, which is asinine.
The game lacks a true tutorial and instead uses in-line help. Unfortunately, the inline help is shown the very first time you go to any screen, which means you spend the first 30 minutes being bombarded by walls of text only to forget it all an hour or two down the line when you're trying to remember how some advanced mechanics worked (which you didn't have access to when the inline help was going).
The game also appears to several necessities that we've come to expect from 4X games (like Civilization). It lacks victory tracking (for you or the enemy) other than some extremely basic percentages that aren't explained and are hidden, an in-game encyclopedia (civlopedia style), advisors to help you when you're just starting out, an online community (there's very basic ones starting up, but they are small), or a mod community. The largest issue I found was that the diplomacy system was extremely shallow and boring. You don't unlock any interesting diplomatic options until several techs into the tree. Once you get them, you'll find that anything sufficiently interesting is missing. There's no way to convince others to go to war, peace doesn't protect your colonies (which makes little to no sense; at least provide a separate option for this), and the game forces you to break your alliance for often trivial, nonsensical reasons.
To top off some failed mechanics, the game has some really obvious and extremely frustrating bugs. My favorites include game screens that are sometimes inaccessible for no discernible reason (spam clicking will sometimes bring them up), buggy math where global % modifiers are applied incorrectly to colonies with negative output (this works both ways amusingly, a negative % modifier and a negative output can cause a positive total output), and some amusing visual bugs where ships and systems will twitch in place. Likely the biggest bugs in the game are those revolving around diplomacy. More than a few times I've had ships get effectively stuck in systems because of an odd confluence of borders, treaties, and ships in orbit defending airspace.

Let me start off by saying that the concept of this game is amazing.  Who doesn't dream of having super powers?  Being able to run, jump, and glide across city blocks in the blink of an eye is quite the rush.  On top of that, being able to shapeshift at will (as a disguise or to transform your body into devestating weaponry).
The problem for me is after about 10 hours of playtime, why am I struggling to find the will to continue playing?
There's a story, but it feels like a narrative that I'm unlocking rather than experiencing.  It's completly mission-based.  The game quickly turns into a free-roam-the-city-to-start-x-event.  To become more powerful I destroy and kill everything.  To complete missions I destroy and kill.  To learn more about the story... destroy and kill.  Let me put it another way... you get reports on how many kills you get and how much money you cost the military, and the higher these numbers are the better your score is.
I could really only reccomend this game to people who:
a. Like GTA style games (maybe only those who really enjoy stealing tanks and trying to evade the police)
or

I remember having given Blockland in Christmas of 2009 (And re-buying and still playing it via Steam at this point). And back in the day, it tended to be a clone of Roblox in terms of building blocks and other notible assets. Which THEN, a few months ago, made people point out "AAAH THIS IS MINECRAFT BUT ALL SCRATCHY AND SHIZZ" and was going like that ever since. Yup, I know how you Minecraft peoples are.
So for this review, I'm not only going to review this game, but compare this to Minecraft a bit, and why I sometimes like to dub this "Hipster Minecraft".
So basically what Blockland is, is a first-person sandbox multiplayer create-your-own-anything game. SOUND FAMILIAR??? You control inhabitants known as "Blockheads" and build anything, Yup, quite familiar. HOWEVER, you do NOT start in a pre-generated world. It is a flatgrass-style area you find yourself in. All saves you make are only builds, and not whole worlds, which is not as convoluted as Minecraft as all you can do to get a build you made is straight-up load it like a schematic.
Now for building things and designing games, functions, etc.: You can see building is quite advanced and more difficult than Minecraft. But it's great if you want a first-person Sandbox building game with more detailed models than Minecraft, as Minecraft is all 1-meter blocks and very flat compared to Blockland blocks. For functions, you can use a Wrench to make blocks emit light and particles, as well as implement functions to make games and programming. Minecraft pretty much does the same thing with Command Blocks, etc., but IMO, Blockland is more simple than Minecraft in terms of functions. Because Minecraft's functioning requires specific functions and assets, sometimes extra mods, to make a good mechanism.
I MIGHT be missing something here, as I have never tried such functions myself in Minecraft, but I should say that you have no information to design Minecraft functioning whatsoever unless you use the internet, which I don't really like doing given how the Minecraft community is nowadays.
Blockland may be difficult and advanced to build than Minecraft, with all the little blocks to use and everything, but I found that it's much simpler to build what I want without getting my♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked in Minecraft trying to obtain a specific asset for my work. People would say Minecraft is waaaay better than Blockland that they hate this game, but I'm one of the few who played it back then and had a good time, speaking of which...
Everybody knows Minecraft is the way to go besides Blockland. But for the nosalgia, or stuff Minecraft can't as mentioned above, I play this. I'm one of the few who actually like this game and I'm glad it doesn't have a fustercluck of a community like Minecraft, which is what I was anxious to point out. I really admire how quiet and underrated Blockland and its community is compared to Minecraft, and even Roblox as well. (I also played Roblox and it was pretty cheezy). Minecraft's majority of fans has pretty much bubble-bursted, where Blockland is "Just right", however getting beat down by Minecraft.
But I will say this as I finish up this review.
. It is not exactly a ripoff of Minecraft, which I apparently am seeing an award of which this game attained. I give this game a thumbs up, as it was what got me going before Minecraft was all the rage. This is just my opinion though. I'm only proving a point about Blockland vs Minecraft, and NO I do not think Blockland < Minecraft. It's all the Minecraft tweenies that are implying that this game is crapple. When I play Minecraft, I have that feeling that I shouldn't be playing this game anymore, whereas in Blockland, it's calm and I don't need to be reminded by the overdose Minecraft has become. (I still like Minecraft though)

For fans of the Mechwarrior series, this is the online competitive version we've been waiting for. It certainly lives up to the previous titles. It isn't 100% perfect, but I think the positives certainly make up for the faults and the dev team is actively working on the game and improving on it. They also listen to and interact with the community pretty regularly through podcasts and town halls.
The most important part is the mechs in a game like this, and in that regard they've done quite well. There is a huge variety of mechs of all sizes from 20 ton lights to 100 ton behemoth assaults and everything in between. Each mech has multiple variants with different hardpoints and options so it's easy to find something to fit your playstyle. They're also operating on a monthly release schedule which sees a new mech released mid-month every month. Initially mechs are sold in packs for real money but become available for in-game currency shortly after, so paying players effectively get the first crack at the new mechs.
Maps could use some work. The maps themselves are great, well designed, look nice, and have pretty good diversity. The problem is they could stand to add another 4 to 6 maps to the game as currently I believe there's only around 10 or so for quick play.
The gameplay is a nice mix of FPS and vehicular combat. While it does operate like an FPS in a sense, you are in giant robots and they do act like giant robots. Once queued and a match is found players are presented with a vote screen to vote for map/mode, which is something I wish other games like this would offer (looking at you War Thunder). The matches themselves are 12v12's and each player has the one mech they dropped with and that's it. There's no respawn, there's no heals, and no second chances; so play smart. This is probably the part of the game that can be frustrating for new players, but I think once you get past the punishing nature of the game you start to prefer it the way it is.
One of the games current negatives is its faction warfare system. This is meant to be a sort of faction versus faction warfare system and is supposed to be more competitive. Unfortunately it's just not very active as the majority of the players still just play in the standard play queue and the motivation to play in the faction system is really rather lacking. It's a good idea, I just think the scope of it is too great for the limited appeal, particularly in a more niche game like this.
One of the games best parts is the mechlab where you can customize your rig. Decide which weapon combos you want, how many heatsyncs, extra hardware, and so on. Clan and Inner Sphere mechs do operate a little differently in here as IS mechs allow you to modify the engines, while the engines are generally locked in clan mechs. However clan mechs offer the benefit of being able to switch out components with those from other variants which IS mechs can not do. Using your mechbay to upgrade and modify your loadout is extremely key in this game to be able to make the most of your mech and how you play it.
The economy of the game is generally done pretty nice. It doesn't take too much to earn the credits in game required to buy a mech unless you're going for the biggest and most expensive clan mech. It really isn't pay-to-win as most of what you purchase using MC's (premium currency) are cosmetics like colors, decals, camo's, and so on. There are hero mechs that are available only for MC's however these mechs don't really provide an advantage, more a c-bill earning bonus while piloting them and a camo that is unique to the hero. I think the biggest hurdle for newer players are the MC costs of some things, particularly mechbays since the number of mechs you can purchase is always limited by how many bays you have available. Colors are another issue as their costs are pretty high and there's only a small selection of maybe 5 basic colors you can buy for c-bills, though once a color is unlocked you can use it on any mech. Camo's may seem expensive at first, but there is a "one shot" option that you can use that will apply the camo to your mech and it will remain so long as you don't change the camo later. Buying the camo outright costs 10x the price and really has no value unless you're constantly swapping camo's.
The game does almost weekly run events that do allow you to earn MC's just through gameplay, and generally one of these events will net you enough for a mechbay. Prizes also often include things like c-bills, cockpit decor, MC's, and occassionally even colors. The events are very practical unlike some other games that offer event prizes where the requirements to get the prizes is often ridiculous.
All-in-all I would say this is a great game that is worth a shot. It offers a lot of gameplay options through mechs of different sizes, speeds and styles and the community is generally pretty decent. I mean, sure you're going to get some jerks now and then, but overall the community is not overly rude or salty. This is particularly valuable given the game does have built-in VOIP for communication in matches, but there is a mute ability if you do run in to the occassional loudmouth you'd rather just not hear. So I would say definitely give the game a shot, particularly if you enjoyed or played previous Mechwarrior games.

Missions require the arrest of individuals to complete. That is a 3 step proccess involving you providing the name of the subject, their residence, and an incriminating file you have downloaded about them.

As of mission 3 I had at least 6 files with evidence to put this guy away, according to the rules of evidence I was given in the very first mission (describing various types of crimes, what constituted evidence, and the amout of time you would put your crim away for depending on the type of crime you provide evidence for).
I submitted that form all 6 or times, each time getting told we falsely arrested this guy.
And its not a quick proccess either, it takes a while to get that form up with its little transition animation, and fill it all in, and WORSE is that it doesn't even tell you the reason it was rejected. I mean, for all I know there is some file on some server somewhere that tells me the guy moved recently, and i've just got his old address in there. Who the hell knows.

This game sucks.
Want an in-depth review why this game sucks?  I found the sound messed up really hard so I could barely hear the dialogue when there was any.  It didn't stop me from understanding the story, but it did♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  The story is boring.  It's a typical amnesiac with super powers trying to figure out the past.  I liked it better when it was the Bourn Identity.
Gameplay started out funny but immediately got stale.  I really don't care for stealth missions and I didn't see a need for them in this game, but it went ahead & gave me stealth missions anyway.  The whole thing felt poorly balanced.  You're this super ultra killing machine and there's always a seemingly infinite number of soldiers on the screen all spread out shooting at you at all times and you're trying to kill enough guys to keep regenerating health.  Then they introduce these mutant alien things that take for god damn ever to kill.  I got really tired of fighting those things after about the 28th time.
You can steal vehicles, but it wasn't really adding anything to the gameplay.  About 8 or so missions in, I just got bored of the game and decided this wasn't worth finishing.  I was on normal and I started out laughing like "hahaha this is so easy" to having a heart attack trying to finish a mission.  I get that there were more super powers to upgrade, they seemed mostly useless from the description.  The novelty of the game wears off after about half an hour or so.  It just didn't seem like it was worth finishing.

이게임역시 완성도 , 중독성 , 몰입감 , 조작법 , 사운드 , 그래픽 , 잔인성 이다.
내용은 군부가 가장처음 레드라이트 바이러스를 배양하며
레드라이트를 토대로 개량을 시켜 탄생한 블랙라이트 바이러스.
블랙라이트 바이러스는 지구 생명체의 진화의 기본에 충실한 유기화합물로,
감염대상을 세포의 DNA 레벨에서 부터 감염시켜 변이시키는 능력을 가지고있다.
하지만 망할 군부대가 그바이러스를 가지고 반응실험을한다. 결과는 멘퉁....
이러이러 저러저러 실험은 계속되고 멘붕은 찾아오고 세월이흘러가다가
드디어 등장하게되는 주인공 " 알렉스 머서 "
그는 맨하탄에 커다란 집도 가지고
케렌 파커라는 여친도 가진 성공한 연구원이었다.
그는 상부의 거짓말에 넘어가 자신의손으로 ..
블랙라이트바이러스를 탄생시키게된다. ( 이런.. )
또 어찌어찌 튀다가 걸린 머서는 결국 즉결처형에걸리게된다... ( 잠시 멘붕 .. )
그러나 그 직전에 바이러스를 깨트린 " 알렉스 머서 "는
통째로 감염되고 먼저 사망한뒤
그자리에서 블랙라이트바이러스에 감염되고만다 ..
그뒤론.. 뭐.. 할튼 도망치면서 싸우는 신세가 된것. ( 에고고.. 멘붕시리어스 ;; )
일단 게임성역시 프토2와 같은 오픈월드식.
하지만 .. 이거역시 오픈월드 방식인데 .... 오픈월드같지 않은 게임 ..
단순 파괴 액션 게임으로서 스트레스풀기에는 딱 좋은 게임 ...
이 이상 이 이하 게임도 아닌 ..

지금와서 보면 그래픽이 뛰어나지도 않고 .. ;

The AI is quite rubbish, but then 99.5% of all games suffer that problem.
I think what a lot of people get frustrated with is the inability to just half♥♥♥♥♥♥an empire and win, which you can do in a lot of 4x games (Civ 5, for all it's acclaim and excellency, can very much be won just by randomly picking technology with a little conservation.)
In Endless Space it's significantly harder. Whether by design or poor AI, the game more or less encourages you to decide on a victory strategy and go for it, and to do that you have to make significant steps backwards to get forwards. Taking the time to build up your navy is necessary for any real chance at a military victory, but doing so early enough to get a foot on the ladder and avoid risk of being flattened by the Cravers and other military empires really does impact your ability to research and build and expand...all three of which are increasingly necessary for building an effective empire.
Similarly you can't just hump one research tree or one tactic to victory. If you only build ships, you won't be expanding and your research is crippled, which means your 70 destroyers will be flattened by a single ship before you realize your mistake. If you want a decent navy you need to unlock the better ships (second tree),spread to multiple worlds for the industrial power to build (second tree but not directly related to military at all), and nab the perks that build up your fleet size (third tree) as well as building better weapons (1st tree, and the only one dirctly 'military'), and to do all that in a timely fashion you need to invest in better research methods (4th tree, which also contains a few very vital techs for your fleet.)
On top of all that, you need to do it in the right order, or you risk spending too much time on one area to the cost of another....and your empire.
Summary: Endless space isn't perfect, but I think it's got the concept of Empire Building down pretty damn good. The reason the AI feels so overpowered and quite often throttles you with ramping up ship strength is because it's a computer, and usually much much better and prioritizing than you.

From all 4X games that I have played, Endless Space captures the feel of ruling over a galactic empire best.
My favorite element of the game is how solar systems work as a whole, and with every system consisting of different numbers and types of planets, with different anomalies and wonders, gives every system you colonize some kind of 'character'. I love getting immersed in the feeling of space exploration and being challenged by every new system. You have to ponder 'Should I colonize this system right now, or wait until I've researched more terraforming technologies? Should I specialize it as an industry system, or use it for economy and research? Is building this huge, expensive improvement worth it, or should I stick to the smaller improvements in this system?'.
The other side of this feeling is that the things you do in this game are at the macro-strategy level. You don't build single buildings on planets, you build improvements for the whole solar system. You don't manage single trade routes, you build trade improvements in systems, and the trade routes will automatically connect your systems with those of other civilizations you are at peace with, in the most profitable way. You don't tell every single ship in a battle where to move, you set fleet formations at the beginning of a battle, and choose general strategies (Things like 'weapon overclock', 'camouflage', 'sabotage', 'repair', and many more) and aiming patters ('spread fire', 'concentrate on one enemy' etc.) for each battle phase (Long-Range, Medium Range, Melee Range), and aside from that, can't influence the course of battle.
Many players criticize this, but I have the impression that this is part of the narrative, and implementing micro-management options would rather hurt the game flow. In this game, you are responsible for the grand strategies, and this is reflected in the mechanics.
Other elements of this game that are important for my recommendation, personally:
- All of the factions are interesting and have a ship style that fits them well
- The music, made by FlyByNo, is magnificent! It enhances the game greatly.
- The User Interface is amazingly clear and elegant. With 4X games generally being complicated, this makes Endless Space significantly more beginner-friendly and comfortable to play.
Once you get past the steep learning curve and reaaly adjust to what this game is all about, it is probably one of the best 4x space games I have ever encountered.

I have semi jokingly renamed this game Endless Waste. Let me explain why.
Sure you have fleets in space check. You have planets you can build stuff on check. You can research technologies all check. What they don't tell you is there are plenty of 4x strategy games that accomplish these basics. The question is does this game accomplish it better? My answer is meh..... Yes, meh.......
Let me ellaborate. Many people complain of the card system for fleet battles in this game. By way of explanation before one of the three rounds starts you and the A.I must choose a card that fits your strategy. You have many options even starting off and more when you research them. How do they work in actual application? The difference is negligible really. Yeah the right card choice can make a tie a victory and the wrong card choice can make a tie a loss. What it can't do is make superior vessels lose. While i respect this choice for balance's sake it has one major drawback. Space conflict does not require much thought. Planning yes, thought no. TBH the disaster that was MOO3 is better in that sense but not graphically of course. The space battles do look nice.
Moving on to planets. Like i said yeah you can build on planets. The way they implement planetary research and production meh.... You can not have individual planetary production queues. I'd be fine with that if it were more like Galactic Civ 3 and you have the option of having a spacedock at every planet producing ships slowly or sending industry to one spacedock. This game does not have that option. Don't take me wrong I am not a Galactic Civ fanboy by any means. IMHO they are mediocre as well for one simple fact. The gaming experience does not evolve that much. Yet this game suffers from that sentiment even more.
Moving on to research. Yeah they have research. How do i rate it a tiny bit above meh.... to meeehhhh??.... While on paper the research ideas are good. The way the game implements them is very meh.... This is not the reaserch tree's fault though. It is the planet building and space combat's fault. Those systems make seeing tangible results not so immersive. Which is where Galactic Civ 3 shines and Endless Waste does not. Endless Waste is not very immersive. In Galciv 3 for instance it is surprisingly clear what effect the combat research has in combat. You can watch the missile hit and do damage to another ship. You see the ship catch on fire if it does not have enough Point Defense and the missile is strong enough. In Endless Waste you don't have that. Point defense don't launch lasers or countermeasures etc. Missile impacts don't leave clouds of debris and ships smoking and/or flaming. Making it feel like frankly not much is happening. It becomes quickly boring except through statistics... if you are a statistical person. The same with planetary infrastructure even though TBH the same can be said about that with majority of 4X strategy games including Galactic Civ 3. The major difference is with nothing truly immersive in Endless Waste you don't really feel compelled to keep playing. Your choices simply do not matter except through statistics. So in essence since neither planetray infrastructure or space combat is immersive how can research be immersive? The other two affect the one.
Leaving to one last consideration money. Is Endless Waste worth the money? To that I say depends. Let me elaborate. If you love statistics, if you love space and the concept of technologies, if you love that when on sale this is drastically cheaper than Galactic Civ 3 this is for you. For everyone else at most just like myself it's meh... at best.
In summary Endless Waste except for the select few is just that an Endless Waste of potential. If they only put in a tiny bit more effort this game would be playable for most of us. Right now not so much. It's too bad because i liked the concept.

Some friends and myself picked this game up for a small lan party we were going to do over New Year's. We were all a bit ambivalent about IF this game would be fun. Disparaging comments were made about the graphics. We even argued about the merits of buying from Steam or directly from the game creator.
So some time in the morning of Jan 1, we booted up the game and muddled our way through getting a server up. We didn't bother with the manual (a few of us did while we tried to figure out how to get our main screen turn on) since things appeared fairly straighforward. We settled down to our command stations, and since I didn't scramble for a specific station I was pegged as the captain. We set the game on the lowest difficulty settings and said "It's only 6 bucks. Not too much of a loss."
We finished that map in 15 minutes. We were clamouring for more, so we made the sector a bit busier, and the enemies tougher. What followed was over an hour of organized yelling, hasty planning and tense staring at our screens as we fought to save the space stations, guide errant freighters away from black holes and deal with angry space life. We all had our moments: Weapons lofted a pair of nukes and blotted out an entire fighter strike. Engineering somehow kept us intact and powered even though we barely managed to keep him ahead of our flailing. Comms got a trio of enemy ships to surrender in quick succession. Our helmsman suckered an invincible alien life form through a minefield to its death. Sensors ID'd targets and made damn certian we knew everything around us and made each beam shot count.
So our opinion after 80 minutes of fast and furious play? We all agreed on one thing. AGAIN.
Who got which seat, on the other hand...

Good game def worth playing--just wish there was more to it's warfare systems, visuals, etc. Seems to lack any idea of repairing or shields even tho its technically a space game. It's like playing tank warfare but with walking tanks, and there's definitely a huge gap to grind and grind and grind for small improvements (mech modules and pilot skills). It's designed to make you want to keep playing to unlock these small benefits, but actually using a lot of them effectively require a level of teamwork that you will not find during solo/quickmatch play, unfortunately. There also seems to be a vast majority of players who can't aim, then a small percentage which can, and an even smaller percentage who approach godhood and seem like hackers. In reality, this is usually to being critically hit, (super low chance) and having components explode and take out your XL engines, or getting shot in the cockpit (super tiny hit box, almost impossible to hit at range) and thus dying instantly. And, death is death (for each match) unless you have multiple mechs to queue with. That in and of itself can be a huge grind since mechs can cost millions of ISK (currency in-game) and you may only get a few thousand to maybe 150k on a really good match with premium time bonuses even higher.. Even at that rate you can see that obtaining the hundreds of mechs available to play and test with will take a very very very long time. Then, there's the issue of mech bays which restrict you from having more than a few unless you spend real money or buy future packs of new mechs that dont come out for months. They also punish you for buying them when they are already out by costing more and often not getting the same deals, so they want you to invest in something you may think you would like months before its even out, at which point you might not even be looking at the same builds. It's kind of a crazy system but the instant satisfaction is there for those who open their wallets/for those who don't you will have a long grind ahead of you but you won't be limited severely and you can do everything in the game just fine without.
Good luck future pilots. o7

So being 100+ hours into the game now, you can definitely accomplish a lot more than many folks here would suggest without paying. I recently passed 1 million prestige, and the only money I spent on the game that influenced my advancement was the second starter pack thing they offer you when you're new, outside of that I bought a couple mounts. There are some points were progress really slows down (just before you get your God form), and it seems almost as if you have hit the "pay wall" many talk about, but you really just need to stick with it, as you'll soon have your God form, and from there progress jumps to a speed that seems insane at first as long as you complete your daily directives. Yes, you'll usually have a PVP quest in your directives, but you are also given 2 stimulants per day that can be used to skip that, and the rest will be provincial adventures that you should easily be able to solo, or group adventures, that you can always find people looking for more in region chat.
I haven't really had any issues with free progression so far, and really don't see the point in "paying to win" as a lot of the PVE content is either equalized, or scales to your current power, and nobody does PVP. Even if PVP were active, and you couldn't pay to power up, there's always going to be the no lifers that are still far ahead of everybody else messing with the balance of it, equalized PVP is the way to go in games like this, though I can't say if it has any equalized PVP as this is not something I was looking for in the game anyway.
Another thing I will touch on is the population of the game, as I see many negative reviews stating the game is dead. I have not experienced this, at very off hours, there are still plenty of players around, enough that you can still run full group content, during peak hours, there's tons of people around. I will note that I play on the North American server, and that this may not be the case on the European server.
Something fairly important to note is that the default server for the game is Europe, if you would like to play on the North American server, you will need to select it in a dropdown in the launcher, so make sure you do this before playing for the first time if you grabbed the free starter pack, or any other packs, as they will be registered to whichever server you enter after obtaining them.
tl;dr
I haven't encountered any issues with "pay to win" players as I only play PVE and it is somewhat irrelevant to do there (and in general as progression is quite fast after you get your God form), and the populations is fine on the NA server. If you enjoy action games, it's definitely worth a look.

Love the idea of having a controller that replaces the mouse/keyboard duo for PC gaming!
I was one of the people who pre-ordered this and the Steam Link when they were announced and got them on launch day. There are several things I could say about the Steam Link, but I'll try to keep those separate since this is a review about the controller itself. I've watched as the controller software has evolved from a minimum viable product that they pushed to market with stability and usability in mind, all the way to the current day with massive configurability and built-in keyboard mapping.
Speaking of the key maps, I love the Xbox 360 controller; it is truly fantastic in a lot of ways. One benefit of this controller over the 360 controller is that you have keyboard and mouse mapping built into steam itself as if it actually is an external device. I *could* use the steam controller (with the steam link, since it's effectively a remote desktop thin client) from my couch to surf facebook on my desktop running Chrome. One part that's unclear is if there is any way to separate the configuration of button mapping to be a separate application that I might, for example, use with GOG Galaxy.
As far as configurability of the key maps is concerned, I find the lack of community submitted key maps a slight downside. I think so many gamers that prefer controllers are used to using the default mappings and those that customize swear by using an actual keyboard and mouse for their games. As of when I last checked, about 8 months ago (I know, I know...), the number of community supported mappings is still really low and the maturity of the mappings is such that there is still no clear crowd favorite for any given game. It's not yet mature enough like the Skyrim modding community to say, "This configuration is essential if you use the steam controller." That said, I could easily see flame wars sprouting up in the far off future about opinionated configurations being better than one another (re: editor wars)
Overall, I love the Xbox 360 controller for its support of so many games already and the easy to press buttons, joysticks, etc. I don't love how difficult the steam controller is to click the thumb touchpads, especially when the left thumbpad is intended to double as a D-pad.
One experiment I have yet to try is interaction of the steam controller with a non-steam game, such as The Witcher purchased from
. I'm curious if Big Picture Mode, and by extension the Steam Controller, will support it with the same custom keymappings, or whether it'll give up and say it's intended for keyboard/mouse only.

Thoroughly enjoyed this game from start to finish - i've never actually enjoyed point-and-click adventures before, but the whole premace of this one caught my eye, and I'm glad it did!
The positives are that its great fun, makes you feel like you could go out and hack the white house, and you actually build up a mental rapport on various people throughout the story - by the final mission just seeing certain names that cropped up elsewhere was enough to push me in the right direction. There-in lies another positive: the game, despite being a point-and-click, has enough 'flesh' in non-important things to allow you to wonder off what you are supposed to be doing, something that I think is often not done in similar games of the genre, and is the reason i dont normally enjoy point-and-clicks.
Amongst other things, the other great positives to this game, in my opinion, is the humor centred around parodying real life, which is not only present in the main story line, but also in areas 'around' it (by which i mean in the file systems of people unrelated to your mission, etc)
The downsides? I sometimes felt as though I was just guessing at what files might be incriminating, and even when i succeeded i occasionally didnt really understand why. The second downside is the fact that I have finished the game in it's current state (7 missions) in juyst 2.5 hours. I mess around a lot, so someone who was really trying and understood everything about the game could probably be doine with it in under 2 hours. Secondly, I dont see much replay value in it - however, i dont usually see replay value in many things so this could just be me.
Overall I do think that this game is worth the money - not only this but the game will soon have a further 6 (or something around that i think) missions added on in early February. I think that if you are reading this and dont know whether to buy or not, just go and get the demo - the missions in that aren't actually directly related to the missions in the full game, so you will get a good idea of what it is like without having to replay parts upon purchasing
Also, the windows XP nostalgia by itself was worth it!

If you're old enough (or retro gamer enough) to remember that Carmen Sandiego game from 1992 where you had to hop around the world gathering evidence of crimes, pinning faces to names, and figuring out who did what crime and where - you'll absolutely LOVE this kind of game.
I love point-and-clicks, and I love hacksims. This doesn't do either seperately very well, but does both together great!
From a point-and-click side of things, the interface is easy to use, the humor is there, the exploration and investigation is thoughtful. Sometimes it doesn't make it too obvious what you must do next, and you have to try a ton of evidence to move on, but it's executed decently.
The hacksim perspective is a little on the tame side compared to others. You get basic hack commands that "just work", and you realize quickly that taking notes isn't usually required since the help screen is always available. You also don't have to rely on advanced commands or speed timed elements as you do with other hacksims (though I've only played the game for a VERY short amount of time at this point, so I'm assuming a lot) making the hacking element very much a secondary aspect of the game.
In that respect, it's definitely more of a point-and-click than a hacksim where you would have to probe networks, get through firewalls, obtain information, delete your trail... instead, in this you just get in and sort through the evidence. It's about proving someone is guilty of something. It's about digging through their personal sites, blogs, photos.... all very Carmen Sandiego, like I said before.
It's one of the best I've played in recent memory and the nods to the various OSes, software, companies, etc. is hilarious and leaves me feeling very satisfied.

TL;DR (good deal of gameplay from free demo):  Mainlining is a fun adventure game with a clever and unique twist where you hack computers, websites, and other devices to mine information on the different cases presented to you.  The game doesn't hold your hand, so the cases can present a fun little challenge beyond the first tutorial.  Highly recommended!  If you want to see a playthrough of the first (tutorial) case, check out this video (Demo version):
FULL REVIEW:  Mainlining, the point-and-click hacking adventure game, casts the player as an employee of MI7 in charge of investigating various cyber-crimes and tracking suspects through electronic means.  You are given tools (e.g., electronic trackers, a simplified command-line, web browser, etc) in order to collect information, put together clues, and ultimately arrest the right person.
There is a lot of unique gameplay in Mainlining since, unlike other adventure games, the puzzles and stories you try to untangle are pieced together from short emails, blog posts, and other electronic files.  The game does a good job of not holding your hand (e.g., by telling you which sites to hack, etc) but does provide sufficient in-context clues so that the task isn’t impossible and/or a guessing game.  It’s also a game that very much should be played with a pen and paper handy because you’ll need to track which websites/IP addresses you have collected, which you have hacked, which files you have or have not read or downloaded, and which suspects you wish to pursue.  Note that there IS a “notes” application (because the game looks like a computer desktop), but that fills up quickly.
Overall, the game is challenging, unique, and very entertaining (it’s got a good self-aware/internet-aware sense of humor) while still retaining the hallmarks of good adventure games: good story, good gameplay mechanics, and good pacing.  I would definitely recommend this game or, at the least, would suggest you check out the demo (which contains the first two cases from the full game—and save files apparently carry over).

What is bad?
Chakra Dash costs too much chakra. Yes it does.

Adventure Mode forces you to follow a spin-off storyline on the Naruto x Hinata romance narrative, whether you like it or not, whether you approve of that story development or not, or whether you actually care or not. (This is the worst part, that far outweighs the best part, imho)
I am definitely not the only person who disagrees with the romance pairing (Naru-Hina / Sasu-Saku) that Kishimoto went for, despite how little Sasuke has done to show care or even deserve affection from anyone.
It just feels like a spiteful kick in your gut to have to trudge through something you so strongly disagree with, just to have some sort of storyline to follow, in a game mode that has so much potential considering the number of playable characters available, and all the other story developments that don't relate to Naruto's lack of choice in his own love life.
Adventure mode really should be something you have a bit more choice in shaping to your personal liking.
It shouldn't be a linear, forced romance, filler-arc littered with "drops of reminiscence" and uninspired, arcade-style side quests, and some more drops of reminiscence, with a few glimmers of heart warming anomalies.
It's a whole game mode devoted to a filler spin off!
It is simply garbage.
Even if you're one of those people who actually think Sasuke deserves human affection at all, or that it's sweet or even admirable of Sakura, despite obvoius hazards to her physical and mental health, to stubbornly and selfishly pursue a romantic interest that treats her worse than the squashed carcass of a gad-fly - it's still garbage.
Story mode is fine tho.

4/10 at full price. 5/10 on Steam sale.
First, consider the source: I am not a huge 4X fan. Don't get me wrong, I don't mind building my empire by exploring, investing in improvements, researching technologies and creating ships. Creating ships to actually fight, but more on this later. Explore, Exploit, Expand and Eliminate are the four elements of this genre, but I believe this game is seriously unbalanced.
Explore is okay. You build ships to go out and find planets. You eventually run into wormholes which you need a specific technology to use. You can research to get it, which has a certain interest. The problem is that expanding your empire results in a happiness hit to your people. I found the subjects of my empire becoming progressively more unhappy because of expansion. Okay, I can see that, but it seemed to be impossible to make them happy by investing in their systems by creating improvements, generating more FIDS (food, industry, dust and science-the point system at the heart of the game), or building ships. It made no sense. One of the other reasons they were unhappy was listed as "population overcrowding", but none of the planets were anywhere near their caps. But if one of the pillars of 4X results in a penalty, it kind of wrecks the experience, doesn't it?
That said, if one enjoys that sort of thing, i.e. fighting the actual game to figure out how to keep your people happy while researching technologies and actually expanding your realm, then this game is probably going to be for you. The tech tree was kind of neat, but it was very unclear what each technology actually did. Some showed up as system improvements, others were weapon systems and ship types. Others required research in other branches of the tree. Some seemed to have no reason other than spending Science points. I don't mind planning and investing in new tech, but I would like to have a clearer idea of where my return on investment is going to lead.
Diplomacy and trade. I never could figure out if the other AI was offering crappy deals or what. I never saw an advantage to trading with the AI. I formed an alliance with the other AI, but to break it when I wanted to expand into its territory, I had to wait 10 turns. Then, I had to wait another 10 turns to declare war. So forget launching a sneak attack or anything like that. Who would want to EVER do that in an empire-building game, right?
The so-called combat mode was the worst part of the game. This is a 4x space game, not Pokemon! You set up one of three tactics, Spread Fire, which is every ship firing at every other ship. Nosebreaker, where every ship targets the first ship, and Guillotine where you target the first 1/3 of the other side's ships. You then have an assortment of strategy cards you can play at various points in the "battle." Battle itself is separated into 5 segments The Approach, Long Range, Medium Range, Melee and Results. Nothing happens during Approach and Results. So during 2/5s of the "combat" system, nothing really happens. That is a problem that doesn't really get much better.
I have to admit, the individual ships look great, and the animations are slow, but smooth as the camera cuts around the Approach.
Then combat starts, and you find that despite the fact that the ships are a mere several ship lengths from one another, the ships can't hit each other! They contain technologies that let them navigate the galaxy. They have thousands of Dust points invested in them, but they make Star Wars Stormtroopers look like Anne Oakley! And it had NOTHING to do with the strategy cards you play as far as I could tell. Even when both ships played Overclock, most of the shots missed at all distances.
And the lack of ability to target individual ships is arbitrary and frustrating! My opponent would show up with a behemoth ship that was all Deflectors and Shields escorting other ships that some of which had damage, but there was no way to "target" any other ship. And it was all very repetitive; the ships Approach in the same order each time in orbit around what seems like the same planet. After I got tired of watching the same animations with ships inexplicably missing each other time after time, and ending in draws, I decided to set my formations and strategies ahead of time and let the computer auto resolve the battle. Then, of course, I lost half my fleet!
And I kept getting draws. If one craft from either side is left alive, the battle is considered a draw. The ships simply drift, right next to one another during the results phase. Overall, the system is very silly.
This system makes the idea of going through the 4x system really repulsive because it takes the "Eliminate" out of the whole system. I want a combat system where movement, formation, offensive and defensive systems, propulsion, ship size and planetary system features allow/require me to formulate my own strategy and fight the battle until one side's ships are destroyed, or they surrender or flee the field.
I've played StarDrive 2, Vangard Prophecy and Sid Meyer's Starships. I enjoy the turn based combat from VP where you set the motion movement of the ships based on a balance of Engines, Shields and Weapons and the ship moves into position on the next turn firing as it goes. How you move and the balance of ESW help determine whether you are successful. Unfortunately, there is no Explore, Exploit and Expand to that game.
The hex grid board game feel of Starships at the in-system level was also enjoyable requiring you to think how you move, when you fire and what system you use. The battle card system is important, but it doesn't necessarily make or break your tactics.
StarDrive simply felt like Gratuitous Space Battles grafted onto Endless Space's 4X system. It needed more tactical movement and targeting options, IMO.
The problem is that even after 20 hours in the game; I really have no idea what I should do different the next time. IMO, you should be able to play a game and learn from the outcomes what to do differently to effect the next outcome. For this reason as well as others listed in this review, I really can't recomment this game.

Definitely one of the more underrated games under Steam's free list of games. 'WoG:GD' might be targeted more towards people with an interest or passion in fire arms, but as someone who doesn't care for weaponry, I found this game to be very well made and quite enjoyable.
Firstly it's a simulator, if you couldn't already tell, in which you assemble, disassemble, and field test weaponry. The main chunks and most polished modes in this simulator are the assembling and disassembling portions, obviously. Being given hundreds of guns to choose from, ranging from pistols, to assault rifles, and even machine guns, every gun will feel like it's own separate entity. Repetition is nowhere to be seen, and I congratulate the devs on achieving this. You'd think for how formula's usually work in simulators that gameplay would get stale, leaving little reason to come back, but this isn't the case for 'WoG:GD'.
Overall, I think this game will appeal to anyone who interested in mechanisms and systems, not necessarily 'gun freaks'. It's a game that that doesn't even require an extensive knowledge on firearms to appreciate. Everything is presented in a logical way, and there's an option for hints to be displayed, if you are having trouble. Give 'WoG:GD' a shot, even you're just the slightest bit intrigued, it will make for tons of fun.

What can I say about ASBS?
Well it's definitely not for everyone, that much is certain. To expect that to be otherwise is foolish.
However, this game is most certainly very fun for those who enjoy LAN parties, playing with friends online, simulator fans or just one of those who enjoy playing as a team.
It's not impossible to play this game alone, but that takes most of the enjoyment and fun out of this game. If you have a bunch of nerdy friends like yourself who are fans of Star Wars, Star Trek, Babylon 5, Firefly etc. Then you're going to have one of the most fun experiences of your life.
You can each take a certain role on a ship and communicating with your friends is key to your success.
It's a dream game for people who have always wanted to live in their favourite sci-fi universe.
If you have a bunch of friends who are interested in this game, what are you waiting for? Pick this up and buy it!
However if you don't, but are interested in playing this game, hope is not lost, approach people online, look for groups who play together!
I have to recommend this game, it's hard not to with the amount of fun I've had with it!

When I clicked that install button, I wasn't aware of how BAD this game is. I knew it was on the last page of the free-to-play adventure-RPG's, but I didn't think it would be that bad. Now that I'm talking about it, where IS the adventure? I've played this game for 20 minutes and no adventure at all, no storyline, no nothing. Isn't that the point of adventure RPG's?
In my opinion the introduction fails a lot. It should introduce you into the game; who are you playing as? What is your main objective? Instead you start off at a poorly decorated login screen. I could make that with Microsoft Word. after you log in and select a server, you will be taken to another window. And then it all begins. You are randomly dropped in some guys house. Oh and what I forgot to mention: the lack of humor. It's like the game is trying to be funny, but it isn't; "An epic adventure to the kitchen"
After the opening you get to some kind of selection room. You can choose between a zombie and a dragon: a fighter and a builder. I chose the dragon, because if I think about dragons I think about combat and not about building. I only did the quest with the dragon, because I simply got bored. There is one thing that I sure don't like: the shop. Okay, this is an RPG, I like the fact that you can always buy swords 'n stuff, but blocks?! Shouldn't those things be collected in the overworld instead of some kind of boring window which says "shop"?
Anyways, this was my opinion about this game. 3/10.
