Crimsonland is a top-down arena shooter. That's about it. I mean, really. Things come from all sides and you shoot them.
And it feels pretty damn satisfying!
I've got to say, this is a game that I'm in 2 minds about. On one hand, it has a pretty bad design, in the places where it counts. On the other hand, it's glorious to paint the field red with the blood of your enemies!
The game has a ton of different weapons, which is great on survival mode! On the survival modes, you also have a ton of perks that alter your play a bit, almost like modern rogue-lites. The game has no bosses, no maps, no levels, nor anything else of that sort. It does have quite a bit of enemy variety, although the differences between the types are very subtle.
The game also has a "campaign" of sorts, with different levels. The campaign is dreadful. If you read the reviews, you can see most people calling the game out as "randomness instead of skill", and it's absolutely true. On these levels, you have to rely on the "right" weapon dropping for you to beat a level. Sometimes that being insufficient, requiring additional power-ups at the right moments.
Beating it on "Normal" is fine, but on Hardcore, there's one particular level that requires astronomical luck. It's called Spideroids and it's dreadful. It features these Spider enemies that work as follows: big, slow spider -> kill it, you get 2 smaller, but faster spider -> kill it, get another 2, smaller and faster -> this happens like 8 times or something ridiculous like that. Your character doesn't run faster than the small spiders, and to add insult to injury, they actually gain speed overtime, so you'll be overrun after a while.
Unless you get a very specific set of drops, it's impossible to win.
The AI in this game is both great and bad. It's more intelligent than to run directly at you. On Spideroids, though, it makes things impossible. I'm not even sure if the game was actually playtested (as in, without cheats -- without choosing weapons and powerups at will, making sure that it is possible, regardless of the chance of those conditions happening)...
Some enemies run at you, while others observe where you're going, and they adjust their direction to meet you at that point.
Each type of enemy also has different characteristic that are quite interesting! For example, zombies are slower and then to flock, while spiders are quick and unpredictable. That sort of thing. They all try to get to you in a swarm, but they have different details that are very much appreciated!
Overall, the campaign is very situational. Fortunately, where the game shines is one its Survival Modes. There are 4 or 5 different ones that you can choose from. The game and your character are rather slow, which is boring. There is one mode, though, called Blitz, where things are a bit faster, and it's freakin' awesome! I really enjoyed that mode.
The sound design is solid, but the music was very uninsteresting to me.
The weapons' sounds are very distinct from one another, but I feel that they lack a bit of power, in general. Nothing too important, as the game still feels great to play!
There isn't much to say at all, here. It's a very old-school type of game. It's like the analog of Painkiller and Hard Reset in 2D. While 3D shooters have the great advantage of a fully fleshed physics and first person perspective to make things visceral (God, bolt weapons in Bioshock felt so good!), Crimsonland swarm you with enemies from all sides, each hit splashing blood on the floor and leaving bodyparts behind. Ones that don't actually vanish!
There's something fantastic about these mindless games that really appeal to me! And if this sounds like your cup of tea, go for it! As I said, the campaign isn't very good (beat it once to unlock all of the weapons and perks), but the core game is great!
Oh, also... I've never played the original game, so I can't compare it to that.

If you're a long-time MechWarrior or Battletech fan like me, you're going to be disappointed. This isn't the game we were waiting for. It doesn't respect the source material, in ways that are especially frustrating because there seem to be some fairly straightforward solutions. Also, through various dumb decisions better explained elsewhere, it's pretty clear that the developers simply don't care about the hard core fans of the series.
However!
The game itself, taken in isolation, as it is right now, is very good. It's fun to play. So, in all fairness, it gets a thumbs-up. When it's good, it's VERY good. Teamwork is not just rewarded but demanded - if you try to go off and solo you'll get swiftly destroyed and put your team one player down. It can be frustrating when you get a team that scatter like headless chooks, so you'll need to cultivate a bit of a zen attitude, but the good moments are worth it.
There's a very satisfying cycle of customising your mechs, trying them out in battle, tweaking them, salivating over the next big engine upgrade or new chassis, taking that out in battle, eyeing the next big upgrade, and so on.
I wouldn't spend any money on it, though.
NB: I've played for a fair bit before this was on Steam. Apparently I have 97 hours of in-cockpit time all together.
-------------------------------------------
e: quick PSA here: you need to stick together. You NEEEEEEED to stick together. You also need to use terrain to your advantage. Going off by yourself to try to flank the enemy WILL get you killed. Pushing through a narrow pass WILL get you killed.
See
. You'll be more successful with your whole team fighting together, targeting one enemy at a time, occupying ground that allows your team to focus fire, than you will by trying to 1v1 everyone. Even in the very heaviest mechs, you cannot reasonably expect to win against more than one opponent at a time, and if you win a 1v1 you'll take far more damage doing it than if you and your buddies were focusing on one target instead.
Even if you don't agree with where most of your teammates are headed, sticking with them will win more often than going off and doing your own thing instead. Trust me. For the sake of your future teammates' sanity, please stick together.

I have been playing MWO for quite some time. I am not a hardcore fan. I did play MW on the Playstation and PC back in the 90s.
MWO is a great game, there aren't many around, not many games that are not pay to win. A lot of cosmetics to your mechs and plenty of discounts and freebies. If you love Mechs or if you watched Pacific Rim and felt like you want a mech game I really do recommend MWO.
Bear in mind that the Mechs are sluggish, they are huge mechs after all, they also behave like tanks, legs and torso move independently. The game is quite similar with World of franchise.
In regards to gameplay, you can customise your mech with any weapons mods and gear you wish which is great as you will never meet the exact same mech on the battlefield. This is where the fun starts. There is no cookie cutter build, some would argue but really there isn't and I suggest to experiment and play YOUR way. Especially if you PUG and don't join a serious Clan. I did but I didn't like the fact they were dictating my mech set-up.
Quick do and don't list:
DO stick together with your team, else going alone you will get picked up and you will die.
DON'T go alone unless you are very confident and you play a fast scouting mech, light/medium mech.
DO quit the match once dead as you can start a new one without having to wait until end of match (something I did not know and wasted so much time looking at my team play, then again by doing so I did learn about mech setups and strategy)
DO experiment with your mech, don't listen to people saying an Assault mech should not have LRMs. Many of the maps in MWO are LRM firendly. After all how will you get LRM 60+ if not fitting on an Assault mech?
DON'T listen to Assault should never have LRMs on them.
DO use LRM (homing missiles) when you first start playing regardless of the mech you use, it is a noob friendly weapon, hell it is a any player friendly weapon and you will do massive damage.
DON'T go for Heavy mechs they are over used and will take forever to queue for a match. Also they take an Assault class spot.
DO manage your heat, try to have rating of at least 1 heat management if not 1.2+
DON'T fire all your weapons like crazy, get heat spikes and shut down, you will die. Cycle your weapons if you must and go for double heat sinks but bear in mind they take 3 slots. You will be surprised how efficient it is firing 3 4 5 LRM's by cycling (BACKSPACE key) than all at once. Same goes for lasers if you overheat.
DO Lock your targets, ALWAYS, no matter what mech you are in. You help others see the target and LRMs hit it. It also helps you see where the target is damaged so you can do even more damage by hitting the same locations.
DO check your weapons details, especially range. Some weapons have a minimum range so if you shoot them at close range they do ABSOLUTELY NOTHING. You would be surprised how many people shoot PPCs and LRMs at close range. Others that shoot them hoping to get people at 2Km distance:(
DON'T test you weapons when you enter a game, you will just shoot your team mates and cause friendly fire. Use the Testing Grounds or If you must turn around find a safe area and do it but remember you will waste ammo if you use ammo. That 10 ammo wasted could make a difference when you have none left.
DON'T block your team mates, and DON'T be a hero going first hoping to get them kills by blocking everyone behind you. You might get a kill but will also die and cause others to friendly fire you. I had highest damage in the game without any kills (you also get an achievd for this). Even with plenty kills your rating can be lower than someone that killed none but did most damage.
MECHS: You no longer need 3 different mech variants to level them up. So go ahead and experiment.
LIGHTS: I have a few but I don't really enjoy playing them. Hit and run tactics, scouts, you will die very fast, frustrating for new players and for old. Can have a light 5x5LRM which is a trolling build but fun as hell. 8 9 medium lasers which wil do a lot of damage but do bear in mind that you have to constantly move and if you go toe a toe with any other mech you gotta circle it, move legs and torso independently to run circles around that mech. Something I can't do well.
MEDIUM: Similar to Lights but can be fun, they are quite fast and can pack a punch, would be used mainly as hit and runs, brawlers or LRM. You will be surprised how much damage 5x5LRMs can do (over 1000 damage in a match). You are an LRM boat that can move around the battlefield at 80 to 100 Kph. Can fit a number of high damage weapons. IE: Cicada with 4 ER Large Lasers which will be a great sniper.
HEAVY: My first mech was a heavy, the CAT, a lovely LRM boat, all I did was sit back and shoot a rain of missiles on my enemies:) I have the least Heavy mechs than any other one. They are great but everyone is using them and it takes FOREVER to queue up for games. As I mentioned earlier they also take 1 assault spot from the team.
ASSAULT: Well, what can I say about these walking fortresses. They pack a punch and can take quite a few. Just remember to stick with other mechs, mediums lights especially as they can protect you. You will be surprised how fast an Assault mech can go down if even 1 good light pilot starts running circles around you and shooting your legs. I say have at least 1 LRM boat. When people say it is a waste of 100 tons, I say well my score and damage says something else. So many maps now are long ranged that if you have any other weapons you are a waste of 100 tons, especially the snow maps which everyone selects because they cannot manage their heat or because they are LRM or long range weapons.
As I said, experiment, have 1 LRM from each class, make sure to check al mechs and select the one with most missile slots. Put 10 medium lasers on an assault, 8 medium pulse lasers on another, 4 x 15 LRMs, 4 x LBX10 or 4 x 20LRMs. Same on heavy or mediums. Since you will be making more money at start I would suggest to get an Assault mech first. Get one that has the weapons you need so you don't spend even more money on upgrades. Test the trial ones and remember if you buy the trial mech you have been using, it has the XP saved which is great as it can be used for skills once unlocked.
You could go for a Heavy mech first but due to longer queues it will take you longer to make the money back so I say get an Assault first then a Medium and a light if you fancy that (run the trial mechs first for as long as you need as it will help you decide which you prefer and you will also see the difference in queue times for the different mech sizes).

I was incredibly surprised by this game. I had received it as a gift awhile back and from looking at gameplay videos on YouTube, I decided at the time it wasn't for me. I was dead wrong. This is my first 4X game (explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate) and have passed on other popular games like the Civilization series thinking that they would not be to my liking. Where should I start?
Graphically speaking, the game looks and performs very well. Are they top of the line, burn your motherboard-type graphics? No, but for what this game offers, I have been very pleased. As you can see from the pictures provided on this page, you'll spend most of your time looking at either the beautiful galaxy map or the various tabs located at the top left of your galaxy screen. Aside from staring at the galaxy map when zoomed out (which I particularly enjoy), the most eye candy you'll see in-game is of course the "manual" fleet battles that I'm sure you'll encounter during play. I have my graphics set to the maximum settings and the frame rate runs easily above 100 per second. "Manual" fleet battles give you a visual representation of the battles as well as an opportunity to change your strategy as it progresses.
The tabs at the top of your screen consist of various actions you may queue up and/or perform on any turn. They range from your overall progression score compared to the other factions in the game to a comprehensive system list to manage your assets, research tree, fleet shipyard, diplomacy and finally your hero cards. These different tabs also range from useful to rather unnecessary. Later in the game (usually after 70 turns) I found myself using this tab the most so I could manage all of my systems happiness, tax rate, system improvements and resources and trade routes. The research tree is absolutely necessary to do anything in the game, but what I found out to be more important was to skip reading guides online and simply just sit down for an hour and read through all of the different tiles. The fleet shipyard isn't required much as you simply just research new ship types in one of the four available tech trees in the research tab along with your various weapons, defenses and support modules in other trees and just make your own designs to build. The hero tab is rather ho-hum as quite simply you look to hire hero cards to place on a system or in a fleet. Managing your ability points as your level them up can be done elsewhere.
Diplomacy on the other hand is somewhat frustrating. Split between a sort of good and evil with some rather in between, 10 factions in the base game offer a wide variety of gameplay. There are tiles that you upgrade diplomacy through your research tab to give you various bonuses, however what it won't take into account is that each faction responds differently to diplomacy. Some won't engage in it and are completely hostile, others are hermits and avoid you almost altogether and others hate your guts if you're beating them economically like I have and take forever to form alliances and cooperative trade agreements. I don't quite like how it was designed and wished there was a little bit better way to draw up diplomatic relations more quickly and efficiently. If you're all for blowing them up and conquering systems, then diplomacy won't even be an afterthought for you.
Personally, diplomacy has been much to what I described. They tend to either be violent due to the inherited nature or they hold a grudge against you for being better than you for a good two-thirds of the game and then suddenly they become bootlickers and ask for the most ridiculous trades imaginable. Example: I was playing as a peaceful Amoeba faction, exploring and expanding to three arms of an eight arm spiral galaxy with 5 other factions. One hated everyone and was suspicious of anyone (Cravers), one was constantly making threats and talking about glory and me being beneath them even though I was the master race for the whole game in terms of knowledge, diplomatic, expansive and economic power (Hissho); and the others kept to themselves and refused to talk to me until they decided I wasn't going anywhere (Pilgrams, Amoeba and another Hissho). The first Hissho decided an alliance would be good, but thought I was worthless and demanded I pay them a bunch of fuel resources to make the deal. After that I invited the pilgrams since they were 2nd to my capabilities and the Hissho eagerly agreed. Next the Amoeba decided that I'm peaceful enough that they may want to trade with me. At this point, for the rest of the game they kept asking for trade deals that are the worst imaginable. "How about I give you 2 marbles and I'll throw in a jacket with a torn sleeve for 5 units of rocket fuel? Promise not to shoot at you? Our people believe this to be for the glory of the Empire!" Blah Blah Blah.
You get the idea.. These "allies" of mine are chumps and couldn't be trusted to fix a crack in the pavement let alone build an empire. Good luck getting good trades in of your own unless they love you to death for not shooting at them all game long. Lastly in regards to diplomacy, take care when you're in an alliance. If you declare war, your allies might not like this and then declare war on you, or in my case, I was in an alliance where one declared war on someone, bringing us into the fight when we didnt want it and I decided to stay whereas my other ally turned on me for staying. Let's just say that didn't end well and I learned my lesson. If you wish to side with other like-minded allies, just be careful when war breaks out.
One other thing to keep in mind with the game is to read through each of the factions before you play. Very important as the traits allocated to each one is specific and will help cater to your particular playstyle. In other words, if you have a certain playstyle in mind, you might later on discover that other factions are better at accomplishing those goals. Once you get the handle on the game, take a look at designing your own faction. I haven't come close to mastering the game yet for me to go there, but I'm looking forward to it.
Over all, as the 4X title suggests, you get to do a bit of everything and even if it doesn't seem like it will be fun, it is worth another look at the very least. I came from enjoying real-time strategy games like StarCraft, WarCraft, Red Alert and Company of Heroes to loving this game to death. I've only put 24 hours into this game and I've barely scratched the surface and will most definitely put many more hours into it. Even though the diplomacy aspect of the game is somewhat limiting, there is something there for someone who wants to build rather than destroy as well as the capability to just wreck havoc in a pretty decent space game. The faction biographies are fun to read as well as the little bits of information you glean from discoveries around the galaxy as you explore, expand, exploit and exterminate. Take the leap!

Artemis is a diamond in the rough. It's very much unlike any other space sim I've ever played. The game has you play a starship bridge officer, responsible for controlling one of the ship's systems. Pretty cool and all, but there's a twist. In most space sims, a player is responsible for running the whole ship. He controls the weapons, he directs the ship to its destination, and so on. Artemis is different in that each of the ship's systems are run by other players. The bridge crew is entirely composed of humans, not AI.
There are five stations to man in Artemis: Helm, Engineering, Weapons, Science and Comms. Helm controls the ship's movement. Engineering deals with repairs and modifying the power levels of each system in the ship. Weapons handles, well, weapons and shields. Science has control over the sensors, scanning targets for information on its systems and crew. Comms handles communication with other vessels, both friend and foe.
This 5-man setup provides a lot of depth to the game, but it is not difficult to learn by any means. The actual mechanics behind the workings of each system are surprisingly simple to learn. The genius of Artemis is how the mechanics of all these systems work together to form a complete, compelling experience for everyone involved. All crew members need to have good synergy if they want to complete the mission. As long as you keep up a friendly attitude, pay attention to your fellow crewmates and do your part to keep the ship running, you will have a high chance of success.
Originally, the game could only be purchased through the developer's website. It could only be played through LAN, and it cost 40 bucks, because that version came with extra copies to be played on other computers for a full LAN party. LAN play is fun as hell, but that alone doesn't make for much mass appeal. Fortunately, the developers have realized this and have added online play. The Steam version of the game costs a mere 8 bucks, because it's only one copy. A dirt cheap price for what could be an endless amount of fun with friends? That's a steal.
If you're going to play online, you'll need to get a program called Teamspeak to communicate with other players. There is a teamspeak server that is decently populated for most of the day. IPs for servers can be found there. Its address is
and its password is Artemis1. The community is very friendly, supportive, and a whole lot of fun to play with.
Give Artemis a shot. This game deserves a lot more attention. It really is unlike any other space sim on the market. It's about as close to being in Star Trek as you can get. I'll see you in Starfleet.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game back in 2003 when it was originally published. I didn't even know about this remake (which actually feels exactly like I remember the original version, right down to the same menacing music) until I just spotted it in the Humble Bundle and just had to buy it immediately.
The game has many different kinds of enemies that are sufficiently different from each other, and even more weapons and perks. Perks are used in the survival mode, where you can activate a new perk every time you cross a certain threshold in scores. They, too, are very diverse, and I like their descriptions that are spiced with some dark humor.
The game has just the right learning curve. The levels get tougher the further you proceed, but you never feel like a level is unwinnable. Sure, you may have to try it five, ten, or fifty times, but you can always see your progress bar at the top of the screen and see that you actually did slightly better than the previous time. And it is of course a very rewarding feeling once you complete a very difficult level.
I would've recommended this game warmly 12 years ago and I still do!

This game is a top-down shooter without a story. Every single mission will place you on a flat map without any obstacles or anything else but monsters that keep spawning.
Each mission will spawn different combinations of enemies, but in each mission your goal is the same and that is to kill everything on screen.
Now can a game without a story and map design be fun? Absolutely! Unfortunately this is not one of those games that managed to pull that off and it's just not fun.
So what's wrong with it? Well you'd expect this kind of game to be fast paced action-filled shooter right? Well that's not really what this game is. Your character is very slow and that really ruins the gameplay in my opinion.
Another issue I have with the game is that weapons aren't balanced. A lot of them are simply underpowered and not worth using. Also the way you get weapons in this game is random. When you kill enemies they sometimes drop weapons or power-ups.
The first enemy you kill in a mission will almost always drop a weapon. So what you'll probably end up doing is keep restarting the mission until your first drop ends up being a good weapon so you have a better chance of beating the mission. You might do that even in easier missions because beating a mission without taking damage will give you a star on that mission.
When it comes to beating missions without taking damage in order to get stars, picking up power-ups is important. However due to your character moving very slowly and enemies moving at your speed or faster and in packs, picking up power-ups without taking damage can be very tricky or near-impossible in certain missions.
Usually in challenging games I feel good when I finally beat a hard level, it feels like an achievement. In this game however that's not the case. I don't end up feeling good, nor that I achieved something. I just end up being glad I got that mission over with and ask myself do I really want to go for another mission or should I just close the game.
I wouldn't recommend this game even if it were freeware as it's just not enjoyable. I really don't know why they think their game is worth 14€.

Playing Prototype was a red haze. The games protagonist Alex Mercer is an unrepentant sociopath and embodies the Prototype worldview. Mercers obsession with vengeance leads him into mass murder, which in turn makes it impossible to root for him. He actually uses civilians as "medi kits", absorbing their bodies to replenish health. One of the primary quest givers is Mercers sister, and not killing her seems to be Mercers most humane act.
In fiction, the most obvious way to justify the anti-hero's acts is to make the villains even more evil in comparison. Prototype is not afraid of the obvious, and the military and the private sector seem to be psychopaths to the last man.
The gameplay is OK but unspectacular, with Mercer having access to various powers but gaining upgrades at a very fast speed indeed. The speed of Mercers movements is very fast too, and going from place to place is actually well made. The typical activities (obstacle courses, kill challenges etc.) do not fit the game, at all.
Prototype is nasty and nihilistic and I cannot recommend it to anyone. Prototype fans were somewhat disappointed when Mercer returned as the primary villain in 2, but that is what he was all along.

So I see a lot of people are giving poor reviews on the Steam Controller for a "Recently: Mixed" where the controller overall has a "Very Positive" Rating. Why? Maybe it has something to do with the early adopters knowing more what they were getting into, very new territory where they'd have to spend some time configuring their controller. They find what kinds of settings they like and can quickly configure their controllers to suit any game they play. Newer users might be having trouble where they think the default or community settings are "tried and true" but aren't actually good for them. Plus, I think more people are getting it on amazon and such and reviewing it there (hence its 4.5 star rating) I figured I'd chime in to defend this gem of a piece of hardware.
First, a warning: This is the best controller out there, but you have to WORK for it to be the best controller out there. You can become very nearly as good as a mouse and keyboard user if you fine tune your settings per game and practice with it. You wont become perfect with it overnight. You won't even be very good with it by the end of the week. But stick with it and you'll have a wonderful extension of your hands. If you don't think that taking the time to set your controller up so you can play the games you want to play on it *competitively* is worth it, and you want to play competitively with a controller, then you're kind of in a Catch 22 situation. It's going to take time, and if you don't take that time, you're not going to have a good time.
Otherwise, the most I can tell you is that so long as the steam overlay can interact with your game, you can use the steam controller on it. Civilization, Dota, Dark Souls, 20XX, you name it. Put some time into configuring it and it'll be effective and fun. The more games you play on it, the more you'll learn about how YOU like your controller working and how best to set it up for you, and the less time it'll take.

(singleplayer only review)
Really good classic doom gameplay with new gfx, huge maps, and nice monster variations.

I initially thought this would be another asinine reboot, but it's not.
It's a very polished gameplay loop. Excellent work. RAGE was fine, this is much better.
I initially had some problems with proper configuration so that it runs well, since this game needs to be played with a minimal framerate over 60, no matter what gfx quality. I now play this on a phenom II x4 with some 2.8ghz and a gf 1050 with 2gb ram, so cpu quite potato, gfx okish. The game engine (ID tech 6) is quite scalable, it runs really good (60-120fps) with render resolution full hd * 0.65, medium to low settings, especially for shadows and lights, 1x temporal aa and motion blur high quality. The game plays and looks beautiful at these settings.The (beta?) vulkan render mode introduced some weird constant stuttering issue, so i use the gl4.5 mode.
Also, the motion blur effect actually works very nice this time, first time i preferred it to no motion blur in any game.
Gameplay is simple but complex:
You kill monsters, retrieve keys to certain doors and find secrets.
The monster killing is done in a way i haven't seen yet in this kind of perfection.
It's all very fluid and seamlesss, with nicely tuned mechanics that grow as you play the campaign.
The base gameplay is totally opposite to the currently dominant slowed down sniper/cover shooters.
Move and shoot, while doing so you get quite some options to continue.
Stand still and die.
Again, very nice ID tech openGl/Vulkan engine and a really good revival of classic doom gameplay without any corporate horseexcrements attached.
Very solid singleplayer campaign with complete replay value around 100%.
Individual pros and cons:
+ very polished & extended classic doom gameplay loop with nice gfx & sound
+ plays very nice with mouse + key
+ nice guns and very polished gunplay
+ nice and scalable engine running on opengl/vulkan, looks beautiful even in low render res
+ lots of options and a level editor
+ no weird microtransactions or dlc ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t
+ no jumpscare-dark-horror-theme - it's brightly-lit
+ nice and varied map design (although the map themes are limited to 2)
+ nice and fluid movement, nice gunplay (although i mostly use the shotguns like in classic doom)
+ the quite-interesting-non-story has been pretty unintrusively wrapped around the gameplay
+ high replayability (mostly for the classic levels)
+ fair price, at discount it's a steal (really nice 2016 game)
+ no more denuvo drm
- initially included some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t denuvo drm
- no linux release
- no moddability further than snap map
- needs some initial settings tuning (default settings were much too low on FPS)
- quite long load times (on mechanical hdd)
- mediocre and sometimes confusing interface (but tolerable)
- vulkan renderer introduces constant microstuttering (nvidia1050_2gb)
- there are only 2 environments (mars & hell)
- enemies can sometimes be hard to spot (not a problem on the classic maps)
- checkpoint system (it's tolerable)
As an end note i want to add that you really need to appreciate the fast paced classic gameplay loop and find a setting for your machine that gives you the 60+FPS at minimum, else you might be frustrated, because the game could be quite impossible to beat and very punishing with a cover-based-mindset approach.

I really wanted to like this game. I played the original version in 2003 and loved it. Now 80% of the time I spend playing Crimsonland I am angry or frustrated or both.
I don't know exactly what changed (aside fromt the obvious nerf to the Telekinesis-Perk). Maybe I as a player have a different approach to games now. Back then it might have been less important to me to finish a game 100% before playing something else.
Now I mostly strife for completion or at least getting as close as I can. And in the case of Crimsonland that turned out to be  an incredible pain in the behind.
So maybe it's due to my attitude and not to questionable gamedesign but my experience with this new iteration of Crimsonland was mostly unpleasant.
What bugged me most was the random factor when it comes to your weaponry. In most levels and Survival runs you start with the pistol and one of the first 3 or 4 monsters you slay will drop another gun. This game has alot of weapons. Most of those are way underpowered. If they were better balanced or if I as a player had at least some kind of influence over which drops I see and which I won't see, that would make a huge difference. Restarting a level over and over again until finally one of those 5 or 6 viable weapons pop up is NOT fun. In most levels that is not necessary but trying to complete the harder ones with a suboptimal gun is just a waste of time.
I have to say though, the carnage and frenzy of the original are still there. The soundtrack is awesome and if you get one of those (sadly) rare runs where everything falls into place and you get the right weapons, perks and drops in the right moment then it is indeed a wonderful experience. This is a great Free-to_play, mostly PVE orientated, MMO RPG hack n slash game. Not going to beat around the bush at all.
So lets break down why:
1. You start off with a choice of 3 classes which you can switch between at any given moment in the game with no cooldown, no need to pay for it, if you feel like playing support, tank or damage, you can switch to your situation. In the end you have 14 classes - 2 support, 2 tank and the rest in DPS to have fun with at any time.
2. The bosses are creative and beautiful not only in design but in mechanics as well. From the single player mechanics which ends you more in a hack n slash effect to the various new mechanics that come into play when you group up. The boss attack tactics change from single player to group/party
3. The graphics looks amazing - there is the few odd bug and some lip syncing is a little off with the standard quality of voice acting but overall, you will go ooooooooo and aaaaaaaaah while running around in the vast world of Aelion
4. You have a few choices on how to play - you can either just finish your "Along the yellow brick road" quest for which you can complete in groups or solo, you can do story as a single player or you can go run around in the pve open world areas that offer their own flair and challenges
5. Upon reaching your divine form, the game almost changes a little until you explore more and see what is there to offer.
6. Game can be a little grindy - getting your prestige up and running can take some time to take some things on
7. Customization - granted you not looking at a Skyrim level of customization but from eye color, fun hairstyles and even height, boob, butt and alike modifiers, there is plenty to get your character looking like how you like it
8. Costumes - there is PLENTY of costumes - some you can buy from the ingame market with credits or things you collect , others you unlock with quests, event AND each unlocked class you receive 2 costumes that you can still go purchase more color schemes for in the market- there is no reason to spend real money unless you feel you want to give something back to the game
9. Spending Real Life Money - unless you want to be premium with those extra creds, chests and weekly gifts of a few stimulants to help skip over quests, the game itself limits you to NO NEED TO BUY unless you feel you want extra. So far we notices no difference between someone who has premium vs someone who dont. So its up to you. Since there is more PVE than PVP areas, pay-to-play isnt really a thing. You cant buy gear ANYWHERE in the game - its purely drop based.
10. Party Mechanics - When entering an intance, the whole party scales up to the highest prestige player. Your power in game is determined by your prestige which is all equipment excluding your weapon. So its easy for higher members to carry lower ones through if they want to help boost them.
This has been what I've found so far. I am sure I am nowhere near the end of it but in all, its a really great game and cant wait to see what coming, happening and in store.

As someone who came into this game with little to no prior expirience with Battletech/Battletech universe lore, ect i'll just run down the pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
-Free2Play setup- realistically, its hard to play this game without spending money. Much like all F2P games, theres the freemium curency, and without it, you dont get many "mech bays" for housing mechs you purchase. I dropped 20$ twice on this game in total, soley for more of these mech bays and ground for the in game curreny to buy more mechs and mechparts.
-Simple mechanics- You join a match, move forward, shoot people with your weapons until one team is dead.
-Limited Weapon types- you know what all 4 types of weapons do (Missle, laser, ballistic), they either just get bigger and do more damage or shoot faster/have a longer range
-Flexible Loadouts- The mechs are totally customizable to your liking depending on what what the mech is specialized for and what you're looking for. You want a bigger engine for more speed? Cut down on the amount of ammo you want, or make the engine more exposed to critical hits. Take long ranged weapons that dont work in close range combat, or stack up on short ranged dumbfire missles. The choice is yours.
-Mech Building- Honestly this is the most enjoyable part for myself. I'll build the most unothrodox mechs to just have fun and screw around with. I'll take a massive mech thats suppossed to be slower, and throw in a massive engine with only a couple weapons and zip around like im a light-scout mech. Theres alot of leeway with that kind of stuff and I have  ablast with it.
-Decent Community: most people in this community are chill, and will even help you. There is a small group of toxic players, mostly pilots that flame their team mates because they die doing something stupid, but the vast majority are players that have been following mechwarrior for years. They helped me out alot, and I found a group to play with in and outside of mechwarrior because of it.
Cons:
-Meta or bust: The game revolves heavily around meta builds/playstyle, especially on the Community Warfare hub. If you arent playing the most optimal builds, you get thrashed match after match, even if your skill is on par (**** Kodiaks- end of story)
-Group heavy: The game requires coordination, planning, and teamwork- solo que can be cancer. Find some friends to play with and this problem is easily fixed.
-Strict F2P is rough: If you dont plan on spending money at all, then you might want to get used to the monthly free-prebuilt un-customisable mechs, because you only get 3 slots for customizable mechs.
-Desire to learn more about the lore: This may just be me, but bein thrown into a world I knew nothing about just didnt suit me, so I found myself spending hours on the wiki learning more on the battletech wiki.
-Skill tree- Skill tree grants bonuses to mechs based on expirience with it, but without the bonus's, the mechs dont operate at the peak, out of the box, efficiency, which really hurt some mechs.
All and all, I'd give the game two different scores:
Strictly Free to Play: 4/10
Spend what you want to: 7/10

PROS
* Play for free, and after 25 matches you have enough money to buy 1 or 2 Mechs
* Awesome custom options/weapons/color schemes/ for Mechs (that you own).
* Playing with a faction of people you know, or friends, is very satisfying for co-op play.
* Mech combat is intense and adrenaline pumping.
* The game rewards patience and positioning, not twitch mechanics or picking up drops.
* The mechlab is fun, for designing a mech with a weapon loadout suited to your playstyle.
* Different mechs play differently, even from light mech to light mech, or Assault to Assault.
* Follows the lore (to a certain extent).
* Colors bought can be applied to any mech you own. Some can be bought with cbills.
* In-game earned credits (cbills) can buy most things, so there are less mechanics that could be singled out as P2W  than in some online games. Hero/Champion mechs bought for MC are rarely the best among variants of a chassis, and so the powerful cbill variants can be had by anyone with cbills instead of real money, nice!
* At some point in the future, there will be a PVE game mode or single player campaign (supposedly in development by PGI). Time will tell.
* There are free mechs (Trial Mechs) one can use in the game until they figure out what they like, to a certain extent. But none of them can be customized.
* Veteran players can now support the game by buying the new mechs that come out (20 dollars a pack, for three) which includes a month of cbill boosted earnings (valued 12 dollars). Yet this will not be great for new players since they will not know what to buy at first (see below in warnings and CONS)
* Cool warhorns and hanging items you can put in your cockpits (which can be won for free during events, or paid for if you have money to burn)
* If you are a fan of the lore you can join a house or clan of your choosing and fight for planets in the Inner Sphere. The game modes/maps for this are quite different from the PuG matches, and last longer.
* Spend some money in the game and there are loyalty mechs/rewards at the end of the year, for various levels of support.
* Eventually buying one steam pack here provides a lot of content (30% cbill boosted mechs, cbill boosted earnings for a month, cool paintjobs, cool colors (that cost money in the game), and give mc (mech credits) for buying hero mechs or colors/cockpit items in the game. Though it would be nice if they came with different colors or patterns from pack to pack.
WARNINGS, and hopefully things that will change in time:
* This game requires a fianacial advisor or tutorial in order to keep new players from spending their first cbills in the wrong way. New players may become frustrated and quit as a result.
* New players might buy their first mech based on nostalgia or knowledge of the lore, only to find out neither have anything to do with how the mech plays in the current meta (gameplay).
* In Tier 5 (lowest ranked players) Pug matches can seem very unbalanced, and rarely do matches seem even; your team is completely destroyed or dominates depending on how many veteran players from upper tiers were forced to play with you (due to few people being available for matchmaking).
* PGI has spent the last couple years trying to balance weapons and mechs, but still a lot of tweaking is required. Often new mechs/patches injected into the game change the way the game is played, especially in faction warfare.
* Bad positioning (or teams splitting up) often means you will lose, and unless you are playing in a group of 12 people on teamspeak there is always a chance this will happen.
* People love lasers and long range combat, so rarely do groups push into the enemy right off the bat, so matches can seem dragged out to new players that want to face-tank opponents.
* Mechs that have a 30% cbill earning boost require real money to buy, but may or may not be the best variant of a chassis. When it is the best, people complain it lies behind a paywall. When they suck, people complain that they wasted their money.
* Game modes are somewhat different, but rarely feel different from each other. (supposedly more are in development, but we will see if and when that happens)
* Fans of the lore might want to play an Assault Mech (the largest), but to do so well requires too much knowledge of the current gameplay and positioning on current maps.
* Make one mistake in positioning and you will die, especially in the higher ranked tiers for PuG. Faster mechs on your team will abandon you when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, so expect to take one for the team again and again until your learn the maps and how to position.
* Clan mechs are crazy expensive, while Inner Sphere mechs are cheap as chips. Newer players might then gravitate to IS mechs, but IS mechs will almost always require a better engine, new weapons, and so on, so the amount of cbills spent to optimize is actually similar.
* To fully upgrade a mech with your mech xp you must play with and upgrade 2 other variants of the same chassis before higher level upgrades are available. This requires a lot of cbills, or real money to buy entire packs of mechs in one shot.
* A lot of mechs have become obsolete, or were never very good. This will not be readily apparent to new players unless they do some research on google, or
.
* Positioning, twisting & shielding (to spread damage when being shot at), and weapon ranges are things that can't be picked up in a day, and require a lot of practice in-game. The learning curve can feel brutal at times.
* Inner sphere mechs were given isane quirks in order for them to compete properly with the Clan mechs, which means they are specialized for one or two styles of gameplay usually and so new players really have to do their homework before buying one.

CONS, and things that are unlikely to change:
* Cbills are hard to get as a novice player. And to get a general boost to cbill earning requires about $12 a month, so often you will be tempted to pay for it to lessen the grind.
* The "Trial mechs" are rarely outfitted to one's liking, and do not have any modules on them (which help veteran players stay alive longer, or kill more effectively). While a veteran player in a trial mech might still be dangerous, a newbie in a trial mech is cbills for the taking. Trial mechs are few in number and rarely change. You could wait months or years to see a mech you wanted to try in this list. As a result, players simply go in blind most of the time and buy the mechs before being able to try them out.
* While new players are grinding cbills, veterans can spend theirs freely on optimizing their mechs with modules (that add efficiencies to various systems on a mech) and cooling abilities to reduce or eliminate heat from their mech when they get too hot. This means they can out DPS anyone who does not have these on their mech (because once your mech gets too hot, you must slow down or stop your rate of fire). Even some in the community call "pay to win" here, and so these elements can rub people the wrong way.
*Unlocking modules not only takes a massive amount of GXP, but then they must be paid for with cbills (2 - 6 million) as well! New players want to spend money on new mechs, not grinding to optimize; this works against the best part of the game which is being able to try new mechs.
* If you want to leave the module on a mech and never move it you have to pay cbills again to have a copy of said module.
* XL Engines for IS mechs turn your mech into a fast moving glass canon (if you lose a torso section, you die), while Clan engines are fast and allow you to lose one torso section and stay in the game. Many argue that this causes balance issues in the game.
* Long range missles make the game a hide behind cover and shoot simulator at times, and only in the higher tiers does this change, a little.
* Faction play is very unforgiving for new players, and where many of the elite players join up to play.

A HOMEMADE POTATO SALAD:
4 cups cubed red potatoes.
10 slices bacon, cut into 1-inch pieces.
¾ cup mayonnaise.
1 tablespoon Dijon mustard.
2 teaspoons granulated sugar.
1 teaspoon salt.
4 hard-boiled eggs, chopped.
1 stalk celery, diced.
1 small onion, chopped.
½ medium green pepper, chopped.
1. Boil the potatoes until they are fork tender. (If you're not sure how to boil the potatoes...well you're♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!) Drain the potatoes and set aside.
2. Meanwhile, cook the bacon in a skillet over medium-low heat until crisp. Remove bacon with a slotted spoon and place on a paper towel-lined plate to drain. Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of the bacon drippings in the skillet.
3. Add the MAYONNAISE, mustard, sugar and salt to the reserved bacon drippings in the skillet and whisk to combine.
4. In a large bowl, combine the potatoes, eggs, celery, onion and green pepper. Pour the dressing over the ingredients and gently stir to evenly coat. Stir in the bacon.
5. Cover and refrigerate for at least 3 hours before serving.
So there you have it. The best potato salad, EVER.

So I see a lot of people are giving poor reviews on the Steam Controller for a "Recently: Mixed" where the controller overall has a "Very Positive" Rating. Why? Maybe it has something to do with the early adopters knowing more what they were getting into, very new territory where they'd have to spend some time configuring their controller. They find what kinds of settings they like and can quickly configure their controllers to suit any game they play. Newer users might be having trouble where they think the default or community settings are "tried and true" but aren't actually good for them. Plus, I think more people are getting it on amazon and such and reviewing it there (hence its 4.5 star rating) I figured I'd chime in to defend this gem of a piece of hardware.
First, a warning: This is the best controller out there, but you have to WORK for it to be the best controller out there. You can become very nearly as good as a mouse and keyboard user if you fine tune your settings per game and practice with it. You wont become perfect with it overnight. You won't even be very good with it by the end of the week. But stick with it and you'll have a wonderful extension of your hands. If you don't think that taking the time to set your controller up so you can play the games you want to play on it *competitively* is worth it, and you want to play competitively with a controller, then you're kind of in a Catch 22 situation. It's going to take time, and if you don't take that time, you're not going to have a good time.
Otherwise, the most I can tell you is that so long as the steam overlay can interact with your game, you can use the steam controller on it. Civilization, Dota, Dark Souls, 20XX, you name it. Put some time into configuring it and it'll be effective and fun. The more games you play on it, the more you'll learn about how YOU like your controller working and how best to set it up for you, and the less time it'll take.

"Endless Space" is a very interesting and fun game. It's almost like nothing you've ever played before. OK, sometimes, it might remind you of the "Civilization" series, but, a little more detailed and complicated. Of course, I do like its concept  myself, so I'm totally into it.
The graphics are beautiful. The player can pick any kind of galaxy out there and a faction with balanced pros and cons and achieve different types of victories. Scientific, economic, military...
Another amazing thing is the game's music. I'll say no more about it, just take a look at YouTube by yourself.
I'll add that the game has a mythology of itself, which makes it unique and not some simple TBS with nothing much to offer.
One last thing that amazes me, is the research behind the game. It seems like the developers trully gave their best so as not to fall in the waters of pseudoscience. Thus, the technologies are actual (present day) ideas and  theories, somewhat futuristic and simplified but real! So, the player will find teleportation, wormholes, black holes, Casimir effect, quantum entaglement and stuff like this that can make a Science student go mad!
There are only two things that bother me:  (a) The Tutorial. It's not messy but it's a lot of information at once, without giving the player the chance to practice it,  a bit. Someone might get overwhelmed but you get used to the game pretty quick. It could be better, though.  (b) The Battles. They don't occur the "usual" (whatever that means) way, but it's all about advancing technologically, picking Heroes as Admirals, having a few ships and most importantly (!) picking the right cards. I've never played anything like this before and I know that the developers don't have unlimited money, time and mood to create a game *that* much detailed, without disappointing the consumers, but, in general, yes, battles could be a little more *alive* and a little more simple!
Nvertheless, I do recommend it! It will be an unforgetable experience!

An average 4X space game, looks fine and  have some nice features. The only concs in my opinion was the combat design, repeated combat fight would drive me crazy if AI have 100+ fleets, the fleet movement was also confusing since some time they would not pick the optimal space routes. Despites of these conc, the game was fun and could be used to kill some time. I would give 7 out of 10 if you want a score.

The majority of the game plays like a double edged sword. Immense and intricate but then hampers or limits the player in one way or another. For instance not only can't you negotiate at the start of the game, every diplomatic action must be researched in your tech tree before hand. Want to form an alliance? Research first. Open trade routes? Research first. It gets obnoxious when it comes time for trading resources.
Say you want to trade X number of your anti-mater for X number of their space peaches.
First you have research the ability to recognize anti-mater as a resource and then research the ability to trade it.
The same issue happens when it comes to fleet customization. The ability to build your own warships and customize their load out was one of the things that drew me to this game. Cause let's be honest, that's ♥♥♥♥ing cool.
You select your chassis and the type of armarments you want. Make a ship that's all offense, all defense, or somewhere in between.
The problem comes first with the lack of real-time combat. It's honestly the biggest dissapointment.
But you get the option to watch cinematic of the destruction and imagine what it would be like to actually play.
Because there's no real-time combat like the Total War series, you can't tell your fleet to target the weakest, strongest, or ship with the lowest current HP. You can't flank, you can't really do much of anything. This could have been solved with more attack formations, but we only get 3.
Combat in Endless space is a card game. It begins like this,
How your fleet is formed...remember pure defense in front, pure attack in back because the ships in front are targeted first.
Every ship attacks another ship, 1/3 your fleet engages 1/3 of theirs, all ships focus fire a single ship.
Bascially you pick cards that have special effects like increased accuracy, increased damage, etc.
These card effects can be blocked or enhanced based on what the enemy chooses for their 3 cards. I can't stress how depressing this is.
Both Medieval 2 Total War and Crusader Kings have strategic positions. Like a portion of land that gives bonuses to attackers or defenders. In  Endless Space the card game option is purely luck based. There is no way of knowing what card your opponent (AI or human) will pick so it's a pure crap shoot.
Knetics are hilariously overpowered giving you no reason to use missles or beams which only further limits your strategic options.
The faling of Endless Space is the fact that the entire foundation of the game is waiting for upgrades. You can't do anything in this game without researching it before hand. Even something as basic as diplomacy with other factions.

Great game! I used to have this on the Xbox so was pretty chuffed to play it again here. This is my first purchase on Steam too and so far im pretty impressed with how it works. Stick Em Up 2 is a primarily a platformer but there's actually quite a lot of variation to the gameplay, you get a different weapon on each level and they really dictate the way you have to play the game.
The first level opens with a quick tutorial and a few basic jumps to get you used to the controls and then its straight into the action. The controls took a minute to get used to (Im playing on my keyboard and mouse) but I soon found myself galloping along and unleashing a sea of bullets on the unsuspecting stick-baddies. The weapon you start with is a machine gun with unlimited ammo, which is pretty handy. Half way through you get to fly a helicopter with a rocket launcher which is obviously extremely badass. The second stage is set in Japan and the soundtrack is really cool, ancient Japanesey music. The weapon here is a ninja star and you have to change your tactics a little bit, if you try and rush through like you did in the first level you'll be massacred in no tiime. The trick I found was to progress slowly and pick the enemies off one by one like a ninja. Theres a massive house at the end of this stage which looks like something out of a 70s Kung Fu flick and you need to scale your way right to the very top to get off the level.
Somehow the next level takes place on the moon. Stars are falling out of the sky and these stars are not your friend, they hate you and they want to kill you. This level is all about firing a continious barrage of missiles up at the sky at the falling stars and running past whenever you get a tiny gap. Level 4 has our stickman fighting pirates at sea. You jump from ship to ship, via whales, slashing the armed occupants to smithereens with just a trusty sword and your wits. Again the weapon really dictates the gameplay here, it IS possible to kill the baddies hand to hand with the sword but the safest way is to use the sword to deflect their own bullets right back at them. I like the idea that our stickman is so incredibly hard he can kill 20 badguys with guns using just a sword. He is a double-hard barsteward and no mistake. Oh yeah and theres a canon on one of the ships which you can comandeer. Its not exactly fair to shoot the enemies at point blank range with a canonball, but it IS fun.
Level 5 finds us back on the moon, thankfully there's no stars this time but there is a moon buggy for us to drive. It's pretty much a straight time trial race against the clock. I can't stress how awesome this level is, blasting along with the accelerator planted to the floor trying to keep the buggy on its wheels. Each difficulty setting gives you a completely different track too, so theres sort-of 3 levels built into 1 here. This is one of those mini-games that you accidentally spend an hour or 2 on, especially in multiplayer. The last level is this weird kind of Ewok treehouse city and the weapon is a javelin thing that you can charge up. It takes a second to get to maximum charge and it's pretty satisfying unleashing it close-range on the poor unsuspecting stick baddies - its goes straight through them - and if theres 2 or 3 standing in close quarters you can kill all 3 with one spear, which aside from being great fun also shows our stickman is very frugal and even in these violent times, has one eye on the environment. The other theme of this level is BIG jumps. Some of them seem only just possible, which I personally really like in a platformer.
One of the coolest things about the game for me is the varied gameplay, each of the 6 levels really has its own unique vibe and you need to adjust your playing technique accordingly to progress. The other thing that stands out is the sound which is truly EPIC, these tunes will stick in your head (In a good way) and I actually hope they put the soundtrack out at some point, I would definately pay another $3 just for the tunes. Some things I would really like to see updated in the future: More levels, especially the moon buggy levels (This needs its own game) and maybe some more flying in the moon rover, that was over way too quick. I found the difficulty level was gauged pretty good, theres 3 settings and the hardest really is very challenging - you get one life and you cant take much damage at all - but even so, its not impossible so you never get too frustrated. Also theres the various achievements to unlock, which I havnt really gotten into them yet but they seem to range from amusing to insane, like the pacifist one which you get by somehow going through the entire game without shooting anyone!
Anyway a very good game & totally worth the $3!

Now you might see a review already for Deus Ex:Human Revolution and think, hang on this game has already been reviewed and you would be right.
But I’m going to review it again for 2 reasons
The game has fundamentally changed enough to warrant it.
You can't purchase the previous version anymore in the store, meaning if you don’t already own it, this is the copy you will likely be buying.
The big changes first
The boss fights have been edited so any style of playthrough can now have the same chance of finishing them so you no longer need to run and gun them. Playing a hacker/stealth run- no worries, just hide and do your magic. Playing like you’re a cyborg death machine- everything is still all good.
The next big change is the The missing link DLC is now integrated into the main game instead of being a separate side story (The other DLC is also included but the big one is the missing link). While I’m happy that everyone can play the DLC now (it's great and adds its own layer of horror on how people are being stolen and experimented on by the government) adding it to the main game for me slightly broke some of the immersion. You were on your way to find the people who did this to you, and then you are suddenly plopped into another area, which doesn’t relate to the main quest line, with a whole new set of problems to deal with. It's explained well on why all your upgrades don't work, and it contains enough exp to get you semi functional to finish while maintaining a challenge. While foreshadowing is great, if you haven't already played the game it's easy to miss what’s coming up by playing this before finishing the game beforehand, which now you are forced to do. Adding this in I felt making getting all the achievements harder (both main game and side story had requirements for certain achievements to pop, and it’s not explained anywhere if doing something in one will invalidate it in the other, leading to a very cautious playthrough).
Overstuffing bodies in vents will still lead to deaths, and there is still no death counter in the game (it would be nice to know how many people I have killed- the man has every other upgrade including the kitchen sink). Hell, even moving bodies when upgrading strength can become risky in case you "accidently" throw them and kill them.

Standard victory types: Military, Science (research), Expansion (% of map controlled), Economic (total per-turn income in Dust), Wonder (build specific things).
Pros: Interesting features that make the game more engaging than the standard Civ-type games.  Pretty.  In space.  Customizable battle units.  Several (7+) factions to choose from, plus "build your own" faction with choosable traits.
Cons: Is a turn based strategy game.  If you like them, great.  If you think they're kinda slow and long winded, that's exactly what this is.

Highly recommended alternative to anyone burnt out from Civ.  An interesting combat system with moderate depth ship design and flavour text and lore everywhere. Can't wait until Endless Space 2!

Prototype is a third-person apocalyptic open-world type of game. It has an interesting plot even if it can be a little bit confusing at times, especially since Alex Mercer wakes up with amnesia and there's a virus spreading. It turns out Alex Mercer also has gained some special powers. By consuming certain people you can find out a bit more story and fit some of it together throughout the game.
The side-events/missions aren't very special and I found myself skipping most of them in the end because they felt repetitive and the points you earn to upgrade your abilities can be earned most of the time through other ways. After completing the game you gain access to free-roam mode (and New Game+), where you can complete all the challenges if you'd like to.
The gameplay is great. I loved running, jumping and soaring around the city in a fast pace. Almost everything earns you points that you can spend on unlocking abilities and upgrading almost everything you can think of. Some upgrades, like weaponry, do require that you do certain side-events but they're not really something that you'll need to use much. In the end Alex Mercer seems almost invincible. Some parts of the game requires a little bit of "stealth" and some parts require that you get things done quickly. It's a nice mix.
The game came out a few years ago but it has aged well, in my opinion. Sure, it's not the greatest looking game compared to some of the current AAA titles - the important thing is that it's not ugly. Alex Mercer's movements are smooth and detailed compared to the rest of the NPCs, but it's to be expected. What's rather nice with the visuals are that as the infection spreads, more and more of the city will look infected, it adds to the immersion.
I can really recommend this game, especially if you like open-world games. It's a great game that I had a lot of fun with.

After using SC for the last year, it became one of my most beloved hardware possessions and has in fact replaced all my other controllers and media center keyboard.
The build itself is robust plastic, with nicely tactile A/B buttons (small but child compatible), very decent analog stick and excellent throttles. Up to this point SC is basically just like any other controller, but enter the custom trackpads. Very smooth and precise, optionally used with the gyroscope for fine control, they offer surprisingly expressive mouse replacement. SC beats your standard XBox analog stick camera without question.
This is cool marketing, but mouse is still better if you mean business, and you usually do. That's why good mouse emulation is actually a bigger deal in the operating system or any other game or software where you want to try and replace it, which is how SC works by default in tandem a virtual keyboard when you turn it on in the OS.
All those games that weren't meant for a controller are playable on SC, in any way you want, since the trackpad comes close in replacing the mouse and buttons can be bound to any keyboard keys, providing the complete experience. No need for xpadder; you just define your presets and while Steam is running, the controller binds work globally.
While SC is past its initial birthing pains and seems to be in a healthy state (the customization is now fantastic), I would say Valve still needs to do some fine tuning with how presets are selected for different environments, solve some of the occasional bugs (saved presets appearing late, keyboard crashing the desktop mode...) and hopefully integrate the UI and configuration into the default client (now only available in Big Picture).
Since no other controller comes close to the possibilities that SC opens, it is without competition in its class. Being a decent game controller by itself and way more, Valve succeeded in creating the ultimate PC controller you can buy and it won't be matched in that area any time soon.

Review:
Combat:
The gameplay and concept itself is solid and frankly the only thing keeping this game afloat. Each class has its own unique abilities and some of them have attack combos. The attack you choose is typically best suited for a particular engagement such as single target vs. a large group. You can evade heavy attacks from enemies by dogding out of the way or using a class skill which is useful for evasion. Alternatively you can just take the shot to the face if your class has an ability that makes them invulnerable or gives them a shield (not advised if the damage you're about to take exceeds shield strength. Each class also has an ultimate which, depending on the class, will deal damage or function as a buff. An important thing to note, this game does not have any healers or active healing abilities. You can use a regenerative consumable once every 5 minutes or so while in combat, or the alchemist can use its ultimate to heal you once every 10 minutes, give or take. If you get tired of one class, you can switch to any other you have unlocked at will as long as you aren't in combat.
The game also has combat mounts, which differ from the regular mounts in that they wont disembark you as soon as combat starts and can actually be used to fight (we even have a spinoff D.va mech).
World Layout:
The world is basically just dungeons, not open world as other mmos are. You go to the hub of the game, the Divine Observatory, where you can form groups for dungeons which range from doable as a solo run to 10 man operations. There are some open areas which are comparable to the size of a small map in... say battlefield but nothing like the open worlds of other games where you walk from one area to the next.
The main attraction:
The biggest feature of the game is that you can eventually enter your god form for a limited duration. Your god form consumes "faith", a resource you aquire from sending out your
followers
into the world of Aelion. They start out with 100% energy and stop collecting things like faith and credits when they hit 0% or you cancel the journey. You will then collect whatever they have found. Not going to lie this new version of the follower system is basically a
spinoff of Fallout Shelter. There's even that text box like in Fallout Shelter where you can see what they've been up to and what they are thinking. While in god form you become many times stronger, and larger, than your normal self and become a reaper of the battlefield with special ultimates for each class catagory that have their own uniqe functions ranging from a damage buff to firing a giant etheral cannon from the sky.
As someone who has had this game for a long time I have seen this game evolve (or devolve depending on your perspective, say... not a blind cave lizard) at the hands of a dev team who REFUSE to listen to their playerbase. If i had to describe the path this game is taking, I'd say its doing a FireFall. So go ahead and play the game, enjoy what it has to offer, just don't invest your money into this game until the devs start listening to the people who provide them with their income.
Edit: with the new "Sparks of Transformantion" that have been implemented, this game has simply gone from "♥♥♥♥ you" to "♥♥♥♥ you, pay me". One of the game's main selling points, not being restricted to a single class, is now locked behind a massive grindfest unless you wish to pay the troll the toll to cross over the bridge past the paywall.
Final consensus: avoid this game until the devs realize that it's the playerbase that sustains online games, not the developers. Will be changing my review to negative until such changes are made.

Now you might see a review already for Deus Ex:Human Revolution and think, hang on this game has already been reviewed and you would be right.
But I’m going to review it again for 2 reasons
The game has fundamentally changed enough to warrant it.
You can't purchase the previous version anymore in the store, meaning if you don’t already own it, this is the copy you will likely be buying.
The big changes first
The boss fights have been edited so any style of playthrough can now have the same chance of finishing them so you no longer need to run and gun them. Playing a hacker/stealth run- no worries, just hide and do your magic. Playing like you’re a cyborg death machine- everything is still all good.
The next big change is the The missing link DLC is now integrated into the main game instead of being a separate side story (The other DLC is also included but the big one is the missing link). While I’m happy that everyone can play the DLC now (it's great and adds its own layer of horror on how people are being stolen and experimented on by the government) adding it to the main game for me slightly broke some of the immersion. You were on your way to find the people who did this to you, and then you are suddenly plopped into another area, which doesn’t relate to the main quest line, with a whole new set of problems to deal with. It's explained well on why all your upgrades don't work, and it contains enough exp to get you semi functional to finish while maintaining a challenge. While foreshadowing is great, if you haven't already played the game it's easy to miss what’s coming up by playing this before finishing the game beforehand, which now you are forced to do. Adding this in I felt making getting all the achievements harder (both main game and side story had requirements for certain achievements to pop, and it’s not explained anywhere if doing something in one will invalidate it in the other, leading to a very cautious playthrough).
Overstuffing bodies in vents will still lead to deaths, and there is still no death counter in the game (it would be nice to know how many people I have killed- the man has every other upgrade including the kitchen sink). Hell, even moving bodies when upgrading strength can become risky in case you "accidently" throw them and kill them.

Maybe some old fans dislike the changes implemented in the past years, but the fact remains: Crimsonland is still one of the best top-down arcade style shooter games ever released.
Crimsonland was originally released in 2003 on the now-defunct Reflexive Arcade, where it quickly raised to fame and glory among the indie game players. With good reason. It features constant action against a horde of aliens in several game modes (chief among them are the campaign and survival) with a plethora of weapons and special player perks– both which have been expanded over and over throughout the years.
Yeah, there is no story, no voice acting, and only a handful of music tracks, but, frankly, they aren’t needed even in the least bit.
This version has some controversy among the older players though. Crimsonland started as a simple 2D top-down shooter, but between its original release and the 2014 debut on Steam, the whole engine was remade, along with most of the game modes. Perks and weapons received an overhaul (new ones added, some powerful ones removed or rebalanced), the typing shooter game mode was replaced with some not so original ones, and campaign mode now lacks perks completely.
But even though if you miss the über-powerful old telekinesis ability and dislike the number of barely useful new weapons, Crimsonland is still a damn good and fun game to play, one that will probably won’t be replaced for at least another decade.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played. Mechwarrior Online is the legacy of a decade of Mechwarrior/Battletech videogames, and an even longer period of tabletop gaming. It's not a twitch shooter; if that's what you're looking for, I wouldn't recommend this. Mechwarrior Online is the "thinking man's shooter" where logistics and strategy are key to win. However, if you just want to run around and derp anyone who comes near you: go for it. There are a wide variety of playstyles and skills in this game. It's definitely not a pay to win game; you don't have to pay a cent and you can still have the time of your life (however, some mech variants and most cosmetics can only be purchased with real money). Gamers who fear RNG (I came here from World of Tanks, so believe me when I tell you I know what RNG is) need not worry: the game has very strict calculations, so if an enemy kills you, you know it wasn't just sheer stupid luck and you don't have to rage as much over a missed shot when you know it isn't just spray and pray. Overall I can't recommend this game enough. If you made it this far into the wall of text, congrats and I thank you for caring about an old pilot's opinion (make sure to vote this as helpful!). If I were you, however, I would watch some videos on Youtube about how to play this game (it can be a bit confusing for new players). A few short tips: always hit the "R" key to mark opponents (this will give you info on how far away they are, how damaged they are, allow you to target them for your long range missile allies, and give you a credit bonus if you are the first to target them... hitting "R" is IMPORTANT), don't underestimate the value of heatsinks (they cool you down faster so you can fire more often and they also add internal health), don't put the maximum number of LRMs as you can on a mech (they are for suppression, not pure damage, so only put a few small ones on most mechs so you can constantly chain fire them), always pay attention to your heat (if you overheat, you're dead. period.) and always assume you can get better. If you haven't committed suicide over the sheer boredom of reading this whole thing, good for you! Enjoy the game and I look forward to seeing you on the battlefield, pilot (look for the name "Sovietshadow").
