I've been playing MWO since closed beta, Summer 2012.  Four years is a loooong time to be playing any one game, but it's kept me and my crew together.  If you want heavy firepower wielding mechs, this is pretty much the best game in town.  Less twitchy than other FPS titles so better for older players.
The Good:
Art and Design of the mechs.  By far this is the best that battlemechs have ever looked in a video game.  Just go look at MW4 and cringe.  While a few of the redesigns were a bit of a miss (looking at you WarHammer), the major are unbelievably good (Atlas, Catapult, Cataphract, Summoner) etc.  Even o es that never looked that good to being with (Jager mech, Stalker).
Gameplay is solid.  The arm+torso movement for aiming is simple brilliant and this is the best mechs have ever handled.  Assaults (except Kodiak...) feel heavy and methodical.  While something as small as the Locust feels insanely fast and nimble.
Mech customization is damn near infinite.  Not very chassis can do what you want, but there's a mech or variant somewhere that CAN.  Build variety and the near endless way to build a mech is solid.
Negatives:
Harsh to new players.  Much like Eve, opening this game up the first time is less of a learning curve and more of a vertical WALL.  There is finally a new player tutorial for driving a mech, but still absolutely nothing for the mechlab.  That said, the community is very helpful, and there are many community run Team speak servers avail with people glad and willing to show players the ropes.
Tiny community.  MechWarrior just isn't that big anymore.  While huge during the 90s, it's very much a niche product today.  After 11 or so Pacific, you'll start seeing familiar faces every drop or two.  Just not a big enough pool to build matches.
Big fish in little ponds.  This game has a "Pilot Skill Rating.". (PSR) Basically it's an XP bar that fills to move you up in tiers.  Play really poor early on and you'll probably start at Tier 5, and over time you'll move up.  Big issue is it is HEAVILY biased to move players up, so you'll hit tier 3 pretty quick.  After that you're just food for the Tier 1 elite crowd.  They tend to be the players that support the game the most financially buying the pre-order mech packs, so to keep them entertained the game is geared to throw easy targets at them.  Unless you run with a crew that WANT to be the best and focus fire and build to the meta, you're going to be rolled a lot at higher tiers.
My crew is a very casual group that play because we love big stompy robots and want to play something that supports 2 to 12 of us at a time.  But because the PSR is biased so heavily, most of us are tier 1 or 2, but we're NOT that caliber of players.  We've just played enough it shoves us against MS, 228, KCOM, etc.  So we get rolled. Small community though so MM is designed to put as many people into the same port as quickly as possible.
Limited game modes.  You've got Assault (kill everything or capture their base), Conquest (kill everything and capture enough bases), and Skirmish (kill everything).  There's none of the real objective based gameplay that MechWarrior is known for.  There was an attempt with community warfare for two years, but it's largely died off because of poor design and developer miss steps.
Glacial development.  The last real issue is development is at a snail's pace.  The core gameplay really hasn't changed since Alpha.  They do have mech creation down to a science, but actual Ballance changes or adjustments are once yearly, at best, with huge imbalances receiving no attention for months at a time.
Overall what you see is what you get with MechWarrior Online.  I don't see it changing much in the next two years, but for solid Team Death Match with Robots, it's pretty much unbeatable.  Just don't go in expecting the Battletech or MechWarrior heritage for objective based gameplay or more.  It's not here

an original implementation of the 4x genre: it's not as complex as Galactic Civilization II, but has some new fresh features.
it's so light that never tires: i keep coming back playing it from time to time.
PROS
- original basebuilding system: the management aspect is focused more on solar systems than single planets
- can hire heroes as governors or fleet leaders
- simple but effective governor feature
- simple but full-fledged diplomatic system
- good ship builder ( it's a little messy, gets improved in the expansion )
- original combat system: can't actually control spaceships, but can issue an order for each of the 3 combat phases with cards unlockable with technologies ( gets deeper with the expansion ), and amazing camera view mode.
- graphic is polished and captivating
- good galaxy view
- great UI: you can get info on almost everything just hovering over; you can go to the previous screen just with a RMB click.
- simple but compelling tech tree
- interesting lore: set in the Endless universe, same as Endless Legend and Dungeon of the Endless  ( nice having the same concepts represented by same icons recurring in all the games )
CONS
- spaceships can move only on paths that join planets ( only later in the tech tree you can unlock free movement in the galaxy ): i feel it like a constrain to exploration and tactical possibilites, but it works.
- no espionage feature
- no starbases or orbital structures
- no political government features
- no ethic alignment features: there are random events that prompt you a choice, but consequences just end there and do not carry over
- no stats and charts, neither of your empire nor other players'
- no "go to event location" feature ( added in the expansion )

As a developer I was thrilled about this controller and eager to add support for it only to be gravely disappointed. I did not like the build quality, the bulkiness and the awkward paddles in the back. The touchpads are interesting and their haptic feedback could have been nice if it wasn't for the noise.
- while other controllers have a steady report rate of 125Hz, the steam controller can only provide that on average with reports coming in at an unsteady pace alternating between 6 and 12 milliseconds (while a reliable 8ms is to be expected); this is guaranteed to drive serious gamers mad.
- The "analog" thumbstick is not so analog after all, providing a meager granularity of about 20 states per axis (no matter the setting)
- wireless dongle interferes with other game controllers rendering them unusable
- to use the controller as a gamepad your application has to be launched through steam which will emulate the API required; alternatively you could possibly install a filter to eliminate the regular events being sent to the OS by the controller and tap into the RAW input API (which thanks to the lack of documentation for this abomination of a controller wouldn't be fun)
This has been my most expensive and objectively worst controller so far. The only good thing is that wirelessly (above mentioned restrictions apply) it works more reliable and over greater distances than any wireless mouse I've seen so far.

Revised my last review and giving a more detailed review of this game.  Verdict still doesn't change, as I think you can buy far better games.
First, let's start with the Pro's of this game.
- The Cinimatics are nice.
- The Soundscore is awesome.
- The U.I. is very clean.
- Ship design is unique and cool looking.
Now, for the long list of Con's.
- The A.I. is cheaty and only seems to play one way.
- There is no real feeling of exploration.
- No visuals of any kind for planetary upgrades.
- Limited ship builds which are very basic.
- Simple bugs such as destroyed enemy ships warping cinematic never fixed.
- Gameplay leaves you longing for more.
Basically, this game feels like a good Beta build.  Much of everything is there, but lacks a lot of polish which would make this game exceptional.  The A.I. does not seem to hide the cheaty nature of what normally would be impossible play for a normal player.  Little things such as showing devlopment of planets when you upgrade them, were never added.  Even building your ships have a severe hindrance of being very very basic in design.
Many little details leave you feeling like this is an unfinished game.  Small bugs which should have been patched out long ago, like seeing a 'warp away' cinematic even if you destroy all the enemy ships, still remain in this game.  Exploration consists of visiting the next planetary system over, but has left out any other type of 'anomaly' exploration.  (ie. no Blackholes, Vagrant ships, Pulsars, etc.)
In the end, with a bit more devlopment, and the addition of just a few things, the game would have improved significantly.  It feels like a format for a game was designed, but a vast majority of content was left out, leaving some nice eye-candy, but nothing filling.
I would not recommend this game if you are looking for something long-term... I mean, unless you are interested in playing Multiplayer only, because Single player, the A.I. pulls fleets of ships from nowhere.  Management is minimal and a lot of the game focuses solely on moving ships around and your research tree.  Really, there is no depth here.

This game is very well done, considering Wargaming has tens of years of experience with the best tank game in the world. It's light, textures are optimized, matchmaking is fast, load time is 4 sec and there are noobs all over the place
So if you're new to tanks I recommend this game and if you are an old WoT player, than try this and blast through tiers in days.
I see a lot of WoT annoying stuff fixed in WoTB, let me list a few points :
No arty whatsoever!
Consumables can be reused multiple times in battle. Also there are cool new consumables that boost speed or reload time.
Modules cost only Experience, but no credits.
One Crew per account and crew skills are more like tallents - When tank is 100% you start contributing EXP to your Crew's light, medium, heavy or TD skills, and when you level up a skill you get benefit from it on all tank types.
Daily 2x experience reset happens twice every day, and missions keep rolling, so still a very addictive model, but overall the grind is way easier in WoTB than in WoT.
You get 2 days of premium + ~1200 gold. I would advise new players to spend that gold towards buying a premium account and grind some line fast in the start to get a tier 6-7-8 tank and start doing missions and clan platoons.
In WoTB there is a built in visual indicator if a shot will penetrate the armor and its very well done, auto aim works the same way as in WoT so overall there is nice skill ceiling so far, the game looks interesting in its 7v7 format.
Good luck tankers

Never have I played a game where you can have so much fun taunting and teabagging an opponent, only to be blasted away in the middle of your stripper pole routine! As others have likely said, a few years back, the developers decided to work on a PS4 version, and while their vision of expanding the game was commendable, their sense of timing turned out to be very lackluster. Instead of polishing, balancing and completing the work which they started, they chose to bite off more than they could chew, and the result now is a very dead game that once had so much promise.
In conclusion, it was most certainly fun while it lasted, but considering that the developers have completely abandoned the PC version in favour of the PS4, and what is left is little more than a game on it's final moments before life support is completely shut down, considering too that the website's security certificate has already expired shows that they have no intention of ever returning, so your time would be better spent looking elsewhere. If you would like to experience what Loadout was like in the past, then I would recommend giving the PS4 version a go, you might find that you enjoy it!

Probably the best reboot ever of a classic cyberpunk IP. While the game balancing has issues, it frequently gives you the option to pursue objectives in multiple non-linear ways to include cover-based combat, stealth, hacking, or a combination of all three. The inclusion of both lethal (noisy, permanent) and non-lethal (stealthy, temporary) melee takedowns makes for an interesting moral and/or gameplay dilemma. The game even posits that you can complete its entire 30+ hour campaign without killing any enemies, which is quite the achievement. The self-augmentation and upgrade system using Praxis Points is ingenious and you can definitely feel your character, Adam Jensen, progressing and improving his abilities throughout the campaign. Has a lot of areas to explore outside the main missions to collect loot or gather snippets of information about the circumstances surrounding the game. If you are a fan of world-building, Deus Ex is the game for you. Pocket Secretaries are littered in various locations that will provide elements of lore to the player and help deepen their immersion into the world of Deus Ex. While the topics in the game with respect to cyberpunk are nothing new, I would argue that it has the most intriguing discussion out of any game in the genre with respect to transhumanism and its potential societal impacts. Again, I would highly recommend this game as it is one of the best I have played in the past 6 years. 9.5/10

Crimsonland probably will not win a price for originality. The main formula of the game is simple: Massacre all the bugs, aliens, zombies and other creatures of the map and while you're at it destroy their hives aswell. It's a formula that has been done in dozens of games.
Everytime you beat a level, you either earn a new weapon (30 in total) or a new perk (50 in total) which are suppose to help you ofcourse. Most of the weapons are fun to play with but obviously some are better than others. I did not really care much about the perks, the dev could've just made the creatures more difficult to kill but instead gave you these perks.
In my experience the difficulty in Crimsonland was mostly based on sheer luck. Every level you start of with your pistol. The first creature you kill drops a better gun, if you're lucky you gain one of the better weapons which already makes the level a lot easier.
Crimsonland also relies heavily on powerups, since they often make the difference of surviving a level. Powerups like: slowmo, frozen enemies, plasma ammo and even a nuke will make the game much easier, sometimes even too easy, especially if you get 6+ powerups next to each other.
Graphically, the game looks pretty good for a top-down game, killing hundreds of creatures is satisfying and the game really makes you feel like you're a total badass, even if you're not.
Overall, Crimsonland is a solid top-down shooter, It's probably the best game of it's sort right now. Although I believe the game is more about luck than about skill, it's still fun and enjoyable.

When the original Crimsonland came out, it was a fun overhead shooter.  But the original Crimsonland came out over ten years ago, and a ton of overhead shooters have been released over that period.  The genre has moved forward, while this new release of Crimsonland has either stayed stuck in the past or even regressed.
Character movement is sluggish and balance isn't even a concept.  Luck is a major factor in surviving, both in the form of getting the right weapon drop and in the battle-reversing power of certain random power-ups.
You can play Quest mode or Survival.  You can unlock weapons and perks as you progress, but both only randomly appear as you play and perks only appear in Survival.
Quest Mode has you facing preset monster waves.  Defeat a wave without taking a hit in order to gold star it.  This pretty much makes your lifebar pointless, as there is little point in beating a stage without getting the gold star.  Further, as said earlier, luck is a major factor.  The starting pistol doesn't do enough damage to control some waves, and bad luck could see weapon drops appearing in groups that you cannot navigate without taking damage (and thus losing that gold star).  On the other hand, getting the right weapon means you can stay ahead of enemy hordes even with poor play/aim.
Survival Mode has you facing screen-filling waves of enemies that have just been thrown together.  You level up as you kill enemies, and leveling up allows you to choose a new perk from a random selection.  The problem here is that Survival mode is simply boring.  You mindlessly mow down colorful bullet sponges, triggering power-ups as they appear, hoping to grab and maintain the best crowd control gun for your style.  Eventually you get overwhelmed and die.
The game lacks "oomph".  Weapons are boring, and most don't feel like they have impact. Movement feels sluggish. Unlocks are largely meaningless, when the game gives them randomly anyway.  There isn't any variety to play.  There is no excitement, and plenty of games have since done the graphical trick of gradually bathing the area in blood.
There is nothing else to Crimsonland.  It may be (based on) a classic, but it is a relatively expensive and fairly mediocre entry in a crowded field.  It has Steam Trading Cards, but the game isn't interesting enough to earn more than one card legitimately (through actually playing the game) versus just idling for cards.

Endless Space is a game for people with patience and interest in complex mechanics, not unlike Galactic Civilizations.  As a 4X game, it succeeds and holds its own well.  The AI works the systems and the difficulties scale well as you learn the game.  If turn-based, steep learning curve games don't scare you then you should at least put this on your Wishlist.
Before giving up in frustration, there are some key mechanics to understand.
Combat - You choose 'cards' in each of three combat phases, and set formations and tactics before starting the fight.  If you choose to 'Auto' the battle, it plays out exactly as it would if you were watching but without being able to shift your card selection.  Sitting through the fight in 'Manual' lets you see the destruction and alter your selected card for the next phase if you want to.  The cards can counter opponent cards and/or simply provide combat bonuses.  Combat mechanics aren't clearly described and can be confusing - the most important aspect is the relationship between ship size, defense, and weapon damage.  Late game AI ship builds will push you to have a good understanding of how to defeat them mechanically.
Ship builds - Ship building is fairly tame and comes down to adding categories of stats.  Ship builds generally stick to themes - the "Tank", the "Glass Cannon", and the "Planet Destroyer".  Trying to create balanced ships early in the game can work, but later they become a liability and it's better to shift to a strategy that involves either making a lot of small glass cannons or a massive tank backed by serious firepower.  Space limitations in each of the 6 chassis types means ships never get insane statistics on their own.
Growth - Colonization is key to conquest and can be tricky to understand at first.  It can be hard to balance happiness, taxes, and production - but with a few key techs it's easy to shift into overdrive and expand as quickly as the AI does.  The combat and conquest does suffer from grinding, especially later in the game, but that seems a common theme is in every 4X game and is expected.
Overall, this is a worthwhile 4X strategy title and is recommended for lovers of the genre.

My favourite was someone who played over 500 hours, saying only 'worst game ever'. Completely useless review, and clearly a lie too! Gave me a good chuckle.
In all seriousness it is not a game that everyone will get in to and there are some important issues to be aware of before you start.
1) Configuring a Mech is complicated. I know Battletech well, but for my friends it was daunting and can be quite a put off. My advice is to persevere, the complexity keeps the game fresh for a long time to come.
2) There are only a handful of maps to play on. This can definitely be frustrating given that some maps are biased towards particular weapons loadouts. Skill still plays a huge role though, and games are short so you don't suffer long if your loadout is completely inappropriate!
3) Spend as much time as you can stand with trial Mechs before spending any C-Bills. You get money rapidly per game over the first few days, then it dwindles to a trickle. You'll find your first and second Mechs really have to last you a long time so choose wisely. My advice is a Clan Heavy OmniMech such as the TimberWolf-S. OmniMechs have the most configurability, and this is essential when buying a brand new Mech costs a small fortune!
4) Although definitely not Pay-to-win, as skill and teamwork always trump any minor advantages of an individual Mech, spending money is very tempting as it can really ease the grind to get new Mechs. I don't begrudge the developer wanting to make money. Every Free-to-play game does, so don't pretend they don't.
Overall I have enjoyed my Mechwarrior Online experience. The ability to customise Mechs with a range of weapons, and the small advantages and disadvantages of each Mech really help to maintain interest. The gameplay is surprisingly well balanced with skillful individuals and team maneuvering being vital to winning most of the time.
I'll admit to frustration at the expense of Mechs and the push to spend money. However it truly is not necessary in order to advance through the game steadily. Matches are short and frequent enough to keep your bank account growing, and there is nothing more satisfying than saving up for a new Mech. Spend money only if you really enjoy it and want to support the developer. Games don't get made for free!
P.S. I thought I should add that this is one of the least toxic games I've played. After playing Dota 2 for so long, and putting up with swearing and childish tantrums, it's been a breath of fresh air to have a game where 99% of the time people talking are positive and helpful!

I probably have close to a thousand hours in-game with Mechwarrior Online and have certainly had some great times across its lifecycle, but I would not recommend putting a single cent into the game.
MWO should serve as a warning to what can happen with a crowdfunded/early access title when incompetence and greed align. The game's original publisher (IGP) was created specifically to organise parts of MWO's development, yet for years it bled the developer (PGI) of incoming funds and directed them towards other, failing, projects. Actual work on the game would pretty much cease for months at a time, or end up focused on features that would increase IGP's revenue without improving the experience.
Eventually the developer and publisher parted ways and just enough change occurred to make you hopeful. But through years of genuine criticism PGI's leadership team has hardened against any kind of feedback, resulting in increasingly slapdash decision making and implementation alongside very public hostility towards parts of the community.
At this point the playerbase has declined precipitously and the free-to-play 'whales' have been bled dry. A complete redesign of one of the core pillars of the game has sat announced for almost a year, with very limited testing and no word on what the final decision will be. Not a positive thing in a game that exchanges real cash for in-game effectiveness.
A palpable sense of desperation lurks in almost every aspect of Mechwarrior Online's experience, in the UI, in the gameplay changes, in the pricing structure and in the organised events. By all means check it out, a solid Mechwarrior title lurks beneath, but make no mistake MWO is dying. It's reached the point all free-to-play products risk hitting, more ponzi scheme than workable game.

It is a really good controller, but it takes some getting used to, especially if you are into FPS games. But in Skyrim, another game made only for Keyboard/Mouse, it feels great and performs just like a mouse. So these issues can vary from game to game. Skyforge, you get to play as a God, an immortal hero called down to the planet by way of desperate NPC’s looking for help.
Loading up the game, the story doesn’t seem so bad, a little corny, but that isn’t always a bad thing. The character customization is a little limited, but better than most, with a choice of fun costumes and other character additions.
You are then introduced to the voice acting, and boy, is it bad. I tried to give it a chance, I really did. Coupled with terrible lip syncing, this did not help. It was a lot like being subjected to a bad movie, bad acting, bad lightning and bad makeup.
Let’s ignore this and move on. After the first cut scene, you are thrown into a relatively good looking world. Until you realise that there are a lot of graphical glitches, npc’s randomly disappearing for a second, and sometimes NPC’s and objects flashing black. This was a little hard to overlook.
However, the graphical options in settings weren’t so bad but the lack of anti-aliasing was very frustrating as the game looked very choppy with rough edges.
The story continues regardless of graphical glitches and mayhem, and we are thrown into a cut scene that is very similar to the origin story of Kingdoms Of Amalur: The Reckoning. Nothing wrong with that, though there were a few minutes where it felt like a blatant rip-off. You become immortal, a chosen one, nothing out of the ordinary. After talking to a few NPC characters about the main storyline, you realise that you have no choice over the fact that everyone is calling you a god, which I’m not entirely sure is necessary but it seems to give a relationship to the world hub in the game, which wouldn’t make sense without that.
The combat at the beginning of the game is very boring, and along with everything else, it is a struggle to stay interested. Thankfully, if you stick around, you will be rewarded with some beautifully animated combat and fun combat mechanics. You are able to switch classes any time you want, so if you’re bored of being a mage, be a warrior for a while. The classes that you can try at the beginning are standard of most RPG’s. It unfortunately feels like they only put all their effort into combat, which is okay I suppose, if you can put up with everything else.
The UI is very clean, your screen is free from the overwhelming information like most MMORPGS, which is very refreshing and if you are new to MMORPGS, this is something to be happy about. The quest giver and tutorial is very straight forward, and the quests are easy to follow which is again, refreshing.
Skyforge has a lot of potential but is sadly spoiled by bad voice acting, terrible graphical bugs and errors, and terrible animations (that aren’t combat related) but this isn’t anything new from
as a lot of their games are very similar and easily forgotten.
If you can stand all of that and stick around for the combat and easy questing and UI that you can understand, this is probably the game for you, if not, you should try it anyway to see if you like it.
With all its flaws and buggy-ness, I’d give this a rating of 6/10 simply because the combat is fun and the idea is nice.

Ok, I post this review after I played this game for 24 hours in steam and unknown numbers in iOS. First of all, I recommend this game since I'm a tank lover. But to put it in general, here's pros & cons IMO for this game :
Pros :
+ Massively consume less disk space than WoT PC
+ Easy to control in PC (since I've played WoT PC 3 years ago)
+ Easier to grinding XP than WoT PC
+ Less specs needed than WoT PC, so I can play WoTB in high resolution
+ 3 golds for watching videos (in mobile though)
+ Easier to rank up crews and skill crews
+ Sixth sense, ammo replacer, module penetration chance indicator, etc. are already trained
+ Daily missions are updates twice everyday
Cons :
- Harder to control in mobile (need more experience to adapt it)
- Update 3.8 ruined equipments. Need spare parts means more hours played/more cash flying
- No dynamic platoon (in WoT PC can)
- Harder to tell what kind of my tanks's position currently are
- Narrower maps than WoT PC
- No base to base capture mode (only encounter and supremacy [from WoWs])
Neutrals :
> No artillery
> No LAV (Light Armored Vehicles) means no infantry
> Only 7v7 battles allowed
> No planes or airstrikes (this World of "Tanks" LOL)
> Almost still P2W like WoT PC
Overall, I hope this game will get better because I'm almost not interested to play this game again. But if you're a fan of tanks or love to drive tanks and have low-end computer like me, this game is for you. If you like an expansive gameplay or more variative vehicles and have great connection and high-end computer, try Heroes and Generals or War Thunder instead

The game is known by some as a child proofed GTA, what a censored GTA clone would look like. This isn't completely inaccurate if looked at with an open mind, but it isn't necessarily a bad thing for it either. Instead of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s giving you health by ♥♥♥♥ing in cars, you kiss girls. Instead of killing your enemies with guns you "knock out" with a fireworks launcher or sling shot. The game plays well and shares greatly the same mechanics and concept as GTA, but that doesn't mean the fanbases cross everytime since they still have a different setting and atmosphere and the mechanics are slightly different enough that it might mean the world of a difference to some players.
The game doesn't give the player a whole lot of freedom, you feel as if you're in a linear game. You cannot do this or that, there is instant pentalties for it and no rewards to encourage it. For example, no hitting girls or little kids or prefects will get the ability to grab you and you cannot do anything to stop it even at full health. While it does ensure players cannot just run around doing complete chaos like the designer's intentions, it also as a consequence feels the way they did it just took some breathing room for fun. I feel there could have been a less lazier design choice that could allow players to have fun doing those things but greatly punish them through some form of reputation system, something that doesn't exist in spite it being a game essentially about cliques!
In fact, you have little to no control over who likes you and who hates you, there is no consequences for your actions. Once you interact with someone, the next time you meet them it's as if it never happened. You can be a huge♥♥♥♥♥♥to someone and they'll still act either friendly or douchey, all entirely depending not on the player's actions in the game but specifically the current placement in the story. When you progress in the story doing various tasks, you then befriend entire factions of individuals.
The problem with the story is the same as many rockstar titles, they give you a very interesting antagonist except you rarely see him. You see him in the beginning and then you never see him until the end. Like GTA:SA with Big Smoke, a very interesting individual that deserved more camera time, you encounter a character named Gary who is a complete sociopath. Gary is very interesting in what he does and what his intentions are, if he ever seems underwhelming to anyone it's because he has never had his full potential exploited as a character. He did this one thing and now you gotta play the story and wait until the very end to see him. How fun.
The main character is Jimmy Hopkins, a somewhat uninteresting protagonist with the goal of making a lot of friends and creating peace in school through force. That's pretty much it, that's his character, he is just the tough justice warrior that will do anything he wants to achieve his goal. Jimmy isn't a bully in nature, even if bullying is an option through gameplay, and will go as far as to comfort tears from his peers because he is just nice like that. He has virtually no character beyond that, they hint he came from a rough home, a mom that lays on her back for a living, but as far as character development or backstory... that's it. I subscribe to the conspiracy theory that maybe the game was originally about a different character that actualy bullies but then the controversy made Rockstar backstepped into turning it into something else, likely why they never touched a potential franchise again in spite its fanbase. Even if this is most certainly not true, the question remains on why he had such a lazy story to tell in spite any other protagonist from any other GTA game. I feel they could have done better.
I also feel it was weird they added certain weapons, almost like they felt it had to be more like GTA and have less emphasis on realistic melee attacks. Maybe they felt something was missing, I don't know. I do not think they had to add them and my initial reaction was I felt it was weird they added them, but I did get used to them... They do make the game feel easy though.
In spite the many bugs, missed potentials, and the overall ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port, I still think this is worth a buy for any non console owner of the platforms this game is on. It's not going to be good for newer players or players that cannot appreciate older games they have no nostalgia for, but I definitely think you could get you $5 worth if you tried. Me? Already placed hundreds of hours on the PS2 version, I am gonna just wait to see if the alleged Bully in College will ever take place.

is a covert action game in which you play augmented cyborg Adam Jensen in his crusade to take revenge for an incident in which the lives of his "friends" were lost (along with most of his appendages and internal organs).
The game itself is quite immersive, a return to form for a franchise that strayed too far from its origin by trying to please everyone. Although the choices you make are railroaded, it still feels like you actually made them, and Jensen is actually a likeable guy. You could even say he is very "human" (pun intended).
The game can be played in several ways, depending on your approach. You can be a killing machine or an invisible ninja; open your way by bursting throgh walls, or hack yourself into places; become a close-combat specialist, or a weapon expert, etc. Be careful with the play style you choose, because boss fights are mandatory... the first boss WILL own you if you don't choose your enhancements well.
Replayability is almost nil, due to your choices having little effect over the outcomes (except at the very end). You can get most (or all) of the enhancements by the end-game, so there really isn't a need to plan a "build", you just have to plan what you get first, and what you leave for later.
However, it is quite fun to try to get all the achievements, although a little discouraging when you mess up
and
, which could require you to play the game all over again... which is actually frustrating.

Pros:
- this really is free-to-play and definitely NOT pay-to-win. Most mechs are purchasable with c-bills which you can earn in-game, and the few 'premium-only mechs are not necessarily 'better' than the non-premium ones (but they do offer a bonus to in-game currency earned in matches). Most of the premium-only items in the game are either cosmetic or boost the rate at which you can earn in-game currency; additional mechbays are an exception, but the 4 you start with are plenty until you want to start building a large mech collection.
- the game is very generous for new players. Just completing the tutorials gives you a load of c-bills, while the cadet bonuses from your 1st 25 matches should get you enough to buy any mech in the game (apart from the premium variants mentioned above).
- huge range of customisable mechs to buy (in 4 classes light,medium, heavy and assault). The game also has a selection of trial mechs in each class that you can use for free (but you can't customise these) - this allows new players to get a feel for the different weight classes before buying their 1st mech (tip: don't do what I did and spend your cadet bonus before being absolutely sure what type of mech suits you).
- lots of mech customisation options (but these may seem complex/baffling for anyone not familiar with mechwarrior games).
- the visuals and audio do a great job in making the mechs feel authentic
- the matchmaking system attempts to match newer players with other players of the same level of experience
- fairly friendly community overall
Cons:
- huge learning curve for anyone not familiar with the mechwarrior universe.
- the basic tutorials are not really sufficient to prepare new players for the online battlefields, so new players may get frustrated at having to learn to play the hard way.
- there is no option to practice against AI mechs, which would help to alleviate the point above. There is an option to wander around empty battlefields to familiarise yourself with the maps, but I suspect that a lot of new players will quickly get get bored with this, if they choose to do it at all.
- despite the attempt to match new players with others of similar experience, a lot of matches seem to be quite unbalanced and I can see that this could put off many new players.

- How's Money?
Like most games, it gets much more fun the more hours you put into it. In other words, it feels more like "pay to speed up" than pay 2 win. I'll admit there are a few mechs that can only be bought with real money, but it's still possible to take them down (,especially if it's an LRM 80 Scorch; veterans you know what i mean lol.) You may be limited to only 4 mechs at first due to the need to buy mechbays to put your giant robots in, but that can be solved easily if you look out for events that give real-money currency known as "MC." If you have the patience, you wont need to spend a single penny on the game.
- Gameplay?
Has a very high learning curve due to lots of mechanics, weapon types, mech geometry, and more. but if there's one strategy i can give to new players it's this: Deathball. If your team moves as one giant deathball, and even more if you all find an enemy alone, you can pick off the enemy team one by one. Enemies will be frightened when they see 12 enemy mechs charging in at them; they wont know who to focus-fire. Which by the way, focus-fire means "everyone shoot the same target." The strategy works because if you have a lot of people shooting one target, they drop fast and your team can go onto the next one, except this time with one less mech shooting back at them.
- Replayability?
When you do get into the game, what makes it so fun to keep playing over and over again is the fact that you can change what weapons are on the mech. If you get bored, just change the loadout; whether it's derp or a meta build, everyone has their own tastes. I wont get too much into detail for builds here because there's a lot of information, but quick summary is you may spend most of your time in the mech lab and testing grounds more than the actual battlefield/game.
- Conclusion?

Excellent game. I would recommend if you like 4x.
Pros: Empire management is done well. Many system upgrades have limited types of planets it can effect, So may not be useful or of limited use on certain systems. I like the race customization, it really gives you many options for your play style.
Cons: Battle system is horrible because it uses a card game system, no tactics or picking targets. Battles tend to be heavily affected by rng. I would prefer a combat system where you can control your ships. Also taking over a star is too simplistic, it can take a very long time if the enemy keeps throwing ships at you since you can not siege a star until all ships are cleared. AI is not that smart, the difficulty levels only affect AI bonuses and player handicaps. The enemy often mass produce cheap/crappy ships and fleets can only attack 1 time per turn....so even if you fleet is super good you can still attack 1 time. The AI will often have like 30-80 junk fleets ( depending on game difficulty) and can become quite tedious to fight them all. Not to mention the AI keeps sending more junk fleets and can really prevent you from capturing a system. Research tends to scale on cost per tier, so if you skip some research you can get it easily when you are 2+ tiers from it....no reason to skip any research only stall till later when they become really cheap; This really leaves  you with a boring way to choose research the same way every game.
I was tempted to give this game a 5, but the AI and combat system are just too poorly made. I hope that in Endless Space 2 they address these issues. I would have also liked to see more types of ships, weapons and customization; it would be better if there were different types of lasers, for example that would have different strengths/weakness instead of just getting the same basic laser with more damage.

Selections for size as well as sliders to fine tune, muscles, hips, hands, head, bust, buttocks, chest, waist, legs, height.
Classes- There are 12 or 13 classes in game, 3 of which you can start as after the tutorial and allows you to unlock more as you complete missions. They range from ranged, melee, and mage types, bows, guns, magic wands, swords, spears, hooks. And varying looks for these same items you aquire through playing missions and getting loot. Which is honestly more like rewarding you for playing a mission rather than getting loot from dead bodies.
-Gameplay-
This aspect is kinda neutral to me, I like how they want to impliment combos into the game, it makes the game feel like Tera almost, a little more dumbed down and less emphasis on actually comboing to me. I feel like you really can just survive by spamming LMB and RMB with 1 and 2 rarely. The level setup is absolutely trash and it's the same throughout as follows
[Kill these little enemies, find bigger enemy, kill it, find boss win.]
[Destroy hive, remove banners, kill enemy, kill boss, leave.]
and it follows this through 90% of the missions.
the only aspect of an mmo in the game so far is the hub, which allows you to speak in vicinity, and region.
There is not a specific world to go to and play around it, missons are the basis for gameplay and progression.
-Cons-
Chapter missions - Go here, kill these, kill that, big monster, kill it. Leave. You go back to the hub, select new chapter, go here, kill this, cutscene, story elements in a game that has a poor setting for scifi fantasy God's, kill this, hub world.
"Pay to win"
I use this very, very lightly, the game offers packs to purchase, which the game really has no need for. You don't NEED it, the way loot drops I think would deter anyone from even worrying about getting more, you get a few weapons from a few missions and just fight stuff over and over and over. The game is very far from a loot grind.
Gameplay - as I said before, it's bland, boring, and samey.
Buggy - only slightly, here and there it shifts back and forth while doing certain attacks, interupts work odd considering the speed at which you can spam your LMB and RMB buttons.
OVERALL - I would give it a try if you like scifi elements, its been a while since we have had any good scifi games that are roughly open and MMO-Likes.
It's not worth sinking any money into however, and it's almost not worth anyone's time I would say if you aren't a huge fan of scifi-fantasy.

It is a really good controller, but it takes some getting used to, especially if you are into FPS games. CS:GO played beautifully on the Steam Controller, and in some ways, felt even better than the Xbox One controller and other Third Party controllers. But with some other games like DOOM, which was not made with the controller in mind, if feels out of place with the camera. For example, in DOOM, the movement was fluid but the camera movement felt strange and not precise. But in Skyrim, another game made only for Keyboard/Mouse, it feels great and performs just like a mouse. So these issues can vary from game to game. Its true home is with indie games, like Binding of Issac, or with games made by Valve themselves (CS, Portal, etc.) and most other FPS games.
The controller itself feels good, yet odd. It is not familiar feeling like console controllers, but because of that, there is a sense of change to it that is somehow satisfying. But it does feel kind of cheap, but this is mostly because of the all plastic build of the controller.
Overall, I'd give this 3.5 out of 5 stars, with the bigges problems being some ways it plays, but your configuration and a software update from Valve can fix that easily.

The Steam controller is the quintessential PC gaming peripheral: customizable, moddable, likely to be taken physically apart and put back together, the learning curve is steep but the versatility is unmatched, and once mastered, it is comfortable in situations for which it was never intended; I wrote this entire review using mine.
For those who really just want an xbox pad that won't crap out in six months it will run reliably and wirelessly on 2 AA batteries for months, though casual users will find the touchpads and need to personally configure most games a pain. For those who really want to dive into what the controller is capable of, the gyro function - while a significant battery drain (those who don't mind a retro feel can simply plug the controller in using any standard usb 3.0 cable), makes any game calling for a bit of precision feel perfectly intuitive after a bit of tweaking, and tweaking each game to perfection is half the fun!
The options available for personal tuning and countering typical pesky console-port interface stumbling points is comprehensive to the point of valuable redundancy; when one method of smoothing input that can't decide if it's a mouse or a thumbstick doesn't work, you can rest assured some combination of three others will.
The biggest downfall of the controller, as is increasingly common in the hardware market, is strictly down to software. Big Picture sucks, and it's all but necessary for using the controller for gaming. One can set a standard desktop configuration for  using the pad like a mouse and handful of keys outside of steam, but for the primary purpose of videogames, custom game-specific configs require booting up Valve's heinous attempt at a typical console interface.
From the starting point of Big Picture, one will confidently arrive at the conclusion that Valve does not think much of the designers of proprietary console OSes, nor the people who use them. The frustration induced by the unnecessary bloat and poor implementation of features useless to anyone on a desktop such as an integrated browser, social media and steam chat, is compounded by the fact that many of these elements override their better made counterparts the entire time Big Picture is active, and active it must be while you have a game open; closing it will irreversibly revert your control scheme for that session.
That said, the Software appears to be a work in progress, and updates often fix nagging little issues, while only occasionally introducing new ones.

Pros :
+ Massively consume less disk space than WoT PC
+ Easy to control in PC (since I've played WoT PC 3 years ago)
+ Easier to grinding XP than WoT PC
+ Less specs needed than WoT PC, so I can play WoTB in high resolution
+ 3 golds for watching videos (in mobile though)
+ Easier to rank up crews and skill crews
+ Sixth sense, ammo replacer, module penetration chance indicator, etc. are already trained

Cons :
- Harder to control in mobile (need more experience to adapt it)
- Update 3.8 ruined equipments. Need spare parts means more hours played/more cash flying
- No dynamic platoon (in WoT PC can)
- Harder to tell what kind of my tanks's position currently are
- Narrower maps than WoT PC
- No base to base capture mode (only encounter and supremacy [from WoWs])
Neutrals :
> No artillery
> No LAV (Light Armored Vehicles) means no infantry
> Only 7v7 battles allowed
> No planes or airstrikes (this World of "Tanks" LOL)
> Almost still P2W like WoT PC
Overall, I hope this game will get better because I'm almost not interested to play this game again. But if you're a fan of tanks or love to drive tanks and have low-end computer like me, this game is for you. If you like an expansive gameplay or more variative vehicles and have great connection and high-end computer, try Heroes and Generals or War Thunder instead

I still stand by the fact that this is one of the most unique games on the market on a gameplay and technical standpoint, but due to how few players there are remaining, the difficult learning curve for new players, and multiple cheaters that exist in the game currently, I can no longer recommend anyone put any time into it.

An incredibly flexible controller, but not for everyone.
The steam controller has some fantastic features.  The touchpads can emulate mouse-like precision fairly well, the gyro can add additional precision for your aim, Steam's controller support lets you creat complex and flexible configurations, and it essentially makes every button in every game remappable.  The grips on the back are not to be underestimated either.  Ever play a game and wish you could jump or reload without taking your thumb off the analog stick?  The steam controller has you covered.
That said, if you are stubborn or unwilling to learn a new controller, avoid this.  With the incredible flexbility comes a learning curve.  You have to get used to the way the touchpads react.  You have to get a feel for how you like it set-up.  One common theme I find among people who hate it is that they gave up and went back to their Xbox controller or thier PS4 controller in a fairly short time frame.  You are going to have it feel a little weird on your first game or two.  We did not adapt to analog sticks in a mere 10 minutes.

Endless Space offers another look on a 4X genre. It was confusing at first glance, but the variety of all the playable races plus the ship customization is something that has kept me entertained and playing.

Endless Space is a fairly traditional 4X game.  Colonize, expand, build a fleet, conquer stuff, and so on.  It does have a small twist of a simultanious turn system(aka everyone is taking their turns at once, so someone could lock down one of your fleets by engaging them before you move them and so on).  Some like this, some don't.  I'm fairly neutral about it myself.  While I'm pretty slow about making my decisions, sometimes it's actually helped that I tend to go later in the turn order as I get to see what everyone else is doing and then make my moves accordingly.  Sometimes of course it hurts as an enemy moves somewhere preventing me from doing what I was originally planning.
Graphically it's nothing amazing by today's standards but the graphics are functional.  The game as far as I can tell is mostly bug free.  There was one game breaking bug I came across and I don't know if it's gone(there have been multiple updates since that happened and I've never been in the situation that caused it the first time) where lots of ship stacks from different empires all going into the same spot would cause the space battle warning but wouldn't allow me to actually go into the fight and wouldn't let me end the turn since there was a battle that needed resolution.  It happened in my second game I haven't seen it since and other than that I haven't seen any bugs at all.
I do wish the empires had a bit more variety than they do(other than ship designs they feel a bit too similar to me with one exception) perhaps via having more unique techs than they do but honestly I've had a lot of fun nonetheless.
Outside of empires feeling a bit samey, my only real complaint is the diplomacy system and to be entirely honest I'm at a loss for a game with a good diplomacy system.  Civilization, Galactic Empires, this, none of them seem able to get diplomacy out in such a way that it doesn't feel tacked on.  The AI especially gets really weird about diplomacy at times wanting you to be at a very specific strength or it'll hate you for being too strong or too weak and if someone attacks you it gets pissy about you building a large fleet to fight off the attacker.  I had excellent relations with two AI empires, then the Cravers went genocidal on me forcing me to build a massive fleet to push them back, by the end of our war the other two empires(both Pilgrims) had gone from excellent relations to neutral ones.  On the other hand kudos for them not doing the whole attack, surrender, attack immediately after they surrender stupidity that some other games(Warlock, I'm looking at you) have done. I put a lot of hours into Skyforge before it came on steam, though my character got wiped for some weird reason so here i am trying to get back to it on steam!  (Rest in peace sweet prince, Le Squish Bootyhunter :~: )
So you die and for some reason and BOOM, today's your day pancakes you're a immortal.   Now your goal is to become a god, how?  Well the progression system is much more different than most mmorpg's,  Instead of xp and Level you get Prestige which is basically your overall power of your character.    You can bring up your prestige by upgrading your cathedral or tower of knowledge to get more followers, more followers equal more prestige,  or you can do bastion quest which are quests available after finishing the region you're in etc.
And the cool part about Skyforge is that you can change classes that you've unlocked anytime during gameplay, don't feel like cryomancer your style? Bam you're a Necromancer now.   And you don't need to worry about getting ingame or cash currency because it's not hard to get, as you can get it through daily rewards and offerings from your cathedral.
It's not to hard to find groups or people either, i found a few cool peeps and i'm already in a guild! :D   (Everyone is so welcoming! ^^)     So yeah, if you feel like you want a mmorpg with a new spin on it try Skyforge it's really fun!

And, as we all learned, Bandai apparently thinks they are an exception to the logic that every other publisher follows.  This is wrong.  The season pass, a twenty dollar investment, contained two story packs, less than two hours of playtime a piece, and included the Sound Four, who should have been in the game in the first place. First things first, if you felt disappointed with the Doom 3, welcome back to the slaughter. This is Doom is more like the original Doom on steroids. Fear? You do not need fear when you have your trusty shotgun and nearly limitless supply of imps to kill in the most gruesome but fun way. Scratch that, you don't even need the shotgun, if you get spooked by something, you can just punch the hell from it (pun intended).
So, why you should play this Doom? If you need to relax after a long day in work being yelled at by your boss, killing few hell spawns can do wonder to your mood. There are plenty various monsters to kill in the most imaginative ways. Hell, you can upgrade guns to wildly change the way they behave and switch on the move if you get bored with it. The difficulty is just right, there are few puzzles along the way to even help you use few brain cells now and again and the story feels familiar. I did enjoy the story being somewhat better explained than in original doom, but the essence of the game stayed the same. Kill everything before it manages to kill you.
As for the negatives, there are none that you don't expect while buying pure FPS. The game is a tad linear, there are no important decisions along the way and the story is very predictable. However, in this case, it is not the story that matters. It's the feeling that you saved the world by smashing all the hell to pieces.
Did I forgot to mention? CHAINSAW!

I played quite a lot of the original Crimsonland and while the updated graphics and new perks are appreciated, for me the main reason to play was always the survival mode. And in this revamped version it just isn't that much fun because the usual game lasts only around 6 level-ups. This is not enough to work towards any consistent perk+weapon set-up. In the original you could always try new combinations and you felt like they really mattered, but here? After reaching level 6 or 7 I am always overwhelmed no matter what I try and my only hope is to keep on hitting power-ups like plasma overload or fire bullets.
This is another problem, fire bullets used to enhance the weapon you use but now they are almost like a weapon of their own. The same goes for the plasma power-up that is new. This means that in the end it doesn't matter much which weapon you use, because it will soon be too weak anyway and your only hope are the power-ups that replace your weapon.
The Quests felt like good old Crimsonland (once I enabled perks in the menu) but the Survival mode is really inferior to the original one.

Most of it comes down to hoping you get the right weapon drop, and hoping that wepon drop isn't in the middle of a swarm of enemies. and hoping that the enemies don't push you into a corner because you'll never out run them.

I wanted to like the Steam Controller. I really did. I wanted to buy into the Steam pipe dream of being able to couch game, and play games that wouldn't otherwise be a controller game. I wanted a gamepad I could take anywhere with me to play when I'm with friends. This piece of hardware has let me down on every single front, and this is after 2 of them purchased.
My first controller was a preorder unit, and arrived on the promised date. After a couple months of occasional use, the analog stick bug hit, making the analog stick useless. Without this, the whole unit is basically broken; it's not worth using for anything in this condition.
The second controller was bought to replace the first with the hope that it wouldn't have the same happen to it. This is when I bought into the steam link, and began using it regularly. Throughout its life, it's had a multitude of small issues. I initially kept the wireless receiver in the steam link, and plugged into my PC, but after a short while, the USB plug on the backside broke, and wasn't usable if I moved the controller (which, spoiler alert, you sometimes do with a controller). The vibration motors in it have always come on at semi random times, and the left touch unit never really worked totally correctly, but it was passable as an occasional D-pad. Finally today, the left bumper no longer works, and just sinks down.
I'm done. I'm not interested in another one. These controllers see use mostly for rocket league, and maybe once a week couch gaming, but neither of them is usable. Both fatally broken in different ways. I don't plan on getting another to see another failure mode. A very promising concept with fatally flawed and poor execution. Unfortunately, it's back to less full featured but still better controllers for me.

Once you really understand how to use the diplomacy system, everything else is pointless when playing against the AI. If you don't understand why this is the case, then you don't really understand how to use the diplomacy system. Master it (which is really nothing more than learning a few tricks, albeit ones that many people inexplicably fail to discover) and even the -195 point race achievement becomes effortless, even boring.
Unfortunately, the game doesn't get much better even when playing stupidly (meaning not taking full advantage of the diplomacy system). Simplistic, counter-based ship design, similar to GalCiv2 (which suffers from many of the same problems), fails to provide much opportunity for meaningful tinkering, and the system of choosing a few tactics when going into battle is not an adequate substitute for actual tactical combat. I suppose that if you're super-interested in economic optimization, and aren't going to look too hard at the diplomacy system, you might find this game interesting.
Otherwise, you might want to look elsewhere.

I was very much looking forward to a decent modern 4X game. Having very much enjoyed the Master of Orion games and Ascendancy from the DOS days, I was hoping for something new and exciting from the genre. I had tried Galactic Civilizations 2 before and it was clunky, uninspired and unfun, maybe this would be different?
This game was completely unfun to play from the beginning. It was very frustrating all around and I couldn't get into the game at all. The star system looks beautiful, I love the way the worlds look and slowly rotate, esp. since you can zoom in on each one... but the UI and game play were not intuitive nor entertaining.
The races seemed largely unoriginal, and almost all of them were based on humans, unlike the vastly different races available in Master of Orion and Ascendancy. The tutorials just had popup text over the actual window and only told you what parts of the view port were, not how to use them. Way too much informationation all at once, and not letting you actually poke at any of them while explaining things did not help you figure it out.
It took a long time to figure out how to even move ships. I noticed a ship icon next to my home world and couldn't figure out how to tell it to move until I right clicked directly on a system and away a ship went. Right clicking a little bit off just unselected the ship, so I kept thinking I was doing something wrong, and the mouse cursor doesn't change to indicate that the ship would move. Ok... So you right click to move. Except after exploring a nearby system, trying to explore the next star system just doesn't work again (unselecting again), probably because I need some research to be able to travel further from my home world, but I couldn't even figure out what any of the drives did, how to move further, or what was wrong. The game didn't give me a message when I tried to go to nearby stars to tell me why I couldn't go to that one vs this one, it just unselected the movement, like slapping my hand for doing something wrong without saying why. A message saying, "You need Long Distance Space Exploration" or whatever would have gone a long way here. In fact, looking things up in the Wiki and doing searches for this never came up with the information necessary to explore, and I looked all over through the research tree, which was it's own lesson in frustration.
The research tree gives minimalistic information in popups, that told you the names of what you could get from the research and some story about that research, but didn't tell you a darned thing about the research itself. And you can't mouse over things in the popups to figure out what the heck they are (though Ascendancy also had this problem). The research tree tells you almost nothing useful, and the names of a lot of things mean nothing.
An example: A research you get near the beginning is called "Compact Fusion Reactors". This has the text:
"While great leaps forward in fusion technology are on the horizon, the ability to miniaturize and simplify existing fusion technology also provides practical rewards." - Ok... this doesn't tell me much.
It says it unlocks "Advanced Magnetics Drive" and "Colonize Arctic". Ok, I get the Colonize one (though who knows why a new Fusion reactor would unlock colonizing arctic worlds), but what the heck does "Advanced Magnetics Drive" do? Does it allow my ships to travel further? Faster? Is it a new module for engines for building new ships? Apparently, it just adds 2 movement speed to all of your ships once you get it. I had to look it up on a Wiki to figure out what it did.
The combat system was incredibly confusing from a new player's perspective. I experienced combat on turn 3 with my scout ship up against a couple of pirates... I didn't want to lose my scout ship, so I had all these cards to pick from, so I just picked retreat cause I knew I was going to die otherwise. Then a weird cinematic-ish battle happened where I couldn't tell what was happening at all... and suddenly my ship ran away, back towards my home system. Which is where another pirate was waiting, and this time succeeded in destroying my scout. On turn 4. Great way to learn the game!
I never even met up with another race because I couldn't travel very far in the couple of attempts to play, and was so frustrated by the game at this point, I switched back to playing old MS-DOS 4x games again.
This game is taking many ideas from Master of Orion 2, which I played again after writing this review and could see all the parallels. But MoO2 is intuitive and doesn't require a tutorial, let along a 3rd party guide to play. It came with a book, yes, but even that wasn't necessary because it was easy to just jump into the game having played 4X games before.
In MoO2, when you click a ship and then mouse over a star system, it does one of two things. If it is in range of your systems, it draws a green line and gives an ETA for how long it would take to get there. If it is out of range, it draws a red line to it and says how far away it is so you can tell it's too far for your fuel to reach. In ES, there is no indication that the game has a clue there is another system there, no cursor change, no highlight, nothing.
In MoO2, when you are presented with the 8 different research trees and which branches you can learn, if you right click on a research, it tells you what it gives you. Right from the beginning, I can right click on "Standard Fuel Cells" and it tells me "Supplies sufficient energy to propel a ship 4 parsecs before refueling." - Ok, I now know exactly what research to work towards if I want to travel further. I don't even know what it says for the correct research in ES, since I could never find it, but I doubt it mentions anything about your ships travelling further from the popup information...
I spent almost 2 hours trying to get this game to work for me, and I could not. I'm certain other people pushed themselves through the problems, but to me spending 2 hours and still not even knowing what to do was frustrating.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution has to be one of the greatest games I've ever played, it brought back the excitement of System Shock when I first played it and had a compelling story to back it up. This version has topped the original with a more immersive story, without taking you away from the action. Much more than an FPS or a Stealth game, with a huge amount of RPG elements thrown in. There are often many ways to complete a task, from charging in with a massive gun, sniping people from a distance, to sneaking past without anyone noticing. My favourite however is using the tranquiliser to silently knock out people one by one, stacking their bodies in a vent. This is the first game I’ve played where once I finished it for the first time, I immediately loaded it back up, set the difficulty to max and started all over again, determined to get that achievement, or find a new way of finishing a mission.
I would definitely recommend it to people who want a blend of FPS that makes you think about what to do next and it is still relevant in comparison to the more recently released sequel.

So its not an awful controller.  I does feel a bit cheap, i dislike the AA batter power...though mines lasted a while...and after a bit of use you sort of get over the feel of it.
My thumbs down isnt 100% the actual physical controller but more the whole package of steam big screen, the steam controller, and how steam functions as a package with the steam link controller and its games.
First of all, the steam controller intergrates fantasically with steamlink and big screen...for some games, not all.
The controllers most interesting feature, the haptic feedback right thumb track pad is great in a very few specific applications regarding a couple games.  Other than that, youll often find yourself wishing for an xbox controller or other twin stick controller.  For most application the track pad is inferior to a second joystick...
Now this can usually be overcame with a solid user created public configuration..which is viable only with hugely popular games....for the most part, occasionally youll come across a good configuration for a lesser played game.  Its sometimes the difference between using steam as a console type platform and giving up, exiting big screen, hopping on to the pc and using an xbox controller or standard KB/Mouse.
And this is my problem.  Other than the few gametypes (turned based games) that usually work flawlessly with the controller and whole steam on my couch package...i find myself flipping through my game library aimlessly looking for a good game to play.
I filter my library by controller support...which often includes games built for any controller...specifically not the steam controller.  Top that off with a lot of simple games that do work great with the controller but dont run in bigscreen mode well...screen flashes or odd issues that cause the game to act oddly.
In big screen mode it doesnt tell you what type of game it is, so you look at screen shots, often it wont show any existing...i cant go to store page to see what exactly is this game that offers controller support.  There are a lot of games that the whole steam on the couch package doesnt work well with, regardless of how well it works with the steam controller.
Bascially valve is on a good path with this set up, however, it feels in alpha mode sometimes...the big screen mode from my couch offers less tools to manage and wade through the mass of games im not familair with that i own.  I spend i feel more time trying out a game, finding out i need a twin stick set up, the game doesnt work well at all with the steam controller but will with an xbox controller from desktop, or just straight up isnt a game that is compatable at all with big screen/controller.
I really dont have an issue with every game working with this set up, im fine with it...im fine with the steam controller preforming hooribly for games desiged for twin stick controllers....but you basically have to try each game to see if its one youll want to play from your couch with the steam controller.  A LOT of wading through games trying to figure out which ones work great and which ones ill stick to desktop.  This is what i mean when i say the steam from the couch experience feels very alpha mode.
Now...if the $50 controller, $50 link is worth it for you to play a few games from the comfort of your couch...its worth it.
If you are looking for the next step in steam gaming, from your couch, its a rocky ride trying to sort out all the games you own that will work...even when filtering to increase those chances many controller compatable games are not compatable without a lot of work, and even then an xbox controller will be far superior...
I will say, i LOVE bigscreen mode when floating through the store, the adaptation of store page video, reviews, and games in general is a very pleasant experience from the couch, and i ♥♥♥♥ing love how easy it is to put a store page video into full screen and watch a crisp, lag free, video from my couch....i will make use of steam as a tv media platform once that happens.
Im not saying any aspect is horrible with valves from the couch set up...its so much in its infancy that it can be fustrating, and youll end up sticking to a few games you know work great (and when they do it is fantastic)
I still havent found a game that i really prefer to play on the couch that utilizes the track pad well...If steam offerd a steam controller with twin sticks and no track pad, id probably pick that up and never use the track pad controller again.  Take that for what its worth i feel its a strong statement.  When it does work well however, its a beautiful thing...but i find that its a small fraction of my game library, and many games that should work well, dont...and getting them to work can be time consuming and fustrating with lots and lots of trial and error.
Moving forward steam needs to intigrate the track pad much better, and games need to be made that really utilize it for it to be an awesome product worth buying.  I feel they need a better grip on which games are steam controller compatable....just because you can doesnt mean its pleasant or fun vs an xbox controller...as well as tidy up their big screen mode library games so i know what the heck the game is about....we all have big game libraries because of steam...so better tools to wade though it, manage it, and enjoy it would be appreciated.  I do think they need to incorporate the big screen library featued and reccomended on desktop...its great to see store page style representations of game i already own.
So unless you have a specific game you know works well, love to tinker with settings to force controller compatability, or like me just wanted to blow $80 on valve in the hopes it gets better over time....just skip the steam controller, go with wireless xbox, and understand that it can be very fustrating to play many games via the steam link on a tv.
Steer clear if you are looking for an easy to use controller and console style experience with steam....it needs a lot more time to remove fustrations and poorly executed controlls.  Youll have to spend hours gettin the controller to work properly unless the community has figured it out, the developer has made it easy to use, or the game is so utterly simple it cant possibly fail (joystick move and no more than 4 functions that land on the 4 buttons)
Oh and i dont think ive ever use the flat left crontrol pad.  Really the track pad and control pad are utterly useless in most cases, your paying for one joystick, four buttons, two triggers, a super handy steam button to turn it off or exit a game (doesnt always work though and youll have to get up and force close)....also the back of the controller flippers are annoying, feel super cheap, and its really easy to accidentially activate them.
Just offer a twin stick steam controller, no need for the flat controller pad or track pad.  Better plastic on the back of the controller, a usb charge battery, and the steam controller is much much better.  Not enough games that will and can utilize the track pad, and even then...those are typically games better played on desktop anyway.
