This is just a short version of a much larger controller round up feature which will appear in my magazine due May 2017. I have been using my controller on a daily basis since Jan 2017. I could write a small book on how it has progressed over the last few months, how to best configure different kinds of games, etc. But I promise I will keep this article short and sweet.
CHEER UP BRIAN
First I'll address the negative points of the device, and there are a couple: Number one, and the biggest issue by far is that you really don't want to play twin-stick games with this controller if you can avoid it. I mean, just look at it and imagine using the right haptic input as a joystick! If you can't picture it let me tell you that awkward ain't the word. Although in it's defence it does seem to allow for a greater degree of analog precision, this comes at a great cost to speed and maneuverability.
As is using the left haptic as a dpad a bad idea, which the indentations on the input would suggest Valve intended it to be used for. The haptics perhaps offer just a little too much resistance when pressing down on them to click. That's why it sucks so much as a dpad, and probably the reason why most configurations map the left mouse button to the right trigger instead of a right haptic click. You can set it up to register a button press when you touch the haptic, but then there's not enough resistance, so you're buggered one way or the other it seems. Oh well, wow onto the good points...
RED RIGHT HAND
The right haptic as a mouse generally works quite well, infinitely better than your average laptop touchpad, with a pleasing slight mechanical feedback vibration and sound when you make a movement which I found quite satisfying as it gave me a greater sensation of physically interacting with the game. And adjustable sensitivity and inertia, as well as being able to place the mouse pointer in a particular section of the screen via the controller configuration means that it can potentially give you quite the edge over regular mouse users in mouse controlled games.
The on screen keyboard is really quite easy to use when accessed with the two haptic inputs, although the afore mentioned issue with the high resistance of the click action is mildly annoying. And I find that sometimes I am able to type a bit faster with two thumbs looking at the screen than I am with all ten digits looking at the screen. Although not all the keys are accessible in this mode (you're going to have to use the configuration editor to assign inputs to those) and as for the word predictions at the top of the on-screen keyboard, well I know from previous experience reviewing for Steam that the word I want to use will be covered in hearts (I seem to recall it caused controversy when used in the school paper in a fairly recent episode of South Park), so let's just say "inherently stupid". Especially when compared to the predictive text on my Android phone.
CONFESSIONS OF S STEAM PUNK
I must confess that I was not really interested in purchasing a Steam Controller, as my initial impression from looking at the images and reading the reviews was that it would be 1) a bit awkward and uncomfortable 2) a poor substitute for keyboard/mouse control and 3) not really suited to replace the standard twin stick controller which has become the norm over the last decade or so.
But I recently purchased a Steam Machine which of course comes with a Steam Controller bundled with it, and I must say that at least the first two out of three parts of my initial impression were, well, just plain wrong. And I would absolutely recommend that any serious gamer purchase one of these.
The first thing I noticed when I picked it up was that it feels surprisingly comfortable in my hands, and after almost a month of usage I might even go so far as to say it's perhaps even the most ergonomic of any controller I've ever used on any system in my 25+ years of gaming. Although it's worth noting that I am a full grown adult male who stands about 5"10' (175cm) tall, I imagine it could possibly be a little on the large side for anyone shorter than about 5"6' and indeed at least one other review confirms that it's a bit large in the hands of a female child.
WHEN THE WEATHER IS FINE
If you're happy using keyboard and mouse and are just looking for an Xinput (Xbox 360 & One as well as Windows 10:) twin-stick controller then you definitely want to look elsewhere and would definitely be advised to be sure you have at least a standard 360 controller in your possession before saving up your pocket money for a Steam Controller. But if you spend more than a few hours a week accessing games in your Steam library then a Steam Controller definitely should be an object of desire for you even if you cannot afford one. Worth saving up for if you are the kind of person who will use it, while the software is slightly unstable the hardware is pretty solid, and like my grandfather might say in cases like these "You tend to get what you're willing to pay for", meaning if you're paying a premium price you can very much expect a premium product. The Steam Controller is both fashionable and functional, the interface is still a little rough around the edges but then this is very much a product which Valve are continuing to develop and support, so what may be a minor technical issue now may no longer be an issue with future updates too.
- Rob O'Malley
UPPERS
I could go on at length but I will simply say that it works! It works well and it works comfortably. I hardly ever use my real keyboard and mouse to control my Steam Machine anymore, and that includes my Ubuntu desktop too.
DOWNERS
Much like all of Valve's Steam products, both hardware and software, it has a distinct "beta version" quality, especially the driver configuration. And it's possibly a bit large for those of small stature. Oh, and it costs about twice what one might expect to pay for a controller as you have probably noticed.
BOTTOM LINE <3
The Steam Controller may be a poor twin stick controller, but it is good for games which only use one stick or the dpad for input and quite brilliant at it's intended application of replacing keyboard/mouse controls. A must have for all serious Steam users. But casual gamers might be advised to think twice due to the price.

So, I decided to spend 30$ on this game not too long ago, and I am beginning to regret it. Do keep in mind, I adore the naruto franchise and it is probably one of the highest spots on my favorite list, but this game just makes me very disappointed with where they decided to go as far as they games are concerned. One of the most recent updates brought 60fps to the game, which is a god-send, but with the amount of players that still using 30fps rather than the new 60fps option, it completely ruins the game and makes it like the game was put in slow-mo (Literally.)
Another thing to go on about, is the connectivity. I've had around 15-20 games recently where after just punching my opponent one time, it would disconnect us from the game and say that the connection was lost, after just one punch. Other times, it's just extremely laggy and puts a huge delay on the match and makes it near impossible to even play.  I kinda feel like it's in their favor when that happens. Also, some of the games mechanics are just plain broken, which is something that I can overlook since most of them are just small things.
BUT, the one very important thing that really got on my nerves, was the seemingly normal release of the Road to Boruto DLC. I believe it added a new character to the game, other than the well known next-gen characters (Boruto, etc) - and that character isn't OP, but just plain stupid and needs to be re-worked. When they do their jutsu, it is 100% unable to be interrupted. I tried punching them while right in front of them, and it did nothing and got hit with the jutsu instead. (I hit them right when they started the jutsu)
Most of the complaints you'll find here are the overpriced DLC that shouldn't be the price they are, or the consistent connection issues that most have. If you want a pro? Well, the visuals are pretty enjoyable, as well the story of the game.
If I had to rate my online experience, it'd most likely be a 6/10, I'll bump it up to 8 or 9/10 once they fix the connection issues. (I understand that most will be due to client side, but most are also server sided.)

I purchased this on sale (35% off - $20) a few months after release (and after a few updates fixing several problems other people may have noted).
Overall, this is an ok game, however I wouldn't recommend it over any of the similar games in the genre. It plays most similar to Sins of a Solar Empire (semi-realtime, not turn based), but lacks the depth. And I don't mean like min-max depth, I mean everything is super basic. Building ships is just adding a new widget in a generic interface. Adding buildings is just putting bubbles into the civic category. Research is extremely linear.  There's also no auto-management for settlements, so you have to go update everything yourself every time, otherwise it'll stop growing.
On top of all of that, the game is relatively boring (you only unlock two planet types during the game, so there's not much new settling/expansion mid-game), and most things are capped (total research is capped, savings are capped, etc). So even if you do expand or build a successful empire, it doesn't really matter. After a certain point, bigger gets you nothing. There's a lot of design decisions that really limit the strategy options, which makes the game far less interesting.
Combat also sucks. The interface doesn't allow you to easily select ships to use their abilities, so more often than not you are either trying to micro ships, or you just let them slug it out hoping the terrible AI will keep all your ships at least attacking an not just sitting idle (even though they are in aggresive mode) watching their friends get shot.
Aside from that, the game seems to run slow. Zooming was choppy. The interface seems to lag. There were no bugs or crashes that I experienced, but it wasn't smooth either. And the music is fairly dull.
Overall, not terrible. 5/10. But I wouldn't recommend this over any other space 4x game currently available. Also, I wouldn't pay more than $15 - $20 for it if you did decide to purchase.

The problem with the game is that while it visually looks good, everything seems to be missing a feature which causes the whole thing to play like you are trying to start a stalled car.

I assume the quality of the planet allows you to eye ball it but it is still guess work and some of the random events include spawning a minor civ or hostile fauna both result in a lost colony ship.
- Economics is basic and boring you have strategic resources which give empire wide bonuses but once you have access to them thats it you have access. You can "trade" for them if an empire is selling them at one of there planets but they do not have an amount value so one empire can sell to the entire galaxy and gain a large economic advantage.
- The prices the things scale way faster than you can reasonably earn anything and to acheive an ecnomic victory is the easiest way to win which is just shocking considering that 12 units can cost you 10k credits and by that time you are in the end game.
- Travel is slow which by itself is not a bad thing but coupled with everything else just grinds the game to a snails pace that just never picks up.
-Combat is uninventive and just amounts to you line up your ships and they attack each other untill one side wins. You can put MODs on your ships to give them certain advantages or abilities which when used can actually turn the tide of a battle which is really nice. The whole thing though just feels lacking, the fleets can never be as big as you want them to be, the battles them selves are basically turn based and tactics are purely based on your mods. Flanking attacking from behind just dosent matter when ships can turn on a dime anyway and have full 360 combat.

A game where you dismantle real-life guns by each and every single pieces, all the little springs and screws being ripped off, and then you have to rebuild it back from the mess you've made.
I'm far from being a gun enthousiast, but this game is still pretty interesting gameplay wise, there's a neat puzzle aspect to dismantling and reassembling, analyzing how the guns are build.  While it's totally fine taking you time with it, the in-game challenges has the more adept players try to make the highest score, taking a lot of precautions to not try to remove/assemble a piece too soon, and as fast as possible; a lot of it is about memorization, but it's still good fun, it "wakes up my brain", which is enough to keep me happy.
It also serves as a very complete educationnal tool.  I've said I wasn't much into guns, but it was still interesting seeing how all this stuff works.
There are a few annoyances though, as sometimes I would click twice on a piece to remove it, but the game counts it as me being hasty and losing points, and sometimes trying to click on the smaller pieces makes the game think you've been clicking on the side.  It's pretty obnoxious as you try for a better score, and the game fails to load quite a few times in each sessions, but it didn't tarnished the whole experience for me, at least.
There are also Shooting Ranges, where you actively use a weapon, which is more of a neat little distraction for me.
Since it's Free to Play, the way it's build has you either retrying the same guns or wait for daily rewards, to obtain Experience Points, which you have to use to unlock new guns.  You could always buy for Gun Packs DLC to not have to use these Exp Points.  There are also exclusive models that may require Credits, which also cost money, unless you miraculously manage to get all challenges on a model, in which case you only get 1 Credit for each 100% guns.  Not the best business model, but eh... could be much worse, I guess.
It's worth a peek at least.

Don't let the 'mixed' ratings draw you away from this game - this game here is the biggest investment I have possibly ever made in gaming. I started playing 2 years ago and have already garnered 2,000+ hours, and that number is steadily increasing. The core game itself has literally all of the little details and touches that work with the player - natural controls for brickshifting, shortcuts, and all sorts of nifty tricks such as being able to repeat a building pattern in the blink of an eye are all found in the base game.
I have nothing to say about the older versions of the game, except that from what I've heard they sounded good, but in my opinion the present version of this game is the best it's ever been for me.
People are saying that the community is 'dead' or 'dying' - yes, there are less and less players and more are VERY GRADUALLY leaving over time, but those that remain, they're great. The best way I can think to explain this game is that if you have an open-world game with memorable characters and certain individuals that stick out - everyone knows them, they are known for their work/memes etc. - making the community feel really close together. That's the best way I can describe this game. Sure, there are a few♥♥♥♥♥♥♥but they're to be expected.
If you're new to the game,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥are left and right, but only if you BEHAVE like a new player. The reason why is that new players have a certain reputation for being clueless kids with no intent to do anything other than whip out lame roasts and make ♥♥♥♥♥♥ builds. Just act smart, and you will be treated smartly. Your building doesn't have to be great - there's lots of time for practise. I reccommend getting the BL Glass add-on for the game since it's really helpful for getting into the community.
This game is literally impossible to sum up in a simple review, which just goes to show how open-ended it is. This is one of the few games I know where anything and everything really IS possible with enough dedication. And the add-on variety basically never ends. Unlike games like Minecraft and/or Garry's Mod (Which, I should mention, this game came before Minecraft and Roblox in its first prototypes) where incompatibility with other players is a huge issue and missing textures after an hour's worth of waiting for downloads is your reward for waiting, add-ons are downloaded while you're joining the server. UNLIKE GARRY'S MOD, however, you are still connected to the chat of the server, allowing you to contribute to the server and whatnot. It may look like a lot of files to start with, but after a few servers they'll be less common.
I whole-heartedly reccommend this game to everyone. EVERYONE.

I really like the game and enjoy playing it.  That being said this game has a steep learning curve.
1. Balancing a mech and playing as an organized unit are hard, especially organizing in PUG matches.  While your mech build is important, the team play and communication are most important.
2. Most mechs are playable and can do well; you just have to find the right heat/firepower/range ratio for that mech model and build. There are usually several and they can be personalized.
3. Pay to Win?  The new mech releases are only available to purchase with real money, but most of the models become available in a few months for in game money.  There are a few obsolete models from the game launch, and a few small bonues on the newer released mechs.
4. Overall, this does not matter much.  I.E. The mech and model that I do best with has been there since launch, cost in game money, and has been nerfed a few times.  Your skill is what matters.
5.  Spending real money, allows you access to the newer mechs, special mechs (The real difference is a paint job), cockpit items, and customizable paint jobs.
6. Grind:  The game has lots of bonus challanges, going on almost every day, that allow you to win in game money, in game cash credits, mechs, and cockpit items.  You can always use trial mechs from the start to earn these bonuses.
7.  Mech and skill advancement; Buy a medium or heavy mech to start with.  They are the most versatile and do well when together.  Save your in game money and buy 2 variants of your first mech so you can master that mech. The hype machine behind big games often mirrors the precarious Icarus myth - fly too close to the sun, promise too much, and you're just as likely to tumble out of the sky as deliver on your potential. Green Lava Studios have promised so much with My Name is Mayo that it's hard to see how they could succeed, how they couldn't burn up in the harsh heat of audience expectation.
My Name is Mayo takes place in a future you can see from here. The world of My Name is Mayo meets somewhere between Blade Runner and Robocop caught between the utopia of revolutionary scientific discovery and the dystopia of the people inevitably left behind.
While My Name is Mayo can't be a revelation, it's an achievement nonetheless. It's a visionary, considered piece of work, and while my thoughts drift to the things that could have been and the compromises made due to the possibilities of video games in 2016, they're just as quick to consider playing through it again. My Name is Mayo is a smart and rewarding.

The cult classic is back. This time with updated graphics, weapons, perks, and game modes.
I was a huge fan of the original and was ecstatic to see it get rereleased on Linux.
When it comes to top down shooters, Crimsonland is by far the best out there. Controls are very percise and mappable. The graphics update is beautiful when compared to the original and quite nice for being a 2D game. The interface also got a face lift. Orignially, your ammo count was an image on the top that showed you how many shots you had left. Now, it is a counter above the mouse. I prefer this seeing as I'm mostly looking at the mouse. In the original, any bonus you picked up would give you a count down in the upper left. Now, if the bonus affects your gun (firing rate, fire bullets, etc.) you get a yellow countdown around your mouse. If the bonus affects your character (shield) you get a clock like counter around your health bar (which is also now around the character instead of in the upper left hand corner). There are no countdowns for 2x, Freeze, or Speed bonuses. Some indication would be helpful, especially for the Speed bonus. But, I won't fault them too much on those. Lastly, the perk selector was overhauled as well. Originally, a window would pop up that listed the perks in a vertical list with a discription on the bottom. Now, they are images listed horizontally with the name under it when the mouse is hovered over it and the discription on the bottom and the biggest difference is that in the original you would hit Tab to open the perk selector. In the new version it appears automatically and you are forced to pick something to continue.
Some of the weapons updates are nice but I feel that there are too many. While they are nice, since the weapon drops are completely at random you might never get the gun you really need for late game. Also, before the 1.9 patch of the original there was a trick to using the Pulse Gun and using the Angry Reloader perk that just made you dominate the map early on. This was "fixed" in 1.9 which was a huge let down in my opinion.
I can't really say much about the perk other than telekenisis. This perk was changed heavily. Originally, you would hover your mouse over a bonus for a full second and you would pick it up. This made you have to be looking in its direction, which made it hard if you had enemies behind you. You basically had to stop shooting at them to pick up the bonus or time it so you could position them between you and the bonus to shot them. Now, the closest bonus will move towards you. I actually prefer this new method over the previous. Lets you focus more on the fight and less about trying to pick up the bonus. My only complaint is that I think the longer the bonus is traveling, the faster it should move. If you are running backwards, the bonus will never reach you because you can out run it. Still a better approach, though.
They also added a new game mode. Nukefism gives you no weapons and only bonuses to pick up. Very hard game mode which is why the achievement is unlocked when you get 75,000 points in it. Unfortunately, they removed the Typ'o'Shooter game mode which was my favorite. An enemy would appear with a word over it and you would have to type it out to shoot at that enemy. Not only was that a great mode to teach typing but like all things Crimsonland would get progressively harder the longer you lasted. It really made you learn the layout of the keyboard. Typ'o'Shooter is greatly missed.
With all of this being said, I feel that the price may be a little bit high considering that the original was only 10 dollars USD in 2004. By no means do I consider this a 14 dollar title, especially when they removed a great game mode and didn't really add anything of a story. When Survival mode will last, at best, 10 minutes before you get overwhelmed by enemies, these quick matches, I feel, makes the 14 dollar USD price tag a little bit much. However, on sale, this is a great buy.
The biggest drawback to Crimsonland is that it relies a bit too rmuch on the random factor. I would have loved to see a game mode like Survival but where you can remove, say, 10 weapons and 15 perks from the pool. This would let someone get rid of some of the bad weapons and perks (like the Blowtorch... seriously, the Blowtorch? Why? I'd rather take the Pulse gun over the Blowtorch).
Lastly, the Linux port was amazingly done. Performance was as expected. Some reports of reversed X axis on game pads which I believe are fixed as of this writing (or will be fixed soon). I did experience 1 random crash but I think that was caused by something else happening at the same time.
If you are a fan of quick match top down shooters, storyless and senseless violence, or simple time killer games, I highly recommend this game. If you were a fan of the original, you might be left with a bad taste, but I wasn't.

If you've come here for a BUlly review, you've come to the wrong place. But if you've come for a recipe for an outstanding and delicious pound cake then you've come to the right place.
You will need:
1/2 pound (2 sticks) butter, plus more for pan
1/2 cup vegetable shortening
3 cups sugar
5 eggs
3 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for pan
1/2 teaspoon fine salt
1/2 teaspoon baking powder
1 cup of milk
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Directions:
Preheat oven to 350 degrees F. With a mixer, cream butter and shortening together. Add sugar, a little at a time. Add eggs, 1 at a time, beating after each addition. Stir dry ingredients together in a bowl and add to mixer alternately with milk, starting with the flour and ending with the flour. Mix in vanilla. Pour into a greased and floured tube pan and bake for 1 to 1 1/2 hours, until a toothpick inserted in the center of the cake comes out clean. You now have a delicous pound cake waiting for you!

I love this game. MWO is set in the battletech universe, in which a number of factions of different ideas and heritages fight among themselves for the control of the Universe. The leading war machines of this futuristic conflict are Mechs, a sort of ultra-giant heavy armoured and armed robots, piloted only by the bravest and noblest warriors of each faction. In this game you'll have to impersonate one of these pilots and manage your Mech, from its loadout configuration to the actual piloting in the battlefield. Let me be clear: the game requires some time to master its mechanics, so if you're new expect some confusion and frustration in the firsts matches. But the great number of options and different play styles you can choose it's exactly what makes this game unique and deeper, and hence better, once you'll start to learn the mechanics. A very positive factor, beside the game itself, it's the affectionate fanbase, which is almost always very gentle and will help you whenever you ask (I found metamechs and mechspecs web sites particularly useful). I spent a lot of time (and no money, this is definitely not a play to win game) on it, and I plan to continue. If you're in structured simulation games this is worth giving a shot!

It's been a while since I played a 4X/RTS hybrid. Despite leaving its Early Access stage yesterday, Dawn of Andromeda proves that a video game which shows great promise, can also keep its word in terms of promises made to its players and early buyers/supporters. Nonetheless, it is the Steam debut of its developer, Grey Wolf Entertainment.
I was playtesting extensively the Early Access when out of the blue, that stage was over and I could finally sink my teeth into the proper Dawn of Andromeda storyline. The highly anticipated (by me) Eras. You may consider them, scenarios focusing on very specific objectives and struggles between two or more factions. Before the campaign was launched, I had to contend with a sandbox mode of sorts, titled “Custom Game”. It was more than fine yet it could hardly fill the void for a proper story. Along came the Eras and while I shall not spoil anything to you, know that its main plotline focuses on the causes and effects of a cataclysmic event, triggered by mindless warfare and religious zealotry. Why does it sound so familiar to me?
It’s still debatable if Dawn of Andromeda’s graphics engine is running Unity 5 assets, but as far as players are concerned, the game looks gorgeous. In the several hours I spent building up my galactic empires, I haven’t met a single bug, glitch or crash to desktop. The frame rate was constantly pushing 60 FPS while rendering at 4K resolution. An Early Access that features absolutely no technical issues, isn’t something you take for granted. I have obviously met none, even after two days since the game’s full release. Textures were featuring the right amount of detail and variety, but I’d still like to see more ship design features, other than a few templates that only have modifiable loadouts and no aesthetic options as well. At least the chance to alter the faction and unit color schemes would be welcome.
The sounds are not quite on par with the eye candy. Sure, the soundtrack is a soothing and genre specific, yet the sound effects are lacking in diversity and there is absolutely no voice acting. Not for the into cinematics or for the various task and interface screens between major or minor species. I probably got too used to the diplomatic screen from the more recent Civilization titles, but I’d like at least a few lines of spoken dialogue when interacting with the AI allies or foes. We’re negotiating intergalactic peace over here, so they should spare the time to properly thank me for that.
I mentioned in the Introduction section, two acronyms. Perhaps some of you are more familiar to RTS (real time strategy) than 4X ("eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate"), yet they both represent old school staples of the strategic gaming genre. Recent years may have been less kind to 4X since this subgenre has always been harder to implement or improve over the existing formula (micromanagement can rarely get streamlined), but I still like to think that it’s more than just a niche demand for strategy games that incorporate in-depth elements of politics and diplomacy. Because 4X is as much about waging total war, as it is about brokering a lasting peace. Ensuring technological advancement, without neglecting society’s constant need for changes in its structure. Politics may be a dreary subject to some players, yet such video games may present a more “digestible” version to the real life negotiations which are never as smooth or straightforward as the mass media portrays them.
The Artificial Intelligence in 4X games needs to be sharper than in many other strategic subgenres, since the gameplay is more static. Even in Dawn of Andromeda’s case, where you experience all the drama and joys of empire building in real time, you will pause the game often enough or at least play at half the “normal” speed. Many decisions to consider, orders to issue and planning your next move should never be rushed, unless you wish to gamble away your units or survival odds. In the Eras campaigns, the AI cannot be fiddled with, but I found its tweaking options in the sandbox mode to be quite efficient. Playing in an custom galaxy and with the specific factions you desire as your competitors, you can set their behavior to either Expansionist, Survivalist or Diplomatic. It goes without saying that if you wish to play the game at a considerably slower pace, you must set your future AI rivals to a more Diplomatic conduct and you can then research the entire tech tree in Dawn of Andromeda before they’d dare to lift a finger against you, no matter how close you get to their homeland.
Speaking of acquiring new territories, colonial expansion is the bread and butter in this game. Your fleets of space ships can be assigned certain roles, such as mining resource-rich asteroids, surveying anomalies or colonizing other planets. Right from the start, you won’t be able to expand on every single world you set your eyes upon, but with proper research in a few unlockable projects, you may inhabit even the most inhospitable environment if you’re interested in the resources hosted by the planet in question. Trading with the other species you encounter, will be your second most important source of income, after taxation itself. You will need all the credits you can squeeze from your citizens, in order to assemble and maintain an efficient defensive fleet.
I hope the dev team shall add the option of retrofitting the ships with newly researched tech advancements, instead of forcing me to disband units and commission new vessels in their place. Never mind the cost, it’s a time consuming process which could spell disaster during an ongoing conflict. You have full control over all crucial aspects of you space empire. You influence the finances, industry, agriculture, diplomacy, internal policies, military and research efforts. If that doesn’t sound like an easy job, it probably ain’t. But this is a video game and unlike real life, you can always load a previous save file, if you think you screwed up things beyond repair. Ideology also plays an important role and your Council of ministers/governors, needs to be reconciled, lest you invite rebellion or civil war upon your doorstep. You will understand soon enough that democracy is just the compromise you accept out of fear for its alternatives.
Dawn of Andromeda is a real-time 4X strategy title done right. It doesn’t sacrifice well established gameplay mechanics for the sake of “modernity”. It’s streamlined enough to appease new players but at the same time, it doesn’t antagonize the subgenre veterans. If you consider it overpriced, just wait for a bundled offer or better yet, a Steam Sale which is more predictable. In case you’re wondering why even old 4X games are seemingly overpriced, you need to understand that the AI, interface complexity and potential for hundreds of gameplay hours, cannot be offered at the price tag of more simple and repetitive genres. Don’t compare apples to oranges. They are priced accordingly. Even if you’re not a die-hard fan of strategy, Dawn of Andromeda’s tutorial screens will guide you towards the galactic conquest you’ve always dreamed of!

This game is quite significantly improved since my original review.  Ticking the 'camera smoothing' box has corrected the visual problems that I was having.  Improvements to the fleet management UI and other aspects of the user experience mean that I've enjoyed returning to it.

Dawn of Andromeda has a lot going for it, with one very serious drawback: it isn't fun to play.
There are quite a few clever ideas here, but headache-inducing graphical 'features' (having the camera wobble after you've moved it is cute the first time, nauseating the thousandth) and under-developed UI suck the enjoyment out of it.
Theoretically, this is a game much like Stellaris, except that the game mechanics are streamlined, so you can get in and play it quicker, without quite so much fiddling about.  Ultimately, this is a shallower game than Stellaris, where you spend four times as much effort completing routine tasks, and ultimately more time to achieve less.
I really want to enjoy this game, and hope to change my review to a 'recommend' after playing a version that doesn't make me want to throw up (seriously, the camera gets glitchy and induces motion sickness) and doesn't make me want to scream in frustration when all I want to do is order a ship to go to the system where I received a notification.  (Let's not start about 'checking the status of the minor races'.)
Enjoying it very much so far, look forward to updates!

Very basic twin stick shooter with somewhat intriguing concept yet horrible execution to say at least.
The game has one and only play mode. You shoot waves of squares that simply fly around you in order to gain points which you then spend on guns and gun upgrades inbetween the waves. There's an aspect of building the ship. You need to expand the size of your ship for every new gun you want to attach making you bigger target and sacrifice your movement speed in exchange for better firepower. If enemy hits your base section, it's game over. If it hits expanded parts, you lose only the guns attached to that part. This is interesting on paper yet you'll find out right after few games that it's more efficient to just keep your ship small with one gun you continually upgrade.
Concept of buying upgrades and new guns is also very much undermined by the fact all guns are very weak against the enemies so you're basically waiting for power-up so you can kill something.
Visual presentation of this game is at least atrocious. Every graphical part of this game seems what you would expect from very first InDev version of a game. Your ship is square, your enemies are square. Background seems to be squares. These graphics would be low for a flash or a mobile game. Everything feels lazy and undone. This theme is acompanied by visual effects that are beyond annoying. Half of the time you won't even see what's happening on screen. And this is game focused on precision. Imagine playing Counter-Strike with screen going bright white every few sec... oh wait.
The game is sold for a very low price of 2€ yet you won't get any content worth that much. If this was free flash game on a site like Newgrounds or Kongregate, it would still have a low score at best. The one positive thing is soundtrack which is very catchy but artists provided the music are not even credited? Shame. Thumb down.

To give an idea of the gameplay, it is essentially a civilization clone. It is streamlined and dumbed down to be more accessible to new players.
Rather than having a terrain system, each planet comes with it's own perks, making it easier for newcomers to understand the habitation system. The research is presented as a web, which is very easy to understand. The resources are more straightforward. The units are where the game shines, where you are allowed a good amount of customization.
What could be so bad about this game, then?
- With the simplification of the terrain, the replay value died. Every game you play has a pretty similar feel, whereas you could change the settings of a Civ game and have it go completely differently. After a few games, I feel I've seen all the game has to offer.
- With the streamlining of the game, there's not a lot to do. Select options. Expand borders. Sometimes attack. The strategy of the game incorporates no abstract thinking, and you find the key to success is how well you can handle the menus. This is boring.
- As I said, customization of units are the best thing about this game. For the first little while, it's fun checking out all the options a ship has. However, especially since a ship has limited stats, the novelty dies off, and you'll wish for pre-sets.
- Each battle comes with the option to view a cutscene. You'll want to see this cutscene twice, at most. It's long and boring.
This game doesn't do anything that Civ hasn't done better. If you want a similar experience for free, "CivFree" is a pretty similar game. Definitely do not pay $30 for this game that I would bet you would not spend 10 hours on.

I recommend this game for anyone who likes 4X and likes to relax while building up thier galactic civilization for hours on end.

This game is a one of a kind and it's amazing. Don't let other people tell you otherwise. While it has its flaws, it's an absolute marvel to play when you are in the upper tiers where people aren't noobs.
As a tier 1 player with well over 700 hours (I played a lot when it wasn't on Steam), I can give you new players tips.
For starters, this game is not your run of the mill CoD clone ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, nor is it like Battlefield. This is a vehicular mech fighting game, and not the gundam type where everything can dash and sidestep willynilly.
Rather, you control like a tank, as in your torso and legs are seperate. You "Strafe" by lining your torso to the side of your legs. I would recommend getting used to playing with your arms unlocked at all times, it makes no sense to use a slower aim point that is locked arms, there is no benefit to it.
By keeping your arms unlocked, you can be sure that your arm mounted weapons can travel faster/further up and down as well as left and right. Keep in mind some mechs do not have arms, only shoulders which can only go up and down.
In terms of mechanics, this game feels great to be good at. Make sure to look up guides on torso twisting, mech parts tagetting and which weapon dooes what.
Also make sure to look up guides on buying your first mech because you will not always be given cbills for free, your first purchase matter in how you will enjoy the game. Make sure you buy what fits you.
I have not felt any game quite like MWO that drives my enjoyment of working as a team. Play with a friend, it's worth it.
If you ever see anyone say "This game is broken with pay to win♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; you can instantly know they are talking♥♥♥♥♥♥ you cannot buy power in any way whatsoever. You can only be good at the game, that's it.
If you need help with the game, feel free to visit MWO's forums, people will gladly answer your questions.
Have fun and good luck, pilots.

So, I bought this back in Late November 2016, possibly early December, I don't exactly remember. It's February now. So it's been 2-3 months since I've purchased it, I use the controller exclusively for Rocket League. I've put in 107 hours as of right now on Rocket League, 80 of that is probably with the controller. At first it was a little tough getting used to, but I adapted quick, yes it's true, some tinkering is involved to set the controller scheme for each game, which can be a hassle if you are constantly buying new games, but it's definitely worth it if you only want the controller for a few games.
However, the controller has some major flaws. The bumper buttons break incredibly fast. Like I said, I've maybe put a total of 80 hours on the controller. And my back bumpers have been broken since early January, so maybe only 40 hours in. I went online to see if maybe there was an easy solution to this, and I found troves of forums with people havign the exact same problem as me. Apparently the build quality on the controller is not ideal and a number of players were having their back bumpers burn out very quick if used even mildly often. So a lot of the suggestions are to simply bind unimportant functions to the back bumpers so that they are used sparingly so as not to break them. But, this controller only has so many buttons on it, and when you need to have a lot of different functions, this controller will fall short because of the fragility of the back bumpers. I've also noticed that the Letter keys (A,X,Y,B) are also intermittently not working. It's possible I just got a bad controller, but it seems awfully odd for any sort of controller to be breakign down this fast after ~80 hours of gameplay.
If you ask me what I plan to do from here on out... I could either attempt to get it swapped out, or buy a new steam controller. But I have little faith in a new controller not simply havign the same problems. Or I could modify an Xbox controller for PC and set that up instead. Despite the additional work, time, and programs it will take for me to do that, I'm leaning towards that, rather than to deal with this faulty controller for another go round.
The Steam controller is a neat idea, but it is not durable or rugged enough to be a practical solution just yet, I think there might be 2 or 3 more versions they'll come out with before they get all of the kinks out of it. Great idea, but frustrating to deal with these problems so fast.

The game features a number of scenarios on pre-designed maps and custom games in randomized galaxies. Each race has slightly different attributes that may alter the general strategy of each match. The interface is a mess: ship and planet lists are both full-screen, making it entirely too difficult to select and issue orders quickly. In addition, there are too many pop-up notifications (the frequency of which cannot be customized), no main screen indication of idle ships (and the ship list says vessels are idle when in fact they may be colonizing or mining), and auto-exploration of two separate ships is uncoordinated. Step one is to explore the galaxy with scouts, revealing colonizable planets, items that can be surveyed (like in Stellaris!), and mining locations. Planet management is almost entirely automated: simply choose which fields (food, population cap, research, defenses, production) to invest extra cash into, and the stats improve on their own. Characters can be assigned to the council for empire-wide bonuses (like in Stellaris!) or to specific worlds as a governor. Policies can be adapted as well. Technologies, artifacts, and foreigners can be studied (like in Stellaris!) through research, and trade of valuable goods can bring in extra money. Diplomatic options are typical, but features vague feedback on why a deal was not accepted. The AI is passable, but combat is uninteresting once war is declared. Dawn of Andromeda is held back by its woeful interface and features stolen from better games.

Before purchasing this game, I read alot of reviews. alot stated that the game was (despite early access) promising, and yet somewhat hollow.
After some reasonable playthroughs, I can honestly say that DoA is like all those chocolate easter eggs. They are big, appealing and at first taste so so delicious, yet ultimately are finished too soon because guys and girls, and not to state it too on the nose.....hollow.
Whats Good: Graphics, Ambience, interface....the gameplay is intuitive, and it doesnt need you to have played any game before for a novice to pick up the mechanics.
Whats Bad: Absolutely nothing......yet everything....its not enough. its too simplistic....yeah yeah yeah I know micromanagement is the biggest bugbear of all 4x games, yet please allow us some variance in our colonies, a reason for having this or that planet. At the mo all the races seem to like the same habitability, so you ultimatley fight over the same terrain for not much of a variance in the colony. It all blends into a land grab to build up economy and military, and then bash the enemy over the head with your new toys. Oh and speaking of your vast armadas, well there is two ways of doing that; build alot, send and smash...wash, rinse, repeat, or build smart....build a tank or two to micromanage and support with a group of missile boats.....the AI allwyas targets your tanks leaving your boats to obliterate even the toughest of foes......pirates no longer hold a threat.
I give this the thumbs up because of what it could be.....just like Stars in Shadow this has so much potential.....but please, please, please for (insert preferred diety or profanity) give this some depth, nuances, creamy soft caramel filling or at least some M&Ms (US)/Smarties (UK) for use to get our sugar high from. MOO 1&2 gave us starship tag, Homeworld gave us ships we cared about, Sins of Solar empire, gave us real time thrill of battle.......this could be all of this and so so much more without compromising its simple game interface and playstyle.

Disapointed.. The game has all the elements to be a good twinstick shooter, but it's just lacking balance. The game itself is split up into questmode where you have to earn all your perks and guns.. Somewhat of a lazy way of lengthening the game lifetime, instead of actually focusing on the game modes themselves.
Once you've got all the guns and perks, you're all set! ..right? No..
The survival mode is much like the quest mode, in that there's an red thread going through most of the game. Being that there are hives spawning all across the board, and you've got to clear them out, else you'll be swarmed and die..
And the guns are just a major lackluster.. There's so many useless weapons, as in slow as **** to reload, or not a big enough clip.  So what this basically forces you to do is to start whichever level and gamemode you're on, until you get a gun that's decent enough.
But the red thread is impossible to avoid, and it'll catch up to you no matter what. And that's fine! It's just not fine when it happens in a matter of 5-7 mins.. No matter what! The hives constantly pour out more and more mobs, and eventually they overrun your pathetic little person.. and then you die. And this happens over and over again, really not differentiating the way in which you die. You always die of being overrun, about 5-7 mins into a game.
It almost feels like the game is forcing you to play it with 1 to 3 other people, completely killing the singleplayer experience.
So the AI mechanics are disapointing, the weapons are mostly disapointing.. What about the perks then? Surely they are the saving grace? Nope..
The perks are plentiful and very helpful (obviously), but they're as cryptic as hell. They pretty much all have lengthy descriptions and tryhard humor on them, and doesn't really help you get the right upgrade in the heat of battle.. Instead you have to pause, break immersion and ponder WTF this actually does to your character. And a lot of them are just plain stupid, like instantkilling you for a better "score"... Yeah, that's helpful! "Gotta get those points!" :P
All in all, the game isn't horrible, as it's got all the right elements and the right idea.. The execution just doesn't seem that well thought out. It doesn't seem tested enough somehow. It's very short lived and anticlimactic when you've died for the 30th time to the same damn problem.
It just makes me want to play Nation Red instead.. Maybe not a fair comparison as this is an indie dev and all, but that's like saying "don't judge an Early Access game as a complete game". It's in the same genre, so I'm gonna.
So yeah, if you want a real solid twinstick shooter, try Nation Red.. Atleast they got it right and let's you play for more than 5 mins at a time. The game has a lot going for it, but it doesn't seem like it's ever going to change. Can't really recommend it at all, for more than a 3-4 hr fun time-killer. It doens't really have much replayability once you've gotten all the unlocks really.. hard difficulty is fine, but impossible is not. Buy at your own risk.

Human Revolution is a worthy return to one of the best PC franchises of all time. Wearing the fashionable leather jacket of protagonist Adam Jensen is an exceptional opportunity to dive into a not so far future setting, where biotic augmentation has a significant effect on society, entailing both advanteges and disadvanteges. The game itself is an action/stealth/RPG hybrid. Following the clues of the main story arc gets you to different, well built locations, so-called city hubs, where you not only have the chance to undertake interesting side missions, which divert you from the main story for hours, but exploring these areas and inhaling the unrivalled atmosphere plays a huge part in Human Revolution's excellence. The foundation of inner areas and a significant part of your arsenal encourage you to take the silent way, creeping in ventilation shafts, hacking computer terminals for valuable information, and sneaking behind unsuspecting guards to take them out silently. On the other hand the game gives you the opportunity to go ablazing should you choose the less pacific solutions. However, the gunfight and the other game mechanics during open confrontation would require a smoother shaping, not to mention, that Human Revolution rewards the sneaky style with more experience points, which can be spent on different augmentations, making the gameplay and approach alternatives more colorful. Thanks to the more developed Director's Cut the annoying boss fights got a fresh facelift guaranteeing that you have more ways to incapacitate them providing you pay attention to your surroundings. The cherry on top of the cake the fantastic developer commentary: here and there I could listen to the little stories behind different elements of the game and become more invested in the world of Deus Ex. Human Revolution is a highly recommended game to anyone who wants to take their time in a detailed world preferring the silent way.

4X games: my anti-drug... and my anti-sleep, too, I guess. No other genre has the power to keep me going, turn after turn, well past the time that any sane person would have collapsed from sleep deprivation. I grew up on Master of Orion, and I honestly have to say that I enjoy it more than MoO or MoO2. That's mostly due to the convenience improvements that this game has over those older games, plus it just looks beautiful. The "synchronous turn" approach works brilliantly.
Ship combat is a bit of a mixed bag, though. I do miss the turn-based combat of MoO, but I recognize the advantages of the CCG-style approach. Ship combat could get tedious in MoO and often wasn't that compelling, since it didn't require a great deal of strategy. In Endless Space, each battle is over quickly, and battles over star systems can last many turns. This means that each battle could be just a small part of a larger, ongoing conflict that is much more interesting. On the other hand, I'm not a big fan of the weapons system. I honestly don't know why you should pick one weapon type over another, but it just so happens that the weapon type I chose worked pretty well. *shrug*
I could go on with the comparisons to MoO, but most of you probably haven't played it. Basically, this is a really great 4X, empire-building game. I highly recommend you give it a try. It could be a bit daunting at first, though, so I'd recommend starting light with a "throwaway" session, where you just try things to see what happens. You'll pick up most of what you really need to know as you play the game. For everything else, there's google. :)

Bully. It's GTA, but without blood and deadly weapons, and instead of playing as an adult man, you play as Jimmy Hopkins. A 15 year old kid who's aggressive and a fighter, but not truly malicious. He only gives people what they have coming to them.
Bully takes place in Bullworth, a town in New England. Your mom, well, Jimmy's mom, drops you off at Bullworth Academy. A boarding school. The school is full of bullies and corrupt teachers and it's up to you to put a stop to it.
The game's storyline will guide you through six chapters (There are 65 missions, the sixth chapter is an endless free-roam chapter, giving you the chance to complete non-storyline missions and to collect collectables.) Each of them takes place in a different weather season. The missions vary, it's never the same. One time you're cleaning a rat infested library and the next time you're helping a teacher escape from a psychiatric hospital. As Jimmy, your main goal is to bring peace to the school by helping and befriending the four school cliques: the Nerds, the Jocks, the Bullies, the Preppies and the Greasers.
Of course you'll have to go to class. These classes are: English, gym, geography, math (ew), music, shop, art, photography and biology. They are simple mini-games which become noticeably harder every time you attend them and make progress. You'll also have to deal with a time schedule. You can skip class, but you won't get any rewards if you do so and prefects will chase you down and send you back to class if they catch you.
Jimmy, your character, is highly customizable. You can buy clothes, change your hairstyle and more. You can even buy a bike, a go-kart or a scooter if you save up enough cash. Money can be earned by either taking a paper route, doing missions for townies or students or by completing storyline missions.
You've got weapons. No, they are not guns and no you can't kill people. There's a super slingshot, you can use firecrackers, stink bombs, eggs, a bag of marbles, a bottle rocket launcher and so much more. You can also pick up one of the many objects around you (umbrella's, vases, bottles) and use them as a weapon.
Interacting with your fellow students is fun too. You can talk to them, give cute presents, put them in trash bins or lockers, steal their books, take their pictures for the yearbook, punch them in their faces (aka bully them) and if you feel like it you can make out with a girl or a guy.
The game has a very impressive map size. You can explore the entire school, the school grounds, the town, a fully functional theme park, an industrial park and a few more awesome places. There are many collectables scattered around the map too.
Bully may be pretty good, but it's not perfect. The graphics are rather outdated, the sound isn't that amazing, the controls are a bit clunky at first and there are some bugs. But don't worry! It doesn't kill the fun. Bully is an amazing game and there's much to do. And for only $14.99 - £9.99 - €9.99, it's certainly worth it.

This game simply doesn't run on newer computers. And by newer, I mean anything newer than Windows 98. I have no idea how the actual game is because it won't run! But it's probably fun if you can make it work.
EDIT:
Since posting this, I got some info for how to make the game work. Yay!
1. Right click on Desktop
2. Select Screen Resolution (if you do not see screen resolution select Personalize then select Display Settings from the resulting pop-up window)
3. Click Detect or Identify Monitors (with no additional monitor connected)
4. Next to your first display, you'll see a grey square with the text "Another display not detected" Click on the grey square
5. Next to "Multiple displays" it will say "No display detected"
6. Click on "No display detected"
7. A drop-down menu will appear
8. Select "Try to connect anyway on: VGA"
9. Click on your primary display (the square with the big "1" in it)
10. Next to "Multiple displays" select "Duplicate Display"
Hit the “Apply” button and start the game.
If duplicating the display does not work, then try choosing “Extend Display.” Extending the displays can cause windows you open to be “hidden” on the non-existent second monitor, so it isn’t the best option, but it should work to play the game – “duplicate displays” is a better option if available. This change can be reversed once you have finished playing the game.

So, I bought this back in Late November 2016, possibly early December, I don't exactly remember. It's February now. So it's been 2-3 months since I've purchased it, I use the controller exclusively for Rocket League. I've put in 107 hours as of right now on Rocket League, 80 of that is probably with the controller. At first it was a little tough getting used to, but I adapted quick, yes it's true, some tinkering is involved to set the controller scheme for each game, which can be a hassle if you are constantly buying new games, but it's definitely worth it if you only want the controller for a few games.
However, the controller has some major flaws. The bumper buttons break incredibly fast. Like I said, I've maybe put a total of 80 hours on the controller. And my back bumpers have been broken since early January, so maybe only 40 hours in. I went online to see if maybe there was an easy solution to this, and I found troves of forums with people havign the exact same problem as me. Apparently the build quality on the controller is not ideal and a number of players were having their back bumpers burn out very quick if used even mildly often. So a lot of the suggestions are to simply bind unimportant functions to the back bumpers so that they are used sparingly so as not to break them. But, this controller only has so many buttons on it, and when you need to have a lot of different functions, this controller will fall short because of the fragility of the back bumpers. I've also noticed that the Letter keys (A,X,Y,B) are also intermittently not working. It's possible I just got a bad controller, but it seems awfully odd for any sort of controller to be breakign down this fast after ~80 hours of gameplay.
If you ask me what I plan to do from here on out... I could either attempt to get it swapped out, or buy a new steam controller. But I have little faith in a new controller not simply havign the same problems. Or I could modify an Xbox controller for PC and set that up instead. Despite the additional work, time, and programs it will take for me to do that, I'm leaning towards that, rather than to deal with this faulty controller for another go round.
The Steam controller is a neat idea, but it is not durable or rugged enough to be a practical solution just yet, I think there might be 2 or 3 more versions they'll come out with before they get all of the kinks out of it. Great idea, but frustrating to deal with these problems so fast.

I've had my SC since Dec 2015, and it has grown to be my preferred input device for gaming, surpassing mouse/keyboard, the inputs I've grown up with. It is outstanding for FPS titles from Ultimate Doom to Doom 2016, providing similar accuracy of a mouse, with Gyro support for fine tuning. It is just fine for FTL, Tomb Raider, Torchlight 2, Diablo 2, Ori and the Blind Forest, Shovel knight, and other top down/3rd person/2d titles. It's also fine for mouse-centric games such as Baldur's Gate, Pillars of Eternity, Homeworld Remastered, and Civ 5. The number of games I have encountered which the SC does NOT support well are few and far between, and given time, solutions seem to arise (for example, there is a mod for Fallout: New Vegas which simply renames NVSE to F:NV's filename to allow full SC config support AND continue to track achievements).
It took me about a month to grow accustomed to the feel of the SC. It is larger than a 360 pad, and the ABXY buttons are in an unfamiliar place for your thumb if you're used to the 360. It takes a little time to learn how to hold the controller - loosely, not tight, with just the index finger on the triggers, and middle/ring fingers resting on the grips. The gyro will take longer to master, but now I use it for everything, from desktop mouse control to aiming in FPS games and minor mouse movements in FTL (such as band boxing). It is perhaps a little heavier than the 360 pad, but the weight is balanced and even, and it's at most only two ounces heavier (I don't know).
I would recommend this controller to someone who likes controllers but hates joystick aiming, who is willing to config each game, who likes to experiment to find the best control scheme. I'd also recommend it to someone who wants a controller that can control both the desktop, and games, from their couch - and for this it is absolutely perfect.

First off, I'll say that while this isn't a terrible game by any means, there are much better 4X space games out there.
The one thing I like about this game that most other space 4X games don't do is heroes. You can recruit and assign heroes to fleets and star systems and the hero will gain experience and level up and provide various bonuses. The graphics are pretty nice as well and the descriptions and the lore are interesting to read.
Unfortunately for the rest of the game, other games have pulled off the same mechanics in better ways, but even though this is a newer game it did not learn from the games that came before it.
First off, the UI could use some work. Some things are hard to find (and the tutorials don't tell you where everything is so you have to dig around) and some things don't make sense. For example, when a random event happens that generates random anomalies on random planets, it doesn't tell you what planets, you have to manually check all of yours to see.
The tech tree is kind of annoying and illogical at times. You start in the middle and can research technologies in 4 independent trees. The thing is, 3 of them have various forms of shield tech but you have to get halfway up in each tree separately to get to that point even though it seems like a basic shield precursor should lead to all those techs. All of the same factions also share the same tech tree which
Combat is also a boring automatic numbers game. You can customize your ships, but in reality this customization is pretty limited and all that really matters is the final combat rating. There's a poorly named manual mode which isn't actually manual, it just shows a little cinematic of your ships blowing each other up but otherwise works exactly the same way as automatic resolution. Whoever has the most ships and the highest combat rating wins, there's really no tactics involved.
The AI is annoying on any difficulty level. They spam combat ships and will overwhelm beginner players regardless of difficulty, but they're one trick ponies (doesn't matter what civilization) and don't learn from your actions so once you learn how to beat them all the difficulty levels become trivial.
All upgrades are built on the system level and their cost doesn't change regardless of how many planets are actually affected by them, so building an upgrade costs the same in a system with 5 planets vs one planet, yet the system with 5 planets gets a much bigger bonus. This illogical behavior is a cornerstone of the game and makes it difficult for me to enjoy. Each system is also limited to a single production queue regardless of the number of planets.
Overall, I was disappointed with this game and have a hard time recommending it over the other available 4X space games, especially at the asking price.

I do recommend this game for the following type of 4x player.
- Those who do not like to get bogged down with colony management
-Those who enjoy a quicker paced game than say Stellaris which can be quite epic depending on settings and style of play.
-Those who appreciate not being able to blitz through the tech tree and have techs / units that are obsolete before built.
- Those who prefer warp lanes travel and choke points....
I like the minor randomization of tech, and other elements.
Having said the above there are some things that need to be fleshed out to make it better and more re-playable.
Colonization should perhaps be more in depth.  Meaning only habitability rating matters, no distinction is made between oceania, desert, ice, gas etc.  If it is listed as habitable you can colonize.
Ship design needs a little more depth I feel.
In depth is not necessary to be a good game but some level of depth is needed to make it feel more immersive.

The game is early access so I won't fault it for crashing and some of the flaws that the devs seem to be actively fixing.

I've been playing this game since closed alpha -- I had to fill out an application and be accepted to join closed alpha testing. That was early 2012 and this is still by far my most played video game of all time.
You need to know what you are getting into with this so that your expectations are not let down.
There still is no single player campaign
There is no story line
Community warfare is just another game mode with virtually zero additional depth
There is a very steep learning curve. You will have to play for many hours before you are really good. There is a lot to learn, many quirks and intricacies.
If you like the gameplay, though, this game may be for you. There are many different strategies you can take -- various mech classes and roles. For me, the game never gets stale because of the customization and different roles. If I get tired of playing the peek-and-poke strategy with a fast, light, agile mech running 2 large pulse lasers, I can switch to an assault brawler build with short range missiles and a large autocannon and have a completely different play experience. So for me, the game never gets stale, I just keep coming back for more.
So just know going into it that it's almost like a porno -- the plot is just some thin BS, it's really about the action. If you like the action enough, this game wont get old.
Tactical gameplay. Very fun for a free game

What I'm referring to about "Unbalancing" is that P2W kills Casual playing. Yes, money flow keeps games like this alive. However, there is a line. To get certain Mech builds, you MUST spend Money. They are not all readily available via c-bills.
Personally, I don't like paying past the one time purchase fee when I buy a game. But.. It's free O_O so. Making one or two in game purchases(if you see fit) won't be a bad thing. Yes the game has bugs. Name one that doesn't. Wall hackers, rubberbanders, etc etc etc. Welcome to Online Gameplay.
If you do want to spend money, i would suggest at, or at least Half the MSRP of a Brand New game. If you buy anything 30$ or under, buy the Steam LIGHT Mechpack. You get two variants that have a perm +30% to cbills, and 30 days premium time which is a flat 50% increase to xp and xbills across all variants. Plus, it's a good idea to master Light Mech fighting. Because for me, it's actually the hardest weight class. Easy for you? Bam. Money.
If you buy MC for Mechs, don't spend them on anything else except premium time. As PT = $$$ and you need that to buy variants to unlock the Elite Skill Tree and Mech Modules. Everything else is really obtainable with Cbills.. except Mech Bays. They have random events where you can unlock them. Or you can purchase them in game.
AVOID QUICKPLAY. If you are serious about Team Play Join a faction as a merc or a loyalist. Get a team so you can coordinate. If you don't team play, You will get slaughtered.
Don't have a Mic/Headset? Don't wanna blow 30-40$ on a Headset? Teamspeak is VERY cheap on the Google Play and Apple App Stores. You can use your phone's headset(which have noise cancel on most) and/or bluetooth and set it to voice activate after a certain range level is met.

I've given this game a fair 30+ hours of playtime so I should be able to make a relatively good base of a review on it.
First and foremost, its not a bad game .  Don't let the Thumbs down actually deter people from actually purchasing the game.  I've done literally everything you can in game in regards to building what's currently available across two single player servers.
The Pro's of the game
* At the start, it is relatively slow to get yourself on your feet.  It took me around 2 realtime days to actually get some sort of broken battery power initiated to actually make any real progress.  Once you get a thermal generator up its smooth sailing for the most part.
* You can make a fair few nice designs for base building.  The map can be varied to small, medium and big so you can get a lot of room to go places or keep the area small and managable.
* The cross-server option is nice.  You make a fake world to mine resources and clear-cut the map to then bring over to your homeworld map (like Savage Lands where you can make a resource map - delete when cleared).
* I do see a lot of potential if the game continues to go in this developing direction.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Now the Cons - and sadly there's a lot more in these than the Pro's
----------------------------------------------------------------------
* Firstly, having aliens popping up ONLY at night (nearly always three and they randomly spawn whever they like) and die in three hits are tedious.  Technically any sort of barrier or even uneven surface they get stuck on and run at you where you can easily just kill them off.  They need a huge improvement with AI and spawning options.
* A lot of the things you can build need to actually be operational and useful.   Currently, things like the Greenhouse, Filler and one or two other items constructed serve utterly no purpose.  They have not been scripted and are currently a construction waste of time as they do absolutely nothing at all.    These need to serve some sort of purpose.
* My biggest headache - and a lot of the community agree - is that there is absolutely NO tooltips on items to be constructed.  I understand what machine (for example) does what by building and use it. (or I've had to refer to the discussions thread with other people asking those same questions).  The items are listed, it tells you what materials are needed to craft, however there's no description AT ALL as to what their purpose is.
* The food side of things.  I am so fed up with just banana trees, oranges and lemons.  That's all I've found on EVERY world I've created and I've make hundreds of servers with different ratios for the resources sides.  but things like the Apple Trees, vegetables of ANY sort, etc etc... none of them exist.  I've never found any at all and really, I've solely been relying on oranges for the most part as a food source.  They decay in hand way too fast and the Freezer only slows it, so there's no real storage to keep them fresh.
* Stuff needs to be described in regards to placement of structures.  I slapped down about 1500 blocks to be able to place the air transport factory as when I tried to place it on the map as its partially hilly, half of it was in a mountain or half underwater so I made a platform large enough (as its f'cking huge!) to place it on.  Total waste of time as it did not place on a flat structure.  This needs to be a possible option.  The Transport Factory has no problem being on a platform so why one and not the other?
* Stuff like fishing, hunting that sort of thing would be good in game.  However, its currently not.. its a 3x tree farming simulator.
* Some items are categorically useless.  The campfire purifies water 1x2 for the bottles.  When you upgrade to a Distiller, its 1x1, the process is a little slower, but you don't lose one bottle to every two.   Then there's the Chem Lab.  All its DOES is purify water and that's pretty much it.  Its the fastest of the three but what's the point of the middle man really?
* Lastly, one other thing that has me a little concerned regarding the game that I read on Forum, I was trying to figure out the use of the Filler machine.  I have a vague idea but as its not doing what its supposed to do, I can't do anything with it.  I'm certain though that someone asked a question in regard to the Filler and the developer responded something like "What is a Filler?"
This actually concerns me as he was the one who put the object in and he himself doesn't know?   Two thirds of the forums are literally nothing but conversations in Russian which makes us english speaking only population at a loss unless we get a broken google translation decipher.   So it does raise my concerns regarding how "user friendly" its going to be.
Please note, the main picture is of Space.  So Far I've found nothing that leads me into space and I'm not even certain if the games even developed that far.  The main picture on the Store page with the picture of Jupiter and one of its four main moons Europa.. that's the night sky spashscreen you see every night on your little chunk of island.  The bigger map may have fragments off shore, but it looks like there's no other islands off where you start.  I swam/walked for a solid 2 hours and saw nothing but ocean.  So I'm assuming its only the land you start on being the map itself.
Personally I would wait to see how the game develops.  Its been enjoyable so far just to build bases and try and get some sort of power grid going.  Other than that, there's really nothing else to do.  So I'd suggest holding your money until it develops further.

So, after tinkering around with this game for a short while, I've got an idea of this game. The graphics are pretty shoddy and look kinda off when you move, but they work (for the most part, anyway, determining what layer a block is on is tricky and overhangs just vanish when you're under them). The music is honestly quite enjoyable, but nothing fantastic.
Gameplay is simple, but effective: both combat and building have little to them but still satisfied me nonetheless. The menus do their job, but aren't special and don't really look pretty. The NPCs have nice designs (and the ones that speak are often humorous) but enemy AI is incredibly simple and similar.
I can't really comment on the MMO aspect, as I prefer playing solo. But for an MMO, I enjoyed my time alone, which is generally a good sign. I've heard complaints of being only playable if you shovel money into it, but I honestly didn't feel that way at all. Overall, the game is lacking. However, there are three factors that stop me from not reccomending this:
1) The game is in early access. The biggest problems I have with this game (namely, the artwork and the simplicity) can be very easily fixed with future updates.
2) There's just a certain...CHARM the game has. With it's designs and it's dialogue and it's style...there's just something about this game that I love, even if it isn't that great on closer examination.
3) The game is free. There is really nothing stopping you from at least trying it out and making a decision.
TL;DR: The game is simple and somewhat lazy, but charming and free.
