This game has a lot going for it...but not enough.
Lets start with the positives:
I love the updated graphics, the new perks, the more streamlined leveling system, the ability to have four players at once, and many other details about this reboot of the classic crimsonland. Killing enemies is as fun as ever and almost every weapon is great and feels good for different situations (except you blowtorch!) and has a legitimate strategy. Perks are incredibly important and add a deep aspect of thought to the game (Do I get regeneration to keep my health up or choose fast reloader so I can kill enemies more?) and the sheer addictive nature of the gameplay will keep you hooked. Its a solid title...or should be...
Which leads me to the negatives:
Outside of the story mode this game isn't really as fun as it used to be. They took out a lot of things that made it fun. In solo survival the average player can expect to get to level 8-9 if they get a decent weapon before being absolutely annihilated by the hordes of enemies. If you add friends to the mix the difficulty ramps up even more and you will be lucky if you clear level 6. Its almost a broken level of hard. Theres no fighting it. No matter which perks you pick or which weapons you have the survival mode reaches a certain point early on that just immediately kills you.
Your choices feel useless and it becomes kind of a drag when you get the perfect weapon combo with the perfect perks and then you just get slaughtered anyways by the sudden wave of splitting spiders and zombie lords that surround you out of thin air instead of coming out of the sides of the screen like they used to. The previous version of crimsonland slowly spiked the difficulty more and more making the survival last longer. It really felt like you were, you know, surviving?
This version of crimsonland has no such subtlety or flair. They let you gain a couple levels and then just murder you outright with a frustrating amount of enemies that are impossible to fight. Let me put it to you this way. I was the 3rd highest ranking player IN THE WORLD in the previous crimsonland but in this one I can barely top level 10 in solo survival. They have taken one of the greatest and most fun modes of the game and just smashed it and made it unplayable. If they had a difficulty choice I think it could mitigate this. This is the only game I think actually NEEDS an easy mode.
Another thing that is absolutely broken in this game is the enemy spawning system. In the previous crimsonland enemies came out of all 4 sides of the screen giving you a chance to plan ahead. You could see a horde of zombies and decide which way you want to bait them to try and get an opening to dive for that powerup or weapon. You can find the big monster that is spawning little ones and put that sucker down before he overwhelms you.
This crimsonland has destroyed that too. It is quite common now to have enemies spawn on top of you and immediately kill you. Nothing sucks worse than to be 10 minutes into a boss battle and to be killed by a horde of tiny red aliens spawning right on top of you. Or to be doing a survival round with your favorite weapon and perks and to have a lizard king spawn right next to you and one shot you instantly. Its painfully frustrating and can make you want to chuck your keyboard across the room. It has happened to me in almost every mission of this game and is the most common way to die. Some enemies still come out of the sides of the screen, but more than half of them just appear with a flash wherever they feel like regardless of how inconvient it is for you.
So in conclusion, the game is fun but ultimately frustrating and not worth your money. They could have had a solid remake of a fun arcade shooter on their hands but they've instead destroyed it by breaking the difficulty and spawning and made it virtually unplayable. If you do buy this game, you'll discover its fun palls rather quickly because of its major stumbling blocks. It is a shadow of its former self and if you want to play a fun arcade shooter, download the first one online someplace (a few places host it for free) and have yourself a grand old time.
But skip this version. Its just not fun anymore.

I should start with a couple of things:
1) I do recommend this game. But it's not a very strong recommendation.
2) My decision to purchase was largely nostalgia-driven.
Those two caveats disclosed, my review is relatively simple. This is a fun top-down shooter that is a bit stuck in the past. It's a game that for me, back in 2003, was a pretty big deal for something that today would fall into a much more competitive indie genre. The basic premise is: you're a guy, you run around in circles, you shoot things and they bleed. Eventually you're going to die, but along the way you can level up to gain perks which propels the arcadey gameplay.
The game is effectively untouched except in superficial, and relatively inconsequential ways. It really needs much more than that to be anything but a game people like me are willing to purchase because they have fond memories of playing. You can use modern resolutions now! The UI is updated (but it's bland)! But that's about it. Effectively, this is a PC game from 2003 ported to a PC platform of 2014.
The gameplay is still fun. But the asking price, and the lack of change and balance to the game over the course of a decade is unlikely to bring in much of an audience beyond people who played Crimsonland prior to its launch on Steam.
I wanted very much to see some new game modes, some new weapons, some new perks, some new something. But really, I have the same game on a new computer with a new UI. Pretty unimpressive.
On sale, this game is worth the time and money I think. Though it's very hard to make the case for something old that isn't doing much to take advantage of a huge sea change in what a game can be, and what the PC platform is able to do. I was happy to buy the game hoping against hope that maybe some additional content will be added, or Steam Workshop integration will come along. Though I doubt that is likely, and I doubt you'll feel as nicely as I do about this game, I think you can still have a good weekend's worth of fun if you give it a shot.
If you like top-down survival shooters, then you must buy this one.

My Problem With The Game:
So far I've enjoyed the game quite well, so why would I not recommend this game? How Ram intensive it is. I know you might be saying "If you don"t run the recommened you should not be playing the game", but currently the recommened ram is 8 GB, and I'm using 16 GB ram and yet it still caps it off. Ram build really heavy into late game, and any saves you had in the game render your game unplayable if the game crashes, because unless you play again with a beefy ram of 32 GB, it still won't work. So far both time I've gotten to end game my run is cut short due to Ram contraints. I've tried lowering the graphics (lol), but that's not where the ram usage comes from. I have a hard time figuring out anyone running the recommended to could finish a playthrough, much less the "minimum". All I have to say is that the game at this point is unplayable for me, even after the update today that was supposed to mend the Ram crashes people have been having..
Game In General:
As for the game concept, I absolutely love it. All elements of the game seemed well thought out and polished (except trading, I found it completely useless and diplomatic A.I). I'm sure this game will eventually be a title to challenge all the other 4x's, Hell I'd even argue that it's one of the best out there. Ingame mechanics all seem useful, and none seem forced into gameplay. The only real thing I can see myself complaining about is how useless the tech tree is. If you really wanted to you don't need to research anything to win the game, or if you do research it's not really going to massively affect gameplay (outside of how much other dudes are willing to pay for it). The game is also really friendly right now for new players, as alot of the mechanics are not too complicated though I can see why many would say the game looks too superficial.
Specific Things:
Now there's a few games I still have to do before I can say how worth it it is. I'VE NEVER COMPLETED THE GAME, as I said in my personal problem with the game bit. I've never been able to recover the body or scavenge any of those guardian things or beasts, it always says for me that It was too messed up to scavenge. I've never found out the fossils (not for lack of trying, after researching I find nothing) and I've never researched all of the tech tree. I've only played up until the first glitch patch of the game. If the game could run on my computer I would say the price tag is fair, but it can't. Overall at THIS STAGE OF THE GAME I would give it a 8/10 considering you can run it.

I only played about 2 hours, but for what it's worth, here is my opinion on the content I had time to approach. So keep in mind I don't know about endgame or grouped gameplay.
NB : I played a closed alpha years ago, and I left the game witout regret. When I've been told about "Skyforge" lately I didn't even notice I already played it, ah.
The first contact is about mapping keys. Some are locked by default, which already got on my nerves, but ok, let's pass on this. Then there is the graphic part, and for what i've witnessed in the trailer, I expected the game to run quite smoothly on my 560, just like TERA. And surprisingly enough, I got huge frame drops while it looked terrible, even on maximum details. So, be warned, the optimization is nowhere to be found, and honestly, I wouldn't bother buying a $$$ rig for such poor visuals. The engine is old and badly hardcoded.
Now the gameplay. Well, nothing stunning really, same ol' stupid m1 smashin with abilities doing almost all the same. The combo system is nice tho (I rarely play mmo's, so maybe i'm being too kind), but I felt the fights were way too easy and boring to be appealing. And what about the useless and ridiculous Dash system? I don't remember having used such short dash in any game ever. Even Lara Croft can do better than that nowadays. Having players to just smash the mouse like returds is unrespectful from a dev. Now perhaps the game is aiming for a casual player base, thus making any sense of progression inexistent. And so are the fights feedbacks. It's simply not satisfying to hit/kill anything because they either vanish, either drop on place. I wish the physic engine was a bit more interactive to give more impact in combat, but it's just bland instead.
Talking bland thing, did I mention the uninsteresting story? Okay, mmo's are garbage at story telling, but this one is way further than others. Playing Zelda BotW is sure not helping my opinion, but I remember FF XIV was fairly correct in the that matter. Skyforge is just sounding like a "mmo maker toolkit" you can grab for 9 bucks...
Now I didn't spent much time in the menus, but the little time I had in the interface was reminding me why I dislike most mmos. Too many tabs, menus, "interactions". Has no mmo rpg's ceo heard of the sentence "less is more"? Still, I don't think it's an important thing in the genre. We'd know if mmo had brilliant UI anyway...
All-in-all, I found Skyforge very generic to be honest, and badly boring on top of it. Bad art, bad feeling, bad "universe", bad optimization, and I read here and there it is p2w like most of
products. And if you are to tell me "you shoulda play further in order to enjoy it", I'd answer : it's the proper goal of a studio to make you like a game right away, if they screwed it in the first hour, then they are probly bad at doing games. I think it's cancer to think one can like a game only in the long run. This is an incredibly misleading game. By looking at the title, Deus Shrex, I thought it was going to be a sequel, or a reboot of the famous game of 1958 called Shrek Simulator 1958. It was quite okay and you had to defend your swamp from a guy called "Player 1" and always lost despite him not doing anything. This new game doesn't deliver expectations, but still turns out pretty awesome.
So naturally you start off playing a guy called Adam Jensen, who doesn't seem like an ogre at all. All of your beloved characters are gone in favour of other non-ogre looking non-beloved characters. You also start somewhere that could have been your swamp if not for all of these towers, industrial buildings and cars and cops and I guess it could have never been your swamp in fact.
Next thing you know you're forced to defend your non-swamp base or home or whatever from evil non-beloved non-ogre characters using highly violent ways like pressing a trigger on an automatic combat rifle to make bullets go rocketing towards your enemies destroying their vital internal organs. Now I know why they abandoned the Shrek concept.
And that sets off a chain of events and sends your non-Shrek character on a globe-trotting adventure, where you continue to defeat enemies using loud and powerful weapons, beat-ups or by bypassing them entirely. This is sure not something I'd want in a Shrek game.
And to add to all of that you can upgrade your non-ogre non-layered character in lots of different ways giving him abilities that all ogres have natively, so he might as well have been an ogre.
Uh so I guess you should not come here for a Shrek Simulator, but rather for a sequel of the game Deus Ex which is a totally different thing, I  don't know why they didn't call it that.

This is an excellent niche game that targets people who enjoy building things, taking them apart, learning about their functionality, and guns.
You will not enjoy this game if you do not have a mechanical mind that takes large amounts of enjoyment from deep exploration of different devices. You must be the type of person that enjoys ripping things apart, and putting them back together repeatedly until you can probably do it in your sleep. Even if you enjoy guns themselves, it may not be enough - you have to actually enjoy the mechanical side of the weapons you love so dearly.
That being said, if you DO fall into that camp, this game will blow you away. It's hyper-realistic, and nails every little detail with extraordinary accuracy. It is easy to use, and names every single part. If you're like me, you can definitely Google search everything you find in this game, and with a bit of invested time you could become quite knowledgeable about guns in general, and a lot of specific weapons.
A lot of people are claiming it is 'Pay To Play', but it really is not. The people calling this out are not what I described above, and are operating under the assumption that you can do a few runs with the gun you're currently working, and you should be able to buy another right away. This is not the case. Remember how I said you have to actually LIKE taking apart the same thing over and over again? That's because you may have to take apart the same guns dozens of times, doing it different ways each time to get achievements and high scores (or even the exact same way, in some cases, as practice for the challenges), before you can afford to buy another weapon. Ideally, you would work the same weapon continually until you have all the achieves (which is like saying 'I know every piece of this weapon by heart') before moving forward.
The purpose of this game, I feel, is to actually teach a bit about the weapons you work with. The only way you can learn something is through repetition. There's no shame in getting some compensation out of this, anyways.
I personally have bought two new guns (beyond the two starters you begin with) at the time of this writing: the Beretta 92 and HKMP5. That's with about 3 hours of play. Pretty decent, especially if you consider I was taking my time to enjoy the mechanics of the game, and I had to take frequent breaks to pay attention to my 2 year old daughter.
So while I don't believe it is 'Pay To Play / Pay To Win', you will have to put a little work into the game to get through more than a couple guns.
I hope you can enjoy this game like myself!

This is the first review I have written and it's because I feel compelled to write one for this product. As a console gamer since 1997 I have always loved the game pad, from ps1 up to ps4/ xbox one, a controller felt so natural and I was able to sit back in my chair and game on the TV. Last November I made the jump to PC and as much as I love it, I game on the TV so it was either get a razer turret or lapdog... all which cost a rather large amount, no thanks. So I see this steam controller, and look at it and think what the hell is this? To briefly sum it up, it's basically a dualshock 4, an xbox one controller and a Wii mote all in one, It looks as radical as an n64 controller in a market full of generic gamepads, you see only one thumbsticks and 2 track pads, what is this thing? Out of curiosity and as a potential resolution to my initial problem I bought it, unboxed it and stared dumbfoundedly at it, how on earth do you use this? Now unfortunately it was at this point that the dualshock 4 beta had literally come onto steam the day I bought this, so I packed the steam controller back into the box for the foreseeable future. It was only a few days ago I looked over and saw the box and thought, I really need to give this a go, not only had I spent money on it, but I could see its potential waiting to be unlocked. So me being me I have a gander on YouTube to see what I can uncover about this and I stumble across a channel by existentialegg who I must say has done great videos showing what the controller is capable of, so I highly recommend people who are debating on buying this to definitely check out his steam controller videos! Anyway the controller came out of the box and I must say I love it, I play war thunder a lot and one of the things I love is the finesse of the gyroscope for aiming in the controller, it's really amazing! And the customisation of the controls too! Honestly if you're on the fence about this, take the plunge, this is without a doubt the best controller available, yes it will take time to get used to because it's so different as steam has reinvented the controller, and credit where credits due, they've done a damn good job. Thanks valve!

I own both Endless Legend and Endless Space and they both suffer from the same basic problems ... it's like the developers haven't played 4x games in the past 15 years. They're missing key features that have become key in modern times. No hotkey binding? Come on. Management screens are devoid of crucial information. I still can't seem to find where it shows how much you're paying on maintenance for your fleets. There's a published formula but why can't I see it at a glance?
That said, the game is very pretty. The artwork is beautifully done. The gameplay is pretty good, though the AI sucks (which seems to be a consistent theme with this developer ... Endless Legend AI sucks too.) It's playable even on older computers and the storyline is engrossing. The default races are wonderfully done. The technology tree has had a lot of thought put into it and is fascinating just to read through if you're a fan of science fiction.
In short, the game is worth playing (especially if you can pick it up on a sale) but it's not as good as even Space Empires IV in terms of a strategic/tactical 4x. I would call it "strategy-lite" in many ways and I don't expect it to have a lot of replayability once I've seen all the events, heroes, and story.

Design a race, define your universe, design your ships, choose your research, expand across the galaxy, and make war. Move fleets of ships from system to system engaging in three phase battles. A remarkable game.

I have HUNDREDS of hours before this came to steam, so dont look at my hours on record.  This is one of the best most overlooked RTS games every to come out. it is VASTLY superior to the socalled KohanII.
The RTS game has simplistic city management, where you have 'cities on the map' that have slots for buildings that you build, but you do not have to micromanage where they go etc... they are 'in the city' they give you benefits like being able to recruit better units or resources, etc.
Resource management is also unique, although it is technically divided up into Wood, Stones, Iron, and Magic Khaldunite, each have a monetary value and will be imported when they are lacking.  so gold is the only real 'resource'.  It updates per second, based on your income.  If you want to build spearmen troops, each unit squad within the unit will take one of the wood for example, so if you have 5 wood produced, you cn make a 5 spearman unit with no penalty, if you make 6 in there, then it will cost you some of your gold income every second to 'supply' the extra wood, etc.
Comabt is also EXCELLENT, the units each can take damage, but also have a unit morale.  Once their zone of control overlapps an enemy unit, they will engage, sending frontline units up while rear units will bring up the rear with raged attacks of possible or charge in secondly if not.  The only order you can give it when to retreat and where to retreat to (or to rout, where they flee willy nilly) if they get broken morale, they will flee without the order.  you have to return them to friendly supply zones for them to restore their combat effectiveness.  Terrain matters, formations matter, Defensive outposts can provide extra garrison and supply zones... special squads can be added to units to change how they fight...
The single player campaign is honestly mediocre, but the multiplayer and battles in this game are still some of the best I've ever played and that's over 12 years since it's been released.
I can't recommend this enough.

Honestly, I'm not completely sure why people are calling this game an abandoned project. Sure, the devs may have quit periodically updating the game, but to be honest, there arren't really any updates needed. This game was good-to-go the second it hit the market. So if you complete something and then not change it, are you really abandoning it? (I'm not meaning to get deep there. :p)
As far as servers go, don't think for a second that that there are none. There are LOADS! On top of that, there are different types of servers for every gamemode. You have your Official Servers and your Community Servers. The Officials are pretty straight forward, they're what you'd expect an Official Server to be like. The Community Servers on the other hand are a whole nother story. Some are normal, but others have crazy modifications, like free vehicles, and Orbital Strikes that only cost 1 Credit (You get about 2-500 per kill).
Not that it needs to be said, because it should be painfully obvious to anybody even looking at the previews for it, but this game is amazing. On top of that, IT'S FREE!!! I don't see how anybody can complain about a game that is this beautifull and free.
If you download this game, I promise, it will slowly begin to consume all of your online life. The adrenaline rush you get in your body as you take the enemy flag while you're flying at 300 km/h is shocking. You'll simply feel your heartbeat in every part of your body. That feeling alone should be enought to make anybody get this game.
Even though I only have about 70-80 hours in on this game, they have been the best hours of any game I've ever played. If I had to give an example of a similar game, it would be a combination of Halo (I know, this doesn't come close, but just the look of it reminds me of Reach), and Call of Duty (Yuck) or Battlefield (Better). The shear fast pacing in this game will make anybody want to play it for hours on end.
Thanks for reading, and I really hope you at least TRY the game. I mean, it's free. If you don't like it, just delete it. At least all your friends that will still be playing it can't say you didn't try it.

I lost my interest in WoTM because of the very broken artillary mechanic (and yes, I used the Arty as well, and found it quite broken, although they claimed to have changed it but I am skeptical), and when I was watching videos on WoTB, it had no arty in it what-so-ever, and I desided to try it out, and I found it to be quite fun, and I have been playing it non-stop ever sense.
PROS:
Smaller matches compaired to WoTM means quicker grinding for tank lines, and sometimes comical more chaotic battles.
New Equipment System: Many players will disagree with my statements (and that is fine), and yes, although the old equipment system was very good, the new one is even better in my eyes. And I will say, at first, I absolutly hated it. The new system allows players to mount 9 different equipment types on there tanks, and all it takes is some grinding for "Spare Parts". Many players think the old one is better, most likely because all the needed to do was grind IGC (in game credits), but it only allowed us to mount 3 equipment types total, and some classes of tank, such as tier 5 tanks, wouldn't even get to mount certain equipments because they were too low tiered, namely the Gun Stabilizer, which in the old system could only be mounted in tier 8+ tanks, and now can be mounted on almost any tier.
Tons of tanks to choose that fit most playstyles:
There are tons of tanks in here, just like WoTM, bar Arty. If you want quick, zippy, deadly tanks, go down light tank paths. If you want a balance of power, go for medium tanks. If you like to camp in bushes and torture your victims, go for Tank Destoryers, and if you like to sit an laugh at people trying to hit your armor, go for heavy tanks. And as the game is still improving just like WoTM, more tanks are in the future.
Good graphics and gameplay - nothing much to say, although they are not as HD as WoTM, for low-to-medium-end systems (somewhat like mine) they are perfect, but I am not into games for fancy graphics, I play for gameplay.
Cash grinding is quicker do to smaller matches.
Cons:
Smaller matches compaired to WoTM. Although it has it's perks, if you come from WoTM, you might have some withdrawls from the old 15v15 and have to deal with the 7 v 7.
Spare Parts System: Although the new equipment system is good, I will say that the Spare Parts system is somewhat flawed. We should at least earn 1000 spare parts for a victory and maybe 250 for a loss. I've only won about 300 for a victory. This makes getting equipment quite slow and somewhat annoying. The only way to get more than 1k spare parts is to complete missions, but these reset only every 12-24 hours (forgot which lol) To be honest people, the new equipment system really is awesome, but the amount we win spare parts at is too slow for it to be truely effective) - Update 3.10 claims to add new ways to earn more parts per battle.
Overpowered tanks:
Although a somewhat realistic feature (example, a Tiger II in real life would blow away a Sherman no problem), many tanks in here are too powerful for what they are. Some notable tanks are the Leopard Light Tank of tier 5, KV-2 of tier 6, LTTB of tier 7 to name a few. What makes them flawed is the raw damage output they can deal, the Leopard only had 2 varients built in real life, so not much is known about it. The KV-2 in game can 1 shot anything at tier 6 and below when using the 152mm gun, however in real life, this thing couldn't even turn it's turret when it was on a hill. LTTB reportedly broke it's suspention when traveling over rough turrain. The LTTB is also a light tank, and it moves as quick as many light tanks of lesser weight and armor, yet it has 90mm of hull armor. I don't think it should be moving that fast (perhaps why it failed in real life) However, these tanks are luckily not without flaws. Leopard has a long clip reload and poor armor. KV-2 has an insanely long reload (upwords of 20+ seconds), and the LTTB is quite large for a light tank and can be easily shot.
There is also somewhat of a "Russian Bias" with this game, and many of the Russian tanks are quite overpowered, and seemingly the German tanks are underpowered (even though a real scenario would have the German tanks with the upper hand, depending on the crew, with a few exeptions on tanks) - luckily this bias isn't as great as it is in some games though. And yes, I am parcial to German tanks, but I also use British, American, and Russian, so this is from personal experience.
The new "Millitary Honor" system:
Absolute **** in my eyes. I've been having some stability issues with my computer, so sometimes my computer will crash during game play, and I don't exactly have the cash to buy an entire new rig (luckily I might know the problem and am fixing it) but because of  this new "Millitary Honor" system, you're "honor" stars go down because random players think you're botting, or AFKing when you could have issues like I am experiencing. In my eyes, this system needs a major reworking or removal.
And my final and main issue with the game: NO THREE MAN PLATOONS LIKE NORMAL WOTM - I understand that 7 v 7 might be difficult to have 3 man platoons, but we need something cause 2 man platoons is just too small. All I can really say about that. - honestly we should start a petition on WoTB for 3 man platoons for those that agree with this.
Another thing for new players is DON'T JUDGE THE GAME UNTIL YOU'RE AT LEAST AT TIER 5, AND THIS GOES FOR WOTM AS WELL. I've seen too many people quit because they don't invest the time into learning this game. It's not just "point and click and get a kill" (unless you're an old arty or KV-2, then it sometime is). There is tons of mechanics in the game for armor, a skill called "sidescraping", and many other things that will help you survive in battle. Learn you tank too. A Panzer IV will have a completely different playstyle than a T1 Heavy or KV-1 (these are all tier 5s too, so not compairng two diffrent tiers). Use youtube for education and training, and you might enjoy this game more.
Note: These are all my opinions, ignore misspellings, etc.
And that concludes this long winded review.

I think this is an excellent game, if you accept it for what it is. I've played most of the big MMO's over the years, and I recently played WoW's Legion expansion, which I thought was excellent; however I am so done with the AP grind that I am not even bothering to earn flying. And the crafting was changed to the point where it's not fun for a casual player like me. I also played ESO recently, and while it's an excellent game, it requires a lot of time and daily busywork (such as upgrading your mount's stats, crafting writs, learning styles/patterns etc) and I just do not have the time or patience that these games require of me, at this point in my adult life.
Skyforge is much more of a casual experience. Like others have said, it's lobby-based, with instanced missions that you can run solo or with groups of up to 3 players. Each region has one or two "open world" areas where you will be running around with other players, and these maps remind me of Guild Wars 2, in that there are quests and objectives scattered everywhere, and you find them by exploring the map. Tagging mobs does not appear to be an issue, at least as far as bosses go. I've jumped in to defeat quest bosses with other players and it's a quick and easy way to finish a questline. The level designs are excellent: maps are detailed and look really nice. Quest text and dialogue are pretty much as bad as everyone says, but not so bad as to ruin the experience.
Combat is a lot of fun, it reminds me of Blade and Soul, but for some reason Skyforge combat is much easier for me to manage. Some classes are combo-based and some are not. Some have "forms" or stances that switch up your available skills. Class design is really quite well done, and it's something I rarely see mentioned. If you want super complexity you can play Monk or Slayer; if you want something easier you can play Cryomancer or Outlaw. I honestly don't think the devs get enough credit for the things the game does well, and class design is one of those elements.
Since everyone can easily unlock every class on the PC version, the pay-to-win arguments usually center on the daily resets of the temples and other buildings that directly tie into your character's power level. I don't know, for me this is just not an issue. You can contribute resources to these buildings and eventually, they reach a point where you can only contribute 3 times per day, unless you reset them with a cash shop item. I don't see this being a problem unless you NEED to keep building up, and you just can't wait for the daily reset. I do my three daily contributions and that's it, I just wait for the daily reset. I'm in no hurry. You can also unlock bag slots for in-game credits and you earn enough of those to unlock a few slots every day, so storage has not been a problem for me. I am taking my time and clearing all of the maps, I'm not in a hurry to reach end game because I know that "end game" is probably where I will hit a wall, and be unable to progress without a pantheon (guild).
So if you don't go in expecting the second coming of WoW, I think there's a lot of fun to be had with Skyforge. It looks great and plays really well, and is a very good casual option to get your MMO fix.

The core game is executed nicely and they have added quality of life designs, such as being able to manage through your planets on one screen.

I've been playing Crimsonland pretty much since its original release, and it was a total time killer at the time. Obviously, I was quite hyped when I heard about the updated version on Steam. And I have to say that I am quite disappointed with it.
The HD graphics are just... meh. Sure, it is in high resolution, and new level backgrounds look nice, but everything else looks like garbage from year 2000. Really, the old version just had better overall design. The new monster graphics are ugly, the weapon icons are beyond any recognition, and the new UI is not just ugly, but it is also less usable. It is virtually impossible to determine how much of your Shield is left when surrounded by enemies, and it is also very hard to determine the exact time left in reloading (why not just leave the clear and accurate "clock" from the old version?).
The game is now released on many platforms. Usually, there is nothing wrong with that, but for Crimsonland it meant that some content was removed because it was unusable on consoles. I really miss the Typ'o'Shooter mode, and some perks like Pyrokinetic and Evil Eyes.
Speaking of perks: the new Telekinetic is just garbage. Instead of allowing you to hover the crosshair over the powerup and wait for a few seconds, ALL powerups are now gravitated towards you even when you really don't need that. Ever wanted to lose the game because a mysterious force made you pick up the Blowtorch? Well, now you can. Say thanks for consoles for one more butchered PC game.
I was also really disappointed by having perks disabled in Quests mode by default. Sure, one can say it is more challenging that way, but I've always perceived Quests as an extended tutorial for Survival mode, where player unlocks the perks and tries them out. Without the perks, the difficulty becomes just absurd on Grim, and the luck factor starts to account on your success way more that your skill. Why not just make an achievement for finishing the game without the perks? I believe that'd have been the best of both worlds for both hardcore and usual gamers.
Some quite significant changes to the game balance were also made. And while I appreciate the new way Fire Bullets powerup works, I will never understand why rockets weapons are THAT powerful now, and why the almighty Splitter Gun is reduced to a useless garbage when compared to the old one. Still, the balance is better than it was in general, I think.
I really dislike new Survival mode. You can barely get 6-9 levels if you are really good (and lucky), and that really limits your chances of survival. The game session is also much shorter now, as monsters gain power and health much quicker than before. I miss the old epic 1+ hour battles.
Online highscores are implemented really well and provide a lot of additional info that helps to identify cheaters.
In conclusion, Crimsonland is still a fun game. Not as fun as the old version for me, but if you are new to Crimsonland - just wait for the sale and go grab it.

Awesome space 4X game with some interesting new ideas to the 4X genre. If you played Endless Legend, you'll find many things (especially the interface) very familiar. If you can, buy the Gold edition with the Disharmony DLC!
+ Beautiful graphics; every planet and every anomaly has its own awesome visual. And space fights look gorgeous as well
+ very clean interface, you normally find all information you need directly on screen or they are at max 1 click away
+ very different species with different playstyles; not only will you have technologies that only you can research but also faction traits that require different playstyles. A war driven species won't bloom with diplomacy only. You can create a fraction with your own selection of boni and mali by yourself (though always using the ship design of an existing faction)
+ planets and systems that basically become available over time; At first you can only populate very basic and life friendly planet types (like Terran, Ocean, Jungle). Through research you are able to populate lava planets, gas giants or even asteroids. But you always have to keep  in mind the happiness of the population. Just putting ppl on a lava planet because it will give you a lot of production won't work because your happiness will go down and decrease productivity. So you need buildings to compensate that or be lucky to have some anomaly or luxury resource that produces happiness in that system.
+ the battle system; while some ppl hate it, I think it is a nice new idea over the old Civ like "Strenght X vs. Strength Y, so both Units get A and B damage"; first you have to design your ships with modules you have researched (no visual editing though). Each ship can carry a certain tonnage but may have a bonus regarding certain modules. While a bit overwhelming at the beginning it is quite easy (and fast) to do later while you can put of lot of time crunching numbers in it, if you really want. There are no things like firing arcs just basically how much of each weapon (3 types), defenses (for each of the 3 types) and other modules do you want on your ship. Your normal battle ship will have about 2/3 weapons and 1/3 defenses so nothing to worry about if you don't like designing ships. But it is a very tacital element of the game because you can hard counter enemies who focus e.g. on rockets by just using flaks (defense against rockets) and use the rest of the tonnage for weapons. After that you have to put your ships into fleets (each battle is 1 fleet vs. one other fleet) which have limited size but can be increased with technology. The battles themselves are divided into 3 phases: Long Range (rockets will do most damage), mid range (beam weapons are most effective) and close range (fire the ballistic weapons!). During each of these phases both players can use a certain tactic with various boni (e.g. +20% on beam damage or defense). Each tactic can be countered by an other tactic (nullifying its effect) of the enemy which gives the battles another nice tactical layer. While some ppl complain that this is pure luck, I think that it is just the reality of war tactics. Also if your enemy uses e.g. mainly rockets you may have an idea of the tactics he will use. And that also does not mean that a small army can completely annihilate a huge army just by using a "lucky" tactic.
+ technology tree; there are basically 4 of them roughly focusing on warfare, diplomacy, expansion and science. While you normally do research in all of them (as the technologies get more expensive later on you will naturally research the cheap technologies in the other 3 trees before researching an expensive one in your favorite tree), it will give you an interesting way of focusing your empire on a certain thing. Your enemy may have a blooming economy but if you can get more advanced weapons faster than him, you will get a nice advantage in warfare.
- lack of late game buildings;  sometimes I have the feeling there is barely anything to build on your main systems in the late game except for more ships (or convert production into money or science) as there is not much to build. Many buildings focus on giving you more food on planets that normally produce barely any food and thus allowing for a faster growth but normally most of your systems are maxed out on population by then anyway (but there are exceptions!). In games like Civ, that normally happens more in the mid game where you are doing a lot of war anyway and you always have new wonders to race for.
- no allied victory; while you can do alliances with your friends, there is always only one winner at the end of the game. Of course you can just stop playing when you annihilate all other enemies but that does not feel the same. And for e.g. the science victory you can't work together
- ship design may be a bit confusing at the beginning; but there are plenty of wikis/forums/videos to help with that.

Note: review only applies to the game with Disharmony DLC; don't bother with the vanilla classic mode.
Endless Space is a fine turn-based space 4x, but it's not on the same level as the timeless classics such as MoO2 or GalCiv2. Compared to contemporaries, Endless Space is nowhere as great and deep as Distant Worlds (but boasts vastly superior graphics), way better than Sins of a Solar Empire in terms of vanilla customization and replayability (but not in replayability due to mods and overall depth/lore/flavor), and vastly superior to Sid Meier's turned-based space 4x games.
PROS:
+ Customizable faction/race (stats/traits-wise, not appearance)
+ Customizable ship modules (stats/traits-wise, not appearance)
+ Can rename star systems
+ Relaxing automated combat; almost no tactical control aside from choosing tactics
+ Decent graphics
+ Good BGM
+ Sleek UI
+ Pleasant gameflow IF you know what you're doing
+ Large skill trees
+ Acceptable amount of planetary/installation customization
+ Stats/traits, etc. are mod-friendly
+ Decent replayability, though definitely not "endless"
+ He is the Horatio. They are the Horatio. Horatio gazes upon the stars and wishes to fill up the galaxies with the most beautiful thing in the universe: Himself. Horatio.
CONS:
- Pre-chosen number of factions; no emergent factions, such as pre-spacefaring species for enslavement, experiment, worship, etc.
- No end-game return of old race/death horde, despite the lore existence of one that features prominently throughout the game
- Vanilla faction/race roster lacks distinctiveness, mostly humans and robotics
- Automated combat gets old fast, the tactic cards system sounded nice on paper but more often than not is no better than "educated" rock-paper-scissors
- Near non-existent tutorial that leads to unnecessarily steeper learning curve; good luck figuring everything out without wiki/faq/forum guidance
- Frustratingly opaque game mechanics, despite the sleek-looking UI; confusing/misleading stat descriptions
- Suffers the same zero-sum AI mentality that plagues many 4x and grand strategy games: diplomacy is highly unreliable because even the most trusted and friendly ally will backstab and hate the player forever because of Win Conditions
- Graphics not moddable, so can't introduce new races or ship skins. Because of this, replayability can drop drastically after a few playthroughs if you don't enjoy the vanilla factions--your mileage may vary
- Severe desync issues in multiplayer campaigns that effectively ruined multiplayer
Overall, Endless Space is a pretty good space 4x that looks nice and plays well IF you take the time to study the mechanics OUTSIDE of the game... or learn through mistakes and repetition. And no, that's not good game design and polish. Despite all of its flaws, Endless Space is still one of the better contemporary space 4x games out there, just a bit below SoaSE and DW.

Where to start...
You play as Adam Jensen (I knew I'd enjoy this game when the character had my name, haha), an ex-SWAT from Detroit, hired by Sarif Industries to protect scientist who are researching human augmentation. Things go wrong, and mercenaries attack Sarif and Adam has to figure out who-dun-it.
The storyline was great, but I won't talk about the plot for the sake of not spoiling it. It was long, too. When I finished the game for the first time I had 28 hours into it. I'd estimate the game to be 25-30 hours long, depending on how fast you play it. In certain parts of the game, Adam is given choices in actions to take and things to say to people. The game has four possible endings. I really enjoy games that give you choices like this, so this really helped my already high opinion of this game.
I really enjoyed that you could play this game in more ways than one. You could either choose to launch full-frontal-assaults on your enemies or you could go about it the stealthy way, crawling through vents and occasionally knocking out a bad guy. I played on the medium difficulty, "Give Me A Challenge," so I typically mixed stealth and going loud together, depending on the situation. When I replay the game on the hard difficulty, "Give Me Deus Ex," I imagine I'll be sticking to being stealthy a whole lot more.
The gunplay in Human Revolution was fantastic as well. The guns sounded like guns and they had actual spray patterns instead of shooting dead straight like in Call of Duty games. The damage the guns did also felt balanced. One problem I had with guns is that I never figured out how to aim down the sights. There may be an ADS function in the game and I never found it, but I thought that should be addressed.
The stealth mechanics were also done really well in my mind. I found it more satisfying to knock people out than to kill them off, but I killed enemies when I had to.
Human Revolution is the first Deus Ex game I played, and it was a phenomenal experience. I hadn't been so into a plot line or game world since my first time playing Halo: Combat Evolved. There were some sections of the plot that I didn't quite understand because the game bounced from place to place, but in the end, I felt as though the story boiled down pretty well. I will certainly play this again. I got it in the Deus Ex Collection when it was on sale, but it is certainly worth full price.

The controller is by no means low quality, and the amount of customization is on a whole upper level compared to any other controller you can buy. The fault of this product is its software which is nowhere near the quality it should be at its price of $50.
The first thing you should understand is that this controller does not have its own software program; it works through steam. This eliminates the possibility of using this with a gaming console. It also means that while it will recognize steam games and automatically switch to their corresponding configurations, it will not recognize non-steam games. You can only use the desktop configuration to interact with these games, meaning you have to manually change and save the configs.
The worst part of this thing is the software bugs. After spending hours tabbing between my non-steam game and the steam big picture, fine-tuning the functions, the program will often refuse to update the configuration to my controller. If I exit the editing page, all the changes I made are gone. The controller is reverted back to the previous save. This bug is extremely inconsistent, and I have not figured out what causes it. This is extremely frustrating as now I have to invest even more time into a task that already consumes a great amount of it.
Other problems I have had include the situation with my configurations and the functions of standard controller input. After putting this controller on the shelf for  months, maybe a year, I took it back down to give it another chance. I found that none of my saved desktop configurations were there anymore which is possibly my fault as it could have been discarded on the occasion that I needed to rebuild my operating system. Presently, steam refuses to save my configs, and the loading screen that says "Working" gets hung often and will not be able to finish. Also, inputs that are normally on a controller never seem to work for me at least with the desktop mode.
Another thing is that you can not search community configs; there's just a page by page list relative to the game you are playing.

Now that the Steam controller has been out over a year now, I figure a review is due. I have had 3 controllers and a link for about a year now and I got to tell ya, It's a great piece of equipment. Does exactly what you want it to do. Stream your favorite games to your couch without sacrificing valuable PC resources. It is my favorite toy when I have friends over for a night of gaming. No more LAN parties hunched over a desk. You get all the luxuries of a home theater setup.
Now that I have given you my honest thoughts about this product, it's time to fill you in on things that some consider short-comings or faults in this equipment.
These controllers have a very steep learning curve. I have had mine for a year now and I still discover cool features and abilities that can be programmed into this controller. The level of customization on these controller layouts is, simply put, unreal. You can do everything from make your PC think its a Keyboard and Mouse, Game controller, Joystick and Throttle, Track pads can be pop open circular menus, and it goes on and on.
But there is good news for the eager newcomer, the steam configuration importing tool allows you to preview and use other players setups for your game. This means you can basically get your controller configured instantly to the most popular setups among seasoned players. This basic function is where you will start to learn of all the wonders these controllers posses. Setups from the well known basics to multi button function based on menus, maps, inventories, etc. They really are a lot of fun to tweak and see how it impacts your game play.

I've been speedrunning, modding, and making YouTube videos about this game for the past 5 years, so I think this review will come in handy for a lot of people.
'Bully' takes place in the town of Bullworth (Which actually exists in the same universe as the 3D 'Grand Theft Auto' games and even 'Manhunt' 1 & 2). The storyline revolves around the mischief and struggles of the main protagonist (Jimmy Hopkins).
Jimmy finds himself abandoned by his mom and abusive stepfather at the worst school in the country. He's quickly targeted by one of the most aggressive gangs, so he sets out to defeat all of the town's rival cliques, thus raising his social status from simply 'The New Kid' to pretty much becoming a local celebrity.
Unlike the dull and almost lifeless streets of Liberty City in GTA IV, the town of Bullworth is full of personality and a great deal of variety. You'll experience different seasons as you progress through the story, allowing the player to see Bullworth in the autumn, fall, winter, and spring. Even Halloween makes an appearance at one point. Each area is easily distinguishable from the other, and so are the characters. Which brings me to my next point.
What makes the storyline work so well is the witty and likeable nature of all the characters, including the main protagonist. This clever writing even extends to most of the background characters. Hell, even the main antagonist has his moments.
And just like GTA, the further you get into the storyline the more areas and features you unlock.
This is why patience is key when playing through the first chapter. There are 6 chapters. Each Chapter consists of roughly 8 - 15 missions, excluding the 6th chapter because it's basically the "You have completed all of the story related missions, so now you can do any remaining optional sidequests you want"-mode.
The more chapters you complete, the more freedom you're given.
The reason I point this out is because I've seen several people give up halfway through Chapter 1 due to their impatience and an eagerness to explore the environment. Take it easy. Get to know the environment and the characters. I guarantee that you will grow to like the game more if you simply give it time to familiarize yourself with it.
Even the soundtrack is superb. Music composer Shawn Lee's talent really shines here as he shows off a range of different genres and influences.
Don't be surprised if you find yourself humming the 'Walking Tune' when roaming around.
I could go on and on about why this game is so likeable, but I think it's about time that we dive into some of the things that don't work so well.
First and foremost, this game performs very poorly on Windows 10. I've seen tons of people come up with all kinds of solutions and compromises to make the game playable, but I've yet to try any of them myself (I never "Upgraded" to Windows 10). Some claim that certain fixes work for them, others say they don't.
Unfortunately, it seems as though Rockstar has no plans on patching the game for Windows 10.
I use Windows 7, which really is the ideal way to play this game. All I had to do was install the game and play it. No problems.
The game also runs on a 30 fps limit, but there is a mod which removes the framerate cap.
I would suggest installing this mod if you have the game. And while you're at it, why not check out some of the other mods people have made for the game.
Pros:
+ Beautiful soundtrack.
+ Likeable characters.
+ Interesting storyline.
+ Comfy environment.
+ Fun missions.
+ Clever writing.
Cons:
- Terrible Windows 10 support.
- 30 fps cap.
- Somewhat slow beginning.
And hey, there is actually a 'Bully Multiplayer' mod in the making.
Perhaps that too will be in the 'Pros'-list some day.
It's not perfect, and it hasn't aged very well on PC. But it still has a strong and active fanbase for several good reasons.

This is game for bringing out your inner butcher! But also, bringing out your inner demon who likes to consume living beings! Prototype is a hack n' slash type of game with an added twist. You can consume enemies to regain health, see their memories and obtain their powers. There's a cool story, tons of things to upgrade through leveling, and a really innovative feature called the Web of Intrigue. This web is a collection of all the memories you obtain, in order to try and uncover the horrible truth about yourself and everything that's happening on the island...

Feels like an "anti-hero" version of Prince of Persia set in Manhattan. I was expecting more of a roaming aspect like GTA but most of the side quests are boring or just not worth the time (I did maybe 20% of them and still maxed almost all my skills by the end of the game). There's three sets of collectables in the city: landmarks (200 blue orbs that give exp), hints (50 loading screen "protips" which are really pointless), and web of intrigue targets. WoI targets are the most interesting because they add more depth to the story but they are hit or miss. Sometimes you get insight into past story events, sometimes you get militant chest beating. The graphics are pretty bland and boring in a city full of grey but I guess there's only so much you can do with Manhattan.
Overall this game is solidly average but a definite console port. If you can get it cheaper on a console go for it.

Played this game for several hundred hours, a founder who spent $250-300 over the course of the past 4 years.
I'd have a hard time in good conscience recommending this game, especially to new players.
- For the $60-100 it costs to get a decent stable of mechs up and running, there's literally hundreds of games better than this
- Very crash prone game. As in, hard crash to desktop OR system lockup every ~2 hours. Every match starts with 2-4 disconnected players.
- The Clan Wars are semi-decent for organized groups. But the population is so small, PGI sacrifices solo queued groups to organized premades and its basically 20-30 minutes of your life lost in a guaranteed loss.
Also, PGI has the license for Mechwarrior until the end of 2017. There's no guarantee this game will be active after that point. You maybe be spending money that will evaporate in 6-12-18 months time.
The game is fun for quickmatch games (12v12), but its a B level franchise trying to sell itself as AAA.
EDIT: While my rating is 'Yes' for recommendation, I would opt for a neutral rating if available. I still have fun with the game, and play it from time to time. I've enjoyed it over the years despite its shortcomings, and there's nothing really like it on the market. That said, people should be aware that they're buying into a diamond-in-the-rough.

2 years experienced player, MechWarrior Online was the first title I came to on PC after being a five year long console gamer and it soon became the one single game I play on a regular basis. After my first year of casual play, I started to become a more competetive player and I became a spender on this title. I didn't feel like I needed to spend money on Mechs to be able to enjoy the game, I just decided I wanted to support the devs since this game felt like a major step up from the direction console gaming has been going in. As far as pay-to-win goes, you can pay to speed up progression with premium time, but that's about as far as it goes, everything else is mostly cosmetic or timed (exclusive with the exception of Hero Mechs), it's up to you wether that crosses the line or not.
The dev team is very open with community feedback and does a fair job of keeping players up to date with their plans to improve the game, so there's almost always some new features to look forward to in the regular updates/patches. Gameplay wise, this is a very competetive title and a lot of information to take in and learn about. If you enjoy having long term thinking and strategic decision making in your shooters, this is for you. The learning curve is steep, but very enjoyable when you start to apply your knowledge in game as you fight your battles and even more fun is when you play with a group of friends and communicate information between one another.
Overall, a unique and in-depth shooter experience and a nice change of pace from the usual fast paced run and gun type shooters most of us are used to from Triple A titles. Definitely recommended to give it a try and at the cost of free, all you have to lose is a couple hours you spend trying it out.

A unique take on the standard Arena-Style FPS, that I think is well worth trying out at least one.
The weapons appear to be well balanced (with a couple exceptions), the maps are large and interesting and well suited to the unique movement mechanics where you build up momentum to slide across the battlefield at high speeds. Plus, it has a jet pack, and everything is made better with a jetpack. The combat is really faced paced, given the movement mechanics, and so hitting somebody with a mortar or rocket launcher is a lot harder than one would think. The game requires actual skill and some tactics to be good at, and that's something that gets rarer and rarer these days. Given that it's a free-to-play, obvious there are microtransactions, but nothing is pay to win. If you blow your money to get all the best gear...lol good for you, but you still need to learn how to use everything effectively, and even if you do, everybody else is still on your level unless you're so good at the game you don't even need to use the best weapons. Plus, anything you can get that actually affects gameplay with real money can be unlocked rather quickly just by playing matches. I unlocked a new class in just one game.
The downsides are, of course, the people who play the game. It's competitive, it's a shooter, and it's free. So you can bet your♥♥♥♥♥there's a bunch of squealing pig-children that play this game. My very first match there was some kid wailing about hackers every time he got killed, when in reality he just sucked. There was another kid who claimed he had reported everybody in the game who used used profanity and that we all "ruin the game for everybody else".
Just mute or block and of the little kids and focus on the game and it's a lot of fun.

Very fun game. Very fast paced but easy to learn. The basic premise is the ability to make yourself frictionless and "ski" across the battlefield at 100+ kph. At it's core, Tribes is a pretty average sci-fi FPS, but with the ski mechanic the entire dynamic of the game changes, transforming a boring shootout into something more akin to a car chase across the large maps. The general feel of the game reminds me alot of the old Blood Gulch Halo 1 multiplayer.
Another refreshing thing about this game was the absence of pay-to-win microtransactions and such. Every class and gun in the game can be unlocked just by gathering experience in-game (as well as with purchasable gold). It makes you want to support the devs, unlike a lot of other similar MP games.
Anyhow, if shooters are your thing, definitely try this one out. It's free, it has a great community and addicting gameplay.  Highly reccomend. See you in game.

This whole game's one of the clunkiest I've played in a while, and not even the funny kind. Just straight up frustrating.
The construction is unwieldy as all heck. First, you have to buy all materials from the shop (I'll get to the cost later). Then it becomes a fight with the camera angle to even build a decent house with a roof. Let me tell you, a "slightly" top down view is NOT a good angle for anything construction related. There are even cases where the walls completely block certain tiles, not only making it feel like you're building blindfolded, but also forcing you to deconstruct everything just to build whatever it was the walls were blocking.
The combat... Oh the combat. Unless you're ranged, it's almost impossible to battle without getting hit. Normally this would be fine, damage is inevitable, but considering how few hitpoints you get, the damage adds up. Ultimately, you'll be finding yourself dying and going back to the beginning of the world. Even as ranged, there's also the case of extreme respawn times, so be prepared to get shell-shocked.
Speaking of worlds, quests are pretty much your only option to even hope of getting decent money and EXP. It takes an EXTREME amount of gold to get enough to build anything past a small house. So unless you like running at cheap enemies, you'll have to do quests. Again, this would normally be fine, but after the initial quests, every quest you get is randomized, and I mean RANDOMIZED. It takes no account what level you are or anything. With some quests taking place in worlds locked behind level requirements, this is a major problem. This is countered with the ability to talk to the quest giver for a different quest, but the number of awful quests to cycle through is astounding. From continuous pixel-perfect gauntlets given to beginners, to ultra vague scavenger hunts, it's like there was no effort put into filtering the good, the bad, and the ugly.
Finally, the cost. Like I said before, every block in the game costs coins, heck, even entering certain doors cost coins. I'm talking about an extravigant number of coins. With the small, convoluted shop menu, it's almost impossible to find what exactly you want. Pair that with the cost of everything, good luck trying to build something actually worth looking at. They're practically making you pay to get anything good, and even good's a strong word.
This game has no soul. It feels like something thrown together and then presented as an enchanting ground breaking indie game. It doesn't even try to hide the amount of cynicism it throws at you. Even what few NPCs are shown are extremely cynical. Jokes are fine, but having sarcastic remarks the only things NPCs say to you in an already soulless husk of a game just spits in your face. I'm sorry.

An amazing unrecognized innovation in the rts/grand strategy genre. Part of a golden age of the last generation of pc strategy games when the 2d formula had been refined refined and innovation was the order of the day. For some unfortunate reason these wonderful games had mixed results in the next generation, think Stronghold, Empire Earth, Kohan 2, etc.
Simplified but good resource and city management, very refined squad level controls with a fully functional experience, moral, and terrain system. Enough rpg elements to make things customizable but not too involved or important to distract you from the larger strategic picture. Wonderful classic pc fantasy style graphics. One of the features that still impresses me about this game today is that you can play on huge maps with tons of other players on a robust random map generator, this makes almost every game feel unique. Lots of factions and ways to play the game, if you are enjoy strategy games at all, pick this one up.

A game that was released back in 2001, yet still has people going back to play (in fact, there is still a small but active MP community which still plays this game!)
That alone says how good of an RTS it is.
In fact, it amazes me that no RTS has been released since that combines what Kohan does (although the Dawn of War series comes close, it was a lot more about micromanaging battes and how fast you can click to activate special abilities).
Key concepts:
- city management, and the cities generate all your resources
- company based combat structure, where companies can heal back to full health over time (as long as even 1 unit survives and returns to your bases).
- companies and heroes both level up and become more powerful and stronger
- once units enter combat, you not longer have control of the unit (barring retreat and rout).  This severely reduces the effect of "microing" (clicking like a madman).  It also makes battle tactics like flanking to kill enemy support units much deadlier.
If there's one con to this game, it's that it has a default resolution and doesn't support widescreen (stretches out the images, making them look ugly).

Great Hardware but garbage Software.
Really a great controller as it fits perfectly into my hands and the controls feel really solid. The feedback of the touchpads is really nice and precisely tells you what you're doing.
The Software side is really terrible however. First of all the controller isn't even detected as such by Windows itself, so you always need Steam to use it. You can't just go over to a friend, plug it in and done.
Instead you get all the configuration in Steam. But you need to launch big picture mode. No matter what.
The settings panel is really nice and lets you configure the controller extensively. It even lets you configure it for each game!
You can also download configs from the Steam Workshop, which is nice.
While in-game you can also configure it on the fly... if the overlay doesn't act up yet again.
First you need to make sure to turn on the controller before you start the game or else the config overlay won't be available.
Then in-game the overlay stutters and lags quite a lot, making it almost unusable. Sometimes not for whatever reason, but for the most part it acts up like that. But the worst part is when you try to close it. Sometimes it works, other times it just stays there but just becomes invisible. So if you try to use the controller in the game again, it won't register any input, as the now invisible overlay catches all input. So you hear that you do something in the menu but you don't see, all while the game now keeps going.
Sometimes it works to just press the steam button on the controller again to re-open the overlay and then use the mouse to click on "back to game". Sometimes you have to do that a couple times. But if you're unlucky you're stuck in the invisible menu forever. The options you have are that you go back to keyboard and mouse or restart the game.
If the software wasn't so majorly and frustratingly flawed, it would be the best controller on the market in my opinion, but as it is right now I can't even recommend it, unless you don't care about your anger management and hair. Because you will pull your hair out and get really angry.

This is the perfect game to buy on sale. I picked it up during the Steam Summer Sale at a fraction of the full price, and I'm very happy with what I got for the money.
Would I feel the same if I had paid full price? Probably not. The simplistic gameplay makes it easy to enjoy without the frustration of a steep learning curve, but does not justify a top-shelf price tag in my opinion.
That said, the Endless Space universe is full of beutifully detailed graphic depictions of all types planets, including various sci-fi anomalies such as ancient ruins and gravitational disturbances. Each star system you discover reveals unique challenges and opportunities for colonization, keeping the experience enticing.
Combat is a little strange, consisting of 3 phases which essentially represent long, medium, and short range exchanges of damage and defence. There are no maneuvers involved; every class of ship is essentially a slow-moving platform for weapon systems and countermeasures closing in on one another, The strategy for each of the 3 phases is selected before combat, and you are given the option to skip straight to the results or watch the action in real-time. The latter provides the opportunity to change the selected strategies along the way, and some decent eye candy. Nothing that would rival the likes of EVE, but far more exciting than a Sid Meyer game's combat system.
Trade and diplomacy are both present, as you'd expect from any sort of nation-building strategy game. Having chosen an empire which relies mainly upon military superiority, I haven't experienced enough of either to judge their implementation. However, the fact that you have a wide of choice of empires ranging from evil militants to peaceful industrialists means you can play-your-way, selecting the definintion of "victory" that suits you.
The game also includes randomly generated events, rare and valuable resources to find, pesky space pirate attacks, and a handful of other surprises which keep things from becoming stale or predictable.
What it does NOT include are cinematic sequences, voice acting, linear storytelling, city-level management  or integrated mini-games. I expect that casual gamers may find that to be a bit bland, but strategy purists will appreciate the lack of distraction.
Bottom Line:
If you're a fan of turn-based strategy, civilization building, sci-fi warfare, and looking to add another solid title to your collection, then put this on your wishlist and wait for the next sale.

UPDATE, November 2017: While I no longer use Steam to launch the game, I've now been playing MWO consistently for over a year.
There have been 2 game modes added since my original review, Incursion and Escort. Incursion drops you and your team on a map with a base to defend, your opponent also has a base to defend (with turrets, structures, and destructible walls). You fight over 3 battery spawn points on the map that can power a radar sweep, a radar jammer, and an 'air control tower', which calls in a friendly dropship to strafe the enemy base. In Escort mode you are either escorting or attacking an AI mech, to bring it to an extraction point or destroy it before it gets there.
The developers have also added an in-client event system, and are running very regular events so players can earn in-game currency, complete challenges, etc. When I first reviewed this game, there was
going on at least once a month, now there's something going on all the time. I would think that it would help a bit with the grind due to the biggest change this game has seen in years:
Skill Tree. Love it or hate it, it does allow players to customize their mechs' performance in a much more detailed way than the previous system. It also adds very much to the grind.
If you are new to this game, or thinking about trying it out: save your in-game money! You're going to need it. (original review is below)
The mechanics of this game are similar to previous MechWarrior titles. You pilot a Battlemech, have to deal with ammunition for your guns and missiles, and manage heat and cooldowns for your energy weapons. There's 4 classes of battlemech (light, medium, heavy, assault) and a variety of roles that each can play, based on loadout, which for mechs you own is fully customizeable. There are two multiplayer game modes: Quick Play and Faction Play. Quick Play is where the majority of pilots spend their time, dropping into 12v12 matches on a variety of maps and with varying objectives (Skirmish/Deathmatch, Conquest, Domination/King of the Hill, Assault/Base Capture). Faction Play allows pilots to participate more in the lore/IP; by signing on with one of the Inner Sphere houses or one of the Clan tribes as a loyalist or mercenary, and shape the Mechwarrior universe (unfortunately, in practice this is not as cool as it sounds - more on this below). I'm 100 hours in as of this review, here's what I like and don't like so far:
Overall, if you've got a few hours a week (or more) to kill, this is one of the better F2P 'puter games I've played. The publisher definitely doesn't get everything right all the time, but I think overall they've done a good job, and I will definitely be playing this game for awhile.
Not convinced?

This is not the MechWarrior game we are looking for.
In its current state, MWO is not going anywhere fast. It is painfully aparent that this Free-to-Play game is supporting itself on very expensive Mechpacks (new mech comes out, preorder commences, nostalgic players drop $80, rinse and repeat). Gameplay is very, very stale. The 'immersive' battlefield known as Faction Play is a barren wasteland that is simply a harder and less-popular clone of Quick Play.
Here is what you will find if you play this game.
You will get massive ammounts of C-bills (probably around 25-million) for your first 25 games. Then your recruitment bonus will end and funds will trickle in like icicles melting in a warm breeze. It becomes EXTREMELY time consuming and tedious grind for a single million C-bills.
Mechs (the ones that are available for C-bills) cost MILLIONS of C-bills to purchase, and you only get 3 free slots for Mechs. So unless you win a Mechbay from an event, you will only be able to own 3 Mechs for free. That is, assuming you manage to earn enough C-bills to buy 3 Mechs.
Quick Play (which is currently the ONLY viable game mode) is the same 12 vs. 12 man match over and over and  over and over again. You have different maps and slightly different objectives (if other players vote for them at the voting screen) but it is hardly enough to keep you engaged and interested for the lenghth of time it would take to afford an Assault Mech.
Oh, and these 12 vs. 12 matches are PUG matches. Which means you will be trying to coordinate a 12-man team of random players. Use your imagination.
All told, game looks great and the mechanics aren't terrible. Sadly it is one of the ever growing number of Free-to-Play titles that are going towards the Pay-to-Enjoy model. And heads up, even if you do pay, it won't make the matches more interesting.
