As a long time fan of Battletech / the Mechwarrior, I'm glad to see the franchise has been picked up and dusted off. I've been playing this consistanly game for 3 years or so now (using the stand alone client) So I've come to share my opinon of this game as a true vet.
So what is Mechwarrior about? From the very beginning, it's always been about piloting giant, multi-ton battlemechs into battle. Smashing trees, stomping cars, high-powered futuristic weapons. Carnage. Destruction! Battlemechs operate as walking tanks. You can move the torso independently from the legs. And you can Aim Arm mounted weapons independently from weapons mounted in the torso. It takes a certain finesse to get the hang of it, but it does lead to a pretty fun experience in battle.
That said, MWO is a solid tactical shooter. It can be a bit slower paced as you really have to be able to land consistent shots in the same component location to effectively destroy your opponents armor so you can get to the internals, who will be doing their best to spread that damage all over his mech. But on the other hand it can be brutally fast paced when a coordinated team focuses down targets. Though there are a few lone wolf roles that can be quite disruptive to the enemy team, Team work as well as positioning and situation awareness is Key in this game.
It cannot be ignored that there is a learning curve to Mechwarrior. It does take a certain finnese outside of twitch shooting. It can be frustrating if you're new and trying to get the hang of the game, as it does take a while to learn proper maneuvering, how to manage your heat and preserve your armor. There are no respawns in MWO, but if you play it right, most mechs can take quite a beating. Once you get the hang of it, combat is seamless and satisfying.
Another crucial part of the Mechwarrior franchise that will keep you coming back for more is the Mechlab. Here you can browse thoughscores of available mechs for purchase (Most mechs and ALL weapons / equipment in the game can be purchased with in game currency that you earn in battle), choose your ideal mech, strip it down and build it up to your preferred role / play-style, finding that balance between heat management, firepower, mobility, ammo and any other support tech. Here is where you will fine tune your mechs and try to squeeze after last bit of performance out of it to fit your needs.  Each chassis is different. They will have different hardpoint types / locations and / or quirks that may make them excel in some areas. PGI has done a great job of making each mech not feel exactly the same as another so there is lots of variation to be found.
Mechwarrior also offers several types of weapons that you can choose from to equip on your battlemech. They fall into 3 main categories.
- Energy - Those are your lasers and particle projection cannons. They come in different sizes and beam duration lenghts for different roles. Damage is done instantly to your target. But damage is DOT, so you have to hold the beam on a specific spot on your target to get the full damage to that location. Energy weapons generate the most heat but require no ammo.
-Missiles - Again, come in different sizes and salvos. Short and long range versions. Can end up weighing a lot. variants that can lock on to an enemy do less damage. Generally low heat, but can get hot with long periods of sucessive fire.
-Ballsitics - your Autocannons and Guass rifles of different calibers. Require lots of space and tonnage to equip on your mech. Rounds do have varying travel time and range depending on the calibre of the round. Ballistcs that don't burst fire will do their full rated damage on impact if within optimal range. Generally very low heat weapons.
Mechs come with combinations of these hardpoints and it's up to the player to figure out what works best for them.
Above:Sniping and harassing in the shadowcat: Medium Omnimechs equipped with Dual Extended range PPC's. Heat managment and positioning are key on this build.
That said there are 4 classes of mechs to choose from.
20-35 tons - Your nimble annoying light mechs that will pick and peck at you. Infuriate you! Low armor, low to decent firepower, high speed and maneuverability. Very effective against slower targets.
40-55 tons - Medium mechs which as less mobile but carry more armor and firepower. By lore, they are the workhorses of the battlefield.
60-75 tons - Heavy Mechs, Good armor, good firepower and decent mobility.
80-100 tons - Assault Mechs - Expensive, Slow, lumbering heavily armed behemoths of destruction. With just as heavy armor.
As far as DLC goes, there is a lot out there. But you don't really need to get any of it. New players only have access to trial mechs, most of which are decent but cannot be customized, but new players also earn money bonuses for their 1st 25 games. Completing the tutorials will also net a nice tidy amount of cbills which should allow new players to buy 1 or 2 maybe even more Mechs of their down. And yes, any mech in the game ouside of hero mechs can be purchased with in game currency. Hero mechs are usually not the preferred variant of a mech, they may have a couple hard-point changes and come with their down custom camospec and a 30% boost to money earned in matches. The only thing that a new player that is into the game should buy is Mechbays - you only have 4 to start with, and if you want more mechs you'll have to sell mechs to free up bays or by more mechbays. Mechbays can also be earned in game by playing faction warfare, completing weekend challenges and more.
Sounds and graphics are all nicely done, though the game could still benefit from some optimization in some areas. This is still a work in process and there is new content in the making and improvements are always being added.
I'll end this review with another video of some of the sights and sounds of mechwarrior.  Hope to see you on the battlefield Future Mechwarriors!

When you are subjected to a piece of art there are two things you must ask yourself: what is this piece trying to say, and what does it make me feel.
Throughout this game you experience the life of another. Their hopes and dreams, struggles with family and intimacy and finding one's self. This game carries a strong message; we are who we make ourselves.
Throughout the game you are rewarded, for the completion of mundane and banal tasks, brief glimpses into the main character's life. The games allows you to reflect upon yourself and attempts to guide you into the realization that it is only through experimentation and discovery that we can find our true selves.
We know what the game sets out to accomplish; what does it make us feel? I found myself profoundly changed after experiencing this game. I laughed, shuddered, got excited, leapt off my seat, and even wept. I feel that in the aftermath of this true piece of art there will come about a social change. I know that many, like myself, will have their view on life irrevocably altered.
I highly recommend this game and as such will give it a perfect score.

Pros:
-Some of the combat mechanics are fun.
-If you like hack and slash games, this MAY keep you occupied.
-Character creation is as good as some of the most recent MMORPGs.
-Doesn't stray too far from the typical starting classes, they should be fairly familiar for new players to this game.
-Had some decent skillsets, interesting takes on abilities.
Mediocre:
-Voice acting. It's not great, but it's not complete garbage either, I suppose.
-Animations are alright, nothing ground breaking, and not near as polished as most paid games.
Cons:
-Story.  I noticed several blatant rip-offs of other games within the hour I played it.  (Portal, Kingdoms of Amalur, Destiny among them)
-Animations during speech.  Often the lip sync doesn't even come close, and frequently I noticed the lips continued to move for some time after the speech was finished.
-Interactions.  Several instances where I was told to interact with something, my character jumped instead.  I would estimate easily 40% of the time, this happened, instead of my interaction with said object.
-Combat. Yes, this probably changes in later levels, but the initial bosses I've encountered were nothing more than meat slabs that you hack away at, No bother dodging or anything, just stab a few times and repeat.
-Graphical woes.  Lots of clipping, character models teleporting slightly, sudden twitches and just overall weird processing to make things appear/disappear suddenly.
I gave this game an hour, which some people will probably cry about, but as far as the story and all else goes, it really just doesn't entice me to play longer, this was enough time.  It has all the staples of a generic freemium pay-to-win type game.  Characters are very generic, voice acting is generic, stry is copy/pasted from numerous sources, and combat just feels like a freemium game.  Not bad freemium, but not quite good freemium.  It's very in the middle of the road in everything. Most of the development in this game obviously went to very bad breast physics.
If you're absolutely at the end of your rope trying to find an MMORPG that you don't have to pay a monthly sub for, then you may want to give this game a try.  For all else, I'd say you can safely avoid downloading, and you won't regret your decision, or miss anything at all.

KAG is my favorite RTS.  I've been playing it since it came out in 2001 and only recently downloaded the Steam version to connect with friends who had lost their CDs (I have one signed by the devs... I know, I'm a KAG geek).

In fact, my partner and I have created 7 epic campaigns that we play all the time, each featuring different Kohan and types of challenges.   Tinkering with AIs is also great fun (look for The Awakening fan site to download tons).
Anyway, I recommend KAG if you like retro games and want to try something different.  Have fun!

What is it about this game that makes it so good?  The random maps?  The squad-based controls?  The RPG elements?  The city-building component?  Micromanagement that's fun and not overwhelming?  Good co-op play?
I'm not sure.  But I can't get enough of it.

In Game of Thrones, an exceptional swordsman is maimed and forced to fight using his left-hand; with which he does so poorly. He says something akin to "it's evident from the training that I wouldn't be able to defend myself against a stable-boy." I can now empathise with that swordman! :D  *I've played Dark Souls 3, and Left 4 Dead 2; both games requiring moderate competence and skill for survival, on the Steam controller*
I purchased this monstrosity so that I wouldn't have to resort to using the popular DS3 tools to play my favourite games with; it was a grave mistake. It should be noted that this review comes from someone conversant in console gamepads; not someone whose primary way of playing games is a mouse and keyboard, which should be punishable by maiming.
Pros:
+the controller is highly customisable; all you need to do, is press the Steam button in the centre of it, and viola, configure away.
+behind the controller are two triggers which you can map to use in-game; they're absolutely wonderful. More gamepads should have this feature!
Cons:
-the button layout is atrocious, being underneath the right trackpad, and the buttons themselves are probably smaller than the ones found on any traditional controller; even more so than those on an SNES or Gameboy.
-the contour design for the gamepad is quite awkward; the bottom of the controller sticks out against your palms which can be quite uncomfortable.
-the Steam menu is converted to Steam in "Big Picture" mode; I don't know anyone who plays with an interface so clumsy that it makes the one for the Playstation 3 blush.
-the right trackpad is so sensitive that it can never fully replace a right analog stick. (I've tried various popular settings as well.)
The sodium levels in my head are quite high as I write this review; I only remember being this salty on two separate occasions in my life: one happened five years ago when I got a haircut so awful, that I let out a stream of invective shortly after leaving the salon. I questioned if the stylist got the certification she displayed on her desk from a McDonald's rather than a proper school for beauty. The second time was, lo and behold, when I visited a barber shop and waited about an hour to get a haircut, while one barber was better at talking to his customer than finishing his work, and the other was too busy doing drug deals in the back of the shop, to finish up his current client and attend me. I never felt like I wasted time I was never going to get back (I left) in my life like I did that day :) Similarly, I've never felt like I've given $50+ dollars away like I did buying this joke of a controller. Somewhere in all of my rage, I truly felt like this was a prank by Steam to its consumers. The women who helped Elizabeth Bathory kill all of those innocent virgins got their fingernails plucked out for their crimes... I'm wondering if such is a fitting punishment for the Steam controller's designers.
"Well, wait a minute! This controller takes time getting used to; so stop throwing a tantrum!" Riding a unicycle needs time to get used to as well, but you don't see people ditching their bicycles in favour of it. Actually, that might be easier and more intuitive to get used to than this new gen., N64 controller to PC, port. Surely, it should be mentioned that some games, like those in the strategy and third person genre, that are slow paced would seem easy or ideal to play using this gamepad, but the actively face-paced FPS, for example, are not.

Decently challenging AI ? Check.
An exhaustive victory conditions set ? Check and doublecheck.
Custom factions, maps, rules and units ? Check.
A huge and well designed tech tree ? Check.
An imaginative and inspiring story universe ? Check. Granted, some of the tech descriptions don't really seem to match their effects, but the writing is excellent (English version). Especially considering Amplitude is French. We aren't exactly aces when it comes to foreign languages.

It's okay.
The fleet vs fleet battle system is essentially a very enlarged game of rock-paper-scissors with three rounds and many cards that all counter each other differently, for a very complex and hard to predict web of cause and effect. It's incredibly satisfying when you pick the right card and blow your opponent to smithereens. Fleet size matters, but small fleets can beat larger fleets with good strategy, so it's well designed. In addition, the heroes you appoint have specialties and command the fleets, so it's all very satisfying to play fleet tactics.
Where the game falls behind a bit is in the overland starmap strategy. There are both size limits on fleets and movement/attack limits per turn on fleets, even if they are in the same system as an enemy. Logically, since the turns are a week, your fleet SHOULD be able to attack every enemy fleet in the system it's located in, but somehow it can only attack one, which is incredibly stupid because then the overland strategy becomes a tedious game of hide, seek, and run around repetitively.
The other way the game falls a bit behind is in fleet vs. planet combat. It's done only passively, and while the mechanics to decide it are sound enough, there's no interaction there, it's entirely automated. I don't understand why we couldn't have gotten an awesome tactical card game for planetary invasions too.
The final big issue is that it's still very unstable and has bugs - none that crash the game, but a lot that break it and make it somewhat unplayable. AI will bug out, mechanics will break, etc.
If you love political intrigue and economics, which I admit I also have a soft spot for, this game is not your thing. It's very polished, but not too deep beyond the fleet battles. It personally didn't work for me, not just because of the lack of depth beyond the combat but because of the strategic flaws. However, if you want a decent space 4x with a great battle system that doesn't take long to get in to, this is your game.

with the important mission to kill various types of

. It sounds like childish fun on paper and thats exactly what it is. It's called Crimsonland because you basically paint the ground blood-red from pulverizing anything that shows up on screen. That basically sums up everything you need to know.
The core gameplay for this game is very simple. You control a soldier from a very retro-esque top down perspective via the WASD layout and aim and shoot monsters for score. Sometimes, monsters drop power-ups, which you can choose to pick up, or not as you need to conserve them while they're on the ground in order to get the fullest potential out of any of them. Having a strategy on how to progress properly is essential in this game so besides blasting Aliens it requires some forsight and mental preperation of things to come. Often your chances of survival your way to the power-up itself so you can pick it up isn't even big as the ever coming monster waves keep you occupied otherwise.
Two of the basic main game modes are a
, which provides the Player with a set of "Missions" where the term only is used in the loosest of senses as the only thing you have to do in each mission is to kill a specific set of monsters until the bar of the upper side of the screen is filled out. It gets interesting however if you like to survive the round without taking a hit since the game at least acknowledges it so you can honor your skills with this game.
Being good at
gets rewarded with a star and an achievement for survivng all normal missions and this game has some of the most difficult to get achievements I've seen yet, apart from
. As it requires a lot of partience to be rewarding, only the most hardcore of players may ever see one of the more difficult to get achievements. By completing missions you can unlock new Weapons, perks and Game Modes.
The other mode is something that gets unlocked during the first few missions and that is the
. Survival mode is the Flesh and Bones of this entire game as this is the game mode where you can get level ups to attain the perks you previously unlocked in the Quest Mode. There is a very well structured On-Line Scoreboard so if you feel competitive you can always try to reach the Top 100.
To get straight to the point the graphics feel a little bit dated but I do believe that in this case it seem appropriate given the age of the game of it and how fluid the gameplay is. In terms of art direction I say that it all feels very pleasant to the eyes, as you can already tell from the pictures on the Steamstore for this game.
In terms of sound effects this game feels a little bit lackluster and is the worst thing this game has to offer regarding everything else
as to offer. Shooting your guns doesn't feel as strong as it should in my opinion and even launching a nuke doesn't feel as good as it should be. However I believe that the Music is pretty spot on given the gameplay as shooting up monsters and Metal seem to go hand in hand with carnage-themed games since Doom 1.
I believe that this game is a fine example on how gameplay throughout the simplier ages of video game design
can still be this refreshing. Sometimes you just want to shoot some monsters and rack up points with not much else. So if you believe that it's the game for you I hereby highly recommend that you should pick it up even if it isn't on a sale right now, as this is one of the genres finest.

- graphics are nice enough for an "mmo" and the game is well optimized even in big areas. I noticed some frame drops here and there mostly due to FX and other players on screen. The characters are well done too. And the skill special effects feel really powerful and are well done, like the Cryomancer ultimate detonating into a bubble freezing everyone around with ice and frost covering the ground and enemies, etc.
- the mechanics are interesting : you are a god, and to increase your power ( Might ) you need more and more followers. The more mortals believe in you, the more a$$ you can kick. In the lore, Gods forgotten by mortals start aging and they die. You have two ways to get followers : you can pay with credits for rituals at the cathedral, and you can rescue mortals during missions.
The other way to increase your Might is by making research on monsters. To do that you have to spend research points that you get by killing monsters, simple enough.
- there's 13 classes in total, 3 at the beginning and the rest is unlocked when you progress through the missions. You can switch your class at will outside of combat.
- the costumes and armors are nice, at least the ones for the classes. The other costumes seem a bit out of place sometimes but it's OK if you don't take the game too serisouly. It's still far from some other games with really silly costumes.
- you begin with several costumes already unlocked and can change them as you wish. You can also change the makeup, tatoos, earrings etc of the character for free in your dressing room.
- there is a Glados-like voiced AI telling you stupid stuff and giving you more or less useful info about enemies.
- missions are generally short so you can just play one from time to time when you fell it.
- plenty of mounts and vehicles to travel with, you get one for free, but the others are expensive ( 18 000 "argents" each, and you don't earn a lot of argents by simply playing ).
- the loot from mobs is obtained by opening gray Pokeballs. I sh!t you not, it's literaly a pokeball and it opens like a pokeball, but there is loot inside instead of a pikachu.
- they didn't even try to do a real story, and that's good. I mean, there IS some kind of story but nobody gives a damn, you play this game to kill monsters and loot stuff, like Diablo 3.
Cons :
- the combat could be a lot more fluid, it's not as fun as Vindictus and other games like this. I think it's mainly due to long animations and the fact that there is some kind of delay between skill activation. Like, if you use a skill and then use LMB too quickly for a normal attack, it won't register because the animation wasn't over, which totally breaks the flow of the combat. There are also several skills requiring you to hold on a button to charge up, it's kinda slow and generally you don't even see the benefit, you could just have used an instant skill instead.
- voice acting isn't really good, and there is like no lipsync with english voices.
- some aspects of the game are not well explained. For example, I played for an hour without understanding why I didn't get new skills for my class. Thing is, you have to open the map, go to your class temple and accept a quest ( kill X monsters with your class, yay ! ), and only then the XP counts to unlock skills. And when the next skill is unlocked you have to accept the quest again, otherwise you're basically wasting your time.
Another issue was with the Bastions quests that tells you to kill X monsters of a certain type. Ok so I go to a mission and kill the monnsters, but the quest didn't update. In fact I had to click on the "Adventure" button which teleports me in the exact same zone, but now the quest is active... Really dumb game design.
- some things in the store seem a bit overpriced, especially anything requiring "argents" ( I wonder why they didn't call that "gems" or "diamonds" because the icon looks like a gem ). The costumes requiring argents instead of cerdits have nothing special, they're even worse than the class costumes.
- the "open world" areas are bad, with a ton of other players all playing solo and waiting for mob respawn, or quest objective respawn, or boss respawn. The normal missions are solo/coop, but those special areas are the "mmo" part of the game and honestly I don't see the point.
- despite the tutorial, menus and game mechanics are extremely confusing at first. 10 hours in and I still don't understand some stuff.

A truly great RTS game with a macro-scale focus.
Units are grouped into companies which must be carefully crafted, can be lead by a hero, and will stay with you throughout the game, gaining experience and so forth. Smart design calls such as stationary units gain a defensive advantage if they stay in the same spot over a long period of time, as well as the retreat/rout/morale system and zone of control means that positioning is very important in Kohan. Additionally, terrain plays a huge role, as different terrains have very large effects on combat and movement, and natural chokepoints are crucial to hold for similar reasons.
Cities are condensed into single buildings, which house a number of 'component slots' that are filled by buildings, and again the design forces careful economic planning, for instance focusing on gold income for the long-run or pumping out valuable resources such as iron to fuel a war effort. Resources in the game are not cumulative besides gold-- meaning that you are rarely encouraged to sit back and do nothing in the game.
The game also comes with several large campaigns, a random map generator, a custom scenario editor, fairly competent AI (with the ability to make your own / download them online), and extensive modding tools. There are a huge number of heroes, secret technologies and monsters to keep the game fresh game after game after game.
Besides this glowing review, I would point out two flaws:
1. A faltering online community. The game is old, and few people play anymore.
2. The game is somewhat unbalanced. While the game is usually tight, there are a few degenerate situations, and on very large maps the game is very unbalanced. However, you can play on very small maps to fix that, and much of the game imbalance can be addressed via modding; personally, I advise a mod which increases the gold penalties for going negative with your resources, as well as making resources scarcer.
Still, it is a game worth playing, and better than its successor. I hope we see a worthy sequel someday.

I have been playing this game for several years, far longer than it has been on Steam. At its core, it is essentially "Virtual LEGOs" and that it still does very well. Thanks to a modding community that has been active for years, a wide variety of bricks are available even beyond what is included with the base game, making it possible to replicate practically any real world LEGO construction with minimal need for replacement or substitution.
This being said, although at its heart this game's bones are good, I would be remiss if I did not concede that it does have some major flaws. The biggest fault in this game is its community, which is immature and sometimes downright toxic; there is a reason that I rarely play on multiplayer servers. Building can sometimes be frustrating, especially if you are used to games like Minecraft, because there is no "Creative Mode flight"; when building above one's height, it is often necessary to erect scaffolding for yourself or otherwise put up with the frustrating and sometimes inadequate jet boots. Finally, the game's highly touted physics are bordering on a joke. This is particularly problematic when trying to complete the game's racing achievement; all vehicles travel very fast and precision speed and steering controls are practically impossible. And should one's vehicle hit even a minor bump, it will be bounced off as if it were weightless and made of rubber. I have yet to complete the pre-built racing course to earn the acheivement.
In spite of these flaws though, I still adore this game. I highly recommend it to those who wish to simply unwind on their own, to hop into the body of a minifig and build their own world. Then populate it wish zombies and see how long they can hold out, or simply fly around with a rocket launcher blowing all of your perfect creations to kingdom come. Because let's face it, explosions are fun.

I was involved in a segway mini accident where the machine took control of it's own accord and threw me off. The touch pads take some getting used to, but feel like second nature after a few plays. It'll take a bit longer to learn how to use the pads with more mouse-oriented games though (Enter the Gungeon comes to mind).
Pro's:
*Fits comfortably in the hands of an adult
*Tactile touch pad function gives a feeling of texture and orientation not unlike a trackball
*Responsive buttons
*Controls can be mapped to most games or existing user controls exported, making most officially unsupported games more or less ready-to-play
*Lengthy battery life on just two AA's
*Barely noticeable latency between the Steam Controller and Steam Link over a decent wireless connection with cable speeds
Con's:
*Not suited to every game style (Don't even think about RTS's or fighters like MKX or SFV).
*While controls can be mapped for unofficially supported games, it's a lengthy trial-and-error process for beginners and not all uploaded control schemes are particularly well thought out
*The transition from analogue stick to touchpad for FPS's will definitely take some getting used to for newbies
*While the battery life is great, they're still batteries. Future models need a rechargeability feature.
*Trackpad sensitivity options are too inconsistent - works in some games, in others the changes are barely noticeable.

Note:  This review was written for just the Emporer Edition of the game.  I have not yet tried it with the expansion.  If I ever get the expansion, I will update my review.
I felt conflicted about whether to recommend this game or not.  In the end, I decided that the pros outweigh the cons.  That being said, it has a lot of missed potential, and I hope they improve on a few things for the sequel.
Pros:
- The game is a lot of fun, especially beginning and mid game.  A lot of thought has been put into certain details, such as the tech tree, which makes it fun to explore all the different techs.
- You can customize your own race, and choose its advantages and disadvantages.  This, to me, is one of its strongest points.  I had a lot of fun creating my own alien races to play as and play against
- The game has an AI function that allows you to automate system management.  I didn't discover this feature until my 2nd playthrough, and let me tell you, it sped up the game a ton!  Now, you still need to keep tabs on what it is building and where, as the AI will not always make the choices that best suits your strategy, but for the most part it really speeds up the mid game.
Cons:
- The game as a steep learning curve.  The tutorial is more or less useless.  It took a lot of playing around with settings and features before I was able to figure out the ins and outs of the game.
- Ship combat is a little boring, albeit fun to watch at least.
- The End game leaves something to be desired.  Once you get past the mid game stage, the game tends to drag on.  This is especially true if you are trying to achieve different types of victories, such as the science or diplomatic.
In conclusion, This game is fun, but requires patience towards the end.  I hope that when they do the sequel, they tap into the potential that this game had.

Endless Space - Emperor Edition is a turn-based strategy game where the object is to meet one of the conditions for Victory, Expansion, Scientific, Diplomatic, Wonder, Economic and so on. You can play in a randomly generated galaxy, the size of your own choosing, with up to 8 opponent empires. Endless Space also allows for full modding and multiplayer capability.
There are several stock empires ready for you to play as, or you can choose to create your own. You start in your capital system and then must explore nearby systems, colonize new planets, research and unlock new technologies, locate strategic resources to upgrade and more. As turn-based games go, this game was a lot of fun. I spent Five hours playing and ended up not getting much done in the way of review writing yesterday. The Space combat portion of the game, involves a different type of combat. Other reviews and game analysis have referred to it as akin to Rock-Paper-Scissors, and I think that is a pretty valid observation. Of course you can always allow the computer to auto-resolve the conflict, in which case the game takes into account the type and strength of ships involved in the conflict and randomly generates an outcome.
All in all, I enjoyed Endless Space - Emperor Edition and may go out on the web to look for player-created Mods to make the game more challenging. If you enjoy these types of turn-based strategy games, give Endless Space a try.

Although I do enjoy playing Blitz doesn't necessarily mean that I support each decision that WG has decided to take with this. In its earlier iterations, it was more akin to WOT-lite, whereas now although still retaining the main components of WOT has changed it's feeling.
1.SPARE PARTS/ "WAITING GAME"
Unlocking equipment with a third currency "spare parts" and including times to wait seems that WG want to hold some key elements in competitive play from it's community and hold hostage until time is up (especially higher in the tiers). Waiting upwards of 3 days for a single slot and unable to research the others in the same file also slows this down; making not only an experience grind but now the "waiting game" as I call it.
2.NOT EVERYTHING IS BAD
Though I am still just quite the casual gamer, I do find enjoyment when I can find those random matches with others and have a bang up time because teamwork is awesome. Being able from time to time unlock premium tanks is a plus. IE Tankenstein and now the GuP "Kuro Mori Mine, Panzer Anko SP., and the Hetzer" is quite nice.
3.GAMEPLAY
Doesn't last all too long and is often quite enjoyable, it's called BLITZ for a reason. Adding new lines slowly and fleshing out old ones is always appreciated. Though there is a disparity in ability for PC vs Mobile since its expansion as PC users can more easily maneuver and aim than when compared to mobile touch controls. The implemented non crossplatform option works as advertised though it does limit the pool of players thus I find that I use my PC as opposed to my iPad.
FINAL THOUGHTS ( June 10, 2017)
-Thouroughly enjoyable for all players looking for tank on tank action though some mechanics are far from perfect
-MOST content unlockable without having to pay, though it is a struggle especially with some glaring "money grabs" though it is a company providing entertainment has to make its revenue somewhere
-Sweet visuals and asthetics as both the vehicles and environment are pleasing to the eye
-Events that keep one coming back for more as well as implemented clan/training rooms

I played the 2003 Crimsonland and it was one of the best top-down shooter and even if I prefer the old art style, this is still one of the BEST top-down shooter I have ever played.

Crimsonland only knows one trick, but it is a very good trick. You are... some guy with a gun, standing in the middle of a completely flat plain somewhere presumably not on Earth. You are surrounded by perpetually spawning monsters- aliens, zombies, giant spiders, giant beetles, giant spider that gradually split up into hordes and hordes of smaller spiders as you shoot them, etc. Shoot them until they die. Collect better weapons and power-ups they leave behind. Level up. Kill more of them with your bigger, shootier weapons until they overrun and kill you. Rinse. Repeat.
Yes, there are quests, but they only exist to give you more stuff with which to kill monsters in the Survival modes. Each quest you complete unlocks a new weapon or Perk (perks are specific character benefits you choose when you kill enough monsters to level up; like exploding when you die, shooting fireballs when you reload, shooting smaller fireball every few seconds, shooting one big fireball every few seconds... you get the idea). These facilitate your blowing up of stuff in subsequent games. No story or dialogue at all, but this game really doesn't need any. Crimsonland is about the simple joy of holding down the left mouse button, emptying your Rocket Minigun's 16-round magazine in three-odd seconds, and watching critters explode like blood-and-meat-filled balloons.
This game is great. It still has the awesomeness from when it was a game several years ago, but has an updated UI, more weapons and perks, and new game modes!

I'll just start by saying, I recommend this with some caveats. Read below for my experience with the controller.
A mouse still is and likely always will be the most accurate method of aiming. Though this controller has two touchpads, it can't quite match the speed and precision of a mouse. HOWEVER, if you are like me and suffer from Repetitive Stress Injuries from the aforementioned mouse, then this is probably your best option.
In some cases where the game was designed with joysticks in mind, a standard xbox controller might still be preferable. I don't particularly like using joystick emulation with the Steam Controller, even though the haptic feedback is eerily good. That said, anywhere a mouse can be emulated the Steam Controller starts to shine. When I first tried playing Skyrim, the default settings emulated a joystick, and it didn't seem to work very well. Eventually, I decided I would create my own custom bindings for the game, and after about an hour of tweaking here and there I was in business.
You can take that as either a pro or a con. Some games work reasonably well out of the box with only a few tweaks here or there, while others are horrendous until you put forth some time and effort to create a custom mapping. I'm the kind of person that tweaks keymapping, mouse settings, graphics settings, and even some .ini files before I ever even start a new campaign, so it's worth the legwork for me up front to get it how I like it. Unfortunately, some games will have issues if you mix and match control types. For instance, if you have everything set up like a controller, but you want to emulate a mouse for looking around, it might not work as you expect. This is usually where I'll use the default controller bindings as a template and remap everything for KBM. The software is VERY customizable, and I feel as though I've only scratched the surface of what's possible.
On to the hardware. The button and pad placement has always felt a little odd and cumbersome. I'm not sure how else you could lay it out given the fact there are two large touchpads on the controller, but it's something to note if you have tiny hands. The grip buttons on the back are simply brilliant, and it's hard to imagine how this isn't a standard feature on all modern controllers. The touchpads are a mixed bag for me. While they are reasonable accurate, I find my finger skipping across the surface if my fingers aren't bone dry. I would rather the surfaces be made of the same glass you find on laptops like the macbooks so your movements can be completely smooth. Initially I wasn't a fan of the + indention on the left pad, but over time I grew to like it since it helps you find the right area of the pad when you're using the menu overlay. I do wish Valve would have included some form of pressure sensitivity on the buttons like you have on DualShock controllers. It would allow for even more possibilities. I have no complaints about the triggers or the joysticks as they seem to do everything I ask from them. The Gyro is actually a surprisingly good feature. Often times I'll set up the right touchpad with a higher sensitivity and then bind the gyro to the left trigger (aim down sight). This allows me to get the crosshairs close to the target with the touchpad, then while aiming I can lean the controller for fine adjustments. This is pretty much required for headshots. Surprisingly, I found games like Left 4 Dead work pretty well with a medium sensitivity on the touchpad and a relatively high sensitivity on the gyro. It makes it possible to target a lot of enemies in quick succession. I recommend playing around with this until you find a combination that works for you.
As I stated in the beginning, I recommend this with a few caveats. If you want something you can plug in and have a flawless playing experience without much configuration, then you might not want this product. However, if you want a controller for PC games and you don't might tinkering with the mapping to get it just the way you like it, then this is a great option for you. I recommend watching a few reviews on YouTube to get a feel for how it works.
Here's a small list of games I've tried (not a complete list):
Left 4 Dead 2: Works pretty well with the right tweaks.
Portal 2: Works pretty well out of the box, but some tweaks make it better.
Bioshock: I personally found the controller emulation to be a bit unremarkable. I ended up creating a custom map for this that worked out decently.
Team Fortress 2: It works reasonably well (better with tweaks), but you had better bring your A-game.
Borderlands 2 and Pre-Sequel: With the right tweaks it is as though the Steam Controller was made for this game. The touchpad / gyro combo works very well here.
Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes: Works reasonably well, but might increase your stress level if you're used to playing with a mouse.
Skyrim: Crap out of the box, but with custom mappings it's quite enjoyable.
Firewatch: Pretty much perfect out of the box.
Skyborn: Works well enough out of the box, but some buttons are duplicated.
Dirt 3: If you find controllers adequate for racing games, then maybe you'll like it. I wasn't happy with either the touch input or gyro in this game. A wheel is probably your best bet for the best experience.
Warframe: Good after tweaking your mapping.
Trine: Works decently out of the box, but I tweaked it anyway.
Alien Breed: After some tweaks it's actually quite enjoyable to play with the steam controller.
Magicka: One of the first games I tried it with and abandoned it due to some weird bugs with the menu overlay. I may revisit this later to see if I can get a working custom mapping. Not good out of the box.
World of Warcraft: Effectively useless out of the box, but I actually spent a while creating a custom mapping that worked surprisingly well. Given the number of buttons you'll need to play it, you will need to use menu overlays and mode switching extensively. It's very gratifying once you get it worked out, though.

Before I purchased this, I read a few reviews on it and got it on sale knowing that it wasn't going to be my main controller.  I have been surprised at how much I've enjoy using it though.  What's most surprising is the depth of customization that this controller offers.  You can tweak every single aspect of how you use this controller in ways that I didn't know were possible.  You can completely reprogram every single button and control and setup profiles for each game with mode switching to change how the controller works on the fly.  It's very impressive to say the least.
The challenge is the fact that it doesn't have a proper right stick of course and that's what's going to be the biggest turn off for most people.  The emulation on the right touch pad is very very good but does take some getting used to, to the point that most people will not favor it when they are so engrained with how and XBox or Playstation controller work.
For me, just holding this controller is far more comfortable than any other that I've used, it just feels natrual.  I also love the buttons on the grip.  The default programing for most games sets those buttons up pretty well for the most needed functions.
The placement of the buttons is a little uncomfortable at first but after I used it for a while I was fine with it.  Speaking of buttons, the right touchpad can also be configured to serve as the buttons either by clicking in the directions of the button or just by touching the pad.  I can't get used to that configuration but I imagine if someone could it would be pretty crazy.
Lastly, the customization doesn't stop at the button configurations.  The controller plays a melody when it powers up and that can be customized as well as the controllers name and that shows up on Steam when in big screen mode.  On top of that, it can be paired up with multiple devices and you can cycle through those when you power it up.
So, yeah it's an amazing controller, it just takes some getting used to and for most people don't expect to replace your current controller.  It's great for games that do not have native controller support though because of all of the options and community profiles out there.  If they would have designed this controller with a right stick it would be the only controller that I would use.

Update: The bumper has broken 5 times now. Although the rest of this review still holds true, I can not recommend a product that repeatedly breaks. This last controller, the bottom paddle broke, the left bumper broke, and the usb connection port became loose causing frequent disconnects. I am trying to return it for a refund at this point as I no longer wish to RMA it every couple of months for a broken button. If they would rework the buttons to improve integrity, it would be one of the best controllers on the market. But as is, it isn't worth the hassle.
To start I love this controller. It makes other controllers like the xbox 360 controller feel 'sharp' on your hands. It did take me a couple of weeks to adjust to holding this controller in which time my hands did experience discomfort. After I adjusted my grip, however, my hands exerience much less fatigue than with a 360 controller. I have to admit that I have not used any of the more recent playstation controllers to compare.
The bottom paddle style buttons are nice, but it takes a while to not press them accidentally and to be able to press them consitently in a pinch, I recommend putting less important actions on the paddles to help alleviate this issue.
Other good things include the adjustability. You can program the touch pads and hat and even use a gyro to control camera in games. I have yet to use these functions to their fullest potential but I still see the value of having the options.
Battery life is also a major plus. Two double A batteries last me well over the 8 hour timeframe stated by Valve.
There are some drawbacks to this controller. Mainly the bumpers are not very durable. Rocket league is the main game I play, and I use the left bumper as my boost (ie: heavy use), and I have broken the part that allows the button to click twice already. I returned the first one to valve and am about to return this one to valve as well. The return process was pretty painless, but getting the replacement took three weeks. I actually had to submit a ticket asking about my return as I had confirmation they had received the controller and then they shipped my new one and 2 minutes later sent me a response that it had already been shipped... lol nice one valve.
Other con is how poor big picture mode is, which isn't really the controller, but it is the interface valve expects you to utilize with the controller so worth a mention. I have mine default off and only use it when I need to set up a profile for a new game.
Pros:
Ergonomic
Great button layout and options
Battery life
Programability
Easy RMA process
Cons:
Poor bumper durability
Adjustment period (minor, but noticeable)
Big picture mode needs work
Lengthy RMA turn around

I purchased one of these over Christmas - before doing so most of the information I looked up seemed conflicting, so I thought I'd right a write summary of my own experiences for anyobody else in the same position.
Basically I had a trapped nerve in my shoulder and was supposed to be resting and I thought this would be good for playing games on my sofa while resting but most people probably don't care about that.  The short review is that I have recommended this device, but in the circumstances it's a cautious recommendation.
The cost of shipping added significantly to the thing - and although it turned up quickly and with excellent tracking information that is something that needs to be taken into account.  When it arrived it looked very cheap and plasticky compared to the picture on Steam.  Mine also arrived with a big ugly scratch down the front.  It also felt very light and flimsy, and while I was feeling quite pessimistic by then once the batteries were stuffed in it felt surprisingly well balanced.
The thing connected with Steam without issue once I stuffed the USB thing into a USB port.  Working with games was another matter.  The first few I tried didn't appear to be compatable with Steam Big Picture mode.  Despite working previously they gave error messages and crashed on start up.  Fortunately both the controller and games worked outside of Big Picture mode - but switching back and forth to change controller settings and actually run the game was a pain in the bum.  Especially as the Big Picture UI appears to have been designed by a sadist.
Some games worked well with the controller without any setting up.  I was happily head-shotting people in Borderlands the Pre-Sequel within seconds and it felt very intuitive - despite the game occasionally flipping between XBox 360 and Keyboard/Mouse prompts I was really happy.  I like strategy games and felt the controller was really great for games like Endless Legend and Civ: Beyond Earth - it would have been nicer if the games had native support to take full advantage of the controller, but I still felt that it did a great job of emulating keyboard/mouse controls to efficiently play the titles.
Other games were a complete nightmare.  It took me three days to get Skyrim Special Edition working with the controller.  Apparently Bethesda games are a major issue because they can't support keyboard/mouse and controller input at the same time.  The solution was supposedly to disable controller support in-game but for me something during the launcher still detected a controller and switched to 360 controller even if I was trying to emulate mouse/keyboard - which left me unable to do anything, let alone take advantage of the controllers unique features.
Eventually I discovered that I had to start the game with the Steam controller emulating a 360 controller and then walk out of range with it and then back in range with it so when it came back in range it would load my previously exported keyboard/mouse settings and work how I wanted.  Simply disconnecting and reconnecting the device didn't have the same effect, only walking out of range...
Although once I had the controller working it was an absolute joy to use, google suggests I’m clearly not the only person to have to use such a ridiculous workaround and plenty of other games seem to require similar levels of mucking about.
To conclude - as hardware this thing works much better than I expected.  But until mainstream software support catches up (if ever) consider it very much somewhat experimental and potentially frustrating.

Endless Space is a fine 4X strategy games from a very enthusiastic developer, however it lacks on certain parts and fails to deliver a fully fun experience.
Let’s just start by saying that the DLC (disharmony) is a
for this game since it improves on numerous aspects and gameplay. So either buy it in the bundle (gold edition) on doesn’t at all.
The game is not a hardcore space simulation rather than a more casual but fun take on the 4x genera.  It’ fairly simplistic and you don’t have much “tools” in your hand to manage your empire. You will colonize planets to planets with your colony ship, discover and exploit resources, build improvements, creating, customizing and assembling ships until your meet the enemy. Leveling your heroes and deal with Random Events are also a thing, but that’s about it.
Combat is similar to Galactic Civilization where you don’t have much “live” impact on the battle. You need to choose a card (representing a battle tactic) and match with the enemy’s card and that’s pretty much it (also you can set formations and attack pattern). The battle will automatically goes on without the player getting involved, and it all comes down on how did you customized the ships and what card you choose.
And that’s where the game lacks a bit. Although combat is fun, there is not much variety to go for meaning that there are no special attacks, weapons or tactics (you will discover cards later on, but none of them are OP) that will surely break the enemy. You can only choose kinetic, beam and missile weapons (or combination of the 3), assemble the ship and hope the enemy did not develop defenses against the chosen weapon. I find this a little bit lacking.
Another problem is the late game/endgame. Victory conditions are ridiculous for Science and the Invulnerable Empire building victory (Wonder) requires 40-50 turns (so around 170 tops) with massive science and labor points already. The game is TOO LONG for these victory types. The only thing you can go for is Domination and/or Score. But the AI is like a brick spamming ships and improvements like hell and even an easy AI will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ When there is just 1 or 2 AI left you will find yourself in a trench war where everyone is ultra-powered and since there are no special weapons or tactics you cannot break each other. And if you go to war it will be a constant battle for one system since the AI will just spam ships faster than you can defeat his fleet. After some turns combat will be so frequent (you will have 4-5 battle every turn) that you just stop caring and pressing the quick combat button.
This is when you will turn to multiplayer instead. However there is a major flaw/bug in the game which is called the De-synch bug. It turns out when you play with a friend to beat the AI the game will freeze up on random turns and you cannot go forward or back. You need to reload a previous save, hovewer the game will stuck at the same turn. THE END! It’s a pretty much
. I have opened threads and contacted support numerous times but these issues have not been resolved for a long time now and there seems to be no fix for it. Many people suffer from this issue, not just me. (see below the forum thread)
This bug essentially makes it impossible to play Multiplayer, and sometimes even when you 1v1 will freeze up.
-------------------------------------
Endless Space is a good 4x game from a pretty much new developer.  I would say even though its flaws I like the game, and did not regret buying and supporting it. The Devs are nice guys, although direct customer service are not their strengths (as mentioned above) Now that Endless Space 2 is announced I hope they listen to the critics and make it a truly awesome game.
If you are looking for a decent 4X game with great graphics and you can overlook its limits than you can safely purchase Endless Space.

Mechwarrior Online, for better or worse its a free to play game.
If you know Battletech then you know this game. Lumbering warmachines known as mechs are used around the universe in order to control or regulate stability. etc etc...
This game is always being updated. So bare that in mind as I give a quick (ehh if you read fast!) review on the game at its current state.
-Graphics: Depending on your graphics card this game can be tolerably nice to fairly good looking. The Crytek Engine is put to use but its nothing exceptional. Its a heavy load for any card when the graphics are cranked. Yes, even with the newer Nvidia cards out there (GTX 1080). Generally the mechs are highly detailed and some are very impressive. They have done a great job at bringing the mechs from the FASA world come to life. However, the maps are not that great looking. They are bland and theres is little interaction between the player and the environment.
-Control: It pilots very similarly to previous mechwarrior games. Everything is there from night vision to picture-in-picture zoom. You will have no problems getting around even from the first time. As long as you think of your mech as tank (main gun may face a separate direction from the tracks) you will have no problems adapting.
- Fun Factor: Alright. I cant lie to you. How fun this game can be is based on several factors. 1) your skill and willing to survive and destroy 2) Skill and cooperation from your team mates   3) your ability to grind for C-bills (in game currency). Yeah this game can be very fun and even addictive, but really you have to get in the mind set that everything you obtain, you have to work for. No other way to puyt it. You can buy mechs using C-bills or with actual cash. Initially, buying them with C-bills may seem easy. That is, until you realize you are getting a bit of a c-bill boost if its your first time. After 24 matches, the grinding begins. Now, dont think this is bad. This game feels mostly complete (80% in my opinion) and paying 30-40$ for real mechs or boosters is not that bad of a deal. Ultimately, you are helping the devs. However, this game can be fun. If you experiment with different tonnages of mechs you'll see they all add a bit of flavor to the fight (except the medium mechs.. man they suck!) Dont let all that turn you off, The devs included a pool of mech variants you can try for free and they constantly keep changing them out of rotation. so you cant B*tch, alright?
-Sound: All the sounds are there. Everything fits as it should. Pulse lasers have a heavy thump sound to them, Lasers sound... lasery? Ballistics have that loud thunderous crack. Yeah, this game nails it. You will feel at home. My only complain is the UI voice. Its a female voice but rather than sounding digitally or robotic she kind of sounds like.. shes right next to you. They should have made her like in the previous mechwarrior games. Yeah seriously my only gripe.
-Game Mechanics: Man, you could really write a whole guide regarding the mechanics of the game. Let's just focus on mech customization. There are 4 classes of mechs. They differ in tonnages. The lights being the lightest are also the fastest, but they lack firepower. Mediums are a bit heavier than lights but they have more armor and sometimes more room for weapons. The heavies are much bigger but also a bit slower. They are well rounded in speed and firewpower. The Assaults are the juggernauts of the game. These mechs are expensive, slow and can carry an array of weapons. You cannot take one one of these on your own. Apart from the four classifications of mechs, there are also 2 types of mechs. There are Inner Sphere mechs, which are traditional and well known. Their capabilities are well rounded. The other Type are known as the Clan mechs. Their origin is unknown but they have newer classes of mechs and are often regarded as superior to I.S. mechs. Every mech can be fully customized, from jump jets, to weapon arrangements (mechs can be allocated weapons according to hardpoint) to arm actuators. Battletech at its finest.
After reading all that (you did, didnt you?) you can pretty much imagine the scale and ingenuity of tactics and mech designs. The community brings this game alive and its been going strong for several years now. The devs do a fine job to keep the game current, from graphics to map design. Its always evolving.
So if you are having doubts about this game, just give it a try. If you are a fan of FASA's battletech lore, this a no brainer. download it. You have nothing to lose.

TL/DR: As a long term (~30 years now) fan of all things Battletech, MWO does some things incredibly well, but the glacial pace of progress combined with a dev team who at this point can only be described as occasionally well meaning but incompetent results in a hollow and frustrating play experience. For fans of MW2 Mercs, MW3 and MW4, sadly this is probably not the game you're looking for. I can only hope that in the future there will be more and better Battletech games.
Longer version:
I paid for a founders package for MWO back in September 2012, long before the game was ever available here on Steam. I paid based on the advertising that was on the MWO site at that time. I paid based on the notion that we were going to get some sort of simulation of warfare in the Battletech universe, the game being some sort of mech-simulator-lite with a long-term game based on actual war, from the grand strategic level across the Inner Sphere (and beyond) all the way down to the tactical battlefield level. The game then came out in closed beta and I was thrilled to finally be back in the cockpit of my beloved Atlas assault mech which, in one guise or another, I've been piloting since the mid 80's.
So why the negative review? Several reasons. Before I get in to them, I should say that the artwork, mech design and general aesthetic of the game is the best that I've ever seen in a Battletech PC game. The chap who models the mechs, the textures etc. has done amazing work and fully deserves to find employment in any AAA game dev studio.
The issues I take with the game are:
1. As a founder & huge Battletech fan, and therefore having financially contributed to the very existence of both the game and PGI as a viable company, being bluntly told by a senior member of the dev team that people like me (hard core Battletech fans) are, and I quote, "Not the target audience" for the game felt like a brutal slap in the face. Thanks for your money, but you're not really who we're aiming the game at. Really? Really? As one of very many founders who directly contributed to enabling the game to be made, being told that felt alienating in the extreme, and was frankly very difficult to forgive. This one thing above all else still makes me feel bitter to some degree.
2. The glacial pace of actual content release. As time went on it quickly became apparent that mech pack after mech pack was produced and released (for exorbitant prices, but that's another discussion) in an obvious ploy to distract the player base with shiny stuff so that fewer complaints would be made about the lack of actual content. Almost FOUR YEARS down the line, and we were given something other than endless variations on the theme of team deathmatch... A couple of months ago? Many view the game as having an unacceptably slow pace of development.
3. Lack of community engagement & listening to the vocal minority. I can understand the lack of engagement on the game forum, considering how blisteringly critical it can be, and I understand that the player base has hardly ever been united on anything. That being said, the two things that come to mind on which the entire player base did agree were that nobody wanted a 3rd person view in the game and that nobody wanted a coolant flush. What happened? We got both, pointlessly wasting an unknown amount of dev time that could have been better spent on other areas of the game development.
4. Communication again. There never really was any sort of 'golden period' of communication from the dev team. I thought, and continue to think, that it's inexcusable that every form of communication is used except the official game forum. Back in closed beta hundreds of early CB players made lengthy detailed threads there, suggesting features using well reasoned and polite argument. Pretty much all of it was summarily ignored. Later someone, I don't remember who, suggested that for the dev team to make more use of the forum - the official game forum - would constitute an unacceptable drain on company time. My response: utter drivel. How long does it take to type an official post on the forum? Minutes? By all means use all available means of communication, but the fact that the least engaged method is the official game forum does not exactly engender confidence in the communication abilities of the dev team.
5. Game balance. Wild changes are made to weapon and mech stats with each new patch, with obviously barely any actual play testing being done. Newly released mechs are usually vastly superior to older models wihch serves only to create a power creep dynamic that essentially forces players to buy incredibly expensive new mech packs in order to remain competitive. I have no idea if this is deliberate or an unintended consequence of the inability of the dev team to play their own game to a high level.
Having taken part in organised team matches and also in the solo match queue I've both been pleasantly surprised and at the same time horrified by the differences between how the game plays in team matches (e.g. MRBC games) and the actual group / solo queues.
Whether or not PGI had or have passion for the BT universe is open to question. From my personal experience I think they at least did at the start of the development process. What I think is more open to debate, and what I'm starting to seriously question, is their professionalism and competence. More fool me really - had I bothered to be diligent and researched their prior history as game developers I would have been unlikely to have ever paid them a penny for anything.
From a personal perspective the game as it is can certainly be fun, but I look back today at what I was lead to believe MWO would be and I can't help feeling frustration at the obvious waste of potential, broken promises and utterly incompetent PR efforts on the part of the company.
If microtransaction-supported e-sport team deathmatch is what MWO is destined to become, then I'm done with the game. I will not support something that has only a thin, superficial veneer of Battletech IP over a fundamental game that I no longer derive any pleasure from playing. I never dreamed that I'd get to this point, but I'm done. I'd genuinely, dearly love to be proved wrong and see some amazing changes in the future, but from everything I've heard and read I think the direction being taken is fundamentally flawed, and certainly isn't the MWO I thought I was signing up for. Those of you who enjoy the game, more power to you, I hope you continue to do so.

I have been playing WoTB for a very long time now, and my hours on PC only represent a small fraction of my total playtime because I came from mobile myself. As of now several people are hating on and downvoting Blitz for the recent "scandal" of WG threatening a Youtuber/streamer by copyright striking his video about speaking against WG's P2P system. First of all, my review will be purely based on WoTB as a game, and not WG's dirty work, but of course I am completely against any threat and attempt to stop somebody from using his free speech.
World of Tanks Blitz as game right now is a fun, enjoyable game that provides entertaining gameplay for mobile gamers and PC gamers alike. With about 6 countries and multiple tank 'lines" to select from, you can be sure that with the right attitude, you will be here for a long time. Gameplay is smooth and easy to learn. Many different systems and modes are there to keep you entertained, like training rooms, tournaments, and seasonal events. Now the largest, and most talked about problem in this game is it's microtransaction system. Many people have complained and have bashed WarGaming for the unfair and biased Pay 2 Play mechanic of this game in where you need to invest real, hard earned money in order to progress and get better at this game. My opinion in this game just like many is that no, you DO NOT need to spend a single dime in this game in order to get better or to progress. And much like many games, all you really need to do is to be patient and grind, any person who has played this long enough knows that. And although I do agree that this WG is at frequent times unfair and greedy due to things like Pay to get tanks, premium shells, and several other implemented tank, crew, performance boosts, I still think that this game is not completely unplayble and is still enjoyable for us that don't have money.
Final Statement: Is it playable for F2Ps? Yes.
Are the microtransactions unbalanced and favored for the P2P? Pretty much, but with the right attitude and patience, getting to tier 10 or even winning a match is still very possible for anybody.

This game is absolutely amazing.
Something that usually lacks in the modern day shooter is challenge and reward. Big titles like Battlefield and Call of Duty all have a similar run and gun style, where kills are racked up and skill is based on kill streaks and reflexes. Tribes Ascend however is a game based on skill in aiming, about being precise with your aim and your movement, and each kill is difficult, and when they happen you feel a greater sense of accomplishment than you find in other shooters.
Tribes Ascend gameplay is fast paced involving hurtling over hills and sliding down them to accelerate to traverse the map. Combine this with around sixteen players and projectile weapons with massive dip and you get a fast paced and challenging shooter.
Unfortunately this game doesn't get enough attention, as a new player it is difficult to get into since the community is so small and many of the people who play now are scarily good. There is a level up system that some servers use to restrict veterans from stomping on newbies, but again you have the problem that there aren't many newbies.

There are Mechwarrior fans, and there are Battletech fans. If you are looking for a game that that is like Mechwarrior 4... this game is not that. You probably won't even like it.
If you are fundamentally incapable of playing on an impromptu team... you will not like it.
If you are not capable of ever adjusting tactics to new situations and the strengths/weaknesses of other random players... you will not like it.
If you think of yourself as being an invincible Rambo who should, through your own sheer awesomeness and force of will, be able to carry a team single-handlely, or at least get a rush of endorphins at how super-duper-awesome you are (i.e. you throw a tantrum every time you are humbled)... you will absolutely hate this game.
This game is not CounterStrike. This game is not Call of duty. This game is not a hum-dee-dum casual game like World of [Whatever].
This game is difficult. You will lose. A lot. You will play against people much better than you while on a team much worse than you. And that's tough, but life isn't fair. You want grittiness? That's it. You want challenge? That's it. You will grind. You must grind. And you will get batter for it. You will be frustrated sometimes. Good. That makes the next victory all the sweeter.
And for all of those things I listed above, this game is totally awesome.
There are plenty of whining people who give this game negative reviews. I strongly suggest you read them and evaluate if that sounds like the kind of stuff you would complain about. If you see a review complaining about the mere existence of "support" mechs... consider how that person must react to being on a team. If you see reviews that say "X weapon is the best and Y weapon is the worst", and especially when you see that from different people about literally every combination of weapons in the game, consider how knowledgable these people must actually be about the system they are complaining about.
And ignore them all.
Try the game. If you don't like it; well, it was free and you can come back here to complain.
But, on the other hand... you might just find it to be the best damned real-time approach to BattleTech that has ever been realized.

Of course I have to use the 'P'-word to describe this game. Test chambers, announcer guide narrator, things placed in a spot to open an exit, gun-tool that does stuff. If you need a break from the thousands and thousands of Portal levels out there but still want to run around and open up doors, definitely give ChromaGun a shot.
The premise is simple: Like-colors attract like-colors. Spray things the same color to attract them, or off-color to let them go. Open the exit door.
I'm halfway through now, and am enjoying the game a LOT. Color coding things is starting to get tougher, where I have to plan many steps ahead, programming the wall colors to lead a color somewhere when I'm somewhere else. Love it.
If there's a negative to the game so far, it's that I wish that I could undo a move. Not re-paint a thing ... but just step back in time to undo / un-paint and proceed again from there. Working on a level for 5 minutes, then realizing that I should have done something differently is ok, but having to restart the level from scratch is a bit of a bummer. Add to that the gun ... I wish that the color pipes roatated or changed to match the color ring. I keep thinking I'm spraying yellow (on top) when my ring is blue or red. That's not a big thing, just me wishing for a neat little improvement.

This game is absolutely amazing.
Something that usually lacks in the modern day shooter is challenge and reward. Big titles like Battlefield and Call of Duty all have a similar run and gun style, where kills are racked up and skill is based on kill streaks and reflexes. Tribes Ascend however is a game based on skill in aiming, about being precise with your aim and your movement, and each kill is difficult, and when they happen you feel a greater sense of accomplishment than you find in other shooters.
Tribes Ascend gameplay is fast paced involving hurtling over hills and sliding down them to accelerate to traverse the map. Combine this with around sixteen players and projectile weapons with massive dip and you get a fast paced and challenging shooter.
Unfortunately this game doesn't get enough attention, as a new player it is difficult to get into since the community is so small and many of the people who play now are scarily good. There is a level up system that some servers use to restrict veterans from stomping on newbies, but again you have the problem that there aren't many newbies.

A little known fact is that guns are a great deal more fun to take apart and clean,
than to fire upon stuff; little known to people who does not know or love guns that is.
Firing guns is noisy and the smell is terrible, and you generally have to do it from fairly uncomfortable positions, such as lying down and oh my actual, was a dog in this very
place a few minutes ago?  How do I know?
And then there's wars, were other people are inexplicably pointing their guns at you and repeatedly squeezing the trigger.  Not cool, man.
Disassembling a weapon is a bit like reading a book: you get to know the mind of
the people who designed and built that thing.  There may not be much to those mind,
admittedly, but it's still communication, and some of them were quite clever, never
mind that mounting a 120 incher on top of a bicycle was a dumb idea.
This game is not a game but a very nice interactive book on guns that pushes you
to learn their make and operations by gamifying them, thanks to the lack in the lives
of many of us of a sour-faced instructor who will ruin your hearing forever screaming
in your ear every time that darn bolt gets stuck into its guide.  And no, bolts come
out and get in flawlessly every time in WoG… and I don't how to feel about that.
The interface is adequate, not perfect, it has quirks, but it's all right they don't get
in the way too much.
Unlocking most weapons does require a fair amount of grinding, but I rather see
that as the point than a P2W feature.  Memorising the correct sequence of
operations IRL requires repeating it many times, hence drilling rather than grinding
would be a more accurate description of what happens.
Which brings us to the way in which WoG is not really a simulation of weapon
dis-assembly: it does not develop muscle memory, which is the thing that makes
field stripping a gun so instinctive that you'll be able to do it in perfect darkness,
but that’s not the developers' fault of course.
Here's waiting for the Holodeck… still waiting.

For a very long while, I used a PS3 controller instead of putting down the money to just get an Xbox controller for my PC gaming. Having long since grown tired of my controller coming disconnected, I decided to buy what was supposedly a better controller for PC gaming, at least compared to an Xbox controller or nameless gamepad. Having heard almost nothing but praise for the oh-so prestigious Steam Controller, I caved and bought it. My feelings are far from mixed. I do not like anything about this controller. Why? Let's get into that.
The feel:
Well, for starts, it feels cheap; dreadfully so. When I first picked up the controller, I was fully expecting it to break if I got a bit too invested in the game and just tightened my grip. This, of course, didn't happen, but the feeling was that of a controller's shell, not of something fully fleshed out.
The play:
Steam wanted something innovative; something grand! They wanted to make a controller that would blow away all other controllers, taking away the bad and leaving nothing to be desired...so what do they do? Take away a joystick and add a touchpad that works about as well as a laptop trackpad for gaming. Hey, if you can use a trackpad like a pro and game all day long on it, this controller might actually be for you, but other than that...no. The point of this controller is to improve one's gameplay experience, so what are the major differences between it and, for example, a typical Xbox 360 controller?
-Bumpers on the grips for easy button access
-Repositioned Y, X, A, and B buttons
-Right Joystick replaced with touchpad in place of typical buttons
All of that is immediately visible from the picture, yes, but from the reviews, I thought that it would be more accessable and comfortable than the typical controller! Alas, I was mislead, and the positioning was not only dreadful, but the bumpers on the bottom were almost completely mandatory for playing Dark Souls III, which was the only game I could stomach with this dreadful "controller".
This wretched device boasts for improved accuracy with a touchpad, but it makes looking around in even a Third-Person game far harder, so I can't even imagine how an FPS would go, which is something they advertise it for as well.
"Experience a new level of precise control for your favorite games." They aren't wrong...it's a whole new level of low, because although yes, I may not like the way it feels, which seemingly, I'm alone in this, but there is a very, very large issue that trumps even just the awful build.

This is purely a STEAMpad. I know, a bit dramatic, but you cannot play any other games than what you have on Steam, at least for the most part. Sometimes, you can manage to play a game by addding it to your Steam Library, opening Steam in Big Picture and running it that way, but I did this with 12 games and only 1 actually worked. Even the game I Am Setsuna, a game with full support for this controller, refused to accept the controller since it wasn't directly running through steam, just launching.
It is safe to say that, even if you have the Steam Beta client, which supposedly is working to fix this, you can still only play games you have in your immediate Steam Library, making it quite the inept controller.
Final verdict: 28/100
Don't buy this; save your money. You can get a controller that works far better and actually doesn't feel like a trashy prototype for far less than half of this.

Not satisfied with it. Purchased during Christmas 2016 Sale - Cost was ~$43 after shipping.
