So I got the Steam Controller & was optimistic & excited. I was sort of burnt from the start when I read a review that mentioned the cheap feel of the controller - that is absolutely correct, in my opinion. That aside, the touchpads seemed pretty innovative and a cool concept. Really wanted to like it.
First of all, I don't like layout or the feel of the controller - maybe it's more comfortable for Xbox owners. I think there's 2 problems - the joystick and XYAB buttons are low and toward the center, which makes you have to reach for them (I do not have small hands, either).
Second, the touchpads are big, to the point where I can't find a comfortable place to rest my thumbs. If you rest your thumbs on the touchpads, (depending on the game, config) you will end up moving something and causing a problem.
First game I played with the controller was MKX. Loaded up a community config to use the touchpads as regular, physical buttons - no presses, just tap the pads. Awesome. Unfortunately, and maybe unsurprisingly, it feels weird as hell, and way less efficient than a standard controller. Bummer.
Most reviews say it takes some getting used to and maybe that's the case. If I come around on it I will change this review. For now, cannot recommend.

Actually very good for a free to play game (or really even for a full price AAA title.) You could very easily play this game and not spend a dime if you wished to. This and Star Trek Online have the best 'free to play' models that I have seen. Combat is very fun and engaging. Obviously there is a wide variety of skill level in opponents so you won't win every time, but you likely won't lose all the time either. You're always in a large team, so if you struggle, you can always stick with the pack and up your chances. Going off on your own is generally not a good idea.
If I had to say something bad about it, it can be a little complicated at first, it has a somewhat steep learning curve and that can be intimidating to new players. It's best not to spend any of your early money on a mech, play the free 'trial' mechs until you know what style you like and then buy something that fits your style. There are A LOT of Mechs to choose between and you're likely going to have to watch some videos and do some research, it's not a simple game.

I have been playing MechWarrior since the 90s. This game brings back everything I love about this game. I started playing when MWO was launched and have been on again off again since. Recently though they have really started paying attention. It has kept me playing consistently for a few months. I put my 200+ hours in only the last 3 months or so.
Not everything about this game is perfect. The intial UI and Mechlab are a joke, the faction warfare ui is even worse. However once you learn its quirks its worth putting up with.
Initially they had some ridiculous pricing when it came to content for the game. $500 Khan mechs were the culmination of that dibacle and there were some pretty heated voices about it. In the last year they have really toned down the pricing. Let me be clear buying a single "Hero" mech is still a rip off you do NOT get your bang for your buck that way. You can however go onto their site and buy the bundles they release every month. $20 USD gets you everything you need to master that paticular mech. These are by FAR the best bang for your buck, if you want the "Hero" variant its only an extra $15 USD. I will be honest very very few "Hero" mechs are worth buying due to the necessity of balancing the game, they can't be much better if at all better than their standard variants.
The game play is engaging especially when your team works together. It's amazing watching a co-ordinated attack from 3 lances. Faction warefare still needs work, it takes WAY to long to get into a game. Once you are in a game for Faction play however it is always a fun experience, things like the cannons need some tweaking 1 shotting an Atlas is B.S.
The game can be very grindy if you aren't willing to put money in and to be honest if thats the case it probably isn't the game for you. I look at it as a game that comes with a $20USD monthly sub which while high I find it enjoyable enough to put that money out.

TL:DR below. Please don't listen to short-sighted, low time negative reviews on any game.
In order for a free to play game to stay alive and continue to provide stellar content, some in the playerbase have to spend money to support the devs.
Most Free to Play games hit you with a paywall after about two hours of playing, where you have to spend money if you want to get any further enjoyment from the game.  This is not the case with Skyforge.  I've gotten a solid 30 hours of enjoyable content for free with no strong-arm tactics to make me buy anything. Many $60 titles can't give you 30 hours of content.
Their model is based on a subscription where subs get double XP gain. You can spend money elsewhere but, I have yet to feel pressured into purchasing anything. The difficulty and progression curve for free players feels natural rather than grind-y.
+ Pros +
+ No crushing paywall.
+ Tons of free content.
+ Characters are unlocked by easily beating map levels instead of grinding for hours (looking at you Rainbow Six Siege wtf...)
+ Solid, optimized graphics. Solid character creation.
+ Only a small amount of lag in hub areas (as a NA playing on an EU server)
+ Several ways to experience the game (solo, open-world maps, groups and guilds, pvp)
+ Pleasant community (easy to find groups or get questions answered)
+ Missions are similar but, do not feel like copy/paste.
- Cons -
- Confusing UI in places.
- PvP is likely pay to win.
- English voice acting is god awful.
- Lots of daily activities that can be difficult to keep up with. (I view this as extra content but, some might not like dailies.  This may mean that MMOs possibly aren't your thing.)
- Some tutorials are more confusing than helpful.
I think the most feelbads I've gotten from this game so far are as a new player trying to figure things out.  Many menus can be needlessly confusing but, make more sense once you figure it out.

the good:
- it's not pay to win. I'm totally fine with the double resource gain for premium accounts. The free use of waypoints is also a great feature for premium accounts. Mounts as well, totally fine. Costumes, another one that's fine.

the bad:

- nobody is doing dungeons. I queued up many times, but never managed to actually play one.
- up to 20k prestige it was all easy. But now I hit a wall trying to complete Factorium. The recommended prestige for this level is well above 30k, so I'm far below that. But still, up to this level it was all good and easy. Now I'm stuck, I can't progress and will have to do a lot of grinding previous levels. But even then, those levels aren't going to give me better gear, so my prestige will not go up much. Unless I can do group dungeons perhaps, but as mentioned before, nobody is doing dungeons.
- unlocking new class skills is done with "kill 100 enemies" quests. ALL OF THEM. Like... couldn't you mix this up a bit?!
----------------
If you're looking for a new mmorpg to play long term, I would have to recommend you look elsewhere.
But if you're looking for a fun solo action rpg experience, you found it.

The easiest way for me to summarize DE:HR is to say that this is a game that will leave the VETERANS wanting, while the NEW players will have an experience untarnished by history.
I kept switching back and forth on YES and NO… But if I think about a situation where I meet myself, would I recommend this to me? Well I would have to, especially at the current price.
DE:HR is a respectable game on its own feet, and I can appreciate why it has so many positive reviews.  But I think it is definitely important to point out the number of issues with it in terms of game design choices. Ultimately the quickest way I can BROADLY summarize this is that DE (original) is more of a puzzle than DE:HR. But ultimately, I got 38 hours of entertainment and the price is low. So despite any personal grievances, it’s worth it (to new players) and even veterans for a low price. Would I pay the original full price? I’d be hesitant.

I appreciate that games have to change an evolve, and I can’t just have a remaster of the original. I’m conducive to this, I’m fine with this: but I subscribe to the philosophy that the new game should have MORE than the old game, not less. That’s where my gripe is. It’s not the differences… it’s the cuts and ‘lazy’ merging of features. Kind of like playing Super Mario 3D first and then going back to 2D.
BUT having said that...
It really isn’t all that bad. I mean despite my ‘disappointments’, I did actually enjoy it. It can still be fun! It just depends on the player. I didn’t abuse the 10mm silenced laser pistol for example, I avoided using it, and went for a non-lethal play-through. Towards the end of the game, I got tired of non-lethal and just went shotgun + crossbow (and I have to say I loved the crossbow!).
Plus, what’s important in a Deus Ex game if not the character, story, lore and side quests? Which for the most part DE:HR delivered and I really enjoyed them, while they lasted! From the DLC onwards, things are a bit of a blur, unfortunately. This is because the game didn’t maintain its very positive early traction.
Exploring Detroit was fun too, the atmosphere was great and there were some fun discoveries. The conspiracy side quests and investigations were spot on because they took you to fun and daring places. The NPCs were also really good. The voice acting was great I thought and the interactions were a lot of fun. I cannot complain about DE:HR in this regard; it was all the things I would expect from a Deus Ex game. I just wish they were able to maintain it past the 40-50% mark.
Ultimately, I did finish the game. I won’t go into the ending, but I will say ‘déjà vu’ haha! To be honest, it was expected, especially if you’ve ever played Deus Ex. You almost have to expect it.
So if you’re a NEW player, buy it, take note of the first half of the game and set your standards! You will enjoy it and have fun, I promise.
If you’re a VETERAN; the same advice. There’s enough content goodness that the gameplay shortcomings mostly stand out DLC onwards.
FIRSTLY- Gunplay: it’s “acceptable” but definitely not ideal. The FEEL of the weapons is where it is lacking. Iron sights aren’t all that good to use. It made the game feel very aged, which is an impressive feat for a game release MID 2011! STALKER and Crysis have better gunplay and that was released in 2007. Technically DE:HR is an FPS now, so fair game for comparison which more closely resembles the original DE from 2000. Unfortunately, it’s not the only one to suffer from this in the last 10 years. Don’t know what’s going on with developers.
Laser sight makes the 10mm pistol too strong. 100% accuracy with no fall off from distance. 1 shot head shot kills, decent damage and more ammo than you’ll know what to do with. Really makes any other weapons pointless.
SECONDLY- guard placement. What were they thinking? No challenge here: the guards are always positioned in pairs or less, and often times are facing in directions that pose you no threat. Too convenient.
Because of this, there was really no reason for me not to literally take out every guard in an area then run around like a fool, making a ruckus, exploring for something interesting.
THIRDLY- Exploration wasn’t rewarding enough. You’d find the occasional cache of goodies which was fun, but nothing that really fleshed out the world or characters. Most of the content was on emails.
FOURTH- The DLC… it adds hours of gameplay sure. But it wasn’t a particularly pleasant experience. Long and comparatively linear which is not the DE way. Plus once you’re in, there’s no way out until the end of it.
FIFTH- The augmentations. I know we all love to power play; but I just don’t think it was well implemented. Instead of spending my augmentation points early on into great, fun, gameplay changing abilities, I’m spending points on quality of life, rudimentary ones such as increasing my inventory space or improving hacking.
Don’t worry though, it doesn’t take long to have enough skills points to buy every augment anyway.
SIXTH- Hacking. Mini-game; need I say more? Also. where are the lock-picks? I don’t approve of hacking improvements being tied into augments; can’t get over this. Combining hacking with lock-picks severly hampers level design diversity.
SKILLS- There are no skills. This was the biggest thing I noticed and the most missed. A clear division between skills and augments allowed for more interesting overall gameplay by allowing for a much better and more NATURAL balance in player power vs environment as proven by the original.
This ties in directly to weapons. You’re able to use all weapons effectively, off the bat. How boring?
MULTIPLE PATHS- DE:HR in this regard really “feigns” multiple paths. It’s an illusion. When they combine everything into hacking (for example) you can go through option A or B, but you simply ‘hack’ a different door.
By having only 1 ability open everything you limit the potential for progression puzzles. I never had to stop and think “My lock-picking is terrible; how do I get through this door? What can I use?” The original did this. Choosing to hack the keypad directly or to hack the computer is not an interesting puzzle choice. That’s like choosing between chicken or beef noodles.
EXPLORATION- No puzzles meant reading stuff was pointless. While there were a few gems of interesting writing, you could skip most of it. You almost never had to find the pass-code, you could just hack it.
While I’ll grant you the original had a few too obscure reading puzzles, it was rewarding noticing a book name on a table and typing it in as the password. Or referring to a birthdate in an otherwise innocuous data cube to unlock the safe.
AUGMENTS- In the original game, you had to pick 1 of 2 augments for each slot. You couldn’t just buy everything. This was brilliant! Why? Because the existence of skills meant that all the augments were game changing in a really fun way by SUPPLEMENTING your arsenal rather than dictating it. You didn’t need any of them, compared to DE:HR where you can and should acquire ALL of them.

This is a super fun first-person puzzle game in the vein of Portal, wherein you are a test subject for a pretty shady corporation with a sarcastic narrator. But besides the fact that they're both puzzle games, that's mostly where the similarities end.
Mechanics:
You are equipped with a ChromaGun, which can shoot three colors: yellow, green, and blue. The colors can also be combined with each other to make magenta, green and orange. You use these colors to attract similarl colored hovering, sometimes murderous spheres to activate switches. Puzzles get more intricate with ones that require a lot of planning (since you can only add color, not subtract it, so level restarts are your only way to erase wrong colors), ones that need split second timing (there are a couple countdown events that require shaving off seconds to beat it before dying), ones that require you to reuse finite resources, ones where you have to complete a puzzle while being charged down by murderous "HelperBots", etc.
Pros:
+There's a great deal of puzzle variety, as stated above, with timed challenges, take-your time color puzzles, don't waste your finite resources puzzles, open doors in the correct sequence or get stuck puzzles, etc.
+Good difficulty curve. Starts easy and gets progressively more difficult. Never seemed impossible, but there are definitely some thinkers.
+Great mechanic.
+Funny narration
Neutral:
~Length: I ran about 6 hours, including getting stuck and retrying a puzzle that I didn't realize I had actually solved, some idling, etc. I thought it felt like a pretty good length, but I could have definitely done with some more puzzles because it was actually really well done! Some people may feel it's too short but I personally don't feel cheated.
Cons:
-As stated above, narration was funny, but if you died a lot you'd get the same 3 or so dialogue snippits upon respawn, no matter how many times you died. It would have been nice if it recognized that you had already died several times in the same manner, so you don't need to be reminded not to touch the murderbots for the 6th time. (Like, I KNOW already.)
-There was one mechanic in the late-game that wasn't really introduced well. It didn't help that the effects of what you were doing weren't visible except from one weird angle, so I didn't know the piece I needed had been put into place until about a half hour later. There's only 1 other puzzle with this mechanic, and it is actually more obvious what is going on in the SECOND puzzle, which isn't a big help, honestly.
Overall: If you like good puzzlers with a fun mechanic, buy this game! 9/10. I'd definitely replay this game once I've forgotten most of the solutions.
If you enjoyed Portal, its highly likely you'll enjoy this.

The main problem with the majority of these 4X space games is that they never feel as if they have any guts to them. By which I mean you select AI opponents which may or may not have some flavour text but they invariably DON'T feel like individual alien races - just a few stats and traits different here and there. Where is the real exploration? The real thrill of encountering a new sentient but strange race? The adventure. It's all very well having varied systems that you slowly dominate with formulaic build patterns but the issue I have with these games is that they always feel just like games. It's like a board game - all tactics and no heart. And this one is no different. Whilst it may well be strategic and tactical it still doesn't feel like you are actually exploring space and for this reason I, personally, can't reccommend it. The whole genre has not really progressed since 1999's Alpha Centauri. After sixteen years one would have expected some kind of tangible progress.

- Too many bugs for a game that has been out for a couple of years. Performance is also an issue on the strategy screen in the late game, on a desktop i7 and a GTX 780.
- AI uses a different set of rules than the player. They get to move their units before, after, or during the player's turn. The player can't do the same. This is not challenging, just very VERY annoying because it feels like the game makes up the rules as it goes, and the rules are not intuitive ("I forgot they could do that. Load last save. They can do that too? Ridiculous. Load last save.") For example if you want to assign 3 ships from one fleet to another, you must first remove them from their original fleet, then add them to their new fleet, which are both orbiting the same system. As soon as you remove the 3 ships from the original fleet, the AI will interrupt your turn and attack the original fleet minus the 3 ships. So you need to remember that you need to remove 1 ship first, then assign it to the new fleet, then repeat 2 more times, instead of just moving the 3 ships. The AI rearranges their fleets instantly.
- Diplomacy is broken. On hardest difficulty the way to win is to finance your empire and drive your enemies into financial ruin by trading anything against X Gold per Turn. The more money an AI makes the more willing they are to give it to you.
The empire building and research tree is mostly well done, altough the finer workings of the expansion penalty are rather unintuitive. This could have been a great game if it had better diplomacy, fewer bugs, and a round robin turn system instead of the abdomination they used instead. If they had also added decent combat it would even have been competition to the 1996 title MoO2, which so far remains unchallenged.

MechWarrior Online is bar-none one of the greatest team based shooters out there. It is extensively well balanced and has a great deal more strategy and teamwork than any other shooter I've played. The mechs are diverse and in the right hands even a garbage mech can be a war hero on the field of battle. It has a steep learning curve and takes awhile before you can find a mech that best suits you, but once you do the game is extremely rewarding.
My biggest complaint about the game it is the name. MechWarrior Online sounds like a trashy free to play mech game so the fact that this is free to play doesn't do itself any favors as far as marketing goes. I've been a fan of the MechWarrior games for over a decade but I took years to try this because I assumed it was going to be a piece of crap due to its name. My Steam friends don't want to try it for this sole reason.
Beside the name I have no issues with the game itself, in fact I would say this is leagues better than other strategy based shooters like CSGO for instance. If you are looking for a game more involved than hiding out in a bomb simulation I would highly recommend this.

Tank Battle Mania is made as though it comes from a 1980s era video game.
The graphics are extremely basic.
As the name implies, it's a tank game.
You have to attack the enemy base, whilst making sure that the enemy don't destroy your base.
The controls are WASD and/or arrows to move about - i.e. they are quite clunky, as there is no mouse input with the gameplay.
Nonetheless, it has some gameplay value.
And it has a range of levels.
As the game is only 99 cents, it is reasonable to say that it gives value for money - especially if you buy it on sale, like I did.
If you don't mind a bit of retro gameplay, then this is fine.
However, do not expect some great fantastic game; this is just a bit of old-time amusement, nothing more.
I can only recommend it on the basis of it being retro and cheap.
If you're happy with those qualifying factors, then go ahead and buy the game - so long as you don't expect a lot from it.

I've Played somewhere around 2.000 battles in - ( May just call it the original WoT ) and I can't say I'm too disapointed with this one... The system requirements are really low and the casual way the battles play out seems pretty suitable for just "a
quick game" maybe before school / work.
There could of course be more vehicles and maps in the game, but I would say it still makes a decent "little brother" of the original WoT.
Now despite what the hardware requirements say, the game ran pretty much flawlessly on a 1.80Ghz single core cpu, 3GB of RAM and a 1GB graphics card, getting 58-60 FPS almost the whole time using the highest preset and no AA.
And to people talking about some "horrendous paywalls".. you can actually claim a premium account for a couple of days for FREE. I currently have an IS (tier VII), a Matilda (IV) and an SU-85B (tier IV) and a couple of lower tier tanks that don't really matter and I've played 70 hours so far, where in the original WoT you would probably be still stuck at some tier 3-4 without a premium account.
Also you don't lose credits by playing the heavy tanks as in WoT i actually wasn't able to pay for the repair + ammo resupply costs thus resulting in having to sell my IS and go back to low tier tanks just to be able to still play the game. Of course you could just pay some real money to get back into the game, but that sort of becomes a damn "Pay2Play", which is not suppossed to be happening in a free game.

The Steam Controller is the most promising and interesting development I've seen in gaming periphery in a very long time. Second only to the VR-controllers bundled with Rift and Vive, it excels in some disciplines, while being a regression in others.
After a full year of studying Valve's update policy regarding the controller and its acceptance within within the community, I decided to finally give it a try. So far I have no regrets, but there are a couple of things I would like to share.
the SC's built-in gyroscope is what makes it truly special. Thanks to this tiny sensor the SC is capable of surprisingly high precision, while there is no noticeable input lag even when paired via bluetooth. Trackpads and gyro combined, with some added tweaking of its respective config settings (smoothing, activation etc.) make for the closest competition to mouse input I have ever experienced. This is where traditional gamepads fail; and it's nice to see a developer step up and try something bold and innovative, albeit imperfect.
It surely is an improvement in games that are played in front of a TV but were never optimized for controllers. However these are also accompanied by issues a controller cannot solve, such as small UI. Games that look right on TV but don't naturally support a controller, and thus profit from the SC's input abilities, are few and far between. At the same time, the SC often is an inferior choice for games that come with well-made controller support: In these cases, its deficits are all too obvious (see below). To no one's surprise, it is first person games requiring mouse-like precision that reveal the Steam Controller's biggest strengths, provided that you pick the right settings and are willing to put in some time to practice. RTS or point & click titles will work well, too, while offering a less steep learning curve.
One is the absence of rumble motors. The built-in linear actuators are fine for creating haptic feedback, but are not suited for heavier effects. Valve offers rumble emulation, which I find rather unconvincing (and way too loud without headphones on). Then there's the design of the triggers, which can only be pulled for a tiny distance and are thus inadequate for precise inputs, as required in racing sims. The absence of the right thumbstick holds true to the original concept, but can be quite irritating no less. The use of conventional AA-batteries has been discussed thoroughly, and while its not a vital criterium, I would have preferred a dedicated lithium battery. Cutting costs, I guess.
to come up with improvements. Not only is the configuration menu the most powerful and complex I have ever seen for any type of PC input device. They also released the CAD schematics for everyone to use, modify and share. A smart move, because now you can reshape a specific part of the controller to your personal liking. Some modeling software is free and easy to learn, 3D printing services are offering low prices – so there's really no limit to how much the SC can be improved (by us). Funny enough, its complexity may be its biggest hindrance; I cannot imagine the average gamer having the patience for trackpad-aiming and micro-managing settings on a per-game-basis. Of course it's possible to choose from a set of popular configs provided by other members of the community but still, it takes considerable initiative to get comfortable with the device.
I can only speculate. There are some
about it. It is probable, but Valve may take its time and see how the current version plays out once people get familiar with it. We are also seeing some titles released with dedicated, in-game SC config settings, so acceptance among developers is another factor. Overall I wouldn't bet on a new SC within the next two years. So if you're interested in this device: Get it now. There are worse things to spend your money on and, frankly, it's not all that much.

Unfortunately ES isn't a very good 4x strategy game, playing it more only reveals all the major flaws of the game, however one major aspect of any 4x game is decently programmed AI, and that is something Endless Space doesn't have at all, since the AI is poorly programmed and starts with more or less infinite bonuses and the ability to do things the player can't -  the outcome of the game almost always leans in favor of the A.I winning no matter the difficulty setting, unless the player has enough experience to know all the aspects of the game, knows the skill tree and how to get important research done first and of course, the player gets an almost legendary start.
Even on the easiest of difficulty settings, the A.I can still easily beat a skilled human player because of the boosted AI stats.  Not to mention, throwing almost endless high powered fleets of ships if war is declared against the player and to add further insult, knowing almost intimate information about the players empire so it can attack your weakest points at any time, like many 4x games - basically the AI is programmed to cheat since thats the easiest way to program an AI to give a human player a challenge, even on the newbie difficulty A.I difficulty makes me want to face palm.   I'd like to know how its possible for an A.I player with a couple of planets to have nearly double the score I have sometimes when I have nearly triple the star systems, wonders and a large fleet of ships?
Some would say its a "Smart A.I" but there is a difference between a proper smart A.I and one that has been programmed with cheap bonuses that more or less gives it a clear winning edge against the player.   Also, I think the galaxy map isn't big enough, the so called "Huge" map feels quite small by comparison to other 4x space strategy games with maybe less than a 100 star systems without mods.  Many of the good mods unfortunately break the game completely as they haven't been updated, these mods we're perhaps the saving grace of the game but now its more or less been abandoned.
Like someone commented, this game seems to be better played co-op against A.I players.  Single player just isn't worth your time, especially if your a 4x fan - ES seems to be more like a zerg rush than empire building, which weakens the gameplay considerably -  so the title really should be changed to Endless Zerg or Endless Fleets.
I think the premise of the game is fairly good, the graphics, sound - all that is fine.   The problem really lies with the execution of the gameplay, thats where it falls down.    I think a sequel that fixes all the major problems the original has would be a good contender for the top 4x space strategy title,  but they need to fix a lot of problems and make sure they don't make the same mistakes.
4x space strategy is about expansion, empire building - in a nutshell turtling out your empire, building fleets - defending choke points - exploring the galaxy.  ES does this, but in such a way it all takes the back burner,  the galaxy without 'working' mods is way too small - The AI cheats too much to make the game fun or interesting, so a sequel needs better programmed AI without infinite bonuses or other stupid stuff.
Overall, 4/10
Endless Space isn't 'terrible' per say, but AI does heavily let the game down.  GalCiv remains the king of 4x space strategy games.  I'm glad I got this from the Humble Bundle sale, I would never pay full price for this.   I would like to see a sequel to see if they can improve the game.

Chaos

VolChaos is a very cute, charming retro-style platformer that conjures the feel and excitement of some of my favorite console hits of days long gone—legendary games like Mighty Bomb Jack and Kid Chameleon... It is a simple game (as many of the great ones are) but what VolChaos lacks in complex variety it more than makes up for with solid execution, wonderfully creative level design, and pure delicious challenge.
This game is very, very accessible to anyone who has ever played Super Mario (or any platformer). I understood *immediately* how to play, with no instructions of any kind. Really nice, smooth controls. Simple, yet beautiful retro-inspired graphics and sound. Tons of killer levels that include the interesting challenge of picking up all the cleverly placed jewels as you rush to avoid the rising lava... Each level has its own "best time" leaderboard, and the times are pretty damn competitive. I give myself mad credit for even getting into the top 100 on some of them. :)
VolChaos had me laughing out loud and screaming horrible words at my monitor within minutes of pressing START. This game encapsulates all the wonder and enchantment that made me fall in love with video games, and most impressively does so without any flashy 3D graphics or showers of animated gore. At the price of $2.99 USD, I cannot possibly recommend this game highly enough. Get VolChaos and get ready to rage! :)

VolChaos is an old-school platformer that reminds me of an Amiga 500 game.
I almost want to recommend the game just to give a big thumbs-up for the great level names, which reminded me fondly of the old mutant camels games (though VolChaos is nothing like them), but after having played for just under five hours, and having rage-quit many times during that (almost all on level 27), I just don't find VolChaos fun to play, and other than fun I can't see that it offers anything else.
The game is mostly well done, with good pixel graphics and a vast array of levels. However, the levels vary wildly in difficulty with no discernible curve leading from easier levels to harder ones, and relying on replay after replay of the same level in order to gain longevity does not lead to a fun game. Some levels are obviously designed to foil early attempts, requiring blind leaps of faith, which is not great level design in my opinion.
To be fair, the game's description does say it is "ultra-challenging", but ti seemed to me that most of the challenge was had from trying to master the player's inertia and remember the tricky bits from the previous attempts at each level, rather than through any devious or clever level design. I had some fun, but unfortunately not enough. I suspect a reordering of the levels would help immensely. As it is, I couldn't bring myself to keep bashing my head against level 27. I knew what I had to do, but the controls just wouldn't let me do it.
Grab VolChaos if it's on deep discount or in a bundle and you enjoy a bit of reminiscing over platform game rage. But if you play games to enjoy yourself, it's probably best to give this one a miss.

Crimsonland is an awesome game, and so are the devs.
I've been playing Crimsonland since it came out in 2003 (over 10 years ago!) and it is still as much fun today as it was back then. This HD remake has everything I loved about the original Crimsonland and more.
Yes, there are changes from the original version, but I feel that these were in good taste. One of the biggest changes I've noticed is that telekinesis no longer lets you selectively pick up powerups. Instead, it pulls all nearby powerups to you.
Additionally, Typ'o'Shooter is nowhere to be found. This was one of my favorite modes and I REALLY hope that it gets brought back in an update.
The gameplay is as insane as it was in 2003, if not moreso. There are so many enemies on the screen sometimes that it's hard to comprehend, and yet the game never skips a beat. The monsters now gib when you kill them, and this effect looks really great.
Although online multiplayer would propel Crimsonland to new levels of awesomeness, the couch co-op is a ton of fun. I just tried it for the first time with a couple friends and we had a blast. The game scales the difficulty based on how many players there are, so be prepared for even more carnage.
All in all, this is mostly the same game it was back in 2003 but with updated graphics and a few (good) tweaks here and there. As a player of the original Crimonsland, I highly recommend this game to fans and newcomers alike. Speaking of which; if you've never played Crimsonland, do youself a favor and buy this game right now.

What used to be an extraordinarily fun, fast-paced shooter with a fair F2P business model, is now an abandoned husk of it's former self. I've put over 40 hours into the game's two iterations, and it really sucks that's it's gone.
Sony offered them money, so they abandoned the PC entirely at the drop of a hat. They made one batch of 'exclusive' content for the PS4 version, and then disappeared off the face of the planet. Little to no communication since the launch of that last PS4 update numerous months ago.
I like multiplayer games when they're done well, but the vast majority of low-budget developers need to realize that unless they get insanely lucky (Rocket League, Path of Exile, etc), their multiplayer game will die quickly, no one will have any reason to buy the game let alone play it, and all of their work will mean nothing. Tons of these games would work just fine as single player experiences, and multiplayer could be added on if they found success. Instead, we keep getting great games that are multiplayer-only and range from completely unplayable to a few days of play during a sale or promotion. I've heard the servers have either been shut down or are on their very last breath, shutting you down before you even hit the main menu. What little single player component was there, the weapon testing room and the "campaign" of the 5.0 beta version aren't even accessible.
A game I'd have recommended as a must-play for fans of hectic shooters, is now 6GB of wasted hard drive space and nothing more. At the very least, I hope this serves as a warning to consumers and developers alike.

I tried this for a while and abandoned it to the shelf. I was having inconsistent inputs, did not enjoy the touchpads vs. joysticks on other controllers, and the layout of the controller didn't feel the best.
After letting it sit for a while, I went back to it and have a newfound appreciation.
First, there was an option which was automatically set for my non-steam game which set each button to rapid-fire when held. Once these buttons were unchecked, it worked wonderfully. Also, modifying the dead-zone on the d-pad made it easier to use without incorrect input.
Second, the options for how the touchpads are used took some getting used to, but the flexibility is what makes them worthwhile. Currently, my touchpad is used as a simulated joystick but once the left trigger (aim) is pulled, it switches to a touchpad allowing much more precise control.
Third, while the controller does still feel a little bit bulky, the ability to use the controller as a mouse is fantastic. Also, the underneath buttons are easily programmable making for unique inputs that other controllers can't do.

I'm an experienced gamer. Of all the controllers, this one is certainly the most innovative, but after forcing myself to use it for 3 months, I can safely say that it's the worse one.
After more than one year, Steam has yet to make it fully compatible with games (many, too many games don't work at all with this controller, and a lot of others are erratic); easily lose 30 to 60 minutes to configure your controller for a game you yet don't know and only want to play it.
Not having rumble may seem like a minor issue, but some games (like car games) rely on that, and you miss the whole perfect breaking/drift feeling.
The touch pads might be a nice idea, but they are too small, if you have medium/large hands like me, they are impossible to use precisely, they should be bigger or at least without a curve; even trying to use different sensibilties (using buttons), still isn't worth the trouble, easier and better with a PS4/Xbox controller.
All in all, it is a nice piece of hardware (I say hardware because on Windows it looks like a mouse and keyboard, only through the Steam platform you can use it as a controller); it's useless because game companies don't optimize games for it, and I'm now fairly sure they never will.
I'm trying to sell mine, but even the price isn't as good as selling another controller, though it costs about the same.

What is "My Name is Mayo"?
No long review here, it is just a clicker game in the purest sense. You click through various story branches where each next option requires you to click x more times after selecting the current achievement from the pause menu. While the story itself is interesting, it is not deep at all. The whole game is more a joke game, an anti-clicker game that is not as bad as the one in the Basement Collection,[1] but dull enough in gameplay terms that you need to reflect on your gaming habits. Do you play games for achievements? Great, grab this, click 10k times and have another 100 percent in under an hour! Do you play for fun? Then avoid this! Or if you really play it, take the lesson you get from it, which is how stupid clicker games really are, why they only work as idle games, and even then only as glorified Skinner boxes.
Graphics:
The graphics are like a flash game. There is not a wide variety, but the different mayo jar styles are humorously done.
Sound:
The sound consists of a forgettable track and minimalistic sound effects.

This game is a remake/improved verison of the original Crimsonland game, which I absolutely loved and spent hours trying to get a decent score in Survival Mode. I instantly bought this one when it was released, and while I liked it at first, I had to give it a thumb down after couple of dozens runs in Survival. My main issues with the game were:
1) Low camera altitude: can't see the field of battle clearly
2) New perk and experience system: no perks in quests (kinda), leveling up is extremely slow, some important perks altered for worse.
3) Interface: power-ups are displayed on crosshair, hp and shield are displayed on player model.
4) Survival Mode: added monster-spawners, average game longevity is ~3 times shorter than in original game, harder to get a weapon you want.
After update 1.1.0, review was changed to positive, mostly because of the inclusion of original Crimslonland game for free. Changes to he game were good, but not good enough, since it didn't fix the main issue with survival mode: toned down exp gains in comparison to the old game, which resulted in very short survival matches, without any feel of buliding up your character.
But now with update 1.2.3 I can totally recommend this one. Increased exp gains and some changes to perks made the game as enjoyable as the original. While in previous versions you died on level 6-7 (my personal highscore was around 350k points), now level 30 is not even impressive (50+ million points is pretty much a real thing). Of course, you're still pretty much screwed, unless you get at least few of the vital perks in first ten levels, but overall, now this game wrecks you with RNG (in terms of obtaining perks, weapons and power-ups) even less than the original did.
Final thoughts:
A great top-down shooter, with the potential to suck you in for dozens of hours, if you're into getting the high scores. The "story" mode (i.e. quests) is more of a training ground before survival, so I don't think it's worth to buy the game if you don't plan on playing survival. But if you do, prepare for absolute carnage, because Crimsonland is finally back.
P.S. Took more than 2.5 years though.

If you've played Crimsonland before, this is essentially the same game from a decade ago with some minor changes. The graphics and UI have been (slightly) updated, and some great new weapons, perks, and powerups have been added. The most notable changes are the removal of perks from the campaign mode and the addition of monster spawners/nests in survival mode, both of which make the game more challenging (in a good way).
If you're new to Crimsonland, this is a fairly straightforward top-town shooter in which you use outlandish weapons and powerups to...well, paint the map crimson. The gameplay is similar to Serious Sam's, in the sense that you'll be constantly circle-strafing around enemies to avoid getting overrun. Don't think to hard, and you'll have a great time. The original game was always a guilty pleasure of mine, and I'm glad that Greenlight has made this subtlely remastered version possible.

Want the tl/dr, skip to the end. Anyone still here? Strap yourself in. I played this game when it launched originally, and for the time I played it, I had a blast. I loved it, and would have GLADLY recommended this game even after I drifted away from it. It had just the right level of complexity, and the old ascension atlas was not the deepest thing in the world, but between it, the various skills you had, the passives, and other little things you could do to tweak and optimize your character, It gave you this feeling that you were making progress (Even if it was a bit of a grind. Lets face it, it's a free mmo. You go in expecting a grind.).
I speak of all these things in the past tense because they are dust in the wind now. The best way to describe it is, "Gutted" which is what has happened here. The ascension atlas is removed, skills are acquired through a canned simple "Kill enemies get bacon system". The overall number of skills has been sliced in half for many classes, and you can't mix and match skills given they don't exist and the option isn't there. Passives....what passives? Cryomancer, the most basic, and in many cases, first attacking class is now limited to 3, something I saw as soon as i grabbed the class and thought that more would open up, or reveal themselves ~there's only 3~. Graphically it has been dumbed down as well from early days of the game, and I think this is the first time I've seen optimization work backwards with the game running worse on the same system than before on lower settings. The icing on the cake is that there is only one stat that matters now when we talk about dealing damage, healing, anything that uses your skills. Might. There are other stats, but this is the god stat (badumtiss) and everything else is secondary to it by way of nothing else being there to make it tertiary.
Long and short is, this game is oversimplified now beyond anything that should be on pc, and yet games like this exist. By that I mean games so simple they could be ported to mobile if not for how pretty the developer (tries) to make them look. In this case, done in the favor of 'streamlining the game' but you can streamline a game without gutting it and leaving it to feel like a pinata not full of treats or angry bees, but rather a wet fart.The game still has potential. They've shown they can do creativei nteresting things with it (outlaw class), but right now that creativity is wasted on this when it could go to a better game.

Background on me and platformers:
I have played many 3d platformer for systems like the n64 and gamecube, but I have not played many 2d platformer like Volchaos. With my background and recommendations from others I decided to play Volchaos with a controller. I will be writing this review from the view of a xbox controller.
Gameplay:
The game is fun. It passes time quickly and I find myself not getting frustrated with the levels if they require me trying over and over to complete. As for how far I am in the game the levels are not crazy hard to the point were I feel that I have no chance in actually beating the level, the levels always fell beatable. As I worked my way through to the point that I am now in Volchaos I saw the level design change as my skill set evolved. As for the controls, (a) is jump and (x) is replay, something that you will probably be pressing a lot when playing. When moving though the levels, I found myself using the dpad button to move instead of using the analog joystick. People talk about the bad controls but I found them easy to get used to as you went along playing the game.
Bugs:
I think for an early access game I should put this here to point out problems. (if I find any more major one then I put them here)
1) When booting the game it often crashes the first boot... the second boot starts the game more times than not though.
The verdict:
For 2.99... yes! I have enjoyed all the time that I have played so far and I am sure that I will continue to play and enjoy the game in the future.

Volchaos is a fun little Speed Platformer where you have to collect gems whilst dodging enemies and watching out for  rising lava. However, the game is exceptional for it's price there are still some pro's and con's which I will list below.
Pros:
♦ Great Price
♦ Good amount of Content
♦ Challenging and Fun
♦ Nice Number of Built in Awardments
♦ Awesome Graphics and fitting Music
♦ Each level is Unique
♦ Decent number of Enemies to verse
♦ Puns before Levels that actually link to things that have happened outside the game (This keeps the game interesting)
♦ Easy Controls that just seem to work
♦ Decent Jumpbox (No delay, no over jumping for no reason etc)
♦ Interesting Intro Story
♦ Good Number of Easy Steam Achievements (Just gotten from playing the Game)
♦ Awesome Looking Steam Cards/Emoticons/Backgrounds
♦ Good replay value due to highscores
♦ Friendly Dev who listens to players/community!
Cons:
♦ If you Quit at Level 21 and Exit the game and come back to play again, it will crash at level select (However, this is inconvenient it is fixable if you select level 21 really quick before the error message appears)
♦ Steals a lot of concepts from Mario (Such as Final Boss, the Spikey Blocks that fall on you and the Angry Sun design + more)
♦ The puns before each level tend to repeat a fair bit (Would be awesome if all 60 levels had their own Pun including Expert levels having their own)
♦ Can collect gems after you've touched the flag (Such as level 16) and shows that you've collected all gems in the ingame information but it doesn't recognise that you've collected all gems for that level
♦ Hit Box on the Spiked Sun Face looking things is way off
♦ Ending for both Normal and Expert is lame wall of text (Could be way better concidering Intro was alright)
Overall, even though there are a number of cons (Most of the cons are minor bugs or things that could be improved to make the game better) this is a great game, with hours of fun content at an awesome price with most of the gameplay being exceptional. Therefore, for the $3 you'll spend on this, you'll defently get your moneys worth and you should pick up a copy if you like Fast Paced, Collect Em All, Dodge Em, Platformers.

Picked this up years ago thinking "Oh look, Civ meets EVE, that should be cool." And just like both of those games, while there are options there to be peaceful and diplomatic and spiritual....its a lot more fun to burn the world down and rebuild it in your image.
I don't have a God complex at all, nopenopenope.
Anyway, its mostly a GalCivs-style 4X, the resource management is a pretty heavy-handed (although you can put much of that under control of the AI, and the AI is trustworthy most times), and when you build your military units, you have to equip/upgrade templates for them else they're pretty useless even in massive numbers; as you progress in the 4 tech trees you'll unlock new abilities and more efficient ship modules and every so often you'll need to bring your fleets in for a refurb. And then you have fleet combat with formations and tactics to contend with, there is some randomness to how that plays out (its a rock-paper-scissors scenario) but it will rarely make a huge difference in the end.
Like most 4X's there's a LOT to learn, in addition to the fact that there's faction-specific lore and technologies to learn; there is a tutorial-esque thing but after reading a few screens of it you'll want some aspirin, basically you just have to dive into the deep end and drown a couple times before everything snaps into place for you (or at least, that was my experience.)
Also like many 4X's, there's a mechanic where you can use your gold - called "Dust" in this game, which I kinda wanna mock but whatever - to bypass production queues, basically you buy the ship/building/etc at a high price and get it on the next turn rather than having to depend on your population's laborforce, and any one resource is dependant on the other three: food (population increase speed), industry (production speed), dust (money), and science (research speed).  Once you get to a certain point in the game, you can have money rolling in if you micromanage the hell outta your early star systems, so that mechanic might be OP to some; since I'm all about domination/expansion victories, personally I abuse it every chance I get, and its fun =D If you think that's BS, however, the higher difficulties really don't permit lavish spending, unless the Random Generator God is pleased with you (and he never is is he, ♥♥♥♥ that guy ^^) Also there's at least one faction that outright cannot use dust, so they basically have one of the four resources removed, which fundamentally changes how you have to approach things.
This was before the Sid Meier's Civ In Space game, if that's what you want you can probably just go that route and be happy, this smells a little more like Galactic Civs, although not quite as hardcore (which for me is a good thing, your mileage may vary).

First thing you should know: This game is gonna hurt you. It's gonna make you realize that you're not half as good -quarter as good- as you thought you were. This game is HARD in the way that there are a million factors to consider, and one extra food on turn 10 can mean victory or defeat 200 turns later. It's much easier on the lower difficulties, but if you try to play this on even the Normal setting first time through, you will cry.
THAT BEING SAID. This game is also deep and interesting. There are almost a dozen different ways to win, and the AI have individual personalities and act accordingly. Resources make sense, and the UI is very easy to use and understand (once you put in a little effort.)
One flaw with the game is that it does have a huge, deep, steep, nearly bottomless learning curve. There are, as I said, a ton of things to learn and consider. However, once that curve is mastered, the game has a ton of replay value. Aside from the dozen different and unique factions, you can design your own, meaning that you can make thousands of different races that all play differently.
The universe is variable to the last detail, but even if you have the smallest settings, it's almost impossible to get even remotely close universes across different games, so everything plays out differently.
Overall, the only grudges I can hold against the game is the learning curve, and the amount of time needed to invest to master it. This is NOT a game to pick up and play for five minutes a day. But if you've got the inclination and time, this is quite possibly the best 4X game in existence.

This game has gripped me like no other.
In Tribes Ascend, you can choose from 9 power armor wielding classes, with every one of them having at least one explosive weapon, jetpacks and ski boots. There are two sides playing, the Blood Eagle and the Diamond Sword. The character animations and armor designs are well done for both. When you first play the game, you'll probably barely hit anything, die a lot, but you'll enjoy every bit of success. As you keep playing, you start to learn to lead for the various weapons (and for your ping), how to ski faster and how to play classes better. A rather iconic part of the game is the VGS system, which lets your character bark your favourite lines after tapping a short combination of buttons. Another gimmick which is quite fun to learn. And when you look back its just hard to imagine how that bronze guy could've ran out of ammo without hitting anything.
As you progress, you will unlock bonuses for things you already own, and also earn XP to unlock new primary or secondary weapons, belt items, packs, primary and secondary perks. They don't require too much grinding, and there is no "pay2win" in this game at all: everything (except voicepacks and skins) can be bought and upgraded to max from XP.
Another thing you might like is that one-hit kills are rather situational in this game. There's no instant-headshot-go-respawn kills, which really lets players put their skills to the test. There aren't any whiney voice-comms either.
While this game is quite remarkable considering only solo play, it gets on a whole new level if you manage to get a good team together. The classes can really do their own parts to contribute towards the team's benefit especially if they can converse by mics, although the VGS does a pretty decent job at it too.
The game's main gameplay type is Capture the Flag, with TDM, Rabbit, Capture and Hold, CTF Blitz and Arena being options.
In CTF and CTF Blitz, both sides have bases with Turrets, sensors and generators, which can be destroyed and then repaired. The generators while powering deployables, the turrets and the sensor, sometimes also generate valuable forcefields which can really benefit the team. On some maps the bases also have vehicle pads powered by the generator, where players can summon tanks, hover bikes or jets.
They do so from money earned by doing various tasks. They can also spend the money on upgrading base structures or calling in tactical/orbital strikes or inventory stations, which refill ammo and allows them to switch classes without dying.
While it sounds truly amazing there are quite a few cons to this game.
Some mentions the devs abandoning it, or say its "dead". There haven't been updates for ages, true, but the game is already much fun. As for the "dead" business, I play on the Amsterdam (EU) servers, and unless I log in between 3AM to 9AM there's always at least 2 servers with people playing. 4 or 5 during the day which is pretty good.
HOWEVER. My personal issue with it is the lack of solutions for skill gaps. You have 2 servers for levels 1 to 10, Then, you are thrown into servers which let players between levels 8 and 50 in, and lvl 50 players have already played thousands of matches, and will wipe your♥♥♥♥♥off in a heartbeat if you don't know what you're doing.
Another issue I have is d-stacking, that is the high level players (high from about lvl 35) joining on the same side, pretty much dominating the entire match, and there is usually nothing you can do against them.
(If you have trouble with a high level player:
- overwhelm with numbers
- get your own high level on your team to kill him (if possible)
- outsmart his skills (there are quite a few tricky weapons, deployables and abilities which might surprise a top-dog)
In conclusion Tribes Ascend is a very entertaining game, where you start as a dumbfounded target, then learn how to go fast, anticipate and lead your targets, develop little tactics and end up as a professional killing machine, respected/dreaded/hated by others and being a critical part of the match by yourself alone.

It's finaly nice to have this legend in Steam also. However there are some features in this new remake version which I have ...even despise.
- First of all, why on earth it is not any longer possible to level-up and use perks in the quests!?
- The Progress bar in the quests is pretty annoying. In my opinion it should be much smaller.
- The new healthbar and reload system doesn't look very pretty although I understand the point behind it: the player doesn't need to take his eyes off of the player when there is alot of action.
- In the survival, it is absolutely horrible when you can't no longer deside yourself when to pick a perk after leveling. There is usually very much action going on and therefore sudden pop-up windows can really ruin the game session.
- I mainly play the game by myself, so the "Press fire to join" infos in each corner are very irritating.
After all that complaining, there are also good new features.
- It is nice how you must unlock the weapons and perks in the quests to be able to use them in the Survival.
- The menus are more graphical, although somewhat crude-looking. (And some menus lack some buttons I'd presume to be there; like replay after winning a level)
- Now it is possible to see each wepon's individual specs.
- The star ranking in in each level (for beating it without taking a hit) adds playability a bit more. However I would like to have even more achieavables (stars) per level, like for instance >40% accuracy or complete the level under par time.
- Four player co-op is nice! (hopefully in the future it will be possible over the net)
All in all it is close to the good old legendary Crimsonland, but I don't completely agree with the new change choises the 10ton team has made. Alse the 14€ price is somewhat steep (at least in my and my wallet's oppinion).

I think that this is a great game. The developers are constantly releasing new content, and  it's a free game as well. I really enjoy the fast pace of the battles, and it shows its roots as a mobile game. I really enjoy the fact that I can play for 15mins or 3 hours and feel a sense of accomplishment. A downside to being a mobile game is that it draws in some young gamers, and to be honest your team can be terrible at times. As stated earlier this is a free to play game, but as you progress up the tree it becomes hard to advance. The in game credits are hard to accumulate at the higher tiers, with some tanks barely breaking even in a good battle. So in short its the lack of credits that become the pay wall. This doesn't mean that you have to pay anything to enjoy the game. Getting to tier 6-7 with a standard account (free) is early doable. You can even progress further for free but it does take time. People complain about this because everyone seems to want the best of everything now and for free. How do you advance (quicker) past this credit pay wall? You need to buy Premium time (+50% xp and $), or buy a Premium tank. Premium tanks as similar to ”regular” tanks but earn much more in game credits, they are NOT "I win" vehicles.  For the most part the game is fairly balanced. I also want to address patch ”the sky is falling” 3.8; there are some terrible decisions that WG made here. Is it the end of the game? No. Does it suck? Yes, but it affected EVERYONE and created a level playing field. One thing that is really disgusting about 3.8 is the timers to unlock the new equipment. Having a long timer that can be rushed for Gold (purchased in game currency) screams greed. Hopefully this trend doesn't continue. Reworking the equipment system is fine, making the player wait days for 1 (out of 9) equipment slot that required in game currency and grinding is a poor choice. UPDATE 3.9 continues the poor choices by the devs. No longer recommended

I never played the original Crimsonland. Well actually that's not true; I tried the demo once and the game didn't really seem like anything special. After reading some great impressions from a friend, I decided to check out this new and improved Crimsonland and I'm very glad I did. It's addictive, bloody, intense, and just one hell of a fun satisfying shooter.
In terms of story and gameplay, Crimsonland is as simple as can be. You and hordes of hundreds and hundreds of creatures on the battlefield, kill them all. But while the actual mechanics are not complex, Crimsonland adds a layer of strategy underneath the run and gun gameplay, turning a game that might seem shallow from the screenshots into a compelling thrilling experience. Every moment consists of countless decisions. Which gun is best for the current situation? Should I rush for that power-up but risk having to run through a horde to reach it? Which order should I use power-ups? Which perks should I choose?
I think the most interesting aspect is how the varied enemies require you to totally change your tactics and influences the weapons and perks you'd want to use. It's not like some shooters where you can just get the most powerful weapon and kill everything. If you're facing fast spiders that replicate when they die, then you're going to want a weapon that's accurate and precise but that fires and reloads fast enough that they won't close the gap, and power-ups that focus on crowd control and defense. Hordes of zombies? You'll want to go for the spray and pray type weapons or explosives and all-out offensive power-ups. Thankfully your arsenal is just as varied as the enemies you face. Weapons range from a simple pistol and shotgun to all manner of flamethrowers, plasma cannons, automatic weapons, and even more exotic weapons. Power-ups slow time, shield you from damage, restore health, imbue your weapon with devastating plasma energy. The RPG-esque perk system offers diverse ways to customize your playstyle. Sacrifice health for damage, move faster, have more ammo, poison enemies, gain a melee attack, and many more perks make each survival attempt feel fresh and exciting
Crimsonland is a must play for top-down shooter fans. Besides the 60-mission campaign (and three difficulty levels), you can test your skills across several survival modes, all of which adds its own twist of the core gameplay. The visuals and effects are stylish, the gameplay is deeper than you'd might expect, and seeing the screen literally turn red with blood and gore as you mow down hundreds of creatures is very satisfying.

Jimmy is dropped off at a prestigious academy by his mom and the foster dad he despises very much. Our objective, initially, is to try to fit in at the school while the parents are off on their honeymoon. While Jimmy looks like a bully he is in fact bullied by other groups of students so he soon learns there are various factions who all have their own territory. By allying himself with one group he can eliminate another. Divide et impera.
If you have played at least one GTA game you'll find Bully's gameplay familiar. Shining beacons indicate you can launch a story or secondary mission that is introduced by a cutscene. Voice acting, as usual, is superb. Throughout the story we get to know all the relevant parties at the school: nerds who are afraid of everybody and hide in the library, greasers who show off by oiling their hair and wearing an outdated black jacket, preppies who are the future "fat cats of the town", the athletic jocks who are extremely short on IQ and of course the bullies who are led by Russell, a guy who could easily be called Hulk if his skin colour was just a little closer to green.
If you don't want to do any missions you can just walk around and do pranks on students, try to kiss girls (make sure you have a box of chocolate or a bouquet of flowers at hand), participate in sports activities and, of course, attend classes. These sometimes require you to pick the right answer (math), do some QTE (chemistry, music or shop classes) or go to town and take photos of the local scenery or known monuments (photography). As you progress in your studies the game slowly reveals all collectibles on the map and you are provided with different perks that ease the gameplay.
Exploring the school and its surroundings with the dormitories, the garage, the library and the gym hall is already quite exciting, however, the game goes further and gives Jimmy the opportunity to visit the local town. You know you have reached a new chapter in the game when a new district becomes accessible. Missions are expanded upon: teachers ask you to go to town and buy stuff for them and you meet a new faction (the townies) that represents an even bigger challenge.
You can do chores in the more posh areas of the town (such as becoming the paper boy or mowing the lawn) and participate in bike races. Shops are available for you to buy a better, faster bike and you can also purchase clothes and have your hair cut. Some of these activities are very similar to the ones encountered in San Andreas. By completing challenges you can acquire a building - a place where saving, sleeping and recharging your weapons are a good opportunity.
At 9 AM and 1 PM your classes begin. I do not believe they are mandatory to be attended, however, I liked these minigames so much that I never missed one. As time progresses you soon realise its nightfall and you notice some new missions have become available. Late in the evening the prefects keep searching the school and its areas to see who's violating curfew. Unlike fellow students, you cannot beat up the prefects (the same goes for townsfolk), so unnecessary violence leads to the principal's office. It doesn't mean game over - actually, it's fun mowing the lawn at school as a punishment. Hitting girls is also severely punished (while hitting on them is encouraged and it yields us a health bonus).
Make sure you keep track of time otherwise you'll miss out on missions and fail to attend classes. Also, staying up late for too long (around 2 AM) results in Jimmy's collapsing. Going to sleep is a must in this game.
Numerous activities are available for you as you stroll around on the campus. It's fun looking for collectibles in the girls' dormitories as you know you are trespassing and you'll be kicked out immediately if caught. You can play dodgeball and beat the jocks you hate so much. Students often run up to you and request you to run some errands: this means, for instance, egging the building of a faction or lock picking some of the lockers at school. Even teachers give you tasks - one is a drunkard who wants you to collect all bottles of alcohol at school while the other wants you to fix a date for her.
Riding a bike or skateboarding both allow for faster travel especially when you go to town. At bus stations you can basically fast travel back to campus. I liked how I could do skitching while skateboarding just like Marty McFly. Our favourite gun will include an accurate slingshot with indefinite ammunition and a bottle rocket launcher for swiftly eliminating a group of bullies. The spud gun is basically Bully's equivalent of a pump-action shotgun. We can also use a lot of melee weapons (such as baseball bats) when the going gets tough.
There is a reason why I used the term "Featherweight Edition" above. Bully includes no gore, no extreme violence and is toned down when it comes to cursing. Considering the dialogues and the gameplay it is still a game meant for grown-ups, though. Just because it is a toned-down version of GTA it doesn't mean it's not fun. Quite the contrary! Some of the missions are creative and a joy to play - since driving is replaced by skateboarding and riding a bike I did miss the opportunity to listening to the radio.
Unfortunately, Bully crashes a lot on modern PCs with particular emphasis on Windows 10. I was 15 hours in the game when completing the mission "Defender of The Castle" the game started crashing in every 15 minutes or so. I noticed launching it in compatibility mode (Windows XP SP 3) helped tremendously. The last 5 hours or so were done without one single crash. Still, reading on this topic in the forums does not confirm that this is a solution for everybody.
Bully is a great game. It has lots of missions and playing a GTA-like game from a student's perspective is just great fun. It wouldn't be a proper Rockstar game if it hadn't had its fair share of controversial moments. Upon its release roughly 10 years ago not everybody liked the fact that the game included a lot of bullying and kissing your own gender was a possibility. The Scholarship Edition of the game is basically a revamped version of it. If discounted this is a great purchase if you like GTA and / or sandbox games and searching for solutions for crashes is not a deterrent factor for you.

The game itself I would recommend to anyone. A great story, plenty of characters, missions, gameplay, and my favorite, the atmosphere of the game. Bully does a great job of making you feel like you're in a school filled with problems and chaos. There are a lot of side activities you can do on faily sized map to explore as well.
The only downside to this game is that it's almost unplayable on PC. Other reviews touch on it, but from my experiance, it is very hit and miss. 2 hours no crashes, 30 minutes 2 crashes, 1 hour 3 crashes etc.
If you've got a console, you're better off playing it on there. But, as far as the PC port goes it's really bad. I've tried multiple fixes, but nothing has worked out for me. I love Bully, it's a great game, I just don't recommend the PC port.

For all that the original game of the series was a such a classic experience, the sequels never quite impressed me the same way. Human Revolution especially had a hard time, with its horrid orange-tinged graphics, DLC-shredded storyline and terrible boss-battles. Still, it did recapture the feel of the original in many ways and that alone is enough to earn it a recommendation.
The Director's Cut edition removed the gold filter from the graphics of the original released version of Human Revolution, which was a welcome change. Unfortunately, without the softening tinge everything looked too harsh and this only emphasized the age of the graphics. Similarly, the Director's Cut rolled the stand-alone DLC into the main storyline. Alas, this too backfired; while the "Missing Link" quest was interesting and added some interesting detail to the storyline, it had obviously been padded out. This was okay when "The Missing Link" was a stand-alone product but - integrated into the main quest - it overstayed its welcome and completely ruined the pacing of the main story. And sadly, nothing had been done about the awful, awful boss-battles which felt so out of place I decided to bypass them using god-mode cheats.
Still, the core gameplay was solid, even though it doesn't feel half as innovative as it did 15 years ago now that every game has imitated the original. The obvious divisions of the solutions (talk, puzzle or fight) available to bypass a problem, were too mechanical and game-like to sell the illusion , and the conspiracies didn't have quite the depth or believability as those in the original. But it was still fun to creep around through the vents and take down enemies (non-lethally!) like some cyber-ninja. Some of the level design was really nice too, especially in the latter half of the game, although I felt there was too much similarity to the original game there as well. So overall it was a fulfilling experience, if nowhere near as memorable or innovate as its predecessors.

Although I'd say that it leans a little more towards the action game side of things than the classic MechWarrior sims, I think it still captures the feeling of being a mech pilot pretty well. I was apprehensive due to admittedly being a bit of a sim snob when it comes to this sort of game, but I'm finding it to be a lot of fun. Sure, they made a few changes from the board game, but even as a fan, I can deal with them. I think it still does a pretty good job of giving each type of mech a job, and not turning it into a simple shooter. You can take a missile boat and provide long-range support from cover, or a fast & light recon machine with electronic warfare equipment, or brawler, etc., and I think they did a pretty good job of making each one feel like what it is.
Regarding the "freemium" thing, the one thing that kind of annoys me is that you have to use MC (the currency you have to pay for, as opposed to C-Bills, which you can earn by playing) to pay for changing the colors on your mech, and it's not exactly cheap. That's pretty minor though, and so far I'm having plenty of fun with the mechs I've purchased using the C-Bills I got from matches (there are "special" ones you can't buy with CB). They give you a bonus amount of CB for each of your first 25 matches, so even if you suck as bad as I did, you can afford to get something cool by the end of that.
Overall, it's better than I expected, and while it's not perfect, it is a lot of fun.
