Borderline recommendation, but only because it's an above average game that could be amazing if the developers shifted focus. I'd say there are two issues holding the game back:
(1) It's currently a game that's torn between realism/adherence to tabletop Battletech versus focus on gameplay/fun in general. The upside is that they got the basic fighting forumla - the fragging in the basic quick match game mode - down well. It's fun, it rewards aim-based skill, and it rewards good mech loadouts. The downside is that PGI (the developers), have shown that they have trouble understanding the gameplay of their own game, with OP mechs, and then over-nerfs (although eventually they sort out mech balance). Similarly this extends to Community warfare (a special game mode), where realism/adherence to tabletop has made for boring community warefare maps. Case and point is further realism/tabletop mechanics poorly implemented like the CW auto-aim, long-tom artillery which basically fires off a mini-nuke every 2 mins, which kills most mechs in 1-2 hits and has a large radius. It's caused people to stop playing CW in the past - this is just one example. Similarly, PGI nerfed agility and speed of light mechs (a class of mechs) making them them basically underpowered in fights, because that's how they were in tabletop, eventhough lights were balanced before and a very fun class to play, even for the fragging. A third example is that community warfare has more then 8+ factions, making it a total mess with certain factions having too low pops, and others too high, once again imho, because of the focus on tabletop/lore/realism over gameplay.
(2) The game is Pay2NotGrind. As a new player you get a huge starting bonus of c-bills that lets you get a couple lights, 2 mediums, or 1 heavy, so it's not immediately noticeable, but put it this way - an average starting player  might  average 100k c-bills per 10-15 min match if they are good (after starting bonus expires), but light mechs typically take 5-7 million deck out; assaults usually closer to 15-18mil. If you're good, you can probably average 150k c-bills/match, maybe higher, but it's still a grind. Thankfully, it's not really Pay2Win, although there are some very good mechs that can only be bought with hard cash; the free to play equivalents are generally just as good. There are also trial mechs (can always be played by anyone without buying them) that are decent as well, though you can't customize them. Overall, the Pay2NotGrind seems to be a purposeful decision by PGI to focus on whales (few players who put lots of money in the game), and this tends to hurt the size of the playerbase.
Overall though, it's still a very fun game, and the quick match - individual or group queues - are very fun, even if community warfare isn't. And you can play private games for scrimmages, and there is a very active league quick match scene, so there is real depth to the game. Just a shame that the developers are holding the game back.
p.s. I have another 100 hours on the non-steam version of the game, several years back. Also, I'm a pseudo-whale - I've played this game on and off three times (2014, 2015, 2016)  and each time I've spent around $50-60 for a total of about $150-180. That amount has bought me about 12 mechs, mostly heavies. In the same time period of time - or about 200 hours total - I've probably grinded enough money to buy 9 heavy mechs, but I definitely wasted some ingame money by selling weapons after buying them, and then needing them later and having to rebuy them.

The game borders between fun and rage-inducing. It hits so many elements of the mechwarrior universe on point but lacks some of the most important things that makes mechwarrior stand out from any other deathmatch game.
Bases aren't bases. They aren't massive round dropships surrounded by a perimeter of turret defenses, repair bays, and vital facilities/objectives. No, your base is just a martian rover with a capture zone.
Clan Wars, an attack/defense game mode, is so horribly broken that practically no one plays it. The recent updates to it just made it worse. Limitations on mech selection AND the obliterate-the-entire-team artillary aside, much of it can be attributed to bad map layout.
I credit this game for being balanced. It has a massive selection of weapons, mechs, and equipment - free mechs, and mechs that cost over $50. Yet, you can still gain an edge over the cash-flush players with skills and the right loadout.
But you can also BLATANTLY CHEAT with macros. Somehow this is still allowed! Exploit the game and alter your weapon firing rates using outside, third-party software to input commands into the game. Defenders of this say "it doesn't affect dps" or the advantage is negligable. It's still an attempt to gain an advantage and it alters the way the game was originally intended to be played. Make whatever excuses you want, you're cheating. I'm not too worried about these people because they're terrible and that's why they use macros in the first place.
So is the game still fun? Yes, but only in QuickMatch mode. And only if you're lucky enough to not get stuck on a team full of complete pansies who hide behind rocks, fail to recognize enemy tactics, or offer strategy suggestions long after the opportunity to act has passed.
The game looks and sounds good, is in continuous development - with new content frequently coming out, and can be fun with the right group of players.
So, it's a love/hate thing.

A silly, cute and surprisingly heartwarming tale about a nerdy, introverted computer programmer and the dragon who comes to live with her in the modern human world. Due to how it relies heavily on cultural knowledge (both of Japanese life and various mythological tales), your enjoyment of this show will vary depending on just how much of it you "get".
On that same note, the major blemish on this anime are the interactions between another character and a little boy with the unfortunate (but appropriate) name of Shouta. As you might expect, it's shota-related jokes, but even the characters in-universe seem to acknowledge how uncomfortable & sometimes creepy it can be having a millenia-old former-goddess flirting with a young boy. There is some character development going on with the two as the season proceeds, which does eventually lead to an adorable moment with no subtext whatsoever; and the offending character also starts covering herself up more. Still, it's the one thing that would keep me from making this a recommendation to everyone, unless you're aware of this and the different attitudes of Eastern and Western nations' views towards such behavior.
There's never anything graphic actually shown or done (sexual OR violent) in any situation, and a lot of the humor reminds me of classic Ranma ½, so if you can go into this with the mental reminder that it's sometimes "very Japanese", I think you'll enjoy it. From what I understand, they've also made some major improvements over the manga, but some characters and plots still haven't been introduced, so hopefully there will be another season.
There's some heavy use of anime tropes and lampshading of others, and while it starts off slowly, the way they build things up and make excellent use of continuity means you'll likely start really liking almost all of the characters, and I was pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed this series. Just.. take a grain of salt with a handful of (thankfully brief) scenes.

Endless Space is a 4X game (expand/explore/exploit/exterminate) in the same vein as Civilization, with a lot of similarities to Civ IV. The game has a lot of interesting unique mechanics in addition to the normal Civ gameplay including a uniquely structured tech tree, purchasable heroes that can lead your troops or your planets, and a unique way to utilize your planets (cities essentially) for resources. In addition, the many traits that the different civilizations have change the dynamic of the game and your priorities. The ability to make custom civilations by mixing and matching these traits also gives a lot of room for creativity and new experiences.
However, the main flaw of Endless Space is that it feels somewhat lifeless. It does a lot of things well, but there isn't anything it does particularly amazingly. The game ends up feeling somewhat generic because despite the unique mechanics there isn't anything that stands out as a large improvement over other 4X games.
Overall I would recommend Endless Space to fans of 4X games, especially those that enjoyed CivIV more than CivV, and for people who enjoyed Endless Legend and want to try a similar game. However, for people who aren't huge fans of the genre I would recommend sticking to Civ or other common 4X games instead.

At first this game seemed generic for a 4x, but as I got better the game got more complex.
The complexity lies in the design of your empire as a whole. Every development is trading one benefit for another and the degree with which you can fine tune your Empire is pretty insane. The ability to sacrifice one aspect like population growth for researching technology. Getting invaded? In a dozen or so turns you can turn that research oriented empire into a production beast. How about repurposing your battle fleet as an extension of your research? Oh yeah, done in one turn.
This game does drop the ball on combat. It's theatrical battles are beautiful and fun to watch, but they don't serve any greater function. The auto-battle button will be worn thin quickly. Also, the AI will instigate war for no reason when you get close to a victory. Then after losing said war, will pretty much all but stop trying. The AI is a very soar loser, I mean that literally. It gets very butt-hurt, very easily.
That said, this game does lose a lot of it's appeal playing small maps and/or quick games. For a quick game it loses most of it's appeal. If you're looking for a quick action packed experience, this is about the farthest thing from what you want.
If you're looking for a time investing empire manager, then this is worth the money. If you're looking for epic space battles, your enjoyment may be short lived with the exception of a couple of the playable races.

The only ones who could make them fall were the Endless themselves with inner conflicts and arrogance. Millions of years later other empires arose from the stars. The Endless were gone but their technology, wisdom and Dust is still there, waiting for new conquerors. Which faction will dominate the others with science, war and dust? Hopefully yours.

with your chosen nation. May it the aggressive bird-like Hissho, the mechanical Automatons or the old human Imperials, they all come with positive and negative aspects that fit differing playstyles. Colonizing your first planet afterwards can be a tough choice. Planets differ and thus do the resources they produce. What you should keep in mind here is
, standing for Food, Industry, Dust and Science. Basically, these four get your planets populated and fed, build ships and structures, offer the possibility for doing research and pay your running costs for ships, planetary improvements and heroes. Improvements can be portals for faster travel, refineries or habitats, just to name some out of a huge amount ES offers. Heroes are specialized commanders who can be attached to starsystems and fleets to further improve certain aspects like production or offense. They get XP, level-up and cost more while doing so. Better ships and improvements need more research and cost more Dust. See, it is the well known cycle you have to bear with. What makes it even more difficult sometimes are random events that can be a blessing but also a plague for the whole empire.
Having established yourself, there is room for
. First, acceptance. Planets, taxes and other effects influence your nation’s happiness. The higher the taxes, the higher the dust outcome. But who wants to pay taxes? People will likely start to get lazy and work less. It works the other way around too. Less taxes, more resources. Next task: luxury ressources. Once your scientists know how to deal with them, you gain the opportunity to build better ships, planetary improvements and use them as trading goods. Trading leads us to task 3, diplomacy. Venturing into the unknown will make you meet new friends. Or Foes. Fight or feed them? Living in peace means building trade routes for dust and science, luxury resources and even full researches. Roughly Explained:  Remember turns as a term that got used in Baldur’s Gate where attacks and effects were happening in a specific amount of time? Take this, mix it with scissor-rock-papers referring to bullets, lasers and rockets and their defensive counterparts and add some tactical influence via abilities, used as “cards” ingame. After around 20 hours I think I can make a fairly well informed opinion on this game.
First the question everyone always asks when it comes to F2P games. Is it pay to win?
The answer is an unequivocal yes. This game is absolutly pay to win.
The next question is how, how is this game pay to win?
The answer is quite simple. The way you increase damage and health is through a single stat called "Might". Might is raised not by killing enemies and finishing quests but through two buildings you aquire faily quickly called the Cathedral, and the Tower of Knowledge. Both of these are simply menus that you click a single button to improve, this costs in game currency and has a daily limit on how many times you can upgrade.
So how does this make the game pay to win? Simple, you can buy both currencies to increase your Might (remember might is more or less levels, it increases every single stat and cannot be found on equipment), and you can also buy items that reset the daily upgrade limit. Eventually the daily limit becomes more and more restricted. Day one you can upgrade dozens of times with seamingly no limit, day two you can upgrade maybe 7 or 8 times, and by day three you can only upgrade each maybe 3-4 times (This could also be linked to progression and not times a day but I have no way to know). I would assume as time goes on you will eventually be restricted to a single upgrade each day. Im sure this is designed to give you the initial impression that you can upgrade without limit and are never required to spend money to level up, but quickly becomes a progression wall incentivizing you to spend money to reset daily timers.
I am three days into the game and I've already hit a solid brick wall where missions are too difficult for me to complete (I simply cannot survive attacks or kill fast enough), but I need to wait a full day to upgrade my character in any meaningful way.
Now... Onto gameplay.
Skyforge is an instance based action RPG, similar to games like Vindictus in zone structure, and TERA in combat. You are given a basic attack, 7 special attacks, an ultimate, and in some cases combos that give additional attacks.
You start the game with three basic classes to fit the three major MMO roles...
Damage (Cryomancer-ranged damage)
Support (Lightbringer-NOT a healer, only has shields and buffs but for some reason does WAY more damage than the cryomancer)
Tank (paladin).
As you progress through the story you unlock more classes (mostly damage dealers) by completing missions. Since there are no levels in this game and all progression is dictated through the might stat, unlocking new skills is accomplished by quests that require you to kill X amount of enemies with the class you wish to upgrade. Most equipment also seems to have a negligible effect giving you a fraction of a percent of damage, the only piece that seems to make a big difference is the weapon and only because it can come with a "X% Damage increase" stat on it. Entire zones seem to drop the same handful of items over and over, the only way Ive found to upgrade your gear are instances (which are REALLY hard due to the lack of a healer) and zone quests which give you a new full set of items to equip.
The combat is psudo skill based, it includes a roll with no iframes so really all it is good for is distancing yourself or moving quickly. And most skills seem to be functionally useless under most circumstances. Generally you will use 2-3 skills and just spam those till things die. Its definitely more fun than most MMOs but is still rather shallow.
Overall I would say its worth playing for a few days, once you hit the point where missions become impossible to solo and the game begins putting up progression walls to try and convince you to buy resets, its worth just hanging up the towel and moving on. I've played this games for hundreds of hours before it came to steam and came back to it about a month ago so this is my opinion on the current iteration of this game.
Pros:
Well thought out mechanics.
Skill is based on precision and teamwork in this game.
Probably the best community I've seen in a game (youngest person I've met online was 16).
Immersive gameplay.
Great visual queues for everything that happens whether dealing damage or taking it.
Teamwork focused gameplay.
Extremely Customizable mechs and mech loadouts.
There are no "bad mechs" as all have strengths and weaknesses.
All weapons are fair and balanced.
Beautiful scenery/models/animations.
Great F2P system (you earn a ton of money early with the cadet bonus which allows you too basicly buy any mech).
Little to no "trolls".
Cons:
Extremely high skill ceiling for new players.
Clan wars (Comp.) can be dreadful and not worth your time if you aren't in a good faction/group.
If you are new and past your cadet bonus you won't be making much money as you won't be getting many points.
If you don't do well then earning c-bills (in game currency) can become a grind instead of a steady income.
Game modes aren't different enough from one another.
Queuing system needs reworking.
Overall this game is its own unique experience as no other game is quite like it. It puts you into a cockpit of a huge 25-100 ton War machine and tells you to go out and destroy the enemy Pilots. The feeling you get when you peel apart enemy mechs and visualing see them being torn to ribbons is a feeling no other game can recapture.
I can't recommend this game enough. It's fun, has a great community, and as of July the dev team has worked out some of the previous hinderances and problems that this game had (that plagued it long ago but no more!). Now is the best time to play this game so Pilots power up your mechs and head out to war!!
9/10 please just try it you are missing out :)

Pay 2 Win Change=Each tank has its own characteristics with a crew of its own.First Wargaming introduced provisions which increased the tank in pretty much all the aspects.This feature, while could be bought for ingame currency, was very expensive and required the purchase of a premium account to profit in high tiers of the game.This change was followed by reducing the profit percentages of all the tanks and now with update 3.8, equipment system is changed.Wargaming introduced timers which could bypassed for gold(currency that can be bought) with new equipment being much varied and stronger than the previous ones.This new system gives the wallet warriors a huge advantage.
Map Design=At its initial release Blitz resembled its pc version a lot more with its varied maps.In order to promote supremacy game mod(capture the base mod), the majority of the maps were flattened.Tank destroyers and heavy tanks lost importance while light and fast medium tanks became the dominant classes.While the penetration values of lights and meds were nerfed not long ago, the game suffered a lot with Wargamings decision to promote brainless fast paced gameplay.

Loadout was one of my favorite multiplayer shooters I have ever played. I only spent a few hours on steam, but I've spent more than 50 hours on the ps4 version. I decided to jump back into the PC version and now I have a verdict on this version.
Loadout is a very unique F2P shooter. You have the ability to create different combinations of weapons and use them to blow up or dismember your opponents. You have a lot of options and every combination is fun to create and fun to use in  combat.
The game also had a very smart approach to Free to play. The game allowed you to use the money for gun parts which didn't make the gun over powered.
The player base is currently still alive and kicking and you can jump into any game mode without any trouble.
All the game modes are incredibly fun, so if you get sick of one game mode you can quickly jump into another without a problem.
You might be asking yourself, why I'm giving this game a negative review then if all the things that I listed make the game seem awesome. Well the reality is the PC version is terrible compared to the PS4 version.
The game has been abandoned by the developers, who announced that the servers will shutdown and not to mention no updates for a while now.
Some connection issues also ruin the fun of the game, but that rarely happens so I doubt you will run into that problem.
In the end this game is incredibly fun, but the devs abandoned the game, so there is next to no reason to play the PC version. If you have a PS4 that is the place to play the superior version of the game.
Final Rating:
4/10 - Don't bother with the PC version

I finally finished the entire game, and did a full walkthrough/let's play of this game on my channel.
Plus, I've earned all the achievements.
Anyways, I wish to thank all of the people who made this game, and with that, come with my honest opinion, so people can find this helpful, and as well, tell the people at Pixel Maniacs what I think.
Despite I got this for free from the company, I don't believe that should effect my opinion.
The price should be lowered, since I can't see it being worth 13 Euros, when you can complete the entire game within a short period of time, around the 10 Euros would be more fitting.
I truly enjoyed the concept, the idea of a puzzle game, which involves colors, was something that I haven't tried before, and that was truly something different, than what I normally play.
However, the game did seem quite short, and it has it's few moments that can be tricky. The only hard times, are when you're forced to make a wild guess. I believe that the game could've easily be longer, and a lot more challenging.
I must say, that I enjoyed the narrator and his evil voice, giving you some kind of hints now and then, but you barely heard from him later on in the game.
What I pretty much asked for, is more gameplay, and a greater challenge as you progress.
With all this said, the game is not bad at all, it's worth playing, but it should be for a smaller price then, since it is as short, as it is.
Big applause to Pixel Maniacs for this nice game. =)

Oh boy, how this game surprised me.. I bought this on a sale and thought I would play it only for a few hours and then get bored, I thought that it would be your common rpg. It has an amazing unique gameplay, interesting mechanisms I have never seen before, a very entertaining story, nicely done humour, hundreds of locations to explore in an open world playstyle, flexibility in building your characters (both in appearance and stats/skills), sidequests, hundreds of different enemies, some choice matters stuff and one of my personal favorites: lots of secrets (even though I had to see some spoilers to solve some of them).
On the other hand, like every game, there were somethings that I missed/disliked in this game like. Stealth skill is bugged and it has been a long time like that. I experienced once (and only once) a bug where I couldn't move my characters so I had to exit the game and lost my progress in that level. The lack of a quest log, the game has LOTS of locations and information, I couldn't possibly remember everything from everywhere. The lack of a written list of the locations in game (some quests require you to go somewhere you still don't know, an in-game written list of the locations would make it easier to guess instead of having to move your mouse to every single location in the map to see it's name). There could be more lore to the enemies since lots of them were really interesting and I would love to understand the developer's idea behind them. As you can see, most of my complaints are personal opinions and really small compared to every good thing this game has to offer (except the ones about bug) so it may not apply to you.
TL;DR: if you like rpg's and/or tactical turn based rpg's, scroll up and buy this. Like someone else said in his review, it's truly a hidden gem in Steam

Pretty disappointed by this "remake"... if you could even call it that. This game has some new perks and a few new game modes, but that's about all that is new.  All of the sound effects and music, for example, are 100% reused from the original-- in 2003, this kind of audio quality was acceptable, but in 2014, it feels tinny and underwhelming, especially with regards to the music, which sounds like it was saved and then resaved as lossy 64kbps mp3s. The graphics are pretty much the same as well, just barely updated for wide screen resolutions. This is such a non-remake, in fact, that the flavor text for perks is exactly the same, poor English included! In 2003, coming from a tiny indie dev, this was acceptable. But to have this in 2014, from what is now a well established, modestly successful casual PC and mobile developer...that's just shameful and embarassing. (If you've played any of 10tons' games on iPhone or Android, that is the kind of quality I expected.)
Now for the new gameplay-- for some reason, someone thought that it would be a good idea to remove perks entirely from the Quest mode. This is such a poor decision. A major part of the 2003 game's charm was getting to make choices and develop your character gradually over the course of each level, with a clear progression in your power as the enemies became stronger and more numerous. Now the quest mode is just a boring grindfest in which the only interesting choices are when to pick up a powerup, and whether to use a shotgun or a plasma rifle. What's worse is that the game forces you play through this quest mode in order to unlock the guns and perks for use in survival mode, which does let you choose perks and develop your character. It's a poor design choice to force your players to trudge through a boring mode so that they can better succeed in the more fun game mode. Please change this back to the way it was!
Perhaps the biggest feature of this "remake" is the introduction of achievements, but half of them are predictable, "complete chapter 1 of quest mode", "complete chapter 2", type achievements. There's also one achievement which is particularly irritating for completionists like myself-- the "no damage" achievement. You now earn a star for each Quest mode level you complete without taking damage, and you have to collect one from every level to get the achievement. Sounds simple, right? Not when your character now moves at 80% of the speed they used to, your success on a level is heavily dependent upon which gun drops from the first monster, and the poor level design is such that monsters sometimes spawn right on top of you (this was rarely an issue in the original). This achievement also goes against everything the original was about: wading into mobs of aliens like a badass, and shrugging them off as you blow them away. To actually get every star for this achievement, you would have to restart your game hundreds, if not thousands of times. Meanwhile, you have to play the game as a super perfectionist SHMUP where you die instantly, rather than the messy, Smash TV style slaughterfest it is meant to be.
Lastly, the UI...I don't know why they decided to change this. In the 2003 game, your health and ammo were shown in the top left corner, in a bar with a black background. You could clearly see how much health you had, and how much ammo you had remaining in your clip. In this remake, they moved it to the aiming reticle, converting the health to a very small blue circle around you, and the ammo to a blue number next to the crosshair. While this does mean you don't have to shift your eyes away from the battle to see your stats, the tiny graphics and the light blue coloring are a pain to read, and they often blend right into the scenery or your enemies.
Unless they patch this game to make it more interesting and closer to the original, I can't recommend it. You will have much more fun with the 2003 version, believe me! And it costs almost the same. I was SO excited about this remake. I wanted badly to love it, and I was looking forward to improvements to the original. Instead, I got a product that is actually worse, and that feels like it was rushed in a month or two for the sake of a money grab.
Edit: The devs have made a post in the Steam discussion forums about how they did include a hidden option to unlock perks in the main Quest mode by typing "grim" at the menu. However, this doesn't solve the deeper underlying issue, which is the super short Quest levels (and to a lesser extent, the poor level design). The original Crimsonland was about starting weak then growing in power over time. The length of these levels is so short that this feeling of progression has been greatly diminished.  So while it's a band-aid, it doesn't fix the actual cause.  This feature (one that shouldn't be hidden, btw) also doesn't make up for the generally poor production values and other issues, such as the unclear UI.

This game used to thrive because there was a mutual understanding between the players and the developers. When you spent money they treated you right, they courted you for keeping their lights on. It was understood that you were a paying customer and that was appreciated. Since their 3.8 update (and a little before, actually), they've ceased to show a smidgen of respect to the playerbase and taken to try and force money from the hands of paying players. I can't even imagine the kind of discomfort experienced by those playing for free. I weep for them. If you take anything away from this review, it's this :
. Free to get robbed and struggle through impossibly long grind periods (We're talking months for
little reward)? Sure.
Update 3.8 brought a change to the equipment that one can load onto their tanks. Keep in mind that the difference between a fully equipped tank and stock tank is night and day. It takes that equipment to play it to its full potential. Pre-3.8 veterans, myself included, had hundreds of tanks that were fully equipped. That took hundreds of hours of gameplay to do. When they announced 3.8 they told us outright that we were going to be short-changed: we'd recieve 1/8th of the equipment we had before. Imagine that. You'd think that they'd do the very obviously fair thing and make the conversion 1 to 1 (nope). Now those of us with garages full of tanks only get to fully equip a handfull at best and the rest is locked away behind timers that take days and grinds that'll take
. Again, I have to say this so you don't get the wrong impression: if the veterans are getting robbed, the "free-to-play" newcomers are at a huge disadvantage. It's in everyone's interest to hold these devs accountable.
This is simply extortion. They want you to spill some cash for gold so you can play the tanks you already worked to equip. Ridiculous. There's been an exodus of players and thread upon thread of complaints on the forums but the devs don't listen. Check their t-shirt reviews on Amazon and their ratings on the Apple store. The devs just nailed the lid on their coffin and unless they make some serious, non-cash-grabby changes, they're going to kill their own game. As it stands this game is not playable and absolutely not worth spending any money on. Heed the bad reviews and remember that the Russians (devs) have bots working to try and skew how badly their game has tanked with fake reviews.
edit: if you choose not to believe me, go look a the other reviewers. Mind you that the only relevant ones are from May onward. That's when this 3.8 fiasco happened.
Still no fix for the equipment system they implemented and they've instead added a rating system that's pretty useless. It limits the amount of votes you can give other players on their behavior/performance in-game to 3 per day. That's useless and it'll let people get away with still being ignoramuses. League has a similar honor system that WG could easily model but they've decided to side with the trolls who cry on the forums about imaginary "abuse". They just want to be able to call people everything under the sun without consequence. The new American line looks unappealing and I wouldn't bother grinding it myself. They nerfed premium ammo damage and made it less costly as well. For the time-being I don't see a problem with that, and I spam the stuff when I see red, if that tells you anything. They resold exclusive event tanks in the tech tree and put out some mediocre camo for the IS-6 (it's terrible and suuuper low-res, I've made my own mod camo that's higher quality). They're nullifying the work the people who ground the event tanks put in after every update and it's just sick to watch them take people's money and then stab them in the back. The game remains in an unplayable state. Wargaming is frantically selling over-powered, formerly "exclusive" tanks at exorbitant prices to try and slow the bleeding from 3.8. They're going to be releasing another crate-gamble event soon to try and recoup their losses because of how successful the last one was. Meanwhile, long-time players and collectors have boycotted them into the red. They went as far as replacing an in-game consumable--adrenaline--with "ToRnAdO eNeRgY". The image that replaced it was a Tornado Energy Drink can. They've been hemorrhaging money so much that they've turned basic game mechanics into advertising space. Let me first let it be known that I love tactical turn based games so this could be a little bias.
I bought this game on sale for about 6 bucks which to me is a steal. I would say 10 bucks is where it should be priced at.
The setting is pretty simple and intriguing you are a prisoner who has comitted a crime which you get to pick, I only think two of the crimes change the experience from what I have read but never the less its still pretty interesting. There is many different locations and some pretty decent lore within in the levels that keep you wanting to learn more about the world you are placed in. I waited until I was about 7 hours in to place this review to get  decent understanding.
Combat in this game is pretty simple yet you still have to be aware of your surroundings and the type of character you have. You can recruit every enemy that I have met so far in a system that is dependent on your stats which is interesting as there is a wide variety in the types of enemies. You can use ranged magic spells as well as healing and for ranged attacks it is dependent on what weapon you equip your characters with. Certain items will give you range for what I have seen up to 5 with different stat bonuses. You can choose to make your characters tanky, have good dodging, critical hitting specialist, magic users, or strong magic defense to name a few.
There is a very interesting stronghold system in this game that makes in unique and separates it from your average strategy game. To take strongholds you must have adequate man power to hold it which in turn gives you the ability to recruit more companions and have shops, traders, or quartermasters which can really make your life easier.
Overall I really enjoy this game due to the setting and lore that keeps you immersed. The combat while a bit simple is made entertaining by the different types of playstyles you can recruit and fight with. The most unique system is the strongholds which gives you something extra besides a basic fight only game.
Graphics are a pixelated master piece if you ask me. I have never been a gamer that has based a game on graphics and absolutely cannot stand people who will dismiss a game on graphics alone. As long as I can tell what is what and am not like WTF is that supposed to be I do not mind.
Biggest cons would be that the AI for your party can be a little dumb with getting stuck on pathings and not automatically staying closer to you. This could be an easy fix for the dev (there is only one) to just have them stay in line so they dont get caught up so far behind or stuck entirely. The enemy AI is decently smart and I have read that they just rush you? This is completely false and they will hold their ground if they see you setting up and just buffing defense. Just wanting to out the false reviewers who have put that. Other than the pathings faults thats my only real complaint.

ChromaGun is an interesting game for me. And I personally have some mixed feelings about the whole package of the game. Let's start by breaking down my Pros and Cons.
So, for those of you deliberating whether to buy this game, I highly recommend it if you enjoy puzzle games such as Portal and others of that specific genre. It's a love letter to the game, containing a few hidden references for the player to find.
The Pros:
The useage of colours to solve the puzzles is a fresh new take on the puzzle genre and provides a fun four hour experience.
The game has eight chapters worth of chambers and almost every chapter has 7 stages tacked on, so you get a lot of gameplay for your money's worth.
The Narrator is entertaining... when he's around.
The droids.
The Cons:
After a while the six colours you can make become a little boring. By chapter 6, I was desiring a new upgrade. Maybe an option that could revive rusted objects perhaps?
The electric tiles and their hitboxes. If there's anything I disliked in this game, it's those electric tiles. I had my fair share of failures from them and they ruined my experience in the final room of the game as I kept getting shocked by them at the end due to the working droids pushing me into them (This is during an escape sequence where you really shouldn't die for maximum impact).
The lack of narration is some portions of the game. I couldn't help but feel like half of the chapters were just romps through the test chambers. We don't have as much interaction with the Narrator as I would have liked and I just couldn't care for the character when he talked. Sometimes I forgot he was there.
The end of Chapter 4. Because a few floors in to chapter 5 we completly ignore what had happened like it had never taken place.
Overall, I'd give this game a solid 7/10 with a recommendation to Buy it! The game works, caters to all audiences and is an easy fix for those with Portal withdrawel symptoms. But keep in mind the game doesn't have much of a story and sweeps any narrative portions under the rug fairly quickly.

I didn't get the controls right and I didn't like the community settings. So after an hour I realised that I should have been playing the game instead. I also had a harder time getting used to rocket league since the 100's of hours I put into this game on multiple platforms has ingrained muscle memory which I can't get rid of. Not the controller's fault but I found myself getting annoyed. The Talos principle and SOMA on the other hand are PERFECT for the controller. Pick up and play and you'll love it.
All in all, I am amazed by the amazing link and the great controller. They are products which appeal specifically to tinkerers and tech savvy people. If that's you, you will LOVE these products! 9/10, would buy again.

I am a fan of the original game. I got it back in 1994 and if a Steam counter existed back then I'd have at least five thousand hours on it. When I saw it available on Steam I bought it and immediatly started playing.
The base game seemed like the original, building my first colonies and manufacturing goods. I enjoyed myself until I decided to get rid of my French neighbours.
I prepared a little army, with several veterans and some artillery. The initial combat went my way.
The combat in this game is basicly a diceroll you can influence by using better units or by using advantageous terrain like mountains or forest. By doing so I was able to first defeat a few French dragoons, turning them into militia(infantry) and then defeated them again and captured them as unarmed colonists. Then I decided to move against his colony and the forces he set up to defend it. I hit his first dragoons, lost the diceroll and my veteran dragoons were destroyed. Uhm, excuse me? I played this game often enough to remember that any defeated unit gets demoted to the next lower level, instead I just lost a veteran, dissapeared, destroyed, not even an unarmed colonist left. I fought a bit more to see what was going on and, in the same fashion, lost several more veteran dragoons. Effectively setting me back to some garrisoned militia and artillery, incapable of offensive actions. what a letdown.
Oddly enough, a unit defending a colony demotes as per the original. For a little while there I thought it was me but nope, I actually got a copy of the original game from somewhere else, this is not how the original works.
If you are a fan of the original game, then I'm sorry to say this isnt a copy of that. If you do not mind that bug or another attempt at a 'better' remake(those were always a step back), then you may enjoy it. I found it horrible, cant recommend.

This game is a gem, and still great fun to play more than two decades after its release. It is up to you to turn that humble beginning into a vast colonial empire - and then rebel against the ever more oppressive rule from across the seas.
It is a game that is fairly simple to get into, but the more finnicky bits of growth and economy can take a while to get the hang of. Do you start a vast agricultural colony, raising new colonials through food, or do you start with cash crops and their refined versions to scrape together enough gold for new recruits from the old world? Perhaps you instead focus on spreading the good word of your faith to lure lost souls across the Atlantic, or use your military might and missionaries to subdue the local natives as converts? Perhaps all of the above, all the while bickering with your fellow European colonies and treading carefully around the sovereign's steady requests for higher taxes, your day only brightened as founding fathers flock to your banner to aid you.
Being an early Civ style game, the four different factions (England, France, Spain and the Netherlands) start at the same time (1492) and with a fairly similar footing. England is the baseline faction. France has a trained pioneer, Spain has a trained soldier, and the Netherlands has a better ship - on top of their unique nation bonuses.
This particular version of the game is the DOS version, wrapped in a quite functional DOS-box. This does mean that you'll get the limitations of that version - namely, there is a unit cap for how many units you can have on the map at a given time. Unless you're really building up your empire for population score, you aren't likely to encounter that issue all that often, though. There is also a cap on the number of colonies, but again, it is fairly high. Barring those inherited problems, I've had no issues with this version of the game - short of lacking the time to play it as much as I'd have liked to.
All in all, a game that still feels as great as rose-tainted memories suggested. That cannot be said or all games one feels nostalgic about. Definitely a worthy purchase, even now.

Where to begin... Upon its release NSUNS4 recieved bad rep for having terrible performance and a 30fps cap (which I will touch on later **no longer applies**), I for one never had an issue with performance running a meager phenom ii quad core from '09 and an overclocked 7950 running the game maxed with super sampling down from 4k. So if performance is a concern for you there's no need to worry, as long as you have a DX11 compatible GPU you should be able to run the game just fine. **EDIT 60fps option has been added to the game** The game is locked at 30fps however, due to the way the animations are created and low frame times it still feels fluid and responsive, this coming from a CS:GO LEM who can't stand less than 100fps in a first person shooter, though the cap isn't an issue, I still wish it wasn't there.
The Game:
When I first picked up the NSUNS series I wasn't expecting much, a generic fighting game involving characters from the naruto series right? As it turns out, I was in for a pleasant surprise. The series became a staple when it came to playing with friends and NSUNS4 is no exception. NSUNS4 is a colorful, action-packed game that's fairly easy to pick up but still manages to have a relatively high skill ceiling. There are a large variety of characters (including around 8 Narutos and 8 Sasukes) and the battles feel epic and fast-paced. While there are many mechanics that differ the naruto series from other fighting games, probably the most discerning is its substitution mechanic, which allows you to basically stop taking damage for a moment and teleport behind your opponent, the catch however, is you only have 4 of these substitutions and they only begin recharge after a cooldown period and its easy for your opponent to continue their assault if you don't immediately take action, timing and "meter management" are everything. In terms of "new" mechanics compared to the older games, you can now switch between teammates in team fights and are no longer restricted to your primary character, switching mid-attack allows you to extend your combos and really makes the feature feel like a seamless edition to the game. Local multiplayer is flawless, though online multiplayer is a bit of a hit or miss. The game has been designed to use a peer-to-peer connection, which means very little in terms of servers or maintenance on the dev's part however if either one of the players has a bad connection or has trouble maintaining the games fps limit. The game time can slow down or become a stuttery mess with a "connecting" bar popping up in the middle of your screen frequently. That with the fact that the game uses open mics and no option to mute opponents, multiplayer can potentially be a nightmare. That being said, if both players have a good connection, can run the game fine (as most can), and either mute their mics or don't have a lot of background noise, the multiplayer works great and can result in some very memorable battles. The story is great, though it starts late in the storyline so its definitely not friendly to those new or unfamiliar to the series. The story features some fantastic battles, though cut-scenes switch between animations and slideshows, which may not sound appealing however overall it's very well done and I would even recommend the game for the story alone as both it and the multiplayer each are great in their own regard. If you're into fighting games, a fan of Naruto, or just looking for something new, this game is great and I would reccomend it to just about anyone.

Got that itch for Portal, but can't be bothered to replay Portal(2) for the umpteenth time? Good, time to stop thinking with Portals and remember how subtractive color addition works!
Chromagun is a first Person Puzzler, and took a lot of inspiration from Portal. The playtime was roughly around 4 hours for me as someone who has played both Portal and Portal 2. There is a "Speedrun" mode implemented as well, so if you're into that.. There's more play time to be had, to really get those best times down.
Graphics and sound are not bad by any means, but they won't be Portal level, of course. They work for the game though since the focus is on the puzzles in the whole game. Speaking about the puzzles, I felt like there were some slight problems in terms of Flow from time to time. I've gotten through some of the apparently more difficult levels with ease, only to be hit i nthe face with a level that is way easier than I anticipated in which I will try to overengineer the solution as much as possible. Then again, that could be a personal quirk as well.
So, this game is about colours, you say, but what about the folks who can't see all the rainbow-y greatness that is this game? Fret not, for this game actually has a pretty snazzy Colourblind mode, overlaying all coloured surfaces with marks that also combine properly when mixing colours.
The ending was somewhat antclimactic in retrospect and is the biggest negative point I have. I mean, the story isn't anything to write hme about either, but serves its purpose - But that ending just felt like a slap in the face compared to Portal. I don't want to spoil too much, but a timed level doesn't make for the best finale, in my opinion.
Would I recommend the game and why/why not?
I'd recommend the game. If you like Portal and want a game for a rainy day/slow night - This is right up your alley. Into speedrunning and want to try something different? Give Chromagun a shot.
Are you looking for a 100hr+ game for $5 max? Go away, deinstall steam and take a looooong walk.

- The play concept seems fun, but the graphics quality themselves is poor and, in spite of what I read in other reviews, I thought the writing for the voice over was a painfully not-funny amateur attempt at Portal 2 like humor. - You'll notice I don't have much play time. The first time a robot killed me I crashed and dropped out of the program. Along with the other issues it wasn't worth it to me to try again and risk crashing all the time. I just bailed and wrote this review mostly to warn people about the keys.

I hate comparing games to other games in a review, but it's almost unavoidable in the first-person puzzle-platform genre, since Portal has basically been the gold standard since 2007. I feel that ChromaGun captures the elements that made Portal great (excellent gameplay, humor, puzzles, progressive addition of new mechanics) without feeling like a clone or a rip-off. It's simple, fun, challenging, and full of color. And you get to shoot robots with paint. Hard to beat that combination.
The only bad thing I have to say is that I think the price is high for the amount of content (playing casually, I completed the game in about 4 hours). That said, I've read rumors (and the game's narrator drops a couple of hints) that there may be more content coming (possibly a level editor?) in the future. If that's the case, then I retract my complaint about the price. I'd love to see the developers build more upon the concepts they've established so far.
(I just have one question for the devs: Why are you able to jump? You literally never need to use it, and you only get about two inches off the ground anyway. :) )

Almost every time I run Steam the controller will reset itself to default configurations (which seem totally non-intuitive to me).  You have to go into Big Picture mode and then exit it just to get the controller to work as a Windows mouse.  Unbelievably, NONE of the dozen or so games I have installed, including ALL the Steam games, are supported - including the ones that have been ported to consoles!  I also don't see any mention of user-made controller profiles
in Big Picture.  If installing them requires a bunch of manual tinkering then Valve has failed completely - the whole idea was to give us console-style simplicity.  I suspect I'll be returning this thing and sticking to proper PC input devices.  If I really end up needing a controller it'll likely be an XB1 type, which supports virtually EVERY game whether its Steam-based or not.  While a joystick isn't as great for aiming as a mousepad, if the controller doesn't support most of the games, what does it matter?

Introduction: 8BitMMO will always be a special game to me for a number of reasons; it's the first MMO that i've taken seriously, it's one of the first free-to-play games that I've ever downloaded (with Tank-Tank-Tank! for the Wii U being the first) and finally it is actually my first Steam game. If all of that wasn't enough for me to see the game in a positive light then the huge amount of content, the great community features and the charm that the game hands out frequently would just about do it.
Gameplay: The gameplay is based on three core-styles; building, combat and exploration. I'd say that the building and exploration aspects are far more prominent in the game rather than the combat. The exploration in the game is a little dodgy but that's just dependent on how well you and other users have developed explorable worlds. You explore by visiting other user's built worlds, villages, dungeons... well, what ever they have decided to make to be honest! Your objectives in these areas are to find a reward block after completing challenges set by the creator/user... but how do these challenges work? Well, the user is supposed to put enemies and other hazards in the way of the player and the reward block. An issue with this is that most people just put a bunch of enemies in the way of a bunch of complicated building structures, the question is though, is this the game's fault? Players are given a number of different choices in design so I'd say no, the game's barrier for design is your imagination. If you're a boring minded gamer then I'm sorry but the truth is that your game is going to be boring. The combat (as mentioned before) plays a key part in this form of exploration because apparently spamming the "insert enemy here" button equals good game design. The combat is very simplistic for a MMO but that isn't a bad thing, it keeps a constant and consistent flow in-between the gameplay styles without completely dumbing it down. You can purchase weapons with money such as a sword, a stronger sword and a stronger sword... ok, they may have dumbed it down a little... ok, a lot... ok, quite a lot. Sure there's a fire arm and it's many bigger brothers but that's about it. Finally there's the element of building that I'm sure has some 4 year olds screaming "MINECRAFT CLONE!" but it's not the same. Rather than crafting and harvesting recources you instead buy them with the money that you take from fallen enemies, it's simple and it works. People can also be seen in your game but interacting with them is far from the attraction of the online.
Presentation: The style is 8-bit and the music is kick♥♥♥♥♥(and obviously 8-bit), that sounds familiar doesn't it? An 8-bit styled game with great music... Oh yea, it's nearley EVERY Steam game ever. Besides that though it's all fairly easy to explain, the style is in the form of a top down 8-bit game and the music is just great and enjoyable.
Story: So uh... some guy called... I want to say Alan, Alan? Alan. Anyway some guy called Alan gets you to talk to... a Zombie and a Dragon. Ok, the story sucks and there's no way around that, it is there to open the gameplay up. With that said there are plenty of witty one-liners and just a ton of cool nods to other series. Not that it makes up for the off pacing though.
Positives: - The exploration, combat and the building all fit well (even if not equally),
- The gameplay is just solid overall,
- The game has a very solid online system which works on so many levels.
Negatives: - The combat is repetetive and is way too simple,
- The design is staggered (but not ruined) by the less creative gamers out there.
Score: 7/10 - I recommend this game.

In a nutshell, Mechwarrior Online is a multiplayer battle arena with gigantic robots. Unlike many other
games with mechs however, Mechwarrior Online does an amazing job of actually feeling like a robot,
rather than a big metal man.
Pros:
-Looks very nice.
-Feels like a real mech. Huge stomping strides and the cockpit rocking are very... Mech-like?
-A huge amount of depth and customisation for those who look into these areas.
-A blend of medium and fast paced combat and variety of Mech classes for varied playstyles.
-Fairly fun to play in general. Very rewarding for team players and those who put in time.
Cons:
-Very complicated to new players. Can be overwhelming if you're not willing to put in time.
-Some cosmetics are incredibly expensive.
-There's a lot of grinding to earn enough credits to purchase and upgrade Mechs to a useful level.
-Furthermore, many Mechs are rather bad in their stock state, which can be misleading.
-Rather mercliess gameplay; no respawns can leave those unprepared feeling destroyed. (Well, you were, I guess)
Overall, Mechwarrior Online is a surprisingly high quality battle arena styled game that doesn't get
the attention it deserves. It's  very complex and hard to learn at first, but behind that, it's an incredibly
fun game that can have you playing many more matches than you'll expect. If you enjoy giant robot games
and are willing to learn, give it a go. If you enjoyed games like Hawken but want something a little more complicated and
interesting, this is your game.

I strongly recommend this game to anyone who likes the idea of fighting in customizable stompy robot tanks.
If you are a Battletech/Mechwarrior fan and haven't yet picked this up, you owe it to yourself to download it and play.  If you played it back and left, you should try it again.  I've enjoyed playing both quick match (which I rarely have to wait more than a minute), and community/faction warfare games.  As a fan of "Instant Action" games from MW 2/3/4, this scratches that itch perfectly.  I really like the variety of maps and mission types.  Plays great with a mouse and keyboard.
Unlike a lot of other F2P games, you don't have to put in money to get enjoyment out of the game.  There are bonuses for completing the tutorial up to about 6 million C-bills (currency), and you get a bonus for the first 25 quick match games you play - win or lose - which amounts to about another 8 million.  This is enough to buy one of the really large assault battlemechs or a couple of the smaller ones (I personally recommend medium or heavy for newer players).  I also don't feel that it is pay-to-win, since real money can get you more variety faster - or cosmetic items, but it won't make you a better player.   Money can't make you more situationally aware, a better team player, or a better communicator.
Summary: If you like customizating robot tanks and shooting at people in a 12v12 team environment, play this game.  It's free.  If you like it, support it by buying a Steam pack or a premium/mastery pack from the MWO website.
Side note: I'm glad that my friends taught me the phonetic alphabet.  It has been really useful!
-----
The stuff below are things that I think new players should know going into this.
- I recommend that you have a mic or headset.  It's not required, but it helps since you aren't going to have time to type meassages while driving your 'mech.
- Weapon groups.  Life is easier at first if you set your weapons to groups 1 & 2 (left mouse button, right mouse button).  Change it once you get a little better and can handle a larger variety of weapons & groups.
- In-game money & grind: I would say this isn't as much of an issue if you are careful with your purchases.  Really try those trial mechs so you can focus on what you like.
- Inner Sphere or Clan?  Pick one to focus on - since in community/faction warfare you will be limited to IS 'mechs for the houses or Clan 'mechs for the clans.  The weapons and equipment are not interchangeable between technology bases.
- Understand that you will lose matches at first - and that's okay.   Learn to communicate, call targets, be a team player.  A lot of the "veteran players" have given good advice on staying alive and being effective.  If you do die - spectate other players to see what they do right and wrong.
- Don't go it alone.  Alone = dead.  Coordinate with your teammates.  A team that talks together wins together.
- Spending *real* money:  Once you have played through the trial mechs and found a size type that you prefer, then look into spending real money.  The Steam packs are pretty good when on sale, and I would buy one if you *really like* one of the 'mechs in the pack.  Just be aware, that you need three of a chassis (which have different weapon loadout possibilities) to "master" a mech, which provides performance perks.  Also look at "mastery" packs - which are sold in the MWO gift store, or premium packages which have different price points.  (Note: before you buy a mech, see if it is included in one of these - that way you can buy a variant that isn't included so you don't have a duplicate mech). I personally have purchased the light 'mech pack from Steam first, since I thought it was good value for money, and the Marauder pack from the MWO website since that is one of my personal favorites.  I have been happy with both purchases.

An orphan disappeared from an orphanage in Venice. The headmaster thinks that now, everything is haunted. Who kidnapped Luciano? Why? Are ghosts real?
Dance of Death is a casual adventure game rated apparently for adults, as Steam asks me my date of birth for age verification. The plot may deal with some ghosts but apart perhaps the dealing with ghosts appearing everywhere and the general ambiance of horror, I don't see why it should be rated high.
The plot in itself is simple: save the boy from the evil man that needs him for his ritual of black magic. However, not every ghost is there to scare everyone, some of them will be friendly. Dance of Death is the name of the partition of the deceased father's boy, so, it's not a surprise to see skeletons in the menu or so many spooky references. However, the ending is quite anti-climatic. Oh hey villiain! Oh no more villain! I'm happy, I didn't have to protect myself! As you can see,
One of the main problems of the game is, for me, the minigames. Some of them are a little disorienting and even with the rules, I had an hard time to finish some of them (like the masks of death as they're not really looking alike). I liked however the originality of some of them, especially those related to the missing parts of the medallion. The hidden objects scenes are quite rare but still easy and also full of originality (with moving stuffs). However, the metamorphs/beyong objects scenes are perhaps harder: you don't always see the appearance changing and I was always under the impression that I needed to find one to unlock the second (when many of them were already there).
While I liked the ambiance and the tries to scare you, some actions aren't really making sense: how can I know that I need to go back to a room so that a ghost can appear and give me the needed item to advance? Also, the navigation inside the villa isn't making sense: why should I click on the bottom of my screen to reach a new location when the rest of the game is using that location to make you go back? I was really bothered by that.
If the graphics are correct, the cutscenes involving real actors aren't as well done as I've seen in other games: I don't know why it's so hurting eyes, why the moves aren't natural at all. I don't know why the developers felt like they needed to add effects.
The soundtrack is nice, so, your ears should be fine.
Dance of Death is very brief, under 2 hours. That's another problem with the game. Usually, the genre has games that can go to three-four hours.
4 bucks for the game seems a little expensive for me, so, if you see a discount, you should acquire the game. Given the fact that at the time of the writing, it's at -87%, it's a good bargain. But I would prefer many other better games if you want to give a try. That's why I can't quite recommend it. I can only do it for those who are curious and those waiting for a good discount.

Deus Ex Human Revolution is my third favourite game ever and a worthy successor to the best game of all time, the original Deus Ex, in every concievable way. It has issues, but goddamn if it isn't one hell of a game. A worthy RPG,
a worthy cover shooter, a worthy stealth game and one hell of a worthy Deus Ex game. A must-play, no doubt in my mind.
++The RPG elements are accessible yet never feel dumbed down
++Characters are well written and very memorable
++The dialogue isn't flawless, but for the absolute most part it's unrivaled in video games
++Voice-acting is as good as you can get within the gaming medium
++Stealth is as enjoyable as the best pure stealth oriented titles out there
++Level design is visually diverse and provides many different challenges
+Game looks decent
+Animations are of a higher quality, with some very impressive first person animations
+Side quests are fun and unobtrusive
+The deep conversations you can have with specific characters are incredibly well written and are highlights of the game
+The dialogue system, unlike certain Bioware titles and a specific Bethesda title, say exactly what you think they will and have effects on how a conversation plays out
+This game is very, very long no matter how you play it
+The inventory system is well designed
+Taking the combat approach is highly enjoyable, even with its faults
+Hub worlds are populated and mostly believable
+The game acts on its own and never for a second feels held back by its storyline sequels
+Game gets better as it goes
+The music kicks♥♥♥♥♥ even if it doesn't hold a candle to the original's
+The sound design is mostly amazing
+-The whole augmentation debate is somewhat ham-fisted, but in comparison to its sequel it is fairly tame. It also makes sense for it to be so prevalent when the whole narrative is focused on it. In my idea, this remark isn't worthy
as being a valid complaint but does remain to be something to note.
-+Performance is lacking
+-The concern of taking a stealth playthrough being the more rewarded type of playthrough is valid, but I've never found it to be a hinderance whatsoever
-+Some of the writing is a bit cliche and unbelievable, but it's rare that it's such an issue
+-Adam Jensen is a bit two dimensional but he is still well voice acted and a kickass protagonist
-+I don't think the boss fights are that bad but they are a tad easy
+-Technology seems to be quite a few decades in advance of the original, not a few decades before
-+The last few areas aren't great in terms of enemy design
-Hubs are fairly empty and a chore to traverse
-I'm not asking for an abundance of side quests (i.e. Elder Scrolls) but more would have certainly been nice
-Combat is made more difficult than it probably should be due to hitbox issues and difficult aiming on a controller
-I always have all the main augmentations I need early on and don't feel the need for any more after about halfway through the game
-The DLC breaks the flow. Should have been made optional in the Director's Cut.
-RPG elements through augmentations and skills don't allow for any playthrough types besides stealth and action
-The game doesn't really give you any reason to care about the bosses whatsoever
-The hub worlds are a little stilted
-The endings ♥♥♥♥ing suck
-Character models look uggggllyyy in close-ups. Not sure why some peoples 'hair' looks like it consists of nothing but a scalp topped with hair coloured gel mixed with petrol adding up to a nice, sleek brown-with-a-hint-of-purple

This game's description is pretty deceptive.
If you're looking for a tactical RPG that can stand on the merits of its gameplay, look elsewhere immediately. There's the seed of a good combat system here (the Risk mechanic is legitimately interesting) but the combat feels much more like a game in early-demo phase than finished-product. Enemy AI is braindead and predictable; once you have a few characters with the specializations you want, you can figure out a trivial strategy that will win you every battle in the game (except one) with nearly no effort, and with the exception of the actually unique legendary weapons obtained near the end of the game, everything about the weapons and magic system is almost as shallow as can be. Other core gameplay mechanics don't fare much better. From the standpoint of gameplay and challenge, this game was thoroughly disappointing.
Where it actually and unexpectedly shines (sort of) is the writing. Like many such games, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bonds has a map of numerous distinct locations. Unlike most such games, most of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bonds's locations tell a story or scenario that has had some amount of effort and creativity put in. In a standard tactical RPG, battle is the core, and settings and story and situations are sort of the window-dressing that helps to showcase the combat. In this game it is the reverse; the entire tactical RPG aspect feels like a shallow garnish for the underlying stories and scenarios. Secrets and optional quests and objectives are thoughtful; characters' special scenes tell interesting stories; on the whole, clearly a lot of creativity and thought was lavished on the writing, which is good enough to redeem some of the lacking qualities...
...if you happen to like big gay male orcs. Because, as it turns out, when this game's not busy trying to act like a tactical RPG, what it really wants to be is a visual novel about big gay male orcs, with the occasional burly werewolf or lumberjack thrown in for seasoning. The game's summary only briefly alludes to this kind of thing, but the game absolutely revels in it. So if that's your thing-- great, you found your game. If not, it's probably best to keep looking.

Pros: Has a massive amount of substance, at least from a development standpoint, rather than a gameplay standpoint.  The gameplay is very simple, overall, which while fine at first, starts becoming a con once you've got your guaranteed-victory-strategy in place.
But still, lots of areas (bordering on too many) and equipment and characters, with a decent amount of customization (despite being very pixely and basically un-animated).  Combat's easy to understand, the dialogue and writing are pretty great, and everything's pretty random, so each playthrough is fairly unique once you've burned through the starting 20 areas or so.
Cons: Doesn't really do a good job of helping you figure out the minutiae of the game, like the impact of character creation options, Stronghold management, or the value of using Risk.  Also, the character designs give off a feeling like they're realizing the developer's fetish - lots of extremely burly, strangely proportioned, nearly nude flirtatious bear-men made up my party and populated my stronghold.  Maybe that was just the luck of the draw, but out of the 20 recruits I found, 2 of them were women, and the rest were the type of men you wouldn't want to share a prison cell with.
Also, DON'T FORGET TO SAVE.  There's no auto-save, so if you find yourself on a tear and just burning through zones, levelling up like crazy and then WHOOPS GLITCH THAT KILLS THE WHOLE PARTY BECAUSE MY CHARACTERS DIDN'T RECOGNIZE THAT THEY WERE IN COMBAT then you basically lose hours of progress.

Now that I have got a substanial number of hours into the game, and have completed all but one achievement (which will be for the next playthrough) I wanted to update my review of the game.
I have always been a fan of tactics style games.  Disgaea, Final Fantasy Tactics, etc, but what i find with most of those games is that while the tactical combat is great, they tend to miss out on the exploration piece.
That is something that this game has added, and is what really made it feel special when playing.  It's not like Disgaea or Final Fantasy Tactics, where you get into your map to fight and go straight into it.  Instead, you get to navigate the map, and this navigation leads allows puzzles that are typically missing from those other style tactics games.  It almost gave it a bit of that Dungeons and Dragons feel.  You go into an area, you search around "oh, here's something that requires me to have a character who can complete a weave challenge" - so then you go back and get your character who can do weave challenges.
And it created a great balancing act - to do those challenges with some amount of consistency, you need to invest points into that skill, but if you invest points into that skill - then you can't invest points into other skills.
The 3x3 system for character advancement was interesting, and one of the aspects I also enjoyed completely.  Its not common in tactics games to get to get this level of detail in character customization, at least in my experience.
It's not without it's flaws - my biggest gripe is a bug that exists with the highest rank skill in the dodge line.  The results are frequently game breaking, but thank fully you can just avoid this particular skill, and the game will work fine.  Other bugs have seemed to be minor, the occasional scripted event that didn't work flawlessly, but compared to some triple A titles, even after patches, this game runs pretty smooth.
Another grip I have found was with the magic system - though I will admit this may primarily be personal bias - I really wish that the Healing magic wasn't bundled in with offensive magic, and at such a high rank of the ability.  But as I said, it may primarily be personal bias/experience with games where you have Fighter/Thief/Mage/Cleric - and I'm just expecting the cleric to really be it's own build.
Beyond that, I had minor nits:  Like I felt that Necromancer might have made more sense to have "Poxsoul" instead of "Touched", and perhaps being a murderer would have been "Maxsoul" to represent the fury in your heart.  This would have allowed for some more variety in the characters designed, as well as random characters, without having to rely on monsters or items to achieve the effect.
But overall, I am really happy I stumbled on this gem.  The themes in this game are right up my alley as well, so that made it even better.  For anyone who enjoys a good tactics game, this game is definetly worth the money.  Now that I've played it, beat it, I'm yearning for more - I'm trying to find a game that has similar aspects...shoot I'm trying to find applications I might be able to use to mod this game so I can make some tweaks/randomizations so I can have another playthrough and have some surprises.

I'm a big fan of this genre from Masters of Orion.   For an indie game this is pretty amazing.   If you are expecting pure combat, I don't think this game is for you.   It is more about system development and expansion.   I lost the first couple of games on weakest AI because I was focused on military.   I finally won a game on easy using Science.
Micro management of the systems.
This is actually very interesting.   I'm 40 hours in and I don't think I've mastered this at all.   My mid game, around 80 turns was very strong.  But my early game is still poor.   What is fun is to put the game in a window.  Then pull up dirty pleasure tv show off to the side and then just clicking through your planets to make them rapidly develop.   You actually have to read the system improvements because one size does NOT fit all.   In other words, on some systems it is a complete waste to build every improvement.
Tech Tree
Again another piece of the game that makes you think.   You don't need everything, especially if your are targeting a specific victory condition like dust, tech, aliance, etc.  Read and decide.  You must look at the planets near your home world before you unlock the colonization for those worlds.   Sure eventually you will get all but you need to race to unlock key strategic systems
Expansion
This is very cool.  It is easier to expand in sytems you own rather than sending out ships.  Makes sense right?   However you still need to send ships out to seed systems.  And you need to seed systems that either block other player's expansion or give you huge development potential.  And you haven't always developed the right technologies to seed the planets on the target system.  This makes for a great game play balance in the game.
Ship Upgrades
I really like the modification and retrofit system.  Very easy to use and key to keeping your fleet uptodate.
Combat
This is a bit dull but not the focus of the game.   You pick attitudes for three rounds of combats, long range, mid range, short range, then your ships do their thing.   I've found repairs to be pretty good.   But again I don't think the focus of the game on combat, especially since you only have about 5 classes of ships to fly with various mods on them.  It is easy to win other ways.
Diplomacy
I'm still a bit lost.   I don't quite understand why I can't initiate peace treaties.   Maybe that is the way amoeba's are.   Not sure.   Alliances seem good until you get thrown into a battle you don't want to be in.
Nay Sayers
It always reminds me of players that want to play the way they think rather than the way the game allows them to think.  Sure we all have had our frustrations with that.   Even I had that with the first couple of games.  But once you start looking for other ways to do things, the game opens up.
Value
I picked this up on steam sale.  Great value.   Fun little game completely worth the money.
